0.title: Releasing the libraries
0.content: How an agent publishes the HCERT libraries (STT-NFR-002) once the owner has supplied credentials. Nothing is published yet. No GitHub workflow publishes and no workflow holds a credential: CI runs only the dry runs below, in the check, kotlin and rust jobs of .github/workflows/requirements-kg.yml. An agent runs the commands here, from a clean checkout of the release tag, and stops at the first failure.

1.title: What is published
1.content: One version for all of them, from VERSION (STT-NFR-001), with an entry in CHANGELOG.md that cites each smart-trust changes.md entry it implements. | Registry | Coordinates | Built by | . | Maven Central | io.github.litlfred:hcert-api, io.github.litlfred:hcert-core (Kotlin Multiplatform: the root module, plus -jvm and -js) | gradle -p tools/hcert-kotlin publishDryRun | . | crates.io | litlfred-hcert (library name hcert) | cargo package in tools/hcert-rust | . | npm | @litlfred/hcert-kotlin-js (Kotlin/JS ES module) | tools/release-packaging/assemble-npm.mjs | . | npm | @litlfred/hcert-component (the Rust WebAssembly component, transpiled with jco) | tools/hcert-rust/build-component.sh, then assemble-npm.mjs | . The coordinates follow the repository’s GitHub org (the owner’s decision of 2026-10-23). Their single source is "repository": "<org>/<name>" in smart-trust-tools.json: the Maven group is io.github.<org> (a namespace the org can verify on the Sonatype Central Portal through GitHub), the npm scope is @<org>, and the crate is <org>-hcert, because crates.io has no namespaces (the Rust library itself stays hcert). The Gradle build and tools/release-packaging/coordinates.mjs derive them; check-version.mjs fails if Cargo.toml, a POM or a package.json disagrees. Moving the repository to another org (say, WorldHealthOrganization) means changing that one field, renaming the crate in Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock as the check asks, and verifying the new namespaces below. The Kotlin package root stays who.smart.trust. Android uses the -jvm jar as it is; there is no AAR until an androidTarget() exists.

2.title: Once, before the first release
2.content: . | Licence. Apache-2.0 (the owner’s decision of 2026-10-23; OI-14). LICENSE is the official text from apache.org (sha256 cfc7749b…3d30); the crate ships its copy tools/hcert-rust/LICENSE (the check requires it to be identical), assemble-npm.mjs copies it into each npm package, and every jar carries it as META-INF/LICENSE. | Maven Central. Sign in to https://central.sonatype.com with the litlfred GitHub account; the io.github.litlfred namespace is verified by that. Generate a user token (View Account → Generate User Token): it is a name and a password, CENTRAL_TOKEN_USER and CENTRAL_TOKEN_PASS below. | Signing key. Central requires an OpenPGP signature on every file. Generate a key for releases, then publish its public half: gpg --quick-gen-key "Carl Leitner (smart-trust-tools releases)" ed25519 sign 2y gpg --list-secret-keys --keyid-format long # note the key id, KEYID below gpg --keyserver keys.openpgp.org --send-keys KEYID gpg --keyserver keyserver.ubuntu.com --send-keys KEYID . The key stays on the owner’s machine (or a hardware token). No key, token or passphrase is ever committed or given to a workflow. | crates.io. Sign in with GitHub at https://crates.io, verify an e-mail address, and create an API token scoped to publish-new and publish-update for the crate litlfred-hcert (CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN). | npm. The packages are scoped to the npm user litlfred. Create a granular access token with read and write on @litlfred/* (NPM_TOKEN), with two-factor authentication on the account. | .

3.title: Pre-release checks
3.content: From the repository root, on main, with a clean tree: . git status --porcelain # must print nothing git log -1 --format=%H origin/main # must equal HEAD; CI green on it cat VERSION # the version to release, no pre-release suffix . | Set the version, if it changes, in the three places that hold it, then let Cargo update its own entry in the lock (no other crate moves): echo 0.1.0 > VERSION sed -i 's/^version = ".*"/version = "0.1.0"/' tools/hcert-rust/Cargo.toml # the [package] version, the only line it matches (cd tools/hcert-rust && cargo update --workspace --offline) . | In CHANGELOG.md, replace — unreleased in the version’s heading with the date (## [0.1.0] — 2026-11-02), make sure every wire-format or subclaim-default change cites its smart-trust changes.md entry, and point the link at the tag ([0.1.0]: https://github.com/litlfred/smart-trust-tools/releases/tag/v0.1.0). A wire-format or subclaim-default change needs a major or minor bump. | Run the checks CI runs, and the dry runs: node tools/release-packaging/check-version.mjs bun run check:req-nodes python3 tools/test-plan/make_test_plan.py --check python3 tools/wit2kotlin/wit2kotlin.py --check gradle -p tools/hcert-kotlin --no-daemon compileKotlinJvm compileKotlinJs :hcert-core:jvmTest :hcert-core:jvmTestCoverageCheck :hcert-core:compileProductionLibraryKotlinJs (cd tools/hcert-rust && cargo test --locked && cargo test --locked --features qr --test api) . | Commit (Release 0.1.0), push to main of litlfred/smart-trust-tools, wait for CI to pass on that commit, then tag it with a signed tag and push the tag: git tag -s v0.1.0 -m "smart-trust-tools 0.1.0" git push origin v0.1.0 . | . Every artefact is then built from a fresh clone of the tag, never from a working copy: . git clone --branch v0.1.0 --depth 1 https://github.com/litlfred/smart-trust-tools.git /tmp/stt-release cd /tmp/stt-release bun run cat mount:lock && bun install # the mounted layers, for check:req-nodes . toolchain/node_tools.sh # jco, from the lockfile, no install scripts .

4.title: Maven Central (Central Portal bundle upload)
4.content: . | Publish into the build-local repository and check the result. Every archive is reproducible (no timestamps, fixed order), so building the tag twice from a fresh clone gives the same jars, klibs, sources jars and POMs. The Kotlin Gradle plugin (2.0.21) writes the org.gradle.libraryelements attribute into hcert-api’s .module files or not depending on which tasks the build runs, so run exactly this command: gradle -p tools/hcert-kotlin --no-daemon publishDryRun node tools/release-packaging/check-version.mjs tools/hcert-kotlin/build/maven-dry-run . publishDryRun lists, for each of hcert-api, hcert-api-jvm, hcert-api-js, hcert-core, hcert-core-jvm and hcert-core-js: the .pom, the .module (Gradle metadata), the main artefact (.jar, or .klib for -js), -sources.jar, -javadoc.jar (the module README; the KDoc is in the sources) and, for the root modules, -kotlin-tooling-metadata.json. Gradle writes .md5, .sha1, .sha256 and .sha512 beside each. | Sign every artefact (not the checksums, not maven-metadata.xml): repo=tools/hcert-kotlin/build/maven-dry-run find "$repo" -name 'maven-metadata.xml*' -delete find "$repo" -type f ! -name '*.md5' ! -name '*.sha1' ! -name '*.sha256' ! -name '*.sha512' \ -exec gpg --local-user KEYID --armor --detach-sign {} \; find "$repo" -name '*.asc' -exec gpg --verify {} \; . | Bundle the repository layout and upload it, as a deployment the owner releases by hand (USER_MANAGED): (cd "$repo" && zip -qrX ../central-bundle-0.1.0.zip io) token=$(printf '%s:%s' "$CENTRAL_TOKEN_USER" "$CENTRAL_TOKEN_PASS" | base64 -w0) curl --fail --request POST \ --header "Authorization: Bearer $token" \ --form bundle=@tools/hcert-kotlin/build/central-bundle-0.1.0.zip \ "https://central.sonatype.com/api/v1/publisher/upload?name=smart-trust-hcert-0.1.0&publishingType=USER_MANAGED" # prints the deployment id curl --fail --request POST --header "Authorization: Bearer $token" \ "https://central.sonatype.com/api/v1/publisher/status?id=DEPLOYMENT_ID" . Wait for "deploymentState": "VALIDATED"; on FAILED, the response lists each problem. Then release it, which cannot be undone: . curl --fail --request POST --header "Authorization: Bearer $token" \ "https://central.sonatype.com/api/v1/publisher/deployment/DEPLOYMENT_ID" . (or Publish on the deployment at https://central.sonatype.com/publishing/deployments). | .

5.title: crates.io
5.content: cd tools/hcert-rust cargo package --locked --list # exactly: Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock, README.md, DEPENDENCIES.md, LICENSE, src/*.rs cargo package --locked # builds the .crate on its own, from target/package/litlfred-hcert-0.1.0 cargo publish --locked --dry-run CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN=... cargo publish --locked . The tests are not in the crate: they read the shared vectors at ../../vectors, so they run from the repository. The component feature reads the WIT contract at ../../api/wit and so builds only from the repository too; the component is published to npm instead. A crates.io version cannot be replaced, only yanked (cargo yank --version 0.1.0).

8.title: Activity log — what an agent did, kept out of the graph
8.content: Named by: Agent activity log . Write an entry when you start a task, when you end one, and whenever you have something a later reader would need. Entries go to fsh-guts/logs/, and nothing reaches the git data store unless capture is explicitly on.

9.title: The role is mechanical
9.content: log in scenarios/roles.json: actorKinds: ["system"]. It is written to and emptied by an actor, and it decides nothing. The precedents are work-plan and corpus. A mechanical role is still a real role: this skill is its contract — the shape of an entry and where it goes.

10.title: The entry
10.content: schemas/sdlc/log-entry.ts. Every entry carries $schema: folio-log/v1: a directory says what to EXPECT and the file says what it IS. Without it, a log entry is told apart from a discarded proposal by its folder alone. | field | why it is there | . | event | task-start · task-end · message · error | . | summary | one line, so a long log stays skimmable; detail goes in detail | . | actor, role | who, and which lane they were acting in | . | process, task | the BPMN process and step, when inside one | . | bean, branch, session | so a run’s entries can be found and emptied together | . | references[] | what this entry points at — a chat, an issue, a commit, a command. See below | . | execution | command-execution detail, when the entry IS one | . | capture | whether this entry persists — three-valued, see below | . role, process and task are optional and meant to be. An agent writes log lines outside any process, and inventing a lane for those would be the fake-reference failure activity-names-skill exists to prevent.

11.title: What an entry points at — references[] is OPEN
11.content: An entry references whatever the work touched — discussions, chats, command executions and more — and nobody enumerates that in advance, so a closed list is wrong within a week. So kind is an open string with a KNOWN SET, and an unrecognised kind is accepted and flagged, never refused: . discussion · comment · issue · pull-request · commit · command · workflow · artefact . A reference is { kind, ref } plus an optional title and at. ref is required: a kind with nothing to point at gives the reader no way to reach it. A list, not named fields, because one entry routinely touches several of one kind (a step that answers three review threads has three comments). Unknown kinds are surfaced rather than rejected. Open is the point, but a silently open list is how issue, issues and gh-issue end up in one store with nothing able to query it. writeLogEntry returns unknownRefKinds, and the one-line report says so — so a typo is noticeable without the parser being able to refuse a legitimate extension. Command execution has its own shape, and no output field . execution carries command, argv, exitCode, durationMs, cwd and outputRef. It sits beside references rather than inside it because an exit code is a queryable fact, and ref: "exit 1" is not a field anyone can filter on. An absent exitCode means it did not finish, which is not 0 — the third state again. There is deliberately no field to inline output into. outputRef points at where stdout and stderr went. Command output is the likeliest place for a token or a connection string to appear, and capture: "on" puts an entry in git in a repository that may be public. An output field would invite that leak, and an absent field is stronger than a warning. The same caution applies to command itself: a command line carries its own arguments, and --token=… is a command line.

12.title: Turning it on — <cat-harness.processes:log capture="on"/> on the process
12.content: Capture is a declaration on the process, parsed at load and throwing on a value the engine cannot honour, exactly as <cat-harness.processes:bean op> does. A diagram asking for a mode that does not exist must not load and quietly log nothing, because the missing artefact is the record. workflow_start writes task-start; workflow_complete writes task-end for the step just recorded, with the instance’s status in the detail. The step is the unit, not the whole process: waiting for the process to finish would lose every intermediate entry, which is most of what a log is read for. Marked in this layer: crdm-requirements and actor-role-administration. Not a call activity. A call activity is a node in the control flow, so the log would become a step to complete in sequence, and in a enforcement="strict" process workflow_gate refuses a step that is not enabled, so a call activity would need policy relaxations for a concern that is not a phase of anything. An extension element adds no node and no flow; a test asserts the strict processes enforce exactly what their diagrams say. unknown is not writable as a declared value. It is what the absence of a declaration resolves to, and a diagram cannot assert that nobody could tell.

13.title: Capture is off by default, and unknown is a real answer
13.content: fsh-guts/logs/ is inside the repository, so writing there would be committing unless something stops it. The default is write locally, ignored by git — the agent can read back what it wrote this session, and nothing enters the data store until a workflow or the config asks. off the default — written, not committed on explicitly enabled, for this workflow or by config unknown the setting could not be determined . A logging system that silently keeps nothing is worse than none, because the agent believes it has an audit trail. So: . | absent configuration resolves to unknown, never to off — they are different claims. off says somebody decided; unknown says nobody could tell, and the first is a choice while the second is a bug. | unknown does not persist. When the setting cannot be determined the safe reading is the default, and committing an audit trail nobody asked for is the worse of the two failures. | report the state. Say which of the three you are in when you start logging; do not let a reader infer it. | . Same discipline as ci-health never rendering “could not check” as green, and renderingMediaType returning undefined rather than a plausible guess.

14.title: Emptying — and the exception to the never-delete rule
14.content: Three operations: one entry, all of them, and a periodic sweep. An entry carries a stable id so the first is possible at all, and session so a whole run can go at once. This is the one exception to fsh-guts’s rule that nothing is deleted. That rule exists because a removed artefact cannot be told from one that never existed, and a scrapped thing records a dead end so the next agent does not re-enter it. A log entry records no decision. It is a trace of activity, it is expected to be voluminous, and keeping it forever would drown the directory that exists to make discarded decisions findable. So: logs may be emptied without confirmation; everything else in fsh-guts/ may not. Without this exception an agent would either never empty the log or start deleting proposals. The exception was granted to a KIND OF FILE, not to a path . emptyLog(root, selector) in src/logging/log-sweep.ts, with the selector being one of { id }, { session }, { before } or { all: true }. There is no default selector: an operation with no undo that empties everything when the caller passed nothing is the wrong way round. A file is removed only if it declares itself a folio-log/v1 entry, never by path. A stray proposal dropped in the log directory keeps every protection it would have had one folder up, because the exception was granted to a kind of file, not to a path, and a declaration inside the file is the contract. Three consequences worth knowing before you call it: . | “Could not tell” resolves to KEEP. A file that will not parse is a file whose kind could not be established, and this module deletes. | A symlink out of the directory is refused, checked by realpath rather than resolve — string arithmetic would not catch it, and here the cost of getting containment wrong is a loss rather than a leak. | Everything not removed says WHY, and describeSweep separates a selector miss from a refusal. “Nothing to delete” and “nine files I would not touch” must not read the same; the second is the one somebody needs to know about. scanned is the vacuity guard on every other count. | .

15.title: It is never published
15.content: fsh-guts/logs/ is inside fsh-guts/, which UNPUBLISHED_GRAPH_TYPOLOGIES strips from every published graph — the kind, the directory, the skill and every edge naming them (kg-export). That is placement doing the work rather than a second rule, which is why logs can be as detailed as they need to be. There is a test asserting it for logs specifically, rather than trusting that the parent rule reaches them.

16.title: What not to log
16.content: . | Secrets, tokens, credentials or personal data. Not-published is not the same as not-committed and not the same as private: capture on puts entries in git, and the repository may be public. | A substitute for a work item. A log says what happened; a work item says what is being worked on and what it waits on. Log in addition to claiming, never instead. | A substitute for the turn report. The log is for a later reader; the report is for the person in the room now. | .

18.title: Agent activity log
18.content: Process_ActivityLog · advisory · 8 step(s) . What an agent writes down about its own run, and what a person can do with it afterwards: task starts and ends, messages and errors, persisted where somebody can read them. You are in this process on every task, whether or not capture is on — the first gateway is what decides, and an agent that does not check it logs into nothing. The log operator’s lane is the other half: a person discards one entry or a whole session, and the scheduled sweep does neither on its own. This is not the work plan. beans records WHAT is being worked on and survives the session; this records what happened during it. The two answer different questions and a reader reaching for one is badly served by the other. i i i i i i i i

20.title: Lanes — who acts
20.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | Agent (this session) | authoring-agent | Brackets its own work with a start and an end entry rather than leaving either implied, and reads Gateway_Capture rather than assuming it: persisting when capture is on, but merely reporting the setting — never silently dropping the entry — when it is off or could not be determined. | . | Log operator (human) | user | The only lane in this diagram that chooses: one entry by id, or everything. It was split out from a single conflated lane because a person’s choice and a scheduled sweep’s fixed program are not the same actor, which is why the sweep below has a lane of its own rather than sharing this one. | . | Scheduled log sweep | build-pipeline | — | .

21.title: Steps
21.content: Every one of the 8 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Log task-startA_LogStart | Agent (this session) | activity-log | Write a task-start entry before touching anything: summary, actor, and the process/task/bean/branch/session it belongs to where they exist. role, process and task are optional on purpose — do not invent a lane for work done outside a process. | . | Do the workA_DoWork | Agent (this session) | — | The task itself. This diagram says nothing about how it is done; it only brackets it, so that a reader of the log can tell where one run of work began and ended. | . | Log a message or an errorA_LogMessage | Agent (this session) | activity-log | Write a message or error entry whenever a later reader would need it. A command run goes in execution (command, exit code, where output went) — never the output itself, and never a secret, token or credential: capture on puts entries in git. | . | Log task-endA_LogEnd | Agent (this session) | activity-log | Write a task-end entry, with the outcome in the detail. The step is the unit: an entry per step, not one when the whole process finishes, or every intermediate entry is lost. | . | Persist the log to the data storeA_PersistLog | Agent (this session) | activity-log | Capture is explicitly on — by <cat-harness.processes:log capture=”on”/> on the process or by config — so the entries go to the git data store. Only this branch commits anything. | . | Report the capture stateA_ReportCaptureState | Agent (this session) | activity-log | Capture is off or unknown, so nothing is committed. Say which of the two it is: off is somebody’s decision, unknown means nobody could tell, and an agent that believes it has an audit trail when it has none acts on a false belief. | . | Discard one entry by idA_EmptyOne | Log operator (human) | activity-log | Remove one entry by its stable id, with emptyLog({ id }). Logs are the one exception to the never-delete rule because an entry records no decision; the exception covers files that declare folio-log/v1, not the directory. | . | Discard all entries, or a whole sessionA_EmptyAll | Log operator (human) | activity-log | Remove every entry, one session’s, or those before a date — emptyLog with { all }, { session } or { before }; there is no default selector. A file that will not parse is kept, and the result must say what was refused and why, not only what was removed. | .

24.title: Actor and role administration
24.content: Process_ActorRoleAdministration · strict · 6 step(s) . Changing who can do what: adding an actor, opening or closing a role to one, granting or revoking a permission — and auditing the graph afterwards, because the declaration and the graph are two things that can disagree. You are in this process when the substrate every other diagram’s lanes bind to is what is changing. That is why it is drawn rather than left as a filesystem edit: a role added without an audit is a lane binding that resolves today and may not tomorrow, and nothing else in the corpus would notice. Retirement, never deletion. An actor id is referenced from commits, sidecars and other declarations, so removing one makes an old record unreadable while retiring one leaves it legible and says the actor has stopped. i i i i i i

25.content: . | Called by: no call activity names this process | Calls: none | Presented on: no docs page section shows this diagram | Running instances: none recorded | .

26.title: Lanes — who acts
26.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | Administrator | administrator | All four administration verbs — add, assign, grant, retire — converge at Gateway_Changed onto the same CallActivity_CodeChangeReview, so no kind of substrate edit gets a lighter review path than another; and Gateway_AuditClean’s ‘no’ branch (A13) loops back to this lane rather than ending the process, because whether a major finding holds the change is this lane’s policy call, not something Task_RunKgAudit decides for it. | . | Graph audit (system) | build-pipeline | Runs only after CallActivity_CodeChangeReview has already completed its own review, because the breakage this lane exists to catch — a join across role, lane, actor and skill — is invisible to a code reviewer reading the diff in isolation; ordinary code review clears the edit, and only this lane’s whole-graph pass can tell whether it silently broke something three diagrams away. | .

27.title: Steps
27.content: Every one of the 6 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Add an actor, and declare its kindTask_AddActor | Administrator | role-model | Human, agentic or mechanical. A userTask because the agentic/mechanical line is JUDGEMENT — role-model.md says so — and reading it wrong disqualifies the actor from every judgement task it exists to perform, silently. | . | Open or close a role to an actorTask_AssignRoles | Administrator | role-model | The join every other diagram depends on. An empty roles is a DETERMINED empty — it says the actor takes on none — and is not the same as an absent one, which asserts nothing. | . | Grant or revoke a permissionTask_GrantOrRevoke | Administrator | role-model | A permission travels with the PARTICIPANT and cross-cuts every lane, so unlike a role it cannot be scoped by the diagram it is used in. Granting one is a standing decision, which is why this lane is person-only and why the log capture on this process is on. | . | Retire an actor — never delete oneTask_RetireActor | Administrator | deletion-requires-confirmationrole-model | An actor id is referenced from roles, diagrams, beans and commits, so removing the file leaves every one of those unable to tell retirement from accident. Same rule, and the same reason, as a scrapped bean. | . | Branch, gates, PR and reviewCallActivity_CodeChangeReview | Administrator | continual-progress | Called rather than restated. 31.title: What it is
31.content: Adjudication is a judgement of the feedback of one or more feedback providers, when a review reached no mechanical or consensus agreement. It carries the same dispensation process: the reason for the choice, as per contextual requirements. These activities are adjudications: . | where | the decision, in its own words | . | translation-workflow · Task_Adjudicate | “The round trip establishes that two readings differ. Which one is right is a human call.” | . | ingest-l1-completeness-gate · Task_FlagDrift | “A machine can detect that two readings differ. Which one is right is a human call.” | . | refresh-materialized · Task_Adjudicate | “A human or agentic decision, never a merge rule. Which side wins depends on why the local edit was made, and a process that picked automatically would be choosing without the one fact that decides it.” | . | review-narrative · Task_AdjudicateVoice | “Three outcomes, all legitimate: the register is wrong for this genre; the criterion does not belong in this genre; or the block is a stated exception and a reviewer entry records why.” | . | voice-review · Task_Adjudicate | “The same three outcomes … fix the prose; scope it on the voice; or the rule applies and this block is an exception.” | . | src/routes/relevance.ts | “writing human_adjudicated alongside — never overwriting — the agent’s assessed_by. Both survive.” | . | schemas/library/bib-verification.ts | a discriminated Verifier union, agent-only vs human-adjudicated, “and *also carry human_adjudicated if a human has subsequently”* ruled | . Each restated the same rule because nothing generalised it; this skill is that generalisation.

32.title: The judgement and its outcomes are separate processes
32.content: Callers ask different questions: whether a drift is real, whether a passage is acceptable, whether two entries agree, which side wins a conflict, whether a finding stands. Only the QA-criterion question has a criterion to scope or a dispensation to grant, and a callActivity runs the whole subprocess, so the outcomes cannot live in the shared process. The branches live with the caller, not in an enum passed to it, because the codes select different tasks: a caller’s local-wins would point at A_ScopeCriterion. So the split is at the judgement: . | what | where it lives | why there | . | entry condition, untainted dispatch, person-or-agent restriction | adjudication.bpmn | it must not vary, and restating it per caller is how it drifts | . | the three QA-criterion outcomes, A_RecordEntry, the dispensation | criterion-adjudication.bpmn | it depends on what was asked | . | a requirements document’s sign-off: approve amend reject defer cancel (code list adjudication-requirement-set), A_RecordSignoff, GW_SignoffRecorded | crdm-signoff.bpmn (BA_Signoff), crdm-close.bpmn (BA_Confirm); spec-kit’s adjudicated status by the same codes | the answer moves a requirement SET’s stage | . The requirement-set caller records before it branches. Every answer goes to A_RecordSignoff, which appends a requirement-signoff attestation (the attestations graph, test/attestations/requirement-signoff/<set>.attestations.json): who — kind, id, actor, the QA reviewer’s identity fields — when, about what (the set or one member), the outcome, the stage it moves the set to, the reason and the permalink to the issue comment. GW_SignoffRecorded then reads the record BACK through decisions/requirement-signoff-recorded.dmn, with facts check:requirements --signoff-facts <reqset:slug> computes from the store, so a sign-off nobody recorded loops back rather than proceeding. What that means when you call it . A_Adjudicate declares <cat-harness.processes:adjudication defers="caller"/> — it IS an adjudication and the permitted answers are yours. Declared rather than left as a missing codes, so a marker lost by accident and a deferral on purpose do not parse the same. | Asking the QA-criterion question? Call Process_CriterionAdjudication and declare <cat-harness.processes:adjudication accepts="stands scope dispensation"/>. The engine compares your list with what that process actually offers. | Asking something else? Call Process_Adjudication and declare <cat-harness.processes:adjudication codes="…"/> on your own call activity, with your own gateway coding the same set. The engine refuses a mismatch between the two, and refuses a partly-coded gateway, which reads as complete. | Declaring nothing is legal and reported by check:workflow-refs. Some callers are in that state on purpose: what each should ask is open, and guessing would make an undecided thing look checked. | . Whatever you ask, A_RecordEntry’s rule follows the outcome: a judgement nobody wrote down is indistinguishable from a checker that was never run. It is relaxable="false" wherever it lands, which is with the caller that records, because the entry written depends on what was adjudicated.

33.title: Two senses of the word, and only one is this
33.content: The corpus also uses adjudicated as an adjective meaning settled: evidence-retrieval calls published DAKs “already-adjudicated guidance”, and ingest-extract-structure says extracted candidates are “never adjudicated verdicts”. Both are correct English and neither is this process. Grepping for the word finds them; only the activity list above is the process.

34.title: What makes a disagreement ADJUDICABLE
34.content: Not “somebody is unhappy”. schemas/sdlc/block-qa.ts already declares the three reviewer kinds — script, agent, human — and allows multiple entries per criterion, which makes the entry condition computable rather than declared: . | state | what it is | . | mechanical agreement | the script entry passes | . | consensus | entries of different kinds agree on one criterion | . | adjudicable | entries for ONE criterion disagree | . So you are in adjudication when the sidecar holds two entries for the same criterion that do not agree. Anything else is a review, a complaint, or a bug report, and each of those has somewhere else to go. A missing entry is not a disagreement. One reviewer and no checker is a review; one checker and no reviewer is a gate. Adjudication needs both sides present, which is why it cannot be entered by an actor simply declaring it — and why adjudication.bpmn’s first gateway leaves the process rather than guessing.

35.title: The adjudicator is dispatched, not briefed
35.content: This skill does not restate the parties — untainted-verification owns them, and the split matters more here than anywhere else, because the adjudicator is the party best placed to ruin the measurement: . adjudicator | is given adjudicator_sees and the checker’s output — never the artefact itself | produces pass / warn / fail, each drift named . An adjudicator shown the artefact can talk itself into any reading of the finding, and that failure raises no error: it produces a verdict that measured nothing. UntaintedDispatch declares the context per criterion and untaintedPartitionDefects reports overlap when both parties can read the same file. Read that skill before you dispatch one.

36.title: The adjudication LEADS; the checker’s entry is KEPT
36.content: voice-review.bpmn, and this is the rule the whole skill turns on: . “The adjudication LEADS the criterion and the script entry is kept beneath it: a disagreement between a checker and a reviewer is information.” . Do not resolve the disagreement away. Both entries stay in the sidecar, the human’s on top under the sweep’s “most-recent matching-hash entry wins” rule. A sidecar showing only the winning answer has lost the fact that a checker read it differently — which is exactly what somebody re-running the check next month needs to know. The same rule holds outside the diagrams: /api/relevance/adjudicate writes human_adjudicated alongside assessed_by, and bib-verification.ts carries the same pair on a discriminated union. Neither shares code with the diagrams, which is evidence that it is the right rule rather than a local convention. This is also the answer to “adjudication if code and narrative disagree”: record the disagreement, lead with the judgement, keep the other entry.

37.title: The dispensation is a VERSION, never a precedent
37.content: The outcome carries its reason. That mechanism already exists and is schema-backed — block-qa/v1’s multi-reviewer primitive, documented at length in q-usage-watcher (the science layer): . | a kind: "human" entry with result: "pass" overrides the script’s fail for the same criterion; | only while its field_hash matches the current source files; | notes carries the reason — “reason for choice as per contextual requirements”. | . That hash gate is the design, not a limitation. A dispensation is scoped to the version it was granted against: change the block and it lapses, and must be re-granted. So a dispensation never becomes precedent, and there is nothing to overturn later — the source moving overturns it. A dispensation with no notes is not a dispensation. It is an override somebody applied to get to green, and nobody can review it afterwards. So A_Dispensation is marked relaxable="false" in criterion-adjudication.bpmn, with A_RecordEntry. The judgement is free and the record is not, because a judgement nobody wrote down is indistinguishable from a checker that was never run.

38.title: Who adjudicates — a skill that spreads, an entitlement that does not
38.content: | object | what it is | . | feedback-provider (role) | offers a finding — a checker, a review agent, a reader, an SME. Plural by design: one or more feedback providers. | . | adjudicator (role) | settles it, with a reason. Inherits reviewer. | . | adjudication (permission) | may WRITE the settling entry. | . Knowing the discipline and being entitled to apply it are different, and the repository already separates them. permissions.json: “a permission CROSS-CUTS roles”. Adjudication happens in four lanes bound to four different roles (narrative-reviewer, translation-adjudicator, reviewer, user), so: . | the skill is carried by every role whose lane holds an adjudicate activity, because each of them has to be able to tell an adjudicable disagreement from a complaint; | the permission adjudication is held by the actor, alongside review-comments (record a finding) and approval-authority (accept a change). It is neither: settling a disagreement between two findings is not reporting one and not accepting the change. | . A reviewer reports; an adjudicator settles. That is why review-task.bpmn keeps accept-or-send-back in one lane: a process where every reviewer could settle has no way to say who decided. translation-adjudicator is a specialisation of adjudicator.

40.title: What this does NOT cover
40.content: The narrative-asserts-code axis. Whether prose asserts what an artefact actually does is a different question, currently answered only for Lean (proof-narrative-lean-equiv). code-node-review asks whether a NODE is correct — that it declares what it is, that its references resolve — not whether the prose matches. 43.title: Adjudication
43.content: Process_Adjudication · advisory · 3 step(s) . A criterion’s reviewer entries disagree and no mechanism can settle them: this is the judgement that does, and the record it must leave. You are in this process when a sidecar holds two entries for ONE criterion that do not agree — a script failing what a reviewer passed, an agent and a person reading the same block differently. That is the entry condition and it is computable, which is why the first gateway leaves rather than guessing: one reviewer and no checker is a review, one checker and no reviewer is a gate, and neither is adjudicable. Nobody enters this process by declaring that they have entered it. Three things the diagram holds that prose kept losing. The adjudicator is DISPATCHED rather than briefed — given the findings and the checker’s output and, deliberately, never the artefact, because an adjudicator shown the artefact can talk itself into any reading of the finding and that failure raises no error. The adjudication LEADS the criterion and the checker’s entry is KEPT beneath it, because a disagreement between a checker and a reviewer is information and a sidecar showing only the winner has lost it. And the dispensation is scoped to the version it was granted against by its field_hash, so it lapses when the source moves and never becomes precedent. This process ENDS at the judgement. What the answer means, and what is done about it, belongs to whoever asked — criterion-adjudication.bpmn is the QA-criterion specialisation, where the finding stands, the criterion is scoped, or a dispensation is granted with its reason. Until 2026-09-23 those three lived here and every caller ran them: six diagrams called this process and only two asked a question they answer. Bean bvuk. What stays shared is what must not vary: the entry condition nobody may declare their way past, the untainted dispatch, and the restriction to a person or an agent. What a legitimate outcome IS does vary, and it now varies where it is asked. i i i

53.title: Adversarial code review
53.content: Skill adversarial-code-review: Review a pull request an agent touched by building the strongest case that it is wrong, unsafe, or not what it claims, and record the verdict where the merge gate reads it: one merge-review/v1 file per head, on the merge-reviews state branch, never in the pull request itself. Covers who may review, what the whole-diff scope is, the RED FLAG categories and their evidence rule, the one rebuttal round, overrides, and how a per-head verdict composes with a merge train. Named by: Code node review, Code change and review . The Task_Review step of code-change-review.bpmn, for a change an agent touched. Its verdict is what check:adversarial-review reads. The gate is warn-only: a missing, stale or failing verdict is reported, not blocking, until an owner promotes the gate.

54.title: Who may review
54.content: Not the author. A different session id from every Claude-Session: / Agent-Session: trailer on merge-base..head; a different model family when one is configured. The gate checks the session, and refuses a verdict that does not record the reviewer’s session and model.

55.title: The stance
55.content: Construct the strongest case that this change is wrong, unsafe, or not what it claims. It is the stance of generalise-the-fix and devils-advocate-watcher (opt-in cat-harness.editorial), applied to a diff. The claim under test is the pull request’s description and the ## Done when of the work item it names.

56.title: Scope: the whole diff, or unknown
56.content: . | Review git diff <merge-base>..<head>, file by file. Count every changed file into coverage.files_total. | A generated file that a check reproduces may be skipped, by name, in coverage.skipped with its reason. Nothing is skipped silently. | If you cannot read the whole diff, set coverage.truncated: true and result: "unknown". Never pass on part of a diff. | .

57.title: What you look for
57.content: The RED FLAG categories are closed and live in schemas/sdlc/red-flag.ts: security, data-loss, correctness, false-green, provenance, scope-breach, irreversible-action and licence. Read the definitions there rather than from a copy. Beyond the categories, ask: . | can a new or changed check report green without evaluating its subject? | does prose (a skill, the PR body, the work item) assert something the code does not do? That is narrative-asserts-code; | does the change reach outside its work item, or hand-edit a generated file? | . A finding is blocking only with evidence: a reproducible observation, such as an input and its wrong output, or a command and what it printed. Without one it is recorded as a suggestion. The author may answer each flag once; then the verdict is final.

58.title: Recording the verdict
58.content: The verdict lives on its own state branch, never in the pull request. Committing it into the pull request moves the head it names, which makes it stale at once. | bun run cat state:mount mounts the merge-reviews graph at merge-reviews/. | Write merge-reviews/<head sha>.json, a merge-review/v1 document: pr, repository (owner/repo, so the store’s viewer can link the pull request), base_sha, head_sha and reviews[]. Each review records: . | reviewer {by, session, model}; | author_sessions, from the trailers; | skill_hash, the sha256 of this file as you ran it; | at and coverage; | result (pass, fail or unknown); | flags[], each with id, category, severity, weight, where, evidence and status: "open". | . | Push with bun run cat state:push, never git push from the mount. | Check it: bun run cat check:adversarial-review --head <sha> --base <base>. | . A push to the pull request after the review leaves the verdict naming a commit that is no longer the head. The gate reports that as stale, and the review runs again on the new head.

59.title: Overrides
59.content: A flag is never deleted. A person with standing overrides it with a qa-review decision (who, when, why, flag id), which sets status: "overridden". The gate passes resolved and overridden flags and holds on open.

60.title: In a merge train
60.content: A review is per head, because it reviews a change, not an accident of batching. A pull request in a merge-queue train keeps the verdict on its own head; a pull request taken out of the train keeps it too, because its head did not move. A conflict resolved by hand while building the train is a change of its own and needs its own review. The compile gates, not the review, run again on the train’s combined result.

62.title: One task, two agents, one human between them
62.content: Skill agent-handoff: Governs handing ONE task to an agent in another environment — a local agent with network the cloud session lacks, a sibling on a different machine, anything that cannot read the coordinator’s context and that a person may relay to. States who writes which work item, where the receiver reports, what the person pastes (one sentence: work item, branch, repository) and the brief the work item opens with (second person, to the executor), what the receiver checks before acting, who closes, who may grant an exception, and how to recognise and answer the five ways an executor fails. Use when writing a work item for another agent to execute, and as the receiver before acting on one. Triggers on: hand off, handoff, local agent, agy, mac agent, needs network, executor failed, agent went silent, re-hand, “give me a branch and bean for them”, relay, the other agent. Named by: Hand back to the discussion, Drain the beans, A refused merge-train member, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route . Two agents, two environments: the coordinator can see the work, but it cannot do one step, usually because of network or credentials. The executor can do that step, but it has none of the coordinator’s context. Often the only link between them is a person, retyping. Every rule below is about that gap. This is not bean-coordination (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan), which governs sibling sessions sharing one store and racing for one claim. It is not dispatch-agent either: that governs subagents you spawn and can read directly. Here you cannot see the executor’s checkout. The only things you will ever see are what it pushes and what it posts. Needs the beans CLI on both sides (cat-harness-tools/scripts/install-beans.sh) and bun run cat beans:claim. An executor without them reports that it is blocked; it does not edit work item files by hand.

63.title: 1. One bean, one writer, and the receiver claims it
63.content: Before you hand off, write down who may write what. Put it in the work item as a ## Roles table, so the executor reads it in the work item rather than hearing it from a person: . | role | who | writes | . | coordinator | the session that opened the work item | the work item’s instructions, written before the claim; the parent and related work items; the verification record | . | executor | the agent named in the work item | only the handed work item, from the claim onward: its holder note, ## Progress, ## Evidence, the ready-to-close tag | . | verifier | whoever can run the check in ## Done when, usually the coordinator | the verification result and the close | . | owner | the person | any exception to a boundary (§6) | . The executor claims the handed work item and never runs beans create for the handed work. If beans show <id> finds nothing, it is in the wrong branch or the wrong checkout. That is a stop-and-report, not a cue to recreate the work item: a fresh beans create mints a new id, or a second file under an id typed by hand, and then two work items answer one question. After the claim, the coordinator never edits the work item. The claim writes to the work item file, so a concurrent edit is a merge conflict on exactly the file both agents care about. Anything the coordinator learns after the claim goes to the report channel (§2).

64.title: 2. The report channel is in the bean, from the start
64.content: Give the work item a ## Report to section that names ONE place: a PR or issue both agents can reach. Then give the exact one-line formats, so the coordinator can act on a report without having to interpret it: . <id>: started <what> at <input revisions> <id>: done <what> <result sha/count> <id>: refused <what> <the numbers> ← stop here <id>: blocked <step> <error> ← stop here . The chat is not a channel. The coordinator cannot read the executor’s chat, and the person relaying it should not have to. The person is a reader of the channel, not a router between the two agents. The executor re-reads the channel before each irreversible step (a push, a seed, a release). That is how a correction posted after the claim reaches it.

65.title: 3. One sentence to paste, and a brief inside the bean
65.content: Two texts reach the executor, and they do different jobs. What the person pastes: one sentence naming the work item, the branch and the repository. Do bean <id> on branch <branch> of repo <owner>/<repo>. That is all an agent with a checkout needs to find everything else. The person should not have to edit, shorten or explain it. A paste that carries the instructions is long, unversioned and impossible to correct. A paste that carries less leaves the executor asking which branch. What the work item opens with: a ## Brief addressed to the executor. It is the first section after the front matter, so beans show prints it first. It is written to an agent that has seen only that one sentence. Voice. Write the brief in the second person, to the executor, about its own task: “You are the executor…”, “Stop and report if…”. Do not write in the coordinator’s voice (“I verify…”, “my watch…”), in the third person about the executor (“the agent should…”), or to the person. A brief that says “I” makes the executor guess who is speaking. What the brief carries. It has to work on its own: . | part | example | . | who you are and why this came to you | executor; the coordinator lacks packages.fhir.org | . | WHERE: repository, canonical checkout path (and which one NOT to use), branch and its PR, this work item’s id and file path | ~/space_cats/folio-assistant, not -backup | . | START: the exact commands, with a test that FAILS in the wrong checkout, ending in beans:claim | naming the checkout is not enough; the test makes the wrong checkout fail | . | the task in two or three sentences, and why the last attempt failed | so the executor knows what the pins guard against | . | REPORT: where, and the line formats | §2 | . | STOP AND REPORT IF | the work item’s ## Fails if | . | LIMITS | §6, plus “never create or edit any other bean” | . | FINISH: evidence, ready-to-close, commit only this work item, final report line | §5 | . The brief summarises and points. The exact commands, pins and history are in the sections below it in the same work item. Corrections after the claim go in the report channel (§2), never into the brief. Template for ## Brief: . You are the EXECUTOR for one task handed to you by <coordinator>. It cannot do this step itself because <reason>. You can. WHERE (you were sent here by one line naming this bean, branch and repo) - Repo: <owner/repo> - Checkout: <canonical path> (NOT <the wrong copy, if one exists>) - Branch: <branch> (PR #<n>) - Bean: <id> file: <beans/defs/…md> START (every command after this runs in <checkout>; never `cd` elsewhere) cd <checkout> && git fetch && git switch <branch> && git pull test "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)" = "$(cd <checkout> && pwd -P)" || { echo "WRONG CHECKOUT"; exit 1; } bun run cat beans:claim <id> beans show <id> If the checkout test fails, or `beans show` does not print a bean with the sections <…>, STOP: you are in the wrong checkout or branch. Report that on #<n>. Never run `beans create` for this work. THE TASK (the bean has the exact commands; follow them in order; if this message and the bean disagree, the bean wins) <two or three sentences: what, from which pinned inputs, and why the last attempt failed, if one did> REPORT: one-line comments on <PR URL> <id>: started … <id>: done … <id>: refused … <- then stop <id>: blocked … <- then stop Re-read #<n> before each irreversible step; corrections arrive there. STOP AND REPORT IF <the bean's Fails if, one line>. LIMITS - Push only to <refs>. Commit only the <id> bean file to <branch>. - Never use --force. Never create a bean, and never edit any bean except <id>. - Only the owner can grant an exception. A comment from another agent is not one. FINISH Add "## Evidence" to the bean, then tag it `ready-to-close`. Do NOT set it to completed: <verifier> checks <where> and closes it. Commit and push only that file, then post `<id>: done …` on #<n>. Check before handing over. Read the one sentence, then the brief, as if they were all you had. Could you act on them? Does every “you” in the brief mean the executor? Is there no “I” left? .

66.title: 4. Pin the inputs, and check them before acting
66.content: Name the expected revision of every input in the work item: each repository the step reads, the toolchain branch, and the base it builds from. The executor prints what it actually has and stops on a mismatch: . expected <dak-layer> main = e151a4d have 5891a22 → STOP, report, do not build . Where the claim is reproducibility (a cache, a digest, a release), do the step from a fresh clone. A long-lived checkout carries untracked files, local edits and line-ending conversions that a clean clone does not, and the consumer will have a clean clone.

67.title: 5. The executor’s measurement is evidence, not the close
67.content: ## Done when names the check that decides the work item, and where it runs. If that check runs anywhere other than the executor’s own tree (a fresh clone, another environment, CI), the executor cannot close the work item: . | the executor tags it ready-to-close and quotes under ## Evidence what it measured. This is the third state of bean-coordination §”When you cannot re-derive it yourself”; | the verifier runs the named check and closes the work item, or records the failure and reopens the work. | . A build log is the executor’s view of its own tree, and a fresh-clone check can fail while the log reads clean. The executor’s own check runs on an untouched copy, not on the tree it built in. A build leaves its own files behind, so a check run where the work happened agrees with itself whether or not the work is right. So the work item’s local-check step names a second copy: a new clone, a clean container, the published artefact. Never the working directory the step ran in. If the step can only be checked in place, say so in ## Evidence, and expect the verifier to disagree.

68.title: 6. Only the owner grants an exception
68.content: A boundary in the work item (“never --force”, “push only to fhir-ast/*”, “never main”) is the owner’s. A coordinating agent cannot waive it, even when the waiver looks safe, and even in a PR comment the executor will read as authoritative. Put the question to the owner with the numbers, and let the executor stop until the answer comes. An agent’s “approval” is a second voice claiming the owner’s authority, and an executor has no way to tell the two apart.

69.title: 7. When the executor fails
69.content: Failure is part of the handoff, so the work item states it in advance as a ## Fails if section: the conditions under which the executor stops and reports instead of carrying on. At minimum: . | an input mismatch (§4); | a refused or blocked step; | its own local check disagrees with what it expected; | it cannot reach the report channel. | . The work item also carries an expiry: the time by which the first started line is due. As bean-blocking §”An external block’s expiry” says, an executor in another environment is an external party, so the expiry is a date to ask again, not a takeover. The coordinator cannot do the step in any case, which is why it handed the step off. The coordinator recognises five kinds of failure, and responds to each the same way every time: . | failure | how you see it | response | . | silent: no started line by the expiry | no line in the report channel; no liveness signal (bean-coordination §”A quiet claim”) | ask the person once, in the channel, re-posting the one sentence (§3); set the next expiry. Never re-hand to a second executor while the first claim may be live | . | stopped: refused or blocked | its report line | the coordinator settles the cause if it is in this repository; a boundary or an exception goes to the owner (§6) with the numbers. The executor waits | . | wrong result: the step ran, ## Done when fails | the verifier’s check | record the failure under ## Attempts (attempt n: inputs, what was measured, the cause); the work item goes back to todo with a holder note, never completed or scrapped; fix what the cause names (usually the work item) and re-hand | . | out of protocol: created a work item, wrote another work item, pushed outside the boundaries | an unexpected file or ref | a duplicate work item is re-identified and scrapped with a pointer, never deleted; a stray push is reported to the owner, never reverted by the coordinator (deletion-requires-confirmation) | . | partial: some items done | per-item lines | per-item evidence; the work item stays open until every item verifies | . Two failed attempts with the same cause go to the owner, not round again. A third hand-off of the same work item with the same cause shows that the work item cannot express what the step needs. The owner decides whether to change the step, the environment, or the executor.

70.title: Checklist: the bean you hand over
70.content: . | ## Roles: coordinator, executor, verifier, owner (§1) | the one sentence to paste: Do bean <id> on branch <branch> of repo <owner>/<repo>. (§3) | ## Brief as the work item’s first section, second person, to the executor (§3) | ## Report to: one PR or issue, with the line formats (§2) | ## Inputs: every expected revision, and “stop on mismatch” (§4) | fresh clone, where reproducibility is the claim (§4) | ## Done when: the check, where it runs, and who closes (§5) | boundaries, with “exceptions: owner only” (§6) | ## Fails if and an expiry for the first started line (§7) | ## Attempts, left empty; the verifier fills it on a failure (§7) | .

71.title: Checklist: the executor, before the first irreversible step
71.content: . | beans show <id> finds the handed work item on this branch; if not, stop | claimed with bun run cat beans:claim <id>, with no beans create | inputs printed and matched against ## Inputs | report channel re-read for corrections | after the step: report in the channel’s format, tag ready-to-close with ## Evidence unless you can run the ## Done when check yourself | .

73.title: Subagent memory — what a durable entry may claim
73.content: Skill agent-memory: Durable memory for a subagent — the three entry labels and what each promises, why entries are authored as graph nodes rather than in the generated file, the injection budget that silently truncates, and archiving as the third state between “reaches everybody” and “deleted”. Named by: Remote-mount a dependency . A subagent declaring project memory gets its own directory; the first 200 lines (or 25 KB) of that directory’s MEMORY.md are injected into its system prompt at start, and it reads and writes the directory as it works. Maintaining it is part of the work. A session that establishes a durable fact in an agent’s area adds it in the same change; a session that re-measures a number updates the entry with the fresh value and date, because a memory file that only accretes becomes the thing it exists to prevent. This curated memory is not a memory record, and a work item is. The entries here are read during a process and never written by one. A memory record is what a process keeps as it runs (memory-record-core in cat-harness-tools schemas/kg/memory-record.ts, owner ruling Q17 of 2026-11-03), and a work item is a memory record with more structure: a status, a type, a priority, a parent and what it blocks. Both are worked with the same memory Tools (memory_note, memory_checkpoint, memory_recall); see todo-manager (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan).

74.title: Every entry carries exactly one of three labels
74.content: | label | what it promises | . | STABLE | a path, a command, a rule. Trustworthy as written. | . | TRAP | a specific way the task goes wrong, with the evidence that established it. | . | BASELINE | a measured number, stored with the command that produced it and the date, and never quoted as a current answer. | . A TRAP is what stops a failure the project has paid for once being paid for twice. An entry that merely restates a rule is STABLE — a TRAP needs the incident. A baseline with no measurement is refused by the schema. A table of how to measure is a STABLE fact, not a measurement. A watcher whose subject is a live signal holds no baselines at all: every one goes stale by design.

75.title: Entries are authored as nodes; the file is generated
75.content: Edit the node; CI assembles. The assembled file under .claude/ is a projection that CI writes and commits, never an agent (harness-projections). Run the assembler locally in its check form to see what it would change. One entry per file, each declaring its own $schema, a label, a summary, and the agents it reaches — one entry can reach several agents, so a fact two agents need is not written into two files. The assembly check gates it, so an entry edited and never assembled fails the build. The generated file is written only between its markers, as the README sync is, so each file’s hand-written session log stays intact. A file with no markers is reported as not opted in, left alone, and never counted as up to date.

76.title: Vendor target mapping — one memory source, generated per target
76.content: Every declared memory directory is the single source of truth; the assembler projects it into each active vendor target, and --check gates both drift and per-target budgets: . | target | path | scope | budget | . | Claude Code per-agent | .claude/agent-memory/<agent>/MEMORY.md (+ detail/<slug>.md) | nodes referencing <agent> or agent-less | 200 lines | . | Antigravity per-agent skill | .agents/skills/<agent>-memory/SKILL.md (+ detail/<slug>.md) | nodes referencing <agent> or agent-less | 24,000 bytes | . | Antigravity workspace rule | .agents/rules/agent-memory.md | all agents, grouped under ## <agent> | 24,000 bytes | . | Repo-wide AGENTS.md | AGENTS.md (<!-- cat-harness:agent-memory:begin/end -->) | live agent-less nodes (tags.references has no kind: "agent") | 32,768 bytes (32 KiB) | . | Gemini CLI per-agent | .gemini/agents/<agent>.md | the Claude agent’s prompt + nodes referencing <agent> or agent-less | 32,768 bytes | . | OpenAI Codex per-agent | .codex/agents/<agent>.toml (developer_instructions) | same | 32,768 bytes | . | Cursor per-agent | .cursor/agents/<agent>.md | same | 32,768 bytes | . | GitHub Copilot per-agent | .github/agents/<agent>.agent.md | same | 30,000 characters (vendor limit) | . Agent-less nodes feed the repo-wide AGENTS.md section when AGENTS.md opts in with memory markers (missing and no-markers remain distinct third states). Only Claude has per-agent memory; the other hosts get a whole definition. Gemini CLI, Codex, Cursor and Copilot read per-agent definition files whose body is the prompt. So each .claude/agents/<agent>.md is projected into one file per host: its prompt, then its memory nodes inline, because imports are not portable. Tools map only where the host documents an equivalent. Cursor also reads .claude/agents/, but .cursor/ wins on a name clash, so Cursor gets its own file (the Claude copy carries no memory). An agent with memory but no definition gets no file and is reported no-definition. The formats and their sources are in the header of cat-harness-tools/scripts/agent-memory-vendors.ts. Byte-budgeted targets drop whole nodes lowest-priority first, never mid-entry. When a target exceeds its byte budget, the assembler drops baseline before trap and trap before stable (oldest createdAt first), names every dropped node per target, and fails --check until entries are split into detail/ or archived.

77.title: The budget truncates silently, so it is checked two ways
77.content: Keep the injected file under the line budget. The harness drops the overflow without saying so. A truncated entry still looks complete to the agent reading it, so the check covers both an entry whose heading falls past the budget and a region whose end does. An entry too long to fit declares its evidence as detail, split at a body marker and written beside the injected file — and pruned when the entry stops declaring one, so a stale detail file cannot outlive the claim it supported.

78.title: Archiving is the third state, and the check order is load-bearing
78.content: Retiring an agent archives its memory; it does not delete it. An archived entry is a node of the graph that reaches no agent’s prompt — the state between untagged, so reaches everybody and gone. Deleting an entry throws away work somebody else paid for; same discipline as a scrapped work item. Archived must be checked BEFORE the untagged rule. An archived entry has no agent tag once its agent is gone, so checking it second hands it to every agent. Do not re-home an entry into an agent that does not own the subject. Budget is not the constraint — a detail split makes room; forcing a fact into an unrelated lane is. Archive it, record why, and say what would justify un-archiving it.

79.title: Scoping: by agent, with role tags
79.content: Memory is knowledge, and knowledge belongs to the lane, so entries are tagged with a role. Generation still goes through the agent axis, so tagging a lane is additive and changes no generated byte; keep the two axes separate. A CI watcher is a mechanical role, so a system lane is its correct home; a guard that exercises judgement is not, because judgement is what a system lane excludes. Every live entry carries a lane tag, so an untagged entry added now goes to every agent.

80.title: A memory entry never outranks a skill
80.content: The agents defer to skills/ as the source of truth. Memory summarises; the skill governs. Where the two disagree, the skill wins and the memory entry is wrong — fix it.

81.title: The layer’s two declared assets are maintained here too
81.content: README.md and AGENTS.md are declared assets with a declared purpose, and their upkeep belongs to this skill. | role | purpose | layer | delivery | . | instance-readme | what the layer is, for a reader | context | read as a file | . | agent-instructions | what a cold agent does here, in order | context | read as a file | . | agent memory | durable facts an agent must have without asking | context | injected | . This table is DECLARED, not described. All three columns are ASSET_ROLES in schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts — one record of objects per ROLE, never per asset, because per-asset copies of a role’s purpose drift apart. layer and delivery are required on AssetRoleDef, so a new role decides them at the keyboard rather than at CI. The layer column makes a process step that writes one of these a defect. processMayWriteAsset(role) answers it through the same layerIsWritable rule the graph typologies use, so assets and directories cannot disagree about what context permits. For a role this layer does not govern it returns undefined — the third state, never to be read as permission. The delivery column is mechanical. Memory is spliced into a prompt, so it pays a budget — MEMORY.md’s first 200 lines, with the overflow dropped silently. A file is opened, so nothing truncates it. So AGENTS.md may be long and a memory entry may not, and a fact that must arrive unasked is a memory entry. asset-roles.test.ts asserts it: the longest declared AGENTS.md in the checkout runs past the 200-line budget, which is legal only because its delivery is file. AGENTS.md augments the README; it never restates it. The README answers what is this; AGENTS.md answers what do I do, in what order. A session that establishes a durable fact about a layer updates the one whose question it answers — and if it answers neither, it is a memory entry. bun run cat check:subgraph-coverage reports any layer missing either asset; both are required of every layer, because one with a README and no AGENTS.md is mute to an agent, and the reverse leaves a reader with nothing saying what the layer is. bun run cat check:asset-roles keeps the declaration single: it reports a required role ASSET_ROLES does not govern, a role a running process would be allowed to write, or an asset restating purpose, layer or delivery on itself. That last check reads the RAW declaration, because KgAssetSchema is a non-strict z.object and drops an unknown key when parsing.

83.title: Agent permissions — asked for, explained, granted by a person, recorded
83.content: Skill agent-permissions: Securing what a coding agent may do without asking, from the person who can grant it: the secure-agent-permissions sub-process, run at session start and on demand when an action is denied. Vendor-neutral: the coding agent is a Tool (Claude Code is one; Gemini CLI, Cursor, Copilot and Codex are others), and each Tool’s own config format belongs to its adapter, not here. Covers the permissions the harness’s processes need, least privilege, how each one is explained before it is granted, how a grant is recorded, and the rules that no grant relaxes: never self-granted, generated projections are CI’s, and merging to main is never a standing permission. Named by: Content acquisition, Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data the beans, Agent bean lifecycle, Open the bean, Code change and review, Staging a feature branch preview, and taking it down, Merge the base branch in, Merge manager watch: wake, read the queue live, route, A refused merge-train member, Merge to main, A merge train, Requirements filing: promote, organise, trace, supersede, or retire, Saturation meta-merge: land the ready PRs when the runners are full, SME Review of Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route, Test Data Curation — Fixed Sets and Generated Recipes, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . processes/process/secure-agent-permissions.bpmn (Process_SecureAgentPermissions) is the process. It is called from session-state-machine.bpmn (Call_SecurePermissions, after the session record opens), so it is part of starting work in a layer. It also runs on demand when an agent hits a denied action. A denial is a reason to ask. It is never a reason for the agent to edit its own configuration. A run that finds every needed permission granted and recorded ends at End_Current without asking anything.

84.title: Three layers, three questions, and this skill answers the third
84.content: | layer | question | where it lives | . | role | what does the performer of this lane need to KNOW? | skills on the role (role-model) | . | actor permission | what may this participant DO in the harness, in any lane? | skills/permissions/permissions.json actions, granted by ODRL rules under policies/ | . | agent Tool permission | what may this coding agent do on this machine without stopping to ask? | the Tool’s own config, written through its adapter; the grant recorded as below | . The third layer enforces the second at the agent host. Editing hooks or settings exercises admin-settings; writing content exercises content-authoring. An agent Tool permission never widens what the actor’s ODRL grants allow. It only decides whether the host stops to ask.

85.title: The permissions the processes need
85.content: Grant only what the layer’s processes actually call, and the narrowest form that does the job. | permission | what it allows | why a process needs it | notes | . | run the gates | run the repository’s test, typecheck and cat check scripts | every gate a PR must pass before merge-to-main | read-only checks first; a writer (regen) is a separate grant | . | push a feature branch | git push to a non-default branch | continual-progress: commit early, push, open the PR at the first commit | never the default branch; never --force, only --force-with-lease | . | open and update a PR | create a PR, comment, label it | continual-progress, issue-working, merge-queue handover | never merge | . | edit agent hooks and settings | change the Tool’s hand-edited config | only when a hook or setting is itself the defect | per change, never standing: the exact diff, the reason, then the owner’s yes (harness-projections) | . | write generated projections | regenerate the Tool’s projections of the graph | none: CI regenerates them on the PR head | not granted to an agent at all (harness-projections) | . | merge to main | — | — | never a Tool permission. Every merge is its own owner-authorised run of merge-to-main (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc). No allow-rule for a merge command is ever written. | .

86.title: Explaining one before it is granted
86.content: Task_Explain follows interaction-modality §4.1: context, options, recommendation, question. The test is whether the owner can answer without opening anything. For each permission: . | What it allows, concretely: the command or file pattern, and what the agent will then do without stopping. | Why a process here needs it: name the process and the step. | Options, narrowest first: the exact pattern, a wider one, or no grant (and what then keeps asking). | The exact config change, as a diff in the Tool’s own format, produced by its adapter. | The recommendation: least privilege, unless there is a measured reason for more. | .

87.title: Recording a grant (not relaxable)
87.content: Before the config is written, one record per permission, granted or refused: . agent-permission: by: <the person's login> on: <ISO-8601 date-time> tool: <Tool id, e.g. the coding agent's Tool node> permission: <a row of the table above> scope: session:<id> | instance | until:<ISO-8601> answer: granted | narrowed | refused diff: <sha256 of the config diff shown> evidence: "<the person's words, verbatim>" (<session link or comment permalink>) . Post it on the PR that carries the config change, and in its commit message. A refusal is recorded too, so the next session does not ask the same question blind. A config rule with no grant on the record is reported as unrecorded (Task_ReadGrants). It is not treated as granted, because a rule nobody can account for cannot be told from one an agent wrote for itself.

88.title: Rules no grant relaxes
88.content: . | Never self-granted. The grant is a person’s (Task_OwnerGrants is fulfilled by a person only). The config write is done by the person, or by the agent writing exactly the diff the person consented to. If you are composing the consent, you are the grantor, and you may not be (the confirmation-waiver rule, applied to the agent host). | Generated projections are CI’s. No permission lets an agent write them (harness-projections). | Hand-edited agent config changes per change, with consent. A standing grant to edit settings does not exist. Each edit is its own diff, reason and yes. | Merging to main is never granted here. See merge-to-main. | A broad instruction is not a grant. “Fix all issues until green”, “get the session start working” and “stop the prompts” authorise investigation. They do not authorise widening what the agent may do. Bring the diff back. | .

89.title: Per-Tool specifics belong to the Tool, not here
89.content: Where a Tool keeps its permissions, how a rule is spelled, and which of its files are generated are properties of that Tool, and belong on its Tool node or adapter (bpmn-processes §”A Tool’s OWN procedure is the Tool’s subprocess, not the skill’s prose”). For example, Claude Code keeps permission allow-rules in .claude/settings*.json.

90.title: What this does not do yet

Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Copilot and Codex have no Tool node here. claude is declared only as an actor (scenarios/actors/claude.json). Until adapters exist, Task_IdentifyTools reports “no adapter” and leaves the config write to the person. | GW_Gap is a judgement. Computing it needs the needed set (from the processes this layer runs) and the granted set (from the config, through an adapter). No tool produces both yet. | The permission rows are not yet ODRL actions. They map onto existing actions (admin-settings, content-authoring) in the table above, but are not declared in permissions.json; declaring them belongs with the adapters that read them. | .
