226.title: Relationship first, visualisation later
226.content: Skill board-diagram-interchange: A board is a DIAGRAM OF a folio, not a container of one. The OMG split between the semantic model and its layout, why the arrow runs one way, and what a note may never carry. Named by: A harness’s default rendering, Board: open and close content, Board: place a note, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . Treat a board like the OMG specifications treat BPMN layout: relationship first, visualisation later. BPMN separates the semantic model — bpmn:process, its tasks and its flows — from Diagram Interchange: BPMNDiagram, BPMNShape, BPMNEdge, which say where each of those was drawn. They are two documents about one subject, and the layout one points at the semantic one, never the other way. A folio board is the same shape: . semantic model notes, anchors, content nodes what is true diagram interchange board-positions.json where it was drawn .

227.title: What follows
227.content: A folio is complete with no board. Deleting every board loses layout and no content. That is the test to apply when you are unsure whether something belongs on the board or in the folio: if losing it would lose a fact, it is not layout. A note carries no x, no y, no board, no position — for the same reason a BPMN task carries no coordinates: layout lives on top of notes, not as data within them. One note may sit on several boards, at different places, without the note arbitrating between them. A coordinate on the note could not express that; a layer above it does so for free. An orphan is swept from the LAYER, which is the easy direction: one file, one pass, and nothing edited out of a note a person owns.

228.title: The arrow, and how it is kept
228.content: folio ──▶ board ──▶ position ──▶ note allowed note ──▶ position / board / folio REFUSED . This is a property a future edit can break silently, so it is checked rather than described. schemas/board-positions.test.ts asserts two things against the SOURCE: . | no field named x, y, board or position appears in todo.ts, carried-note.ts, landing-sticky.ts or note-anchor.ts; | board-positions.ts imports zod and nothing else — it names notes by id, and an id needs no type from the layer below. | . The first guards the failure that actually happens: somebody adding coordinates to a note “for convenience”, which makes a content node carry state and gives one note two answers on two boards.

229.title: Two graph typologies, because they are two things
229.content: | kind | holds | what it is | . | boards | content | what a board is and what it shows | . | board-positions | state | where each note was drawn | . content-context-and-state-graphs refuses a content node that carries state, which is the same rule one level up. And check:graph-typology-work asks a sharper question of the second: it is state, written by a running process every time somebody moves a note — but state that records a position in a PROCESS is work, and state that records a position on a CANVAS is not. Both kinds declare recordsWork: false.

230.title: A board declares what it SHOWS, and absent means everything
230.content: schemas/ui/board.ts: an optional filter over pages and kinds, OR within an axis and AND across them. Absent is the default and it means the whole folio — a query rather than a stored list, because a list of content nodes needs something to notice that a listed node was renamed and that a new one was never added, and a query has nothing to fall behind. Every harness above the floor has a board filled with all contents, which is the absent filter — so the minimal board and the total board are the same document.

231.title: Mergeability is the reason for the shape, and its limit is stated
231.content: Positions are the most concurrently-edited state a folio has: two sessions moving two notes is the ordinary case. So the document is sorted and indented, one note per line-block, and the sort is idempotent — a writer that reshuffled on save would conflict with every other save. It is a partial fix. Two notes that sort adjacent still conflict, because the inserted lines overlap. This removes the guaranteed conflict, not every conflict, and it should not be trusted further than that.

232.title: What this skill is NOT
232.content: Not the rendering. How a board draws, when a card becomes its avatar and what an open window does are board-windows. Not the tiles. Which boards and viewers a reader can reach is harness-tiles.

252.title: Start in the avatar, open into a window
252.content: Skill board-windows: Everything starts as its avatar; opening projects a window onto the board. The two mechanisms that must not be conflated, z-order, and the fixed chrome a content kind fills in. Named by: A harness’s default rendering, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . Everything starts as its avatar, and [x] closes a window back to it. Opening projects a window onto the board; selecting any part of a window raises it. Each content kind controls its own avatar and rendering, and opens into a full-screen panel with fixed controls such as [x], [linksrc] or [edit].

253.title: TWO mechanisms, and conflating them is the defect
253.content: |   | trigger | who | . | semantic zoom | the card’s rendered width crosses a declared threshold | automatic | . | open / close | [x], or opening a card | a person | . An open window is not a zoom state: it is projected onto the board rather than being the card grown large, so it survives zooming out. Only [x] closes it. Collapsing the two gives a board where a card can close itself with no action taken, and where [x] and a zoom-out are indistinguishable. Semantic zoom is the GLASS’s, not the board’s . Every board slot — a landing sticky and a todo sticky alike — is one component: the same closed square tile (--fa-sticky-tile-size) with the theme’s faded art, and the same compact icon row underneath it. A slot is its closed tile at every width, so semantic zoom does not run on the board. It decides what a card shows on the folio glass, where a card is resized freely. Do not add a width observer to the board grid: it would be a zoom with nothing to change, and the next agent would read it as the card’s state.

254.title: One sticky, one icon row, in one order
254.content: Under every sticky, on every panel: view, edit, pin, send to fsh-guts, as icon buttons. An icon-only control carries aria-label (what a screen reader announces) AND title (the same words on hover); they are not interchangeable. No control sits inside the card body. The open window’s bar uses the same icons for the same acts. A link the sticky cannot serve is absent, never dead.

255.title: Pin is a toggle onto the FOLIO glass
255.content: There is one store answering “what is on my glass”: the folio. A second store holding a page-level copy of the card gets no glass tools, no folio geometry and no shelve, and has to be special-cased by the glass filter and count. | Pin makes the sticky a folio asset — todo/<id> (the key the glass’s own Todos panel pulls a todo out under, so the two ways onto the glass agree) or landing/<slot> — with shown: true, drawn by the glass’s own card path and placed by placeOnGlass. A landing sticky’s theme, picture URL and text travel in the entry as data, never as stored markup. | Unpin is shelveFromGlass — the middle of the three states below. The entry stays; the same pin puts it back, where the reader left it. | The pressed state is the store’s answer (folioStateOf(key) === "glass"), never the button’s memory. The glass’s own × shelves too, and the row’s pin follows it. | .

256.title: Send to fsh-guts asks first
256.content: A control a reader has to ask about has not said what it does, so discard is named for where it goes (Send to fsh-guts, the trashcan that is kept) and opens a confirmation that names the sticky, says it is restorable and per-browser, and says where it is restored from — the fish in the navbar’s icon row. Focus starts on Cancel; Cancel and Escape do nothing but close it. A dialog whose dismissal performs the act did not ask. The window bar’s send is the same act and takes the same confirmation. The inverse is Restore in fsh-guts.

257.title: The threshold is declared, inherited, and traceable
257.content: schemas/kg/semantic-zoom.ts (instance data: semantic-zoom.json): a folio default (belowPx) with a per-kind override (byKind) — the repository’s inheritance rule (inherit everything, override anything; a variant states only what it CHANGES). So: . | the folio always has a number, and every kind resolves to one; | a kind that states nothing is complete, not invalid — requiredness is checked after resolution, never on the declaration; | an override carries a required because, and the resolver returns the source alongside the value, so a reviewer can tell a deliberate override from a folio default that does not fit. | . The boundary is stated once. Strictly below the number, so the declared width is the last one that still shows words. A boundary written one way in a comment and the other way in the renderer makes a card flicker.

258.title: Z-order: selecting any part raises
258.content: Windows stack, and selecting any part of one raises it — not a title bar, any part, because a reader who clicks into a window’s content has already said which one they mean. Z-order is session-only. The DI layer carries no z: a committed stacking order would make every raise a file write and every two sessions a conflict, on the most concurrently-edited state a folio has. If that proves wrong, z is one optional field in the positions document.

259.title: The chrome is fixed; the kind fills it in
259.content: A content kind declares which controls it offers, and the platform fixes the frame: . | [x] is always present and always in the same place, so a reader learns the frame once; | a declared control that names nothing known is a finding, not a missing button; | a control the environment cannot perform is hidden, and the reason reported — a dead [edit] 404s for exactly the reader who cannot edit, which reads as “this page is broken” rather than “you cannot do this”. | .

260.title: Closing must have a reachable inverse
260.content: An action whose inverse is not reachable is not a toggle. On an overlay, close may set hidden, because the launcher tile re-opens it. On a board that IS page content, hidden removes a section of the page, so the inline board collapses to a control in its own position, and focus follows it — left alone, focus lands on <body> and the keyboard position is gone. A control two clicks deep inside a collapsed launcher does not count as reachable. A default of “hidden” is allowed only with the inverse on screen. The glass’s tile strip starts slid away; its “Show tiles (N)” tab stays in view, in the strip’s own position, and the same tab hides the tiles again. See harness-tiles §”The glass strip”.

261.title: The floor, which is not negotiable
261.content: This layer’s declared interaction profile is low-dexterity. Every board action is keyboard-operable; drag is an accelerator and never the only way in. Targets are at least the tile size. And the board is ALWAYS collapsible to a linear, tile-based listing — a board that cannot be read linearly cannot be read by a screen reader, printed, or translated. The listing is the ARTEFACT and the board is the overlay . The board is an extra laid over a simple tile-based listing. So the floor must be correct with no JavaScript at all, not merely when the board is toggled off: notes built only by docs-ui.js from a fetch of assets/todos/index.json give a reader with JavaScript off no note, no count, and no hint that notes exist. Three checks follow: . Document order, never the board’s order. The board may stack by BPMN subprocess depth; the floor does not, because document order is what a screen reader and a printout depend on, and a floor that reordered would be a second answer to “what comes next”. Collapsed, never removed. When the board mounts it moves the listing into a disclosure so the page does not show the same notes twice. It does not delete it, hide it from assistive technology, or display: none it: a listing the board removed would have no way back while the board is open. Assert against the SERVED HTML. A test that reads the DOM passes because the board built that DOM. The assertion is on bytes the server sent — a browser context with javaScriptEnabled: false over the same renderer the generator writes with.

262.title: The folio belongs to the HARNESS, not to the library
262.content: A content library is something a reader browses — a replica, a published layer, any folio published as a site. A folio is the reader’s own surface: their notes, the assets they have materialised, the documents they created or linked. So the folio visualisation is cat-harness’s, available by convention on any harness, and a library never implements its own. A library may have its own landing page and its own harness; neither is licence to build a second folio. Consistency is the requirement: a reader moving between libraries must find the same folio, because the point of carrying a folio is that it does not change underneath them. A note or a todo MAY reference nodes in another KG library. The folio is not scoped to the library it is pulled down over, so a renderer must not assume local resolution.

263.title: A tile, or an avatar?
263.content: A tile is what the HARNESS declares, an avatar is what the FOLIO holds, and a theme is how either one looks rather than a third kind. The test is in harness-tiles §”A tile, or an avatar?”, and only there, because one rule with two homes is free to drift.

264.title: An asset has THREE states, not two
264.content: Pulling the folio down gives a glass — a surface over whatever is being browsed, carrying sticky notes and the avatars of materialised assets, including materialised KG like cat-bootstrap or cat-harness themselves. | state | where the asset is | how it got there | . | in the library | not the reader’s at all | the default | . | in the folio, not displayed | materialised into the folio’s own reproduce directories — library/ for the bytes, uploads/ for a source — off the glass | the reader closed it, “back in library” | . | on the glass | displayed in the pulled-down folio | the reader pulled it out of the library | . “In the folio” is not folio/. The folio is the reader’s REPOSITORY, of which library/ and uploads/ are declared parts — both carry dependents: "reproduce". folio/ is a different graph typology: renderable authored content. corpus-grep searches library/ only, so a node materialised anywhere else reads as ABSENT to every consumer. Closing returns an asset to the middle state and NEVER to the first. Only its display goes. Putting it back on the glass is a separate act performed from the library, not from the glass it just left. A two-state model would make closing a sticky and un-materialising an asset the same gesture, and a reader tidying their glass would silently discard work; the middle state is what makes closing cheap enough to do freely. When you implement close, check that the library offers the way back — not that the glass does. Close says where the way back is, at the moment of closing. The glass’s [x] opens a confirm that names the layer’s library and links it; Escape and Cancel leave the card where it is, and only the confirm shelves it — after which the glass says, with the same link, where the asset went. Naming the library matters because a reader holding assets from several libraries would otherwise have to remember which one each came from. The place is the card’s own, so there are three. A library card goes back to its layer’s library, a todo to the Todos board, and a landing sticky pinned to the glass to the page it was pinned from; calling a sticky “your Todos” would send the reader to a list it was never on. One function answers “where does this card go back to”, and the confirm, the status after it and the [x] button’s own label all read it, so the three cannot disagree. The confirm is the page’s one confirm dialog, shared with sending a sticky to fsh-guts, so focus-on-Cancel and Escape-cancels are stated once. Opening a library card goes to the asset’s visualizer when its index entry declares one, else to its entry page; resizing is a corner drag, with +/− in move mode and the move bar’s buttons as the non-drag path.

265.title: Two settings panels, two names, each points to the other
265.content: The glass has its own settings (theme, avatars, opacity, blur), and the page has its own under ▦ Actions (scheme, reading preferences, the Discarded fish, Declared kinds). They are named “Glass settings” and “Page settings”, so a screen reader does not read two controls identically, and each panel opens with a link to the other, as its first control, because a reader who opens the wrong panel needs a pointer to the right one. Site chrome and board state are unrelated settings but they are neighbouring places, and a reader moves between places. | The names are declared once (SETTINGS_NAMES in docs-ui.js), because each panel’s link prints the OTHER panel’s name; a panel renamed in one place only would leave the other panel’s link naming something that no longer exists. | The link must OPEN its target, not toggle it, and not open it underneath. The glass’s openPanel closes a panel that is already open, and the open glass covers the sidebar where Page settings lives. So the glass-to-page link shuts the glass first, and the page-to-glass link shuts the launcher first. In both cases focus lands on the target panel’s heading. | No link to nothing. A page with a glass and no sidebar has no launcher. Each panel registers an opener, and the link is drawn only when its target registered one. | . The same holds for any future pair of panels that share a word: name each one for what it acts on, and point each one at the other. scripts/tests/settings-labels-distinct.test.ts checks the source; test/settings-crosslinks.e2e.ts checks the rendered page at 1280×800 and 390×844, by mouse and keyboard.

266.title: Lazy window content fetch and render safety
266.content: Rendering the board with N cards makes 0 per-card detail fetches up front: each board slot (todoSlot / renderBoardTiles) renders only its summary tile/avatar. When a card carries a per-card detail or artifact URL (detailHref, bodyHref, artifactHref, or a non-inlined jsonldHref), opening its window (openCard / createLazyWindowLoader.openWindow) fetches that card’s content lazily on open, caches the result by card id (so re-opening uses the cached result and never pre-fetches the other N - 1 cards), and renders any body or tool/skill output through the declared renderToolOutput (RENDER_AS: text, url, markdown, json) and safeHref boundary (schemas/ui/render-output.ts, site-chrome/assets/js/docs-ui.js). A refused URL scheme (such as javascript:) is never fetched and is shown as escaped text.

267.title: Not this skill
267.content: The layout layer and why a note carries no coordinates: board-diagram-interchange. Relocating content out of a folio is deletion-requires-confirmation, applied by the content core’s processes/ui/board-relocate.bpmn.

268.title: board-windows (skill)
268.content: The skill board-windows as its source file cat-harness/skills/ui/ui-core/board-windows.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

269.title: Reading a knowledge graph before you have anything
269.content: Skill bootstrap-kg-navigation: Read and navigate a knowledge graph with nothing installed — no MCP server, no tools, no harness. Named bootstrap- so it cannot be confused with a navigation Skill of a Harness that is installed. Named by: Complete initialization, Determine the harness and repositories, Initialize a harness . This skill assumes a text editor and nothing else. No MCP server, no skill-fetching tool, no work-plan store, no build. If those exist they are not yours to rely on yet — see AGENTS.md.

270.title: A graph is files that declare what they are
270.content: Three facts carry the whole model, and every one of them is checkable by reading: . | A layer declares the directories it scans, in its declaration at its root. Each entry is an id, a path, and the kinds of graph found there. | A directory is a place to look, not a type. One may hold more than one part of a graph, so the directory does not say what its files are — the files do, in their own front matter or $schema. | Ids are stable across a relocation; paths are not. An override matches on an entry’s id, never its path. Matching on path turns one relocated graph into two, and every consumer then scans a directory that is not there. | . Two more words you will meet in a declaration. A field this skill does not describe is an Extension: a Harness added it, and you ignore it. A Harness’s own kind of declaration, which requires everything bootstrap’s does and adds Extensions, is a Subkind of bootstrap’s: read it as bootstrap’s, and it still means what it says. Versions and addresses. A declaration may state its version (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) and an iriBase. Every identifier it mints, and every page meant for a person, is then <iriBase>v<major>/…: the address carries the major alone, so only a breaking release moves it. The exact release you read is fixed by the pin that brought this repository to you, not by the address. Bootstrap’s own are in its declaration; read them there rather than trusting a copy.

271.title: Do this, in order
271.content: . | Read the repository’s declaration. If there is none, this repository is not a layer yet, and that is the case bootstrap exists for. | Find the entry whose graphTypologies name the kind you want. In bootstrap they are named for what they hold: skills, processes, scenarios (the Roles), schemas and models. The entry’s path is relative to the declaration. | Read the files in that directory. A markdown file declaring name: and description: in front matter is a skill — its body is the instruction you were looking for. A file declaring $schema: is stating that it is something else, and is not a skill however it is named. | Follow a reference by id, not by path. A node that names another names it by id; resolve it through the declaration rather than guessing a filename. | .

272.title: What “I could not determine” means here
272.content: An absent declaration and an unreadable one are different: . | what you found | what it means | what to do | . | no declaration | not a layer yet | this is bootstrap’s case — continue | . | a declaration that will not parse | a layer asserting something broken | stop and say so; do not fall back | . | a declared directory that is not there | the declaration is wrong | stop and say so — scanning nothing and reporting a clean run is the defect | . | no declaration for a kind you want | this layer has none of it | that is an answer, not a failure | .

273.title: What this skill is NOT
273.content: It does not describe what a Harness above bootstrap holds, such as its content or its checks: those belong to the Harness you have not loaded yet. If you need one of them to finish bootstrap, the boundary is in the wrong place — say so rather than importing the definition.

Skill id: bpmn-authoring · Package: workflow · Named by l2-dak-authoring.bpmn (Business processes · BPMN 2.0, Business analyst lane) and crdm-requirements.bpmn (Phase 2: Map current workflow (BPA), Agent lane). Author BPMN 2.0 business process diagrams — both a DAK’s L2 business processes and this repository’s own processes/**/*.bpmn.

276.title: Inputs and outputs
276.content: schemas/skills/bpmn-authoring/: . | in — processName (required), sourceWorkflow, existingBpmn, participants | out — bpmnFile, diagramFile, taskCount, gatewayCount, participantCount | . graphviz is a declared capability with degradation: skip — layout help degrades, authoring does not stop.

277.title: Diagram Interchange is not optional
277.content: A .bpmn with no DI section — no explicit x/y on its shapes — parses and renders blank, although the XML looks complete. bun run cat render:bpmn renders every diagram to docs/assets/img/workflows/ with bpmn-js in headless Chromium; bun run cat render:bpmn:check fails when an SVG is stale. Run the renderer and look at the SVG before you call a diagram done.

278.title: Readable at 100%: check it before and after (author check)
278.content: Every diagram you write or touch must, when you are done: . | fit 1400 × 900 in diagram units, so its 16px text reads at about 14px in a 1200px band without zooming; every task a fixed 120 × 120 square: boxes never grow to fit their names, and a name that does not fit is shortened (TASK_SIZE in the tools layer); | have no label on another label, on a flow (its own included), on a box or across a lane line: a gateway’s question above the diamond, its answers beside their flows, every label inside one lane; | have right-angled flows and every name inside its box, pool and lane names inside their strips; | have no crossing flows, and the lane order that keeps flows between lanes shortest: each lane sits next to the lanes it exchanges flows with, so no flow crosses a lane it does not stop in. A lane that talks to only one other lane, such as an owner who only approves the merge steward’s card, goes on the outside, next to that lane (owner, 2026-11-07: “swap owner lane down to reduce arrows across non interacting actor lanes”). | . bun run cat bpmn:detangle <file> reports all of it, and --write fixes what it can (lane order, right angles, box and lane sizes, label places). Run it before and after, and put both counts in the PR. Zero findings on every diagram you touch, or it does not merge (owner, 2026-11-02, after 63 of 80 harness diagrams were found with findings: “improve bpmn authoring process/skills so doesnt happen again”). A report nobody has to act on is how they piled up. Run bpmn:detangle <file> --check last; a finding you leave needs a reason in the PR, and only diagram-too-wide / lane-order may be left that way. Then look at the render: the check cannot yet see a box drawn across a lane line or outside its own lane, two flows drawn on top of each other, or a flow that wanders through a lane it does not stop in. Those are found only by looking. The same findings are in render:bpmn’s warnings and the process’s QA report, so a reviewer sees what the author left. The procedure, and why the budget is 1400 × 900, is bpmn-detangle.

279.title: In this repository, a diagram is executable
279.content: processes/**/*.bpmn are not pictures. workflow_start / workflow_next / workflow_complete run them, and workflow_complete refuses a step that is not enabled. That has consequences for how you author: . | Every activity carries <bootstrap.processes:skill ref="…"/> naming the skill that implements it, and <cat-harness.processes:bean store="beans/"/> where it touches the work plan. bun run cat check:workflow-refs fails on a ref that resolves to nothing, and bun run cat kg:audit additionally fails when the named skill exists but no package can serve it. | Every lane names a role. Declare the role once as a top-level <bpmn:resource id="<role id>" name="<title>"/> (before the collaboration and the process), and set partitionElementRef="<role id>" on the lane; the id is the role’s in scenarios/roles.json, verbatim. Lane names are free text; an explicit ref is the join that does not depend on spelling. <bootstrap.processes:role ref> is the deprecated form. A diagram using any bootstrap.processes: element declares the namespace as the first child of <bpmn:definitions>: <bpmn:import namespace="https://litlfred.github.io/bootstrap/v0/processes/ns/" location="https://litlfred.github.io/bootstrap/v0/processes/ns.jsonld" importType="http://www.w3.org/ns/json-ld"/>. | A store is not a lane. Lanes are for people and agents, the roles that act. A place where things are kept, such as the work plan (work items), a corpus, a session record, an activity log or a published bucket, is a <bpmn:dataStoreReference>. The tasks that read or write it point at it with data associations, and each task sits in the lane of whoever does it. A “Work plan — beans” lane holding “Open the bean” says the store does the work, when the agent does. | The process’s own bpmn:documentation opens with what it is for. Its first sentence is the diagram’s row on the publication-workflow page. kg-export carries it on the Process node as summary (the whole text as description), the page reads it from the published named-subgraph JSON-LD (bun run cat subgraph:jsonld) rather than from anything written by hand, and check:process-index fails when a declared diagram’s node has none. So that sentence says what the process does or answers — not who asked for it, which work item or issue it came from, or where the work got to. Those belong later in the documentation, or in the work item. | A gateway may be computed rather than chosen — see dmn-authoring. | Policy is declared on the process. <cat-harness.processes:policy enforcement="strict"/> means workflow_gate refuses a step that is not enabled; absent policy means strict. Steps marked relaxable="false" may never be relaxed by any package. | .

280.title: Readable diagrams: what the research supports
280.content: These rules are what holds up from the BPMN comprehension research, checked mechanically. kg:audit reports each rule below per process (src/workflow/diagram-quality.ts in the tools layer). The sources, and how strong each rule’s evidence is, are in the process-model-quality methodology. | Separate routing from work. A task never has two outgoing flows: put an exclusive or parallel gateway after it, or a reader must guess fork vs choice (activity-implicit-split, major). A loop-back INTO a task is fine. A gateway either joins or splits, not both (gateway-mixed). A question is a gateway, never a task: a box named “Should it leave now?” or “Separate this graph?” is a decision drawn as work. If someone must judge first, draw that as a task (“Judge whether it should leave”) or a call to Process_AskThePerson, then the question on the gateway after it. | Keep it small. Split by phase into call activities past 20 flow nodes (process-size). That 20 is house style. The only threshold with evidence is 7PMG’s 50 (process-decompose, major), and it predicts modelling errors such as deadlocks, not reading speed. | One start event per process level (process-single-start). Several named end events are fine, and the work item CLOSE pattern needs them. | A decision is a question, its branches are the answers (decision-label-question). | Label activities verb-object: imperative verb, then its object (Review the draft, not Draft review) (activity-label-verb-first). The evidence is one study of how ambiguous labels felt (29 students), so this is reported, never gated. | A name says the step, nothing else. No trailing [skill] slug: the skill is in <bootstrap.processes:skill ref>, and the page links it from there. No step numbers (“1 ·”, “Phase 2:”, “P1.1”): the flows already give the order, and a number in front breaks verb-first. A number that cites a section of a source document goes in the task’s documentation. A list of numbered steps is a sign the diagram copies a document’s outline; group the steps into phases instead. | . Split by phase: how . A diagram can be right in every step and still unreadable on its page. When process-size fires, or a diagram has a start event per lane, split it like this: . | The top-level process shows the phases. Each phase is a <bpmn:callActivity calledElement="…"> to its own process. Keep at the top only what moves the work between phases: who hands off to whom, and the decisions that send it back (rejected → revise). A loop that crosses phases is drawn at the top; a loop inside a phase stays in that phase. | A phase lives in its own file, <parent>-<phase>.bpmn, next to the parent, with its own process id (Process_<Parent><Phase>) and a first documentation sentence that says what the phase does. It becomes the phase’s row on the publication-workflow page like any other diagram’s. | A phase that ends two ways ends in two named end events, and the caller’s gateway right after the call reads which one it reached, as GW_BeanYours reads Process_BeanOpen’s. | Keep the node ids when you move nodes into a phase. A test, a schema or a skill that points at Task_X then changes only its file and process, not its id. | Open and close the work item at the top, once. A process that is only ever called runs on its caller’s work item, so a phase calls neither Process_BeanOpen nor Process_BeanClose (check:bean-calls). “Once” holds for the top as well: a process with several outcomes routes them all into one Process_BeanClose call, which decides itself whether the work item is completed, scrapped or blocked, and only then branches to its named end events. One close per outcome repeats the same box and makes the diagram wide. | A caller’s adjudication accepts looks one level down. If the judgement moves into a phase, put accepts on the call to that phase, and take it off any caller further up. | Name a call activity for the phase, verb-object like any activity (“Review the change”), not for its file. | . A phase that only one parent calls is still worth its own file: the point is the page a reader opens, not reuse. Untangle every diagram you touch . The same discipline as ArchiMate views (archimate-models §”Untangle every view you touch”), and the same geometry: a change never adds a tangle. Run bun run cat kg:audit before and after, and compare edge-crossing, edge-through-node and edge-rectilinear for the diagram, and check that no shape has a flow in and a flow out on the same point and that each lane’s rows sit at k/(n+1) of its height (bpmn-processes §”Edge routing”). Say both counts in the PR. Route loop-backs in the channel below the lane (bpmn-processes §”Edge routing”), then look at the rendered SVG. What the evidence does NOT support . Do not import these from style guides or model output; each was checked: . | Mandatory left-to-right flow. Figl & Strembeck 2015 (44 people) found no significant difference in accuracy or time across four directions. Lay out left-to-right for consistency, not because it reads faster. | A word cap on labels, a gateway fan-out cap of 4, and a fixed colour palette. No study behind them. Colouring matching split and join gateways made novices more accurate and experts faster, not more accurate (Reijers et al. 2011). | OR-gateways need no rule: the process model refuses inclusive gateways at load. | .

281.title: If it has actors, activities and a control flow, it is BPMN
281.content: Not a Mermaid fence. Mermaid stays for the things that are not processes — component maps, lattices, navigation graphs. The audit of which is which is on the publication workflow page, which the content core authors.

282.title: Why this skill is in a platform package
282.content: It covers both a DAK’s L2 business processes and this repository’s own processes/**/*.bpmn, and platform processes such as crdm-requirements.bpmn name it, so it cannot live in a content-type package: a platform process depending on a content-type package crosses the boundary the platform-boundary-guard subagent keeps. Its DAK material stays here rather than in a second skill, because a generic skill naming a domain worked example is ordinary, and two skills that must be read together to author one diagram are not.

283.title: When a layer above transforms it
283.content: A layer built on this one may transform an authored business process into another artefact — FHIR Shorthand, for instance — and then the BPMN is a source artefact rather than documentation of one. Author it knowing it will be transformed: names and ids you choose here appear in what is generated. That layer’s own tooling skill has the mechanics; this one names no layer above it.

286.title: Branch archaeology: what each branch holds that main does not
286.content: Skill branch-archaeology: Classify every remote branch against the default branch (merged, landed by squash or cherry-pick, partially landed, unlanded, undetermined) by commit ancestry, patch-id and merge-tree, not by subject line. Report only, never delete. A branch touching content or mathematics is a salvage-review item and never a delete candidate. Covers the treeless fetch that makes thousands of branches cheap, caching by tip sha, and the report’s shape. Read before answering “which branches can go?” or “what work never landed?”. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Agent activity log, Close the bean, Drain the beans, Agent bean lifecycle, Open the bean, Code change and review, Merge the base branch in, A refused merge-train member, Requirements filing: promote, organise, trace, supersede, or retire, SME Review of Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route, Test Data Curation — Fixed Sets and Generated Recipes, Watching a pinned upstream dependency, Adopting an upstream version bump, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Editing and HCI validation, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . The question sounds like git branch -r --no-merged, and that command answers it wrong. It tests ancestry, so a branch landed by squash or cherry-pick (which is how most PRs land here) shows as unmerged forever. lsi:epics uses it to find unmerged branches, which is fine for filing and wrong for disposal. Measured in one folio, 2026-10-04: 6,480 remote branches, of which 461 held mathematics not on main. Those 461 are the reason for the rule in §2. A sweep that labelled them “stale” would have offered the only copy of proofs for deletion.

287.title: 1. The five classes, decided in this order
287.content: | class | test | meaning | . | merged | git merge-base --is-ancestor <tip> origin/main | every commit is on main | . | landed | git merge-tree --write-tree origin/main <tip> produces main’s own tree, or every commit’s patch-id is on main (git cherry origin/main <tip> prints only -), or the branch’s combined diff patch-id matches a main commit (the squash case) | the CHANGE is on main under other commits | . | partial | some commits’ patch-ids are on main, some are not | part landed; the rest is unique work | . | unlanded | none of the above, and every test ran | unique work | . | undetermined | a test could not run: an object could not be fetched, or merge-tree conflicted and patch-ids disagree | not unlanded and not landed. Report it as unknown | . Some notes on the tests: . | The merge-tree test is the strongest. If merging the branch into main changes nothing, then nothing on the branch is missing from main, however it got there: squash, cherry-pick, a re-implementation with the same result, or a revert-and-reapply. A conflict proves nothing either way, so move on to the patch-id tests. | git cherry compares per-commit patch-ids. It catches cherry-picks. It misses a squash, because one squashed commit’s patch-id equals the sum of the branch, not any single commit. Hence the combined test: . base=$(git merge-base origin/main "$tip") git diff "$base" "$tip" | git patch-id --stable # the branch as one patch git log --format=%H "$base"..origin/main | while read c; do git show "$c" | git patch-id --stable # each main commit since done . | Subject lines are never evidence. Two commits titled “fix build” share nothing, and a squash usually renames. | undetermined must never be folded into either neighbour. A census that counts it as unlanded inflates salvage work. One that counts it as landed offers unique work for deletion, which is the dh4f shape: a clean report over what the tool could not read. | . Two flags sit beside the class rather than inside it: . | open-pr: #n — any branch backing an open PR is live, whatever its class. | beans: […] — work item ids named in its commit messages, the same extraction lsi:epics performs. This is the link that lets work-plan-restructure (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan) close a work item whose work this census shows landed. | .

288.title: 2. Content protection: a content branch is salvage-review, never delete-candidate
288.content: If an unlanded or partial branch touches content, it goes on the salvage-review list and is never offered for deletion, at any age or size. “Content” means any path under a directory the layer declares with a content kind (folio, library), any .lean file, and the folio’s block, chapter and computation sources. Read the declaration (<instance>.json); do not use a hard-coded path list. The reason is asymmetric cost. A platform branch’s unique work can usually be re-derived from the issue that motivated it. A proof, a computation or an authored chapter often cannot, because the session that wrote it is gone and its scrollback with it. So: . | branch | goes to | . | merged / landed, no open PR | delete-candidate list, with size, age, last author and the evidence that it landed | . | partial / unlanded, no content touched | review list, with unique commits, size and age | . | partial / unlanded, content touched | salvage-review list, with the unique paths and hunks, and work item ids | . | undetermined | unknown list, with the test that failed | . | any class with an open PR | not listed for disposal at all | . The delete-candidate list is a report, not an action. deletion-requires-confirmation: the owner reads it, with sizes and ages, and says which go. A branch is the last copy of its commits once the PR is closed, and plj1 is that skill’s worked example of a workflow whose shape deleted work nobody decided to delete. The content census — “absent on main” is the signal, “differs” is not . For a branch on the salvage list, the question is which of its content is nowhere on main. Compare at three levels, strongest first: . | By name, not by path. For each Lean module and declaration, and each block label, the branch adds, search main for the name anywhere. A module that moved directories is still on main. Measured in the qou orphaned-content census, 2026-10-04: of 60 recent unlanded branches, 32 touched content and 27 carried content not on main. After excluding schema files, the residue was 12 Lean modules on 7 branches whose names occur nowhere on main. That residue is the salvage list. The other 55 files that merely “differ” are not. | Path-remapped. A branch cut before a layout move uses the old paths (qou’s branches all predate its content/ → folio/ move). Remap through the move before comparing, or every file reads as absent. Take the remap from the commit that made the move. Do not guess it. | “Differs from main” is not unique work. Main moved on after the branch was cut. Count it separately, and never as math. Only a three-way comparison against the merge-base says whose change a hunk is. | . Salvage is filed per CLUSTER, not per branch. 461 branches are not 461 work items. Work items are not sidecars, and one work item per branch is the generated-template flood work-plan-restructure exists to clean up. Group the salvage list by the subject its unique paths touch (a chapter, a Lean namespace), and propose one work item per group to the owner.

289.title: 3. Making 6,000 branches cheap: a treeless fetch
289.content: git fetch --filter=tree:0 origin '+refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*' . This fetches every head’s commits without their trees or blobs: 15 s for ~6.5k branches in qou. That is enough for the ancestry test and for the commit-message work item extraction. The merge-tree and patch-id tests need trees and blobs, which the partial clone then fetches on demand, per branch. So order the work to fetch as little as possible: . | Ancestry for every branch (commits only, cheap). Most stale branches end here as merged. | Open-PR heads from the API, once. | Merge-tree, then patch-id, only for what is left. A branch whose objects cannot be fetched is undetermined (§1), not skipped silently. | .

290.title: 4. Cache by tip sha, and know which classes go stale
290.content: Key each row by branch tip sha and record the main sha it was computed against. | merged and landed are monotone: main only grows, so they stay true while the tip is unchanged. The exception is a revert on main, which the next full run catches. | partial, unlanded and undetermined must be recomputed when main moves, because the work may have landed since. | A changed tip invalidates the row whatever its class. | . A re-run then costs only the branches that moved plus the non-monotone rows. The full answer is never re-derived from scratch, which is the waste goal-review and the survey graph (beans/surveys/) already exist to stop.

291.title: 5. The report
291.content: For each branch: name, tip sha, main sha, class, the evidence (which test decided it, patch-ids matched of total), open-pr, beans, commits ahead, size of the unique diff, last commit date, and the last author or Claude-Session: trailer. Then the four lists in §2, each with counts, and the undetermined count stated beside the others, never dropped. Where it goes: summarised on the issue or in a work item note (bun run cat beans:note) for the owner, and the per-branch rows as a file attached to that review. A committed, declared home for a recurring census (a qa-reports sidecar) is not built yet. Do not invent an undeclared directory for it. Name the gap instead.

292.title: What this skill does not do
292.content: . | Delete, prune or close anything. Not branches, not PRs, not work items. | Judge whether unique work is wanted. unlanded means “not on main”, not “should be on main”. That call belongs to the owner, through salvage review. | Replace branch-freshness (your own branch against main) or coordinate (live sibling PRs). This skill is the census of everything else. | .

294.title: Branch freshness — stay current with main
294.content: Skill branch-freshness: Read what changed on main often, and re-analyse the session workplan. Put main INTO the branch rarely: freely before a PR exists, and on a branch with a PR only when it conflicts, when the work needs something that just landed, or once just before it merges, because each such push re-runs the PR’s whole CI. Prevents stale assumptions, merge conflicts, and duplicated work without spending CI on churn. Named by: Hand back to the discussion, Drain the beans, A refused merge-train member, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route . A feature branch that drifts from main accumulates three kinds of debt: . | Merge conflict debt — the longer the branch lives, the harder to merge | Assumption debt — siblings may have renamed, moved, or restructured | Workplan debt — siblings may have completed overlapping work items | .

295.title: Reading main and merging main are two different things
295.content: Reading main (Steps 1, 2 and 4: fetch, look at what changed, re-check the work plan) costs nothing and catches assumption and workplan debt. Do it as often as the table below says. Putting main into the branch (Step 3: rebase or merge, then push) is different once the branch has a pull request. Every push to a PR re-runs its whole CI: the gates and the preview, about 30 runner-minutes or more. And it proves little, because a PR’s pull_request runs already test refs/pull/N/merge, the head merged with main as it was when the run started. While main moves every few minutes, a branch kept “current” this way restarts its CI over and over and queues every other PR behind it (owner ruling 2026-11-05, CI speed II, work item folio-assistant-6h4p). So, on a branch that has a PR, merge main only when: . | it conflicts with main. A conflicted PR has no merge ref and no CI run at all, so here a merge is work, not churn; | the work needs something that just landed on main, such as a fix your change builds on, or a gate that is red on your branch only because main’s fix is missing; | once, just before it merges, when the merge steward asks or the PR is at the front of the queue (merge-queue §”After submitting: do not spend CI you do not need yet”). | . Before a PR exists, rebase as often as you like: nothing re-runs. Rebase before you open the PR.

296.title: When to check
296.content: | Trigger | Read main (Steps 1, 2, 4) | Put main into the branch (Step 3) | . | Session start / resume | Always, before anything else. | No PR yet: yes. Has a PR: only on the three conditions above. | . | Long idle (> 30 min) | Before resuming work. | Same. | . | Before opening a PR | Yes. | Yes: rebase first. | . | After a sibling PR merges | If git fetch shows new commits on main. | No PR yet: if it touches your files. Has a PR: only on the three conditions above. | . | Periodically | Every ~10 commits or ~1 hour of active work. | Same as the row above. | . | Before posting a round summary | So the summary reflects current main. | No. | .

297.title: The freshness check
297.content: Step 1 — Fetch and measure drift . git fetch origin main git log --oneline HEAD..origin/main | head -20 . 0 new commits → skip to Step 4. Step 2 — Scan what changed . git diff --name-only HEAD...origin/main git log --oneline HEAD..origin/main . Look for: . | Files you are also editing → merge conflict risk | Schema changes (schemas/*.ts) → types may be stale | Pipeline changes (pipeline/*.ts) → behaviour may differ | Skill changes (cat-harness/skills/**) → guidance may be out of date | BPMN changes (cat-harness/processes/**/*.bpmn) → diagrams may conflict | Work item changes (beans/, on its state branch: bun run cat state:mount) → work items may have been created/resolved by sibling | AGENTS.md changes → rules may have changed | Directory restructuring → paths you’re writing to may have moved | . Step 3 — Rebase (or merge), only when the rule above says so . git rebase origin/main . If conflicts arise: . | Resolve one commit at a time | Check whether your change or upstream is correct — don’t blindly keep yours | Non-trivial conflicts → flag to the BA | . After successful rebase: . git push --force-with-lease . Step 4 — Re-analyse the workplan . beans list . Ask: . | Are any open work items redundant (sibling completed equivalent work)? | Did upstream introduce new defects or requirements? | Did a schema/pipeline change invalidate implementation assumptions? | Do I need to re-run tests? | . If yes: update work items, re-run tests, note in turn summary. Step 5 — Report . > **Rebased** on origin/main (12 new commits). Notable: schema type Foo > renamed to Bar (adjusted). Bean xyz1 resolved by sibling (removed from > workplan). Tests pass. Or: . > **Checked** origin/main — 0 new commits. Current.

298.title: Rules
298.content: . | A branch with a PR takes main only on the three conditions above — reading main stays free | Never rebase over review comments — merge instead (git merge origin/main) | Never rebase someone else’s branch | Re-run BPMN render after rebasing BPMN files | Re-check work items before creating — a rebase may pull in sibling work items | .

301.title: Cache-first CI — a step is a pure function of its inputs
301.content: Skill cache-first-ci: Every CI step is a pure function of its inputs: derive the inputs, hash them into a key, restore on a hit, run and save on a miss. Read before adding a cache to a workflow, before writing a cache key, before trusting a restored output or a skipped verdict, and before pushing a change that moves a cached step’s key. Covers the one primitive (cached-step + cache:key), the trust classes, what a committer publishes, the 10 GB budget, and the hit-rate report. Named by: The cache process: restore and save every cache a run can use, Incremental IG build . The principle. Derive a step’s inputs, hash them into a key. On a hit, restore the output (or the verdict) and skip the step. On a miss, run the step, then save. The full set still runs on main’s integration run, nightly and on every release candidate (release-gated CI, owner card Q-CIB-4 A, 2026-11-08), and that is what catches a key that missed an input.

302.title: One primitive, not one cache per author
302.content: A checkout’s CI has ONE cache primitive. In folio-assistant it is the composite action .github/actions/cached-step (its README is the operational detail). A new cache goes through it, and an old bespoke one is ported onto it by its owner. Then every cache has the same key shape (cs1-<step>-<key>), the same trust policy, the same hit | warm | miss — why line in the job summary, and a row in the daily hit-rate report. A cache that bypasses it is one nobody can audit.

303.title: The key is DERIVED, never hand-declared
303.content: Owner ruling, work item 4rbc: “derived is BEST”; “DERIVED = no drift, no extra data fields”. A key comes from one of these: . | bun run cat cache:key <script> (cat-harness-tools scripts/cache-key.ts). This is the f017 fingerprint of the script: its import closure, audited for every environment, network, clock and git read (input-sites.ts); the tool versions; bun.lock; and its task-io declaration, where {tracked} means the whole tree. | A lock’s digest, when the lock pins every input. index.lock.json pins every mounted tree. cache:key --hash-files prints what the runner’s hashFiles() prints. | A digest script that hashes the tree and the exact tool versions (bundle-cache.sh digest). | . Never narrow a key by hand to get more hits. A hand-picked list of input globs is a claim nothing checks. When the key does not hit often enough, the fix is to derive the inputs more finely (the cone, ci-cone.ts). Hand-listing is not the fix. Could-not-determine is never a hit. An undetermined key runs the step and saves nothing.

304.title: The trust classes (owner, 2026-11-05)
304.content: Committers, both people and agents, produce cache entries locally where CI can verify them cheaply, so CI only verifies. | class | what | who produces it | how CI accepts it | . | (a) exactly verifiable (trust: exact) | verify checks the output against a reference derived from THIS tree — the mounts and the layers ref against the lock’s digests — so a bad entry is only a miss | main, a PR into its own scope, or a committer with cache:publish (never consumed on main) | a hit only after verify passes; a prefix restore is a warm start, never a hit | . | (a′) verifiable with provenance (trust: exact + a source rule) | a bundle checked only against the manifest it carries, from a deterministic producer | main, or a run whose head is this head, a parent, or a commit with this tree | the manifest check AND the source rule; never from a committer | . | (b) verdicts (trust: verdict) | “this gate passed on these inputs” | CI (main, or a PR into its own scope); a committer’s local gate record goes through #2957/#2958 | exact key only; reported SKIPPED, not passed, naming the run that recorded it; committers’ records are re-verified deferred or sampled | . | (c) everything else (trust: main-only) | outputs neither checkable nor deterministic | main only | exact key only | . The Actions cache scopes an entry by ref. A PR’s save is readable only by that PR’s own runs, so a PR cannot poison what main or another PR reads. pull_request_target never saves. A manifest the entry carries proves it intact, not built from these inputs: a poisoner ships a matching manifest. That is why (a′) needs a source rule, and why only (a) is safe to take from anyone. A producer the determinism audit (determinism-audit.sh: build twice in one tree, diff the bytes) has not cleared cannot hit across commits at all. A private cache scheme is held. A pull request that adds a cache outside the primitive is held and returned to its author with a pointer here, the same rule the merge manager applies.

305.title: What a committer runs before pushing
305.content: For each class-(a) step that the change moves the key of, run: . bun run cat cache:publish <step> . This builds nothing. It publishes what you already built to refs/cache/cs1-<step>-<key>. The mounts have their own committer path, the layers ref (refs/cat/layers/<key>; bun run cat layers:publish, which mount:remote runs after it changes the lock). Its replayer verifies each layer against the lock and serves every layer that did not move, which is finer than a single all-or-nothing hit. So it is declared as a cache node and is not wrapped in cached-step. One committer path per cache.

306.title: The budget
306.content: GitHub keeps 10 GB of Actions cache per repository. It evicts the least-recently-used entries beyond that, and any entry left unread for 7 days. | Big bundles go to GHCR or to git refs, never to the Actions cache. The prepared image, the QA working copy and the publish-time pages are all big bundles, and any one of them can evict every small entry. | Small outputs and verdicts go to the Actions cache, namespaced by step. | Pruning deletes only what no run can read any more: entries scoped to a closed PR’s merge ref. | .

307.title: The hit-rate report
307.content: Every restore writes hit | warm | miss and why to the job summary. The daily report (folio-assistant cache-report.sh, run from sweeps.yml) gives the hit rate per step, the cache usage and the size of each namespace. When you claim a speed-up, report the hit rate and runner-minutes before and after, with run ids. A claim without run ids is a guess.

310.doc: The cache process: restore and save every cache a run can use
310.title: The cache process: restore and save every cache a run can use
310.content: Process_Cache · advisory · 9 step(s) . One optional process for every cache in the harness, used by render, CI, publish and every other consumer, whose components run in parallel where they are independent and in order where they are not. The rule every component follows is the skill cache-first-ci: a step is a pure function of its inputs; the key is DERIVED from them (cache:key, a lock digest, key.sh), never hand-listed; on a hit restore and skip, on a miss build and save; the full set still runs on main and nightly. OPTIONAL, AND SKIPPING IS ALWAYS CORRECT. Every consumer — the render pipeline, the code-quality gates, feature staging and the preview, publish, the docs-site publish, the merge train, and a committer’s local mount — may call it as a call activity, once with phase restore before its own work and once with phase save after that work came back green. A consumer that does not call it, or a run that cannot reach a store, simply builds: every component’s miss is the consumer doing its own work, so this process can cost a run time, never correctness. PARALLEL WHERE INDEPENDENT, IN ORDER WHERE NOT. The layers come first, because every other component reads mounted content. Then the prepared image and node_modules, the bun/pip downloads, the gate results and the generated sets restore side by side. Then the compiled Lean artefacts. Then the render seed (derive:publish’s writer records) and the FHIR IG ASTs side by side; the IG ASTs in their own lane, as the FHIR IG layer’s Process_IgAstCache, whose “valid for this commit?” is the component’s verify and whose AST refresh is its save. The Jekyll cache is last, because it caches the rendering of what the rest produce. ONLY WHAT THE TARGET NEEDS, ONLY WHAT IS STALE (owner, 2026-11-05: “not all rendering/CI/merge processes need all caches. be optimal in what needs caching” and “… be optimal in which caches need to be updated to perform a specific render”). A component runs only when the plan (cache:plan, the first gateway) marks it needed for this target; a component the target does not read is passed through untouched, neither restored nor refreshed. A needed component that is fresh is RESTORED, never rebuilt. A needed component that is stale, or whose staleness cannot be determined, is REFRESHED, incrementally where its node says so (the changed writers, the changed Lean modules over the restored .oleans, the IG AST delta, the moved layers), never wholesale when a delta is valid. A stale component no target here needs is left for the next target that needs it, or for main’s run. The plan and what actually happened are both reported (cached-step phase report), and the daily report flags a component restored and never read. EACH COMPONENT, BOTH PHASES. Restore: look up the derived key, verify the entry by its trust class — (a) against a reference derived from THIS tree, so a bad entry is only a miss; (a′) a bundle’s own manifest plus a source rule; (b) a committer’s verdict, honoured then re-verified off the critical path; (c) main-only entries, by exact key — and report hit, warm or miss with why. Save: only after the consumer’s work is green, only from main or into the run’s own ref scope, never from pull_request_target. Each component is a cache node in the knowledge graph (key recipe, derived inputs, producer, consumers, trust class, location, budget), and the cache viewer compares its current key with the key today’s pins imply, so staleness is computed, never claimed. i i i i i i i i i

313.doc: The cache process: restore and save every cache a run can use
313.title: Steps
313.content: Every one of the 9 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Layers ref: restore / saveTask_Layers | Build pipeline | cache-first-ci | Component 1, which everything else needs. RESTORE: mount-from-lock replays the lock from refs/cat/layers/<key> (key = sha256 of the lock’s layers), verifying every layer’s tree digest, declaration and asset sha256 against the committed lock — class (a), verified against THIS tree, so a bad entry is only a miss, and a stale refs/cat/layers/main still serves every layer that did not move. 316.doc: Is CI actually working on the default branch?
316.title: Is CI actually working on the default branch?
316.content: Process_CiHealth · strict · 2 step(s) . Is CI actually working on the default branch: record each workflow’s state on one tracking issue, and fail the job only when the state could not be determined. A WORKFLOW’S OUTCOME IS INVISIBLE FROM A CHECKOUT. Bean xom7: one workflow here fired on every push to main and FAILED ALL 30 TIMES OVER TWO MONTHS with nothing in the repository saying so. This is the backstop. WEEKLY, NOT DAILY, and the cadence is an argument rather than a default: the defect is “nobody noticed for two months”, not “nobody noticed for a day”, and the session-start sweep already covers every day somebody is working. A weekly run bounds the blind spot to seven days without turning the tracking issue into a feed. Could we tell? IS NOT SIMPLY THE EXIT CODE, and that is the subtlety worth drawing. bun exits 1 on an uncaught exception as well as on a live failure, so exit 1 alone does not separate “found something red” from “crashed”. The REPORT FILE separates them: --out writes it before any exit path, so a genuine red always has one and a crash before that point does not. Exit 1 with no report is reclassified as unknown. Without that, a crash would open a tracking issue quoting a stale file. THE THIRD STATE IS THE WHOLE POINT, AND IT IS THE ONLY ONE THAT FAILS THE JOB. Verified 2026-09-20 by reading the if: guards: unknown runs exit 1; a finding does NOT. A repository in trouble leaves this workflow GREEN and speaks through the tracking issue, while a sweep that could not look turns the job red. That inversion is deliberate and is invisible from the run list, which is the argument for drawing it. ONE TRACKING ISSUE, EDITED IN PLACE, never a comment and never a second issue — a feed nobody reads is the failure mode a watchdog invites. On unknown the issue is left UNTOUCHED: not closed, not opened, not edited. Closing it would assert the thing the sweep just failed to establish. Ensure the tracking label exists sits AFTER Could we tell? and before the split, because both issue paths need the label — the clean path filters on it too, and on a repository where nothing has ever gone wrong it would not otherwise exist. It is skipped on unknown, where neither path runs and a label hiccup must not be what fails the job. The verdict is reported through the shared tracked-watch process (Process_TrackedWatch), with the label ci-health. Its three ends say what happened: unknown (job red, issue untouched), clean (issue closed), or found (issue opened or edited, job green). i i

321.title: CI health — a red workflow looks exactly like a green one from in here
321.content: Skill ci-health: A red workflow looks exactly like a green one from inside a checkout. How to read a default-branch health report, the three verdicts that keep it honest, why a watchdog needs both a session-start print and an unattended run, and the separate external question the Pages deployments need.
