460.title: Two relations — read this first
460.content: A block participates in two different dependency relations, and this skill is about the first one: . | Relation | Source | Answers | Maintained by | . | editorial | uses[] | “what must a reader have read to follow this?” | agent / human — it is authored content | . | formal | the content type’s formal reference → its dependency graph | “what does this block’s formal layer actually invoke?” | machine-derived, never hand-written | . They diverge in both directions, legitimately: a formal layer invokes helpers nobody needs to read about; a claim is motivated by an example it never formally cites. Never populate uses[] from a formal graph — it destroys the editorial signal every heuristic below is computed from. The layer that ships a formal content type defines its formal dependency graph and links down to this skill. The reorganisation heuristics in this skill (forward references, coupling, section balance) are editorial-only by design: reading order is a question about readers, so mixing formal edges in would make the answers wrong, not richer. Impact questions (“what breaks if this changes?”) want the union of both. Build it with pipeline/content-graph.ts, whose accessors default to the union and take an optional EdgeKind filter: . bun run pipeline/content-graph.ts content/<paper> . Auditing whether uses[] is well used is a separate skill: uses-editorial-review (plus the mechanical uses QA axis).

461.title: Overview
461.content: This skill analyses the full content graph of the project at two levels: . | Block graph — Every content block is a node. Edges represent editorial relationships: uses[] (reader-prerequisite), interprets (remark → statement), proofs[] (proof → statement), examples[] (example → statement). The block graph captures the argument structure as presented to a reader. | Chapter/section graph — Chapters and sections are nodes. A directed edge from section S₁ to section S₂ exists whenever a block in S₁ uses a block in S₂. The section graph captures the pedagogical reading order. | . These two graphs are used together to apply heuristics and generate ranked reorganisation suggestions.

462.title: When to Use This Skill
462.content: . | “content graph” / “content organisation” | “cross-chapter arrows” / “cross-section dependencies” | “forward references” / “minimise forward refs” | “sections too small” / “sections too large” / “section balance” | “disentangle content” / “reorganise chapters” | “analyse content connections” | “show me the block graph” / “show me the chapter graph” | “what blocks should move?” / “suggest reorganisation” | .

463.title: Prerequisites
463.content: . | Python 3 and graphviz (installed automatically if missing) | Content block .ts files in content/<paper>/ | Chapter manifests with sections → blocks structure | .

464.title: Heuristics
464.content: The skill applies the following heuristics, each producing a severity- ranked finding: . H1 — Forward references (severity: HIGH) . A forward reference occurs when block A uses block B, but B appears later in the document than A. These cause readers to encounter concepts before they are defined. A block’s position is its (chapter_number, section_index, block_index) tuple in document order. forward_ref: A (pos P_A) uses B (pos P_B) where P_B > P_A . Ideal: 0 forward references. Acceptable: ≤ 5 (genuine architectural cycles). Flag for action: > 5. H2 — Cross-chapter coupling (severity: MEDIUM) . A cross-chapter edge occurs when block A in chapter C₁ uses block B in chapter C₂ (C₁ ≠ C₂). Count cross-chapter edges per chapter pair (C₁ → C₂): . | Edges going forward (C₁.number < C₂.number): blocks in early chapters depend on later chapters’ content → may be a problem (forward reference by chapter). | Edges going backward (C₁.number > C₂.number): normal; later chapters build on earlier ones → fine. | . Flag: chapters with more than 10 cross-chapter forward edges. H3 — Cross-section coupling (severity: MEDIUM) . Same as H2 but at section granularity within a single chapter. Report any section pair where ≥ 3 blocks reference each other across section boundaries. Ratio metric: cross_section_edges / total_edges_in_chapter. | Ratio < 0.20: well-structured | 0.20–0.40: moderate coupling | 0.40: high coupling — restructuring likely needed . | . H4 — Section too sparse (severity: LOW) . Sections with fewer than 3 content blocks (excluding intro prose) risk fragmenting the narrative. They are candidates for merging with an adjacent section. Threshold: < 3 non-prose blocks. Exception: Intro/overview sections (first block is prose). H5 — Section too dense (severity: LOW) . Sections with more than 18 content blocks are hard to navigate. Threshold: > 18 blocks. Suggestion: Split along natural dependency boundaries within the section. H6 — Isolated blocks (severity: LOW) . A block with no uses[] edges (other than prose/intro) and no block in uses[] of other blocks is isolated. It may belong to a different section or chapter, or may be dead content. H7 — Remark / example ratio (severity: INFO) . Sections where remark + example blocks outnumber the content type’s claim-bearing blocks (for a paper folio, definition + theorem + lemma + proposition + corollary + conjecture) by more than 2:1 may have too much interpretation and too little substance — or vice versa.

465.title: Placement Principles for New/Changed Content
465.content: The heuristics above detect problems post-hoc. The placement principles below are proactive: agents must follow them when creating new blocks or significantly changing existing ones. PR1 — Topical home chapter . Every block belongs in the chapter whose topic it primarily addresses. Build a topic map for the project (chapter directory → primary topic scope) and use it to decide. If a block spans two chapters’ topics, split it (see PR5). PR2 — Forward-reference avoidance . A new block should appear after all blocks it uses[]. Run content-graph-analysis.py after placement and verify zero new forward references. PR3 — Section density bounds . When adding blocks to a section, check the count stays within 3–18 blocks. If adding would exceed 18, split the section first (H5). If a removal would drop a section below 3, consider merging (H4). PR4 — Cross-chapter dependency direction . New blocks should depend backward (on earlier chapters), not forward. If a new block in Ch 3 needs to use something from Ch 7, either: . | Move the dependency to Ch 3 first, or | Place the new block in Ch 7 instead. | . PR5 — Topic-coherent blocks . Before accepting a new block, verify it addresses a single topic. If the .md content contains material belonging to multiple chapters, split it into separate blocks placed in their respective chapters. Defer to block-density R1 for the full audit. PR6 — Table extraction on creation . If a new block’s .md contains a table with > 5 data rows, extract it immediately to a table block (kind: "table", label: tbl:<name>-data). Reference it from the parent block via uses[]. Do not wait for a later audit. See block-density R3 for details. PR7 — Reorganisation map update . After any block move, section split/merge, or directory rename, update docs/reorganization-map.md with the change. This is mandatory — it is the downstream debugging reference for tracing broken labels and imports.

466.title: Placement Checklist (for agents)
466.content: When adding a new block or significantly changing an existing block: . | □ Identify the primary topic → select home chapter (PR1) | □ Check uses[] deps appear earlier in document order (PR2) | □ Check target section has 3–18 blocks after insertion (PR3) | □ Verify no new forward cross-chapter edges (PR4) | □ Verify block is single-topic; split if not (PR5) | □ Extract tables > 5 rows to table blocks (PR6) | □ Update docs/reorganization-map.md if anything moved (PR7) | □ Run python3 pipeline/content-graph-analysis.py to confirm | .

467.title: Workflow
467.content: Step 1 — Parse the content tree . Read the paper manifest to enumerate chapters. For each chapter, read its manifest to enumerate sections and their block lists. Assign each block a document position (chapter_number, section_index, block_index). For each block .ts file, extract: . | label, kind, uses[], interprets, proofs[], examples[] | . Step 2 — Build the block graph . Build an adjacency map: . edges[(from_label, to_label)] = edge_type # "uses"|"interprets"|"proof"|"example" . Index every block’s document position: . position[label] = (chapter_no, section_idx, block_idx) . Step 3 — Build the chapter/section graph . For each chapter pair (C₁, C₂) count directed edges from blocks in C₁ to blocks in C₂: . chapter_edges[(c1_num, c2_num)] += 1 . For each section pair within the same chapter, count cross-section edges: . section_edges[(s1_label, s2_label)] += 1 . Step 4 — Apply heuristics . Run each heuristic (H1–H7) and collect findings. Each finding has: . | severity: HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW / INFO | heuristic: H1–H7 | description: human-readable explanation | blocks: list of involved block labels | suggestion: proposed action | . Step 5 — Generate visualisations . Two DOT/SVG outputs (via Graphviz): . 5a. Chapter/section graph (/tmp/content_chapter_graph.svg) . | Nodes: chapters (large boxes) containing sections (small boxes) | Edges: weighted directed arrows between sections | Color: red = forward cross-chapter edges, orange = high cross-section coupling, gray = normal backward dependencies | . 5b. Block graph heat-map (/tmp/content_block_heatmap.svg) . This is the DEPENDENCY heat map, for a paper’s structure. For “where should a reviewer of this edit look first”, the heat map is the review page’s section-by-metric table, and the review-heatmap skill says what each of its columns means. | Nodes: blocks (grouped by chapter/section in clusters) | Edges: forward references only (red), cross-chapter edges (orange) | Isolated blocks highlighted in yellow | . Step 6 — Report findings . Print a ranked report (HIGH → LOW → INFO): . ## Content Graph Analysis: <paper> ### Summary - Total blocks: N | Chapters: N | Sections: N - Total block edges: N (uses/interprets/proof/example) - Cross-chapter edges: N | Cross-section edges: N - Forward references: N ### HIGH — Forward References (H1) - block A (ch1/sec2) uses block B (ch3/sec5) ← B defined later Suggestion: move B earlier, or add stub to ch1 ### MEDIUM — Cross-Chapter Coupling (H2) - Ch4 → Ch1: 14 forward edges ← Ch4 blocks depend on Ch1 Top offending blocks: ... ### LOW — Sparse Sections (H4) - sec:my-section (Ch3): 2 non-prose blocks Suggestion: merge with adjacent sec:other-section ### LOW — Dense Sections (H5) - sec:my-dense-section (Ch4): 20 blocks Suggestion: split into two sections along a dependency boundary . Step 7 — Interactive suggestions . After the report, offer the user a numbered menu of actions they can approve: . What would you like to do? [1] Move block X from sec:A to sec:B [2] Split sec:large-section into two sections [3] Add a new section "Preliminaries" in Ch3 to absorb forward refs [4] Merge sec:sparse-1 and sec:sparse-2 [5] Show detailed block graph for chapter N [6] Re-run analysis after changes [0] Done . For each approved action, make the minimal changes to the .ts manifest files. Step 8 — Implement approved moves . For a block move (action [1]): . | Remove the block name from blocks[] in its current section. | Add the block name to blocks[] in the target section at the correct position (after its uses[] dependencies). | Re-run the analysis to confirm improvement. | . For a section split (action [2]): . | Ask the user to name the two new sections and choose a split point. | Rewrite the chapter manifest with two section({...}) entries. | Move blocks to the correct new section. | . For a section merge (action [4]): . | Combine the two blocks[] arrays in document order. | Remove the merged-away section from the chapter manifest. | . Always show a before/after energy comparison: . Before: energy=142, backward_edges=12, sparse_sections=3 After: energy=87, backward_edges=4, sparse_sections=1 .

468.title: Python implementation
468.content: The core algorithm is a standalone Python script: . pipeline/content-graph-analysis.py . Usage: . # Full heuristic report cd content && python3 pipeline/content-graph-analysis.py # Write report to /tmp/content-graph-report.md cd content && python3 pipeline/content-graph-analysis.py --md # Generate concrete, implementable reorganisation proposals cd content && python3 pipeline/content-graph-analysis.py --proposals # → output also written to /tmp/content-graph-proposals.md # Specific chapter only cd content && python3 pipeline/content-graph-analysis.py --chapter <chapter-dir> # Generate visualisations cd content && python3 pipeline/content-graph-analysis.py --visualise # Export graph as JSON (for MCP consumption) cd content && python3 pipeline/content-graph-analysis.py --json > /tmp/content-graph.json . Proposal kinds (–proposals output) . | Kind | Description | Trigger | . | split | Split a dense section (> 18 blocks) along natural comment boundaries | H5 | . | merge | Merge two adjacent sparse sections (< 3 non-prose blocks each) | H4 | . | move | Move a block that is forward-referenced by ≥ 3 earlier blocks | H1 | . | reverse | Fix an interprets/example block that appears before its target | H1 | . Each proposal includes: . | A unique ID (P1, P2, …) for stable reference | Exact chapter manifest path and section labels to edit | Concrete blocks[] array changes to make | Expected forward-reference reduction | . Chapter naming convention . Directory names are descriptive slugs with NO chapter numbers: . | introduction/, <topic-a>/, <topic-b>/, etc. | The paper manifest chapters[] array defines the chapter order | Chapter numbers are auto-derived: numbered chapters get sequential 1, 2, 3… | Chapters with tabLabel set (e.g. "I", "G") are unnumbered (\chapter*{}) | To reorder chapters: just reorder lines in the paper manifest — no renames needed | . Key functions: . | parse_paper(root) → {chapters, sections, blocks, positions} | build_block_graph(blocks) → {nodes, edges} | build_section_graph(blocks, positions) → {chapter_edges, section_edges} | apply_heuristics(graph, positions) → [Finding] | generate_proposals(...) → [Proposal] (split/merge/move/reverse) | generate_dot_chapter(graph) → SVG path | generate_dot_blocks(graph) → SVG path | report(findings) → formatted text | .

471.title: Drawing it
471.content: bun run cat content:graph:uml --root <content dir> --out <dir> [--status <status file>] (Tool content-graph-uml) draws this graph under the graph-rendering rules: . | chapters as packages; | uses[] and interprets solid, the content type’s formal edges dashed purple (supplied by the content type’s formal-graph builder); | status fills from the content type’s status file; | one diagram per chapter, with blocks in other chapters as dashed stubs; | portrait and landscape views, and a --check that needs no Java. | . 475.title: Lanes — who acts
475.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | Programme manager | programme-manager | Opens and closes the cycle rather than running any of it: Task_Plan commits scope, team and artefacts before Lane_WorkPlan turns them into beans, and Task_Retire is reached only when Gateway_NextCycle finds nothing left to do. | . | Editors + authoring agents | editor | The re-entry point for every round of the cycle: Gateway_NextCycle’s ‘yes’ branch loops back here, not to Task_Plan. Runs once per proposed change, and makes the accept decision on each before the corpus-wide Task_Test. | . | Validation and QA (mechanical + agents) | validation-pipeline | The corpus-wide check no single block’s HCI validation gate can perform — cross-references, whole-folio build status, proof status and QA axes — between the editor’s accept and the publication manager’s release: a change that passed block-level review still has to clear folio-level checks before CallActivity_Publication runs. | . | Review team and SMEs | reviewer | The only reviewing this lane does happens AFTER publication, not before it: Task_Feedback triages what implementers and readers report on the LIVE folio, by severity and scope, and Task_FeedbackBeans turns that triage into the next cycle’s work. | . | Publication manager | publication-manager | The single point in the cycle where the corpus becomes public, reached only after Task_Test has cleared the whole folio; draft-to-publication.bpmn is the last gate before readers see anything. | .

476.title: Steps
476.content: Every one of the 10 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Plan scope, team, artifactsTask_Plan | Programme manager | content-plan | Scope the work, identify artifacts and actors, form the team, set the timeline. | . | Seed the work planTask_SeedBeans | Editors + authoring agents | shared step GT_SeedWorkPlantodo-manager | The plan becomes beans, so a resumed session or a sibling agent can pick it up. The run’s own bean was claimed by the Process_BeanOpen call before this step, so this step only notes the seeded plan on it; the beans themselves are written with the agent’s own beans create, which no engine op performs. From here on, beans/ is the shared answer to ‘what is done, what is next’ — for humans and agents alike. | . | Editing and HCI validationCallActivity_Editing | Editors + authoring agents | calls Editing and HCI validationcontent-authorcontent-validatecontent-review | See editing-hci-validation.bpmn. Runs once per proposed change, not once per cycle. | . | Integration test and QA sweepTask_Test | Validation and QA (mechanical + agents) | content-test | Corpus-wide checks that a single-block gate cannot make: cross-references, build green, proof status, QA axes across the whole folio. | . | Draft, review and publishCallActivity_Publication | Publication manager | calls Draft, review and publishcontent-reviewcontent-publish | See draft-to-publication.bpmn. | . | Triage published feedbackTask_Feedback | Review team and SMEs | content-feedback | Implementer and reader feedback on the published folio, triaged by severity and scope. | . | File feedback as beansTask_FeedbackBeans | Editors + authoring agents | todo-managercontent-feedback | Triaged feedback re-enters the work plan as beans, which is how the next cycle knows what it is for. | . | Retire or archiveTask_Retire | Programme manager | content-retire | No more content is planned: deprecate the folio. Post a deprecation notice and timeline, update its status metadata, archive it, point references at any successor, and remove it from active publication. The programme manager decides; retirement archives rather than deletes. | . | Open the beanCall_BeanOpen | Editors + authoring agents | calls Open the beanbean-coordination | Process_BeanOpen: check before you create, find out whose the bean is, and claim it — or leave it alone when it is someone else’s. The one place a claim is drawn; the gateway after this reads which end it reached. | . | Close the beanCall_BeanClose | Programme manager | calls Close the beantodo-manager | Process_BeanClose: end the bean in a state that says why — complete and archive it, scrap it with its reasons and archive it, or record the blocker and hand it back. The one place resolve and archive are drawn; placed straight before the end so the engine’s resolve sees nothing left but the archive step. | .

508.content: . | Execute test plans and test scripts | Run the content type’s own build, extraction, and verification checks (as specified by the layer that ships the content type) | Dispatch the repo’s CI workflow on your branch and fold the result into the PR — see below; a local build is not CI green | Test cross-component integration | Run regression tests against previous versions | Document test results | .

509.title: Running CI, not just assuming it
509.content: A local build runs on a warm cache, your toolchain and your flags; CI runs cold on its own. A local green is evidence about your machine, not about the branch. Push, then dispatch the workflow against your branch (gh workflow run <workflow>.yml --ref <branch>, or the actions_run_trigger MCP tool), wait for it, and record run URL + conclusion in the PR body. Red → fix and re-dispatch. If dispatch is refused for lack of actions: write, say so in the PR and give the command a maintainer should run. Also check when CI last ran (actions_list → list_workflow_runs): a workflow nothing dispatches can sit red on main while the content it checks stops building.

510.title: A green build only covers what the target reaches
510.content: Before reading “build green” as a claim about the corpus, check what the build target actually compiles. Build systems often default to narrow roots: the target compiles its root plus whatever that root imports, not every source in the directory. Where sources are found and what is built are separate settings. The check is cheap in any build system — count build artifacts against sources. A ratio far from 1 means the green is scoped, and any corpus-wide number read off that build — open-obligation counts, coverage, warning totals — is an undercount by construction. Say what the build covered, not just that it passed.

514.title: Where the results go — not into a commit
514.content: A test run’s results are derived: re-running the plan over the same tree and data reproduces them. They are kept where every derived QA result is kept — the orphan qa-reports branch, keyed by the commit they were computed on (main/<sha>/, pr/<n>/<sha>/), written by bun run cat qa:publish (the CI job qa-publish) and read back with bun run qa:fetch. Do not regenerate a results file in order to commit it. Two things a test run produces are not derived, and they stay on main: . | A reviewer’s judgement of a case — an SME or QC reviewer’s verdict, an agent’s adjudication — goes to test/attestations/ (qa-attestations/v1), because no re-run can reproduce it. | A certification — an accountable decision taken on a plan’s rollup — also stays on main, beside the attestations, and is then signed through qa-report-signing (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc). | . “Regression comparison” against a previous version is a comparison against its stored results: --against <ref> on a gate, or qa:fetch --ref for a report. A previous version with no stored entry is UNKNOWN — say so; never read it as “no regressions”.

524.title: /continual-progress — trackable, always-PR’d, continually-committed work
524.content: Skill continual-progress: Make in-flight work trackable by others in real time — open a PR from the first commit, push small coherent increments continuously (never hoard uncommitted work), keep a live status checklist in the PR body, and post brief intent on the PR + any overlapping sibling PRs. Use on any multi-step or long-running task, especially when siblings/agents or the author may need to follow, cherry-pick, or take over mid-flight. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, KG to public portal, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Actor and role administration, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Agent activity log, Close the bean, Drain the beans, Agent bean lifecycle, Open the bean, Code change and review, Merge the base branch in, A refused merge-train member, Merge request: find or elect the merge manager, Requirements filing: promote, organise, trace, supersede, or retire, SME Review of Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route, Test Data Curation — Fixed Sets and Generated Recipes, Watching a pinned upstream dependency, Adopting an upstream version bump, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Editing and HCI validation, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . Sibling agents and the author can only coordinate with work they can see. This skill makes every in-flight task trackable in real time: the PR is open from the first commit, progress lands as a stream of small pushed commits, and the PR body carries a live status checklist. It is the visibility complement to /coordinate (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) (which triages across PRs); this one governs how your own PR stays legible while you work.

525.title: The four invariants
525.content: . | Always have an open PR (from commit #1). Branch, make the first (even stub) commit, push, open the PR — before further work. The PR is the durable, visible artifact; the chat session is ephemeral. Never accumulate work on a local branch with no PR. Never ask permission to open one — branch, commit, push and PR are all pre-authorised. | Commit + push small, coherent increments — continuously. Each logically distinct change is its own commit (a single fix, a single module, a single unit of work). Push after each commit (or every 2–3 if moving fast). A watcher should be able to git log your branch and see a legible, bisectable trail — not one giant drop. Target: no more than ~20–30 min of work between pushes on a long task. | Keep a live status checklist in the PR body. Maintain a - [ ] / - [x] checklist of the task’s sub-parts in the PR description (or a pinned top comment), updated as each increment lands. A sibling or the author should be able to read the PR body and know exactly what is done / in-flight / remaining — without reading the diff or asking in chat. | Post brief intent — on your PR and overlapping siblings. One short intent line on PR-open (“doing X on <files>; will touch <scope>”); a one-line comment on any sibling whose scope overlaps (“starting <theme> on <files>; flag conflicts”). Don’t stream comments — update the checklist (invariant 3) for routine progress; comment only for genuine coordination (overlap, a blocker, a handoff-relevant finding). Defer to /coordinate (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) for the full cross-PR triage protocol. New work posts its intent only after the collision review in coordinate §”Starting new work” has been run and recorded in the workplan work item. | . Bean edits are pushed to the state branch, not the PR . Work item and workflow-instance edits (beans/defs/*.md, beans/workflows/*.json) do not belong in the PR’s commit set. The code PR contains code, test, and documentation changes destined for main. Work-plan progress, work item claims, status updates, and notes are written directly to the work-plan store through its configured Tool (work-plan-store (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan); on a git state branch, bun run cat state:push per work-plan-store-git-branch). The PR description references the work item via Closes-bean: <id> (or in the status checklist), but commits on the PR branch must not bundle work item file edits. This avoids merge conflicts on work item files and prevents work-plan edits from triggering code CI workflows.

526.title: The fifth invariant, and the one agents get wrong
526.content: . | Do not hold a green change proposal back waiting for someone to look at it. This is the rule that gets inverted in the name of care, and inverting it is not caution — it is a blocked reviewer. | . An agent that has built something it cannot fully verify — a rendered page, a diagram, a UI — must not leave it open and ask the human to confirm from a preview first: . A human cannot assess a rendered artefact from a description of it, and a preview pasted into chat is a strictly worse proxy than the deployed thing. Holding the merge does not transfer the verification to them — it withholds the only form in which they could do it, and asks them to adjudicate from a screenshot. Link the PAGE, never the site root . When you ask somebody to look at a rendered artefact, link the artefact. Not the site it is on, not the preview’s front door — the exact URL of the thing you changed. Linking the root makes the reader reconstruct a route the agent already knew, and every extra click is a cost passed to a reader who may type with difficulty. It also hides a real failure: an agent that links the root has not checked that its page is reachable at all. So: . | One link per thing to look at. Two changed pages is two links, each labelled with what to look for on it — not one root and a sentence of navigation. | Deep-link past the index. If the change is on /docs/<iris-replica>/kg-to-portal.html, that is the URL, not /docs/<iris-replica>/. | Take it from the preview’s page list, never from memory or a source path: a branch slug is exactly the kind of string that is almost right. The rule, and where the list comes from, is feedback-deep-links. | The root is the right link for precisely one thing — a change to the landing page itself. | . This is the same rule as the invariant above, one step further on. A human cannot assess a rendered artefact from a description of it; they also cannot assess it from a link to somewhere near it. What to do with the thing you could not verify . Say it in the body, and merge anyway. ## Not verified is a real section and an honest one; an unmerged proposal is not a substitute for it. Reversibility is what makes this safe — a docs or content change is one revert away, and the cost of reverting is far below the cost of a human blocked on a decision they have no artefact for. A pipe discards the exit code — so a piped run cannot verify anything . cmd | tail makes $? the status of tail. Every claim that a command PASSED must come from a run without a pipe, or from ${PIPESTATUS[0]}. This is mechanical rather than a matter of care, because care does not prevent it. A command whose output sounds like a failure, run through a pipe, reads as a silent pass, and one whose output sounds like a pass hides a failure; a silent pass is what this repository treats as worse than a loud failure. So: when the question is “did this pass”, run it bare. When you want both the output and the verdict, run it twice or capture the status first. Reading a verdict off prose you piped is the same error as quoting a count from prose. A template is not a page — verify the BUILD, not the source of it . The invariant above says a human cannot assess a rendered artefact from a description of it. This is its twin, and it is the one an agent breaks: . An agent cannot assess a rendered artefact from the template that generates it. A correct template and a correct page are different claims, and only the second is what a reader loads. Every source gate can pass over a defect that exists only in the build’s output. For example, a Liquid -%} that strips the space between two attributes makes Kramdown stop treating a block as HTML and escape it into visible text, while unit tests, lint, type checks, gates, e2e and accessibility suites all read valid sources and pass. So the rule is mechanical, not a matter of diligence: . | When the artefact is a built page, the evidence is the built page. Build the site and read the output. Reading the template proves the template. | A screenshot of a scratch render is not a screenshot of the build. If the real build cannot run locally (here the just-the-docs remote theme 403s through the agent proxy), stub the theme and build anyway — a pass-through _layouts/default.html is enough to see what Kramdown did. Stub the part that cannot run; never substitute the part under test. | State which one you looked at. “Rendered and checked” is ambiguous between the two, and the ambiguity is where this hid. | . check:escaped-markup, run in docs-site.yml against the assembled _site/, covers the escaped-markup case, because the assembled site is the only place the answer exists. It does not retire the rule: the next defect of this shape will be in whatever the build does that no source gate can see. The exceptions, and none of them is “I am unsure” . | Never merge red. A failing or unrun required check is a real blocker. | Never merge over an unresolved review thread you have not answered. | Where the repository requires explicit merge permission, that wins, and nothing here relaxes it by a word. Some folios require an explicit “merge it” from the author for every merge to the default branch. There the rule reads: get it green, get it mergeable, say once that it is ready, then stop — do not re-ask on a timer, and do not let “not merged yet” become a reason to stop pushing. | . Green means handed to the Merge Steward — an agent never merges to main here . The merge policy for folio-assistant. It is the “explicit merge permission” case above, made into a hand-off rather than a question: . | Never merge to main yourself — not with gh pr merge, not with the MCP merge tool, not after a green run, not under a standing “merge it” from earlier in the session. | When CI is green on EVERY job (the run list, not the PR page — see prepare-merge §”NO CHECKS IS NOT GREEN”; on a draft, the fast tier), and when the queue allows (§”Pace the ready marking” below): mark the PR Ready for review, add the label ready-to-merge, and comment ready: <head sha> — the full sha of the head that went green, so a push after it is visibly not what was declared ready. | Ask the merge manager to merge, in six lines (owner ruling, 2026-11-07). First check that a merge manager is active and live: the latest merge manager: <session id> announcement, and that session answered within the stall window. Send it the PR URL and full head SHA, your session URL, 1-3 sentences on what changed, the rendered preview URL for that head (or no preview: <reason>), what to look for in the preview, and the CI verdict on that head. A PR green except for a re-pin is sent as repin+merge:: do not re-pin it yourself (owner ruling, 2026-11-13). It posts them in its chat and asks the owner by card. An approval the owner gives in your own session does not authorise a merge. With no live merge manager, follow merge-manager-watcher (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) §”The sibling’s side: find the merge manager first”: elect one with your siblings, and never merge yourself unless you are the one elected. If your request is not acknowledged within the stall window, the merge manager has stalled: re-elect without it. The format is in §”The merge request: six lines” there. | The Merge Steward session (“Separation”) merges. It brings main in, runs regen, re-checks and merges. That is its lane, not yours. | If it reports red, it is yours again: fix, push, wait for green on every job, then re-label and comment ready: <new head sha>. | . Wherever a merge does happen, it is the merge-to-main (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) sub-process: evidence on the head, the owner’s authorisation for that merge, recorded, then the merge. So “merge anyway” in §”What to do with the thing you could not verify” reads here as mark it ready anyway, and “merge it as soon as it is green” in the fix-forward section below reads as hand it over as soon as it is green. The point of both is unchanged: a green PR is not held back. Pace the ready marking — the runner pool is shared . The Actions runner pool is shared across the owner’s repositories. A draft PR runs only the fast tier, and marking it ready starts the full tier, about 10 jobs. So the number of PRs marked ready at once is what fills the queue: . | Open every PR as a draft. | Mark it ready only when its own change is done and its fast checks pass. | Check the queue first: gh api "repos/<owner>/<repo>/actions/runs?status=queued" --jq .total_count. If it is more than about 2 queued runs per runner (5 runners on 2026-10-24, so more than about 10), hold the marking and check again later. | At most 3 ready, CI-pending PRs per agent per repository. Hand one over or let it finish before you mark another. | A fix that unblocks other work may jump the line: a link in the repin chain, or a fix for a red main. | . Holding a PR as a draft for pacing is not holding back a green PR: the fast tier is green, and the hand-off above waits for the full tier. The merge manager enforces this rule (owner ruling, 2026-11-07, card “Cancel CI”). When the runners are saturated, it closes superseded PRs, cancels stale queued runs that never started, and asks the owners of the lowest-priority PRs to return them to draft: merge-manager-watcher (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) §”Runner relief”. A new gate is proven downstream before it lands . A PR that adds a gate or check:* script to a lower layer passes on its own main, says how downstream layers run it, and shows a dry run over a fresh folio-assistant mount. Otherwise the next re-pin inherits the breakage (prepare-merge (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) §”A new gate in a lower layer must pass downstream”). One pusher per PR branch . Only the session that owns a PR pushes to its branch (owner ruling, 2026-11-07). Anyone else sends the owner the change, on the PR’s thread or by message. Every push restarts the full CI run: on 2026-11-07, three sessions pushed to folio-assistant#2985 within 10 minutes, and each push restarted it. Stack instead of waiting . Do not wait for a dependency to merge before starting work that needs it (owner ruling, 2026-11-07: “they dont need to wait for a merge to start working on a feature branch needing a dependent feature branch. They can stack”). The process is the first row of merge-request.bpmn (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc). | In the same repository: branch from the dependency PR’s branch, and open a draft PR whose base is that branch. Pull later changes of the dependency in with merge commits. Never rebase or force-push another session’s branch. | Across layers: develop against the dependency’s branch laid over a fresh mount. A draft may pin the dependency PR’s full head SHA (never a branch) so that CI sees it (remote-mount §”Stacking across layers”). | A re-pin is its own PR. Put the pins, and nothing else, in one PR, and stack the work that needs them on it. A fix the re-pin needs lands in its owning layer first (owner ruling, 2026-11-07; remote-mount §”Re-pinning”). | Say so: write stacked on <repo>#<n> in the PR body, and list the order in the merge request. | When the base lands: retarget the PR onto main and merge main in, then mark it ready by the queue rule. Across layers, send repin+merge:: the merge manager re-pins to the dependency’s merge commit on main. Never merge the stacked PR into its base branch, and never mark it ready while it pins an unmerged commit. | . Two green PRs can merge into a red main, and the answer is to fix forward . A PR is tested against the main it last merged, not the main it lands on. Two PRs that are each green can still combine into a failure that neither branch contained, and no regen on either branch can see it. The policy is to fix forward, not to add a merge queue or an “up to date” requirement. So: . | Watch main’s CI after every merge of yours, not only your PR’s — whoever pressed the button. “My PR was green” does not mean main is green. | A red main whose failure your diff did not cause is still yours to fix when you find it. Establish the cause from the failing run and each parent’s history first, then regenerate or repair in a small PR of its own, and merge it as soon as it is green. | Do not blame the last merge because it is the last merge. Check whether the parent was already red. | .

527.title: Why — the failure modes this prevents
527.content: . | Stepped-on work. A branch that hoards uncommitted work collides with siblings the moment it lands. Continual push surfaces intent from minute 1 so siblings triage around it. | Lost work on session reclaim. Cloud sessions are ephemeral; an uncommitted change vanishes when the container is reclaimed. Push it. | Opaque progress. “What’s the status?” should be answerable from the PR body, not a chat scrollback. The checklist is the source of truth. | Un-takeoverable tasks. If you go idle/blocked, a sibling can pick up a continually-committed, checklist-annotated PR; they cannot pick up an opaque local branch. | .

528.title: Checklist (run this as you work)
528.content: . | PR open? If not: branch → stub commit → push → open it now. | Anything uncommitted older than ~20–30 min? Commit + push it. | Does the PR-body status checklist reflect the current state? | Any sibling whose files I just started touching un-notified? One intent line (not a stream). | Blocked or going idle? Update the checklist + a one-line “blocked on X / handoff-ready” note so a sibling can continue. | .

529.title: Relationship to other skills
529.content: . | pr-description (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc): what the PR body says ABOVE the status checklist (the problem, why, approach, constraints, solution, usage, what is not done), for a reader who was not here. | /coordinate (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) — cross-PR triage (scope map, sibling intent, cherry-picks, ledger). continual-progress keeps your PR legible so /coordinate (yours or a sibling’s) has something to triage. | A folio’s own AGENTS.md may carry these rules for that repository, and a stricter merge gate — litlfred/qou §”Branch + PR workflow” is the worked case. This skill is the platform-side statement; where a folio is stricter, the folio wins. | /todo-manager — the session work-plan; the PR-body status checklist (invariant 3) is its externally-visible projection, so a watcher needs no access to the session’s work item queue. | .

531.doc: Contributor feedback on a working draft
531.title: Contributor feedback on a working draft
531.content: Process_ContributorFeedback · strict (defaulted) · 9 step(s) . A document is still being written, and the Authoring Committee gives feedback on it in a shared Contributor Feedback sheet. This is what happens to ONE change set, one row of that sheet: a member starts it with a title, the sections it is about and their feedback; the agent proposes a direction; an Editor lets the agent edit; the agent makes the edit in the row’s one pull request, whose staging preview shows what changed; the committee answers on the row; and an Editor lets the agent merge. If the row’s feedback changes after the agent wrote its proposal, the proposal is marked stale and the row’s Ready for agent goes back to No, so the agent proposes again and an Editor decides again. The sheet’s colours follow the lanes: Blue for the committee, Green for the agent, Orange for the Editor. Skill: review-sheet-script. i i i i i i i i i

533.doc: Contributor feedback on a working draft
533.title: Lanes — who acts
533.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | Authoring Committee | authoring-committee | The people writing the document with the editor: contributors, each with their own Contributor Feedback column (Blue). They start rows, give feedback and answer the preview. They recommend; they do not set the Ready columns. | . | Authoring agent | authoring-agent | Writes only Green cells and the Agent tab. Proposes a direction for each row, edits the document in the row’s one pull request once an Editor says so, and merges it once an Editor says so. | . | Editor | editor | The one lane that decides, through the Orange Ready columns, which only the people in the sheet’s EDITORS list may set. Ready for agent lets the agent edit; Ready for merge lets it merge. | . | QA reviewer (independent) | qc-reviewer | Whoever runs the QA gate: an agent session that did not write the row’s pull request, or a person. 534.doc: Contributor feedback on a working draft
534.title: Steps
534.content: Every one of the 9 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Start a change-set rowTask_StartRow | Authoring Committee | review-sheet-script | A member adds a row on the Contributor Feedback tab: a title, the Selected Sections it is about (a dropdown from the document’s table of contents) and their feedback in their own Blue column. The script gives the row its Change-set id and links each section. | . | Propose a directionTask_Propose | Authoring agent | review-sheet-script | Reads: the row (Title, Selected Sections, the Contributor Feedback columns, Disposition) and the sections it names. Writes: a proposed direction in Feedback (agent) (Green), and the row’s feedback basis on the Agent tab, so the script can tell when the feedback has moved on. A question for people goes in Feedback (agent) as a Decision needed block with options and a recommendation, and the row’s Agentic status becomes Needs human; a chat card may repeat it, but the sheet is the record. An answered question leaves the feedback: its decision is added to the change set’s Disposition (change set) on the Agent tab, shown in Disposition (agent), whose decision history is appended to and never removed. It ends with Record agent step (record-agent-step.bpmn): the Agent tab row first, then Feedback (agent) from it, then the sheet read back, never Feedback (agent) alone. | . | Set Ready for agent to YesTask_ReadyForAgent | Editor | review-sheet-script | An Editor agrees the direction and sets the row’s Ready for agent (Orange) to Yes. Person-only: the agent never sets it. | . | Edit the document in the row’s pull requestTask_EditInPullRequest | Authoring agent | review-sheet-script | One row, one branch, one active pull request: the agent edits on the row’s branch and opens its pull request, or updates it when the row comes round again. A closed pull request the committee wants back is reopened, or replaced by a new one on the same branch; earlier ones stay listed in Agentic status. Agentic status (Green) says where it is, and Staging review opens the preview’s what-changed page. Before the preview is staged, the agent writes the change set’s Disposition (change set) on the Agent tab: one line per feedback item, starting from the people’s Blue Disposition, after an optional Overall statement; the sheet shows it in Disposition (agent) and flags any item without a disposition, or one that differs from the people’s. It ends with Record agent step (record-agent-step.bpmn): the Agent tab row first, then Feedback (agent) from it, then the sheet read back, never Feedback (agent) alone. | . | Review the preview and answerTask_AnswerPreview | Authoring Committee | review-sheet-script | Members read the preview and answer in their Blue columns, or leave them as they are when the change is right. They record the row’s Disposition (Blue): Pending, Accepted, Partially accepted, Not accepted, Noted, Duplicate or Out of scope. | . | QA gate: check dispositions and PRTask_QaGate | QA reviewer (independent) | review-sheet-script | Reads: the change set’s Disposition (change set), the people’s Blue Disposition and feedback, the pull request’s diff at its head commit, and the staging QA report. Checks that every feedback item has one disposition; that each agrees with the people’s Blue Disposition; that each Accepted or Partially accepted item has the change in the diff, and a Not accepted, Noted, Duplicate or Out of scope item has none; that the diff changes nothing no disposition accounts for; and that the QA report for the staged commit has no failing gate. Writes: QA gate (change set) on the Agent tab, first line “Passed <head sha>: …” or “Failed <head sha>: <why>”, and QA report (change set), the report’s link. The sheet shows the gate under Staging review; a pass for an older commit reads as stale. It ends with Record agent step (record-agent-step.bpmn): the Agent tab row first, then Feedback (agent) from it, then the sheet read back, never Feedback (agent) alone. | . | Set Ready for merge to YesTask_ReadyForMerge | Editor | review-sheet-script | An Editor sets the row’s Ready for merge (Orange) to Yes once the QA gate has passed for the pull request’s head commit. Person-only. Set earlier, the agent does not merge until the gate passes, and its feedback says so. | . | Merge the pull requestTask_Merge | Authoring agent | review-sheet-script | The agent merges the row’s pull request, and Agentic status says merged. The change set’s Dispositions blurb, as it stands when Ready for merge is set to Yes, is the summary: it goes into the merge, and closes the change set’s issue. It ends with Record agent step (record-agent-step.bpmn): the Agent tab row first, then Feedback (agent) from it, then the sheet read back, never Feedback (agent) alone. | . | Close the change set: the issue, then the sheet rowTask_CloseChangeSet | Authoring agent | review-sheet-agent-columns | Closing is one step with two tools, GitHub and the review sheet. The agent closes the change set’s issue on GitHub, with the merge or the reason it closed unmerged, then records Agentic status Closed (or Change merged) on the Agent tab through Record agent step (record-agent-step.bpmn). The sheet script then hides the row and strikes the whole row through (“make sure complete changeset rows are hidden so not cluttered and that text of that whole row is crossed out”). The agent never hides or strikes a row by hand, and never deletes one: reopening the issue and writing a new status shows it again. Hiding and striking are formatting only, which the review-log watcher ignores. A change set closed without a merge, at a person’s request, takes this step too. | .

537.title: /coordinate — multi-agent / multi-PR coordination
537.content: Skill coordinate: Coordinate work across multiple in-flight Claude PRs working toward a shared goal. Post intent + asks on related PRs, identify cherry-pickable work, respond to code-review comments on your own PR, periodically triage sibling PR activity (new comments, CI status, new commits), watch main + newly created branches/PRs, escalate inconsistent findings to the author, and keep a coordination ledger up to date. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Agent activity log, Close the bean, Drain the beans, Agent bean lifecycle, Open the bean, Code change and review, Merge the base branch in, A refused merge-train member, Requirements filing: promote, organise, trace, supersede, or retire, SME Review of Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route, Test Data Curation — Fixed Sets and Generated Recipes, Watching a pinned upstream dependency, Adopting an upstream version bump, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Editing and HCI validation, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . When several Claude branches are converging on the same long-term goal (e.g. “reach the precision target”, “close all violators of a rule”, “infrastructure overhaul”), each agent has only its own context. Without coordination they will: . | duplicate work (two agents both implementing the same helper), | silently diverge (one renames a symbol, another keeps the old name, the merge conflicts), | miss cherry-picks (one agent already wrote the template the others need), | accept inconsistent findings without flagging them to the author, | accept review-tool feedback without checking it against the actual artifact / sibling change proposal’s — pull request’s (PR’s) — framing (e.g. accepting an off-by-one “fix” that contradicts a definition another PR is also using), | miss new sibling PRs that opened mid-session (new branches landing on main with overlapping scope). | . /coordinate is the protocol that prevents this. None of the agents has all the answers; they look to the author for clarification on inconsistencies, and they cherry-pick from each other.

538.title: Workflow rule reminder
538.content: This skill assumes you’ve already created a branch + opened a PR for the work tranche being coordinated. Per continual-progress (STRICT, supersedes default “no auto-PR” guidance for this repo): always create a branch and open a PR at the start of every work tranche — ASAP, and never ask the user “want me to open the PR?” Branch + PR creation is pre-authorized; the only git action needing explicit permission is the merge. Commit early, commit often. Small structured commits cherry-pick cleanly; big mixed commits do not. Exception: integration-watcher batch audit-job sweeps may use a single bulk commit.

539.title: When to invoke
539.content: . | Start of a session where the user mentioned other branches/PRs by name (e.g. “coordinate with claude/foo and claude/bar”). | Whenever you start a new substantive task in a multi-PR effort — before making code changes, post intent on the relevant PRs. | When you finish a substantive task — post progress + concrete cherry-pickable artefacts (file paths, function names, templates, fixtures). | Periodic triage between substantive commits (§7) — even with no external trigger, sibling PRs may have landed commits or comments that change your scope. Run a quick triage every ~3–5 commits or when you finish a task and pick up the next one. | When main lands new commits during your session — if any touch the same files, blocks, or scripts you are editing, treat as a sibling PR for §3 classification purposes. | When a code-review comment lands on your own PR (gemini-code- assist, copilot-pull-request-reviewer, codex, or human reviewers) — see §5 Responding to review comments. | When you encounter a finding that contradicts another PR’s framing — write the disagreement up explicitly, post it to both PRs, and tag the author for resolution. | A COLLISION — coordinate. A merge conflict caused by a sibling’s landed work is not merely a thing to resolve; it is the signal that two sessions are editing one subject. Resolve it AND coordinate. | A POTENTIAL collision, seen in the work items — coordinate. Before you start a topic, and at each triage, scan for an in-progress work item whose scope overlaps yours. That is the cheapest collision to find, because it is the one found BEFORE either of you has written anything. How to read a sibling’s state out of the store, and the boundary of that inference, is bean-coordination (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan) §”Where a sibling session is visible from” — not restated here. | When you START any new unit of work — before the first edit. A new story, epic, feature or task work item, an issue, CRDM Phase 6, a workplan tranche, or a handover pickup runs the collision review in §”Starting new work” below, scaled to its blast radius, and records it in the workplan work item. | .

540.title: Inputs
540.content: . | The current PR number (your branch). | A list of sibling branch names or PR numbers (the user gives this, or list the open PRs labelled in-flight with the list change proposals forge-operation Tool). | The shared goal in 1–2 sentences. | .

541.title: Where each section lives
541.content: This skill was 732 lines and the Protocol was 478 of them — an agent reads the whole thing before acting, and at that length it skims. The Protocol now sits beside this file. Nothing was deleted and no step was renumbered, because other skills cite coordinate §0a and coordinate.md §8a and those citations have to keep resolving. | section | where | . | workflow rule, when to invoke, inputs | here — read before you start | . | Protocol §1–§11 — the eleven coordination steps | coordinate/protocol.md | . | output, anti-patterns, §11 STATUS.md, §12 same-goal coordination, related skills | here | . Coordinating: read this file for whether and when, then protocol.md for how.

542.title: Output
542.content: After invocation, you should have: . | Read every sibling PR’s body and changed-files list. | Posted at most one coordination comment per sibling PR (intent + asks), unless you’ve made progress that warrants a separate progress comment. | Triaged every open review-tool thread on your own PR (§5) and posted a single consolidated status comment. | Run a §7 periodic triage every 3–5 of your own commits, capturing new sibling-PR comments + commits + CI status in one table. | Run §8a (git fetch origin main) at each triage cycle and react to any main-landed changes that touch your scope. | Run §8b (newly-opened PRs / branches) at each triage cycle and prompt the author when a new sibling overlaps your scope keywords. | Identified the next concrete, non-overlapping task on your own workplan and started on it. | (Optional) Created or updated docs/coordination/<goal-slug>.md with the current state. | Escalated any inconsistencies via §6 with @<author> tagging. | .

543.title: Anti-patterns
543.content: . | ❌ Post a coordination comment that just summarises your own PR. Sibling agents already read your PR body. | ❌ Pick the same task as a sibling without posting first. Even if their PR has been quiet, the human author may have given them a verbal lead. | ❌ “Resolve” an inconsistency by rewriting your finding. Escalate to the author. | ❌ Accept a review-tool fix without verifying it against the artifact and sibling-PR conventions. Bot suggestions can flip conventions silently. | ❌ Reply per-thread on a 6-comment review pass. Use one consolidated status comment + per-thread accept / reject-with-reason flags. | ❌ Skip §7 triage between commits because “I would have heard if something landed” — you wouldn’t. Sibling agents work in parallel and rarely interrupt each other. Run the triage anyway. | ❌ Silently merge / cherry-pick from main without §8a classification. Main commits can also be inconsistent findings. | ❌ Add a newly-opened PR to your scope without prompting the author (§8b). The author may want it independent. | ❌ Long prose. Coordination comments are tables, file pointers, and one-line asks. | .

544.title: §11 STATUS.md + master ledger pattern
544.content: A repeated flip-flop episode (a claim asserted and retracted across several sessions) motivates a more structured coordination layer that overlays this skill: . | Root STATUS.md — single dashboard listing every goal + pointer to its master ledger + active PRs. | Master ledger per goal — docs/coordination/<goal>.md holds the durable narrative: current canonical status, open tasks, flip-flop history, sessions log. | Per-goal queue — the beans queue (beans/); each open task is one entry. | . When /coordinate runs, it now ALSO: . | Reads STATUS.md to find which goal(s) the current PR touches. | Reads the goal’s master ledger to identify the current canonical status — overrides recent commit claims if the ledger records a retraction. | Reads the queue to find sibling tasks in flight. | References the ledger session log when posting intent comments on sibling PRs, so the comment is grounded in the durable record, not just session memory. | . See session-intent for the session-start / session-end ledger + queue update protocol — /coordinate is the sibling-PR arm; /session-intent is the durable-state arm. They are run together at session start.

545.title: §12 Multi-agent same-goal coordination
545.content: Multiple agents MAY work the same goal in parallel. Per author directive: agents coordinate with the user on goals, not with each other on task-level locks. Model: . | Goal = product (author’s directive). User-level concern. | Queue = per-goal item list (the beans queue). | Tasks are NOT exclusively claimed. Two agents may attack the same task with different methods — both threads have value. | Coordination is with the USER on goal-level decisions, not agent-to-agent on task-level locks. | . When you detect a sibling agent on your task . Signals: . | The queue entry has co_assignees populated, OR | A sibling PR (listed with the list change proposals forge-operation Tool) has commits touching your task’s scope files within the last 24h, OR | The ledger session log shows another agent declared intent on the same task ID. | . Workflow: . | Do not silently abandon. Your independent attack is valuable. | Post intent on the sibling PR (this skill §3) so the sibling sees you’re also working it. | Ask the user with AskUserQuestion whether to keep both threads or have one stand down. Include rich context per AGENTS.md §User accessibility — quote what each agent is doing, what method, what’s been found, cost of running both. | If user says one stands down, the standing-down agent appends partial results to the ledger and updates queue status: "open" (releasing the task). The continuing agent may pick up the partial results. | . Watching for sibling-PR contradictions . Per §8 of this skill: at each triage cycle, look for sibling-PR commits or comments that contradict your branch’s framing. Per §6: escalate inconsistent findings to the user. Do not silently adopt the sibling’s framing without an §6 conversation.

546.title: What actually reaches a sibling
546.content: Do not assume you can message a sibling session. Measured from a cloud session with eleven siblings live on one repository: . | channel | reaches a cloud sibling? | . | list_sessions | sees them — id, title, branch, task summary | . | ListAgents | no — “no other Claude session is running on this machine” | . | SendMessage | no — the send is refused, target not reachable | . | a committed work item | yes — every session reads the store at session start | . | a PR or issue comment | yes — to whoever looks, and it is durable | . So list_sessions tells you WHO is working and on WHAT, and then the message has to travel through something committed. The practical order: . | list_sessions (or the work items) to find WHO overlaps and how. | Write the coordination INTO the artefacts they will read — the work item, the PR body, the issue. A work item is the strongest, because bean-coordination §”The store on main is the one every sibling reads” makes it the one surface every session opens. | Only then consider a direct message, and only for a sibling ListAgents actually lists. | . A spawned helper is reachable, and the owner’s authority is not relayed . The table above is for a session without the remote-session tools. A session that has create_session and send_message (the claude-code-remote server) can seed a helper session and message a cloud session it lists. Reaching it does not give it the owner’s authority: a helper’s permission layer may refuse pushes, messages back and even reads when its task arrived from another session, and it must refuse a relayed ruling (such as a merge window) as the owner’s. That refusal is correct. conduct/security/zero-trust-handover §”Who the principal is” puts a message relayed from another session on the NOT-the-principal list. So, when you seed a helper session: . | Quote the owner’s own words verbatim in the seed prompt, with the session they were typed in, and say which part the helper serves. The helper then knows what was asked, though it still cannot treat the words as instructions the owner gave it. | Relay no rulings. A merge window, a re-pin consent, or an answer to an owner decision binds the session it was given in. Tell the helper to open PRs and leave them green, not to merge. | Tell the owner, in your own turn, that each helper may ask for confirmation in its own session, and name the sessions. That is the only way the owner’s authority reaches it. A helper that stops to ask is working as designed. The ask is not a failure to route around. | Give the helper a lane it can finish without the owner: a work item store or a set of repositories, the lanes of its siblings, and the report-back channel (send_message to the coordinator). | Carry the interaction-modality rule in every seed prompt and subagent brief, and require the helper to pass it on. A helper that asks the owner directly must present every question twice in order — first the full question in chat (context, what differs, every identifier expanded, ≤ 4 numbered or lettered options with pros/cons/downstream/reversibility, recommended option first and marked (Recommended), and stated default on silence), then the tappable card (AskUserQuestion, request_decision, ask_question, or post_widget) with the same option labels — never in prose alone and never asking the owner to type. A subagent or a sibling running beside a live discussion returns any owner question to the coordinator in the hand-back-to-discussion schema format. See opening-brief §”Briefing a sibling or a subagent — pass interaction-modality on (STRICT)”. | . Eleven sessions is the normal case, not the exception . Measured with eleven sessions on one repository, each merging main on a loop: one branch took four base merges in three hours, three of them conflicted. The rate IS the environment; coordinate earlier, not merge harder. The worked example: a voice landing in a directory being deleted . A branch migrated every voice from <instance>/voices/ to <instance>/skills/voices/. Mid-flight, main landed a NEW voice in cat-harness/voices/ — the directory the branch removes. Git’s rename detection then placed the new file inside another voice’s folder. Nothing was wrong with either piece of work. What was missing was that neither session knew about the other, and the work items said so the whole time: the migration’s work item was in-progress and names the directory. A work item scan by either session would have caught it before a line was written, which is exactly why the trigger above is worth having.

547.title: Crossing into a sibling’s subject — permitted, and what it costs
547.content: Crossing into a sibling’s stream is allowed, but coordinate, watch for collisions, and avoid duplicating work. Two rules follow. 1. The stream that owns a milestone’s WORK may repair the milestone. A checker must not rewrite a milestone — a gate that guesses replaces a stale belief with an invented one. A session that has re-measured the goal’s whole surface may. So the line is checker vs. session, not owner vs. non-owner. A session repairing somebody’s milestone re-measures every line it rewrites, in a fresh container, by running the thing — and says which clause it could not verify. 2. Crossing is permitted; colliding silently is not. Cross freely, but the crossing is what triggers this skill rather than what excuses skipping it. 3. Crossing never means pushing to a sibling’s branch. Only the PR’s owner pushes to its branch. Send the owner the change instead (continual-progress §”One pusher per PR branch”, owner ruling, 2026-11-07). 4. Merging and re-pinning go through one session. Siblings never merge (owner ruling, 2026-11-13). Each sends the merge manager a six-line merge request (PR and head SHA, session URL, what changed, rendered preview, what to look for, the CI verdict on that head), or repin+merge: when the PR is green except for a re-pin, and the owner approves only in the merge manager’s session. Find it first: the latest merge manager: <session id> announcement, noted on the coordination work item, names a live session. With none active, the siblings elect one by a fixed rule, and a lone session is elected alone. A merge manager that does not acknowledge within the stall window has stalled, and the siblings re-elect without it: see merge-manager-watcher §”The sibling’s side: find the merge manager first” and §”Liveness and stalls” (owner rulings, 2026-11-07). 5. Stack rather than wait. Work that needs a sibling’s unmerged PR starts now, stacked on that PR’s branch (or, across layers, on its head SHA), with stacked on <repo>#<n> in the body. Pull the sibling’s changes in by merging. A re-pin is its own PR, holding only pins: work that needs the new pins stacks on it. Never push to its branch: see continual-progress §”Stack instead of waiting” (owner ruling, 2026-11-07). The collision surface is FILES, and it is predictable before you touch one . A work item scan finds sessions working the same subject. It does not find two sessions about to edit the same file from different subjects: . | file | why two sessions want it | . | scripts/stale-paths-baseline.json | two lines long. Every milestone repair removes its own entry. Two repairs in flight = a conflict whose wrong resolution silently empties a file whose stated property is that it shrinks rather than fossilises — and an empty baseline fails every finding, “which is the safe direction” only if somebody notices. | . | a shared work item | every stream appends its own outcome. “An append cannot collide” is false when two sessions append, because both land at EOF. | . | generated dirs (auto-docs/, skill-instructions/, kg-qa sidecars) | nobody edits them, everybody regenerates them. Take main’s copy and re-run the generator — never hand-merge. For test/results/**, bun run cat qa:resolve-conflicts: those are derived QA results whose record is on the qa-reports branch. | . | test/attestations/** | judgements, not generated — no generator can reproduce one. Read both sides and keep both unless they are the same judgement; see prepare-merge §”Conflicts in test/results/ and test/attestations/”. | . Name the files you will touch, not just the work items, when you post intent. A sibling can dodge a file; it cannot dodge a subject it cannot see. Duplicated work is measured in what was already pushed, not in what is open . Before re-deriving a measurement, check whether a sibling’s pushed commit already carries it: an open PR’s diff is a fact, and reading it costs one call against a session’s worth of re-measurement.

548.title: Starting new work — a collision review, recorded before the first edit (STRICT)
548.content: This section is the rule’s only home. bean-coordination, session-intent, continual-progress, opening-brief, issue-working and crdm-requirements-workflow point here. They do not restate it. When it runs — the start of any new unit of work . Run the review once, before the first edit, whenever you start: . | a new story, epic, feature or task work item; | work on an issue, before you announce the branch; | CRDM Phase 6, implementation; | a new tranche of a workplan; | a pickup of someone else’s work from a handover. | . A pickup runs its own review. The previous session’s review is dated, and PRs may have opened since it was written. How deep — scale the review to the blast radius . The review is proportional. The question is how much other work your change can collide with, not how big your diff is. | A platform refactor gets the full review: all five steps, with messages to the owners. A platform refactor is a change to something that many pages, generators or open PRs depend on: . | shared layout and includes: _includes/, docs-ui.css, docs-ui.js, the navbar; | a generator whose output is committed or published, such as gen-ig-pages.ts or gen-navbar-include.ts; | a schema, a BPMN process, a workflow or a gate that other work is checked against. | . A ten-line change to a shared include collides with every PR that regenerates it. | A small, local story still runs steps 1 and 2, quickly. When they find nothing, record “no overlap found” in the work item, together with what you checked: the PR search, the work item search, and the terms you used. That takes about two minutes and one work item note. | Only an overlap triggers steps 3 and 4. If steps 1 and 2 find a sibling on your files or your subject, name its owner and message it, whatever the size of your change. | . “No overlap found” with no record of what was checked is not a review. The next session cannot tell it from a review that was skipped. The work item trigger above catches a sibling working on the same subject. §”The collision surface is FILES” catches two sessions editing the same file from different subjects. A refactor causes both kinds at once, which is why it gets the full review and does not rely on either trigger. The five steps, in order, before any file is edited . | List the open PRs and the files they change. Use the list change proposals forge-operation Tool, then list changed files for each PR. Intersect the result with the files your work will touch. A PR that changes only generated files you will also regenerate is not a collision; say so and move on. | Scan the in-progress work items for overlapping scope. Use beans list --status in-progress --search <term>, and search the subject as well as the ids: the file names, the generator, the page type. A work item id finds nothing when the overlapping work has no work item of its own; see bean-coordination §”The trigger is STARTING WORK”. | Name the owning sessions. Use list_sessions, the Claude-Session: trailers on each PR’s commits, and bun run cat sessions --since <window>. bean-coordination §”Where a sibling session is visible from” says how far that inference goes. | Message each owner with your intent and your asks. State what you will change, phase by phase, and the files each phase touches. Then ask two things: which order do we land in, and who owns each overlapping file. Send it through a channel that actually reaches them; §”What actually reaches a sibling” says which ones do. A PR comment also leaves a durable copy. | Record the review in the workplan work item before editing. Write down each overlapping session, its PRs and work items, the files you share, and the phases affected; or “no overlap found” and what you checked. A review that exists only in the chat is gone when the container goes, and the next session has to run it again. | . Phases that overlap a sibling wait. They wait until the sibling has agreed an order, or until its overlapping PR has landed. Phases that touch none of the sibling’s files can go ahead, and the review says which ones those are. Worked example: a platform refactor . A refactor moving the per-page nav, the harness bar, icons, scripts and the IG chrome CSS into shared cached assets touches the layout of every page. Before any edit, the review found active sibling work on every layout file the plan needed: a navbar session (four PRs on docs-ui.css, docs-ui.js, the navbar include, harness_details.html, head_custom.html), and two IG sessions on gen-ig-pages.ts. The review went into the work item, the three owning sessions were asked for an order, and the only work that started touched none of their files. Without the review, five PRs would have been rebased into a refactor of the files they were editing.

550.title: Flag-bearer reflections
550.content: Lessons from acting as flag-bearer across many sibling PRs on a shared goal. Apply when you hold the flag. | Build the ledger hub FIRST, then post. Create docs/coordination/<goal>.md with: the direction (one boxed statement of the target), the common infra everyone rows toward (cheat-sheet step table, watcher queues, dashboards, a falsification anchor), and a per-PR “which way to row” roster with report-back slots. Post intent only after the hub exists, so every comment can link one canonical place. This is what makes “make sure all use common infra” actionable rather than a slogan. | Tailor per-PR; then LISTEN. A flag-bearer that only broadcasts is half-doing the job. Pull each sibling’s current state (a background Explore agent reading PR bodies + last comments is ideal), and fold their findings back as sharpenings to your own plan. Record sharpenings in the ledger and amend the workplan — do not silently keep the stale plan. | Anchor the cluster to one falsifiable target. Give every sibling a shared regression target. It turns “which way to row” into a checkable claim and prevents divergent re-derivations. | Push-race coordination with background agents. When a background sub-agent and you both push to the same branch, wrap every push in a fetch → rebase → retry loop: for i in 1 2 3 4; do git push && break || { git fetch origin <br> -q; git rebase origin/<br>; sleep $((2**i)); }; done. The agent’s commits may already be in your local history (shared working dir) — check git log before assuming a divergence. | Billing-CI is noise — do not let it derail coordination. If CI fails setup-phase (≤5 s, simultaneous, no logs) on every push while local validation stays green, recognise the billing signature (litlfred/qou AGENTS.md “CI billing failures”), note [skip-ci: billing], and keep working; never re-diagnose it as a code problem or pause the cluster for it. | .
