559.title: Working on materialized content — copy it out
559.content: Skill copy-out-materialized: Materialized content is read-only. To work on it you take a copy into your own folio/, and the copy records what it is a copy of — the local-provenance edge, which is not the upstream one. Named by: Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes . Materialized content is a copy of somebody else’s bytes, and this repository does not edit it in place. The contents of a materialized <stub>/<sub-graph> are immutable, and the rule is enforced: to work on them, copy them into your own folio/. Diagram: copy-out-materialized.bpmn. Schema: the folio-materialization/v1 record (MaterializationSchema, owned by the content layer above this one — named here, not linked). Where they disagree, the schema wins and this file is wrong.

560.title: What the rule protects, and what it does not
560.content: It protects the CLAIM. A materialized record asserts “these bytes are what upstream published”. Editing them in place leaves that assertion standing over bytes it no longer describes — and check:materialized-fixity is what catches one that happened, by hashing the bytes against the digest the record carries. It does not protect against the copy being wrong, stale or badly chosen. Those are the five gates’ job, at materialisation time (materialize-remote), and a copy-out re-opens none of them: you are copying something this repository already decided it may hold.

561.title: Who may copy out
561.content: Any reader. This is deliberately not a permission: refusing a copy would not protect the original, because the original is protected by being read-only. A gate here would only stop people working. What copying out does NOT confer is the right to publish. The copy inherits its source’s restrictions and copyright verdicts, and it is a new artefact in your folio whose publication is your folio’s decision, judged the way any other authored content is.

562.title: Where the copy goes
562.content: Into the copier’s own folio/, with provenance — never a scratch area, which makes the copy publishable by accident: a directory nobody declared is a directory nobody gates.

563.title: The copy records what it is a copy of
563.content: This is the part that is easy to leave out and impossible to reconstruct later. materialization.provenance is a pair: . | field | points at | . | upstream | the remote thing — a URI, upstream | . | local | the original in this repository it was taken from | . A copy-out writes local. It does not overwrite upstream, and it does not reuse upstream for the local original. Without local, one rename later a copy is indistinguishable from original work. That is the whole failure this step exists to prevent, and nothing downstream can repair it: the information was never written down.

564.title: The copy is NOT read-only
564.content: A materialized node is frozen because it is a claim about somebody else’s bytes. A copy in your own folio/ is yours, makes no such claim, and is ordinary authored content — so it is writable, and its directory’s readOnly is false. If it were frozen too, the copy-out would achieve nothing, and the next person would need a copy of the copy.

565.title: The exception is “say what you did”, not a list of who may skip
565.content: The exception — for publication workflow purposes and the like — is a rule, not an allowlist of writers that would go stale: . A step that rewrites a materialized artefact records the new fixity in the same change. Then check:materialized-fixity passes and the record describes what is actually there. A step that rewrites without updating fixity fails, correctly, because it has forked upstream without saying so — which is exactly what the rule exists to prevent. The check asks a question about BYTES and never about who wrote them, so it needs no attribution of a commit to a process step. Where it applies . refresh-materialized.bpmn’s Task_Apply is the one step in the declared corpus that rewrites bytes a materialization record describes, so it writes the new fixity in the same change; otherwise a correct run of it would fail the gate as an unannounced edit. No publication process writes to materialized content. kg-to-portal.bpmn’s S_Sign signs a subgraph cut from the KG — derived content, not held upstream bytes. So the publication case is a rule with no instance yet, stated here rather than drawn as a step no diagram does, because a declared-but-absent step makes a consumer report a clean run over nothing.

566.title: What to check afterwards
566.content: . | bun run cat check:materialized-fixity — the original still hashes to its recorded digest. If it does not, the copy-out was an edit in place. | bun run cat check:read-only-graphs — your folio’s directory is not accidentally declared read-only, and the source’s still is. | .

568.doc: Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else's bytes
568.title: Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes
568.content: Process_CopyOutMaterialized · strict · 5 step(s) . Somebody wants to change content this repository holds a read-only materialized copy of: copy it into their own folio/, recording which original it came out of. Materialized content is read-only, and that is enforced, not advised. STRICT, and the reason is narrow. Only one step here is a gate, and it is Gateway_Frozen: whether the target is read-only at all. Everything after it is mechanical. What makes the process strict is that skipping it does not fail loudly — an edit in place succeeds, and is only caught later by check:materialized-fixity hashing bytes against the digest their record carries. A process whose omission looks exactly like compliance cannot be advisory. The copy-out re-opens NONE of the five materialisation gates. Those were answered when this repository decided it may hold these bytes at all (materialize-remote.bpmn); copying something already held is not a second acquisition. What the copy does inherit is the restrictions and copyright verdicts — the copy is a new artefact in the copier’s folio, and publishing it is that folio’s decision. The three states, the five gates and the provenance pair are folio-assistant-core/schemas/materialization.ts. Nothing here restates them. i i i i i

574.title: Corpus — committing an accepted edit
574.content: Skill corpus-commit-contract: The contract the corpus role is held to when an accepted edit is committed into it: take the write only on the editor’s acceptance, as one change with its QA sidecars, under the commit-hygiene requirement and with no relaxing of that policy. The narrowest contract the editing diagram requires. A mechanical role’s skill is a contract to test against, not instructions to read. Named by: Editing and HCI validation . corpus (declared below this layer) is played by a mechanical actor: the versioned content store, which is written to and decides nothing. A role played by a machine is still a role, and its skills are its contract: the responsibilities it must perform, which a test can hold it to. This skill is the part of that contract this layer’s diagrams rely on, and nothing more.

575.title: Where the diagrams lean on it
575.content: Lane_Corpus in editing-hci-validation (opt-in folio-assistant-core.collab) names this role and holds one activity, Task_Commit. What that lane’s documentation and the task’s say is the whole contract.

576.title: What it must do
576.content: . | Receive the write only after the editor accepts. Task_Commit is reachable from no path except Gateway_EditorDecision’s accept branch (the lane’s documentation). A change the editor discards, or one that has not reached the editor, never reaches the corpus. | Take the change together with its QA sidecars. “Only now does the change become corpus content, together with its QA sidecars” (the task’s documentation): the block and the findings about it arrive as one change. | Hold the commit to the commit-hygiene requirement (req:commit-hygiene), and allow no relaxing of it: the task’s policy is relaxable="false", because this is the one step that is irreversible in a way nothing upstream is. | .

577.title: Not its responsibility
577.content: Drafting the change, validating it, or deciding whether to accept it. Those happen in the author’s, the pipeline’s, the reviewer’s and the editor’s lanes before anything reaches the corpus. Resolving the bean afterwards is the work plan’s.

580.title: Corpus-Grep Skill
580.content: Skill corpus-grep: Pre-declaration corpus check. Before declaring any item “open”, “gap”, “TODO”, “open problem”, “pending derivation” — or asserting in chat that something is unresolved in the corpus — run the four-path grep checklist. A source file’s ## Status note lags the corpus by weeks; the corpus is the source of truth. An item is open only after all four paths come back empty (modulo the originating file itself). Named by: Hand back to the discussion, Drain the beans, A refused merge-train member, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route . Disambiguation. This skill formalizes the backward check (“has this already been resolved somewhere in the corpus?”). Its forward complement is the formalize-first discipline (“can a structural claim prune the hypothesis class before I run a wide search?”). Run corpus-grep before declaring an item open; run formalize-first before launching an expensive numerical scan. The two are duals — backward against known results, forward against the hypothesis class.

581.title: Role
581.content: Gate every “this is open / unresolved / a gap” declaration behind a mechanical four-path search of the corpus. The originating source file’s status note (## Status, Open question, Phase 3 open, a TODO in a code or formal-source file, a PR-description “still open”) is not authoritative — prior agents routinely land a resolution as an audit doc, an adjacent chapter’s block, an implemented witness script, or a coordination ledger entry weeks before the source file’s note is updated. This skill catches that lag.

582.title: When to run this skill (STRICT)
582.content: Run the checklist before any of the following land in a durable artifact (audit doc, content block .md/.ts, code or formal-source comment, PR description, coordination ledger) or are asserted as fact in chat: . | “X is open” / “Open X” / “open problem” / “open question” | “TODO: derive X” / “pending derivation” / “still missing” | “this is a gap” / “no proof exists” / “not yet implemented” | “X is not wired into compute” / “nothing computes X” | . If you are about to type any of those about a corpus topic, stop and run the four paths first.

583.title: When NOT to run it (scope boundary)
583.content: The checklist gates factual corpus-status claims only. It does not gate, and must never be used to suppress: . | Skeptical assessments — “this looks fitted”, “this is numerology”, “hidden degrees of freedom here”. | Outside-view critique of a derivation’s rigor. | Reception / publishability / referee forecasts. | . Those are critical-distance judgments (see the repo’s Critical-distance license), not open-item declarations, and are never gated by this skill. Voicing them in chat does not require running corpus-grep first.

584.title: The four-path checklist (run all four)
584.content: | # | Path | What it catches | . | 1 | grep -rln <topic> docs/audits/ | Owner-authorised resolutions land as audit docs ahead of the source file’s status note being updated. | . | 2 | grep -rln <topic> content/ (full tree) | Related conjectures / propositions cross-cut chapters: a block in one chapter may answer a question raised in another. | . | 3 | grep -rln <topic> folio-assistant/computations/ | Implemented code may already discharge the content. | . | 4 | docs/coordination/<theme>.md | The coordination ledger — a prior agent may have already closed the item. | . Search the full content/ tree, not just the chapter you started in. The whole point of path 2 is that the resolution lives somewhere you did not expect.

585.title: Mechanical recipe
585.content: Pick a TOPIC that is the keyword / regex of the claim (an identifier, a label fragment, a phrase — e.g. delta_lambda, bring_color, c_3.*Taylor, kashaev.*density). Then run all four paths in one sweep: . TOPIC='delta_lambda' # ← keyword or regex for the claim under test for d in docs/audits content folio-assistant/computations docs/coordination; do if [ -d "$d" ]; then echo "=== $d ===" grep -rln -e "$TOPIC" "$d" 2>/dev/null fi done . Prefer the harness Grep tool (output_mode: "files_with_matches", one call per path or a single call with path set to the repo root and a glob) over shell grep when running inside an agent — results integrate with the permission UI and file links. The shell snippet above is the portable fallback. Widen the topic if the first pass is empty: try a synonym, the formal declaration name, the block label, the function name, and the witness-JSON key. A single spelling is not a clearing.

586.title: Decision procedure
586.content: . | Any non-trivial hit in (1)–(4) ⇒ the item is NOT open. Read the hit, then document the existing resolution instead of declaring a gap. Cite the file (audit doc / block .md / witness / ledger entry) that resolves it. | All four empty, modulo the originating file itself ⇒ you may declare the item open. “Modulo the originating file” means: a hit that is only the source file you are auditing does not count as a clearing — it is the very note you already mistrust. | Unsure whether a hit is the resolution ⇒ open the file and read it. A filename match is a lead, not a verdict. Treat a hit as resolving only if it actually discharges the claim (an audit verdict, a proved block, a passing witness, a ledger “CLOSED”). | .

587.content: This skill is the canonical, self-contained statement. It is invoked by, and consistent with, these codified instances: . | The folio’s own AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, where it states the rule for its corpus. | A content type’s own audits, which apply the checklist to their declarations. For a paper folio these are the science layer’s proof-gap-audit §K (proof-gap declarations), compute-author and compute-audit (before declaring a statement “not wired into compute”) and lean-environment-setup (before declaring a capability unavailable). | .

589.title: Covered is not reachable — and check:tools cannot tell you which
589.content: Skill covered-is-not-reachable: A skill can be satisfied by the neighbours of its mechanism while the mechanism is reachable from no Tool node. Read before concluding from check:tools that a command is reachable, and before adding a Tool node or a maintains claim. Named by: Code node review, Code change and review . A skill can be satisfied by the neighbours of its mechanism while the mechanism itself is reachable from nothing. check:tools reports the skill as covered and is right to: coverage is a relation between a Tool and a skill, never between a Tool and a command. For example, kg-export can be satisfied by a publishing node, a serving node and schema carriers while no node runs an export; translation-manager by extract, inject, status, signoff and validate nodes while none reaches the round-trip QA.

590.title: The two questions, kept apart
590.content: “Does this skill have a Tool?” — bun run cat check:tools, and bun run cat tools:coverage for which of the uncovered ones warrant one. “Is this command reachable by asking the graph?” — no instrument answers this yet; it has to be measured by hand. A skill showing as covered is not evidence that its code is reachable. Do not use the first question to answer the second: the cause of an invisible mechanism is structural, because nobody asks the second question.

591.title: What to do when you meet one
591.content: Add the node for the mechanism. Then two things not to do: . | Do not widen an existing node’s satisfies to make the gap look closed. That makes the graph assert a node does something it does not. | Do not give the new node the same I/O as an existing one unless it really is a substitute. Alternatives are derived from a shared skill plus an identical I/O signature (deriveAlternatives), and export-then-publish-then- serve are complementary steps, not competing arms. | .

592.title: Two reasons NOT to write maintains
592.content: maintains.artefact is a single path. A generator that writes one file per subject — gen-skill-docs, gen-schema-docs, gen-block-jsonld — has no single artefact to name. A declaration naming one file out of tens is worse than absent: it looks like a complete provenance record. A maintains claim asserts the artefact is published. Verify that by reading the build, not by assuming: cat-harness/ns.jsonld is a real claim because .github/workflows/docs-site.yml writes it. Remove a claim in the same change that retires its artefact: a claim outliving its artefact is the same 404 from the other side. An artefact nobody publishes is exactly the 404 the drift check exists to prevent. And the drift check only covers its own producer . kg:schema:check reconciles maintains both ways, but its unproduced direction runs only over artefacts whose declaring Tool invokes bun run cat kg:schema, because a maintained artefact is not necessarily produced by the schema exporter. So a maintains claim on any other producer’s artefact is unchecked: it can rot to a 404 and nothing notices. The fix — not yet built — is to assert every declared artefact is present after _site/ is assembled, with could-not-determine kept distinct from present.

593.title: Adding a Tool type is fail-closed, and that is deliberate
593.content: check:tools refuses a command-line input whose type could express a shell payload, against the membership list in schemas/tools/tool-types.ts. A newly added type is absent from that list and therefore unsafe by default. Adding it is a deliberate step, not an oversight to route around — and the fix for an enumerable input is the enum, never a looser type that happens to pass. Where the enum duplicates a union declared elsewhere, guard it in both directions: satisfies catches a member that stops being valid, and a conditional type catches a member added to the union and not here. An unavoidable duplicate is fine; an unchecked one is not — see directory-conventions.

594.title: Five cases, most invisible to the instruments
594.content: | case | what exists | what is missing | what sees it | . | 1 | a skill | a Tool | check:tools, tools:coverage | . | 2 | a skill and Tools for its neighbours | a Tool for the mechanism | nothing — this skill | . | 3 | a mechanism | any skill stating the capability | nothing | . | 4 | a skill, a mechanism, a Tool | a command — it runs in-process only | nothing | . | 5 | a skill, a mechanism, a command | anything that invokes it | nothing | . Case 5 is case 4’s inverse — the entry point is present and the callers are absent — and it is discussed under §Reachability is PLURAL below, because the useful question there is how many dispatch points this should have. A script whose only references are its own usage string and a line of skill prose telling a human what to type is case 5: its mechanism is inlined in prose.

595.title: The third case: a mechanism with no skill at all
595.content: A generator that renders theme and avatar nodes into the site’s stylesheets is a textbook maintains pair, and yet no generic skill need state the capability. tools:coverage cannot see this: it enumerates skills and asks which lack Tools, so a capability nobody has stated is absent from the list it walks. (site-presentation-assets is the skill that now states that one.) . satisfies requires at least one skill, so a node cannot be written without one: . | Do not stretch a neighbouring skill to make the node validate. The resulting satisfies edge is simply false. | Do not write the skill as a wrapper for the command. A skill states a capability generically and names no script; one that exists to give a script somewhere to point is a Tool with front matter. | . Authoring the skill is a design act — a claim about the platform’s capability vocabulary, inherited by every dependent layer — so it goes to the owner rather than being decided in passing. Write the skill before the nodes. Once the gap is closed, remove any note announcing it: an agent that believes a stale gap either avoids the capability or rebuilds it.

596.title: The fourth case: a mechanism with no command, reachable in-process only
596.content: Cases 1–3 are about a missing node or a missing skill. This one has both, and is still unaskable: the mechanism has no command, so no CI job and no person can run it. For example, checkFolioProfile in pipeline/profile-check.ts catches what schema validation structurally cannot — a block valid against its own schema but wrong for the folio’s content profile, because adapters partition disjointly while profiles nest. Its only caller is the MCP tool registration, so it is reachable by an MCP-connected agent and by nothing else: not a gate, not a sweep, not a person at a shell. Every instrument that asks “can this be reached” answers yes. Ask which callers, not whether. “Reachable from MCP” and “reachable from CI” are different claims, and a durable verdict needs the second. Giving a library function its first command . Prefer a qa-sweep axis to a one-off check script: a sweep verdict is durable where a printed one is not — a printed verdict cannot distinguish “wrong since it was written” from “broken in the commit under review”. Watch the library’s defaults. checkFolioProfile resolves through readFolioProfile, which turns an undeclared profile into "paper" — correct for a validator, which validates against the wider vocabulary, and wrong for a reporter, which must use readDeclaredFolioProfile or report pass on a folio that declares no content type at all. A library’s defaulting is usually what erases the third state. When you give a library function its first entry point, the value it resolves for its own use is not the value a verdict may report. Check which of the two you are reading — by running it, not by reading it.

597.title: Reachability is PLURAL — “which caller should this have?” presumes one
597.content: One mechanism can have several dispatch points, so the question to ask is not which caller should this have but: . What should be able to start this — and is each of those a trigger or a Tool? . The two are different objects, and which one a dispatch point is follows from who initiates: . | dispatch point | it is a | because | . | a named command | Tool | a caller invokes it; that is what a Tool node IS | . | a BPMN activity | trigger | the process fires it when the step is reached | . | a QA sweep axis | trigger | the sweep fires it per subject | . | a schedule or a watcher | trigger | time or an event fires it | . None of them is an alternative to another, by the same argument deriveAlternatives makes about sharing a skill: they are different ways the same work gets started. Enumerating the dispatch points also finds the ones already built. For each candidate, check whether it exists (an activity may already carry the skill, so workflow_next already hands it to an agent), whether it is possible (a sweep cannot run a check whose verdict originates outside it), and only then what is missing. Presented as a choice, the options waste proposals; enumerated as dispatch points, they are a short audit with one action. Read the mechanism’s entry point before proposing dispatch points. A name and a position in a diagram say what something is for; an argument list says what it does — for example, whether it performs a check or only records a verdict somebody else produced.

598.title: The same failure one level out: a KIND, not a mechanism
598.content: Ask what is missing of a kind of node and the same mistake appears: counting kg-qa sidecars over the work item store, finding zero, and calling work items unaudited when several gates audit them. Coverage is a relation between an instrument and the question it was built for — see audit-coverage, with bun run cat audit:coverage as the second question.

600.content: Process_CRDM_Close · strict · 5 step(s) . The stakeholders sign off, the BA confirms every criterion is met, the feature lands on main through the merge-to-main sub-process, and only then does the agent close the issue. Never the other way round: an agent must never assume completion. i i i i i

606.title: CRDM — the data-modelling phase
606.content: Skill crdm-data-model: The CRDM data-modelling phase — when in the requirements process a model is built, what it is built from, who confirms it, and what it hands to the phases either side. The technique it invokes is data-modelling; this skill carries only the sequencing and the sign-off. Named by: CRDM data model . This skill says WHEN and WITH WHOM. It does not say how to model. That is data-modelling, and it is deliberately free of CRDM so a folio modelling data outside a requirements process can read it without inheriting a methodology it is not running. Where the two disagree, the technique wins and this page is wrong.

607.title: Where it sits, and why there
607.content: Between requirements (phases 2–4) and sign-off (phase 5). Requirements are statements about things; the model says what the things ARE. The entities come from the business-process analysis (phase 2), and phase 5 must not sign off requirements whose nouns were never pinned. Drafted too early, the model is invented from nothing; drafted too late, two stakeholders approve the same sentence meaning different things. Call_DataModel in crdm-requirements.bpmn is the callActivity after Call_Requirements and before Call_Signoff.

608.title: What it consumes
608.content: | from | what | . | phase 1, needs | the domain vocabulary the BA actually used | . | phase 2, BPA | the activities — every verb whose object is a candidate entity | . | phases 3–4, requirements | each requirement’s nouns, which the model must be able to express | . A requirement the model cannot express is a finding, not a modelling failure. It means the requirement is about something nobody has named, and the remedy is to name it. That is why this phase sits after requirements rather than before.

609.title: The sign-off, and who gives it
609.content: The agent drafts; the BA confirms the entities are the ones they meant; the stakeholders confirm the cardinalities. Those are two different questions and are asked of two different lanes on purpose: . | Are these the things? — a naming question, and the BA owns the domain vocabulary. | Is it really one per? — an operational question, and the people who run the process know where the exceptions are. | . The agent asks both and decides neither: the BA knows the domain, the agent does not guess, because a wrong cardinality is invisible until the data arrives.

610.title: What it hands on
610.content: A declared model, readable by a tool, per step 6 of the technique. Phase 5 signs off requirements against it: whether each requirement is expressible, not only whether it is wanted.

611.title: The loop, and when to leave it
611.content: Like every other CRDM phase this one loops until confirmed, and the gateway is the phase. Leave when the BA recognises the entities and the stakeholders have answered every cardinality — not when the model looks complete, because an unanswered cardinality is a hole exactly where the exceptions live.

612.title: Not decided by this skill
612.content: Whether the model is expressed as Zod, JSON Schema, a class diagram or prose is placement’s question and the folio’s choice. This phase requires only that the artefact is declared, so the next phase can read it rather than be told about it.

620.title: CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance
620.content: Process_CRDM_Deliver · strict · 9 step(s) . One phase and not three, because the loops say so: an increment the BA rejects, an MVP that is not ready, and stakeholder findings all route back into implementation. A subprocess has one exit and cannot be re-entered once finished, so splitting this region would have changed what the diagram says. i i i i i i i i i

621.content: . | Called by: CRDM requirements | Calls: Options analysis, Review task | Presented on: no docs page section shows this diagram | Running instances: none recorded | .

622.title: Lanes — who acts
622.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | BA / Feature Requestor | business-analyst | Every signal that can send the loop back to A_Implement is filtered through this lane first: BA_ReviewIncrement judges behaviour rather than code, GW_MVPReady decides whether accumulated increments are worth showing stakeholders at all, and BA_TranslateFeedback is the only step that turns S_TestMVP’s raw findings into direction the agent can act on. Nothing stakeholder-facing reaches Lane_Agent without passing through here. | . | Agent | authoring-agent | Every loop-back in this phase — a rejected increment, an MVP not ready, stakeholder feedback — lands on A_Implement rather than on Call_OptionsAnalysis, so this lane always reworks an approach already chosen and never re-selects one. Deciding that the APPROACH itself is wrong is not this lane’s call: that belongs to the calling step in crdm-requirements.bpmn, one level up. | . | Stakeholders | stakeholder | Tests in the stakeholder’s own workflow and data rather than against the acceptance criteria BA_ReviewIncrement already checked — a second, independent pass rather than a repeat of the first. GW_StakeholderOK’s findings branch does not hand the agent anything directly; it hands raw results to BA_TranslateFeedback, which is this lane’s boundary: it reports what works and what does not, and translating that into direction is somebody else’s lane. | .

623.title: Steps
623.content: Every one of the 9 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Options analysis how to implementCall_OptionsAnalysis | Agent | calls Options analysis | On the single edge from Start_Process_CRDM_Deliver into A_Implement, so the approach is chosen before any code exists. By Phase 6 the needs, requirements and data model are signed off, which is exactly the evidence an options analysis needs and the reason it belongs here rather than earlier: at Call_Needs there is nothing to weigh, and after A_Implement the choice has been made in code.The three loop-backs into A_Implement — _5 (increment rejected), _7 (MVP not ready), _13 (feedback translated) — deliberately BYPASS this call. Routing them through it would run the subprocess on every iteration of the inner loop, which is the ceremony this design refuses: a gate invoked on every pass stops being read. An iteration reworks an approach already chosen; if the APPROACH is what is wrong, that is not a loop iteration and it belongs to the calling step in crdm-requirements.bpmn.Contrast upstream-version-adoption, where the loop DOES re-enter the analysis. There the loop-back returns to A_Impact, which re-gathers the evidence, so the second pass weighs genuinely different inputs. Here the loop returns to implementation with the evidence unchanged.A_Implement carries a note on the bean (its claim is the OPEN that Process_CRDM calls first); this step carries no bean op, because Process_OptionsAnalysis ends with its own decision-audit note on the bean the caller claimed. | . | Phase 6: Implement (feature branch + PR)A_Implement | Agent | continual-progress | Inner loop: agent claims a bean, implements onfeature branch, opens PR, posts summary to the issue.When the requirement changes a rendered surface, implement against thewireframe candidate the requester or BA chose in Phases 3–4(Process_WireframeDesignReview, called from Process_CRDM_Requirements), notagainst a fresh design; and the delivery summary links the chosen candidatebeside the after-screenshot, so the reviewer can see the build matches what wasapproved. | . | Audit the code nodes the increment addsA_CodeAudit | Agent | calls Review task | Descend into the review task for what this incrementCHANGED IN THE GRAPH — Tool definitions in tools/ and schema definition nodesunder schemas/. 626.title: Feature-request detection (CRDM trigger)
626.content: Skill crdm-detect: Detect when a request needs requirements agreed before anything is built, and which of the two parallel requirements methodologies governs it. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Agent activity log, Close the bean, Drain the beans, Agent bean lifecycle, Open the bean, Code change and review, Merge the base branch in, A refused merge-train member, Requirements filing: promote, organise, trace, supersede, or retire, SME Review of Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route, Test Data Curation — Fixed Sets and Generated Recipes, Watching a pinned upstream dependency, Adopting an upstream version bump, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Editing and HCI validation, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . Detect when a user request is a feature request (platform capability change) rather than a content request (writing, editing, reviewing folio content). When a feature request is detected, the agent works through requirements rather than implementing directly.

627.title: Applies when
627.content: Requirements that come from stakeholders who must sign them off, on work tied to a folio’s domain — WHO SMART Guidelines, an IG, a programme’s content. The requester is a content developer working through a BA, and the answer depends on what the folio says. Not for a platform capability change raised by somebody building the tooling with a content-agnostic answer — that is spec-kit.

628.title: Which requirements methodology — the fork this detection now carries
628.content: Detecting a feature request does not select CRDM by itself. There are two parallel requirements methodologies, and methodology-adoption forbids blending them. The signals below tell you a request needs requirements; this fork tells you whose. |   | governs | requester | the answer depends on | . | crdm — this methodology | stakeholder-facing WHO/IG work: needs assessment, BPA, stakeholder sign-off | content developers, via a BA | a folio’s subject matter | . | spec-kit (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) | folio-assistant feature development; software-development best practice, closer to a scrum process | tool developers | nothing a folio says — content-agnostic | . Most of the signals listed below are spec-kit’s, not CRDM’s — the “Platform-level change requests” and “Direct capability requests” categories especially, since both describe somebody building the tooling. Read the categories as this needs requirements, then apply the fork. Two things bind under either methodology and are not a reason to pick one: the issue-association rules at the end of this file, and the spec-before-code gate.

629.title: Detection signals
629.content: Scan every user request for these categories of phrasing. A single match is enough to flag; two or more from different categories is high confidence. Direct capability requests . Phrases where the user explicitly asks for new functionality: . | “I need a way to …”, “can you add …”, “we need a tool that …” | “there should be a skill for …”, “add a QA check for …” | “the renderer should support …”, “make the pipeline do …” | “can we add a new block kind for …”, “we need a content type for …” | “it would be great if the agent could …” | “the agent should …”, “the agent needs to …”, “we will need to …” | “build me …”, “create a tool …”, “develop a feature …” | . Workflow gap descriptions . Phrases where the user describes a process that does not work today: . | “right now I have to manually …”, “there is no way to …” | “the current process for … is broken”, “this workflow doesn’t handle …” | “we can’t do … yet”, “it’s missing …”, “it doesn’t support …” | “every time I need to …, I have to …” (manual workaround pattern) | “other people need to be able to …” | . Platform-level change requests . Phrases that imply changes to folio-assistant itself (not folio content): . | “change the schema to …”, “modify the pipeline …” | “add a new adapter …”, “the constraint should …” | “update the CI to …”, “the workflow should fire when …” | “the MCP tool needs to …”, “register a new tool for …” | “the upstream change requests to …”, “upstream asks” — a change asked of a tool this platform DEPENDS ON is still a platform change; the folio is not where it lands either way | References to files under schemas/, pipeline/, adapters/, src/, scripts/, .github/workflows/ | . Cross-cutting concerns . Phrases that affect multiple folios or content types: . | “for all papers …”, “every folio should …”, “across all content types …” | “when any user …”, “the platform should …” | “this needs to work for both document and paper folios” | . Review-surfaced needs . Phrases that emerge during content review: . | “this review process would be easier if …” | “we need a way to triage these comments …” | “the feedback workflow should …” | “stakeholders need to be able to see …” | “can we make the review process more …” | . A request for a plan . A request for a plan ALWAYS produces a requirements document and a work plan for review before implementation. | “plan”, “make a plan”, “plan the …” | “approach”, “what approach would you take” | “proposal”, “propose …” | “how would you …” | “come up with …” | . A plan request needs requirements under either methodology, and content requests are not exempt: “plan the edits to chapter 3” triggers it as surely as “plan the new validator”. The fork above still decides WHOSE requirements — this signal never selects a methodology and never blends them. The operation is the same for both and lives in the content layer, in the plan-request-gate skill (skill_fetch plan-request-gate): produce a requirements document and a work plan, put them where this methodology says (CRDM: committed under docs/proposals/), hand both over as absolute GitHub permalinks, and stop until sign-off is recorded on the issue. The definition of a requirement both methodologies share is the requirement-definition skill (skill_fetch requirement-definition). Self-declared genre . The mirror of "Migration record: …" below. Some documents say what they are in their own first line, and a proposal or a design document argues for a change that does not exist yet — which is a feature request whichever category its sentences fall into. | “Proposal: …” as a document’s OPENING line | “design document for …” | . Anchored to the opening line. On the adjudicated corpus an unanchored proposal adds no false alarm and catches one more item (a change register for pipeline changes not yet built). The anchor stays until an owner decides, because changing a detector to fit its own 27-item eval set is tuning to the test.

630.title: What is NOT a feature request
630.content: Do not trigger CRDM for: . | “Write the next section of chapter 3” — content authoring (but “plan the next section” is a plan request — see §”A request for a plan”) | “Fix the typo in the overview” — content editing | “Run content_validate” — tool invocation | “What does this block kind mean?” — information request | “Review chapter 5” — content review within existing workflow | “Create a bean for …” — work-plan management | “Migration record: …” — a record of work already DONE, not a request for work; the tense is the signal | Bug reports about existing features (unless they imply a redesign) | .

631.title: On detection — what to do
631.content: Do NOT use the term “CRDM” with the user. It is internal methodology jargon. If new session and the first request is a feature: . | Acknowledge the request as a feature/capability change | Explain that you will help them work through the requirements before building | Start Phase 1 (needs assessment) | . If existing session and the user is already in a CRDM cycle: . | Incorporate the new request into the current requirements document | Continue with the current phase | . If existing session and the user is doing content work (not in CRDM): . | Synthesise what you have heard as a feature need | Ask the user: . | “This sounds like a platform change rather than content work. Would you like to pause and work through the requirements now, or should I note it for later?” | If pause: enter CRDM Phase 1, return to content work when done | If later: create a work item with as much context as possible, linking to any relevant GitHub issue | . | .

632.title: Issue association
632.content: Feature work should be linked to a GitHub issue: . | Scan open issues for a match — search by title/body keywords | If match found — ask user: “This looks related to #NNN — should I add your requirements there?” | If no match in open issues — scan recently closed issues | If no match at all — ask the user to create an issue (do NOT create without permission) | Do not proceed without an issue link — the issue is where stakeholders do feature sign-off; without it, there is no review surface | . Requirements may span multiple issues. The agent should link to all relevant ones and note the relationship.

633.title: After implementation
633.content: When a PR is merged that addresses a feature from this process: . | Post a summary comment on the linked GitHub issue describing what the PR accomplished | PRs are for code review (agent and human coders, code reviewers) | Issues are for CRDM stakeholders — the requestor, the BA, and updates from the coding team for feature sign-off | Many work items per issue — they are not synonymous | .

634.title: A feature is a COLLABORATION you are joining, not a fix you are making
634.content: When a feature comes up in conversation, it starts or joins a collaborative design between this user, other users and authors, and other agents. It is not a one-off fix: put it into epics and stories, create or update the artefacts it needs, and link them from the owning harness’s docs/ page. The default that is wrong . A feature surfaces mid-conversation, the agent understands it, and the agent builds it, with the conversation standing in for requirements. Everything needed to review the decision — the alternatives, the reason, who else it affects — stays in a chat log nobody else will read. What to do instead . 1. Assume the conversation is not the first. Before treating a feature as new, look for the collaboration it belongs to: an open issue, an epic, a work item, a sibling session’s branch, a spec. This repository has many of each and they are cheap to search. A feature that arrives without a home usually has one. 2. There are OTHER PARTICIPANTS, and they are not all present. Other authors, other users, other agents working other branches. Two consequences: . | the record has to be legible to somebody who was not in the conversation — which is what the issue is FOR, as against the PR (code review) and the work item (work plan); | a sibling session may already be solving it. Check before you build, and if their answer differs from yours, that is a design discussion to have on the issue rather than a merge conflict to win. | . 3. Structure it: epics and stories, not a task. A feature that is worth doing is worth a place in the roadmap. This store’s hierarchy is milestone → epic → feature → task, and check-bean-parents enforces that every open work item has a home. A feature filed as a bare task with no parent lands in the roadmap’s Miscellaneous section, where it stops being planned. An epic cannot parent an epic here. When the subject already has an epic, the new work is a FEATURE under it — a second epic beside it splits one subject across two roots, which is how a roadmap becomes unreadable. 4. Write the artefacts, and LINK them from docs/, because an artefact nobody can navigate to is one nobody reads. The harness that owns the capability owns the link — so a change to cat-harness’s pipeline is linked from cat-harness’s docs/, not from wherever the agent happened to be working. Which harness owns it is usually answered by which layer declares the directory the change lands in. The test . If this session ended now, could somebody who was not in it pick the feature up — find what was decided, what is still open, and who else is affected — without reading the chat? . If the answer is no, the collaboration has not been joined yet, whatever has been built. What this does NOT mean . It does not mean every small change becomes an epic. The trigger is the same one opening-brief uses: irreversibility and surprise, not size. A one-line fix to a typo in a generated file is a fix. A one-line change to a schema that three layers resolve against is a feature, because other people have to live with it. Nor does it mean stopping work to do paperwork first. continual-progress still holds — branch, commit, push, open the PR from commit #1. The point is that the record is collaborative, not that the work pauses.

635.title: Related work first
635.content: When a requirement is initiated or updated in chat, find the related work before anything else. That means work items, issues and open PRs, each categorized and summarized, followed by one question to the user about whether and how to coordinate. The procedure is related-work-coordination (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc), and crdm-issue-linking.bpmn calls it as Process_RelatedWork.

650.title: Phase 1 — Needs assessment (detail)
650.content: Skill crdm-needs-assessment: Facilitate Phase 1 (Needs Assessment) of the CRDM requirements workflow. Guide the BA through stakeholder identification, source material gathering, and synthesising a domain-language needs statement. Post to the GitHub issue and iterate until the BA confirms the need is correctly captured. Named by: CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Options analysis, SWOT situation analysis, Requirements filing: promote, organise, trace, supersede, or retire, Questionnaire wireframe review, Guideline Updates . This skill expands the Phase 1 summary in crdm-requirements-workflow.md. The agent facilitates; the BA provides domain knowledge.

651.title: Identifying the requester
651.content: Determine who is asking and their role: . | Role | What they bring | . | BA / Feature Requestor | Domain knowledge, stakeholder access, sign-off authority | . | Content Author | First-hand experience with the gap | . | Managing Editor | Cross-folio perspective | . | Technical Reviewer / SME | Deep subject-matter expertise | . | Programme Lead | Strategic priority, resourcing | . The requester is the BA for this CRDM cycle. They interact with the agent; stakeholders interact with the BA.

652.title: Identifying stakeholders (systematic 4-step approach)
652.content: . | Check each active folio’s <name>.config.json roles — authors, editors, reviewers, contributors, affiliations | Check .github/CODEOWNERS — subsystem ownership | Check recent activity — gh issue list --search "...", gh pr list --search "..." for who’s been working in the area | Ask the BA directly: “Who else is affected by this change?” | . Categorise stakeholders: . | Approvers/Governance — must sign off (e.g. review committee) | Direct Operators — will use the feature daily | Downstream Consumers — affected indirectly (e.g. country adaptation teams) | .

653.title: Gathering source material
653.content: The request may arrive through any of these channels: . | Source | How to access | . | Chat messages in the current session | Current context | . | GitHub issue body or comment | gh issue view <number> | . | Uploaded document (Word, PDF) | uploads/ directory | . | Referenced document in library | library/ directory | . | Issue comment attachment | Download via gh | . | Pasted Teams/email discussion | Current context (motivation, not spec) | . Probing discipline: begin with the end in mind. Distinguish: . | Symptoms vs root causes | Workarounds vs missing capability | One user’s need vs shared need | .

654.title: Synthesising a needs statement
654.content: Every needs statement follows this structure: . | Current state — what exists today (specific, not vague) | Gap — what is missing or broken (the actual problem) | Desired outcome — what should happen after the feature | Who benefits and how — named roles, concrete improvements | Workflow rationale — how this fits the broader process | . No jargon (STRICT) . Write for business stakeholders and domain experts, not developers: . | ❌ Avoid | ✅ Use instead | . | Zod schema validation | “the system checks the structure” | . | AST traversal | “scanning the document” | . | TypeScript types | “the data format” | . | Pipeline stage | “processing step” | . | CLI flags | “options” | . | MCP tool | “assistant capability” | .

666.title: Requirements from a recorded walkthrough
666.content: Skill crdm-recorded-walkthrough: Turn a recorded requirements walkthrough (a video call where a business analyst demonstrates a feature and a stakeholder asks for changes) into CRDM Phase 3 requirements with evidence: transcripts compared, an independent transcript where one can be made, screenshots cut at the moments the speakers point at the screen, and every requirement traced to a timestamp. Use when someone uploads a meeting recording, a Teams/Zoom transcript (.vtt, .docx) or both, and asks for requirements from it. Named by: CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Options analysis, SWOT situation analysis, Requirements filing: promote, organise, trace, supersede, or retire, Questionnaire wireframe review, Guideline Updates . A walkthrough recording is the best source a CRDM round can have: the stakeholder reacting to a working thing, in their own words. It is also easy to over-trust, because a transcript reads like a record and is not one. The tool is cat-harness-tools/scripts/meeting-recording.py (stdlib + ffmpeg; --help per subcommand).

667.title: 1. Inventory what was actually uploaded
667.content: List the files before promising anything, because a request can promise a video that was not uploaded. A Teams .docx transcript never contains the shared screen; its images are speaker avatars. Say what is missing, do what can be done, and list what waits for the missing file.

668.title: 2. Two exports of one recognition are one transcript
668.content: meeting-recording.py compare A B gives word similarity and where they differ. | pair | similarity | what the differences were | . | Teams .docx against its .vtt | 0.980 | interjections in another cue; words joined at a .docx line break | . | Vosk small-en (independent) against Teams | 0.802 | mostly Vosk’s errors, but also Teams’ (“Lightner” → Leitner, “philtres” → filters) | . The first number is not confirmation: both files carry every word Teams misheard. Only an independent recognition can disagree with it. A lower similarity from a weaker model is expected and still useful, because what you read is where they disagree, filtered with --keys to names and domain terms. Record the names the recogniser mangled (“Tini”, “Jiun” for Chinni; “Saroop” / “Swarupu” unresolved) in the requirements document, and ask rather than guess any name neither transcript settles.

669.title: 3. An independent transcript, offline
669.content: meeting-recording.py transcribe VIDEO --model DIR --out vosk.json needs the vosk package (PyPI) and a model directory. It downloads nothing. In a sandbox whose proxy refuses Hugging Face and the Vosk model host, find a model already packaged somewhere the network allows, take only the model files, and never run code that came with them.

670.title: 4. Screenshots: where the screen changed and where a speaker points
670.content: . | scenes VIDEO --min-gap 10 lists when the shared screen changed. | Grep the transcript for deictic phrases: “you can see”, “here”, “this”, “looking at the screen”, “select these”. Their timestamps are the candidates; a scene change a second or two later is the frame to take. | frames VIDEO --at 1:52,2:26 --out DIR --crop W:H:X:Y --width 1280 --webp. Crop out the participants’ camera tiles: a requirements document needs the screen, not the faces. Check the crop on one frame first. | Look at every frame you keep. A frame cut for one thing can show a defect or a requirement that is already half-built, and either changes the requirements document. | WebP at quality 80 cut nine 1280-wide frames from 2.8 MB to 476 KB. | .

671.title: 5. From transcript to requirements
671.content: Follow crdm-requirements-template. In addition, for a recording: . | Every requirement cites a timestamp, and every defect the demo exposed is listed separately from the requirements, with the timestamp and “not yet reproduced” until it is. | Say what already exists (Today:) for each requirement, measured against the code or the data, not recalled. | Who signs off is part of the requirement set. Ask who it is if the recording does not say. | Do not build from the recording. A speaker telling the recording agent “implement them on a staging site” is a requirement about the process (P-1), not approval of the requirements. | .

This skill expands the Phase 3 summary in crdm-requirements-workflow.md and applies the crdm methodology.

680.title: Requirement format
680.content: One definition, shared with spec-kit: a statement, a conformance level, a source, at least one success criterion with its verification method, and a sign-off owner — the requirement-definition skill (skill_fetch requirement-definition) in the content layer. The fields below are CRDM’s rendering of it; Acceptance criteria are the success criteria. A requirement with none is not ready to post. Each requirement has: . | Field | Format | Example | . | ID | REQ-### | REQ-001 | . | Title | Short phrase | “Beans filtered by epic type” | . | Description | Plain language, no jargon | “The agent can filter work items by their type (epic, story, task)” | . | Conformance | SHALL / SHOULD / MAY / SHALL NOT (RFC 2119 / RFC 8174) | SHALL | . | Acceptance criteria (= success criteria, ≥ 1) | Testable, measurable, each with a key and a verification method (test / inspection / review / analysis) | “SC-1 (test) — Given an epic with 3 child stories, when filtered by epic, then all 3 appear” | . | Sign-off owner | Who says it is met — a named person or role | “The BA” | . | Priority | Must-have (High) / Should-have (Medium) / Nice-to-have (Low) | Must-have (High) | . | Source | Phase 1 needs statement / Phase 2 process activity ref | “Needs statement §2 — BA cannot see work grouped by release” | . | Impact | Phase 4 footprint | “Schema: new type field on bean. Pipeline: none” | . | Estimated scope | Work item count / PR sizing | “2 beans, 1 PR” | . Priority scale and conformance keywords . CRDM separates implementation priority (how essential a requirement is when sequencing work or trading off scope) from normative conformance (how strictly an implementation must behave once it claims conformance to that requirement): . 1. Priority scale (High / Medium / Low = Must-have / Should-have / Nice-to-have) . Aligned with PHII’s Defining and Validating System Requirements Guide (library/phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, p. 2) and PATH & PHII (2012) (library/path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm, p. 1): . | Priority label | PHII / PATH CRDM scale | Meaning | . | Must-have (Must) | High | Essential to the core business process; the system cannot satisfy the process goal without this capability. | . | Should-have (Should) | Medium | Important for operational efficiency or completeness; expected in standard operation, though a temporary workaround may exist. | . | Nice-to-have (Nice-to-have) | Low | Desirable enhancement that improves convenience or secondary workflows when resources permit. | . 2. Normative conformance keywords (SHALL / SHOULD / MAY / SHALL NOT) . While PHII’s informal prose grammar phrases requirement statements as “The system must or should…” (phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, p. 1), the separate Conformance field uses uppercase normative keywords governed by IETF BCP 14 — library/rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels (RFC 2119) and library/rfc8174-uppercase-vs-lowercase-2119-key-words (RFC 8174, specifying that only UPPERCASE words carry RFC 2119 normative meaning): . | SHALL (MUST) — mandatory requirement of the specification | SHOULD (RECOMMENDED) — recommended; valid reasons may exist in particular circumstances to ignore, but full implications must be understood and weighed | MAY (OPTIONAL) — truly optional capability | SHALL NOT (MUST NOT) — absolute prohibition | .

681.title: Generating from conversation
681.content: 4-step elicitation . | Listen and deconstruct — identify the nouns (entities), verbs (capabilities), and adjectives (qualities) in the BA’s description | Disentangle what from how — “I need to see beans grouped by release” is a requirement; “use a Jekyll page” is an implementation choice | Formulate testable criteria — every requirement must have a Given/When/Then or a checkable statement | Validate with the BA — read it back. “Does this capture what you need? Anything missing?” | .

682.title: The document is a requirement set
682.content: The requirements document as a whole is a RequirementSet (bootstrap-tools/schemas/requirement-set.ts, published as bootstrap/schemas/requirement-set.schema.json): reqset:<slug>, the methodology, the issue, a stage — draft → proposed → approved → planned → in-progress → delivered → accepted, or rejected, cancelled, superseded — its members (req: references, each with its own decision), its work plan (work item ids) and its sign-offs. Commit it beside the proposal as <slug>.requirement-set.json, or as a requirementSet: key in the proposal’s front matter; check:requirements judges it. The set’s stage and each member’s status are independent — a requirement outlives the document that proposed it — with one link enforced: a set is accepted only when every member it approved is in-force. The stage moves only through a sign-off (Phase 5’s BA_Signoff, close-out’s BA_Confirm), and check:requirements refuses approved/accepted without a human sign-off, planned without work items, and cancelled without a reason.

684.title: Posting to the issue
684.content: Format as a markdown checklist: . ## Requirements — [Feature name] ### Must-have - [ ] **REQ-001** (SHALL) — Beans filtered by epic type - _Source:_ needs statement §2 - _Acceptance:_ `SC-1` (test) — Given an epic, when `beans list --type epic`, then only epics appear - _Sign-off owner:_ the BA - _Scope:_ 1 bean, 1 PR - [ ] **REQ-002** (SHALL) — Release lifecycle skill - _Source:_ needs statement §3 - _Acceptance:_ `SC-1` (inspection) — Skill exists at `cat-harness/sdlc/skills/sdlc-core/release-lifecycle.md` - _Sign-off owner:_ the BA - _Scope:_ 1 bean, 1 PR ### Should-have - [ ] **REQ-003** — ... ### Deliverables summary | ID | Title | Priority | Beans | Status |---|---|---|---|---| REQ-001 | Beans filtered by epic type | Must | 1 | ⬜ | REQ-002 | Release lifecycle skill | Must | 1 | ⬜ | . UI / wireframe . Every requirement set carries this section, filled or marked not applicable. When a requirement changes a rendered surface (a page, a visualiser, the navbar, a form, an app screen), the wireframe is designed and chosen before implementation, by wireframe-design-review in Design use; its output (schemas/skills/wireframe-design-review/output.schema.json) supplies every row: . ### UI / wireframe - _Surface:_ the review page's heat map (REQ-004, REQ-005) - _Candidates:_ `docs/proposals/<slug>/wireframes/` — assets of this proposal - `a.html` — [staging](https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/blob/main/skills/process/crdm/%E2%80%A6) · web ![](https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/blob/main/skills/process/crdm/%E2%80%A6/checks/a-web.png) · mobile ![](https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/blob/main/skills/process/crdm/%E2%80%A6/checks/a-mobile.png) - `b.html` — [staging](https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/blob/main/skills/process/crdm/%E2%80%A6) · web ![](https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/blob/main/skills/process/crdm/%E2%80%A6/checks/b-web.png) · mobile ![](https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/blob/main/skills/process/crdm/%E2%80%A6/checks/b-mobile.png) - _Chosen:_ `b` by @requester ([where they chose](https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness/blob/main/skills/process/crdm/%E2%80%A6): the conversation, the issue or the PR), because …; `a` rejected because … .
