903.title: Evidence Appraisal
903.content: Named by: Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes, Translation review and adjudication, Translation Workflow, Review task, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, KG to public portal, Remote-mount a dependency, Publish an ArchiMate model — every picture derived from it, Publish a web app — declared, translated, built at its own route, Authoring a document, Content Change and Review, Content lifecycle, Draft, review and publish, Editing and HCI validation, Evidence for a recommendation, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Public comment on a review draft, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Board: place a note . Appraise and grade a body of evidence against the grading system the folio declares. This skill supplies the procedure; it does not supply the system.

904.title: Why this skill names no grading system
904.content: Which grading system applies is a methodological commitment of the folio and the body that publishes it; the platform holds no subject matter, and a hardcoded system would leave every folio that uses another one working around the platform. An evidence-retrieval process in the content layer judges certainty “per the grading system the folio declares”. This skill covers what appraisal is, what it attaches to, and what has to survive as a record afterwards. Domain layers supply concrete grading systems as refinement skills and code lists (certainty levels, rating reasons, recommendation strength). Each applies only when declared, never as a default; with nothing declared, appraisal is refused.

905.title: Responsibilities
905.content: . | Appraise the body of evidence assembled for one question, not a citation | Record the grade with its reasons, not as a bare label | Distinguish “the evidence is weak” from “there is not enough to judge” | Re-appraise when the body changes, and say what moved the grade | Refuse to grade when no system is declared, rather than picking one | .

906.title: The unit is the body, not the citation
906.content: The grade attaches to the body of evidence for one PICO question. This is why appraisal sits after retrieval’s parallel join and not inside the fan-out: the three retrieval classes (trusted L1 sources, trusted L2/L3 content, data repositories) contribute to one judgement; grading each branch separately would produce three numbers that answer no question. A single citation does not carry a certainty grade.

907.title: “Cannot appraise” is a third state
907.content: Three outcomes; “not appraisable” is not a low grade: . | outcome | means | . | graded | the body was appraised and carries a certainty | . | not appraisable | too little retrieved, or no declared system, or the question was not framed as PICO | . | gap recorded | nothing authoritative was found, and that is the finding | . Never collapse “not appraisable” into the lowest grade: “we looked and the evidence is poor” is not “we could not look”. A recommendation resting on the first is weak; one resting on the second is unsupported.

908.title: Inputs
908.content: . | The framed PICO question — without it the search is not reproducible and the appraisal is not checkable | Candidates that passed an authority check, so authority is a resolved fact rather than an assertion in the citation | The grading system declared by the folio | .

909.title: Outputs
909.content: . | A certainty judgement for the body, in the declared system’s own vocabulary | The reasons, in enough detail that a later reader can tell whether they would still hold (decision-audit); a grade without them cannot be reviewed, only re-litigated | Any gap, recorded as a gap rather than as a low grade | .

910.title: This has nothing to do with formal content
910.content: A graded body of empirical evidence is never an input to a formal deductive proof. In a content type with a formal proof layer, a formal claim’s assertion is discharged by its machine-checked proof sibling and by nothing else; certainty grading belongs to empirical guidance about the world, where the question is what the evidence supports. An empirical grade in a formal proof obligation is a category error.

911.title: Actors
911.content: . | Author / guideline developer (lead) | Domain SME (domain judgement, supplied by the content-type layer) | Content Reviewer (checks the grade’s reasons survive, not the grade itself) | .

919.title: Evidence review — the same rule, a second instance
919.content: Skill evidence-review: Evidence review as an instance of untainted verification — the separation of the appraising party from the drafting party, what recurring surveillance in a living guideline shares with a stale QA verdict, and which of guideline methodology’s rules are fenced rather than shipped. Named by: Is the incremental IG AST what a full build would have produced?, Incremental IG build, L3 FHIR IG pipeline, Make a decided public comment change, Contributor feedback on a working draft . Skill id: evidence-review · Package: folio-core . untainted-verification states a generic discipline. Evidence review — the appraisal of the evidence behind a recommendation — is one instance of it; the translation round trip is another. Two unrelated instances are evidence that the discipline is generic, where one would only be an example.

920.title: The rule
920.content: The party that drafted the recommendation does not write the evidence appraisal for it. Guideline methodology already separates the systematic review team from the guideline development group for the same reason: a party assessing its own output is comparing a thing with its own paraphrase of itself. | untainted-verification | here | . | producer | whoever drafts the recommendation | . | checker — given the artefact, and nothing that would let it shortcut | the appraisal, given the question and the evidence, not the draft’s conclusion | . | adjudicator — given the intent and the checker’s output, never the artefact | the evidence-to-decision judgement | . An appraiser shown the drafted recommendation is told the answer before being asked the question; its “the evidence supports it” measures the instruction, not the literature.

921.title: Recurring surveillance is staleness, generalised
921.content: A living guideline is updated as evidence appears, so its appraisal is a verdict with an expiry. A QA verdict is hashed to its subject and stales when the subject is edited; a living-guideline verdict stales when the evidence base changes, even though the subject did not. The field_hash covers only inputs in the repository; an external corpus is not covered. Either way, “verified on DATE against THESE inputs” is a different claim from “verified”, because a reader given the second cannot tell a current verdict from a lapsed one. A folio implementing surveillance gives each verdict an explicit expiry, as bean-blocking (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan) does for a block: a verdict with no expiry cannot be told from an abandoned one.

922.title: The fencing analysis — which rules are the platform’s, and which are not
922.content: Run through domain-fencing (opt-in cat-harness.kg-ops)’s three questions, in order, first-to-answer wins: . | candidate rule | Q1 rationale survives translation? | Q2 domain in mechanism or vocabulary? | Q3 needs the domain installed? | verdict | . | appraiser ≠ drafter | yes, word for word | vocabulary | no | platform — it IS the spine | . | a verdict carries what it was verified against, and when | yes — it is the field_hash argument | vocabulary | no | platform | . | a finding is upheld by opening the cited source, never by trusting the rule’s wording | yes | vocabulary | no | platform — and already the practice in voice-who-guideline-development | . | certainty rated across the GRADE domains | no | mechanism | yes | fence | . | PICO question formulation | no | mechanism | yes | fence | . | evidence-to-decision framework tables | no | mechanism | yes | fence | . | a search strategy is re-runnable — databases, dates, query recorded | yes in rationale | mechanism is bibliographic | yes | fence the mechanism, keep the rationale (it is the row above) | . Three rows are platform rules; the four fenced rows are a folio’s methodology, not a backlog. Nothing is shipped for the fenced rows — empty criteria would let a consumer scan nothing and report a clean run. A folio that wants them declares them in its own repository.

923.title: What this skill does NOT do
923.content: It asserts no clinical or empirical claim, and the platform must not. The mechanism carries process — who may rule on what, given what. The evidence is the folio’s and the judgement is the guideline group’s; a platform that shipped a default answer to either would be asserting on their behalf.

926.content: Skill external-registry-contract: The contract the external-registry role is held to: what a trusted registry outside this layer must provide for a portal to verify what it received, and what the verifier does when it cannot. The narrowest contract the diagrams require. A mechanical role’s skill is a contract to test against, not instructions to read. Named by: KG to public portal, Evidence for a recommendation . external-registry in scenarios/roles.json is played by an external actor: trusted registries and observatories outside this layer’s control. A role played by something we do not run is still a role, and its skills are its contract: what we rely on it to do. A contract is not an instruction; it is what the diagrams assume.

929.content: An unreachable registry is unknown, never a pass: GW_Verified routes it as it routes a mismatch, to the last good version (End_Rejected). This side of the contract is ours, and it is what makes relying on a party we do not control safe. Needs the owner’s review: this contract is inferred from one diagram. The test in tested-by: holds the side of it that is ours: one lane names this role, it holds P_Verify and GW_Verified, and GW_Verified serves the bytes only on a match, sending every other answer to End_Rejected. Lines 1 and 2 above are the registry’s own behaviour on a network this repository does not reach, and nothing here tests them.

932.title: When to use this skill
932.content: When a content change is being reviewed and the reviewer (or the author) needs to see the rendered result before merging. The staging deployment puts the feature branch’s rendered site at: . https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/branches/<branch-slug>/ . A preview is the general publication step with a different root. The push itself is render-kg-to-cdn with branches/<branch-slug>/ as the publication root URL and the gh-pages Tool as the target — the same step a release takes with the site root. What this skill owns is everything around that call: the slug, the banner and staging.json, the render log, the PR comment, and taking the preview down. Which site — the repository the change lives in . <owner>/<repo> above is the repository that holds the change, not the repository of the index the agent happens to be working in. Read that repository’s index.config.json first: . | the change lives in | its preview is at | published by | . | a repository with its own site (its index.config.json has a site entry) | https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/branches/<slug>/, and the root from its default branch | that repository: stage-local.ts --repo . from its checkout when it declares site.agentRun (below), else its own staging.yml | . | a layer an index mounts and publishes as part of its own site (no site of its own) | branches/<slug>/ on the index’s site | a staging re-pin: a pull request on the index that points the mount at the branch’s commit, recorded with bun run cat mount:remote --staging (basis staging, no consent needed) | . A repository with a site of its own is previewed there, even when an index also mounts it. The index’s site shows it as one layer among its layers, which is the wrong page for that repository’s reviewers. If the repository’s own build cannot run yet (its publisher refuses for a missing cache or an undeclared input), say what is missing and ask. Never fall back to the index’s site in silence.

933.title: How it works
933.content: 1. Feature branch → staging deployment . When an agent pushes to a feature branch with an open pull request, drafts included, feature-staging.yml automatically: . | Builds the docs site (Jekyll + TypeDoc + BPMN diagrams) | Writes the build’s facts — commit SHA, timestamp, branch, PR, issue, build log — once, to staging.json at the preview root | Injects a constant staging banner at the top of every HTML page, which reads those facts in the browser | Comments on the PR that the preview is staged and queued, with the earliest push time and when it should be live | Waits for the rate-limit window (§8), then deploys to gh-pages/branches/<branch-slug>/ only the files that differ from the live site (staging-share.ts apply). The preview’s staging-sw.js serves the rest from the live site in the browser and puts the banner back on its pages; the live site’s root 404.html (staging-share.ts write-404, written by docs-site.yml) installs that worker for a deep link opened before it exists. A page is shared only when it matches the live one once the per-preview edits are set aside (banner, SEO strip, fa-staging and fa-search-index, TypeDoc’s title suffix); anything else keeps the preview’s own copy. The footer build stamp is filled in the browser on every build, the live site’s from build.json, so an unchanged page is byte-identical across deploys | Rewrites the same comment: pushed at a time, live by about five minutes later | . 2. The staging banner . Every staged page carries a muted-sage banner: . 🔀 FEATURE BRANCH — claude/update-schedule · commit a1b2c3d · built 2026-09-18T00:30:00Z · PR #42 · issue #215 · compare with main ↗ · build log . Its colour, #4F6F52, measures 5.63:1 against its white text, above the 4.5:1 WCAG AA threshold. Check any replacement the same way; the pale decorator sages (#9CAF88, #87A96B) land near 2.5:1. The facts are fetched, not baked — and that is a storage decision . cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-banner.ts injects a fragment that is byte-identical on every page and across every rebuild, and the browser derives its preview root from location.pathname, fetches staging.json and fills the banner in. A per-build value in the fragment makes every page unique on every build, so each re-push adds the whole site to gh-pages as new objects. Three rules: . | Nothing per-build may go back into the fragment. staging-banner-constant.test.ts runs two builds with different facts and compares the emitted bytes, so any leak fails regardless of how it is spelled. Add the fact to staging.json instead. | A failed fetch must still say PREVIEW. The static markup carries “FEATURE BRANCH” before any fetch happens, and the fetch only ever ADDS detail. “Could not determine” is never rendered as “this is the real site” — the same third-state rule the rest of the repository runs on, and here the failure mode is a reviewer approving the wrong artefact. | Every value from the JSON goes in as textContent, never as markup. Git ref names may contain <, > and " — they are not in git’s forbidden set, which stops at space, ~, ^, :, ?, *, [, \ and the control characters. staging-banner.e2e.ts pins this with a branch name carrying an onerror payload. | . Pages still differ between previews, because Jekyll’s relative_url prepends the baseurl to ~235 hrefs per page and the fa-translation-index island publishes site.baseurl to JavaScript. Both are coupled to the language switcher. 3. Commit SHA stamping — and the four fields staging must NOT write . Both builds write docs/_data/build.yml, and they do not write the same fields. The difference is deliberate: it is the second half of the deduplication above. |   | docs-site.yml (main) | feature-staging.yml (a preview) | . | sha, short_sha, built_at, run_url | written | DELIBERATELY ABSENT | . | branch, staging, staging_slug, pr_number, search_index | — | written | . Why staging omits them. site-chrome/_includes/footer_custom.html renders short_sha, built_at and run_url into the footer of every page, so writing them per build changes every page on every deploy. The client fills those three in from the same staging.json the banner already fetches — one request, two consumers — and a failed fetch leaves Jekyll’s | default: 'dev' in place rather than blanking the footer, which is the same third state §”The facts are fetched, not baked” requires of the banner. On main there is one copy and nothing to deduplicate, so the include’s own reason stands: “a stale browser cache and a deploy that has not run look identical.” . Adding a per-build field back to the staging stamp will not fail a test. staging-banner-constant.test.ts compares the banner fragment, which is genuinely constant; the footer is not in it, because it lives in a Jekyll include rather than in the workflow’s injection step. Check the deploy commits on gh-pages, not the code, to confirm pages do not differ across rebuilds. A Jekyll layout can read site.data.build.sha to display the deployed version — on main. Under a preview, read it from staging.json. 4. Before/after comparison . The reviewer opens both URLs side by side: . | Surface | URL | What it shows | . | Main (current) | <pages-url>/ | The published state on main | . | Staging (proposed) | <pages-url>/branches/<slug>/ | The feature branch’s changes | . The commit SHA on each page confirms exactly what is being compared. 5. Cleanup . When the PR is merged or closed, the cleanup job in feature-staging.yml removes branches/<slug>/ from gh-pages so stale previews don’t accumulate. The full retention rules — merged vs closed-unmerged, the label, the dispatch — are in staging-review §”Staging retention”. 6. The cap — 3 GB of previews in total, the oldest rotated off . Previews are capped by size, at 3 GB in total, and the oldest are rotated off. The cap is by size rather than count because one preview can run to hundreds of megabytes. Per-PR cleanup bounds nothing in total, every preview is a full copy of the site, and a gh-pages branch past GitHub’s 10 GB Pages limit freezes the live site. So every stage run, inside its push loop, runs cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-rotate.ts: it stamps the preview it is staging (branches/<slug>/.staged-at), keeps that one plus the most recently updated others while the total fits MAX_PREVIEW_BYTES (3 GB, 3 x 1024^3 bytes, defined there and nowhere else), and removes the rest, oldest first — each with a removed render-log entry, its record retired into branches/_retired/, and a line (slug, age, size) in the commit message and job log. _retired/ and non-preview entries are never touched. Two things to know when editing it: . | The push loop re-reads gh-pages on every attempt; it does not rebase. The commit carries removals decided against one read of the branch, and a replayed removal is a stale one — it could delete a preview another run has just refreshed. Same shape as publish-gh-pages.sh. | A rotated-off preview is regenerated by the next push to its PR branch. It can reach an OPEN PR’s preview; the cost is a 404 until the author pushes, not lost work. Detail and the reviewer’s remedy: staging-review §”The cap”. | . 7. The cone — a preview rebuilds only what a changed file can reach . A preview rebuilds only the dependency cone of the changed files, at FILE level, with each derived directory’s generator declared as writer. The rule is general across rendered kinds. A rendered directory is in the cone when a changed file is . | under its own path (its pages, or its source data), or | in the import closure of a writer it declares, or under a writer directory (a path ending in /: what a generator reads, such as its templates, rather than imports), or | in a directory it is derivedFrom, transitively (check:derived-from --downstream <instance/id> prints that half on its own). | . cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-cone.ts computes it; compose-docs.ts carriedInstances applies it to the composed layers. Three rules: . | Any doubt carries. No file list, a writer that does not exist, or an import that does not resolve carries the directory, with the reason in the build log. A preview missing the pages under review misleads a reviewer, while an oversized one only costs bytes. | A computed import() is bounded, not ignored. It can load only a module, so it carries on a changed module file and never on a page. The two such sites a generator reaches today (harness-config.ts’s contributes loader and block-module.ts’s block loader) have DECLARED targets and are walked exactly; DECLARED_COMPUTED_IMPORTS lists them. | The instance-prefix match is a floor. The cone can only add to it. Narrowing below it is a separate decision, made once the cone has been measured in previews. | . A skill-only change carries no IG; a change to gen-ig-pages.ts or to the DAK layer’s themes/chrome.json carries all three. staging-cone.test.ts holds these cases as tests. Built sites follow the same rule. An IG’s own Jekyll site and its AST site are BUILT in the preview from an upstream repository pinned in the layer’s own files, not composed from the checkout. stage-ig-sites.ts and stage-ast-sites.ts take --changed-files and stage only the layers siteInCone reaches. Its reasons, in order: no file list; a change to the build environment (SITE_ENVIRONMENT: the docs Gemfile and this workflow); a change under the layer; the cone reaching any of the layer’s directories (a theme change arrives this way); or a change in the stager’s closure. Each decision is printed with its reason. When you add a generated directory, declare its writer and derivedFrom. Without them the cone cannot reach it through code or data, and the prefix floor is all it gets. 8. The rate limit — a preview never cancels the main site’s Pages build . Staging previews are pushed to gh-pages at a limited rate. GitHub’s pages build and deployment keeps only the NEWEST run, so every push cancels the build in flight, the main site’s included; a build takes about three minutes. So before each push attempt the stage job re-reads gh-pages and runs cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-push-gate.ts gate, which holds the push until the branch tip is old enough: . | tip of gh-pages | wait until it is | . | a staging commit (staging(...)) | STAGING_WINDOW_MS — 5 min | . | anything else: the main-site publish, publish.yml, any other publisher | MAIN_WINDOW_MS — 10 min | . The numbers live once, in that script. Exit 75 means it slept until the window should open (plus up to a minute of jitter) and the loop must re-read and ask again; exit 1 means the job has waited MAX_WAIT_MS (two hours) and fails rather than pushing; exit 2 is an unreadable tip, never read as open. Three things to know when editing it: . | git’s fast-forward rule is the lock. Two jobs that both find the window open both build on the same tip; one push is rejected, re-reads, finds a tip younger than the window, and waits. So at most one staging push lands per window with no shared state. A rejection whose tip MOVED is therefore a lost race, sent back to the gate without spending one of the three attempts; only a rejection with the tip unmoved counts as a failure. | No concurrency group, and none should be added. Every waiting preview would pend in one group and each arrival would cancel the last. The per-branch group at the workflow level stays: a newer push to the same PR cancels a preview still waiting at the gate, so a superseded preview is never pushed at all. | A staging push BEFORE a main-site push is harmless; only one AFTER it cancels the build that matters. The main push then cancels the staging build, and the build that runs carries both. That is why the gate looks at the tip, and why it does not wait for docs-site runs that have not pushed yet. | . A rate limit is used rather than a batching flush job because the gate is one script and one loop whose correctness rests on git, while a flush job needs a second workflow, an artifact round trip per preview, a record of what is deployed, a best-effort schedule and a write token over content built from a pull request. The cost is latency under load: with K previews waiting, the last one pushes about 5 × K minutes later, and the PR comment gives its own estimate. The cleanup and cleanup-dispatch jobs do NOT pass through the gate. They push once per closed PR rather than once per push. 9. Build types — preview and full . There are two build types. A public comment (PC) build is a full build, and so is a release. | build type | used for | builds | . | preview | every pull request’s branches/<slug>/ preview | only what the change can reach (the cone, §7); every whole-corpus index is main’s copy, put back rather than rebuilt | . | full | the main site deploy, a public comment release, a release | everything; every index rebuilt from the tree being published | . An index is computed over the whole corpus: the search index, the LSI viewer, the SQLite slices, the handler index, the glossary pages, the translation status pages and the node-kind pages. A builtAtPublish entry says so with index: true; a writer is borrowed only when every entry it writes says so. Rebuilding an index in a preview shows the reviewer almost nothing and costs minutes, so in a preview derive:publish puts back main’s copy from main’s writer-cone recording and logs borrowed <writer>; the search index is served from main the same way (§”Serve the published search index” in the preview workflow). So a preview of a glossary, translation or node-kind change shows main’s copy of those pages: review such a change on a full build (dispatch with build_type: full) or in its source. The switch is CAT_BUILD_TYPE (cat-harness-tools/scripts/lib/build-type.ts). Any doubt builds full: unset means full, and a value that is neither word is refused. A preview whose main recording holds no copy of an index builds it. A public comment release must be frozen from a full build. A frozen release is cited by page and line for the whole comment period, so its search and slices must describe the draft, not main. Dispatch the preview workflow for the branch with build_type: full, then run pc:release freeze. Freeze refuses a copy whose staging.json says buildType: "preview", and records the build type in release.json. 10. Agent-built previews — deferred on the critical path, verified by a full CI rebuild . When an agent builds and pushes a preview with stage-local.ts, it writes branches/<slug>/_build-record.json (scripts/preview-record.ts) recording builder: "agent", the git tree hash tree of the source tree it built (HEAD^{tree} or the merge tree with origin/main), the head and base commit SHAs, and the SHA-256 of every deployed file outside the per-build metadata (staging.json, _build-record.json, .staged-at, build.yml). When feature-staging.yml runs on the pull request: . | Defer on the critical path. conflict-gate checks branches/<slug>/_build-record.json on gh-pages. When builder is "agent" and record.tree equals MERGE_SHA^{tree} (refs/pull/<n>/merge), the preview is already live for that exact merge tree: the workflow sets the preview/agent-build commit status on the PR head to pending, posts a <!-- preview-build-verify --> notice on the PR, and skips the critical-path stage build so the runner is free. Any missing record, CI-built record, or tree mismatch (including when main moved under the branch) builds on the critical path as usual. | Verify off the critical path. preview-verify-sweep.yml (triggered when feature-staging.yml completes and on a 15-minute schedule) checks that no Feature Staging run is queued or in progress, finds the oldest open PR whose head commit has preview/agent-build in state pending, and dispatches feature-staging.yml with verify_pr=<number>. | Compare or replace. The verify run rebuilds refs/pull/<n>/merge in full and runs preview-record.ts compare against the agent’s _build-record.json on gh-pages: . | Files match (same=true): nothing is redeployed; preview/agent-build is set to success (or failure if a built-site check failed) and the PR comment records the verified tree. | Files differ (same=false) or the base moved (same=stale): CI’s build is deployed to branches/<slug>/ (guarded so a newer preview tree is never overwritten) with a rendered log entry, and when the agent’s build differed, preview/agent-build is set to failure with the differing file paths listed in the PR comment. | Merge guard: merge-guard check 5 (src/coordinator/merge-guard.ts) reads preview/agent-build alongside check runs; pending holds the PR as not ready, and failure refuses the merge. | . | .

934.title: Agent workflow
934.content: When an author requests a content change: . | Detect scope — use content-graph and integration-watcher to identify affected blocks and downstream implications | Create feature branch — branch from main, open PR immediately | Make changes — edit content blocks, deterministic logic, translations | Push — on a folio whose staging.yml runs on push, the staging deployment happens automatically. On an agent-run repository, run stage-local.ts (below). | Report staging URL — tell the author the preview is at <pages-url>/branches/<slug>/ | Iterate — each push updates the staging deployment with a new SHA | . The BPMN for this workflow is the content core’s processes/content/content-change-review.bpmn. Publishing without a runner — stage-local.ts, one command . When the Actions queue is backed up, the agent can build and publish itself: it already has the checkout, the platform and bun. On an agent-run repository (below) this is not a shortcut. It is the only publish path. It is one command for a preview and for the main site, for a folio and for a FHIR IG: . bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/stage-local.ts --repo <repo> --plan # what it would do; nothing built bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/stage-local.ts --repo <repo> --dry-run # build, compose the commit, push nothing bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/stage-local.ts --repo <repo> # build and push bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/stage-local.ts --repo <repo> --artifact <dir> . It prints its plan first, every time: which workflow it mirrors, where the output lands, what it replaces and what it keeps, the commit message, and what it does not run. The size review. Owner, 2026-11-10: “add size review as part of authoring process”. Every build, preview or main, prints a size report before its push (site-size.ts, bun run cat site:size). The report gives the total against the published root, the top directories, the size by extension, the biggest files, byte-identical duplicates, source maps, the directories named after another layer of index.lock.json, and the directories the shared-assets host could serve. It writes site-size.json beside the build, never into the site. The review is advisory: growth over 10% or 10 MB is a warning, and nothing is refused. Read the report before you hand over the preview. The usual culprits each have one fix: . | another layer’s pages copied in: link that layer’s own site; | the same bytes under several names: publish one index, and serve each file once; | vendored libraries: serve them from the shared-assets host; | .map files: do not publish them. | . When the growth holds and none of these fixes applies, raise a decision card with the owner, with the comparison line and the top contributing directories on it. Which publisher is read from the repository’s own workflow files, from the reusable workflow each one calls: . | a caller of folio-staging.yml is a folio. The build inputs (build_command, site_dir, publish_branch, …) are read from that caller. | a caller of a reusable workflow that a mounted layer declares as a site publisher is that publisher’s kind. The IG layer declares one: a caller of its fhirbuild.yml or ghbuild.yml is an IG, published by that layer’s own code, which stage-local.ts reaches through the layer’s declared site-publisher-ig pipeline slot and never by path. The reusable workflow is fetched at the ref the caller names, and its build job is run step by step as written: run: blocks with the environment a runner gives them, docker:// steps in their image. Steps that read a secret, push to the source branch, or need an Actions runtime are skipped, and the plan names each one with its reason. fhirbuild.yml itself only triggers build.fhir.org’s auto-build, so the Pages build is the ghbuild.yml beside it, and the plan says so. | a repository that calls both (smart-ra carries an IG under input/) gets the folio, unless --publisher ig is given. The folio owns the publish root. An IG’s root deploy is a clean one, and it is refused on a publish branch that holds a folio’s branches/, _render-log/ or _main-site.json. | . Main site or preview follows the branch, as the workflows do. The default branch publishes the main site; any other branch publishes a preview. --main says the same explicitly, and it is refused off the default branch. The main site is published only from a HEAD that is the pushed tip of the default branch. |   | folio | IG | . | preview | branches/<slug>/, replaced wholesale; held by the rate-limit gate (§8); commit staging(<slug>): from <sha>; render log staging-preview | branches/<last path component>/, nothing deleted; commit Deploy candidate branch | . | main site | the root, through publish-main-site.ts: only the files the last publish’s _main-site.json lists are replaced, and branches/, _render-log/ and anything a person put at the root are kept; commit main-site: from <sha>; render log main-site for / | the root, cleaned except for the deploy step’s clean-exclude (branches, sitepreview) and the action’s own exclusions; commit Deploy main branch | . Every path refuses an empty build before it deletes anything. | Pushing removes the first wait and not the second. Pages deploys on a runner, so say the page is live once that deploy has run, never sooner. | --artifact <dir>: no GitHub at all. It writes the same build as a bundle for a claude.ai Artifact: index.html plus the files listed in <dir>/artifact.json. Publish that, and it is live in about a minute, private until shared. | An Artifact holds at most 254 files plus the page per publish. Whole top-level directories are left out to fit, the ones with the most files first. artifact.json names each one, and links into a left-out directory 404. | Before publishing a folio whose content belongs to a real organisation (a WHO draft, say), ask the author: an Artifact is a new place that content appears. | . | What it does not do, and says in its plan: . | the folio preview’s QA sweep, screenshots, review-comment ingestion and PR comment (the banner says the preview was built locally); | the IG workflow’s PR comments, its branch-history page and README write-back (each reads a token, or writes the source branch); | the IG deploy action’s single-commit, which force-pushes one orphan commit and erases the publish branch’s history. This path commits on top and never force-pushes. | . | An IG build needs what its workflow needs. The workflow runs IG Publisher in a Docker image, so a machine with no Docker daemon gets the plan from --dry-run, and a real run stops naming the missing prerequisite. | An IG repository’s own site is built from its AST, not from the Publisher’s HTML. The repository declares site.build in its index.config.json entry (inline — never a <instance>.config.json), and that recipe’s first step restores the AST from its cache branch and refuses one that is not valid for the commit. The cache is refreshed by a Publisher run on a runner, through the IG layer’s reusable refresh workflow. It is the one workflow an agent-run IG repository dispatches, and only a person, or an agent the owner names for that run, dispatches it. The layer that owns IG builds owns the rule and the workflow; this skill names no IG step. | . Agent-run repositories — the GitHub Actions path is documented, not run . A repository is agent-run when it says so in its own index.config.json: "site": { "agentRun": true }. An agent builds and publishes its site, and its publish workflow keeps only workflow_dispatch. This skill keeps no list of them: the declaration is the list, and stage-local.ts says in every plan whether the repository declares it. For these repositories the GitHub Actions path is documentation. It says what the workflow does, so that the agent path can match it. It is not a fallback for an agent to take. | what | agent path | GitHub Actions path (documented, not run) | . | a folio preview at branches/<slug>/ | stage-local.ts from the branch | folio-staging.yml job stage | . | a folio’s main site at the Pages root | stage-local.ts from the default branch | folio-staging.yml job publish-main | . | an IG preview at branches/<branch>/ | stage-local.ts from the branch | the IG publisher’s ghbuild.yml, “Deploy candidate” | . | an IG’s main site at the Pages root | stage-local.ts from the default branch | the IG publisher’s ghbuild.yml, “Deploy main” | . | QA sweep, screenshots, review comments, PR comments | not run (the plan says so) | jobs in the workflows above | . Never dispatch the workflow, to cover a gap or for any other reason: a dispatched run contradicts the repository’s agent-run setting. When the agent path cannot do a step, say which step it is and ask. Skills that drive GitHub Actions are not to be implemented. Document what the workflows do, here and in the workflow files, so that an agent-run step can be checked against them — stage-local.ts reads the workflow files rather than restating them, so a change to a workflow’s build or layout is a change to the agent path too.

935.title: Staleness detection
935.content: The SHA stamp means staleness is always detectable: . | Staging matches PR head → the staging preview is current | Staging SHA ≠ PR head → the staging preview is stale (push again) | Main site SHA = merge commit → the publication is current | Main site SHA ≠ latest main → docs-site.yml needs to run | .

936.title: Example — a change that spans several blocks
936.content: An author needs to change the immunization schedule: . | Agent detects the change affects: . | Narrative content in the immunization chapter | Decision logic (CQL) for scheduling the next visit | Indicators that count doses administered | Referral logic for follow-up visits | . | Agent creates feature/update-immunization-schedule | Agent edits all affected blocks, assesses downstream impact | Push → staging deployment → author reviews | Author submits to the guidance review committee | Committee compares main vs branches/feature-update-immunization-schedule/ | Committee approves → merge → staging cleaned up → main site updated | .

937.title: Before you hand a staging URL to a person
937.content: Check the ref, then say how long and come back. A preview push is not a served page, and the bot’s “Staging preview” comment reports at most the first, not the second — and while it says queued, not even that. List branches/<slug>/ on refs/heads/gh-pages before relaying the URL; quote the comment’s own push and live-by times (the rate limit in §8 can hold a push for several windows), or say the stage job takes about 22 minutes plus the wait and Pages adds 3 to 4 on top; schedule the re-check rather than promising it. The three states, and why the third is not yours to assert, are in staging-review §”Before you hand a staging URL to a person (STRICT)”. It is the same rule and it is written once, there.

938.title: Before you report a staging URL as broken
938.content: Look at the publish ref, not the site. A staging URL is LOOKED UP in gh-pages under branches/<branch-slug>/, never composed from the source path — cat-harness/docs/guides/x.md publishes to /docs/cat-harness/guides/x.html, and composing it from the source path yields a 404 for a page that is there. From an agent container a curl against a Pages URL fails on the proxy regardless, so a failed fetch is not evidence either way. Full rule: github-state-inspection (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc).

939.title: Staging links
939.content: When a staging preview exists, every request this skill makes for feedback, review or sign-off carries it: one deep link per changed page, to the anchor where the change sits, with the same page on main as before. Where the skill declares an output contract, they go in its stagingLinks field. The rule, and where the page list comes from: feedback-deep-links.

941.doc: Staging a feature branch preview, and taking it down
941.title: Staging a feature branch preview, and taking it down
941.content: Process_FeatureStaging · strict · 13 step(s) . The lifecycle of a feature branch’s review preview: staged on a push, taken down when its pull request closes, or removed by an explicit dispatch. THE LIFECYCLE OF A REVIEW PREVIEW, drawn rather than described. Bean 7yvd, owner: “make sure all workflows documented as bpmn”. This is the first .github/workflows/*.yml documented here, and it was chosen because its shape was the least visible: three jobs, eight if: branches, a confirmation gate and a deletion trigger, written down only in a sixty-line YAML comment. Three entry points, and they are three different processes sharing a file. A pull request opened or pushed to STAGES a preview — or, when branches/<slug>/_build-record.json on gh-pages shows the agent already built this exact merge tree via stage-local.ts, DEFERS the critical-path build, sets preview/agent-build to pending, and lets preview-verify-sweep.yml dispatch an off-critical-path full CI rebuild (verify_pr) that either confirms the agent’s files in place or replaces them on mismatch (#2881). A pull request CLOSED asks whether the preview should go. A dispatch removes ONE preview that the first two can no longer reach — bean w2g5: the health sweep can only ever report a preview whose pull request is already closed, so by the time anybody reads the finding the event has fired, the job has run and the label was absent. Labelling afterwards fires nothing. TWO GATEWAYS, and both are three-state rather than yes/no. Removal confirmed? reads a merge as confirmation in its own right (bean 1feu) while still requiring a label for a close without a merge. Still in use? refuses on a live signal AND on could-not-tell, because a preflight that has gone blind must not read as permission. EVERY PATH THAT CHANGES branches/ WRITES TO THE RENDER LOG, and the two removal paths write the record in the SAME COMMIT as the removal. A separate log push can fail alone and leave a preview that vanished with nothing saying why, which is the state bean plj1 left the publish branch in for months. The single human step is the dispatch confirmation. Everything else is mechanical, which is what makes build-pipeline the right lane rather than a convenient one. i i i i i i i i i i i i i

942.doc: Staging a feature branch preview, and taking it down
942.title: How it connects
942.content: . | Called by: no call activity names this process | Calls: Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDN | Names the feature-staging skill without calling this process: CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, Publishing the docs site, and keeping the previews alive, Adopting an upstream version bump, Questionnaire wireframe review, Make the content change, Merge and publish a content change, Stage the content change — activity-calls-skill-process asks whether each should be a call activity. | Presented on: no docs page section shows this diagram | Skill: feature-staging | Running instances: none recorded | .

943.doc: Staging a feature branch preview, and taking it down
943.title: Lanes — who acts
943.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | CI/CD Pipeline | build-pipeline | Runs all three entry points — stage, cleanup, cleanup-dispatch — as one actor because none of the work in any of them needs judgement; the one step that does, confirming a dispatch deletion, was carved out into Lane_Human rather than left here. Every path that changes branches/ writes its render-log entry in the SAME commit as the change, because a log push that can fail on its own is exactly how a preview vanishes with nothing on the branch saying why.A FOURTH trigger starts none of them, and that is deliberate rather than an omission from this diagram. merge_group is declared on the workflow so it REPORTS in the merge queue — a required check that never reports on a merge_group event leaves every queued pull request pending forever — and all three jobs skip on it. A preview exists for the reviewers of a pull request; a queue entry has none and lives for minutes. Without the skip, stage’s existing guards all pass on a queue run (github.event.action is empty and the event is not a dispatch), so it would publish branches/<slug>/ named after the ephemeral gh-readonly-queue/... ref, and nothing would ever remove it — Start_Closed below fires on pull_request_target: closed, and a queue branch is never a pull request that closes. That is the plj1 shape arriving once per MERGE rather than once per pull request. | . | Human actor | user | The only lane whose actor cannot be a machine — deletion-requires-confirmation is not satisfied by a click, so H_Confirm must repeat the slug rather than approve generically, which is what stops a confirmation from an earlier run being replayed against a different preview. It precedes Start_Dispatch rather than following it, so the dispatch entry point cannot fire at all until this lane has acted. | .

944.doc: Staging a feature branch preview, and taking it down
944.title: Steps
944.content: Every one of the 13 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Defer build and queue verify sweepTask_Defer | CI/CD Pipeline | feature-staging | Set the preview/agent-build commit status on the PR head to pending, post the preview-build-verify notice on the PR, and exit the critical-path run so the runner is free. Off the critical path, preview-verify-sweep.yml (on staging workflow completion and every 15 minutes) waits until no Feature Staging run is active or queued, selects the oldest open PR whose head still has preview/agent-build = pending, and dispatches feature-staging.yml with verify_pr to rebuild and verify the agent’s preview. | . | Build the docs siteTask_Build | CI/CD Pipeline | feature-staging | Build the preview from the PR’s head (or, on an off-critical-path verify_pr dispatch, rebuild refs/pull/<n>/merge in full to verify an agent-built preview) and write _build-record.json: regenerate the generated docs, trim what this preview does not need, render the BPMN diagrams, then Jekyll, TypeDoc and the knowledge-graph export, with the staging banner and SEO identity claims stripped. It is a PREVIEW build (CAT_BUILD_TYPE=preview, owner 2026-11-01): only what the change reaches, and every whole-corpus index (builtAtPublish entries marked index: true, and the search index) is main’s copy, put back rather than rebuilt. A branch frozen for public comment is dispatched with build_type: full instead. Skill feature-staging, section Build types. A PREVIEW REBUILDS ONLY ITS DEPENDENCY CONE (owner cards Q-CONE-1 C and Q-CONE-2 B, 2026-11-01): main’s writer records say what each derive:publish writer and each step of the QA working copy READ. A writer or QA step whose recorded reads all match is not run, and main’s outputs for it are put back. Every other one runs. QA is not left out of a preview, only narrowed to what the change can reach. Inside a preview’s QA build, skill:register also leaves to derive:publish the two pages that derive:publish builds anyway and that no later QA step reads (skills:docs and lsi:viz), so they are built once. | . | Push to the CDN under branches/Task_Deploy | CI/CD Pipeline | calls Render a Knowledge Graph to a CDNrender-kg-to-cdn | A PREVIEW IS THE GENERAL STEP WITH A DIFFERENT ROOT (owner, 2026-09-30: “independent of staging vs publication … just rendering”). Process_RenderKgToCdn, entered with the tree Task_Build rendered, branches/<slug>/ under the site root as the publication root URL, and GitHub Pages as the target, so its gh-pages Tool pushes. For this target the push is keep_files: true with a destination_dir, so it adds one directory beside whatever else is on the branch; it is also RETRIED once: five other workflows push to gh-pages without joining this one’s concurrency group, and a queue does not help because GitHub CANCELS a pending job when a newer one arrives for the same group rather than queueing it. Measured 2026-09-19: three staging runs from three different branches inside 17 seconds, two cancelled. The call returns the push’s status and message; the render log and the PR comment that follow are this process’s own. THE PREVIEW CAP rides in the same commit (owner ruling 2026-10-02, issue #1868: “cap the maximum number of previews (<= 10) and rotate old ones off”, amended 2026-10-04 to a SIZE budget: “Cap by size, not count”, “3gb”): staging-rotate.ts keeps this preview plus the most recently updated others while their total fits MAX_PREVIEW_BYTES = 3 GB and removes the rest, oldest first, each with a removed render-log entry and its record retired into branches/_retired/. Every push attempt re-reads gh-pages and re-decides rather than rebasing, so a lost race never pushes a stale removal. A rotated-off preview is regenerated by the next push to its PR branch. | . | Append rendered to the render logTask_LogRendered | CI/CD Pipeline | render-logging | Its OWN commit, not part of the deploy. The publish action writes only into destination_dir, so an entry riding in _site would land at branches/<slug>/_render-log/ — inside the directory a cleanup removes, which is the one place a record of the removal must not be. continue-on-error: a preview that deployed and whose entry did not is a gap in the record, not a failed deploy. | . | Comment the preview URL on the PRTask_Comment | CI/CD Pipeline | staging-review | Post, or update in place, one comment on the PR giving the preview URL (branches/<slug>/) and the commit it was built from. On an off-critical-path verify run (verify_pr), also set the preview/agent-build commit status on the PR head (success when the agent build matched and built-site checks passed, failure when files differed or built-site checks failed) and record the verification outcome in the PR comment. | . | Derive the slug from the head refTask_Slug | CI/CD Pipeline | feature-staging | Derive the slug from the PR’s head ref: every character outside [a-zA-Z0-9._-] becomes ‘-‘, runs of ‘-‘ collapse, and leading or trailing ‘-‘ is trimmed. It must be one safe path segment, checked by value. | . | Remove the preview and log itTask_Remove | CI/CD Pipeline | deletion-requires-confirmation | ONE COMMIT for the removal and its record. A separate log push can fail on its own and leave a preview that vanished with nothing saying why — which is the exact state bean plj1 left the branch in. render-log.ts refuses a removed entry with no reason, so this step fails loudly rather than writing a record that says an artefact went and not why. | . | Append retained, with why it staysTask_LogRetained | CI/CD Pipeline | shared step GT_LogRetainedrender-logging | Records that a removal was considered and refused, or that a preview still stands because a signal fired; without the entry that leaves no trace, and nobody can tell why a preview is still up. A reason is REQUIRED — the tool refuses without one. | . | Post the retention notice on the PRTask_Notice | CI/CD Pipeline | staging-review | Removal was not confirmed, so the preview stays: post a retention notice on the PR giving its URL and saying it has NOT been removed, and the two ways to remove it: the staging:cleanup label while the PR is open, or, once it is closed, a Run workflow dispatch with cleanup_slug and a matching cleanup_confirm. | . | Check the slug and its confirmationTask_Validate | CI/CD Pipeline | deletion-requires-confirmation | Guarded three ways because a dispatch input is a DELETION TRIGGER. workflow_dispatch is available only to an actor with write access; the slug must match exactly the characters the sed pipeline can produce, with . and .. refused by name; and the confirmation must repeat the slug, so a confirmation cannot be carried over from an earlier run against a different preview. | . | Re-evaluate liveness AT REMOVAL TIMETask_Preflight | CI/CD Pipeline | deletion-requires-confirmation | Re-evaluated AT REMOVAL TIME, through the same previewLiveness the health sweep uses rather than a second implementation of it. The sweep runs daily and proposes; this acts. Between them a branch can come back to life — bean w2g5 documents exactly that, a session reusing one branch across five successive pull requests. | . | Remove it AND append removed — one commitTask_RemoveDisp | CI/CD Pipeline | deletion-requires-confirmation | Say what is going — size and file count — then remove branches/<slug>/ and append removed to the render log in the SAME commit, so a preview cannot vanish without a record of who dispatched it and why. The slug is a dispatch input, so the tool re-checks it by value rather than trusting the guard. | . | Repeat the slug, exactly, to confirmH_Confirm | Human actor | deletion-requires-confirmation | The one step in this process that is a person’s. Repeating the slug is not ceremony: it names the artefact being confirmed, so a confirmation cannot be inherited by a later run pointed at a different preview. | .

945.doc: Staging a feature branch preview, and taking it down
945.title: Decisions
945.content: Every one of the 4 decision(s) is documented. | decision | what decides it | branches | . | Agent build matches tree?GW_AgentBuilt | Check whether branches/<slug>/_build-record.json on gh-pages was written by the agent (builder = “agent”) for the exact git tree of refs/pull/<n>/merge (record.tree = MERGE_SHA^{tree}). When an agent has already built and pushed the preview for this exact merge tree via stage-local.ts, the preview is already live on gh-pages and the critical-path PR run does not rebuild it. Any missing record, CI-built record, or tree mismatch (including when main moved under the branch) takes the critical-path build. | yes — defer → Defer build and queue verify sweepno — build now → GW_MergeBuild | . | Verified identical to agent build?GW_VerifyMatch | On an off-critical-path verify run (verify_pr), preview-record.ts compare checks the CI rebuild’s _build-record.json against the agent’s record on gh-pages across every file outside the per-build metadata (staging.json, _build-record.json, .staged-at, build.yml). When every file hash matches (same = true), the agent’s deployed files on branches/<slug>/ stand untouched and the deploy and render-log commits are skipped. On a normal CI build, or when the verify rebuild differs (same = false) or the merge tree moved (same = stale), the flow proceeds to push CI’s build to branches/<slug>/ (guarded on verify runs so a newer preview is never overwritten). | no, or CI build → Push to the CDN under branches/yes — keep agent files → GW_MergeComment | . | Removal confirmed?GW_Confirmed | THREE inputs, two outcomes, and bean 1feu set the split: a MERGED pull request needs no label, because the merge IS the confirmation — a person decided the content belongs on main, which says more about the preview than a label does. A pull request closed WITHOUT merging still needs staging:cleanup, because there the preview is the only rendering of that work: not redundant, the last copy.The branch taken is emitted as reason=merged \| labelled \| closed-unmerged-and-unlabelled and written into the log entry, so an audit of a removal can tell which rule did it. | merged, or labelled → Remove the preview and log itclosed unmerged, no label → Append retained, with why it stays | . | Still in use?GW_Live | THREE states, and the third is why this gateway exists. Still in use → refuse, exit 1. COULD NOT TELL → refuse, exit 2. Only a determined absence of every liveness signal removes anything. Refusing to delete is the only recoverable direction, and a preflight that has gone blind must not read as permission. | no signal — safe to remove → Remove it AND append removed — one commitlive, OR could not tell → REFUSED — nothing removed | .

947.title: fhir-questionnaire-wireframe
947.content: Named by: Incremental IG build, L3 FHIR IG pipeline, Questionnaire wireframe review . Skill id: fhir-questionnaire-wireframe · Package: fhir-ig-authoring · Process: questionnaire-wireframe-review.bpmn (Process_QuestionnaireWireframeReview). Show a built FHIR Questionnaire the way a person will meet it — a mid-fidelity wireframe at web and mobile width, and a live form — have it reviewed as a design, check that it says what the wireframe it was derived from says, and take change requests on either side back through authoring. Sourcing. What a Questionnaire means is defined by the FHIR specification and the Structured Data Capture IG; what the live form supports is defined by NLM’s LHC-Forms. This skill states how the two are wired in this harness.

948.title: Rules
948.content: . | The renderer is NLM LHC-Forms, vendored into the site: never a CDN at runtime. Its BSD-style notice travels with the vendored files. | The field ↔ item check is scripts/check-wireframe-questionnaire.ts (Tool check-wireframe-questionnaire). It knows nothing about any one IG; a layer above uses it by name. | Either side may be edited. A change request says whether the Questionnaire or the wireframe was changed, and the agent brings the other back in line. Neither is regenerated from the other. | .

949.title: Inputs and outputs
949.content: fhir-harness/schemas/skills/fhir-questionnaire-wireframe/: . | in — questionnaire (required: one built JSON path; several are several runs), mode, wireframe, renderer, assetDir, suggest, issueForm, channels, branch | out — the output shape of wireframe-design-review (use, topic, assetDir, candidates[] each with its source HTML, web and mobile screenshots and their staging links, chosen, changedAssets, stagingLinks), plus renderer, fidelity[] (the checker’s findings per layout), sdcChecks[] (step 4b) and changeRequests[] (issue URL, which side was edited, status). | . stagingLinks is an inline copy of cat-harness schemas/staging-comparison.schema.json, as every contract carrying it keeps one; changedAssets is the staging preview graph’s changed-assets record, with three kinds of its own: questionnaire-wireframe, questionnaire-rendering, questionnaire-screenshot.

950.title: Roles
950.content: | role | does | . | fhir-modeller | authors: renders, runs the checks, applies change requests | . | business-analyst | reviews the form against the workflow it serves | . | clinical-sme | reviews what the form asks and in what order | . | build-pipeline | the mechanical steps: rendering, screenshots, the fidelity check | .

951.title: Steps
951.content: . | Read the built Questionnaire JSON, never FSH: fsh-generated/resources/Questionnaire-<id>.json, or the IG’s published Questionnaire-<id>.json. FSH is what the author wrote; the JSON is what every renderer and reader receives, so it is what is judged. | Render. | A mid-fidelity wireframe: one field per answerable item, in item order, each carrying data-element="<id>" (the item’s definition, or its code) and sitting in a data-layout="web" or data-layout="mobile" subtree. Monochrome, the item’s own text, no placeholder text — the rules of wireframe-design-review step 2. | A form view: the same JSON in <lhc-forms>, from the vendored LHC-Forms build, on the IG site’s Questionnaire form page (build-ig-site). | . | Screenshots at web and mobile width with the cat-harness Tool wireframe-check (1280×800 and 390×844; renders, no-overflow, no-placeholder). A candidate missing either viewport does not enter review. | Fidelity, when an L2 wireframe exists — the form was designed first and the Questionnaire derived from it: . bun run fhir-harness/scripts/check-wireframe-questionnaire.ts <wireframe.html> <Questionnaire.json> . Each layout is judged on its own: a field with no item, an item with no field, an item naming no data element, a data element twice, the first place the order differs. Exit 0 faithful, 1 a finding, 2 cannot tell — and 2 is never a pass. The findings go in fidelity[], per layout. This is fidelity, not design: a faithful form can still be a poor one. 4b. SDC build checks, with CSIRO’s libraries (Apache-2.0; used for checks, not UI), Tool sdc-checks: . bun run fhir-harness/scripts/sdc-checks.ts --ast output-ast --fixtures input/tests/questionnaires [--out <dir>] . | check | library | passes when | . | assemble | @aehrc/sdc-assemble 2.0.3 | an assemble-root’s sub-forms all resolve in this IG; --out writes the assembled Questionnaire, so assembly is a build step too | . | template-extract | @aehrc/sdc-template-extract 1.0.16 | extraction from the fixture’s response.json yields every resource in extract-expected.json | . | populate | @aehrc/sdc-populate 4.7.2 | FHIRPath pre-population from populate-context.json gives the answers in populate-expected.json | . | behaviour | @aehrc/questionnaire-test-toolkit 0.1.0 | the IG’s behaviour.test.tsx passes. Warn-only: the toolkit is early, and needs its React and Smart Forms peers installed with the IG’s tests | . The fixtures are the IG’s, one directory per Questionnaire id. Nothing is fetched from a server. not-applicable, no-fixture and could-not-determine are said, and never read as a pass. The results go in sdcChecks[], one entry per Questionnaire. | Review by wireframe-design-review, as-is use for a form that exists, design use for one being designed: blind, per criterion, at both viewports, adjudicated where reviewers disagree. That skill is the method; this one does not restate it. | Stage by feature-staging, and ask for review with staging-review: one deep link per rendered Questionnaire and wireframe, before and after. Where the request goes — the conversation, an issue, the pull request — is a judgement, and more than one may be right: staging-review’s deep-link rule, point 5. | Change requests come in in one of two ways, and both end as an issue: . | ✍ suggest, in its Questionnaire mode, on the form page: the reviewer edits the Questionnaire or the wireframe and the editor opens an issue; | the questionnaire-change issue form, filled by hand. | . Each goes to content-feedback for triage (to public-comment when a review round is open), then to l3-fhir-authoring, which edits the side the request did not touch so the two agree again, then back to step 1. changeRequests[] records each issue, which side was edited, and where it stands. | .

952.title: The change-request payload
952.content: What the ✍ editor writes into the issue’s body, and what the issue form asks for, by these field ids, when it is filled by hand: . | field id | holds | . | questionnaire | the Questionnaire’s canonical URL or Questionnaire/<id> | . | edited | questionnaire or wireframe: the side the reviewer changed | . | patch | an RFC 6902 JSON Patch over the built Questionnaire, its paths annotated with the item’s linkId | . | items | a readable before/after table of the items that changed | . | source | the FSH file and line the item comes from, when known | . | rationale | why | . The issue form is templates/ig-repo-site/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/questionnaire-change.yml, which an IG repository copies to .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/, as it copies the workflows beside it. It is for people filing by hand: the ✍ editor does not open it, because GitHub ignores a prefilled body when template= names an issue form, and the patch would be lost. The editor opens a plain issue whose body carries everything. A pre-filled link longer than about 7000 characters is too long for GitHub; the body then goes to the clipboard and a stub issue opens, as the ✍ runtime does.

953.title: The form view and the ✍ Questionnaire mode
953.content: build-ig-site writes one page per Questionnaire in the IG’s AST, Questionnaire-<id>-form.html, through scripts/questionnaire-form.ts: . | the form, drawn by the vendored LHC-Forms build (scripts/assets/vendor/lhc-forms/<version>/, its NLM LICENSE.md beside it, vendored.json recording the npm tarball and a SHA-256 per file) from a rendered copy of the built JSON, questionnaires/Questionnaire-<id>.json. The source Questionnaire is never changed. Nothing is loaded from another origin; | ✎ (the FSH source the AST names), 📣 (feedback) and ✍ (suggest a change), through the platform’s edit-links recipe and a #fa-edit-cfg block whose suggest.profiles names the mode for the ✍ runtime’s mode registry, [{ id: "questionnaire", module, extensions: [".json"], kinds: ["questionnaire"] }], beside the mode’s own builder, sw, fhirVersion, source and slug. The form host carries data-suggest-mode="questionnaire" and data-block="questionnaire:<id>"; | a plain open in CSIRO Smart Forms link-out, as a rendering cross-check. Nothing of it is embedded. | . The ✍ Questionnaire mode is scripts/questionnaire-mode.js, a plain ES module with no build step. It exports the three roles the ✍ suggest runtime’s mode registry calls (cat-harness-tools EDIT_LINKS_RUNTIME), by these names: . | export | does | . | open(host, ctx) → { get, dispose } | ctx is { text, sourceText, sourcePath, why, src, path, label, kind, repo, branch, config, status(msg) }: text the BUILT Questionnaire JSON (the host’s data-suggest-text), sourcePath / sourceText the FSH it was built from, why the reader’s reason (live). A panel: which side was edited (the Questionnaire or its L2 wireframe), and a raw-JSON fallback; with config.suggest.builder, the self-hosted NLM Form Builder in a window, its updateQuestionnaire / closed result kept (its API.md hand-back). Progress goes to ctx.status. get() is awaited on Submit, never polled, and is ctx.text itself while nothing was edited; dispose() closes the builder window | . | check(before, after, opts) | findings [{ severity, message }], from checkSuggestion below; an error blocks Submit | . | issue(before, after, ctx) | { title, body } and no template: the side edited, the FSH source link (ctx.sourcePath, anchored on the Instance: line found in ctx.sourceText), the page, the item table and the JSON Patch with each operation’s linkId. Not the Why: the runtime appends **Why:** to a mode’s body that lacks it, so the mode writing one too would file it twice | . The side edited and the builder’s round-trip baseline reach check and issue through the session open keeps. Everything else is ctx’s: the mode reads no Why from the dialog’s DOM and does not re-derive the source path from the page. Which path opens it. The form page’s host names the profile (data-suggest-mode), the source in the repository (data-src, the .fsh file) and the URL of the BUILT text the mode edits (data-suggest-text, questionnaires/Questionnaire-<id>.source.json, the unexpanded copy the IG compiled; not the copy LHC-Forms renders, whose value sets were expanded). A runtime with the mode registry serves any host that names its mode: it fetches the built text as ctx.text, reads the source as ctx.sourceText, and its dialog offers a Form | FSH switch: the Form pane is this mode, the FSH pane edits the source as text and files a source diff with the reader’s Why. Without such a runtime, the form page’s loader (scripts/templates/ig-pages/questionnaire-form.js) opens the mode itself, with the same ctx (built text fetched from data-suggest-text, sourcePath, a live why; no sourceText), its own Why field, withWhy to append the Why as the runtime does, and issueUrl for the link. Where the runtime has put its ✍ link in the host, the page’s own link hands the click to it. The self-hosted Form Builder, and no cross-site call . The editor is the NLM Form Builder (formbuilder-lhcforms 12.9.0), self-hosted. The site makes no cross-site call. | The builder is vendored unmodified (scripts/assets/vendor/formbuilder-lhcforms/). The site serves a rewritten copy of its index.html, also as window-open.html (its hand-back route): jQuery from this site (vendor/jquery/3.6.0), the Google font rules removed, and a guard that registers the service worker and reloads before anything else loads. | The service worker (scripts/terminology-sw.js, scoped to the builder; the mapping is the pure scripts/terminology-map.js) answers every request to another origin from this site: . | request | answer | . | clinicaltables /api/loinc_items/v3/search | the IG’s terminology index, in the CTSS shape. LOINC comes only from the IG’s cache; a code it does not hold shows “not in this IG’s terminology cache; add it via the FSH source” | . | clinicaltables /api/ucum/v3/search | the full UCUM list (vendored @lhncbc/ucum-lhc definitions) | . | lhcforms-static /lforms-versions/… | the vendored LHC-Forms | . | lforms-fhir.nlm.nih.gov (import and export), anything else | a local error saying it is disabled on this site | . | The terminology index is written at build time by scripts/terminology-index.ts (Tool terminology-index) from the IG’s own restored cache: output-ast/expansions.json and input-cache/txcache/ (ig-build-pipeline, §”The AST cache lifecycle”). | The form view needs no terminology server either: each item’s answerValueSet that the expansions hold becomes answerOption in the rendered copy. The source Questionnaire is unchanged; a value set the cache does not hold is reported. | A code the cache lacks is added through the FSH source. A ✍ change request can carry it as free text. | .

954.title: The suggest checker
954.content: checkSuggestion(before, after, { wireframe }) in check-wireframe-questionnaire.ts is the checker a suggest editor runs on the reviewer’s edit, in the editor-checker shape { errors, warnings }: . | errors are syntax only — not JSON, not a Questionnaire; | warnings never block, and only what the edit introduces is reported, computed against the editor’s own round-trip of the original: a duplicate linkId, an enableWhen naming no item, and the fidelity findings of step 4 when a wireframe is given. | . It is not declared as an editor-checker profile (contentType: questionnaire; a folio-editor-checker/v1 node naming open, check and issue with extensions: [".json"]): the editor-checkers typology is declared by folio-assistant-sci, which this layer does not need. The page config names the profile directly (QUESTIONNAIRE_PROFILE in questionnaire-form.ts).

955.title: What this skill does not do
955.content: . | It does not build the IG: l3-fhir-authoring and ig-publication do. | It does not regenerate one side from the other on its own. Which side is the source of a change is the change request’s to say. | A clean fidelity check is not a design review, and a clean design review is not conformance: fhir-validation still decides that. | .

958.title: fhir-validation
958.content: Named by: Incremental IG build, L3 FHIR IG pipeline, An IG site, built from the AST on its cache branch, An IG release: the owner tags, a draft is built, the owner publishes . Skill id: fhir-validation · Package: fhir-ig-authoring · Named by l3-fhir-pipeline.bpmn (Validate against profiles, Build pipeline — SUSHI · validator · IG Publisher lane) and ig-incremental-build.bpmn (Validate the cone (fhir_validate), Publisher + validator services (JVM) lane). Validate an IG’s FHIR artefacts against the profiles and packages they claim to conform to. Sourcing. Conformance is defined by the FHIR specification and by the packages an IG depends on; the validator is HL7’s. This skill states how it is invoked in this harness and what each outcome is allowed to mean.

959.title: Inputs and outputs
959.content: fhir-harness/schemas/skills/fhir-validation/: . | in — igRoot (required), validationLevel, targetProfiles | out — overallStatus (required), sushiResult, publisherResult, conformanceResults | . SUSHI compiling is not conformance. FSH can compile to JSON that the validator then rejects, so a green sushiResult with an unrun publisherResult is not a pass.

960.title: The binaries
960.content: The package declares these capabilities (providesCapabilities in package-manifest.json); each is defined, with its detection command, in scenarios/capabilities/: . sushi --version # sushi-compiler (requires node-runtime) java -jar "${FHIR_VALIDATOR_JAR}" -version # fhir-validator (requires java-runtime) java -jar "${IG_PUBLISHER_JAR}" --version # ig-publisher (requires java-runtime) . fhir-validator is the standalone validator, distinct from ig-publisher, which builds a whole IG. An authoring loop runs the validator on single resources between builds; a release is cut from the publisher.

961.title: When a package host refuses you
961.content: SUSHI and the Publisher resolve the IG’s dependencies: from packages.fhir.org. Where that host is refused, the failure looks like a broken IG and is not one. Ask for the remedy: . bun run cat tools:remedy packages.fhir.org # → fhir-cache-seed-npm, with its command . Every network-dependent Tool declares remedies per host it reaches (check:tools enforces it), and fhir-harness/scripts/ig-cache.sh doctor prints the same answer for each host it finds unreachable. For packages.fhir.org it is fhir-cache-seed-npm --sushi-config sushi-config.yaml, and for versions npm does not carry, --mirror from a repository that fhir-package-mirror filled on a machine that reaches the host. Pin that repository with --mirror-commit <full 40-character SHA>: git cannot fetch an abbreviated SHA from a remote, and the seeder refuses one. A cloud session can fill the mirror without a person’s device, through a GitHub Actions runner: push a claude/mirror-* branch that edits packages.txt in the mirror repository, wait for its mirror.yml run, merge, re-seed. SUSHI also adds packages that sushi-config.yaml does not list, such as hl7.fhir.uv.tools.r4#latest. A #latest needs the registry to name a version, so offline it fails with errors that look like the IG’s own (for example logical-target … does not exist), even with the package in the cache. Serve the mirror as a registry on localhost, answering GET /<name> with dist-tags.latest and GET /<name>/<version> with the tarball, and run FPL_REGISTRY=http://127.0.0.1:<port> sushi build .. Check which version latest resolves to: it is the mirror’s highest, which is only right when the mirror holds the current release. Do not report “SUSHI cannot run here” before running tools:remedy. A refusal that tools:remedy answers with none is “could not determine” in the sense of the next section: say so, with the reason it gave.

962.title: A capability that is absent did not pass
962.content: If a probe fails, overallStatus is not a pass with an empty findings list. It is “could not determine”, and it is reported as such: a clean run over a validator that never started looks exactly like a clean IG.

963.title: Validating a cone
963.content: ig-incremental-build.bpmn validates a restricted cone — the artefacts a change touches — rather than the whole IG, and reports the cone it chose. That is a latency optimisation for the authoring loop. It does not gate a release: the full publisher build in l3-fhir-pipeline.bpmn does. Do not let a green cone stand in for a green IG: a profile the change did not touch can still be broken by it.

964.title: After validation
964.content: Quality gates on the aggregate are quality-control; publishing is ig-publication. A validator’s verdict is an input to the QC reviewer’s decision, not the decision.

967.content: Skill folio-getting-started: The content-folio half of the harness’s getting-started skill: binds collab/processes/conduct/getting-started.bpmn and decisions/folio-intent.dmn, interprets describeRepository() content-type markers (folio, harness, dak, sushi), and routes new-content and specialised IG/DAK creation requests. 968.title: 1. Repository membership vs. isFolio
968.content: describeRepository() (schemas/content/content-type.ts) returns every marker a repository carries — folio, harness, dak, sushi — with the facts each states and any disagreement between them. describeRepositoryClosure() (schemas/kg/harness-config.ts) extends that through the dependency tree, attributing each membership to the layer that carried it. | folio and harness are distinct memberships. The declaration (<name>.json) says this is a layer; a config that declares contentType (<name>.config.json or inline in index.config.json) says this authors folio content. isFolio in folio-intent.dmn tests membership of folio specifically. | Multiple markers do not perturb the five branches. A folio that is also a DAK or carries a sushi-config.yaml takes the same branch in folio-intent.dmn as one that is not: use describeRepository() to inspect what the repository is, and isFolio to drive Gateway_Intent. | .

969.title: 2. Content-type routing on new-content and specialised harnesses
969.content: . | new-content branch: stop the onboarding process immediately and hand off to the folio’s content authoring workflow (such as document-authoring for a document folio, or the paper authoring skills in a paper folio). Scaffolding anything on new-content is a defect. | Specialised IG or guideline creation: when the user asks to create a domain Implementation Guide or guideline in a harness that specialises this layer, hand over to that layer’s creation skill discovered via skill_list. In a harnessed repository, default to staging the new sub-KG in place first (sub-kg-lifecycle) until the owner confirms creating or writing to an external repository. | .
