972.title: When to use folio-init
972.content: Reach for folio-init when triage in getting-started or repo-conversion has settled that a new folio structure should be created: . | new-repo — a brand-new repository is being stood up to author a paper, document or DAK folio. | add-folio — an existing repository wants a new folio added alongside its existing directories (overlay), without overwriting its tracked files. | . Do not run folio-init when: . | The repository already has a <name>.json declaration and only needs a lower harness layer brought in at a pinned SHA — that is materialise, served by remote-mount (bun run cat mount:remote). | The user is converting existing prose in place (convert in repo-conversion.bpmn) — that uses ingestion, not a blank scaffold. | . Because folio-init runs before the target repository has a content type, the Tool is registered among the generic harness tools rather than inside a content-type adapter.

973.title: Write capability requirement and read-only degradation
973.content: folio-init is a writing verb: it creates directories, writes manifests and agent stubs, and (when git is available) prints the command that seeds the cat/<instance>/beans and cat/<instance>/todos orphan state branches. Before invoking folio-init to write, check that at least one write capability is present (scenarios/capabilities/): . | git-push — local filesystem write plus git remote push capability for the target repository and its state branches. | github-api — GitHub API token (gh / REST / GraphQL) able to create or populate the target repository and refs. | github-connector — MCP GitHub connector able to push the scaffolded files into the target repository. | . When no write capability is available (a read-only container or an unauthenticated session), folio-init degrades cleanly via --dry-run (dry_run: true on the MCP tool): it computes and returns the complete Markdown report of every directory, manifest, builder shim and config file it would write, without touching the filesystem or git refs. Never attempt a partial write when write capability is absent, and never report a failed capability probe as a completed scaffold.

974.title: What folio-init writes
974.content: Given title and one or more authors (plus optional content_type, slug, dir, link, assistant_path, force, dry_run), folio-init lays down: . | The folio directories and initial manifests — folio/ (or content/), uploads/, library/, the root <slug>.json layer declaration and <slug>.config.json, and the root index.config.json that instantiates it (index-config). | The builder shim (content/schema/builders) — block manifests in the folio import ../schema/builders rather than importing the platform path directly. 987.title: “NOT clean” is a verdict about the RUN, not about your diff
987.content: Skill gate-tree-mutation: Reading bun run cat gates’ “NOT clean” verdict. Why every gate can pass and the run still exit 1, the two causes and how to tell them apart in one command, and the question that settles whether a churning field is a defect in the writer: does it describe the SUBJECT or the RUN? . Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Agent activity log, Close the bean, Drain the beans, Agent bean lifecycle, Open the bean, Code change and review, Merge the base branch in, A refused merge-train member, Requirements filing: promote, organise, trace, supersede, or retire, SME Review of Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route, Test Data Curation — Fixed Sets and Generated Recipes, Watching a pinned upstream dependency, Adopting an upstream version bump, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Editing and HCI validation, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . bun run cat gates snapshots the tree before the first gate and after every one, so a gate that repairs something on its way past is named. Every gate can pass and the run still exit 1: . ✗ every gate passed, and the run is NOT clean — 1 gate(s) changed the tree. The gates that ran after the mutation were handed the repaired tree, so their verdicts describe a state you have not committed. No gate can observe what another gate did, which is why the detector can only live in the runner (gate-tree-guard.ts) and why its predicate is a per-gate delta rather than “the tree is dirty”: running gates over your own uncommitted work is the normal case. A failure to read the tree is carried as undetermined and reported rather than thrown, because undetermined is not clean. Two causes, and they are answered differently. Read git status --short before you decide which one you have.

988.title: Cause 1 — you changed an input and did not regenerate
988.content: The ordinary case, and platform-gates §”What a *:check failure is telling you” is the whole of it: run the generator, commit its output, and run the gates after the last edit. Never hand-edit the artefact into agreement.

989.title: Cause 2 — the artefact records the RUN, and your run differs
989.content: This is the one that looks like cause 1 and is not. The generator is behaving correctly, the input has not changed, and the file still gets rewritten — because a field in it describes the run that produced it rather than the subject it is about, and your run is not the last one. The question that settles it: . Does this field describe the SUBJECT the artefact is about, or the RUN that produced it? Only the first is a reason to write. A field that records the environment — a timestamp, the checked-out HEAD, the runtime version — will differ on every machine, so counting it as a reason to write makes the artefact churn everywhere and reports that churn as though an input had moved. Example — QA script sidecars . The committed QA script sidecars under cat-harness-tools/pipeline/script-sidecars/ carry three run fields: . last_run_at wall-clock time of this run last_run_sha the checked-out HEAD engine_version `bun-${Bun.version}` — the local runtime . saveQaScriptSidecar writes only when a substantive field moved, and none of the three counts. Counting engine_version would make a run under any other Bun rewrite every sidecar whose recorded engine disagrees, so that bun test dirties the tree and bun run cat gates ends NOT clean on every branch. Two measures are kept, and they answer different halves: .bun-version pins Bun for CI (check:bun-pin holds every oven-sh/setup-bun site to it), which makes the recorded engine consistent where the repository controls it; the comparison skip stops any other engine — an agent container’s image, which a repository cannot pin — from rewriting a file whose checker did not change. “A verdict produced by a different engine is a different verdict” is true, and about a different artefact. A script sidecar holds no verdict — it records a checker’s source file, its hashes and its dependencies; verdicts live in block sidecars. No reader consults a script sidecar’s engine_version for freshness: entryIsFresh compares field_hash and the script hashes, nothing else. The same field can be load-bearing in one artefact and pure provenance in another, so check the argument against the artefact in front of you. Where the rule is already implemented . | where | the guard | . | scripts/qa-results.ts writeQaResult | compares withoutTimestamp(prior), so only updated_at differing is not a write; shared by every *.qa-results.json family | . | pipeline/qa-sweep.ts | wroteSomething = verdictChanged \|\| metadataDrifted, and updated_at advances only then | . | qa-utils.ts saveQaScriptSidecar | content-derived fields only; engine_version and the two last_run_* fields are excluded | . writeQaResult’s docblock states the principle: the timestamp answers “when were these findings established”, not “when did somebody last run the script”. A churn you meet is more likely a family that MISSED this rule than a new question — look for the nearest of these three before designing anything.

990.title: If you meet a churn whose writer has not been fixed yet
990.content: Discard it rather than committing it, and then fix the writer: . git checkout -- <the churning paths> . Committing such a churn stamps whatever your environment happens to be as though it were a fresh measurement — with an older local runtime, a downgrade. The generator records your container correctly, and your container is not the repository. Discarding is a workaround, not a fix. A signal that is always red is one nobody reads, and then it cannot report the next real in-run repair. So the sequence is: discard, ask the question at the top of cause 2, and fix the comparison. Do not add the paths to an ignore list — that removes the signal instead of the cause.

991.title: Do not read past the line
991.content: Cause 2 has a narrow signature. If NOT clean names paths outside the artefact family you expect, or fields other than the run-provenance ones, it is not this: the gate is telling you something new, and cause 1 is the likelier answer.

994.title: Generalise the fix, then attack the generalisation
994.content: Skill generalise-the-fix: You have a fix. Before it ships, ask what CLASS of defect it belongs to and whether the fix sits at the right layer — then attack your own answer: name what the fix now catches that the bug did not. Two axes go wrong, SCOPE and STATE, and widening either past the problem is how a fix becomes the next defect. Applies to a bug fix, a schema change, a detector, or a claim in a paper. Use after the fix works and before the pull request. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Agent activity log, Close the bean, Drain the beans, Agent bean lifecycle, Open the bean, Code change and review, Merge the base branch in, A refused merge-train member, Requirements filing: promote, organise, trace, supersede, or retire, SME Review of Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route, Test Data Curation — Fixed Sets and Generated Recipes, Watching a pinned upstream dependency, Adopting an upstream version bump, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Editing and HCI validation, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . A fix that repairs one instance and leaves its siblings is half a fix. A fix widened past the problem it solves is the next defect. This skill is the pass between those two, and it is two moves in order — generalise, then adversary — because the adversary has no subject until a generalisation exists. Run it when the fix works and before the pull request. Not while debugging: this asks what the defect was, which you cannot answer until you know.

995.title: Move 1 — what class is this?
995.content: Three questions, in order. The first is the one that is usually skipped. 1.1 What was the defect, as opposed to the symptom? . The symptom is where you noticed it. The defect is the rule that was wrong. They are rarely the same, and the fix belongs at the defect. Symptom: two work items reported as having no options. Defect: the counter recognised one markdown form — top-level list items — while MADR, the authority, is format-agnostic. The corpus was fine; the detector had invented a requirement. Fixing the two work items would have left the rule free to misjudge the next one. The tell that you are fixing a symptom: the fix names a specific instance — two work item ids in a rule, document-ingestion.html in a selector, one filename in a condition. 1.2 What else has this shape? . Look, do not guess. The corpus answers this and your memory does not. The same detector. A twelve-bean sweep over the store found ten using list items, two using bold enumerations — and one using subheadings and being over-counted ten for four options. The sweep found a second error direction nobody had reported, and it changed the design: three forms, most structured wins, never summed. A fix designed from one example handles one example. A fix designed from the sweep handles the class, and the sweep is usually one command. 1.2a A sweep must report its own coverage . The sweep in 1.2 is a measurement, so it answers to the same rule every other measurement here does: say what you covered, or a silent under-match reads as a clean corpus. Sweeping the health checks for more findings whose action could not clear them. The first pass regex-matched action: followed by string literals and reported 6 actions, all sound. The file has 15. The nine it missed included a ternary, and the pass would have concluded the class was closed after seeing 40 % of it — while looking for exactly that kind of blind spot. The fix is one line of output: parsed 15 of 15. The count of subjects found against the count that exist, printed beside the verdict. So a corpus sweep prints the denominator. grep -c for the crude marker, parse for the real one, and show both — if they disagree, the parse is the thing to fix before reading anything into the result. This is rendered-verification’s “assert the conditions” rule with the browser taken out of it: a check that cannot tell an empty walk from a clean one is not a check. 1.3 Is the fix at the right layer? . Walk outward from the symptom until you reach the thing that is actually wrong, and stop there. Both directions are failures: too deep and the siblings stay broken, too high and see Move 2. The search field was 44 % of its panel. Our rules said width: 100 % and flex: 1 1 auto and they were all correct — walking the box chain found the theme’s own .search-input-wrap at max-width: 536px, two layers above where the change felt like it belonged.

996.title: Move 2 — the adversary
996.content: Now attack what you just wrote. One question, and answer it in writing: . What does this fix now apply to that the defect did not? . If the honest answer is “nothing”, say so and move on — the pass is cheap when it passes. If it is anything else, that is the list to justify or narrow. The two axes, and they go wrong independently . Most over-generalisation is one of these, and the worked case below is both at once. | axis | the question | widened past the problem looks like | . | SCOPE | which things does it apply to? | the fix names a container when the problem was one child | . | STATE | when does it apply? | the fix is unconditional when the conflict only arises in one state | . The worked case. A rule was written so ONE panel could paint over a full-bleed figure. It was applied to the whole sidebar (scope) in every state (state), as :root.fa-has-fullwidth .side-bar { z-index: auto }. At specificity (0,3,0) it beat the open-nav rule’s (0,2,0) always — so on every page with a wide figure the navigation opened behind the page content, which the open-nav rule’s own comment had predicted in as many words. Neither axis needed widening. The panel is position: fixed; only the panel was in conflict; and only while a figure was expanded. Four tells, all cheap to check . | The fix names a container, the bug named a child.side-bar when the problem was .fa-qr-panel. | The fix is unconditional and the conflict is not. Ask when the defect can occur. If the fix is broader than that window, narrow it or say why not. | You summed where you should have chosen. Recognising three forms is right; adding their counts gave one work item 14 options where it has 4. When alternatives are alternatives, take the most specific present — do not add. | The label is doing work the relation should do. A stale-claim check keys on parent rather than type: epic, because type is a label a work item sets about itself while parent is a fact another work item asserts about it. Keying on the label would also have forced a ruling on what feature means. | . Keep the discrimination the check exists for . A generalisation that excuses everything has deleted the check. Name the case that must STILL fire, and test it. The stale-claim check excuses a claim whose child moved recently. The case that must still fire: a parent all of whose children are also quiet — 8 open children, none moving — and it has a test of its own. Without it the change would have excused every parent. The strongest outcome is when the adversary reverses you . Expect to find a trade, and measure it rather than reasoning about it. The sidebar case. I expected z-index: 100 to fix the nav at the cost of the panel the old rule protected, so I synthesised that panel and measured. Under auto it was not visible at its own centre — covered despite its z-index: 1200. Under 100 it was. The old value failed the case it was written for, so the new one was better on both counts and there was no trade to weigh. An adversarial pass that only ever confirms you is not being run.

997.title: Move 3 — falsify the guard
997.content: A guard that would not have caught the bug is worth nothing, and you cannot tell by reading it. Reintroduce the defect, watch the guard fail, restore, watch it pass. Two commands. The sidebar case: sed the value back to auto → both assertions fail; restore → 25 pass. A health finding: it fired before, is silent after, and the adjudicated group is still counted so “never created” and “all resolved” cannot read the same. If the guard cannot be falsified — because the defect needs a state you cannot produce — say so where the guard lives, and say what does cover it instead.

998.title: Where this is NOT a bug fix
998.content: The moves are the same; only the vocabulary changes. | A schema or model change. Scope is which records must now satisfy this; state is from when. A field made required is a fix applied unconditionally to every record ever written — the sidebar shape in a schema. | A detector or gate. Its class is the set of inputs it judges. Sweep the corpus (1.2) before changing the rule, or you will tune it to the two examples in front of you. | A claim in a paper. The generalisation is the theorem’s hypothesis; the adversary asks which objects now satisfy it that the proof does not cover. The falsification is the counterexample you look for on purpose. Widening a hypothesis past what the argument supports is over-generalisation with a different name. | .

999.title: What this deliberately does not do
999.content: It does not ask you to generalise everything. “Nothing else has this shape” is a complete and common answer to 1.2, and one worked example is not a class. The cost of the pass is a few minutes; the cost of inventing a class that is not there is a rule nobody can satisfy. It does not replace rendered-verification or a test. It asks whether the fix is aimed correctly. Whether it works is a different question and comes first. It does not decide a trade the owner should decide. When narrowing the generalisation costs something real — say, a corner magnifier under the staging banner, where raising it defeats the banner and lowering it costs the position — report the measurement and the two options rather than picking.

1008.title: The landing page is the layer’s own description
1008.content: A folio’s home page opens with its description inside its backdrop, both declared in the repository’s declaration. Nothing about any particular layer is written into the template, so a downstream folio does not inherit the platform’s grumpy cat. Where the markdown node is: description in <name>.json. It is markdown and it is rendered as-is. There is no separate landing page to keep in step with it, because a description in two places will disagree with itself. How the picture is declared: an image with role: "landing" and a layout (laptop, mobile, card), plus a textRegion giving, as fractions of the image, where words may safely be drawn. textRegion is authored, not computed. It states where the composition is quiet, which is a judgement: find it by rendering candidate boxes over the image and looking at them, not by deriving a number from the aspect ratio. Run bun run cat docs:harness after editing, and --check in CI. Three states: . | declared | rendered | . | backdrop with region | description drawn inside it | . | backdrop, no region | picture shown, words placed below it | . | no backdrop | words alone | . An undeclared region means do not overlay, never anywhere is fine, because text positioned by guesswork lands on the picture. A folio with no art is ordinary. A viewport with no variant falls back to the widest available, and the fallback is reported — that crop’s region is wrong for a narrow screen, so a consumer can decline to overlay rather than place text somewhere nobody chose. Reader-facing walkthrough: docs/start/getting-started.md §8. A new layer’s beans/ and todos/ are not written into its checkout. By default folio_init declares them on their own branches, cat/<instance>/beans and cat/<instance>/todos, and prints a one-time seed command. Say so when you hand the scaffold over: until the seed has been run and mounted, an empty beans list means not mounted, not no work. The rule, the branch naming and the override live in directory-conventions §”Where a NEW layer’s state lives”.

1009.title: 0. Why this skill exists
1009.content: folio_init scaffolds a folio, and it does it well. What it cannot do is know whether scaffolding is the right move, because the sentence that reaches it — “create a folio”, “set me up with folio-assistant”, “I want to start a paper” — is spoken by at least five different people: . | they mean | what they have | the wrong move costs them | . | new-repo | nothing yet, or an empty directory | — (this is the safe default, and the only one an agent may assume) | . | overlay | a repository with their own work in it | a folio scaffolded on top of a project the agent never looked at | . | add-folio | a folio-assistant layer already | a second repository they did not want, and a split corpus | . | new-content | a folio, and they wanted a document in it | an entire empty folio, and the chapter they asked for still not written | . | ask | any of the above, undeclared | — | . Four of these five states look identical from the user’s sentence, and three of them look identical from the filesystem, so the triage always runs.

1010.title: 1. Read the facts — mechanical, read-only, before anything is written
1010.content: Three facts, and nothing else. Gather them by looking, not by asking: . # isFolio — does an instantiated config here declare a contentType? # The root <name>.config.json files, and index.config.json, whose instances # may carry contentType inline (index-config skill). grep -lq '"contentType"' ./*.config.json 2>/dev/null && echo isFolio=true || echo isFolio=false # repoHasContent — does the tree hold somebody's project, as opposed to being bare? # Ignore VCS bookkeeping and editor droppings; count anything else. git ls-files | grep -vE '^\.(git|github|vscode|idea)/' | head -1 . statedIntent is the third, and it is a fact about the conversation: one of new-repo, overlay, add-folio, new-content, or unstated. It is unstated until the user has actually said which — never inferred from tone, from the repo, or from what would be convenient. A user who says “I want to add a chapter” has stated new-content; a user who says “create a folio” has stated nothing, because that sentence is what the five requests have in common. isFolio is ONE MEMBERSHIP of a set, and the set is what a repository is. describeRepository() (schemas/content/content-type.ts) returns every marker a repository carries — folio, harness, dak, sushi — with the facts each states and any disagreement between them. describeRepositoryClosure() (schemas/kg/harness-config.ts) extends that through the dependency tree, attributing each membership to the layer that carried it. folio and harness are different types. The declaration says this is a layer; a config that declares contentType says this authors folio content. That config is a root <name>.config.json, or its entry in index.config.json, where inline fields overlay the imported file (index-config). Listing a layer in the index makes it instantiated, not a folio. cat-harness/ carries the first and not the second — it is a harness and is not a folio. isFolio is exactly membership of folio: the DMN documents the input as a config in the working directory that declares a contentType, not its mere presence. So a repository being several things at once does not perturb the five branches. They key on folio-ness alone, and a folio that is also a DAK takes the same branch as one that is not — it is still already a folio, still has content, and the user has still either stated an intent or not. Use describeRepository when you want to know what a repository is; this probe when you want to know which branch to take. isFolio is about the working directory, not about the user. Somebody who has used folio-assistant before, in another repo, is still in an isFolio=false directory. Their experience is not a fact this table reads — it changes how much you explain, not which branch you take.

1011.title: 2. Let the table decide
1011.content: Feed the three facts to workflow_complete on Gateway_Intent, or read folio-intent.dmn directly. Do not supply an outcome: the gateway is computed, and workflow_complete refuses a hand-supplied answer there on purpose. The table returns one of five branches. Two of its seven rules return ask, and that is a result, not a failure to produce one: . | already a folio, intent unstated → ask. add-folio, new-repo and new-content are all consistent with what is on disk. | not a folio but has content, intent unstated → ask. overlay and new-repo are both consistent, and overlaying somebody’s repository on a guess is not recoverable by a git checkout. | not a folio, nothing here → new-repo. The one state that answers itself. | .

1012.title: 3. Ask — as options, never as prose
1012.content: When the branch is ask, put the question as a short list of selectable options. Not a paragraph, not an open “what would you like to do?”, and not a question whose answer has to be typed out. Load interaction-modality first; it decides the form the question takes, and for some users free text is not an available input at all. The list, phrased in the user’s terms rather than the branch names: . | Start a new folio in a new repository — nothing here gets touched. | Add folio-assistant to this repository — keeps what is here; I’ll look through it first and show you what I find before importing anything. | Add another folio to this repository (offer only when isFolio=true). | Add something to the folio that’s already here (only when isFolio=true) — a chapter, a document, a DAK component. | Tell me more — for the user who wants to describe it in their own words. | . Then ask what they want to get started on, offering the top-level content types this platform knows about, because “a folio” is not something anybody actually wants: . | content type | what it is | profile | . | paper | a scientific paper or book, with formal claims backed by Lean and typeset through LaTeX | paper | . | document | structured prose — policy guidance, a standard, a report. No Lean, no required TeX | document | . | WHO SMART DAK | a Digital Adaptation Kit (L2): personas, business processes, data elements, decision tables | dak | . | WHO SMART IG | a FHIR Implementation Guide (L3) built from an L2 DAK | dak | . Record the answer as statedIntent and evaluate the table again. The user’s answer is a fact like any other — it feeds the gateway, so the loop in the diagram runs back to Task_ReadFacts rather than jumping straight to a branch. When a remote repository is involved, ask which mode — and never infer it from push access. A remote git repository is assumed read-only (read-from). Having push access to a remote is never permission to modify it, and instantiating on a remote repository writes nothing there without the user’s explicit permission for that repository. Ask which mode they want, with materialize-or-reference as its own question: . | Keep it here (read-from) — build and render from the remote KG in this repository (stage-ig-sites into /<instance>/), and ask whether to materialize its assets locally or reference it in place (materialize-remote / materialize-on-demand). | Put a harness on the remote repository (written-to) — instantiate the harness in that remote repository itself and build in its own CI (stage-ig-sites --only <instance> --source .), only after explicit permission for that repository. | .

1013.title: 4. Route
1013.content: | branch | do | . | new-repo | Ask for the name. Create or use the empty directory, then folio_init. | . | overlay | Hand off to repo-conversion — scan first, import second, and never in the other order. The scan’s markers are offered as picks (§2a, Task_ChooseHarnessed): the harness declares only what the person chose — declare, don’t slurp. | . | add-folio | folio_init against a new top-level slug in the existing layer. Do not re-link the platform; it is already linked. | . | new-content | Stop. This process ends here. Hand off to the active content type’s authoring skill. Scaffolding anything on this branch is the bug. | . An empty repository gets main before any feature branch. GitHub makes the first branch pushed to an empty repository its default, so run init-folio (it seeds main first) or push main yourself before pushing anything else. A specialised content type is routed by its own creation skill. When the answer to step 3’s second question names a domain content type shipped by a higher harness layer, hand over to that layer’s creation skill (discover it via skill_list). It reads the same facts and adds the in-repository staged sub-KG option — staging inside the current repository first so nothing outside the repository changes until the owner confirms. Where folio_init does not handle that content type directly, the new-repository route scaffolds with --instance. A second folio can leave later. What add-folio creates, and any staged sub-KG, may later move to a repository of its own. That is sub-kg-lifecycle: stage it in place, then create the repository and delete the in-repo copy, each only on the owner’s confirmation.

1014.title: 5. After scaffolding — seed the plan, then publish
1014.content: . | Seed the work plan. One work item per top-level thing the author named in step 3. Run the exact-title existence check in todo-manager.md (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan) §”Check before you create” first — beans create is not idempotent. | Provision gh-pages — before Pages is switched on. This is Task_ProvisionGhPages in the process, and it carries the semantics of A_Provision in bootstrap-tools’ render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn (the gh-pages Tool’s subprocess — render-kg-to-cdn): a gh-pages branch must exist before Pages can be switched on to serve it. Run bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pages-bootstrap.ts --provision: it checks git ls-remote --heads origin gh-pages and, only if the branch is absent, pushes an orphan gh-pages holding a placeholder index.html and .nojekyll. It is idempotent and never forces a push; without --provision the script creates no remote branch, it only reports unprovisioned with the exact command. Then switch Pages on with Source: “Deploy from a branch: gh-pages, / (root)” — not “GitHub Actions”, when the publish workflow pushes gh-pages (the script prints the source it expects). Every publishing route reaches this step: new-repo, add-folio, and the overlay route through repo-conversion — including an overlay or new repo that remote-mounts its dependencies, which never reaches this section by itself. | Start the Pages build and report the URL. Run bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pages-bootstrap.ts --wait. It checks the branch first, derives the site address, says whether a publish workflow exists and which Pages source it needs, and probes until the site answers. | Say which of the four states you got, and never blur them: . | unprovisioned — there is no gh-pages branch (exit 3). Go back to step 2; nothing later can succeed until it exists. | live — hand over the link, and say what is on it. | not-yet — a measured 404. Give the address, say the first build has not landed there yet, and say roughly how long it takes. | unknown — no URL could be derived, or the probe failed. Say that. “Should be live shortly” is a claim you do not have evidence for. | . | Tell them the corpus is by reference, and how to change that. A fresh harness holds references, not the remote content itself, which can be hundreds of gigabytes. When they need part of a remote subgraph locally, that is an ask made later, as the need appears. Name the skill (materialize-on-demand) and the one command that shows what is already held (bun run cat cache:index), so they learn the option exists here rather than by finding a schema. Do not materialize anything now. | .

1015.title: 6. Anti-patterns
1015.content: . | Scaffolding on ask. The table returned a question; answering it yourself with the convenient branch defeats the table. | Treating “I’ve used this before” as add-folio. Experience is not a filesystem fact and not an intent. | Asking in prose. “Could you tell me a bit about what you’re hoping to build?” is a wall for a user who types with difficulty, and it produces a worse answer than the numbered list. | Announcing a Pages URL you have not probed. See step 5. | Going straight to folio_init because the request seemed obvious. Every one of the five requests seems obvious to the person making it. | Switching Pages on before gh-pages exists, or choosing “GitHub Actions” as the source for a workflow that pushes gh-pages. Step 2 first; the source is “Deploy from a branch”. | .

1023.title: GitHub Pages’ contract
1023.content: Skill github-pages: The contract GitHub Pages keeps as the host of a rendered Knowledge Graph: serve the gh-pages branch at the publication root URL, exactly as committed, and answer 404 for what is not there. A mechanical Actor plays this Role; this is what it must do, and what it is tested against. Named by: Render a Knowledge Graph to GitHub Pages . A host plays a Role, and this is the Role’s contract: what it must do, and what it is tested against. It decides nothing. pages-status is the test: it asks the publication root URL and each document address, and reports pushed, not-pushed or could-not-determine. It sits in the GitHub Pages lane of render-kg-to-github-pages. The Site Publisher, following render-kg-to-github-pages, is the other side of each step.

1024.title: Responsibilities
1024.content: . | Serve the gh-pages branch at /, once Pages is on with that source. | Serve what is committed. After a deployment commit, the publication root URL, its README.html and every document address answer with the committed files. | Answer 404 for what is not there, so a missing page is a failure a check can see, not an empty success. | .

1025.title: Not its responsibility
1025.content: Choosing the root URL or the Subgraphs, staging, or deciding whether a push landed. Those happen in the Site Publisher’s lane.

1027.title: Reading GitHub state — resolve the ref, do not compose the URL
1027.content: Skill github-state-inspection: Answer questions about GitHub-hosted state — is a page published, where does it live, did CI pass, does a branch exist — by reading the ref or the API, never by composing a URL or fetching one. The first check for any deployment or 404 question is git ls-tree of the publish ref. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Agent activity log, Close the bean, Drain the beans, Agent bean lifecycle, Open the bean, Code change and review, Merge the base branch in, A refused merge-train member, Requirements filing: promote, organise, trace, supersede, or retire, SME Review of Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route, Test Data Curation — Fixed Sets and Generated Recipes, Watching a pinned upstream dependency, Adopting an upstream version bump, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Editing and HCI validation, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . Skill id: github-state-inspection · Package: sdlc-core . Every question of the form “is it published?”, “why is this 404?”, “did that deploy?” has an authoritative answer in a ref, and a misleading one in an HTTP request. This skill says which to reach for and in what order.

1028.title: The rule
1028.content: A published URL is LOOKED UP in the publish ref’s tree. It is never built from the source path. cat-harness/docs/guides/agent-onboarding.md publishes to /docs/cat-harness/guides/agent-onboarding.html: the layer segment moves from in front of docs/ to behind it. Anyone composing the URL from the source path gets a 404 and concludes the page is missing. Source paths also move, and some pages (proposals, for one) are kept in the repository but deliberately unpublished. A URL composed from a remembered source path can assert a page exists where the repository has decided none should.

1029.title: First check for ANY deployment question
1029.content: Look at the branch. Not the site. git ls-remote origin refs/heads/gh-pages # does the publish ref exist at all git fetch origin gh-pages git ls-tree --name-only FETCH_HEAD # what is at the root git ls-tree -r --name-only FETCH_HEAD | grep -i <thing> # where does it actually live . For a staging preview, the subtree is branches/<branch-slug>/, and git ls-tree --name-only FETCH_HEAD branches/ lists every branch with a live preview. The slug replaces / with -: claude/festive-galileo-s7ibx0 becomes branches/claude-festive-galileo-s7ibx0/. The MCP GitHub tools answer the same question without a fetch — get_file_contents with ref: "refs/heads/gh-pages" and a directory path returns the listing. Use whichever is to hand; both read the ref, which is the point.

1030.title: Present on the ref is not the same as SERVED — read the Pages deployment
1030.content: The step above is authoritative for what exists. It is not authoritative for what a reader gets, and the gap between them has a mechanism worth knowing. Pages-from-a-branch publishes through a pages build and deployment run, and a new push to the publish ref cancels the run already in flight. So a commit can sit on gh-pages with the file plainly there while the last successful deployment is an older tree. git log --format='%h %ad %s' --date=iso -10 origin/gh-pages # how fast is the ref moving . and the deployments themselves, which only the API has: . actions_list method: list_workflow_runs workflow_runs_filter: { branch: "gh-pages", event: "dynamic" } . Read conclusion per run, not just the newest — cancelled is the one that misleads, because nothing is red and yet nothing shipped from that commit. Each staging deploy pushes two commits about ten seconds apart, the payload (staging(<slug>): from <sha>) and then render-log: rendered …, and the second reliably cancels the first’s build, so on a busy publish ref many recent deployments read cancelled. So when a preview 404s and the file is on the ref: . | Check whether a deployment has succeeded since the commit that added it. A cancelled newest run with an older success means the tree being served predates your push. | Check whether your subtree survives in that older tree too — on a ref this busy, git cat-file -e <commit>:<path> over the recent commits answers “was it ever missing” directly, and a path present at every one of them rules the ref out as the cause entirely. | Only then is the question about Pages rather than about the repository, and it is a wait-or-escalate, not a fix. | . What this does not license. A cancelled run is an explanation to verify, never one to assert: it is equally consistent with a page that is serving fine. From a container that cannot reach the host, the honest report is the mechanism plus what you could and could not establish — not “it is probably propagation”.

1031.title: Why curl is not the first check, and often not evidence at all
1031.content: Three distinct failures produce an identical-looking result, and only one of them means the page is missing: . | what you see | what it can mean | . | 404 | the page is not published — or your URL was composed wrong | . | 000, CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403 | the agent’s proxy blocks the host. Says nothing about the site | . | 200 on a stale page | the deploy has not run yet; the old build is still served | . In a Claude Code container, outbound HTTPS goes through a proxy that blocks github.io. A curl against a Pages URL from here returns 000 and a 403 tunnel error regardless of whether the page exists, so “could not determine” from a fetch is no answer when the ref holds one. “Could not determine” is a third state and must never be rendered as a pass — but it is also not a place to stop when another source can determine it. Reach for the ref first, and a fetch only to confirm something the ref cannot tell you (that a redirect works, that a asset loads).

1032.title: CI state — read check RUNS on the head sha
1032.content: Commit statuses and check runs are different APIs and this repository uses the second. pull_request_read with method: "get_status" returns {"state":"pending","total_count":0,"statuses":[]} on a PR whose eight checks are green, because there are no legacy statuses to report. Use method: "get_check_runs". Further traps: . | Check the sha. A check_suite.completed event names a head_sha that may already be superseded by your own later push, and the staging workflow’s own commits appear as shas that are not PR heads at all. Compare against the PR’s current head before concluding anything. | mergeable_state: "unknown" means GitHub has not finished computing it, not that the PR is fine. "dirty" is a real merge conflict and is work now. | “No suite failed” over ZERO suites is not a pass, and neither is a clean run list that is only PART of the check set. See below. | . A clean check set and a COMPLETE check set are different questions . A check_suite.completed event says no third-party suite is still running or failed. Its own harness note admits the gap: suites with no runs, cancelled suites and legacy statuses are not covered; verify the PR’s overall state before acting. So the event is evidence about the suites that EXIST, and silence about the ones that do not yet. The same hole exists one layer down: a classifier that guards only the EMPTY run list passes a PARTIAL one — one clean run where thirteen are owed reads as PASS — 1 check(s) completed clean. So before reading a clean check set as green, ask whether it is the whole set. check:head-has-run answers it — coverageFor reconciles the runs against the workflows the tree itself declares, and mergeStateForHead returns conflicted for the case below. bun run cat ci:watch composes both. Do not build a second reconciliation; two answers to one question are free to disagree. Four causes of an absent-or-inert run, which must not collapse into one silence. The fourth is not an absence: the run exists, it completed, and it executed nothing. | cause | how it reads | what to do | . | a conflicted head | no pull_request run is published AT ALL — the forge mints no refs/pull/N/merge, and a pull_request run checks that ref out | merge the base in. The checks are not slow; they are never coming | . | a filtered trigger that owed no run | genuinely nothing was due | stay silent — loosening this produces false fires | . | a run never created, unexplained | a workflow the tree declares on: pull_request has no run and the head is mergeable | a finding, not a wait | . | a bot-actor push | the runs EXIST and are completed, with conclusion: action_required — approval was owed and never given, so no job ran | read the dispatched run instead; see below | . A draft PR is a fifth reading of the same silence: Code-quality gates does not fire from pull_request while a PR is a draft, so a draft head owes those runs no more than a filtered trigger does. Mark it ready, do not dispatch. conclusion: action_required is not a failure, and not a pass . Counting conclusions makes this invisible. action_required is a terminal conclusion that is neither success nor failure, so a predicate written as conclusion != "failure" reads it as fine and one written as conclusion == "success" reads the head as merely incomplete. Neither says what is true: the workflow was reached, approval was owed, and no job body executed. A head pushed by a bot actor gets pull_request runs that are all action_required; a head pushed by a session gets runs that execute. The merge-forward bot does not void the gates. With no MERGE_MAIN_TOKEN set, merge-main.yml dispatches both gating workflows — code-quality-gates.yml and jsonld-gen-check.yml — so the merge commit is proved by CI rather than trusted; Feature Staging is left alone because it is preview-only. Such a head shows the pair pull_request: action_required beside workflow_dispatch: success, on the identical head sha. So the rule for reading a head is by workflow and sha, never by event: a workflow_dispatch run of an owed workflow on the exact head is proof, and after a merge-forward it is arguably better proof, because the branch tip already contains the base and the dispatch tests the merged content rather than a synthesised merge ref. check:head-has-run already reads it this way, so do not add an event filter to it. MERGE_MAIN_TOKEN is a convenience, not a correctness fix: it makes the PR’s own runs fire on the bot’s push instead of needing a dispatch. Do not hand-push commits to “restore” gates that already ran. Ask whether the BASE moved before calling any verdict non-deterministic. A pull_request run tests the head merged with main as it was at push time, so main moving flips verdicts in both directions with no change to your branch — a green head can become a red merge commit, and a red check can turn green when a sibling’s fix lands. That is not a flapping gate.

1033.title: Order of resort
1033.content: . | The ref — git ls-tree / get_file_contents. Authoritative for what exists and where. | The API — check runs, PR state, branch list. Authoritative for what happened. | The workflow run — actions_list / get_job_logs. Authoritative for why it happened. | An HTTP fetch — last, and only for what the first three cannot answer. From an agent container, treat a failure as a proxy result until proven otherwise. | . From a cloud agent container, use REST. The proxy blocks GraphQL, so gh pr view and other GraphQL-backed gh commands fail; gh api repos/... works. Actions log blob URLs return 403 through the same proxy, so read logs with the GitHub MCP get_job_logs (return_content, tail_lines), not by fetching the URL it would hand you.

1034.title: github-state-inspection (skill)
1034.content: The skill github-state-inspection as its source file cat-harness/sdlc/skills/sdlc-core/github-state-inspection.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

1035.title: Glossary terms
1035.content: Skill glossary-terms: Add terms to a layer’s glossary: local SKOS terms (folio-glossary/v1) with a definition, a code and links to external SKOS concepts, and references to whole external schemes. Rendered on the glossary/ page; gated by check:glossary. Authored terms go to gettext (.pot) for translation; a paper’s glossary is one more scheme. Named by: Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph . A glossary can reference external SKOS schemes, and that is the preferred way.

1036.title: Where terms go
1036.content: Core declares the glossary directory in folio-assistant-core.json. Its graph typology is perInstance, so every folio built on core has a glossary/. Each *.glossary.json is one SKOS concept scheme, $schema: "folio-glossary/v1" (folio-assistant-core/schemas/glossary.ts).

1037.title: Reference first, define second
1037.content: | you have | write | . | a term somebody else already defines in SKOS (ISCO-08, an EU authority table, a W3C vocabulary) | a local term with exactMatch (or closeMatch, broadMatch, narrowMatch) to the external concept IRI. Do not copy its definition. | . | a list of external terms this folio uses | members: the external concept IRIs, emitted as a skos:Collection | . | a whole external scheme | a remoteGraphs entry in the declaration with graphTypologies: ["glossary"]: known about, not held | . | a term only this folio defines | a local term with prefLabel, definition, and notation for its code | .

1038.title: Three states, never two
1038.content: . | authored: a person wrote or approved the definition. It must have one. | candidate: extracted from a source and not yet curated. It may have no definition, and the page marks it. | could-not-extract: the source names a term the extractor could not read. It carries a reason a person can act on. | . A candidate is never presented as a definition. An extractor writes candidates; only a person moves one to authored. A paper’s definition block counts as that person: its author wrote the definition and marked it (see “A paper’s glossary” below).

1039.title: How a term is linked: the workflow
1039.content: Terms are linked across the glossary, the narrative and the knowledge graph with a few shared joins, not a framework. One join key: the SKOS term (its id, or its IRI from another layer). Everything else points at it, and nothing copies it. | thing | how it names the term | . | the defining site | the term’s source: its glossary row (an L1 section line, or the document’s glossary table block). One node-kind structure for every term. | . | a narrative block that explains the term at length | the block’s defines: [<term id>] (and :defterm[...]{#id} inline). Provenance, not a second definition. | . | other uses in prose | nothing to write: matched at build time (term-passages.ts) and linked by --link-terms | . | an acronym | notation on the term, never a second list. The acronyms table is drawn from it (glossary:table). | . | an organization | focus (W3C ORG), shared ones in smart-ra organizations.glossary.json | . | an ArchiMate element | the element’s skosConcept property (glossary-archimate.ts) | . | a BPMN lane or task, DMN decision, skill, Tool | the generated candidate schemes (glossary-extract.ts); exactMatch when one is the same concept | . | a FHIR code | exactMatch / closeMatch to the CodeSystem concept; the code stays a CodeSystem | . | an external glossary | exactMatch to its IRI, members, or a whole scheme in remoteGraphs | . Where terms come from. | Ingesting a source (L1, DTH, DAK): bun run cat glossary:from-source reads its glossary and abbreviations sections into verbatim candidate terms with source: <file>#L<line> (l1-document-ingestion). No per-handbook script. | Authoring in the narrative (dth-hrh): the glossary file is edited, and the chapter is drawn from it (glossary:table, or the folio’s own build). A block that explains a term lists it in defines. | External: reference, don’t copy (below). | . What a reader gets. Every authored-scheme term has a page (glossary:page, glossary/instance/<instance>/<scheme>/<term>/). It shows the definition and acronym, Defined in (its glossary row), broader, narrower (computed), related terms, matches, ArchiMate elements, and In the narrative: the blocks that explain it, then those that use it. A Capitalized label in prose links to that page when the document build passes --link-terms, which dth-init sets for every DTH. Warnings, never failures. bun run cat glossary:links reports a source that is missing from a mounted layer, and a defines id that no scheme holds. With --all it also lists terms the narrative never uses. The acronym report is glossary:acronyms.

1040.title: Conventions
1040.content: Every folio follows these; none re-decides them. The layer namespace. A term’s IRI is <instance namespace>glossary/<scheme id>/<term id>. The layer namespace is built from the layer’s declaration (iriBase, version, and the stub of a sub-layer) by instanceNs in folio-assistant-core/scripts/glossary-page.ts; schemeIri and termIri are in folio-assistant-core/schemas/glossary.ts. For example: . | layer | namespace | . | folio-assistant-core | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant-core/v0/ns/ | . | ihris (its own site) | https://litlfred.github.io/ihris/ihris/ns/ | . The namespace is never the asset’s path: moving the asset must not move the term. A term is minted by the layer that owns its source. A scheme and its terms live in the namespace of the layer whose root holds the SOURCE ASSET, not of the layer whose glossary/ directory holds the file: . | In a folio with sub-layers, that is the sub-layer (instanceNs(<sub-stub>), under the folio’s own publication root). It is never the root layer, even when the glossary/ directory is declared at the root. In ihris, a term drawn from ihris-manage is minted in ihris-manage’s namespace, not ihris’s. | A code list extended by several packages belongs to the layer that DEFINES it. Say so with the scheme’s own source (a repository path in that layer). Each term’s source still points at the package that contributed it. | A scheme whose terms are sourced in several layers and that names no defining source is refused, never guessed: split it, one scheme per layer. folio-assistant-core/glossary/ holds two platform schemes for that reason, core’s and cat-harness’s. | No two layers share a namespace, and a scheme IRI is unique across every layer. | . check:glossary enforces all of this (schemeOwner and collect in glossary-page.ts, and the checks in glossary.test.ts); glossary-extract.ts mints extracted terms by the same rule. When a check fails, fix the generator or split the authored scheme. Never edit the output. One ConceptScheme per code list. This follows schemas/code-list.ts (codeListToSkos): “a code is addressable and two lists may share a code without sharing a concept”. The same code in two lists gives two concepts. A relation between them is a SKOS match, never a merge. The basis of a match is recorded, never assumed. A match comes from a mapping the repository verified, such as a FHIR ConceptMap whose equivalence implies one: . | equal/equivalent gives exactMatch; | wider/subsumes gives broadMatch; | narrower/specializes gives narrowMatch; | nothing else gives a match. | . Any other basis needs the owner’s explicit acceptance. One example is a ValueSet that binds a local code list to the external code system itself, so that the local code is the external code. Once accepted: . | the scheme’s description names the basis and the ruling; | the builder lists the accepted systems explicitly; | QA recomputes the matches from the same source. | . ihris’s ISCO-08 lists to ESCO are the worked example. An IRI built from a publisher’s pattern but never dereferenced says so.

1041.title: Then
1041.content: bun run cat glossary:page writes the index, docs/glossary/index.md (the authored terms with A–Z and a filter box, the counts, the sources, schema.org DefinedTermSet JSON-LD, and a link to every asset type’s page), one page per asset type at docs/glossary/<type>/index.md (skills, tools, bpmn-activities, dmn-decisions, schema-fields: that type’s extracted terms, with A–Z and a filter box), and one SKOS JSON-LD file per scheme under docs/assets/glossary/. Each term is on exactly one page. bun run check:glossary is the gate: it fails on a document that does not validate, on a stale page, and on a page over its size budget (64 KB for the index, 1 MB for an asset type’s page). A page over budget is split further, never given a bigger budget. The harness’s swimlane-role terms (swimlane-glossary, the swimlane-glossary skill) are one more source the page links to, not copies of.

1042.title: Extracted terms
1042.content: glossary:page also extracts a candidate term from every knowledge-graph asset that carries a title and a description (folio-assistant-core/scripts/glossary-extract.ts): skills, Tool nodes, BPMN tasks and call activities, DMN decisions, and schema fields with a doc comment. One scheme per asset type per layer (kg-skills, kg-tools, kg-bpmn-activities, kg-dmn-decisions, kg-schema-fields), written to generated/<instance>/<type>.glossary.json inside core’s glossary/. | They are generated. Never edit them: fix the asset, then re-run. | The kg- scheme prefix is reserved for them. An authored scheme that takes it fails check:glossary. | A definition is the asset’s own text, verbatim. An asset with no description gives a candidate with no definition. | To promote one, author a term in a glossary of your own with a definition you have checked, status: authored, and the same source. | BPMN lanes and roles are not extracted: the swimlane ledger carries them. | Extracted terms are on their asset type’s page, never on the index, and each carries the “candidate, extracted” badge. Only authored terms go into the schema.org DefinedTermSet, which is on the index. | .

1043.title: Ordered glossaries — logical order, not A–Z
1043.content: Some glossaries (bootstrap’s, for one) are read top to bottom: each term is defined only by terms above it, and never by itself. Do not sort them A–Z. | ordered: true on a glossary says its terms array IS the order. Each term’s requires lists the local ids its definition uses; the schema refuses one that is later, itself, or not in the glossary. checkDeclaredOrder (schemas/dependency-order.ts) is the same check for any authored order. | In SKOS the order is a skos:OrderedCollection (memberList as an RDF list), each use is dcterms:requires, and isDefinedBy — the schema or standard that defines the term — is rdfs:isDefinedBy. | On the page an ordered scheme is its own numbered section at the top of the index, with its “Uses” links, and is not repeated under the A–Z bar. | A schema whose $defs carry uses IS an ordered glossary, read by termsOfSchema in glossary-page.ts: the definitions stay in one place, the schema, and the glossary cannot drift from it. They are authored, not candidate: a person wrote and approved them in the schema’s source, and the collector only reads them out. | The uses list is authored, not inferred. A text matcher over the definitions is a guard that the list and the prose agree (graph.test.ts); a word can appear without being used as a term. | .

1044.title: Translation: authored terms only
1044.content: bun run cat glossary:pot writes one gettext template per scheme that has an authored term, to translations/<locale>/glossary/<instance>--<scheme>.pot under cat-harness’s declared translation-sources directory, beside the BPMN templates in processes/, through the same pipeline (formatPot, the same timestamp-blind comparison); the translation status page counts them. bun run cat glossary:pot:check is the gate. | Only authored terms are extracted: prefLabel, each altLabel, and the definition, in the source language (en when given per language). A candidate reaches a template once a person promotes it. | The term’s IRI is the translator comment, never a msgid. It stays the same in every language; only labels and definitions are translated. | translations/<locale>/glossary.po is a different file (terminology hints for translation-block-qa). Do not confuse it with the glossary/ directory. | . Translations and the per-locale pages . A translation is a .po beside its template: translations/<locale>/glossary/<instance>--<scheme>.po. bun run glossary:page reads every such file (readGlossaryTranslations, through glossary-pot.ts’s potPath) and produces two things: . | a page per locale, docs/<locale>/glossary/index.md, listing every authored term with its translated label, alternative labels and definition. An entry with no translation shows the source text marked (untranslated) — never silently English, never dropped — and the page states how many terms are fully translated; | language-tagged SKOS: the published <instance>--<scheme>.skos.jsonld carries skos:prefLabel and skos:definition once per language (@language), the source as en. | . check:glossary covers both, stale and orphan alike. A translation is UNOFFICIAL until a person signs it off. Every glossary .po says so in its header and records Last-Translator: folio-assistant agent (drafted, unofficial) when an agent drafted it; every locale page carries translation_status: unverified. Keep code, identifiers and standard names (BPMN, SKOS, ODRL, PROV-O, JSON, IRI, $schema, needs) as written, and give each capitalised defined term ONE rendering per locale across every scheme. Subject areas and fixed translations . Owner, 2026-11-07 (glossary review, “scoped fixed terms”). Three fields and one rule, in schemas/glossary.ts: . | field | where | meaning | . | subject | scheme, optionally a term | the subject area the translations bind in (dcterms:subject), a local id: harness-vocabulary, digital-health-trust, who-health-guidance. A term’s overrides its scheme’s; with neither, the term binds only within its own scheme. | . | translationStatus | term | per locale, official or unofficial; a locale not listed is unofficial. It records sign-off, never the translation. | . | (none) | the scheme’s .po | the translation itself. | . A fixed translation is derived, never flagged: an authored term whose scheme catalogue holds a non-empty, non-fuzzy msgstr for its prefLabel (isFixedTranslation). There is no #, fixed flag and no label in the JSON, so the .po stays the one place a translation lives. Precedence applies within a subject area. Across the layers a layer needs, the more authoritative (lower) layer fixes a term’s translation for its subject area, and a higher layer only adds. A match in a different subject area — the harness’s policy (策略) in a health guide’s sentence (政策) — is a sense check note for a person, never a violation. translation:glossary:check reads these fields. Use scopeNote for the prose a reader needs; it is never compared.

1045.title: Source glossary first
1045.content: When a folio is written from a source document (a WHO handbook, say), its terms come from that source’s own glossary before anyone writes one. | Latest edition. Use the most recent edition in the library. If it lacks something an older edition has, use the older one and say so on the term. | Verbatim, as candidates. Extract every glossary entry as a folio-glossary/v1 term, status candidate, the definition copied word for word with its page. Keep the source’s spelling as an altLabel when the prefLabel is normalised. | Read the PDF when the ingest missed it. A glossary the library entry does not hold (a missed section, a missing indicator sheet) is read from the PDF, and the scheme says so. | Structure the source gives is kept. Modules, indicators and the like become concepts too, linked (broader, related) to the glossary terms they cite. | Record what the source never defines. A term the source uses but does not define is a candidate with no definition and a scopeNote saying so, not a definition we write. | Place the scheme with the source. It lives beside the document’s library entry (for WHO publications, in the WHO publications IG), so every folio that cites the source shares one scheme. | Use the source’s words downstream. Blocks, diagrams and ArchiMate names use the source’s terms and link to their concepts, not a paraphrase. | . A conflict between the source’s definition and another scheme’s is raised as an issue on the repository that owns the other scheme, quoting both. Neither is chosen by the agent.

1046.title: Deprecating a term: a change set, decided later
1046.content: Replacing one term with another (for example “Core Data Element” replacing “MDS-HRH”) is proposed, not applied. The agent records a change set with the old term, the new term, the reason, and every place the old term appears. It changes no text and no glossary entry. An agent review, started later by an editor, decides it. Once decided: . | the old term stays in the scheme, so old links still resolve, with a scopeNote saying it is deprecated and why, and related to the new term (folio-glossary/v1 has no deprecated status yet; adding one is a schema change, not part of this rule); | the folio’s own prose moves to the new term; | quoted source text is never changed: a quote keeps the term it was published with. | .

1047.title: A paper’s glossary
1047.content: The paper builder (folio-assistant-core/scripts/build-glossary.ts, skill glossary-build) also writes the paper’s terms as one folio-glossary/v1 scheme, paper-<paper directory>, into the glossary directory the paper’s OWN layer declares. The page picks it up through collect() like any other scheme, so the IRIs are in that layer’s namespace (a sub-layer’s for a paper in a sub-layer, never the root’s). | the owning block | its :defterm paragraph | status | . | kind: "definition" | found | authored: the author wrote the definition | . | any other kind | found | candidate: extracted from a theorem, remark, … | . | any | not found | could-not-extract, with the reason | . The definition is the :defterm paragraph, verbatim, with directives replaced by their labels. The slug is the term’s notation. Never edit the scheme: edit the paper and re-run the builder. A layer that declares no glossary directory gets a notice and no scheme; add { "id": "glossary", "path": "glossary/", "dependents": "reproduce", "graphTypologies": ["glossary"] }.

1048.title: Organizations and acronyms
1048.content: An organization (WHO, HL7, ISO, GS1, a national regulator) is a glossary term like any other, plus a focus: SKOS’s foaf:focus link from the concept to the organization, which is typed with W3C ORG. The concept keeps the words: prefLabel is the full name, notation is the acronym, and altLabel holds other spellings. The organization keeps the facts about the organization. { "id": "who", "prefLabel": "World Health Organization", "notation": "WHO", "definition": "…quoted from its source…", "status": "candidate", "focus": { "type": "FormalOrganization", "homepage": "https://www.who.int/", "subOrganizationOf": ["un"] } } . | type is a W3C ORG class: Organization, FormalOrganization, OrganizationalUnit or OrganizationalCollaboration. | subOrganizationOf names a local term that has a focus, or an organization’s IRI. sameAs links the same organization in another register, such as ROR or Wikidata. Give an identifier only when you have checked it; never guess one. | Without iri, the organization’s IRI is <term IRI>/_focus. | . One home per organization. An organization that several handbooks use (WHO, HL7, ISO, GS1, UNICEF, USAID) is defined once, in the shared reference architecture’s organizations scheme. A handbook lists it under members and does not copy it. An organization only one handbook names, such as a country’s regulator, stays in that handbook’s glossary. An acronym is scoped to its meaning. Use the document’s own expansion, and check it in context. In the WHO product catalogue handbook, “FDA” is the Rwanda Food and Drugs Authority, not the US Food and Drug Administration. When the document’s acronym would mislead a reader, record it as a candidate and raise it in the document’s review log. Do not fix the quoted text yourself. Finding the acronyms that are missing. The QA criterion acronym-in-glossary warns, block by block, about an acronym that no glossary the folio can see holds as a notation, prefLabel or altLabel. It warns and never fails. For the whole folio, with counts and the expansion the document gives (its abbreviations table, or “Long Name (ACR)”), run: . bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/glossary-acronyms.ts --folio folio . Each row is a candidate for a person to decide on. Words set in capitals (RESOURCES in a figure), plural forms (GTINs) and the folio’s own ids (PC-R-05) are left out.

1049.title: Architecture elements: the model drawn from the graph
1049.content: A reference architecture’s elements live in the knowledge graph, and the ArchiMate model is drawn from it, with the relationships on each glossary term. A term that names an element is a glossary term like any other, plus a focus that is the element: its ArchiMate type, and its relationships to other terms’ elements. { "id": "client-registry", "prefLabel": "Client Registry", "definition": "…quoted from the document…", "status": "candidate", "focus": { "archimate": "ApplicationComponent", "relationships": [ { "type": "Realization", "target": "client-identification" }, { "type": "Access", "target": "client-record", "accessType": "read" } ] } } . | archimate is the element type, as ArchiMate’s exchange format names it. | relationships[].type is one of ArchiMate 3.2’s eleven. target is a local term whose focus is an element, or an element’s IRI. accessType is only for Access. | In JSON-LD the element is <term IRI>/_focus, typed archimate:<Type>, and each relationship is a predicate such as archimate:serving. | . The Tool archimate-from-glossary (bun run cat archimate:from-glossary --instance <dir> --model <id> [--write] [--prune] [--check]) makes the model agree. It matches each element by its skosConcept property, never by name. It names and documents the element from the term, creates any element the model lacks (on no view: place it in Archi, or with archimate-detangle), and adds the relationships the terms list. A type that disagrees is reported, and a person decides. A relationship between linked elements that no term lists is removed only with --prune. Archi keeps the layout: no box moves. Its report counts the elements that still point at no term. An authored ArchiMate model is never a source of the glossary. Never write a term, label, definition, focus or relationship into a glossary from a model someone authored in Archi. The words come from the source documents; the model only depicts them. The one exception is a model that was ingested: received from elsewhere and held as a source under the layer’s library/. Such a model can seed the glossary once with --seed --from library/<entry>/<file>.archimate (--write to write). Every term an element of it already points at, and that has no focus yet, takes the element’s type and its relationships to the other linked elements. From then on, the glossary is the source. The Tool refuses --seed on any model outside library/. The read-only “depicted by” links on a term’s page (glossary-archimate) read the model’s skosConcept on each build and write nothing into the glossary, so they are allowed.

1050.title: Not here
1050.content: A clinical code system is FHIR CodeSystem/ValueSet, not a glossary: convergence stops at SKOS. A glossary term may exactMatch a clinical concept; it does not become one.
