3289.doc: Technical Writer — SDO register with RFC 2119 requirement levels
3289.title: Technical Writer — SDO register with RFC 2119 requirement levels
3289.content: technical-writer · shipped by folio-assistant-core · folio-assistant-core/skills/voices/technical-writer · every folio-assistant-core voice . IRI: https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/folio-assistant-core/voice/technical-writer · JSON-LD . The voice for technical documentation of standards, software and knowledge assets, written as an SDO writes (W3C, IHE). Requirement levels are RFC 2119's, read from the ingested RFC rather than from memory, and constrained by RFC 8174: only UPPERCASE usage carries the defined meaning. Applies to drafting AND to review QA. Nine rules; five cite the two ingested RFCs, three cite the `technical-documentation` skill, a node of this layer's own knowledge graph, because a rule that cites a document it was not read from is the false provenance this schema exists to prevent. 9 rule(s) · overlay voice-overlay-technical-writer at major · provenance assertion · derived from RFC 2119 — Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels (S. Bradner, Harvard University, BCP 14, March 1997) (1997); RFC 8174 — Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words (B. Leiba, BCP 14, May 2017) (2017) . | rule | what it asks | category · severity | the passage it was read from | . | tw-rfc2119-absolute-requirement | MUST, REQUIRED and SHALL mean an absolute requirement — nothing weakerUse MUST, REQUIRED or SHALL only where the requirement is absolute. They are interchangeable by the RFC's own definition, so choose one per document and keep to it rather than varying for rhythm. A MUST that a reader may reasonably decline is not a MUST; it is a SHOULD, and mislabelling it teaches readers to discount every other MUST in the document. | terminology · critical | 1. MUST This word, or the terms "REQUIRED" or "SHALL", mean that the definition is an absolute requirement of the specification.rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels#page-001, p1 | . | tw-rfc2119-absolute-prohibition | MUST NOT and SHALL NOT mean an absolute prohibitionReserve MUST NOT and SHALL NOT for absolute prohibitions. Do not soften a prohibition into 'should not' when it is absolute, and do not inflate a discouragement into MUST NOT because it feels important. | terminology · critical | 2. MUST NOT This phrase, or the phrase "SHALL NOT", mean that the definition is an absolute prohibition of the specification.rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels#page-001, p1 | . | tw-rfc2119-should-carries-a-burden | SHOULD and RECOMMENDED admit exceptions, and the writer owes the reader the implicationsSHOULD and RECOMMENDED mean valid reasons may exist to ignore the item — but the RFC puts a burden on the reader to understand and weigh the implications, which the writer can only discharge by stating them. A bare SHOULD with no account of what departing from it costs is an instruction the reader cannot act on. | terminology · major | 3. SHOULD This word, or the adjective "RECOMMENDED", mean that there may exist valid reasons in particular circumstances to ignore a particular item, but the full implications must be understood and carefully weighed before choosing a different course.rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels#page-002, p2 | . | tw-rfc2119-sparingly | Imperatives are used sparingly, and only where interoperation or harm requires themThe RFC constrains its own key words: they are for what is actually required for interoperation, or to limit behaviour that can cause harm. They are NOT for imposing a preferred method where the method is not required. A document in which every paragraph carries a MUST has not been made rigorous; it has made its genuine requirements unfindable. | register · major | Imperatives of the type defined in this memo must be used with care and sparingly. In particular, they MUST only be used where it is actually required for interoperation or to limit behavior which has potential for causing harm (e.g., limiting retransmisssions) For example, they must not be used to try to impose a particular method on implementors where the method is not required for interoperability.rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels#page-003, p3 | . | tw-rfc8174-uppercase-only | Only UPPERCASE key words carry the requirement meaningRFC 8174 updates RFC 2119: only all-capitals usage has the defined special meaning. So 'the parser must handle this' is ordinary prose and 'the parser MUST handle this' is a conformance requirement, and the difference is visible rather than inferred. A reviewer MUST read lowercase 'must' as narration, and a writer who meant a requirement MUST capitalise it. | capitalization · critical | This document updates RFC 2119 by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.rfc8174-uppercase-vs-lowercase-2119-key-words#page-001, p1 | . | tw-elaborate-consequences | State what not following a requirement costsRFC 2119 asks authors to elaborate the implications of not following a requirement, on the grounds that most implementors lack the experience and discussion that produced the specification. Generalised here beyond security: a requirement whose consequence is unstated is one a reader cannot weigh, and is the single most common reason a correct instruction is ignored. | structure · major | Document authors should take the time to elaborate the security implications of not following recommendations or requirements as most implementors will not have had the benefit of the experience and discussion that produced the specification.rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels#page-003, p3 | . | tw-glossary-terms-capitalised | Glossary Terms are Capitalized throughoutA Term defined in the Glossary is Capitalized every time it is used, so a reader can tell a defined Term from the same word used loosely. Before introducing a term, ask whether it is defined; if not, whether it is defined later, whether it belongs in the Glossary, and whether it is used in several places or only here. A term used once and nowhere else does not earn a Glossary entry. | capitalization · major | Glossary Terms are Capitalized on every use, so a reader can tell a defined Term from the same word used loosely.skills/authoring/authoring-core/technical-documentation.md | . | tw-no-repetition-logical-order | After the first draft: repetition, order, defined termsThree questions the writer runs against their own draft before review. Have I repeated anything? If so, consolidate — the same fact in two places is free to drift, and the copy a reader finds first is the one with no test. Does the content flow in logical order? If not, apply the detangler rather than reordering by taste. Is each Term defined? This is a drafting rule, not a reviewer's courtesy: it is cheapest to fix while the draft is still the author's. | structure · major | Have I repeated anything? If so, consolidate. The same fact in two places is free to drift, and the copy a reader finds first is usually the one with no test behind it.skills/authoring/authoring-core/technical-documentation.md | . | tw-link-schema-and-uml | Link the schema source and its UML when the prose names a schemaNaming a schema without linking it makes the reader guess which file is meant, and the guess fails precisely when the schema has moved. Link the source, and the UML documentation where one exists. This is the resolve-do-not-compose rule applied to prose: a written-out path is a composition nothing checks, a link is a reference a checker can falsify. | citation · major | When the prose names a schema, link to the schema source and to its UML documentation where one exists. A schema named but not linked forces the reader to guess which file, and the guess is wrong exactly when the schema has moved.skills/authoring/authoring-core/technical-documentation.md | .

3297.doc: Linked data — how a coding agent emits and reviews JSON-LD
3297.title: Linked data — how a coding agent emits and reviews JSON-LD
3297.content: linked-data · shipped by folio-assistant-core · folio-assistant-core/skills/voices/linked-data · every folio-assistant-core voice . IRI: https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/folio-assistant-core/voice/linked-data · JSON-LD . The voice for a coding agent writing or reviewing code that EMITS JSON-LD: what makes the output linked data a processor can follow, rather than JSON that merely carries an @context. Six rules, each read from a held W3C text. Owner, 2026-10-01: "make sure that these issues are part of the one voice for jsonld" and "it is a voice for a coding agent, in a code authoring or review task". Every rule was found broken or fragile in this repository before it was written down (beans jcet, 9y9j): the PROV-O QA/QC reports carried prov:agent, prov:hadRole and prov:hadPlan as plain strings in all 100 activities, and the content context's @base resolves only because jsonld.js applies @base from a remote context. 7 rule(s) · overlay voice-overlay-linked-data at major · provenance evidence · derived from JSON-LD 1.1 — A JSON-based Serialization for Linked Data (W3C Recommendation, 16 July 2020) (2020); PROV-O: The PROV Ontology (W3C Recommendation, 30 April 2013) (2013); The PROV-JSONLD Serialization (W3C Member Submission, 25 August 2024; acknowledged, not endorsed) (2024) . | rule | what it asks | category · severity | the passage it was read from | . | ld-object-property-is-a-link | A property whose value is a node is emitted as a link, never as a stringWhen the vocabulary defines a property as an OBJECT property (its value is another node: prov:agent, prov:hadRole, prov:hadPlan, prov:used), the emitted JSON-LD must make the value an IRI — through a term whose definition says "@type": "@id", or as {"@id": …}. A bare string under an uncoerced key expands to {"@value": …}, a literal: valid JSON-LD, but a graph in which the activity was done by the TEXT "owner" and nothing joins it to the actor. Review test: expand one emitted document with a real processor and look for @value where a node was meant. | structure · critical | Alternatively, the keyword @id or @vocab may be used as value to indicate that within the body of a JSON-LD document, a string value of a term coerced to @id or @vocab is to be interpreted as an IRI.w3c-2020-json-ld-1-1#sec-053-note | . | ld-know-which-properties-are-object-properties | Read the ontology for which properties take nodes; do not guess from the value's shapeWhether a value is a node or a literal is decided by the vocabulary, not by what the string looks like. PROV-O marks each property op (object) or dp (data); prov:agent, prov:hadRole and prov:hadPlan are all op, so a role id like "user" is still a node reference. Code that decides by shape ("it has a slash, so it is an IRI") gets every short id wrong. | methodology · major | The superscripts op and dp denote that a property is an OWL object property or data property, respectively.w3c-2013-prov-o#sec-016-41-starting-point-terms | . | ld-link-is-the-node-release-address | A link names the node at its dereferenceable address; when it has none, say so instead of minting oneCoercing a bare id to @id is not enough: "owner" then resolves against whatever @base is in force, naming a node that does not exist there. Emit the node's release address — <iriBase><version>/<path in its knowledge graph>[#fragment], the rule check:node-iris enforces — resolved through the OWNING layer's declaration. When the owner declares no iriBase, keep the value as a literal and record a finding naming the layer; an invented address is worse than an honest string. | structure · critical | IRIs are a fundamental concept of Linked Data, for nodes to be truly linked, dereferencing the identifier should result in a representation of that node.w3c-2020-json-ld-1-1#sec-023-note | . | ld-no-base-in-a-remote-context | Do not rely on @base inside a context that documents reference by URLA context referenced by URL is an external context, and JSON-LD 1.1 ignores @base there. Measured 2026-10-01: jsonld.js applies it anyway, so this repository's relative @ids resolve today only through that processor's behaviour; a conforming processor resolves them against each document's own location. Emit absolute @ids, or put @base in the document's own (inline) context. | structure · major | Please note that the @base will be ignored if used in external contexts.w3c-2020-json-ld-1-1#sec-033-413-base-iri | . | ld-no-context-fetched-at-run-time | Hold every external context locally, pinned by hash; never fetch one while processingA context needed to understand a document is part of the document. Code that expands or verifies JSON-LD resolves context URLs through a documentLoader that serves a committed copy (with its sha256 recorded), and refuses anything else — the way publish:verify's localLoader does. A context that can only be had over the network makes the meaning of our data depend on somebody else's server being up and unchanged. | methodology · major | To protect against this, publishers should consider caching remote contexts for future use, or use the documentLoader to maintain a local version of such contexts.w3c-2020-json-ld-1-1#sec-133-11-security-considerations | . | ld-coercion-belongs-to-the-term | A compact-IRI key does not inherit another term's coercionType coercion lives in a TERM's definition. Writing "prov:agent" as a key uses the prov prefix and no term definition, so it is NOT coerced even when the active context defines a term agent with "@type": "@id". Either use the defined term (agent) or define the compact IRI itself as a term. Mixing the two — PROV-JSONLD's context with prov:-prefixed keys — silently yields literals. | structure · major | A compact IRI has the form of prefix:suffix and is used as a way of expressing an IRI without needing to define separate term definitions for each IRI contained within a common vocabulary identified by prefix.w3c-2020-json-ld-1-1#sec-013-terms-imported-from-other-specifications | . | ld-prov-in-prov-jsonld-shape | Emit PROV in PROV-JSONLD's shape, with its termsPROV is written with the PROV-JSONLD context and its terms: an Activity node with startTime/endTime, and each qualified relation as its own typed node — an Association carrying activity, agent, role and plan — so the context's coercions and @reverse mappings apply. The context is held locally (see ld-no-context-fetched-at-run-time). PROV-JSONLD is a W3C Member Submission, acknowledged and not endorsed by W3C; it is adopted here by owner decision (2026-10-01) because W3C publishes no JSON-LD context for PROV-O. | methodology · major | The JSON properties activity and plan map to the object properties prov:qualifiedAssociation and prov:hadPlan, respectively.w3c-2024-prov-jsonld#page-037, p37 | .

3498.title: Glossary
3498.content: Derived: every term this instance's swimlanes define — the role's title and description, the lane names that bind it, and whether the term has been retired. This is an index, not the documentation. It says what exists and what each artefact declares about itself. What a process is for, when you would be in it, and what it is not, is authored beside it and reuses these entries rather than restating them — see the auto-docs skill. Filter this table | Artefact | What it declares about itself | . | Activity logglossary-ledger.json | The agent activity log. A MECHANICAL role: it is written to at task start and task end, and emptied by an actor — one entry, all of them, or on a periodic sweep — and it decides nothing. Modelled on work-plan and corpus, the two existing stores; its skill is the contract it is held to. Its entries are held in the layer's unpublished store and never reach a published graph; the activity-log skill names the location, which is deliberately not repeated here because a role description IS published.notation role/logfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Actorbootstrap/glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation process/Process_LogMessage/lane/Lane_Actorfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Adjudicatorglossary-ledger.json | Settles a criterion whose reviewer entries disagree, and records WHY. Inherits reviewer because an adjudicator is a reviewer with one added entitlement — the adjudication permission — and the separation is the point: a reviewer reports, an adjudicator settles, and a process where every reviewer could settle has no way to say who decided. The KNOWLEDGE spreads (several roles carry the adjudication skill, because each has to tell an adjudicable disagreement from a complaint); the ENTITLEMENT does not, and lives on the actor as a permission.notation role/adjudicatorfirst seen 2026-09-22status current | . | Administratorglossary-ledger.json | Administers the role graph itself: who exists, what they may act as, and what they may do. The ONE lane whose activities change the substrate every other diagram's lanes bind to — which is why it is drawn rather than left as a filesystem edit. Declared 2026-09-20 on the owner's answer that administration is a swimlane; role-model.md's rule is that a role is never invented to make a diagram drawable, so it waited for that.notation role/administratorfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Agentbootstrap/glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation process/Process_HumanAgentDiscussion/lane/Lane_Agentfirst seen 2026-10-01status current | . | Archimateglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/archimatefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Attestation serviceglossary-ledger.json | Signs a QA report's run hashes over an API. A MECHANICAL role, and the one that DISAPPEARS when the actor performing it cannot reach out — which is why the signing process carries a second, human lane rather than a retry.notation role/attestation-servicefirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Attestationsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/attestationsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Auditorglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/auditorfirst seen 2026-11-07status current | . | Authorglossary-ledger.json | Writes and revises folio content. The position, not the person: an editor and a guideline developer both act as author when they are changing a block.notation role/authorfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Authoring agentglossary-ledger.json | The session agent doing the work. The broadest skill set here, and the one whose membership most needs auditing.notation role/authoring-agentfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Authoring Committeeglossary-ledger.json | The people writing a document with its editor, while it is still a working draft: contributors who give feedback through the Contributor Feedback sheet, one change set per row, in their own Blue column. They recommend; an Editor decides, through the sheet's Ready columns. Added 2026-10-31 by the owner, so the drafting sheet names a process role rather than a job title, as the public-comment sheet names the Feedback Review Committee. The lane it binds is in folio-assistant-core/processes/content/contributor-feedback.bpmn and authoring-a-document.bpmn.notation role/authoring-committeefirst seen 2026-10-31status current | . | Auto docsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/auto-docsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Back-translatorglossary-ledger.json | The checker of a translation round trip: renders a sample of the target-language text back into the source language from the target text alone, with no tools and without seeing the source. It rules on nothing. Its rendering is the intermediate the adjudicator reads (untainted-verification, rule 1: neither party sees what would let it shortcut).notation role/back-translatorfirst seen 2026-11-07status current | . | Basic CDN siteglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/basic-cdn-sitefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Basic cdn site (node kind)glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation node-kind/basic-cdn-sitefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Bean notesglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/bean-notesfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Binary releasesglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/binary-releasefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Block kindsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/block-kindsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Board positionsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/board-positionsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Board rendererglossary-ledger.json | Draws a board and performs what the reader has already decided: reads each kind's declared zoom threshold and the layout layer, swaps a card for its avatar, projects an open window onto the canvas, and carries out a confirmed relocation. A system lane — it runs a fixed program and exercises no judgement, which is exactly why every decision in board-open-close.bpmn and board-relocate.bpmn sits in the reader's lane instead. It is NOT the build pipeline: it runs where the reader is, once per request, and publishes nothing.notation role/board-rendererfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Boardsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/boardsfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Bootstrapbootstrap/glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation harness/bootstrapfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Bootstrapping Agentbootstrap/glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/bootstrapping-agentfirst seen 2026-09-23status current | . | Build pipelineglossary-ledger.json | Validates, renders and publishes, and watches whether that actually worked. A system lane: it runs a fixed program and exercises no judgement, so anything needing a decision belongs in a different lane. It carries todo-manager for the two CI-watcher dispatch points in content-change-review, which claim and note a bean and never resolve one -- claim is idempotent and note appends, both fixed programs, while deciding that a publish SUCCEEDED is the judgement this lane must not make (bean xom7: docs-site.yml failed 30 times while reporting its own exit code).notation role/build-pipelinefirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Building blocksglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/building-blocksfirst seen 2026-11-05status current | . | Business analystglossary-ledger.json | Turns a stated need into a modelled requirement. Owns the CRDM lane and the BPMN/DMN that come out of it.notation role/business-analystfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Business processesglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/business-processesfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | C@T Harnessglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation harness/cat-harnessfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Carried noteglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation node-kind/carried-notefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Cat harness declarationglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation node-kind/cat-harness-declarationfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | CDN siteglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/cdn-sitefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Cdn site (node kind)glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation node-kind/cdn-sitefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Certificate Issuerglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/certificate-issuerfirst seen 2026-11-07status current | . | Certifierglossary-ledger.json | Takes the certification decision on ONE test report: applies the DMN the plan's exitCriteria names (computed from facts, never asserted) and records the decision as a judgement under the declared attestations graph, from which it is signed through qa-report-signing.bpmn. A specialisation of stakeholder — accountable sign-off — but NOT judgementOnly: the exit criteria are a table it applies, and only the decision on top of them is the judgement (owner ruling, 2026-10-01). Never the tester and never the system under test. Bean 3o5b.notation role/certifierfirst seen 2026-10-01status current | . | CI cachesglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/cachefirst seen 2026-11-07status current | . | Clinical / scientific SMEglossary-ledger.json | Reviewer whose judgement is about the subject matter rather than the artefact. Acts by domain judgement (judgementOnly: no procedure yields the answer, which is why a person is in the lane; bean vljz).notation role/clinical-smefirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Cloudflare git (Artifacts)glossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/cloudflare-gitfirst seen 2026-10-31status current | . | Cloudflare R2 and CDNglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/cloudflare-r2-cdnfirst seen 2026-10-31status current | . | Codeglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/codefirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Code listsglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/code-listfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Code reviewerglossary-ledger.json | Judges the knowledge graph's CODE nodes — Tool definitions in the tools graph and schema definition nodes under schemas/. Not ordinary code review: the question is whether the NODE is sound — does it declare what it is, do its references resolve, is the mechanism it advertises the one that runs — which a passing test suite does not answer. Entered by DESCENDING into Process_CodeReview.notation role/code-reviewerfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Compute authoring agentglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/compute-authoring-agentfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Consent Recorderglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/consent-recorderfirst seen 2026-11-07status current | . | Consent Registryglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/consent-registryfirst seen 2026-11-07status current | . | Content adaptersglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation kind/content-adaptersfirst seen 2026-11-04status current | . | Corpusglossary-ledger.json | The versioned content store and the L1 source knowledge graph. Like the work plan, a MECHANICAL role: written to, deciding nothing, and held to the contract its skills state.notation role/corpusfirst seen 2026-09-21status current | . | Data Provider Administratorglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/data-provider-administratorfirst seen 2026-11-07status current | . | Data Recipient Systemglossary-ledger.json | no description in the artefactnotation role/data-recipient-systemfirst seen 2026-11-07status current | . | Deep researcherglossary-ledger.json | Answers a question FROM a corpus already held, and is answerable for the answer. Distinct from librarian, which decides what to capture, and from ingestion-agent, which derives structure from what was captured: both produce the corpus, and this role consumes it. Added 2026-09-23 with the doc-researcher methodology, because the accountability it names — somebody who must stand behind a synthesis and its citations — belonged to no declared role. 3624.doc: SPDX 3 — a bill of materials as a graph of elements, for what crosses a trust boundary
3624.title: The load-bearing idea, in the specification’s words
3624.content: “The System Package Data Exchange (SPDX®) specification defines an open standard for communicating bill of materials (BOM) information for different topic areas. SPDX defines an underlying data model as well as multiple serialization formats to encode that data model.” — §1 Scope (sec-007) . Its scope lists, among others, “software composition”, “software build information”, “provenance and integrity”, “licenses and copyrights, including a curated list of licenses and exceptions”, and “security vulnerabilities, defects, and other quality data” (§1). It is profiled. “The Core Profile is mandatory. All others are optional” (§5.2, sec-015): Core, Software, Security, Licensing, Dataset, AI, Build, Lite and Extension. A producer conforms at a profile, not to the whole. The Lite Profile “captures the minimum set of information required for license compliance in the software supply chain” (§5.10, sec-023). Everything is an Element with creation info. CreationInfo requires specVersion, created and createdBy (Figure A.1). The specification qualifies created in a way that matters here: “The dateTime created is often the date of last change (e.g., a git commit date), not the date when the SPDX data was created, as doing so supports reproducible builds” (CreationInfo, sec-044, where the page split carries it; also sec-072). A generator that uses the source commit’s date writes the same document twice for the same commit. Serialisation is JSON-LD with ONE global context. “The SPDX global JSON-LD context file must be used universally for all SPDX documents in JSON-LD format that adhere to a specific SPDX version … "@context": "https://spdx.org/rdf/3.0.1/spdx-context.jsonld"” (sec-032). There is also a “canonical serialization”: “a single, consistent, normalized, deterministic, and reproducible form” (sec-029). That is the form to hash and sign. “Known unknown” is not the same as absent. For licences: “a missing hasDeclaredLicense is not the same as a relationship to NoAssertionLicense since the latter is a ‘known unknown’ whereas no assumptions can be made from a missing hasDeclaredLicense relationship”, and “A written explanation of a relationship to a NoAssertionLicense MAY be provided in the comment field for the relationship” (Licensing, sec-210).

3625.doc: SPDX 3 — a bill of materials as a graph of elements, for what crosses a trust boundary
3625.title: How it would sit beside what this platform already holds
3625.content: These are the mappings the proposal rests on. Each is ours, read against the held text, and none is adopted. | house fact | SPDX 3 term | fit | . | licence.json status: stated + id | simplelicensing_LicenseExpression via hasDeclaredLicense | exact, once ids are validated against a pinned License List | . | status: unknown + searched[] | hasDeclaredLicense → NoAssertionLicense, the search log in the relationship’s comment | exact. The three states survive: SPDX’s absent relationship is our absent record | . | bun.lock, python-deps.ts | software_Package + purl (packageUrl) + dependsOn | exact for npm. Python is blocked: requirements*.txt pin no versions | . | kg-to-portal’s manifest of digests | software_File with verifiedUsing: Hash inside a software_Sbom | exact | . | a published layer’s needs[] / FHIR dependsOn | dependsOn between software_Packages | exact, but only GENERATED from one authoritative record (#592) | . | folio-tool-run/v1, attribution.ts toolchain / inputDigest | build_Build (buildType, configSourceDigest, parameter, environment) | close, and it competes with prov-o-provenance for “what ran” | . | a QA or test report about a released package | ExternalRef with externalRefType: qualityAssessmentReport, “A reference to a quality assessment for a package” (sec-123) | exact as a POINTER. The report stays ours | . | bun audit advisories | security_Vulnerability + security_Vex*VulnAssessmentRelationship | exact, and a VEX not_affected needs a person’s decision | .

3626.doc: SPDX 3 — a bill of materials as a graph of elements, for what crosses a trust boundary
3626.title: What it refuses, with reasons
3626.content: . | A QA verdict store. SPDX 3.0 has no verdict class. A result is an Annotation (“An assertion made in relation to one or more elements”, free-text statement; sec-039) or a relationship (hasEvidence, hasTest, testedOn). A house sidecar holds {criterion, result, reviewer, field_hash} per criterion, many reviewers over time, with four-state freshness. Serialising that into SPDX turns validated fields into a string. 3.1 changes the first half of this, and the change is recorded rather than smoothed over: the RC1 schema has functionalsafety_EvaluationResult (evaluation ∈ {pass, fail, inconclusive}, a required evaluationBasedOn → RequirementVerification with verificationMethod ∈ {analysis, assessment, audit, demonstration, inspection, review, test, other}, and a required rationale), plus a Core Requirement class. That is a verdict class. It makes an SPDX export of a certification report plausible, once 3.1 is final. It does not make SPDX the store, for the remaining reasons: the records are mutable, they would churn, the class sits in a functional safety profile whose semantics a non-safety QA run would be borrowing, and “stale” and “absent” have no SPDX term (inconclusive covers only could-not-determine). | A second execution log. “What ran, as whom, under which plan” is prov-o-provenance’s, by owner decision. A release document that must say how it was built references the PROV record, or generates build_Build from it. It never authors one beside it. | The AI profile for agent authorship. ai_AIPackage describes a model distributed as a package (training, energy consumption, limitations). The platform ships no model. Who wrote a block is provenance. | Authoring SPDX by hand, or committing it where its facts already live. A document generated from bun.lock that is also committed is a second answer to “what are we running”, the failure upstream-pins.json names. | .

3627.doc: SPDX 3 — a bill of materials as a graph of elements, for what crosses a trust boundary
3627.title: What the source does NOT establish
3627.content: . | Anything about 3.1. The held specification is 3.0. Every 3.1 statement above comes from an RC1 schema that was not compared with its published copy, or from a conference deck. | That the OMG edition and the Linux Foundation 3.0.1 web edition are identical. Not compared. | Which buildType IRIs to use. The Build profile requires one (buildType: anyURI[1], Figure A.7) and leaves it to the producer. | How to sign. SPDX carries verifiedUsing integrity methods. Signing the document is outside it, and is qa-report-signing.bpmn’s question. | .

3628.doc: SPDX 3 — a bill of materials as a graph of elements, for what crosses a trust boundary
3628.title: SPDX 3 — a bill of materials as a graph of elements, for what crosses a trust boundary
3628.content: ← All methodologies . spdx-3 — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Describing an artefact that LEAVES this repository so that a party who does not run our tooling can check what is in it, what it depends on, under which licences, and that it arrived intact — a release, a signed package, a published layer’s dependency set, the licences of what we redistribute. It answers what is this, what is it made of, who supplied it, under what licence, with what known vulnerabilities. It does NOT answer what happened inside the repository or who answers for it (prov-o-provenance), what an actor may do (odrl-policies), how a node is serialised internally (json-ld-serialisation), or whether a block passed its QA criteria (the house QA schemas; see §”What it refuses”). Origin. The Linux Foundation and its Contributors, with SPDX Model contributions from OMG, “System Package Data Exchange (SPDX) Specification Version 3.0”, OMG formal/24-11-01, March 2025 (https://www.omg.org/spec/SPDX); its model is the SPDX 3.0.1 model (Annex A points at https://spdx.org/rdf/3.0.1/spdx-model.ttl). Licensed Community-Spec-1.0, with pre-existing portions CC-BY-3.0. SPDX® is a registered trademark of The Linux Foundation. SPDX 3.1, a release candidate since 2026-01-26, is held only as a secondary source (a 2025 conference deck, CC-BY-SA-3.0) and as its RC1 machine-readable schema queued in uploads/, NOT as a specification. Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/omg-2024-spdx-3-0 | library/strauch-carbno-2025-spdx-3-1-supply-chain | . Node file: spdx-3.md .

3629.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
3629.title: Specification-compiled agents
3629.content: Adopted 2026-09-23, on the owner’s “ingest into library for use as evidence and skills as subgraph on processes in cat-harness”. The authors’ own sentence for the mechanism: . “we compile an industry standard BPMN 2.0 process model into a ReAct style control graph. Each BPMN node provides a typed tool contract and a node local policy, while the control plane enforces branches and joins, scopes context per node, and applies contract derived runtime validation with targeted retries.” .

3630.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
3630.title: The load-bearing idea, in one sentence
3630.content: The control flow is COMPILED from a specification the model did not write, so the model never rediscovers the plan at runtime. Everything else in the paper follows from that. The model still reasons — it is a ReAct agent, not a state machine — but it reasons locally, inside a node, against a typed contract, with the branches and joins enforced by something that is not it.

3631.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
3631.title: Three principles, and they are separable
3631.content: The paper names them together; they are three distinct commitments and a reader may take one without the others. | principle | what it does | what it costs | . | constrained execution | branches and joins come from the diagram, not from a plan the model produced | the diagram must exist and be right | . | targeted context management | each node sees the minimum it needs, rather than the accumulated transcript | somebody must decide, per node, what that minimum is | . | modular decomposition | prompt, tools and orchestration are generated as separate artefacts | more upfront authoring than a single prompt | . The second is the one with an argument behind it rather than an intuition. The paper cites evidence that model performance degrades as more of the context window is consumed, and observes that a generalist system cannot scope context per subtask because it does not know, at construction time, what each subtask will need. A specification does know — which is why scoping is available to this design and not to the other.

3632.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
3632.title: What the paper measured
3632.content: Ten workflows, 9 to 52 nodes, all deterministic, spanning e-commerce, costing, risk, labelling, news, social, promotion, tournament registration and weather. Ten successful agents per workflow per system, evaluated across all control-flow paths — 300 agents over 30,543 test cases, from 371 generation attempts. Baselines: Roo and Cline. AutoGen, MetaGPT and FLOW were tried and produced nothing executable — MetaGPT emitted prompts and tools but no agent, AutoGen needed manual wiring even with GraphFlow, FLOW produced decompositions rather than code — so they were excluded rather than scored, which is the honest handling. Aggregates (Figure 4), specialist vs Cline vs Roo: . |   | specialist | Cline | Roo | . | tool-use exactness ↑ | 57.7 % | 48.6 % | 38.1 % | . | tool-call errors ↓ | 1.27 | 3.19 | 3.22 | . | latency (s / effective step) ↓ | 2.49 | 6.59 | 9.08 | . | process adherence ↑ | 54.7 % | 51.6 % | 42.4 % | . | repair iterations ↓ | 0.00 | 1.85 | 2.04 | . | total tokens | 53.8 k | 1 021.8 k | 1 468.6 k | . The two robust results are the last two rows, and they are robust because they are not close: zero repair iterations across every successful generation, and an order of magnitude in tokens. Those are properties of the pipeline rather than of the generated agent, which is why they do not vary the way the run metrics do.

3633.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
3633.title: What the figures say that the prose does not
3633.content: Read off Figure 3 directly, 2026-09-23, as part of ingesting the images. This is a reading of the paper’s own chart, not a claim about the authors’ work, and it is recorded because the surrounding text does not say it. The paper writes of tool-use exactness that “the per-workflow breakdown in Figure 3(a) confirms this advantage holds consistently across all ten workflows regardless of complexity.” Figure 3(a) does not show that. On three of the ten the specialist system is not best: . | workflow | specialist | Cline | Roo | . | Cost | 49.6 | 76.0 | 67.6 | . | Tournament | 46.2 | 99.4 | 94.9 | . | Weather | 81.8 | 90.1 | 61.0 | . Tournament is not a near miss — it is 46.2 against 99.4. The same two workflows invert in panels (b) and (d): on Cost the specialist has the most tool-call errors (1.43 against 0.55 and 0.34) and the lowest process adherence (57.2 against 87.1 and 76.2), and Tournament repeats both. And the aggregate advantage is carried disproportionately by two workflows. On Risk the specialist shows 0.20 tool-call errors against 13.19 and 11.94, and 98.6 % exactness against 0.4 % and 0.9 %; Social contributes a smaller version of the same. A mean over ten workflows, two of which contain an order-of- magnitude gap, is a mean dominated by those two. Separately, §4.3.1 gives the aggregate repair figures as “2.08 for Roo and 1.89 for Cline” where Figure 2(d) is labelled 2.04 and 1.85. Small, and noted only because this node quotes one of them. None of this makes the method wrong. It makes the aggregate run metrics the wrong thing to quote, and it is the reason the section above marks the generation metrics as the robust pair. It also suggests a real question the paper does not ask: what do Cost and Tournament have in common that inverts the result? Looking at their diagrams, both are shallow and branch-heavy — the regime where a compiled control graph has least to contribute, because there is barely a plan to rediscover.

3634.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
3634.title: What this checkout already does, and where it differs
3634.content: methodology-adoption §”Extract the PROCESS, not the paper’s tools” requires this comparison before any tool is proposed. Read from the repository, not assumed: . | the method asks for | this checkout has | gap | . | BPMN 2.0 as the authored control flow | processes/, 69 diagrams, .bpmn as the source of truth | none — this is already the premise | . | a control plane that enforces branches and joins | workflow_start / workflow_next / workflow_gate / workflow_complete, with workflow_complete refusing a step that is not enabled | none of substance | . | a node-local policy | cat-harness.processes:policy enforcement, relaxable, cat-harness.processes:decision, cat-harness.processes:judgement — four mechanisms, already finer than the paper’s one | this checkout is AHEAD | . | a typed tool contract per node | <bootstrap.processes:skill ref> names the instruction body; there is no typed input/output contract | the real gap | . | context scoped per node | not modelled. A step returns a skill; nothing says what the agent may or must see | the second real gap | . | contract-derived runtime validation with targeted retries | nothing. A step that goes wrong is not caught by the control plane | follows from the first gap | . | compilation to an executable agent | nothing, and deliberately: the diagrams here govern agents rather than generating them | out of scope, not a gap | . The last row is the one to be careful about. The paper’s system emits a deployable service; this repository’s engine runs alongside an agent doing the work. Those are different products of the same specification, and adopting the method here means taking the first three principles, not the code generator.

3635.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
3635.title: Where this rendering stops
3635.content: . | No implementation is adopted. ReAct, FastAPI, LangGraph and Langfuse are the paper’s tools, not obligations. | The benchmark is not adopted. Ten workflows the authors built themselves, and they say so: “author-constructed workflows may introduce design bias”. A benchmark of somebody else’s processes measures their processes. | The numbers are not adopted as evidence for anything here. See the figures section: three of ten workflows invert, and the aggregate is dominated by two. What survives is the shape — zero repair iterations and an order of magnitude in tokens — and even those were measured on that corpus. | The deterministic scope is inherited, not argued away. Every workflow evaluated is deterministic by construction. The authors state the limit plainly; this node does not extend the result past it, and deterministic-and-agentic is where the open question lives. | “Specialist beats generalist” is not a conclusion this node draws. The paper compares one specialist pipeline against two general coding assistants operating unconstrained at their defaults, and says future work will examine “more heavily optimised baseline configurations”. That is a fair comparison of realistic low-configuration usage and it is not a claim about ceilings. | .

3636.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
3636.title: The owner’s own statement of the two ends
3636.content: library/kg-folio-asst-2026-09-30 is the owner’s deck of 2026-09-30. It is cited as evidence of intent, not of effect. Slide 7 draws the axis this node sits on: “BPMN Execution Skill: given a Process, Context, State, Role utilize one or more Skills in order [to] execute a Task”, run by either of two Tools. One is an open-source BPMN engine with “state and swimlanes strictly enforced”. The other is “an agentic swarm with ungoverned state”, mitigated by mechanical and agentic QA/QC reports. This node is the method for the first end. The deck measures nothing, so it says where the owner wants the harness to go and nothing about how well either end works. That is what the paper above is for. The diagrams this method executes are OMG BPMN 2.0.2 (formal/2013-12-09), recorded as library/omg-2013-bpmn-2-0-2. The entry identifies the exact specification and its clause outline, so a citation can name a clause and page. It holds none of the text, because OMG’s licence forbids posting copies on a network.

3637.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
3637.title: See also
3637.content: . | specification-compiled-agents — the part an agent here acts on. | deterministic-and-agentic — the open research agenda this is evidence for, and the four mechanisms this repository already has. | hybrid-llm-deterministic — the same shape at a different grain: emit a rule, validate it, run it. | .

3638.doc: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
3638.title: Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model's plan
3638.content: ← All methodologies . specification-compiled-agents — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. A process is already written down as a diagram, and something must now EXECUTE it. Use it when the control flow is external and authored — a BPMN process, a DMN table, a pipeline someone drew — and the question is how an LLM should act inside it. It answers where the plan comes from, never what the plan should be: authoring the diagram is bpmn-authoring, deciding a branch from a table is dmn, and choosing between options is kepner-tregoe. Its companion is hybrid-llm-deterministic, and the two are the same shape at different grains: that one has the model emit a RULE that machinery validates and runs; this one has the model act inside a CONTROL GRAPH that machinery derived from a specification. Reach for this one when the artefact that constrains the model already exists as a diagram. Do NOT reach for it where no specification exists, or where the process is genuinely open-ended. The paper’s own evaluation is scoped to deterministic workflows and says so; a setting with ambiguity, stochasticity or open-ended human decision-making is outside what it measured, and outside what this node claims. Origin. Harris Borman, Herman Wandabwa, Fusun Yu, Sandeepa Kannangara, Justin Liu, Anna Leontjeva and Ritchie Ng, “Beyond Generalist LLMs: Specialist Agentic Systems for Structured Code Workflow Execution”, Commonwealth Bank of Australia. Published as a workshop paper at SCALE, ICML 2026 (PMLR 306); arXiv:2607.14456v1 [cs.SE], 16 July 2026. Open access, ingested whole and read before this node was written. It is a SYSTEM paper reporting one implementation against a benchmark its own authors built, so what is adopted below is the METHOD, and §”Where this rendering stops” says which parts were left behind. §”What the figures say that the prose does not” carries a reading of the paper’s own charts that changes how its headline numbers should be used, and it is the reason this node quotes almost none of them. Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/arxiv-2607.14456v1 | library/kg-folio-asst-2026-09-30 | library/omg-2013-bpmn-2-0-2 | . 3639.doc: Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) — process-centric requirements engineering and harness adaptation
3639.title: Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM)
3639.content: Adapted from the Public Health Informatics Institute (PHII) and PATH. The harness’s CRDM requirements workflow (crdm-requirements-workflow (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc)) and specification template (crdm-requirements-template) adapt PHII’s Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) and PATH’s 2012 application of CRDM to health information systems, combining their process-centric requirements method with the platform’s own agentic facilitation, codebase impact analysis, work-plan decomposition, and pull-request sign-off gates. | Canonical SKOS glossary concept: https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/glossary/platform/collaborative-requirements-development-methodology (docs/assets/glossary/cat-harness--platform.skos.jsonld) | . | Ingested source | What it establishes | Library entry | . | PHII (2021/2023), Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM): A Collaborative Approach to Public Health Systems (https://phii.org/crdm/, 10 pp.) | The three concentration areas (Business Process Analysis, Business Process Redesign, Requirements Definition), the Business Process Matrix, and swimlane Task Flow Diagrams | library/phii-2023-crdm | . | PHII (2016/2021), 5. Analyzing Technical Options: Defining and Validating System Requirements Guide (EHR Toolkit, 6 pp.) | Functional vs. non-functional requirement grammar (“The system must or should…”), the three-level priority scale (High / Medium / Low = Must-have / Should-have / Nice-to-have), nine requirement quality criteria, and three validation techniques (Desk checking, Walkthrough, Peer review) | library/phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide | . | PATH & PHII (2012), Common Requirements for Maternal Health Information Systems: Produced with the Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (36 pp.) | Domain-scale application of CRDM: a four-column Process Framework (Table 1), swimlane Task Flow Diagrams across facility and community pools with numbered activity narratives (Appendix 1), Activity-Linked Functional User Requirements (Appendix 2), and General System Requirements (Appendix 3) | library/path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm | . | IETF BCP 14 — RFC 2119 & RFC 8174 (Bradner 1997; Leiba 2017) | Normative conformance keywords (MUST / SHALL, MUST NOT / SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, MAY) in uppercase | library/rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels, library/rfc8174-uppercase-vs-lowercase-2119-key-words | .

3640.doc: Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) — process-centric requirements engineering and harness adaptation
3640.title: 1. The PHII and PATH CRDM method
3640.content: PHII developed CRDM as a process-centric methodology grounded in business process management that brings multi-disciplinary subject matter experts (SMEs) together to document how work is performed, redesign how it should be performed, and derive what an information system must do to support that work (phii-2023-crdm, pp. 1–3; path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm, pp. 4–7). 1.1 The three concentration areas . PHII organises CRDM around three sequential concentration areas (phii-2023-crdm, pp. 2–9): . | Concentration area | Guiding prompt | Core artefacts | What happens | . | 1. Business Process Analysis (BPA) | Think: How do we do our work now? | Business Process Matrix (process goal, inputs, activities, outputs, actors/roles, business rules, issues/opportunities) and Task Flow Diagrams (swimlane diagrams showing the sequence of tasks across pools and actors) | SMEs map current-state operations end to end, making implicit workflows, hand-offs, and decision points explicit (phii-2023-crdm, pp. 3–6). | . | 2. Business Process Redesign (BPR) | Rethink: How should we do our work? | Redesigned Business Process Matrix and updated Task Flow Diagrams | Before automating anything, participants examine the current-state model to eliminate bottlenecks, redundancies, policy barriers, and information gaps (phii-2023-crdm, pp. 7–8). | . | 3. Requirements Definition | Describe: How can an information system support our work? | Functional User Requirements (anchored to numbered task-flow activities) and Non-Functional / General System Requirements | Every activity in the redesigned task flow is examined to state the information system capabilities needed to support it, followed by structured SME validation (phii-2023-crdm, pp. 8–9; phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, pp. 1–5). | . 1.2 PATH (2012): domain-scale health information system artefacts . PATH & PHII (2012) demonstrate how CRDM scales across a clinical and public health domain (path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm): . | Process Framework (Table 1, PDF p. 8): Inventories all domain business processes across functional columns (Patient Administration, Patient Care, Patient Fees and Accounting, Planning, Management & Surveillance) and selects priority processes for deep modeling (sec-009-outputs-of-the-crdm-process.md). | Task Flow Diagrams with Activity Narratives (Appendix 1, PDF pp. 11–20): Draws each priority process using a ten-element notation (Pools, Swim Lanes, Start Event, End Event, Sequence Flow, Activity, Subprocess, Decision, Multi-Page Connector, Annotation) paired with numbered activity details and narratives (sec-013-appendix-1-business-process-flows.md). | Activity-Linked Functional User Requirements vs. General System Requirements (Appendices 2–3, PDF pp. 21–36): Groups functional requirements by process and numbered activity ID, and separates cross-cutting system requirements (security, audit logging, reporting, interoperability, offline operation) into a dedicated general system requirements catalogue (sec-014-appendix-2-requirements.md, which also holds the general and nonfunctional requirements). | . 1.3 Quality criteria and validation techniques . PHII’s Defining and Validating System Requirements Guide (phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, pp. 3–5) checks every requirement against nine quality criteria — Correct, Unambiguous, Complete, Consistent, Ranked for importance and/or stability, Verifiable, Modifiable, Traceable, and Comprehensible — using three validation methods: . | Desk checking: Individual review of the specification against the business process models and quality criteria. | Walkthrough: Facilitated step-by-step group traversal of task flows and requirements with the SMEs who perform the work. | Peer review: Independent structured inspection by peers to catch ambiguities, omissions, and conflicts before sign-off. | .

3641.doc: Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) — process-centric requirements engineering and harness adaptation
3641.title: 2. How the harness adapts PHII and PATH CRDM
3641.content: The relation between crdm-requirements-workflow and PHII/PATH CRDM is adapts: Phases 1–3 and the SME validation walkthrough follow PHII/PATH CRDM directly, while the facilitation channel, Phase 4/4b codebase impact and dependency analysis, Phase 5 work-item and filing decomposition, and Phase 6 pull-request sign-off are the platform’s own extensions. | Workflow phase / mechanism | Relation to PHII & PATH CRDM | What follows PHII/PATH CRDM vs. what is the platform’s own | . | Facilitated elicitation channel (crdm-requirements-workflow § Core Principle) | Platform adaptation of CRDM workshop facilitation | PHII/PATH run multi-stakeholder SME workshops facilitated by a human business analyst. The harness adapts this into an LLM agent acting in the Business Analyst role (Role_BusinessAnalyst) conversing with the human SME (Role_SME) over an issue/PR thread before any code is modified. | . | Phase 1: Needs Assessment & Problem Framing | Follows PHII CRDM (Business Process Analysis — context & scope) | Establishes the business problem, actors/personas (Role_*), scope boundaries (in-scope vs. out-of-scope), and information inputs/outputs, matching PHII’s Business Process Matrix header and PATH’s process framework scoping. | . | Phase 2: Business Process Analysis & Redesign | Follows PHII & PATH CRDM (Concentration Areas 1 & 2: BPA + BPR) | Models current-state (“as-is”) and redesigned (“to-be”) workflows using swimlane task-flow diagrams (BPMN 2.0 / Mermaid) across pools and actor lanes, paired with a gap analysis table (bottlenecks, redundancies, missing rules). | . | Phase 3: Requirements Definition (Functional, Non-Functional & Data Model) | Follows PHII & PATH CRDM (Concentration Area 3) + BCP 14 keywords | Derives atomic Functional Requirements (FR-001, …) linked to redesigned process steps, Non-Functional / General System Requirements (NFR-001, …), business rules/decision tables, and domain data entities with cardinalities and validation criteria. | . | Phase 4: Impact Analysis & Effort Estimation | Platform’s own extension | Inspects the repository’s existing schemas, skills, BPMN/DMN models, UI components, pipelines, tests, and downstream consumers across 7 impact dimensions to identify breaking changes and t-shirt effort estimates. PHII/PATH CRDM is technology- and codebase-agnostic and has no code impact phase. | . | Phase 4b: Capability Area Grouping, Dependency Ordering & Formalize-First Rule | Platform’s own extension | Groups requirements into capability areas (CA-1, CA-2, …), orders them by a dependency DAG, and enforces the platform’s formalize-first rule (formalizing existing implicit behavior before adding net-new capabilities). | . | Phase 5: Work Breakdown, Work Items & Specification Filing | Platform’s own extension (+ PHII Walkthrough / Peer review) | Writes the specification to docs/proposals/<slug>.md (and upon filing to docs/requirements/<slug>.md per requirements-filing-and-organisation), decomposes work into agent work items (beans/) and human todos (todos/), and conducts the SME walkthrough on the proposal PR. | . | Phase 6: Implementation & Merge Sign-Off | Platform’s own extension | Implements approved requirements on a feature branch, publishes a branches/<branch-slug>/ preview, verifies every acceptance criterion against automated gates, and requires explicit human owner sign-off before merging. | .

3642.doc: Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) — process-centric requirements engineering and harness adaptation
3642.title: 3. Priority scale and normative conformance keywords
3642.content: In CRDM and in the harness’s requirement template (crdm-requirements-template), implementation priority and normative conformance level are two distinct fields with different semantics and different standards origins: . 3.1 Priority weighting (High / Medium / Low = Must-have / Should-have / Nice-to-have) . PHII’s Defining and Validating System Requirements Guide (phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, p. 2) and PATH (2012) (path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm, p. 1 / Appendix 2) rank requirements by relative implementation importance using a three-tier priority scale. The harness aligns its three priority labels one-to-one with PHII’s scale: . | PHII / PATH priority rank | Harness template label | Meaning when sequencing or trading off scope | . | High | Must-have (High / Must-have) | Essential to the core business process; the system cannot satisfy the process goal without this capability. | . | Medium | Should-have (Medium / Should-have) | Important for operational efficiency or completeness; expected in standard operation, though a temporary workaround may exist. | . | Low | Nice-to-have (Low / Nice-to-have) | Desirable enhancement that improves convenience or secondary workflows when resources permit. | . 3.2 Normative conformance keywords (SHALL / SHOULD / MAY / SHALL NOT) . While PHII’s informal prose grammar phrases requirement statements as “The system must or should…” (phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, p. 1), the harness’s separate Conformance field (SHALL / MUST, SHOULD, MAY, SHALL NOT / MUST NOT) uses uppercase normative keywords governed by IETF BCP 14: . | RFC 2119 (Bradner 1997, library/rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels): Defines MUST / SHALL (absolute requirement of the specification), MUST NOT / SHALL NOT (absolute prohibition), SHOULD (recommended; valid reasons may exist in particular circumstances to ignore, but full implications must be understood and weighed), SHOULD NOT (not recommended), and MAY (truly optional). | RFC 8174 (Leiba 2017, library/rfc8174-uppercase-vs-lowercase-2119-key-words): Clarifies that only UPPERCASE words carry the RFC 2119 normative meanings; lowercase “must”, “should”, and “may” in surrounding prose carry only their normal English meaning. | . Keeping Priority (High / Must-have, Medium / Should-have, Low / Nice-to-have) separate from Conformance (SHALL, SHOULD, MAY, SHALL NOT) avoids conflating when a capability is scheduled for delivery (priority) with how strictly an implementation must behave once it claims conformance to that requirement (BCP 14 modality).

3643.doc: Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) — process-centric requirements engineering and harness adaptation
3643.title: Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) — process-centric requirements engineering and harness adaptation
3643.content: ← All methodologies . crdm — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Eliciting, structuring, prioritising, and validating functional and non-functional requirements from current-state and redesigned business processes before implementation begins. Use it when a capability, specification, or workflow spans actors and tasks that must be analysed and redesigned first so every requirement traces to a concrete business activity. Not a replacement for filing and lifecycle governance (requirements-filing-and-organisation), interchange standards mapping (requirements-standards-assessment), one-off option trade-offs (kepner-tregoe), recurring decision logic (dmn), or architecture decision records (madr). Origin. Public Health Informatics Institute (PHII, a program of The Task Force for Global Health), “Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM): A Collaborative Approach to Public Health Systems” (2021, updated 2023-08-29, https://phii.org/crdm/) and companion EHR Toolkit guide “5. Analyzing Technical Options: Defining and Validating System Requirements Guide” (2016/2021, https://phii.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Defining-and-Validating-Requirements-Guide_0.pdf); applied to health information systems in PATH & PHII, “Common Requirements for Maternal Health Information Systems: Produced with the Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology” (December 2012, https://media.path.org/documents/MCHN_mhis_crdm.pdf); combined in the harness’s requirement statement template with IETF BCP 14 / RFC 2119 (Bradner 1997) and RFC 8174 (Leiba 2017) for normative conformance keywords.
