Two sentences of the first draft were wrong and are corrected below (the choice of k, and stemming). | source | held | what this node takes from it | . | Deerwester et al. 1990 | ✅ library/deerwester-1990-indexing-by-lsa | the method, read whole | . | Landauer, Foltz & Laham 1998 | ✅ library/landauer-foltz-laham-1998-intro-lsa | the only HELD description of log-entropy weighting (its p. 17) | . | Halko, Martinsson & Tropp 2011 | ✅ library/arxiv-0909.4061v2 | the engine’s algorithm (Algorithms 4.4 and 5.1) | . | Qi, Hessen & van der Heijden 2023 | ✅ library/qi-hessen-vanderheijden-2023-ca-vs-lsa | the critique in §”What it is not good at” | . | Hang, Schnabel, Yang & Neville 2022 | ✅ library/arxiv-2202.02427v1 | a parallel track for incremental updating; not adopted | . | Dumais 1991 | ❌ not held | cited for the log-entropy FORM the engine uses — unverified, see below | . | Berry, Dumais & O’Brien 1995 | ❌ not held | cited for updating — the claim the node relies on is also in Deerwester 1990, footnote 3 | . | Landauer & Dumais 1997 | ❌ not held | the cognitive reading, refused | .

3702.doc: Latent Semantic Indexing — retrieve and relate by co-occurrence structure, not by shared words
3702.title: The load-bearing idea, in the paper’s words
3702.content: “users want to retrieve on the basis of conceptual content, and individual words provide unreliable evidence about the conceptual topic or meaning of a document. There are usually many ways to express a given concept, so the literal terms in a user’s query may not match those of a relevant document. In addition, most words have multiple meanings” — Deerwester et al. 1990, §1. The paper names the two sides synonymy (hurts recall) and polysemy (hurts precision), and its empirical premise is Furnas et al.’s: “two people choose the same main key word for a single well-known object less than 20% of the time” (§2). And it is explicit about what “semantic” means — only this: . “By ‘semantic structure’ we mean here only the correlation structure in the way in which individual words appear in documents” — §2, footnote 1.

3703.doc: Latent Semantic Indexing — retrieve and relate by co-occurrence structure, not by shared words
3703.title: The method, as the 1990 paper defines it
3703.content: | # | step | what the paper does | . | 1 | Units and vocabulary | title + abstract as the document; “all terms occurring in more than one document and not on a stop list of 439 common words used by SMART” (§5). No stemming. Terms in one document, or evenly in all, “have little or no influence on the SVD solution” (fn. 6) | . | 2 | Term × document matrix | raw counts: “each cell indicates the frequency with which each term occurs in each document” (§5). The paper deliberately adds no weighting, stemming or phrases, “in order to better evaluate the utility of the basic representation technique” | . | 3 | Truncated SVD | X = T₀S₀D₀′; keep the k largest singular values; X̂ = TSD′ “is the matrix of rank k which is closest in the least squares sense to X” (§4.2.1) — the Eckart–Young theorem, stated there without the name | . | 4 | Choose k | “The proper way to make such choices is an open issue”; the paper uses “an operational criterion - a value of k which yields good retrieval performance” (§4.2.1). It works with 50–100 factors, reports ~100, and on MED precision rises from .25 to .52 as k goes 10 → 100 (§5.1, Fig. 5). Solutions are nested: the first 10 coordinates of a 100-factor solution are the 10-factor solution (fn. 9) | . | 5 | Compare | documents by rows of DS, terms by rows of TS, term-to-document by TS^½ against DS^½ — “it is not possible to make a single configuration of points in a space that will allow both between and within comparisons” (§4.2.3) | . | 6 | Query (folding-in) | a query is a pseudo-document: Dq = Xq′TS⁻¹, “placing the pseudo-document at the centroid of its corresponding term points”, then scaled by S for document comparisons (§4.2.4). Retrieve by cosine | . | 7 | Update | “simply folding-in new terms or documents will result in a somewhat different space than would have been obtained had these objects been included in the original analysis … How much of this can be done without rescaling is an open research issue” (§3.2, fn. 3; again §6). An index is therefore stale by construction once its corpus changes — the property the QA criterion checks | . The paper does not interpret the dimensions: “We make no attempt to interpret the underlying factors, nor to ‘rotate’ them to some meaningful orientation” (§4.1).

3704.doc: Latent Semantic Indexing — retrieve and relate by co-occurrence structure, not by shared words
3704.title: What the paper found, exactly
3704.content: . | MED (1,033 abstracts, 30 queries, 5,823 terms, k = 100): average precision .51 vs .45 for term matching, “a 13% improvement”; the gain is at high recall, because “latent semantic indexing is designed primarily to handle synonymy problems (thus improving recall); it is less successful in dealing with polysemy (precision)” (§5.1). The authors warn MED “may have resulted in unrealistically good results” — it was built from keyword searches, so it is unusually well-segmented. | CISI (1,460 abstracts, 35 queries): .11 for both LSI and term matching; SMART, which stems, did better (.14). Re-run on SMART’s own terms, LSI tied SMART at .14. So: “Stemming … seems to capture some structure that LSI was unable to capture” (§5.2). | Their own summary: “modestly encouraging” — better than term matching in one standard case and equal in the other (§5.3), and “a potential component of a retrieval system, rather than as a complete retrieval system” (§6). | .

3705.doc: Latent Semantic Indexing — retrieve and relate by co-occurrence structure, not by shared words
3705.title: What this platform adopts, and what it refuses
3705.content: Adopted . | Steps 1–7. Units are the graph’s own nodes — a library section, a skill file, a work item — because the KG already chunks semantically (work item p2en). | Log-entropy weighting by default, which the 1990 paper does not use. The paper asks for weighting to be added (“refinements such as stemming, phrases, term-weighting … generally result in performance improvements”, §5) and Landauer, Foltz & Laham (1998, p. 17) describe the customary transform: “the word frequency (+ 1) in each cell is converted to its log. Second, … entropy, of each word is computed as −Σ p log p over all entries in its row, and each cell entry then divided by the row entropy value.” The engine uses a different form of the same idea — global weight 1 + Σ p log p / log n, i.e. one minus the normalised entropy — which is the form attributed to Dumais (1991). That paper is not held, so the attribution is unverified; the held source’s form (divide by entropy) is not what runs. Measured here, on the one task that has a ground truth (epic filing, 2026-09-29): log-entropy 59 % vs tf-idf 52 % agreement. raw is available and is what the engine’s test uses, against the paper’s worked example. | The first dimension is reported but read as a margin, not a theme — see Qi et al. below. | Recompute rather than fold in whenever the input fingerprint changes: at this corpus size a rebuild takes about a second. Folding-in is used only for things that are not units of the index (a query, a branch, a PR). | . Refused, with reasons . | A latent cosine is never merged with a lexical match. graph-search refuses to rank because a made-up order hides that everything matched equally. A cosine is defined, but it answers a different question — and the paper itself positions LSI as “a potential component”, beside term matching rather than instead of it. | A dimension is not a topic until a person names it. The paper makes “no attempt to interpret the underlying factors”; dimension summaries are published for review, not as labels. | LSI output never writes a relation. It proposes a parent for a work item, a uses[] candidate, a duplicate pair; it writes none. uses[] is the editorial relation and a score would destroy its signal. | LSI similarity is never evidence for a claim in content. It is a retrieval aid. Nothing it computes enters a proof, a formal statement, a recommendation or a GRADE judgement. | The cognitive reading is not adopted. Landauer, Foltz & Laham (1998) and Landauer & Dumais (1997) present the same computation as a theory of human meaning. The 1990 paper claims only correlation structure (fn. 1), and so does this platform. | No stemming — and this is a cost, not a free lunch. Stemming is language-specific and the corpus is multilingual by design, so it is not done. The first draft of this node said LSI recovers much of what stemming would; the paper’s own CISI result says otherwise, and its authors write that in theory LSA can extract commonalities between stemmed forms but “In practice, we may often have insufficient data to do so” (§5.2). The loss is accepted, and stated. | .

3706.doc: Latent Semantic Indexing — retrieve and relate by co-occurrence structure, not by shared words
3706.title: What it is not good at
3706.content: . | Polysemy. “every term is represented as just one point in the space. … a word with more than one entirely different meaning (e.g. “bank”), is represented as a weighted average” (§6). | The first dimensions carry margins, not meaning. Qi, Hessen & van der Heijden (2023) show “The initial dimensions extracted by latent semantic analysis (LSA) of a document-term matrix … mainly display marginal effects, which are irrelevant for information retrieval” — document length and overall term frequency. Observed here: dimension 1 of both the IRIS replica and skills indexes has no negative pole at all, the signature of a margin. | Word order and negation. A bag of words; the paper lists “a method of handling negation” among refinements it did not add (§5.3). | k has no rule. The paper says so, and the calibration here (59–63 % over k = 50–250) found the choice barely matters for filing. | Search is exhaustive. “the only way documents can be retrieved is by an exhaustive comparison of a query vector against all stored document vectors” (§6) — fine at thousands of units. | .

3707.doc: Latent Semantic Indexing — retrieve and relate by co-occurrence structure, not by shared words
3707.title: The parallel tracks, and why they are not this node
3707.content: | track | answers | why it is separate | . | lexical search (graph-search) | which nodes contain these words, and what is adjacent | exact, explainable, no score; LSI sits beside it | . | correspondence analysis (Qi et al. 2023) | the same retrieval question, by an SVD of the standardised residuals from the independence model rather than of the weighted counts | its own node, correspondence-analysis (adopted 2026-09-29): margins removed, χ² structure. Measured here against this node on work item filing: no significant difference (McNemar p = 0.17–0.71) — not blended into this one | . | incremental compositional embeddings (Hang et al. 2022) | how to place newly arriving nodes without retraining: explicit vectors for the stable node type, the rest “represent[ed] implicitly, through a composition function based on their interactions” | the same shape as folding-in (a new document = centroid of its terms), but a learned model evaluated on recommendation; not adopted | . | dense neural embeddings (docs/proposals/rag-document-ingestion.md) | the same question, from a model pre-trained elsewhere | needs a model download (403 in the sandbox), not reproducible from the corpus alone | . | skill-pipeline-subject-indexing | which controlled-vocabulary terms a work should carry | closed vocabulary, policy-governed; LSI has no vocabulary to validate against | . Pick one per question (methodology-adoption §”Parallel, not composable”).

3708.doc: Latent Semantic Indexing — retrieve and relate by co-occurrence structure, not by shared words
3708.title: How it is performed here
3708.content: The skill is lsi-indexing; the engine is pipeline/lsi.ts, computed by Halko et al.’s randomized subspace iteration (their Algorithm 4.4: Gaussian test matrix, oversampling p = 10, re-orthonormalisation between every pass) and direct SVD of the small matrix (Algorithm 5.1). One deviation, stated: the small SVD is taken from the eigendecomposition of BBᵀ, which squares the condition number and so loses relative accuracy on the smallest retained singular values; acceptable for ranking, not for reporting those values to many digits. pipeline/lsi.test.ts checks the engine against the 1990 paper’s own worked example: the nine singular values of its 12 × 9 matrix to the two decimals printed, and the query “human computer interaction” retrieving c3 and c5, which share no term with it.

3709.doc: Latent Semantic Indexing — retrieve and relate by co-occurrence structure, not by shared words
3709.title: Latent Semantic Indexing — retrieve and relate by co-occurrence structure, not by shared words
3709.content: ← All methodologies . lsi — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Finding or relating units of text that discuss the same thing in different words, across a corpus too large to read whole, where no controlled vocabulary has been assigned. Use it to ask “what else in this graph is about this?”, to propose a home for an unfiled item among existing groups, to find near-duplicates, and to surface clusters nobody named. It answers which units are close in co-occurrence structure. It does NOT answer whether a unit is relevant, correct, or a dependency: every output is a PROPOSAL a person or an agent confirms. Not for assigning terms from a controlled vocabulary (skill-pipeline-subject-indexing), not for judging an assignment (consensus-grounded-subject-evaluation), and not for any decision (kepner-tregoe, dmn). Origin. Scott Deerwester, Susan T. Dumais, George W. Furnas, Thomas K. Landauer and Richard A. Harshman, “Indexing by Latent Semantic Analysis”, Journal of the American Society for Information Science 41(6):391–407 (1990), for the method. Susan T. Dumais, “Improving the retrieval of information from external sources”, Behavior Research Methods, Instruments & Computers 23(2):229–236 (1991), for the log-entropy term weighting. Michael W. Berry, Susan T. Dumais and Gavin W. O’Brien, “Using Linear Algebra for Intelligent Information Retrieval”, SIAM Review 37(4):573–595 (1995), for folding-in and updating. Thomas K. Landauer, Peter W. Foltz and Darrell Laham, “An Introduction to Latent Semantic Analysis”, Discourse Processes 25:259–284 (1998), and Thomas K. Landauer and Susan T. Dumais, “A Solution to Plato’s Problem”, Psychological Review 104(2):211–240 (1997), for the cognitive reading of the same computation (there called LSA), which this node does NOT adopt. Nathan Halko, Per-Gunnar Martinsson and Joel A. Tropp, “Finding Structure with Randomness”, SIAM Review 53(2):217–288 (2011; arXiv:0909.4061v2), for the randomized SVD this platform computes it with — an implementation source, not part of the method. Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/deerwester-1990-indexing-by-lsa | library/landauer-foltz-laham-1998-intro-lsa | library/arxiv-0909.4061v2 | library/qi-hessen-vanderheijden-2023-ca-vs-lsa | library/arxiv-2202.02427v1 | . 3710.doc: WireGen: wireframing from a written design intent
3710.title: WireGen: from a written intent to a reviewed, mid-fidelity wireframe
3710.content: Adopted in part, 2026-09-23, by the owner’s direction. In the owner’s words: “make methodology/utilize/integrate into existing processes. need both web and mobile layouts in usability reviews. wireframe is part of design process for adjudication”. Integrated into CRDM, 2026-10-14. crdm-requirements-definition.bpmn calls Process_WireframeDesignReview (Call_Wireframe) whenever a requirement changes a rendered surface, before anything is built; the candidates become assets of the request’s proposal, and the requester or BA chooses one at BA_ReviewReqs. See wireframe-design-review. Placed in cat-harness (owner, 2026-09-23: “put wireframe in cat-harness, not folio-assist(-core)”). The method is domain-neutral, and methodology-adoption §4 puts a domain-neutral method in the harness. It was first drafted in litlfred/ihris, and its first use was that folio’s data-model site. Issue #1023.

3711.doc: WireGen: wireframing from a written design intent
3711.title: What the method says (rendered faithfully)
3711.content: Section numbers below are the paper’s. | Design intent comes first, as language (§3, §5.2). A short natural-language description of what the screen is for and what it holds. | Mid-fidelity is the target (§3.1.1). The wireframe is monochrome and simplified, but it carries real content, semantic icons and interactive elements, not boxes and placeholder text. | HTML is the carrier (§3.1.2, §3.3). The screen is expressed as a UI-specific HTML-like language. Raw output is post-processed against UI guidance: icons chosen by meaning, typography, and layout guidelines (§3.3). | Evaluation is blind and comparative (§4.3). Independent raters with design background see the description and a shuffled grid of candidates, without knowing which generator produced which. They mark candidates significantly better or significantly worse. | Usefulness is asked separately (§5.2): whether a wireframe is effective for inspiration, whether it relates to the description, and whether the candidates are diverse. These are rated on a 5-point scale. | Refinement is iterative (§6). Intent, then wireframe, then a revised intent, then a revised wireframe. | .

3712.doc: WireGen: wireframing from a written design intent
3712.title: What this platform adopts, and what it refuses
3712.content: |   | adopted | refused, with the reason | . | intent statement | yes: every candidate set starts from one, and it is the criterion candidates are judged against | none | . | mid-fidelity with real content | yes: real content from the folio (for iHRIS: real form classes, fields, lists) | none | . | HTML carrier + guideline post-processing | yes: wireframes are HTML, and the mechanical checks are the post-processing gate | none | . | fine-tuning an LLM on Rico / Screen2Words (§3.1, §3.2) | no | That is how the authors generate; it is not a review method. Candidates here may come from a person, an agent or any tool. The method applies to what they produce. | . | blind, shuffled comparison | yes: reviewers are not told a candidate’s author | none | . | better/worse marks and Likert ratings | the structure, not the arithmetic | methodology-adoption refuses scoring and summing. A mean of Likert ratings reads as a measurement of a judgement. Reviewers record per-criterion pass / warn / fail with a reason. | . | mobile only (the paper’s data is Android, §3.1.1) | extended: both web and mobile layouts are required in every usability review (owner, 2026-09-23) | The source’s scope is narrower than our need. We state the extension rather than claim the paper supports it. | . | the reported numbers (77.5%, the user study) | no | They describe the authors’ model and datasets. Nothing here depends on them. | .

3713.doc: WireGen: wireframing from a written design intent
3713.title: How it plugs into existing processes
3713.content: . | Review record: each criterion gets entries from a script (the mechanical checks), an agent and a human, in block-qa/v1 sidecars. This is folio-assistant’s existing multi-reviewer primitive. | Disagreement: when entries for one criterion disagree, the candidate set enters Process_Adjudication (processes/process/adjudication.bpmn). The adjudication leads, the checker’s entry is kept, and the dispensation carries its reason. | Choice between surviving candidates: a one-off choice, so it uses the decision-analysis methodology. Rejected candidates are kept with the reason they lost. | After build: the rendered result does not go through theme-ui-review.bpmn any more. Theme and UI review moved to ingestion only, by owner ruling (work item 9fdi, 2026-09-24): it runs when the graphical assets arrive, from ingest-theme.bpmn, and still requires both web and mobile layouts (#1023). A post-build visual look for a wiregen output is therefore not provided by that process — recorded so it is not assumed. | . The executable form is processes/ui/wireframe-design-review.bpmn. The operating skill is wireframe-design-review. The mechanical checks are the Tool wireframe-check.

3714.doc: WireGen: wireframing from a written design intent
3714.title: Refusals
3714.content: . | Never review a single candidate as if it were a choice. The method is comparative; at least two candidates, or say why only one exists. | Never accept a wireframe reviewed at one viewport. A web-only or mobile-only review is incomplete, not passed. | Never show a reviewer who made a candidate. Blindness is the method’s evidence of fairness. | Never let placeholder text through. Lorem ipsum makes it a low-fidelity wireframe, and the method is about mid-fidelity. | Never average the ratings into a score. | .

3715.doc: WireGen: wireframing from a written design intent
3715.title: WireGen: wireframing from a written design intent
3715.content: ← All methodologies . wiregen — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Designing a USER INTERFACE, for example a page layout, a navigation scheme or a visualiser, where the choice between candidate designs has to be reviewed and, when reviewers disagree, adjudicated. It is a design-generation and design-evaluation method. It does not choose between non-UI options (use the decision-analysis methodology) or grade evidence. It does not by itself settle a disagreement: that is adjudication. Origin. 3716.doc: Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirement
3716.title: Assessment of open standards for requirements and bootstrap mapping
3716.content: Status: evaluated and recommended, NOT adopted into bootstrap. Issue #1164. Owner, 2026-09-23, choosing markdown front matter for requirement documents: “1 for now. need bean to assess open stds for requirements/methodologies that fit in”. The bootstrap Requirement (bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json) is deliberately free of outside concepts. This methodology assesses open standards across three categories — interchange formats, statement templates & grammars, and quality models — evaluating their licensing, governance, serialization overhead, and exact field-by-field fit to the bootstrap Requirement. It concludes with concrete architectural recommendations on layer placement and verifies the no-outside-concept boundary.

3717.doc: Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirement
3717.title: 1. The bootstrap baseline: the six parts of a requirement
3717.content: In the bootstrap and harness architecture, a requirement is defined by six essential parts (formalized in Issue #2405, FR-007/FR-008, and documented in skills/content/requirements-planning/requirement-definition.md): . | Identifier (id): A globally unique URI/slug (req:<slug>), with each individual requirement statement addressable as req:<slug>#<key> and each success criterion addressable as req:<slug>#<key>/<criterion>. | Title & Label: A concise human-readable heading (title for the document, label for each atomic statement). | Statement & Conformance (requirement, conformance): Exactly one sentence that a reviewer or test can say yes or no to, qualified by an RFC 2119 conformance verb (SHALL, SHOULD, MAY, SHALL NOT). | Rationale / Benefit (benefit, description): The justification explaining why the obligation exists and what value it delivers. | Parent & Lineage (derivedFrom): Direct upstream references in the specialization/conformance lattice. | Acceptance & Verification (successCriteria[]): At least one concrete success criterion (criterion) with an explicit verification method (verification ∈ {test, inspection, review, analysis}). A requirement without a success criterion can be filed and never judged. | . A requirement document is authored in Markdown with YAML front matter or stored as JSON, and grouped into a RequirementSet (reqset:<slug>) tracking stages (draft → proposed → approved → planned → in-progress → delivered → accepted), member decisions, work plans (work items), and recorded human sign-off attestations.

3718.doc: Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirement
3718.title: 2. Survey of open standards
3718.content: Category A: Interchange formats . 1. ReqIF (OMG Requirements Interchange Format v1.2) . | Origin & Governance: Object Management Group (OMG formal/2013-10-01), originally standardized by ProSTEP iViP. Also ISO/IEC 17506:2022. | Licence: Open specification, royalty-free (RF). | Maturity: High. De facto interchange standard in automotive, aerospace, and defense systems engineering (supported by IBM DOORS / DOORS Next, PTC Integrity, Siemens Polarion, Dassault, Eclipse ProR). | Serialization Overhead: Very high. XML-based schema with extensive metamodel indirection: REQ-IF → CORE-CONTENT → DATATYPES → SPEC-TYPES (SpecObjectType, SpecRelationType) → SPEC-OBJECTS → SPEC-RELATIONS → SPECIFICATIONS (SpecHierarchy). Attributes require multi-level XML wrappers (<ATTRIBUTE-VALUE-STRING>, <THE-VALUE>). Line-based Git diffs of raw ReqIF XML are unreadable. | Semantic Alignment to Bootstrap: . | SpecObject maps to a bootstrap Statement (or an atomic Requirement). | SpecObjectType defines attribute metadata. | ReqIF.Name maps to title / label. | ReqIF.Text maps to requirement (statement text). | SpecRelation (type derives or parent) maps to derivedFrom. | Verification items can be modelled either as separate SpecObjects linked via SpecRelation (type verifiedBy), or as structured attributes on the SpecObject (VerificationMethod, SuccessCriteria). | . | Verdict: Excellent for enterprise import/export projection; totally unsuitable for native storage or authoring in Git. | . 2. OSLC-RM (OASIS OSLC Requirements Management v2.1 / OSLC Core 3.0) . | Origin & Governance: OASIS Open Standard. | Licence: OASIS Royalty-Free (RF) on Limited Terms. | Maturity: High in ALM/PLM linked-data ecosystems (IBM Engineering Lifecycle Management, Siemens, Eclipse Lyo). | Serialization Overhead: Moderate to High. RDF graph representations (JSON-LD, Turtle, RDF/XML). Relies on URI dereferencing, Linked Data Platform (LDP) protocols, and ontology vocabularies (oslc_rm:, dcterms:). | Semantic Alignment to Bootstrap: . | oslc_rm:Requirement resource type. | dcterms:identifier maps to id / key. | dcterms:title maps to title / label. | dcterms:description maps to requirement statement text. | oslc_rm:derivedFrom and oslc_rm:elaboratedBy map to derivedFrom / dependsOn. | oslc_rm:validatedBy links to test artifacts or verification definitions. | . | Verdict: Natural fit with knowledge-graph / JSON-LD export pipelines (ns.jsonld, kg-export), but introduces unnecessary REST/graph server assumptions if forced into the local authoring loop. | . Category B: Statement templates and grammars . 3. EARS (Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax) . | Origin & Governance: Alistair Mavin, Philip Wilkinson, Adrian Harwood, Mark Novak (Rolls-Royce plc / IEEE International Requirements Engineering Conference 2009). | Licence: Unencumbered, open methodology. | Maturity: High. Widely adopted across aerospace, automotive, medical device, and agile systems engineering. | Serialization Overhead: Zero. Operates directly on the requirement statement natural language text. | The Five EARS Patterns: . | Ubiquitous: “The <system> shall <system response>.” . | Example: “The harness SHALL validate every block against its declared schema.” | . | Event-driven: “When <trigger>, the <system> shall <system response>.” . | Example: “When a plan is requested, the agent SHALL produce a requirements document and work plan.” | . | State-driven: “While <in a state>, the <system> shall <system response>.” . | Example: “While the requirement set is in draft stage, the tool SHALL allow modification of statement keys.” | . | Unwanted behavior: “If <trigger/error>, then the <system> shall <system response>.” . | Example: “If a statement lacks success criteria, then check:requirements SHALL emit a validation finding.” | . | Optional features: “Where <feature is present>, the <system> shall <system response>.” . | Example: “Where LaTeX tooling is installed, the adapter SHALL generate typeset math blocks.” (Complex requirements combine While, Where, When, and If clauses). | . | . | Semantic Alignment to Bootstrap: . | Fits directly inside the requirement string in bootstrap Statement. | The <system> noun maps to actors / harness components. | Conformance verbs align 1:1 with RFC 2119 / bootstrap SHALL, SHOULD, etc. | Can be validated deterministically by regular expressions or syntax AST checkers in check:requirements without altering the data schema. | . | Verdict: The optimal statement syntax pattern for authoring requirements in the harness. | . 4. ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 (Systems and software engineering — Requirements engineering) . | Origin & Governance: Joint ISO/IEC/IEEE standard. Replaced and consolidated IEEE 830, IEEE 1220, and IEEE 1233. | Licence: Formal international standard (copyright held by ISO/IEEE; concepts open for reference). | Maturity: Definitive international benchmark for requirements engineering. | Serialization Overhead: Zero (process and semantic standard, not a file format). | Core Elements: . | Requirement Construct (Clause 5.2.4): Defines standard syntax comprising Conditions, Subject, Conformance Verb (“shall”, “should”, “may”), Action/Object, and Constraints. | Verification Methods (Clause 6.4): Explicitly standardizes the four fundamental verification methods: . | Test: Quantitative verification using automated or manual test cases with controlled inputs and measured outputs. | Inspection: Visual or manual verification by examining the product, code, or documentation without executing it. | Analysis: Verification using mathematical models, calculations, simulations, or formal logic proofs. | Demonstration: Qualitative verification of observable operation under specified scenarios (analogous to review). | . | . | Semantic Alignment to Bootstrap: . | Bootstrap’s verification method enum (test, inspection, review, analysis) is an exact 1:1 realization of ISO 29148’s verification quartet (with review representing demonstration/adjudication). | Traceability relations (derivedFrom, dependsOn) align with Clause 5.2.7. | . | Verdict: The conceptual foundation for the harness’s requirement definition. | . 5. IEEE Std 830-1998 (Software Requirements Specifications — SRS) . | Origin & Governance: IEEE Computer Society. | Status: Officially withdrawn and superseded by ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2011/2018. | Licence: Historical IEEE standard. | Maturity: Historic benchmark, but obsolete in modern systems engineering. | Fit to Bootstrap: Premised on large, monolithic, document-centric Software Requirements Specification (SRS) manuals (Section 1 Introduction, Section 2 General Description, Section 3 Specific Requirements). Bootstrap requirements are atomic, graph-linked statement nodes in Git rather than monolithic text chapters. | Verdict: Superseded. Retained only for historical traceability; all modern harness mappings should cite ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018. | . Category C: Quality models . 6. ISO/IEC 25010:2011 / 2023 (Systems and software Quality Requirements and Evaluation — SQRE) . | Origin & Governance: ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 7. | Licence: Formal international standard. | Maturity: Universal international taxonomy for software quality characteristics and Non-Functional Requirements (NFRs). | Structure: Defines 8 product quality characteristics (expanded to 9 in 2023): . | Functional Suitability (completeness, correctness, appropriateness). | Performance Efficiency (time behaviour, resource utilization, capacity). | Compatibility (co-existence, interoperability). | Interaction Capability / Usability (recognisability, learnability, operability, aesthetics). | Reliability (maturity, availability, fault tolerance, recoverability). | Security (confidentiality, integrity, non-repudiation, accountability, authenticity). | Maintainability (modularity, reusability, analysability, modifiability, testability). | Portability (adaptability, installability, replaceability). | Safety (2023 addition: operational risk, hazard mitigation). | . | Semantic Alignment to Bootstrap: . | Bootstrap Statement differentiates kind: "functional" and kind: "non-functional". | For kind: "non-functional", bootstrap requires a category string. | ISO/IEC 25010 characteristics provide the canonical controlled vocabulary for this category field (e.g. security, performance-efficiency, maintainability, reliability). | . | Verdict: Strongly recommended as the controlled taxonomy for non-functional requirement validation in cat-harness. | . 7. INCOSE Guide for Writing Requirements (INCOSE-TP-2010-006-04, 2023) . | Origin & Governance: International Council on Systems Engineering (INCOSE). | Licence: INCOSE copyright; educational / professional guidance. | Maturity: Universal de facto standard for requirements authoring quality and automated linting rules. | Structure: Defines 9 Requirement Characteristics (Necessary, Appropriate, Conforming, Singular, Feasible, Verifiable, Correct, Conforming, Complete) and 40+ specific quality rules: . | Singularity: One requirement per statement; no compound sentences with “and/or”. | Verifiability: Must state conditions that can be definitively verified. | No ambiguous words: Avoid vague terms (“user-friendly”, “rapid”, “cost-effective”, “easy”, “robust”). | No escape clauses: Avoid “where possible”, “as appropriate”, “to the extent practical”. | Active voice: Clear subject acting upon an object. | . | Semantic Alignment to Bootstrap: . | Directly justifies the bootstrap requirement rule: “one sentence a reviewer can say yes or no to” and “at least one success criterion with a verification method”. | Provides the precise linting rules for automated QA criteria in check:requirements. | . | Verdict: Strongly recommended as the rule basis for requirements quality linters. | .

3720.doc: Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirement
3720.title: 4. Architectural assessment: complexity, cost, and layer placement
3720.content: Why nothing is adopted into bootstrap (the no-outside-concept rule) . Bootstrap (bootstrap/) is the foundational, zero-dependency substrate of the entire folio-assistant platform. It defines the core data contracts and schemas that every tool, harness, and workspace inherits. | No External Dependencies: Bootstrap cannot import or depend on heavy XML parsers (for ReqIF), RDF/triple-store engines (for OSLC), or specialized NLP libraries. | Git Hygiene and Line-Oriented Diffs: Markdown front matter (.md) and lean JSON files (.json) produce readable, clean Git diffs on PR reviews. ReqIF XML produces massive, unreadable multi-thousand-line diffs for minor attribute changes. | Speed and Portability: Validating bootstrap schemas via Zod is nearly instantaneous in Bun or Node. It introduces zero runtime overhead. | Conclusion: Any standard mapping or projection must live in higher layers (cat-harness, or a content layer above it). Injecting outside formats into bootstrap would violate the repository’s foundational architecture. | . Architectural layer placement . The diagram below illustrates the strict separation of concerns across layers: . ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Layer 2: Projection & Integration Adapters (tools / folio-assistant) │ │ - ReqIF Exporter/Importer (.reqif XML for DOORS, Polarion, Cameo) │ │ - OSLC-RM Linked Data Provider (JSON-LD / RDF / LDP) │ └──────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┘ │ maps to/from ┌──────────────────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Layer 1: Harness Validation & Quality Linters (cat-harness) │ │ - EARS Pattern Validator (checks statement regex / grammar in CI) │ │ - INCOSE Requirements Linter (flags vague words, compound sentences) │ │ - ISO 25010 NFR Category Checker (validates non-functional categories)│ │ - check:requirements gate & requirement-set adjudication │ └──────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┘ │ validates ┌──────────────────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Layer 0: Bootstrap Substrate (bootstrap/) │ │ - Pure Markdown Front Matter + Zod Schema │ │ - Zero outside concepts, zero external dependencies │ │ - 6-part requirement structure: id, title, statement, conformance, │ │ derivedFrom, successCriteria (test, inspection, review, analysis) │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ .

3721.doc: Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirement
3721.title: 5. Concrete recommendations
3721.content: . | Maintain Markdown Front Matter + Zod as Native Format: . | The current Markdown front matter format for requirement documents (and JSON for programmatic requirement nodes) is optimal. | It is human-readable, machine-checkable via strict Zod schemas, and perfectly suited for Git pull request workflows. | Do not replace the front matter format with ReqIF XML or raw OSLC RDF. | . | Implement EARS Grammar Verification in cat-harness: . | Add an EARS pattern checker into check:requirements (or as a dedicated script scripts/check-ears-patterns.ts). | Every requirement statement should be checked against the 5 EARS patterns (Ubiquitous, Event-driven, State-driven, Unwanted behavior, Optional features). | This provides immediate authoring feedback and enforces rigorous syntax without changing the underlying data schema. | . | Standardize NFR Categories on ISO/IEC 25010: . | In cat-harness validators, enforce that for statements with kind: "non-functional", the category field belongs to the ISO/IEC 25010 quality taxonomy (security, performance-efficiency, compatibility, interaction-capability, reliability, maintainability, portability, safety). | . | Build Projection Adapters in Higher Layers on Demand: . | When interoperability with enterprise requirements tools is required: . | Develop tools/reqif-adapter: converts RequirementSet and Requirement nodes into standard OMG ReqIF 1.2 XML packages and vice versa. | Develop tools/oslc-rm-adapter: exposes requirement graphs via OSLC-RM JSON-LD contexts mapped through ns.jsonld. | . | Keep these tools isolated from the core bootstrap package. | . | .

3724.doc: RASCI — RACI plus Supportive, for when doing the work and owning it come apart
3724.title: RASCI — the fifth letter, and when it earns its place
3724.content: Adopted on the owner’s ruling, 2026-09-23 (issue #1004), as a parallel track to raci, not a replacement for it. methodology-adoption: “Two or more methodologies may answer the same question. Do not blend them… pick one per decision, name it, and follow it.” A process here declares which it is written in, and declaring nothing means raci.

3725.doc: RASCI — RACI plus Supportive, for when doing the work and owning it come apart
3725.title: ⚠ This rendering is not backed by a source
3725.content: No RASCI source is ingested here, and nothing below is asserted on a source’s authority. What follows is the method as commonly understood — weaker than a cited rendering, and marked as weaker on purpose. check:methodology-evidence reports this node as unbacked, correctly. Do not remove that finding by pointing evidence at the RACI paper. It was searched: zero occurrences of rasci, racsi, supportive or five roles. Citing it here would be the failure methodology-adoption §”Never write a method from recall and cite a paper nobody fetched” names, made worse by the citation being checkably about something else.

3726.doc: RASCI — RACI plus Supportive, for when doing the work and owning it come apart
3726.title: The five letters
3726.content: | letter | means | direction | . | Responsible | does the work | may be several | . | Accountable | carries the decision; answers for the outcome | exactly one | . | Supportive | contributes effort or resources to the work, without owning the deliverable | may be several | . | Consulted | asked for input before | two-way | . | Informed | told after | one-way | . Four of these are raci’s and are not restated here — the node is raci.md, including the exactly-one-Accountable constraint, which RASCI inherits unchanged.

3727.doc: RASCI — RACI plus Supportive, for when doing the work and owning it come apart
3727.title: What S is, against its two neighbours
3727.content: S is not a weaker R. The line is ownership of the deliverable, not quantity of effort: a Supportive party may do more work than the Responsible one and still be S, because the deliverable is not theirs to hand over. S is not a Consulted who happened to help. C is asked for input and gives an opinion; S does work. Collapsing them is the same error as collapsing C into I — it turns a contribution into a conversation, and the chart still reads as complete. The test: if this role stopped participating, would the activity be late (S), or merely less well informed (C)? A role whose absence changes nothing but opinion was never S.

3728.doc: RASCI — RACI plus Supportive, for when doing the work and owning it come apart
3728.title: When NOT to use it
3728.content: A five-letter chart where every S column is empty is worse than a four-letter one, because it advertises a distinction the author did not actually make. The fifth letter is justified by a Supportive party existing, not by wanting a more complete-looking matrix. raci remains the default here for exactly that reason.

3729.doc: RASCI — RACI plus Supportive, for when doing the work and owning it come apart
3729.title: How this platform applies it
3729.content: S is declarable; R still is not — and the asymmetry is structural rather than an omission. A BPMN activity sits in exactly one lane, and that lane is Responsible. So the lane is a discriminator, not a description: R is the owning lane, S is a declared role that is not it, and no case can be both. This was checked against the corpus before the letter was added — no activity anywhere declares involvement="responsible" — so the premise holds and S inherits no ambiguity from it. It buys real expressiveness rather than a letter for its own sake: BPMN cannot place one activity in two lanes, so before this there was no way to say “this role also does the work here”. A process opts in: . <bpmn:process id="Process_X"> <bpmn:extensionElements> <cat-harness.processes:involvement vocabulary="rasci"/> </bpmn:extensionElements> . and may then declare <cat-harness.processes:raci ref="<role>" involvement="supportive"/>. In a process that has not opted in, a supportive is a reported breach — neither coerced to a neighbouring letter nor silently dropped. That refusal is what makes this a choice rather than a spelling rule; check:raci and the raci-involvement-vocabulary QA criterion carry it, and the skill skills/process/raci/raci.md holds the platform overlay both vocabularies share.

3730.doc: RASCI — RACI plus Supportive, for when doing the work and owning it come apart
3730.title: RASCI — RACI plus Supportive, for when doing the work and owning it come apart
3730.content: ← All methodologies . rasci — declared by cat-harness — cited, not ingested . Applies when. Who is involved, when a role does the work without owning the deliverable. Use it where a separate Supportive party is real — someone who contributes effort or resources to an activity that another role answers for. If no such party exists, use raci instead: a fifth letter nobody fills is a column that makes the chart look more considered than it is. Like raci it answers who, never what or whether — a one-off choice among options is kepner-tregoe, a recurring rule is dmn, certainty of evidence is grade, the record of a decision is madr, situation analysis is swot. Origin. NOT ESTABLISHED FROM ANY SOURCE HELD HERE, and that is stated rather than guessed. RASCI (also written RASIC) is the five-letter member of the responsibility-assignment-matrix family from project-management practice. No text for it is ingested in this repository and none was reachable when this node was written. The one RACI source this checkout does hold — library/dusengumuremyi-2026-ai-mediated-raci — was searched and contains ZERO occurrences of rasci, racsi, supportive or five roles, so it backs raci and expressly not this. The candidates are the same paid standards and books listed in raci’s §”The primary is still not held”. See literature-search. Node file: rasci.md .

3731.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
3731.title: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
3731.content: This methodology node completes work item folio-assistant-qh1s (Issue #1164): a literature search over requirements-management practice across the five lifecycle dimensions (organisation, identifiers, traceability, change, and retirement), the explicit adoption or rejection of candidate methodologies through methodology-adoption, and the proposed executable BPMN filing process (sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc)) put to the owner before automation is built. Whereas sibling methodology requirements-standards-assessment.md (work item folio-assistant-1gf7) assessed open interchange and syntax standards (ReqIF, OSLC RM, EARS, RFC 2119 / RFC 8174, IEEE 29148, Planguage, SysML, Gherkin) to map their constructs onto bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json and bootstrap/schemas/requirement-set.schema.json, this node governs how requirements are organised, identified, traced, amended, superseded, and retired as they are filed into docs/requirements/ once docs/requirements/ grows past a flat hand-maintained list.

3732.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
3732.title: 1. Literature search over requirements-management practice
3732.content: Per literature-search, every surveyed source is recorded below with its provenance/access status (ingested library/<bib-slug> node where held on disk, or external standard / open-source specification where copyright or scope keeps the full text outside library/) and with what it offers here across the five dimensions of work item folio-assistant-qh1s: . | Organisation — how a growing corpus of filed requirements is structured and navigated without breaking path stability. | Identifiers — how requirements and sub-clauses receive durable, collision-free, human- and machine-addressable IDs in a distributed Git workflow. | Traceability — how backward lineage (to proposals, user needs, and L1 sources), horizontal dependencies (between requirements), and forward verification (to work items, skills, processes, and test attestations) are recorded and checked. | Change — how in-scope amendments versus scope-altering replacements are distinguished, reviewed, and versioned. | Retirement — how obsolete or superseded requirements leave active force without breaking historical links or audit trails. | . 1.1 Summary matrix across the five filing dimensions . | Source | Provenance / library status | Organisation | Identifiers | Traceability | Change | Retirement | . | ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 (Systems and software engineering — Life cycle processes — Requirements engineering, Clauses 5.2.7, 6.4, 6.5) | Proprietary ISO/IEEE standard; assessed via public clause structure (no full-text redistributable PDF in library/) | Separates stakeholder requirements (StRS) from system/software requirements (SyRS/SRS); organises by system architecture or functional domain | Unique, persistent requirement identifier (id) independent of document section position | Clause 5.2.7 mandates bidirectional traceability: backward to source/parent need, forward to design elements and verification records | Clause 6.5 requires formal change control, impact analysis over dependent items, and baseline sign-off | Explicit lifecycle status attribute (retired / obsolete / superseded); historical records retained for audit | . | Volere Requirements Specification Template (Robertson & Robertson, Mastering the Requirements Process, 4th ed.) | Commercial book / template; assessed via published Volere atomic “Snow Card” specification | Groups requirements by functional area / business event / concern rather than implementation module; card number is never reused | . | IREB CPRE Foundation Level (Pohl & Rupp, Requirements Engineering Fundamentals, 3rd ed.) | Standard RE body of knowledge; external textbook | Contrasts tree-structured chapter hierarchies against faceted / attribute-driven views over atomic requirement objects | Recommends immutable object identifiers decoupled from chapter headings so restructuring views never renumbers requirements | Defines three explicit trace link directions: pre-RS / backward (to origins), post-RS / forward (to artefacts/tests), and within-RS / horizontal (dependsOn, refines, conflictsWith) | Configuration management and baseline versioning; change impact propagation along trace links | Status state machine (draft → agreed → validated → implemented → deprecated/retired) | . | Doorstop (Browning & Adams, Doorstop: Text-Based Requirements Management Using Version Control, JOSS 2014; github.com/doorstop-dev/doorstop) | Open-source Git-native requirements tool (lgpl-3.0); external software reference | Stores one text file per requirement (YAML or Markdown-with-front-matter) inside version-controlled directories representing document trees | Prefix + identifier per file, addressable in git diffs; Leiba 2017 — BCP 14 key words) | Ingested in library/rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels and library/rfc8174-uppercase-vs-lowercase-2119-key-words | Separates normative statements (MUST, SHOULD, MAY) from explanatory prose within a specification | Statement-level addressing (statements[].key → req:<slug>#<key>) so each normative keyword clause is individually citable | Pairs each uppercase keyword statement with its own successCriteria and verification witness | Changing a statement’s modality (SHOULD → MUST) is a normative change requiring re-sign-off | Retiring or relaxing a MUST statement requires explicit normative adjudication | . | Specification-Compiled Agents & Issue-Driven Work Plans (arxiv-2404.04834v4; filed requirements remain in-force as the persistent invariant until superseded or retired | . | IEEE Std 830-1998 (IEEE Recommended Practice for Software Requirements Specifications, superseded by ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148) | Historical IEEE standard (superseded); external baseline | Monolithic single-document SRS organised by deep numbered outline (3.1.1.1 Functional Requirement 1) | Positional section numbers (§3.2.4.1) tied to document outline location | External traceability matrices (spreadsheets) mapping section numbers to test cases | Document-level revision history table at the top of the monolithic SRS | Striking out or deleting sections in a new SRS edition, causing section renumbering unless placeholder sections are kept | . 1.2 Detailed source notes: what each source offers this harness . 1.2.1 ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 (Clauses 5.2.7, 6.4, and 6.5) . | What it offers here: . | Attribute canon (Clause 6.5): Defines the essential metadata attributes every managed requirement needs beyond its statement text: unique identifier, requirement status, source/origin, rationale, priority/modality, verification method/criteria, and trace links. Our bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json directly embodies this attribute set (id, title, status, proposedIn, derivedFrom, dependsOn, statements[], beans, skills, processes, supersededBy). | Bidirectional traceability (Clause 5.2.7): Establishes that forward traceability alone (requirement → test) is half a system; backward traceability (requirement → originating proposal/need/source via proposedIn and derivedFrom) is what prevents gold-plating (orphan requirements with no stakeholder origin) and explains why a constraint exists when an agent later considers changing it. | Change and retirement discipline: Distinguishes an approved baseline from working drafts (RequirementSet.stage: draft → proposed → approved → accepted in bootstrap/schemas/requirement-set.schema.json) and requires any transition into or out of active force to carry human sign-off. | . | . 1.2.2 Volere Requirements Specification Template (Robertson & Robertson) . | What it offers here: . | Atomic “Snow Card” structure with Fit Criteria: Volere’s primary contribution is insisting that a requirement is not filed until its Fit Criterion (our statements[].successCriteria) is written beside the description (statements[].statement). A requirement whose fit criterion cannot be stated is still a proposal or open question. | Organisation by semantic concern / business domain: Rather than organising requirements by the code file they touch or chronological filing date, Volere organises requirements by functional domain / concern area so a reader auditing one domain sees all governing invariants together. In cat-harness, the eight canonical concern groups in code-lists/concern-group.json (sdlc, process, tools, kg, library, content, ui, conduct) already partition skills, processes, schemas, and tests; projecting filed requirements under those same eight concern groups in docs/requirements/index.md aligns requirement navigation with the rest of the knowledge graph. | . | . 1.2.3 IREB CPRE (Pohl & Rupp, Requirements Engineering Fundamentals) . | What it offers here: . | Decoupling identification and storage from presentation views: IREB highlights the classic failure mode of hierarchical specifications: when chapter structure is used as both the file path and the requirement ID, reorganising chapters breaks every incoming reference. Storing atomic requirements at stable paths with immutable IDs (docs/requirements/<slug>.md → req:<slug>) while providing faceted views (grouped by concern group, by RequirementSet, or by lifecycle status in docs/requirements/index.md) gives both stable URIs and structured human browsing. | Three-axis trace topology: Clarifies the distinction between backward trace (proposedIn, derivedFrom), horizontal trace (dependsOn between peer requirements), and forward trace (beans, skills, processes, and verification attestations). | . | . 1.2.4 Doorstop (Browning & Adams, JOSS 2014) . | What it offers here: . | Git-native file-per-requirement architecture: Doorstop proved that storing requirements as individual text files with YAML front matter and Markdown prose in the same Git repository as the implementation eliminates external ALM database drift. Every requirement filing, amendment, or retirement travels in the same pull request as the code, process diagram, and test attestation that implements or verifies it. | In-place retirement (status: retired / superseded): Doorstop retires requirements by flipping a front-matter status field rather than deleting the file (git rm), ensuring that historical commits, test runs, and child requirements never point to a missing file. | Suspect-link awareness: Doorstop flags downstream items when an upstream requirement changes. In our harness, check:requirements (scripts/check-requirements.ts) provides the deterministic equivalent: it verifies that every derivedFrom, dependsOn, and supersededBy target exists, that no cycle exists in derivedFrom, that no in-force requirement depends on a retired or superseded requirement without updating its own lineage, and that every RequirementSet at approved or accepted has a matching human requirement-signoff attestation and only in-force members. | . | . 1.2.5 Nygard ADRs & MADR 3.0.0 (methodologies/madr.md) . | What it offers here: . | Proposal-to-Requirement continuity (git mv + proposedIn): In cat-harness, a feature starts as a proposal in docs/proposals/<slug>.md (where options are weighed using Kepner-Tregoe, SWOT, and MADR). When the feature ships and is signed off, git mv docs/proposals/<slug>.md docs/requirements/<slug>.md promotes the file in place, preserving its slug, its git log --follow history, and the options analysis that justified it, while proposedIn records the commit SHA and path of the proposal before the move. | Immutable supersession chain: When a shipped requirement’s fundamental contract is replaced by a new design, the old requirement file is not overwritten into a different contract; instead, the new proposal is filed as docs/requirements/<new-slug>.md, and the old requirement’s front matter is updated to status: superseded with supersededBy: req:<new-slug>. | . | .

3733.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
3733.title: 2. Candidate methodologies: adopted vs rejected with reasons
3733.content: Following skills/process/process-core/methodology-adoption.md, we do not invent an unattributed house method. We adopt four orthogonal practices from the surveyed literature—naming their origins, what is taken, what is left behind, and how each binds into bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json and check:requirements—and we explicitly reject five candidate practices with documented reasons. 2.1 Adopted methodologies . M1 — Doorstop + MADR git-native file-per-requirement and two-level semantic identifiers (req:<slug> and req:<slug>#<key>) . | Origin: Doorstop (Browning & Adams 2014) for one-file-per-requirement in Git with YAML front matter + Markdown body; MADR (methodologies/madr.md) for human-readable <slug>.md filenames; RFC 2119 / RFC 8174 (methodologies/requirements-standards-assessment.md) for statement-level normative clauses. | What is adopted: . | Each filed requirement lives in its own Markdown file at docs/requirements/<slug>.md with id: req:<slug> matching its filename stem (^req:[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*$). | Individual normative clauses inside a requirement are declared in statements[] (key, modality, statement, successCriteria) and addressed as req:<slug>#<key> (^req:[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*#[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*$). | Across docs/proposals/ and docs/requirements/, every <slug> is globally unique: a slug exists either as an unshipped proposal in docs/proposals/<slug>.md or as a filed requirement in docs/requirements/<slug>.md, never both (check:requirements refuses a collision). | . | What is left behind and why: . | Doorstop’s auto-incremented numeric filenames (REQ001.yml, REQ002.yml) are left behind because concurrent feature branches in a multi-agent repository collide on sequential integers and opaque numbers hide meaning in prose and test logs. | Doorstop’s content-hash “fingerprint” clearing on whitespace edits is left behind because explicit lifecycle status + human requirement-signoff attestations (test/attestations/requirement-signoff/) provide stronger, semantically intentional governance than raw byte hashes. | . | . M2 — Faceted concern-group organisation (code-lists/concern-group.json) over flat docs/requirements/<slug>.md storage (Volere + IREB faceted view) . | Origin: Volere functional-area grouping (Robertson & Robertson) combined with IREB CPRE’s separation of stable storage identifiers from faceted navigation views (Pohl & Rupp), bound to the harness’s eight canonical concern groups in code-lists/concern-group.json. | What is adopted: . | Physical storage stays flat at docs/requirements/<slug>.md: Every filed requirement sits directly in docs/requirements/<slug>.md, preserving 1:1 path parity with docs/proposals/<slug>.md for git mv, keeping req:<slug> → docs/requirements/<slug>.md resolution O(1) without directory searches, and ensuring check:requirements (mdFilesIn) reads 100% of filed requirements. | Logical organisation in docs/requirements/index.md groups by two orthogonal views: . | By Concern Group (sdlc, process, tools, kg, library, content, ui, conduct from code-lists/concern-group.json), so a reader or agent working in a concern domain sees every in-force invariant governing that domain. | By Requirement Set (RequirementSet) and Lifecycle Status (in-force vs superseded / retired), so CRD baselines and historical records are cleanly separated from active invariants. | . | . | What is left behind and why: . | Physical subdirectory nesting (docs/requirements/<group>/<slug>.md) is rejected (see R3 below) so that reclassifying a requirement’s concern group or cross-cutting scope never breaks markdown links or requires a second git mv. | . | . M3 — ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 + IREB + W3C PROV-O three-axis bidirectional traceability . | Origin: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 Clause 5.2.7 (bidirectional traceability), IREB CPRE (backward / horizontal / forward trace links), and W3C PROV-O (library/w3c-2013-prov-o, methodologies/prov-o-provenance.md). | What is adopted: . | Backward traceability (to origin and parent sources): . | proposedIn: required on every requirement promoted from docs/proposals/<slug>.md (commit SHA + path: docs/proposals/<slug>.md), binding prov:wasDerivedFrom to the exact pre-move proposal revision. | derivedFrom: array of parent req:<slug> IDs or library/<bib-slug> L1 sources from which this requirement is derived (checked for existence and acyclicity by check:requirements). | . | Horizontal traceability (between peer requirements): . | dependsOn: array of req:<slug> IDs that this requirement relies on at runtime or design time (checked for existence by check:requirements). | . | Forward traceability (to work items, implementation, and verification): . | beans: work-plan work item IDs (folio-assistant-xxxx) that delivered or amended the requirement. | skills and processes: the Skill and Process (Process_*) nodes that implement the requirement. | Verification & Sign-off: test runs (test/runs/) and attestations (test/attestations/) citing req:<slug> or req:<slug>#<key>, plus RequirementSet membership and human sign-off attestations in test/attestations/requirement-signoff/<set-slug>.attestations.json. | . | . | . M4 — MADR / ISO 29148 immutable lifecycle for change, supersession, and retirement (proposed → in-force → superseded | retired) . | Origin: MADR 3.0.0 (methodologies/madr.md) and ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 Clause 6.5 configuration & change control. | What is adopted: . | Four lifecycle states (status in requirement.schema.json): . | proposed: drafted in docs/requirements/<slug>.md (or in a RequirementSet at draft / proposed / approved stage) awaiting final delivery and acceptance sign-off. | in-force: shipped, verified, and accepted by human BA/owner sign-off; actively binds the codebase and knowledge graph. | superseded: replaced by a newer requirement; must carry supersededBy: req:<new-slug> (enforced by requirement.schema.json allOf rule and check:requirements). | retired: no longer applicable (the feature or constraint was intentionally removed without replacement); supersededBy is omitted, and the retirement rationale and authorising issue/bean are recorded in the document body. | . | Change decision rule (Amendment in place vs Supersession): . | In-scope amendment (edit in place, keep req:<slug>): When clarifying prose, adding a statements[] sub-clause, tightening a successCriteria check, or updating skills/processes/beans links without reversing the core invariant, edit docs/requirements/<slug>.md in place and record a fresh requirement-signoff attestation if its RequirementSet is approved or accepted. | Scope-reversing replacement (file req:<new-slug>, mark old superseded): When a new proposal reverses or fundamentally replaces an in-force requirement’s contract, file the new proposal at docs/requirements/<new-slug>.md (status: in-force, derivedFrom: [req:<old-slug>]), and update docs/requirements/<old-slug>.md to status: superseded with supersededBy: req:<new-slug>. | . | Set membership consistency: Because check:requirements enforces that an approved or accepted RequirementSet may only contain in-force (or proposed at approved stage) members, superseding or retiring a requirement requires updating any RequirementSet that lists it (replacing the old ID with req:<new-slug> or removing the retired ID under a re-signed set amendment). | . | . 2.2 Rejected candidate methodologies (with reasons) . | Candidate methodology | Verdict | Reason for rejection in this harness | . | R1 — IEEE Std 830-1998 monolithic SRS & positional section numbering (§3.2.1.4) | Rejected | Tying a requirement’s identifier to its outline position in a single monolithic file causes cascading renumbering whenever a section is inserted, split, or reordered. Renumbering breaks req: URIs in test runs, attestations, and work items, and a single monolithic SRS file creates constant Git merge conflicts across parallel agent branches. | . | R2 — Centralised sequential integer IDs (REQ-0001, FR-0042) | Rejected | In a distributed multi-agent Git workflow (worktrees, branches, subagents), two branches filing requirements concurrently will allocate the same next integer (REQ-0043) unless gated by an external lock server. Even when unique, opaque integers convey no domain meaning in test logs or prose compared to req:<slug>#<key>. (Note: FR-NNN may still appear as a local table label inside a single CRD proposal during discussion, but the canonical graph identifier is req:<slug>#<key>.) | . | R3 — Physical subdirectory sharding (docs/requirements/<group>/<slug>.md) | Rejected (kept as faceted index view in docs/requirements/index.md instead) | 1. check:requirements (scripts/check-requirements.ts, mdFilesIn) scans docs/requirements/ and docs/proposals/ non-recursively and enforces a 1:1 slug namespace between docs/proposals/<slug>.md and docs/requirements/<slug>.md.2. Many proposals span multiple concern groups (e.g., sdlc + process); forcing a single directory path would make paths brittle when concern boundaries evolve.3. Faceted grouping in docs/requirements/index.md delivers the navigational benefit of Volere/concern-group organisation with zero path churn. | . | R4 — ReqIF XML / OSLC RM RDF triples as the primary authored store | Rejected (consistent with requirements-standards-assessment.md) | XML UUID graphs and raw RDF triples are unreadable in GitHub PR reviews and cannot be naturally co-authored as prose + front matter by humans and agents. Our YAML front matter (bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json) exports cleanly to JSON-LD (bootstrap/ns.jsonld) without burdening authors with XML. | . | R5 — Destructive deletion (git rm) of superseded or retired requirements | Rejected | Deleting docs/requirements/<slug>.md when a requirement is retired or superseded breaks historical provenance: past test/runs/, test/attestations/, beans/, and derivedFrom links would become dangling references. Keeping the file in docs/requirements/<slug>.md with status: superseded (supersededBy: req:<new-slug>) or status: retired preserves referential integrity across the graph. | .

3734.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
3734.title: 3. Proposed filing process (sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn)
3734.content: To fulfil Criterion 3 of work item folio-assistant-qh1s (“a filing PROCESS proposed as BPMN, to be put to the owner before it is built”), the executable BPMN diagram sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn (Process_RequirementsFiling) models the end-to-end process for filing, organising,superseding, or retiring a requirement in docs/requirements/. 3.1 Where Process_RequirementsFiling sits in the lifecycle . In the CRDM lifecycle (skills/process/crdm/crdm-requirements-workflow.md): . | Phases 1–4 (crdm-needs.bpmn, crdm-requirements-definition.bpmn, crdm-data-model.bpmn, crdm-signoff.bpmn) produce and sign off a proposal in docs/proposals/<slug>.md (and optionally a RequirementSet moving from draft → proposed → approved). | Phase 5 (crdm-deliver.bpmn) builds and verifies the MVP in code, skills, and processes. | At Phase 6 (crdm-close.bpmn), when the feature ships and stakeholders/BA confirm acceptance criteria are met, Process_RequirementsFiling (sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn) governs the transition of the proposal into docs/requirements/<slug>.md (or the amendment, supersession, or retirement of an existing filed requirement). | . 3.2 Lanes and responsibilities . | Lane | Role (partitionElementRef) | Responsibility in Process_RequirementsFiling | . | BA / Feature Requestor (Lane_BA) | business-analyst | Reviews the filed requirement’s organisation, traceability links, normative statements, and any supersession/retirement transition (BA_ReviewFiling), and issues the human sign-off decision (approve, amend, reject, defer, cancel) required by check:requirements before a RequirementSet can reach accepted. | . | Authoring Agent (Lane_Agent) | authoring-agent | Executes the deterministic filing steps: classifies the requirement’s concern group and filing mode (A_ClassifyFiling), moves or updates the file in docs/requirements/<slug>.md (A_PromoteOrUpdate), binds the Requirement front matter (A_BindFrontMatter), updates superseded/retired records (A_UpdateLifecycle), indexes the requirement in docs/requirements/index.md (A_UpdateIndex), runs check:requirements (A_RunCheck), and records the human sign-off attestation (A_RecordFilingSignoff). | . 3.3 Step-by-step walkthrough of sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn . | A_ClassifyFiling — Classify filing mode, concern group, and req:<slug> identifier (skill: crdm-requirements-workflow): . | Determine which of the three filing modes applies: . | New filing from proposal: promoting docs/proposals/<slug>.md → docs/requirements/<slug>.md. | In-place amendment or supersession: amending an existing docs/requirements/<slug>.md or superseding req:<old-slug> with req:<new-slug>. | Retirement: retiring an obsolete docs/requirements/<slug>.md (status: retired). | . | Assign the primary concern group from code-lists/concern-group.json (sdlc, process, tools, kg, library, content, ui, conduct) for indexing in docs/requirements/index.md. | . | GW_FilingMode — Which filing transition? (cat-harness.processes:judgement): . | Branches on the three modes: promote (from docs/proposals/<slug>.md), amend-or-supersede (on an existing requirement), or retire (marking an active requirement retired). | . | A_PromoteOrUpdate — git mv proposal to docs/requirements/<slug>.md and capture proposedIn (skill: crdm-requirements-workflow): . | On the promote branch, record the pre-move commit SHA (git log -1 --format=%H -- docs/proposals/<slug>.md), execute git mv docs/proposals/<slug>.md docs/requirements/<slug>.md so Git history stays unbroken, and populate proposedIn: { commit, path: "docs/proposals/<slug>.md" }. | . | A_BindFrontMatter — Bind Requirement front matter, statements, and 3-axis lineage (skill: specification-management): . | Validate or author the YAML front matter against bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json: . | id: req:<slug>, title, status: in-force (or proposed prior to acceptance sign-off); | statements[] with stable #<key>, RFC 2119 modality (MUST / SHOULD / MAY), normative statement, and measurable successCriteria; | Backward lineage (proposedIn, derivedFrom), horizontal dependencies (dependsOn), and forward implementation links (beans, skills, processes). | . | . | A_UpdateLifecycle — Update superseded or retired requirement records and RequirementSet membership (skill: specification-management): . | When superseding req:<old-slug> or retiring a requirement, set status: superseded + supersededBy: req:<new-slug> (or status: retired with retirement rationale in prose) on the old file without deleting it, and update any RequirementSet in docs/requirements/*.set.json so no approved/accepted set retains a non-in-force member. | . | A_UpdateIndex — Organise entry in docs/requirements/index.md under its concern group and status (skill: crdm-requirements-workflow): . | Add or update the requirement’s row in docs/requirements/index.md under its code-lists/concern-group.json section (for in-force requirements) or the Superseded and Retired Requirements archive table, and regenerate directory READMEs (subgraph-readmes.ts). | . | A_RunCheck — Run check:requirements gate (skill: specification-management): . | Execute bun run cat check:requirements to verify schema validity, slug uniqueness across docs/proposals/ and docs/requirements/, derivedFrom acyclicity, resolution of all derivedFrom / dependsOn / supersededBy / skills / processes references, and RequirementSet invariants. | . | GW_CheckPassed — Does check:requirements pass?: . | If fail, loop back to A_BindFrontMatter to fix schema, collision, or broken-link findings before asking a human reviewer. | If pass, proceed to BA_ReviewFiling. | . | BA_ReviewFiling — BA / Owner reviews filed requirement, organisation, and sign-off (calledElement: Process_Adjudication, skill: adjudication, fulfilment: person): . | The Business Analyst / Owner reviews the filed requirement, its concern-group placement in docs/requirements/index.md, its traceability links, and its verification evidence, deciding approve, amend, reject, defer, or cancel (adjudication-requirement-set). | . | A_RecordFilingSignoff — Record requirement-signoff attestation and set stage (skill: adjudication): . | Append the human decision to test/attestations/requirement-signoff/<set-slug>.attestations.json and update the RequirementSet stage (accepted on approval). | . | GW_FilingAccepted — Filing accepted?: . | approve / amend → End_RequirementFiled (“Requirement filed and indexed in docs/requirements/”). | reject / defer / cancel → End_FilingHeld (“Filing held or deferred — recorded with reason”). | . | . 3.4 Open design choices put to the owner before automation is built . Before any new CLI subcommand or schema extension is built on top of check:requirements, the following three design choices from this proposal are put to the owner: . | Concern-group tagging — index-only vs schema field: . | Option A (current zero-schema-change baseline): Keep bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json unchanged (additionalProperties: false) and organise requirements by concern group in docs/requirements/index.md. | Option B (optional schema field): Add an optional "concernGroup" (or "concerns": string[] referencing code-lists/concern-group.json) to bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json so docs/requirements/index.md can be generated deterministically from front matter. | . | Enforcing in-force dependency health in check:requirements: . | Today check:requirements verifies that every dependsOn and derivedFrom target exists. Should check:requirements also fail (or warn) when an in-force requirement dependsOn a requirement whose status is retired or superseded? | . | Standalone requirement sign-off vs RequirementSet sign-off: . | Today test/attestations/requirement-signoff/<set-slug>.attestations.json attaches to a RequirementSet (*.set.json), and a standalone docs/requirements/<slug>.md promoted via git mv only needs proposedIn. Should every filed requirement belong to a concern-group RequirementSet (docs/requirements/<group>.set.json), or remain standalone unless grouped by a CRD? | . | .
