Like raci it answers who, never what or whether — a one-off choice among options is kepner-tregoe, a recurring rule is dmn, certainty of evidence is grade, the record of a decision is madr, situation analysis is swot. | cited, not ingested | cat-harness | . | Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing processrequirements-filing-and-organisation | Filing a requirement from docs/proposals/.md into docs/requirements/.md, organising filed requirements by concern group, assigning collision-free identifiers (req: and req:#), recording bidirectional traceability (derivedFrom, dependsOn, verification), and governing requirement change, supersession, or retirement | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirementrequirements-standards-assessment | Evaluating how requirements authored or verified in the harness map to or from open industry standards, interchange formats, statement grammars, and quality models — and deciding which transformations belong in higher harness layers (cat-harness, and content layers above it) while keeping the bootstrap Requirement schema strictly self-contained and free of external dependencies. It answers how bootstrap requirements translate to ReqIF, OSLC-RM, EARS, ISO 29148, and ISO 25010, what each standard costs in serialization and semantic complexity, and where mapping adapters must live. It does NOT govern runtime execution logs (prov-o-provenance), decision table structures (dmn), software package bills of materials (spdx-3), or access policy enforcement (odrl-policies). | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | Skill-pipeline subject indexing — one policy-grounded stage per cognitive step, each output inspectableskill-pipeline-subject-indexing | Assigning terms from a closed, rule-governed controlled vocabulary to a work: deciding what it is about and saying so in the vocabulary’s own authorised form. Use it when the vocabulary comes with a written policy manual (LCSH has the Subject Headings Manual; MeSH, AAT and FAST are the source’s own named candidates) and an authority file that can be queried, and a wrong but plausible term would be acted on in cataloguing, retrieval or linking. It answers how to produce the assignment. It does not answer how to tell whether an assignment is good: that is consensus-grounded-subject-evaluation, which is a parallel node and is not folded into this one. Not for choosing between options (kepner-tregoe), a recurring decision rule (dmn), or making a model emit a rule instead of a result (hybrid-llm-deterministic); §”Against hybrid-llm-deterministic” explains why the last is a separate method and not this one’s parent. Not for free keywording with no vocabulary to validate against, because the authority step is what the method rests on. | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | SPDX 3 — a bill of materials as a graph of elements, for what crosses a trust boundaryspdx-3 | Describing an artefact that LEAVES this repository so that a party who does not run our tooling can check what is in it, what it depends on, under which licences, and that it arrived intact — a release, a signed package, a published layer’s dependency set, the licences of what we redistribute. It answers what is this, what is it made of, who supplied it, under what licence, with what known vulnerabilities. It does NOT answer what happened inside the repository or who answers for it (prov-o-provenance), what an actor may do (odrl-policies), how a node is serialised internally (json-ld-serialisation), or whether a block passed its QA criteria (the house QA schemas; see §”What it refuses”). | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | Specification-compiled agents — the control flow comes from the diagram, not from the model’s planspecification-compiled-agents | A process is already written down as a diagram, and something must now EXECUTE it. Use it when the control flow is external and authored — a BPMN process, a DMN table, a pipeline someone drew — and the question is how an LLM should act inside it. It answers where the plan comes from, never what the plan should be: authoring the diagram is bpmn-authoring, deciding a branch from a table is dmn, and choosing between options is kepner-tregoe. Its companion is hybrid-llm-deterministic, and the two are the same shape at different grains: that one has the model emit a RULE that machinery validates and runs; this one has the model act inside a CONTROL GRAPH that machinery derived from a specification. Reach for this one when the artefact that constrains the model already exists as a diagram. Do NOT reach for it where no specification exists, or where the process is genuinely open-ended. The paper’s own evaluation is scoped to deterministic workflows and says so; a setting with ambiguity, stochasticity or open-ended human decision-making is outside what it measured, and outside what this node claims. | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | SWOT — situation analysis over internal and external factorsswot | Situation analysis, before a decision — never instead of one. Use it to assemble what is true about a subject’s internal attributes and its external environment, when the point is to see the field whole rather than to choose between candidate options. Not for choosing: a one-off choice among options is kepner-tregoe, a recurring rule is dmn, certainty of evidence behind a health recommendation is grade, and the record of whatever is decided is madr. SWOT produces the INPUT to those; it is not a substitute for any of them. | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | WireGen: wireframing from a written design intentwiregen | Designing a USER INTERFACE, for example a page layout, a navigation scheme or a visualiser, where the choice between candidate designs has to be reviewed and, when reviewers disagree, adjudicated. It is a design-generation and design-evaluation method. It does not choose between non-UI options (use the decision-analysis methodology) or grade evidence. It does not by itself settle a disagreement: that is adjudication. | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | . | Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — trust is never granted implicitly, it is evaluated per request at a decision pointzero-trust-architecture | A participant is about to act on something another participant gave it, and the question is whether to trust it. That covers an access decision at a boundary, a hand-over between agents, a tool or a dependency graph reaching this platform, and the design of a check that decides any of these. It answers how trust is decided: never by location, per request, by policy, at a named decision and enforcement point. It is NOT a method for choosing among options (kepner-tregoe), for recording a decision (madr), for a recurring business rule (dmn), or for who is involved (raci). It is also not a threat-modelling or risk-scoring method: it says where trust is decided, not how likely an attack is. | citation does not resolve | cat-harness | .

3843.title: Where each one came from
3843.content: The three states are different facts and are kept apart deliberately. Source held means an evidence: reference resolves to a document in a declared library — you can open it from this checkout. Cited, not ingested means the node names an origin and nobody has fetched it; that is an open question, reported by check:methodology-evidence and gated by nothing. Citation does not resolve is neither: the node claims a source and the slug names nothing, which reads as evidence in every listing and is strictly worse than declaring none. Adequacy-for-purpose modelling — a model is judged against what it is FOR, not against reality . adequacy-for-purpose-modelling — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. A formal model is being built, and somebody will later ask whether it is right. Use it when the artefact is a mathematical model of a process — agents, action and reward spaces, update rules — and the question is what the model is allowed to claim. It answers what would count as this model succeeding, and nothing else. Reach for it BEFORE the model is written, because its whole force is that the purpose is declared first and the evaluation follows from it. Reaching for it afterwards turns it into a defence of whatever the model happens to do. Do NOT reach for it to choose between options (kepner-tregoe), to grade evidence, to settle a recurring rule (dmn), or to pick an algorithm (probabilistic-decision-analysis, mcdm-aggregation). It is not a decision method at all: it is a rule for judging a model, and it is filed here because methodology-adoption routes “how do we evaluate X” to a methodology node. Origin. Kavya Ravichandran, “Algorithmic Approaches to Sequential Decision-Making and Social Epistemology”, PhD thesis, Toyota Technological Institute at Chicago, August 2026; arXiv:2607.20636v1 [cs.DS], 22 July 2026. Chapter 5, “Why Algorithmic Approaches” — an essay inside the thesis rather than a result of it. Open access, ingested whole. The view it builds on is Wendy Parker’s (2020) “adequacy-for-purpose”, quoted directly in that chapter; the how-possibly / how-actually distinction is from the philosophy-of-explanation literature the chapter cites, and the confirmatory / applied prediction split is Elliott-Graves’. Ravichandran’s contribution adopted here is the ORDERED three-purpose taxonomy and the evaluation rule that follows from it. The method, as extracted: read it . Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/arxiv-2607.20636v1 | . Automatic term extraction — propose candidate terms from prose, rank them, and let a person decide . automatic-term-extraction — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Finding which words and phrases in a body of prose are the TERMS of its domain, so that a glossary can be proposed from the text rather than typed from memory. It answers which strings are candidate terms, ranked. Every output is a candidate: a person decides what is a term and writes its definition (glossary-terms: an extractor writes candidate, only a person moves one to authored). Not for assigning terms from a closed controlled vocabulary (skill-pipeline-subject-indexing), not for keywords that summarise one document against the others (lsi, correspondence-analysis, the keyword graph), and not for reading definitions a source already states in its own glossary section, which are copied verbatim and need no extraction. Origin. Automatic term extraction (ATE) as surveyed by Hanh Thi Hong Tran, Matej Martinc, Jaya Caporusso, Antoine Doucet and Senja Pollak, “The Recent Advances in Automatic Term Extraction: A survey” (arXiv:2301.06767v1, CC BY 4.0), ingested whole and read. The C-value measure for nested multi-word units is Katerina T. Frantzi and Sophia Ananiadou, “Extracting Nested Collocations”, COLING 1996 (ACL Anthology C96-1009, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0), ingested whole and read; its equations were checked against the printed page, because the Anthology’s own text layer is a poor OCR. The later C-value/NC-value papers that apply the measure to terms (Frantzi, Ananiadou & Tsujii 1998; Frantzi, Ananiadou & Mima 2000) are not open access and are not held. The method, as extracted: read it . Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/arxiv-2301.06767v1 | library/frantzi-ananiadou-1996-c-value | . Consensus-grounded subject evaluation — independent indexers as the answer key, and a panel instead of one score . consensus-grounded-subject-evaluation — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Judging how good a set of controlled-vocabulary assignments is, when qualified people would themselves disagree about the exact answer. Use it to evaluate a subject-indexing system, compare two of them, or decide whether one is good enough to draft for a human reviewer. It is also for any labelling task whose gold standard is expert judgement with a subjective surface. It answers how to measure. It does not answer how to produce the assignment, which is skill-pipeline-subject-indexing, a parallel node. Not for certainty of evidence behind a recommendation (grade), and not for choosing among options (kepner-tregoe). Not applicable where the answer is decidable, meaning a single correct output a checker can verify, because then there is no disagreement for a consensus to absorb. Origin. Kwok Leong Tang, “LCSHBench: A Multilingual, Consensus-Grounded Benchmark for Library of Congress Subject Heading Assignment” (arXiv:2606.04382v1), 2026. Open access, ingested whole and read before this node was written. The method is rendered from that paper. The parallel design it is contrasted with is the one used by the shared task the other ingested subject-indexing papers were entered in: D’Souza, Sadruddin, Israel, Begoin & Slawig, “SemEval-2025 Task 5: LLMs4Subjects — LLM-based Automated Subject Tagging for a National Technical Library’s Open-Access Catalog” (arXiv:2504.07199v3), TIB Hannover. It was ingested and read too, so that design is described from its own text. The method, as extracted: read it . Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/arxiv-2606.04382v1 | library/arxiv-2504.07199v3 | . Correspondence analysis for retrieval — decompose the departure from independence, not the counts . correspondence-analysis — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. The same question as lsi — which units of a prose graph are close in what they are about — when the answer must not be dominated by how LONG a unit is or how COMMON a term is. CA removes those margins by construction, so it is the method to reach for when LSI’s first dimensions are margins (a first dimension with no negative pole) or when the question is which units are UNUSUAL — outlier pages, specimen text, a list among prose. It answers which units have similar term profiles, relative to independence. Like lsi, every output is a PROPOSAL. Not for choosing between the two methods by blending them (methodology-adoption §”Parallel, not composable”), not for a controlled vocabulary (skill-pipeline-subject-indexing), and not for any decision. Origin. Correspondence analysis is Jean-Paul Benzécri’s (L’Analyse des Données, 1973) and is set out in Michael Greenacre, Theory and Applications of Correspondence Analysis (Academic Press, 1984) and Correspondence Analysis in Practice (3rd ed., 2017). Its application to information retrieval, and the comparison with latent semantic analysis this node rests on, is Qianqian Qi, David J. Hessen and Peter G. M. van der Heijden, “Improving information retrieval through correspondence analysis instead of latent semantic analysis”, Journal of Intelligent Information Systems (2023), doi:10.1007/s10844-023-00815-y — open access, ingested whole and read. The method, as extracted: read it . Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/qi-hessen-vanderheijden-2023-ca-vs-lsa | . Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) — process-centric requirements engineering and harness adaptation . crdm — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Eliciting, structuring, prioritising, and validating functional and non-functional requirements from current-state and redesigned business processes before implementation begins. Use it when a capability, specification, or workflow spans actors and tasks that must be analysed and redesigned first so every requirement traces to a concrete business activity. Not a replacement for filing and lifecycle governance (requirements-filing-and-organisation), interchange standards mapping (requirements-standards-assessment), one-off option trade-offs (kepner-tregoe), recurring decision logic (dmn), or architecture decision records (madr). Origin. Public Health Informatics Institute (PHII, a program of The Task Force for Global Health), “Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM): A Collaborative Approach to Public Health Systems” (2021, updated 2023-08-29, https://phii.org/crdm/) and companion EHR Toolkit guide “5. Analyzing Technical Options: Defining and Validating System Requirements Guide” (2016/2021, https://phii.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Defining-and-Validating-Requirements-Guide_0.pdf); applied to health information systems in PATH & PHII, “Common Requirements for Maternal Health Information Systems: Produced with the Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology” (December 2012, https://media.path.org/documents/MCHN_mhis_crdm.pdf); combined in the harness’s requirement statement template with IETF BCP 14 / RFC 2119 (Bradner 1997) and RFC 8174 (Leiba 2017) for normative conformance keywords. The method, as extracted: read it . Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/phii-2023-crdm | library/phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide | library/path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm | library/rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels | library/rfc8174-uppercase-vs-lowercase-2119-key-words | . DMN — Decision Model and Notation . dmn — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. The criteria RECUR and the inputs are data. A gateway that must branch the same way on the same facts every time. Not for a one-off judgement — that is kepner-tregoe, recorded per madr. Origin. Object Management Group, Decision Model and Notation (DMN) Version 1.5, OMG document formal/24-01-01, January 2024 (omg.org/spec/DMN). RECORDED, not held: its licence forbids posting copies on a network, so the library entry identifies the exact PDF (sha256) and its outline and holds no text. The method, as extracted: read it . Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/omg-2024-dmn-1-5 | library/arxiv-1603.07466v1 | library/djurica-2024-decision-model-comprehension-emisa | library/hasic-2018-5pdm-decision-intelligence | library/hasic-2019-complexity-metrics-dmn | . Doc-Researcher — parse for multiple granularities, then research iteratively against a sufficiency threshold . doc-researcher — declared by folio-assistant-core — citation does not resolve . Applies when. A question must be answered from documents this folio has ingested, and one retrieval pass will not do it. Use it when the answer is spread across several documents, or across text and figures within one, or when the asker will follow up. It answers how to search a corpus you already hold, never what to hold — library-ingestion and the L1 completeness gate answer that, and this method assumes their output. Do NOT reach for it for a single lookup in a known document. The loop below costs iterations, and a method whose cheapest path is more expensive than reading the page is the wrong method. Origin. Kuicai Dong, Shurui Huang, Fangda Ye, Wei Han, Zhi Zhang, Dexun Li, Wenjun Li, Qu Yang, Gang Wang, Yichao Wang, Chen Zhang and Yong Liu, “Doc-Researcher: A Unified System for Multimodal Document Parsing and Deep Research” (arXiv:2510.21603v1, Huawei Technologies, 24 October 2025). Open access. THE PRIMARY IS HELD AND PROMOTED, at library/arxiv-2510.21603v1, which is what evidence: below points at. It was staged and unpromotable for a day: the extractor reported 383 images, 335 of them on page 3, and its image-descriptions requirement could not be met. It holds fifty. See §”What this checkout holds” — the first reading of those 383 was wrong, and the correction is kept there rather than tidied away. It is a SYSTEM paper reporting one implementation against a benchmark its own authors built, so what is adopted below is the METHOD, and §”Where this rendering stops” says which parts were left behind. The method, as extracted: read it . Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/arxiv-2510.21603v1 | . Hybrid LLM/deterministic — the model proposes a RULE, machinery validates and runs it . hybrid-llm-deterministic — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. An agent must produce an artefact that something downstream will act on. Use it when a language model is in the loop and a wrong output would be acted on rather than merely read — a schema, a mapping, a classification, a branch, a judgement. It answers how to get the output safely, never which option to choose: a one-off choice among options is kepner-tregoe, a recurring rule is dmn, certainty of evidence is grade, the record of a decision is madr, who is involved is raci, and situation analysis is swot. Those pick an answer; this one constrains how an answer is produced. Not applicable where no model is involved, and unnecessary where the output is only ever read by a person who will notice it is wrong. Origin. Felix Neubauer, Jürgen Pleiss and Benjamin Uekermann, “AI-assisted JSON Schema Creation and Mapping” (arXiv:2508.05192v2), University of Stuttgart. The authors’ own word for it is a “hybrid approach that combines large language models (LLMs) with deterministic techniques”. Open access, read whole and ingested here — unlike most nodes in this graph, the primary IS held. It is a tool paper reporting one implementation (MetaConfigurator), so what is adopted below is the METHOD it generalises, and §”Where this rendering stops” says which parts were left behind. The method, as extracted: read it . Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/arxiv-2508.05192v2 | . JSON-LD 1.1 — the knowledge graph serialised as Linked Data in plain JSON . json-ld-serialisation — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Choosing how a node of the knowledge graph is written to disk or published, so that it is ordinary JSON to a reader with no RDF tooling and RDF to one with it. Use it when adding a generated .jsonld sibling, a term to a published @context, a prefix, or a new exported document. It answers how a node is identified, typed and linked in the serialisation. It does NOT answer what a node means (that is the vocabulary and the schemas), whether a relation is true (uses-editorial-review), or how a table is modelled (CSVW, bound as a vocabulary, not a serialisation). Origin. W3C, “JSON-LD 1.1 — A JSON-based Serialization for Linked Data”, W3C Recommendation 16 July 2020 (https://www.w3.org/TR/2020/REC-json-ld11-20200716/), editors Gregg Kellogg, Pierre-Antoine Champin and Dave Longley; produced by the JSON-LD Working Group. Held as the Working Group’s own publication snapshot of the REC (github.com/w3c/json-ld-syntax, commit 029777cf), under the W3C Software and Document License. The companion Recommendations — JSON-LD 1.1 Processing Algorithms and API, and JSON-LD 1.1 Framing — are NOT held. The method, as extracted: read it . Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/w3c-2020-json-ld-1-1 | . Kepner-Tregoe Decision Analysis . kepner-tregoe — declared by cat-harness — cited, not ingested . Applies when. A decision with several candidate options and no recurring rule — a platform choice, an architecture question, which of three fixes to take. Contextual, not default: if the criteria recur, use dmn; if the question is certainty of evidence for a recommendation, use grade. Origin. Charles H. Kepner and Benjamin B. Tregoe, The Rational Manager (1965); The New Rational Manager (1981) . The method, as extracted: read it . No ingested source. The origin above names one; nothing in this checkout holds it. literature-search is the skill that closes one of these. L1 publication coverage — the report contract . l1-coverage — declared by folio-assistant-core — cited, not ingested . Applies when. An L1 extraction of a publication has been made and must be shown not to have dropped anything normative. Use it to say what a coverage report must contain and what its numbers mean, so two tools’ reports compare and a reviewer knows what was counted. The skill l1-coverage runs it. Origin. The coverage contract written for folio-assistant#2406 (FR-009) as docs/COVERAGE.md in litlfred/smart-kg (main, 0e11ce1), the L1 type graph’s repository. smart-kg was deprecated on 2026-10-16 and its schema moved to the WHO SMART layer that mounts this one; this layer, which implements the check, took the contract with it (folio-assistant#3108). Substance unchanged: the marker list (§1) and the exclusion reasons (§2) are as written there. The method, as extracted: read it . No ingested source. The origin above names one; nothing in this checkout holds it. literature-search is the skill that closes one of these. Latent Semantic Indexing — retrieve and relate by co-occurrence structure, not by shared words . lsi — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. Finding or relating units of text that discuss the same thing in different words, across a corpus too large to read whole, where no controlled vocabulary has been assigned. Use it to ask “what else in this graph is about this?”, to propose a home for an unfiled item among existing groups, to find near-duplicates, and to surface clusters nobody named. It answers which units are close in co-occurrence structure. It does NOT answer whether a unit is relevant, correct, or a dependency: every output is a PROPOSAL a person or an agent confirms. Not for assigning terms from a controlled vocabulary (skill-pipeline-subject-indexing), not for judging an assignment (consensus-grounded-subject-evaluation), and not for any decision (kepner-tregoe, dmn). Origin. Scott Deerwester, Susan T. Dumais, George W. Furnas, Thomas K. Landauer and Richard A. Harshman, “Indexing by Latent Semantic Analysis”, Journal of the American Society for Information Science 41(6):391–407 (1990), for the method. Susan T. Dumais, “Improving the retrieval of information from external sources”, Behavior Research Methods, Instruments & Computers 23(2):229–236 (1991), for the log-entropy term weighting. Michael W. Berry, Susan T. Dumais and Gavin W. O’Brien, “Using Linear Algebra for Intelligent Information Retrieval”, SIAM Review 37(4):573–595 (1995), for folding-in and updating. Thomas K. Landauer, Peter W. Foltz and Darrell Laham, “An Introduction to Latent Semantic Analysis”, Discourse Processes 25:259–284 (1998), and Thomas K. Landauer and Susan T. Dumais, “A Solution to Plato’s Problem”, Psychological Review 104(2):211–240 (1997), for the cognitive reading of the same computation (there called LSA), which this node does NOT adopt. Nathan Halko, Per-Gunnar Martinsson and Joel A. Tropp, “Finding Structure with Randomness”, SIAM Review 53(2):217–288 (2011; arXiv:0909.4061v2), for the randomized SVD this platform computes it with — an implementation source, not part of the method. The method, as extracted: read it . Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/deerwester-1990-indexing-by-lsa | library/landauer-foltz-laham-1998-intro-lsa | library/arxiv-0909.4061v2 | library/qi-hessen-vanderheijden-2023-ca-vs-lsa | library/arxiv-2202.02427v1 | . MADR — Markdown Architectural Decision Records . madr — declared by cat-harness — cited, not ingested . Applies when. Bean context — the owner’s binding, 2026-09-20. When a bean records a decision, this is the form. Not for the decision METHOD (see kepner-tregoe) and not for a recurring rule (see dmn). Origin. Michael Nygard, “Documenting Architecture Decisions” (2011), for the ADR form; MADR (github.com/adr/madr) for the Markdown template with an explicit Considered-Options section. The method, as extracted: read it . No ingested source. The origin above names one; nothing in this checkout holds it. literature-search is the skill that closes one of these. Aggregation-type MCDM — an alternatives-criteria matrix collapsed to one score per alternative . mcdm-aggregation — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. A FIXED, FINITE set of alternatives is to be ranked against several explicit criteria, all known up front. The input is an alternatives-criteria matrix: every alternative scored on every criterion, with weights obtainable. The output is a ranking. Use it when the decision is made ONCE, from data already in hand. Choose within the family by what you can supply. SAW and MEW need only weights and normalised scores. AHP needs pairwise comparisons, which grow as the square of the criteria count, and gives a consistency ratio in return. ANP needs those plus the interdependence structure, and is the only member that admits feedback between criteria. COPRAS, MOORA, FUCA and WASPAS sit between SAW and AHP in what they ask for. Do NOT reach for it when the alternatives are explored REPEATEDLY and information accrues as you go — that is probabilistic-decision-analysis. Do not use it for a recurring rule (dmn), for a decision whose criteria are MUSTs and WANTs rather than weighted scores (kepner-tregoe), or for grading evidence. It also assumes the criteria set is complete: a criterion nobody wrote down is weighted zero, silently. Origin. Zhiyuan Wang (Singapore University of Social Sciences) and Gade Pandu Rangaiah (National University of Singapore; Vellore Institute of Technology), “Multi-Criteria Decision-Making: Aggregation-Type Methods”, Chapter 8 of a forthcoming volume; arXiv:2509.06388v1, 2026. The copy ingested is the authors’ preliminary draft manuscript, produced in Word and carrying no arXiv stamp, headed “Preliminary Draft Manuscript” and paginated 8-1 onward. _pdf_doc_id.py reads the arXiv id off page one’s text layer, so this copy derived no arxiv- slug and fell back to the basename. Filed instead under the author-year convention the repository’s other non-arXiv entries use (owner, 2026-09-29), which is why the bib-slug and the citation differ: cite arXiv:2509.06388v1; the slug is a filing key and nothing more. The method, as extracted: read it . Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/wang-rangaiah-2026-mcdm-aggregation | . ODRL 2.2 — what a party may do, as permission and prohibition rules over actions . odrl-policies — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. What an actor may DO — may this party perform this action, here? Use it when a grant or a refusal has to be written down so a machine can evaluate it: who holds an action, scoped to a process, a task or a role, and which broader action it falls under. It answers permit, deny or nobody has said. It does NOT answer who is involved in an activity (raci), which lane an actor may act in (role-model), or how a decision is reached (kepner-tregoe, dmn). It is not used here for source licences, which are recorded as SPDX ids in each library entry’s licence.json. Origin. W3C, “ODRL Information Model 2.2”, W3C Recommendation 15 February 2018, edited by Renato Iannella and Serena Villata, produced by the W3C Permissions and Obligations Expression Working Group. The held copy is the Working Group’s own staged REC snapshot (github.com/w3c/poe), not compared byte for byte with the w3.org copy and without later errata — see the entry’s licence.json. The companion “ODRL Vocabulary & Expression 2.2”, which the model defers to for normative serialisation and the Common Vocabulary, is NOT held. The method, as extracted: read it . Cited sources — at least one does not resolve: . | library/w3c-2018-odrl-model-2-2 | . Probabilistic decision-making algorithms — and what their regret bounds are claims ABOUT . probabilistic-decision-analysis — declared by cat-harness — citation does not resolve . Applies when. The alternatives can be TRIED, repeatedly, and what you learn from one try changes what you should try next. Bandits, Bayesian optimisation and tree search all live here. The defining features are that the alternative set is sampled rather than scored, that information is gathered adaptively, and that each trial costs something — the monograph’s motivating setting is scientific discovery, “where experiments are costly”. Reach for it also when the question is not which algorithm to run but what an existing bound entitles anyone to say: the monograph is an analysis text first, so it is the right source for reading a regret guarantee rather than quoting one. Do NOT reach for it for a one-shot choice from a fixed matrix — that is mcdm-aggregation — nor for a recurring rule (dmn), a MUST/WANT decision (kepner-tregoe), or grading evidence. And do not reach for it when you cannot actually run the alternatives: adaptivity is the whole premise, and without it every guarantee in the book is vacuous. Origin. A monograph, open access, ingested whole. Its stated aim is accessibility: “theoretical analyses in the literature are often inaccessible to non-experts”, and it assumes only basic probability and statistics plus some Gaussian processes. 3937.title: Write one JSON-LD node per IG artefact, and check a built site’s nodes
3937.content: write turns an artefact index into artifact/<Type>-<id>.jsonld under a docs root, with no .json twin: one folio-ig-artifact-jsonld/v1 node per artefact, in borrowed vocabularies only (the FHIR RDF class, dcterms, schema.org, PROV), naming the artefact’s canonical URL, its representations and, for a compiled copy, what built it. With --root-resources (the IG site’s default) the first representation is the reduced <Type>-<id>.json the site serves at its root (local), the second the full copy in the AST cache by raw URL (mirror), and each index entry names the root file (schema:contentUrl). check is the kind’s QA: over a BUILT site, every artefact has its node and no node is an orphan, each node is its own file’s, no .json twin is served beside it, and every local resource it names is on the site. It also writes and checks the index node, artifact/index.jsonld (folio-ig-artifact-index-jsonld/v1): every artefact once, each entry naming its node. 3938.title: Skills it satisfies
3938.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. ig-build-pipeline . The bare FHIR IG pipeline — FSH to SUSHI to the IG Publisher to a pages branch, with no pre-processing and no post-processing. What this layer runs, what it emits, and the list of things it deliberately refuses to know about. Owns the AST cache lifecycle: an IG site is built from the AST on its cache branch, the publish refuses a stale one, and the reusable ig-ast-refresh.yml is the one writer. Owns what an IG reader may read: contentTypes.ig.include in the repository’s index.config.json, and the legacy warning for a repository that declares none. Read before adding anything to fhir-harness, before onboarding, converting or changing the workflows of an IG repository, and before publishing an IG site. Source: fhir-harness/skills/fhir-ig-base/ig-build-pipeline.md. 3977.title: Build an IG repository’s own site from its cached AST, with no instance declaration
3977.content: The three checkout scripts the platform’s site build runs for a repository that holds an IG and only mounts layers (index.config.json): ig-site:ast restores the AST from the IG’s cache branch (ig-cache.sh restore) and judges it, refusing a stale, cannot-tell or absent one (a stale one is accepted for a preview by default, refused with SITE_ACCEPT_STALE_AST=0, and never accepted for the root); ig-site:compose derives the artefact index from the AST (binding any IG API sidecars a layer above left in $SITE_WORK/ig-api/), writes the thin artefact pages, stages the IG’s input/ and sushi-config.yaml (menu read at build time, palette from the webpage theme of the top layer the repository mounts, edit links from its origin) and composes it at the ROOT of the host site source; ig-site:publisher-pages serves each of the AST’s resources once, as <Type>-<id>.json at the root (no ast-data/ mirror) — reduced (minified, no narrative, no ELM data, the ELM attachment pointing at the full copy) when the pages read the full resources by raw URL from the AST cache commit, and off with SITE_ROOT_RESOURCES=0 — the artefact index (or fhir-artifact-index/index.ref.json, pointing at the cache’s copy) and the sidecars (or none, read from the cache), refuses a page wearing the IG Publisher’s chrome, repairs repeated element ids and stamps folio-build.json. Never runs the Publisher and never reads its output. Compose lists the pages it puts in the site in FOLIO_SITE_UPSTREAM_PAGES, so the site build reports the IG’s own dead links rather than refusing the publish over them. |   |   | . | Tool | ig-repo-site | . | IRI | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/fhir-harness/tools/ig-repo-site.jsonld | . | part of | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/fhir-harness/fhir-harness.jsonld | . | type | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/Tool | . | declared by | fhir-harness | . | source | fhir-harness/tools/ig-repo-site/ig-repo-site.ts | . | invoked | shell | . | qa | qa-reports | .

4002.title: Skills it satisfies
4002.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. ig-build-pipeline . The bare FHIR IG pipeline — FSH to SUSHI to the IG Publisher to a pages branch, with no pre-processing and no post-processing. What this layer runs, what it emits, and the list of things it deliberately refuses to know about. Owns the AST cache lifecycle: an IG site is built from the AST on its cache branch, the publish refuses a stale one, and the reusable ig-ast-refresh.yml is the one writer. Owns what an IG reader may read: contentTypes.ig.include in the repository’s index.config.json, and the legacy warning for a repository that declares none. Read before adding anything to fhir-harness, before onboarding, converting or changing the workflows of an IG repository, and before publishing an IG site. Source: fhir-harness/skills/fhir-ig-base/ig-build-pipeline.md. Also satisfied by: build-ig-site, fhir-core, ig-artifact-jsonld, ig-ast-refresh, ig-index-build, ig-page-render-qa, ig-pages, ig-publisher-i18n, ig-repo-site, ig-site-data, ingest-ig-menu, jsonld-vocabularies, logical-model-schemas, strip-library-binaries, strip-library-content, terminology-index, valueset-schemas. The skill declares no I/O contract (schemas/skills/ig-build-pipeline/{input,output}.schema.json). docs-generation . How a checkout of this harness generates and publishes its docs site: regenerating derived references, composing the docs layers and each layer’s site into one Jekyll source, building it with just-the-docs, the post-build passes, the TypeDoc API reference, the knowledge-graph export, and the full-replace publish to gh-pages and its branches/ previews. Source: cat-harness/skills/ui/ui-core/docs-generation.md. Also satisfied by: bpmn-checklist, bpmn-render, ci-post-merge-regen, pages-index, pages-publish, readme-audit, readme-sync, render-order, schema-docs, shared-assets, site-build-local, site-search-index, site-search-scopes, skill-docs, subgraph-readmes. 4021.title: Skills it satisfies
4021.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. ig-build-pipeline . The bare FHIR IG pipeline — FSH to SUSHI to the IG Publisher to a pages branch, with no pre-processing and no post-processing. What this layer runs, what it emits, and the list of things it deliberately refuses to know about. Owns the AST cache lifecycle: an IG site is built from the AST on its cache branch, the publish refuses a stale one, and the reusable ig-ast-refresh.yml is the one writer. Owns what an IG reader may read: contentTypes.ig.include in the repository’s index.config.json, and the legacy warning for a repository that declares none. Read before adding anything to fhir-harness, before onboarding, converting or changing the workflows of an IG repository, and before publishing an IG site. Source: fhir-harness/skills/fhir-ig-base/ig-build-pipeline.md. 4092.title: Refer to HL7’s published FHIR core definitions by canonical URL, and derive their UML class model
4092.content: Read HL7’s own core package for each stable FHIR release (https://hl7.org/fhir/R4/hl7.fhir.r4.core.tgz, R4B, R5) at the sha1 and sha512 fhir-core/pins.json pins, and keep, under fhir-core/<release>/, only what refers to it or is derived from it: index writes the manifest (each resource, complex, primitive and root type by canonical URL, with HL7’s published JSON for it, its kind, base and the sha256 of its bytes in HL7’s package); uml derives the UML class model HL7 publishes only as pictures, citing the definition and element of every class and attribute; materialise fills a labelled local cache, never committed; check holds all of it to the pins offline; resolve answers with HL7’s URL for a canonical (--cache for the cached copy); diagram prints a type’s Mermaid class diagram. HL7’s publication is the authority: a mirror may only fill the cache. A package that cannot be fetched or verified is recorded as unread with the reason, never as an empty graph. |   |   | . | Tool | fhir-core | . | IRI | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/fhir-harness/tools/fhir-core.jsonld | . | part of | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/fhir-harness/fhir-harness.jsonld | . | type | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/Tool | . | declared by | fhir-harness | . | source | fhir-harness/tools/fhir-core/fhir-core.ts | . | invoked | shell | . | qa | qa-reports | .

4140.title: Scan every page of a built IG site in a headless browser for markup shown as text
4140.content: The checkout script ig-site:page-render-qa, the IG site build’s last final step: it serves the built site locally, opens the root pages and the artefact pages (not the JSON views, mappings views or redirect stubs) in headless Chromium, waits for each to draw, and lists every text block that shows markdown as text (bold, list markers, links, images, code, headings, tables, HTML tags), code and preformatted text left out. 4180.title: Cut an IG release as a GitHub draft that carries its packages and AST, and report a version left untagged or unreleased
4180.content: Gather a release’s files from a full Publisher build (package.tgz and its R4/R4B variants, and ast-data.zip, the IG’s AST with the Libraries’ ELM), say from sushi-config.yaml whether it is a pre-release, and make or refresh the GitHub DRAFT release for the tag with the files uploaded. 4188.title: Write the IG AST viewer: a page per instance holding ig-ast directories, and a hub

4205.title: Skills it satisfies
4205.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. ig-build-pipeline . The bare FHIR IG pipeline — FSH to SUSHI to the IG Publisher to a pages branch, with no pre-processing and no post-processing. What this layer runs, what it emits, and the list of things it deliberately refuses to know about. Owns the AST cache lifecycle: an IG site is built from the AST on its cache branch, the publish refuses a stale one, and the reusable ig-ast-refresh.yml is the one writer. Owns what an IG reader may read: contentTypes.ig.include in the repository’s index.config.json, and the legacy warning for a repository that declares none. Read before adding anything to fhir-harness, before onboarding, converting or changing the workflows of an IG repository, and before publishing an IG site. 4215.title: Tools — fhir-harness
4215.content: The Tool nodes fhir-harness declares in its tools graph — one instance’s slice of every instance’s tools. As an API: OpenAPI document · MCP tool list · API reference. A skill states a capability generically: what an actor needs to know to perform a task. A Tool is one concrete way to exercise it, with an installation, an invocation and typed inputs and outputs. One skill may be satisfied by several tools, and one tool may satisfy several skills. They are separate graphs and this is the tools one. The relation between them is satisfies, and it runs from a tool to a skill — this tool is one way to do that, never this skill is a tool. 39Tool nodes 9skills satisfied 39invoked as a shell command 0reachable over MCP

4217.title: Skills it satisfies
4217.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. prepare-merge . Take a feature branch to a clean, conflict-free, green, pushed state so it can be merged with no surprises: base merged in, generated files regenerated, the folio’s content-type gates run, then pushed. It does NOT merge and does NOT push to the default branch. Use for “prepare-merge”, “make it mergeable”, “ship it”. Source: cat-harness/sdlc/skills/sdlc-core/prepare-merge.md. Also satisfied by: gates-merged, judge-tree, merge-train. The skill declares no I/O contract (schemas/skills/prepare-merge/{input,output}.schema.json).

4224.title: Pin third-party GitHub Actions to full commit SHAs
4224.content: Rewrite every third-party uses: owner/repo@ref outside the declared staging-only workflows to @<full commit SHA> # <ref>, so Dependabot keeps the pair current. A tag resolves to its PEELED commit (an annotated tag’s object is never pinned), else a branch head, by git ls-remote with argv. A ref that resolves to nothing, or to more than one commit, is refused and reported, never guessed. This repository’s own reusable workflows are first-party and left alone. 4379.title: Skills it satisfies
4379.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. repo-conversion . Lay folio-assistant over a repository that already exists, without losing or silently moving what is in it. Scans the tree read-only, classifies candidate files into library (external source) and content (authored here) with an explicit third bucket for what it cannot classify, scans outside the content tree for mathematical evidence and refutations, lists the content markers (an IG, a DAK, processes, work items, library, Lean, folio manifests) the harness could declare and declares only the ones the person picks, puts the three questions the scan cannot answer to the author as selections, and hands ingestion to one agent or a small swarm. Use when a user wants an existing repo converted to a folio, asks to import what is already there, asks whether their PDFs/notes/drafts can come along, or asks what else in a repository an existing harness could declare. Source: cat-harness/skills/conduct/conduct-core/repo-conversion.md. Also satisfied by: instantiate-harness. The skill declares no I/O contract (schemas/skills/repo-conversion/{input,output}.schema.json). getting-started . Triage what a person means when they ask to create a folio, and route them. Five requests share one sentence — a folio in a new repo, folio-assistant overlaid on an existing repo, a second folio in a layer that already has one, a content object they called a folio, or something the filesystem cannot tell apart. Reads the repository facts, runs them through the folio-intent decision table, asks a selectable question for what facts cannot settle, scaffolds, and reports the published URL. Use whenever a user asks to create, start, set up, or initialise a folio, a paper, a DAK, an IG, or “folio-assistant” itself. Source: cat-harness/skills/conduct/conduct-core/getting-started.md. The skill declares no I/O contract (schemas/skills/getting-started/{input,output}.schema.json). folio-init . Scaffold a new folio layer from the harness — the instantiate affordance of the knowledge graph. Covers when to run folio-init vs remote-mount, what the scaffold writes, the builder shim, state branch seeding, write capability requirements, and –dry-run degradation. Source: cat-harness/skills/kg/kg-core/folio-init.md. The skill declares no I/O contract (schemas/skills/folio-init/{input,output}.schema.json).

4556.title: Is this repository’s cutover from the monorepo complete? Measured, condition by condition
4556.content: Run in a separated repository. Six conditions, each decided by an existing gate: mounts (every declared layer on disk at its pin — remote-mount --check), declarations (every path a declaration names resolves — declaration-resolution), monorepo-paths (no wiring still names the monorepo: livesAt on it, a submodule of it, a reusable workflow called from it, a path into its old checkout — the one condition implemented here), import-direction and reference-direction (no layer reaches a layer above it), and site (the site builds from the mounts alone, every link resolving — build-instance-site --no-mount, only with --site). Findings inside a MOUNTED layer are listed and not counted: a defect in a layer pinned from upstream is fixed upstream and re-pinned. 4557.title: Skills it satisfies
4557.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. kg-separation . Separate a Knowledge Graph into its own repository — as a CONTENT repository (files to read, no code) and a TOOLS repository (the code that writes and checks it) — once it is too large, or its consumers or cadence differ. Bootstrap + bootstrap-tools and cat-harness + the tools layer are the worked examples. Source: cat-harness/skills/kg/graph-management/kg-separation.md. 4573.title: Mount remote harnesses at a pinned commit, only when trusted
4573.content: Lay down each declared remote mount — a source.remote layer in the root index.config.json, or, in a folio with no index, a remoteMounts entry on its declaration (both at once is refused) — and its dependency closure, from another repository at a full commit SHA. Write the lock, index.lock.json (a legacy <name>.mount-lock.json is read, and renamed onto it when rewritten), and, with an index, regenerate the root .gitignore block that ignores each mount path. It READS the declared mounts and never writes them: a tool that changes a mount writes through writeDeclaredMounts into index.config.json. Before anything is checked out, each mount must pass the trust gate (schemas/kg/mount-trust.ts, rule H8): a person’s consent recorded for THIS pin, or a signature in a declared trust network. No signature verifier exists yet, so a signature alone is could-not-determine and does not mount. Unsigned and unconsented is refused. --staging mounts for a preview and needs neither. A directory id an override or mountDefaults names may be one the layer declares in its <name>.json or one it declares FROM WITHIN a declared directory (skills/skills.json naming voices), resolved at the pin through instanceDirectories; an id in neither is refused at plan time. tools on an override names Tools by id and mounts each one runnable: its definition (<tools dir>/<id>/<id>.ts), its implementation (the inProcess.module, or the script its bun run cat <key> resolves to) and their import closure, walked by bootstrap-tools’ importClosure (the one closure walker), as every declared directory that closure touches — the lock still records directories only. A hydrated mount lays each chosen directory down as its published index.hydrated.jsonld only: read from the pin’s git tree when a commit carries it, otherwise fetched from the pin’s subgraph index package (the subgraph-index-<sha> release asset subgraph-index-package publishes), its tarball checked against its folio-binary-release/v1 record, its manifest against the repository, pin and harness asked for, and each file against its sha256, SubgraphHydratedSchema and the subgraph IRI; the lock records the package’s URL and sha256 so a replay fetches the same bytes. --check compares the disk against the lock and never fetches. When a run CHANGES the lock, it then re-renders the agent surface (skill:commands → .claude/commands/, agent-memory → .claude/agent-memory/ and .agents/) from the checkout root, so a re-pin commit carries the skills and memory the new layers define; a generator that fails fails the run, and --no-agent-surface opts out. |   |   | . | Tool | remote-mount | . | IRI | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/tools/remote-mount.jsonld | . | part of | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/cat-harness.jsonld | . | type | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/Tool | . | declared by | cat-harness | . | source | cat-harness/tools/remote-mount/remote-mount.json | . | invoked | shell | . | qa | qa-reports | .

4658.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. translation-adjudication . A person’s verdict on a machine translation, carried from the translation review page to the record: the reviewer accepts a catalogue, or flags a mistranslation and picks a candidate or writes their own text; the verdict is filed as a translation-adjudication/v1 issue; a workflow checks the author and the catalogue’s hash, writes the records and opens a PR; a maintainer merges it. Use for “review the translations”, “this string is mistranslated”, “why was my review not recorded”, and when wiring a layer for review. Locale sign-off is a separate act, not this one. 4665.title: Build, check and (on request) publish a layer’s own site, or a branches/ preview
4665.content: From a checkout whose layers arrive by remote mount: mount the pinned closure, install, run the layer’s own gates (--pre), compose the harness chrome for THIS layer, run its source steps, build with Jekyll at the base path read from the git remote (/<repo>, or /<repo>/branches/<branch> for a preview), run the post-build steps (mount-instance-docs, pdf-viewer, set-html-lang, publish-id-lookup, rail-standalone-pages), and check that every relative or base-rooted link in every page resolves to a file under the site, reading each page with an HTML parser. Any failing step stops the run; a link that does not resolve means nothing is published. It never decides to publish: only --publish does, and then a root publish keeps branches/ and _render-log/ on the branch, and a preview replaces only its own branches/<branch>/. |   |   | . | Tool | build-instance-site | . | IRI | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/tools/build-instance-site.jsonld | . | part of | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/cat-harness.jsonld | . | type | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/Tool | . | declared by | cat-harness | . | source | cat-harness/tools/build-instance-site/build-instance-site.json | . | invoked | shell | . | qa | qa-reports | .

4698.title: Convert a checkout to a root index.config.json
4698.content: Write the root index.config.json (folio-index-config/v1) that says which layers the checkout instantiates, where each comes from (source.local or source.remote) and which owns / (site.landing), from the root *.config.json files and the declaration’s remoteMounts. With --write it moves remoteMounts off the declaration into source.remote entries, writes the generated .gitignore block, and renames a legacy <name>.mount-lock.json to index.lock.json. 4764.title: Instantiate a harness over a repository that has none: pin, mount, open the setup-only PR, render the preview
4764.content: The scripted step of the initiation process (getting-started.bpmn, the repo-conversion skill §4). Reads the harness’s declaration at its pin and every needs, transitively (a need beside the layer that needs it unless –repo-of says otherwise, at its default branch’s tip unless –pin says otherwise, its declaration’s name checked), seeds them all into the repository’s index.config.json with the consent given (remote-mount --seed --whole), sets site.landing to the harness, site.agentRun and mountApprovers, mounts the closure (remote-mount: index.lock.json and the .gitignore mounts block), installs it as root workspaces with the hoisted linker, writes the root bootstrap (.github/cat.ts and .github/mount-from-lock.sh from cat-harness-tools templates/root-bootstrap/) and sets the root’s cat script to bun .github/cat.ts, so bun run cat … mounts the layers itself on a later fresh clone, re-renders the agent surface from the mounted generators, runs the harness’s instantiate:<harness> checkout script when a mounted layer declares it, and commits on a branch (default harness/). Then, unless --local, pushes the branch, provisions gh-pages when absent (`pages-bootstrap --provision`), opens the setup-only PR, runs `prepare:` when declared (what the site is built from and nobody commits, such as an IG's AST) and renders the branch's preview at gh-pages branches// (`stage-local`); with --local the site is built and composed and nothing is pushed. It imports only node:*, so it runs from a fresh clone of cat-harness-tools before anything is mounted: it lays the platform's own closure, at the pins the repository will mount, into a temporary root to run the mount from. On a repository with nothing mounted yet, run the same file from a fresh clone: `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness-tools /tmp/cht && bun run /tmp/cht/scripts/instantiate-harness.ts …`. Two more flags, not declared as ports because no constrained type carries them yet: `--pin =` pins one layer of the closure, `--repo-of =<owner/repo>` says where a need lives. |   |   | . | Tool | instantiate-harness | . | IRI | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/tools/instantiate-harness.jsonld | . | part of | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/cat-harness.jsonld | . | type | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/Tool | . | declared by | cat-harness | . | source | cat-harness/tools/instantiate-harness/instantiate-harness.json | . | invoked | shell | . | qa | qa-reports | .

4765.title: Skills it satisfies
4765.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. repo-conversion . Lay folio-assistant over a repository that already exists, without losing or silently moving what is in it. Scans the tree read-only, classifies candidate files into library (external source) and content (authored here) with an explicit third bucket for what it cannot classify, scans outside the content tree for mathematical evidence and refutations, lists the content markers (an IG, a DAK, processes, work items, library, Lean, folio manifests) the harness could declare and declares only the ones the person picks, puts the three questions the scan cannot answer to the author as selections, and hands ingestion to one agent or a small swarm. Use when a user wants an existing repo converted to a folio, asks to import what is already there, asks whether their PDFs/notes/drafts can come along, or asks what else in a repository an existing harness could declare. Source: cat-harness/skills/conduct/conduct-core/repo-conversion.md. Also satisfied by: folio-init. The skill declares no I/O contract (schemas/skills/repo-conversion/{input,output}.schema.json). remote-mount . Bring a harness, and every layer it depends on, into a checkout that does not hold it, from another repository at a pinned commit, as declared directories with a lock: a source.remote entry in the downstream’s root index.config.json (legacy: remoteMounts on its declaration) and mountDefaults on the harness. Covers when to mount and when to subscribe instead, why there are no submodules and no .deps/, the transitive closure through needs and gitlinks, overrides by id, the lock, and the three states. Source: cat-harness/skills/kg/kg-core/remote-mount.md. Also satisfied by: build-instance-site, index-config-migrate, kg-retrieve-npm, mount-from-lock, npm, subgraph-index-package, ci-standing-repin. The skill declares no I/O contract (schemas/skills/remote-mount/{input,output}.schema.json).

4781.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. archimate-models . ArchiMate models as knowledge-graph content: how a layer declares the Archi models it holds, what the archimate subgraph gives every model, view, element and relationship (an IRI, a thin page, and every view drawn as SVG from the model’s own diagram, and its metamodel derived and checked), how to version the models, how to wire them into a folio’s staging build and navbar, how to count and lower the crossed lines in a view before committing it, why every view carries a plain-language key, why names are the source’s own terms linked to their SKOS concepts, and why no Java, no Archi CLI and no Archi HTML report is ever part of the pipeline. 4796.title: Run every existing security check as one named release step
4796.content: Run the repository’s security checks — workflow injection, secret leaks, lockfile pinning, the toolchain pin, QA reviewer permission, materialised-asset fixity — plus two advisories (dependency advisories, third-party action SHA pinning), each by name as argv. Every check is reported as pass, fail or unknown; a blocking check that fails OR could not be run refuses the release, because could-not-check is never clean. Advisories are reported and never block. 4813.title: Skills it satisfies
4813.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. kg-separation . Separate a Knowledge Graph into its own repository — as a CONTENT repository (files to read, no code) and a TOOLS repository (the code that writes and checks it) — once it is too large, or its consumers or cadence differ. The end-to-end method: the signals that trigger it, the preconditions, eleven stages each with the command that gates it, the owner’s decision points, how identifiers, QA and publication move, how the parent consumes the result, rollback, and the post-move sweep that a move between the pair owes before the parent re-pins. graph-detanglement owns stages 1–3; this skill owns the rest. Bootstrap + bootstrap-tools and cat-harness + the tools layer are the worked examples. Source: cat-harness/skills/kg/graph-management/kg-separation.md. Also satisfied by: mount-from-lock, package-exports, rewrite-moved-paths, separation-cutover-check. The skill declares no I/O contract (schemas/skills/kg-separation/{input,output}.schema.json). kg-affordances . The four affordances of a conformant knowledge graph — browse, materialise, instantiate and copy-into-folio — which capabilities each requires, how each writing verb degrades cleanly when no write capability is available, and how copying an asset stamps KgAsset.source provenance. Source: cat-harness/skills/kg/kg-core/kg-affordances.md. The skill declares no I/O contract (schemas/skills/kg-affordances/{input,output}.schema.json).

4829.content: After a move between two layers lands, find every mention <from>/<prefix>/<rest> in the scanned tree’s tracked files and rewrite it to <to>/<prefix>/<rest> only when the file exists under the destination root and not under the source root. 4840.title: Verify a separated repository from a fresh clone
4840.content: Clone a separated sub-KG’s repository (with submodules, and any sibling checkouts it needs) into an empty scratch directory, install, and run its gates: its gates script, else its test script (a person may pass --gate on the command line instead; it is not part of this contract because it is a shell command). Reports green, red or unknown; an empty tree, a failed clone or a repository with no gate is unknown, never green. 4841.title: Skills it satisfies
4841.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. sub-kg-lifecycle . A sub-KG is a knowledge graph staged as a directory inside a harnessed repository, declared as its own layer, that may later leave for a repository of its own. The lifecycle: declare it in place, grow it, stage it for separation (one import seam, the separation guard, a self-contained rehearsal), and then, each behind an explicit owner confirmation, create the repository, copy the staged contents in with history, re-point the declaration, verify on a fresh clone and delete the in-repo copy. The light sibling of kg-separation: use this for a DATA layer that leaves whole, and kg-separation when a graph must split into a content repository and a tools repository. Source: cat-harness/skills/kg/graph-management/sub-kg-lifecycle.md. The skill declares no I/O contract (schemas/skills/sub-kg-lifecycle/{input,output}.schema.json).

4857.title: Apply a vocabulary mapping table
4857.content: Carry one source record into a target vocabulary by a declared folio-vocab-mapping/v1 table: each source field becomes the predicate its row names, in the table’s order, with a DERIVED target (such as dcterms:title rendering skos:prefLabel) copied from its authoritative one so the two cannot drift. A table is shaped like a FHIR ConceptMap: an existing ConceptMap, R4 or R5, is representable as one without loss (fromConceptMap), and a table can be produced as a ConceptMap (toConceptMap), which returns every loss rather than dropping anything silently. 4896.title: Provenance
4896.content: narrative-queue (2) tool.selection.when . | historyTo find out what is waiting on a person, or to discover that this queue exists at all — which was the actual gap. Before this node, grep narrative tools/*.ts returned nothing, so an agent asking the graph how a person confirms a narrative got no answer, and that is exactly the population the command is for. | . tool.selection.limits . | historyThat refusal is load-bearing rather than defensive — driving the CLI in an agent container once wrote "rejected_by": {"kind": "human", "id": "Claude"}, because git config user.name is the agent's and the schema could not tell. So this node deliberately does not offer the confirming arms: an agent may read the queue and must not answer it. A rejection with no reason is refused too, not defaulted, because one lets the next agent redraft the identical thing. | .

4951.title: How it is deployed and reached
4951.content: . | Command line. From the repository root: bun run cat pdf:cover. cat pdf:cover runs python3 cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-cover.py (declared in cat-harness-tools/package.json). | GitHub Actions. No workflow in this checkout runs its command. | . As an API: its operation in the OpenAPI document and the MCP tool list of its layer. |   |   | . | install | cli: pip install pymupdf | . | runtime | python3, pymupdf | . | network | no | . | when to choose it |   | . | when | A listing needs a cover and the bytes are already held. It renders page 1 by default and calls that the cover, because page 1 is a determined answer and “the cover” is not — the same choice pdf-pages.py makes about sections. | . | limits | It decides nothing beyond the raster. WHICH documents get a cover, where the file lands, and what the catalogue must say about the derivation are the catalogue’s to declare — see the content core’s scripts/gen-covers.ts, which reads them from a layer’s catalogue and refuses to write bytes for a THUMBNAIL that does not declare itself derived. It also cannot tell you whether the page it rendered IS the cover; it can only tell you it is page 1. | . | cost | One PyMuPDF wheel, no network at run time, and a few milliseconds per page. Deterministic — identical input gives identical bytes, which is what lets a caller gate on --check rather than re-deciding. | .

4956.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. translation-candidate-source . The one interface every candidate-translation engine meets: for a layer’s catalogues, append candidate translations per string to the translation-candidates/v1 sidecar, each carrying its source, and seed an empty msgstr with the first candidate marked fuzzy. 4988.title: Merge train
4988.content: Build a train branch from a base SHA: merge each member (a PR number or branch) with merge-base.ts --no-regen, refusing — never hand-resolving — a member whose conflicts no declared pattern covers; then one bun run cat regen, check:l1-complete --write, every check a layer declares afterMerge (its declared writer run when red), and kg:audit:all:check; then merge origin/main, taking main’s side of generated conflicts and regenerating once more. 4989.title: Skills it satisfies
4989.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. merge-conflict-patterns . Merge the base branch in and resolve, without a person, only the conflicts a DECLARED pattern covers — generated files, generated README regions, QA sidecars — then prove the result with the gate set. Refuses the whole merge when any conflict is authored or undeclared. Use for “merge main”, “resolve the conflicts”, “the PR is conflicted again”, “auto-resolve”, and when adding a pattern for a new kind of churn. Also governs what a merge steward does with a merge-train member it had to refuse: one deduplicated work item under the PR’s own epic, a hand-back to the owning session with a fail condition, one dispatched agent when nobody owns it, one PR comment, and the close. Source: cat-harness/sdlc/skills/sdlc-core/merge-conflict-patterns.md. Also satisfied by: merge-leftover, merge-overlap. It does NOT merge and does NOT push to the default branch. Use for “prepare-merge”, “make it mergeable”, “ship it”. Source: cat-harness/sdlc/skills/sdlc-core/prepare-merge.md. 5012.title: Check that an ArchiMate model’s fhir-actor tags point at the IG’s FHIR ActorDefinitions
5012.content: Actors come first: the IG’s ActorDefinitions are written from the DAK’s personas, and an ArchiMate model only points at them. For one model a layer’s cat-archimate.config.json names, this reads every element carrying the Archi property fhir-actor, whose value is an ActorDefinition’s canonical URL, and the IG’s ActorDefinitions: FSH InstanceOf: ActorDefinition under input/fsh/, and FHIR JSON under fsh-generated/resources/ or input/resources/, each canonical being <sushi-config canonical>/ActorDefinition/<id> unless its url says otherwise. It fails on a value that is not a canonical URL, a tag that names no ActorDefinition, an element kind that cannot be an actor (a data object, a goal), and a type mismatch (a #person actor on an application or technology element, a #system actor on a business actor or role). It warns about each ActorDefinition no element realizes; --strict makes that a failure. --json prints element → actors and actor → elements, for page back-links. It never writes an ActorDefinition or any FSH, and never matches boxes to actors by name. |   |   | . | Tool | archimate-actors | . | IRI | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/tools/archimate-actors.jsonld | . | part of | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/cat-harness.jsonld | . | type | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/Tool | . | declared by | cat-harness | . | source | cat-harness/tools/archimate-actors/archimate-actors.json | . | invoked | shell | . | qa | qa-reports | .

5054.title: Skills it satisfies
5054.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. merge-conflict-patterns . Merge the base branch in and resolve, without a person, only the conflicts a DECLARED pattern covers — generated files, generated README regions, QA sidecars — then prove the result with the gate set. Refuses the whole merge when any conflict is authored or undeclared. Use for “merge main”, “resolve the conflicts”, “the PR is conflicted again”, “auto-resolve”, and when adding a pattern for a new kind of churn. Also governs what a merge steward does with a merge-train member it had to refuse: one deduplicated work item under the PR’s own epic, a hand-back to the owning session with a fail condition, one dispatched agent when nobody owns it, one PR comment, and the close. Source: cat-harness/sdlc/skills/sdlc-core/merge-conflict-patterns.md. Also satisfied by: merge-overlap, merge-train. The skill declares no I/O contract (schemas/skills/merge-conflict-patterns/{input,output}.schema.json).

5078.title: Does every node have an IRI, a .jsonld, a page and a row?

5103.title: Screen a hand-over for injected instructions, field by field
5103.content: Before a model reads a sub-agent’s report, a delegated prompt, a tool result or a comment from someone who is not the principal, screen it against a declared schema whose top-level fields are control (steers what the receiver does) or data (content it reads). A finding in a control field, or any field the strict schema does not declare, is REFUSED, so a report cannot extend the delegator’s plan. A finding in a data field is QUARANTINED: the original is kept and marked, never stripped. The patterns are a deterministic tripwire (instruction overrides, role and turn spoofs, fence breaks, tool-call syntax, hidden Unicode, exfiltration links, pipe-to-shell), a mitigation and not a guarantee. 5127.title: Publish a folio’s or an IG’s site from the agent’s own checkout — the one agent publish path
5127.content: Build a repository’s site in the agent’s checkout and push it to the publish branch, as a preview or as the main site, without an Actions runner. Which build is read from the repository: a declared site.build recipe (built by build-instance-site), else the reusable workflow its own workflow files call — folio-staging.yml for a folio, the WHO SMART Base IG’s ghbuild.yml for a FHIR IG, whose build job is planned step by step and run as written. For an IG it then applies the harness chrome over the built output (sync-docs-harness, then rail-standalone-pages --foreign-site --instance <the IG>): every page gains the rail and the icon row #fa-navbar-row, and the IG’s own content is left byte for byte. A root publish is REFUSED when the chrome cannot be applied, and a clean root deploy is refused over any root whose index.html wears the icon row unless the new output does too, so a chromed root is never replaced by bare IG Publisher pages. Every run prints its plan first, and the plan lists the chrome step; --plan stops there, --dry-run composes the commit in a temporary worktree and pushes nothing, --artifact writes a claude.ai Artifact bundle instead. |   |   | . | Tool | stage-local | . | IRI | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/tools/stage-local.jsonld | . | part of | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/cat-harness.jsonld | . | type | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/Tool | . | declared by | cat-harness | . | source | cat-harness/tools/stage-local/stage-local.json | . | invoked | shell | . | qa | qa-reports | .

5208.title: Package one pin’s subgraph index files for a hydrated mount
5208.content: Pack every built index.jsonld and index.hydrated.jsonld under a layer’s <docs>/subgraph/<harness>/ into ONE npm package for one pin — <harness>-subgraph-index@0.0.0-pin.<sha>, with a folio-subgraph-index/v1 manifest giving each file’s sha256 — through pack-tarball (bun pm pack), which also writes the tarball’s folio-binary-release/v1 record. 5248.title: Replay a committed mount lock with nothing but Node
5248.content: Lay down every remote mount index.lock.json records — each layer fetched at the lock’s full SHA (sparse, blob-filtered), each directory verified against its treeDigest, a mismatch undone and reported — importing only node:*, so it runs on a fresh clone before any layer is present. It never decides what to mount: remote-mount writes the lock (and checks trust); this only replays it. Refuses to write over a path with tracked files or bytes that no longer hash to the lock. Separate a Knowledge Graph into its own repository — as a CONTENT repository (files to read, no code) and a TOOLS repository (the code that writes and checks it) — once it is too large, or its consumers or cadence differ. Bootstrap + bootstrap-tools and cat-harness + the tools layer are the worked examples. Source: cat-harness/skills/kg/graph-management/kg-separation.md. 5273.title: Publish a built site to gh-pages as a full replace
5273.content: Lay a built _site onto a gh-pages checkout as a FULL REPLACE and push it, keeping the open pull requests’ staging previews: each attempt re-reads the branch, re-runs restore-staging and keep-shared-payloads against what is on it now, replaces the tree, commits docs(gh-pages): site from <sha> and pushes. A rejected push is rebuilt, never rebased (a rebase would re-apply the replace over a preview a sibling just deployed), up to three attempts. A restore that cannot read the branch stops the publish. A site that matches the branch is a no-op, not a failure. It publishes and does not verify: the workflow’s verify step runs after it. |   |   | . | Tool | publish-gh-pages | . | IRI | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/tools/publish-gh-pages.jsonld | . | part of | https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/cat-harness.jsonld | . | type | https://litlfred.github.io/cat-harness/v0/ns/Tool | . | declared by | cat-harness | . | source | cat-harness/tools/publish-gh-pages/publish-gh-pages.json | . | invoked | shell | . | qa | qa-reports | .

5338.title: Skills it satisfies
5338.content: A skill states the capability; this Tool is one way to exercise it. Each skill’s declared input and output contract follows, where it has one. cache-first-ci . Every CI step is a pure function of its inputs: derive the inputs, hash them into a key, restore on a hit, run and save on a miss. Read before adding a cache to a workflow, before writing a cache key, before trusting a restored output or a skipped verdict, and before pushing a change that moves a cached step’s key. Covers the one primitive (cached-step + cache:key), the trust classes, what a committer publishes, the 10 GB budget, and the hit-rate report. Source: cat-harness/sdlc/skills/sdlc-core/cache-first-ci.md. The skill declares no I/O contract (schemas/skills/cache-first-ci/{input,output}.schema.json).
