6536.title: Every initialization step, as the declarations name them
6536.content: Skill initialization-steps: Walk every initialization step the declarations name (the layer’s own and each one it needs), check each before doing anything, do what can be done, ask for what only a person can do, and report every step as done, not done, could not determine, or stated. Named by: Complete initialization, Determine the harness and repositories, Initialize a harness . You are making sure a harness’s initialization is complete: right after installing it (initialize-harness calls complete-initialization), or because you were dispatched to do exactly this with nothing but the diagram and the repository. Either way the steps are the same, and they are not listed in this file. They are named by the declarations.

6537.title: Where the steps come from
6537.content: Read <name>.json at the root, then each name in its needs, from a sibling checkout at ../<name>/<name>.json. Each step below names the declaration that names it, so a reader can see why it is there. | step | named by | done when | . | declaration | the file itself | <name>.json parses and its name is its file name | . | needs:<name> | needs | the dependency is beside it, and its declaration parses | . | instructions:<name> | FR-4 | stated: <name>/docs/bootstrap/initialization.md was read and followed | . | schemas:staged | each $id / @id under iriBase (FR-11) | the site build stages every JSON Schema and JSON-LD document at its IRI | . | schemas:published | the same IRIs (FR-11) | every one of those IRIs answers | . | directory:<id> | directories[] | the declared path exists | . | asset:<id> | assets[] | the declared file exists | . | readme | FR-8 | the root has a README.md | . | readme-sections | the README’s own markers | every section the README opts into is current | . | site:workflow | repository | a workflow commits the rendered site onto gh-pages | . | site:branch | repository | a gh-pages branch exists — it must, before Pages can be switched on | . | site:enabled | repository | Pages is on, serving gh-pages | . | site:live | iriBase, else the Pages address | the address answers | . The two schemas: steps are the primary ones. They are checked first once the declarations are read, and the report leads with them: publish-documents. A harness above bootstrap names more steps the same way. A work-plan store it declares as a directory is a directory: step, and a harness’s own set-up instructions are its instructions: step. Bootstrap does not need to know which harness declares what. The site steps are in publish-site.

6538.title: Four states, not two
6538.content: . | done: checked, and it holds. | not done: checked, and it does not. Say exactly what to do next. | could not determine: the check could not run (no forge CLI, no network). Never reported as done. A check that could not look is not a pass. | stated: the declarations name it but nothing can observe it (reading and following a harness’s instructions). Follow it, say you did, and leave it stated. | .

6539.title: Idempotent by construction
6539.content: Check before doing, every time. A done step is left alone, so running the process twice changes nothing the second time, and an interrupted run is resumed by running it again. Performing is not the same as done: after you do a step, check it again, and only the check says done. Replace nothing. A step that would overwrite what somebody wrote (an existing README, a Pages site built from a branch, a declaration that disagrees with the directories on disk) is a step for the person. Ask through human-agent-discussion, with the exact step written out. Do not create an empty declared directory to make its step pass. Git does not track an empty directory, so the check would pass on your machine and fail on every clone. Put its first file in it, or ask whether the entry should go.

6540.title: Where tools are available
6540.content: A toolset may perform the checks for you — for example https://github.com/litlfred/bootstrap-tools, whose init command reads the same declarations, does what a tool can (regenerating README sections; switching Pages on when an authenticated gh is present), and prints each step in these four states with what to do next: . bun run scripts/init.ts --root ../<instance> # from a toolset checkout beside it bun run scripts/init.ts --root ../<instance> --dry-run # check only . Where no tools are available, do the same by reading files. The diagram is the same either way, and so is the report.

6541.title: The report
6541.content: One report through log-message, led by the primary step’s state (the JSON Schemas and JSON-LD at their IRIs): then every step, the declaration that named it, its state, what was seen, and for anything not done, what to do and who does it. End with the counts (done, not done, could not determine, stated). An initialization that finished with steps open says which. It is not hidden behind “installed”.

6549.title: instance-publication — draft is a state, not an absence of one
6549.content: Skill instance-publication: Every asset carries an id and a version and sits in DRAFT. Publication is a state, not a boolean, and published is refused by the schema because the formal process does not exist yet. Carries the id namespace rule, why a mirror never takes its subject’s identity, and what a consumer may assume of a draft. Also the one home for which graph each layer publishes, where, under which IRI and schema, and what is stripped from it. Named by: Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, KG to public portal, The cache process: restore and save every cache a run can use, Alert the publication manager, QA report signing, Adopting an upstream version bump, Incremental IG build, L3 FHIR IG pipeline, An IG site, built from the AST on its cache branch, An IG release: the owner tags, a draft is built, the owner publishes, Content lifecycle, Draft, review and publish, Guideline Updates . Skill id: instance-publication · Package: folio-core · Layer: cat-harness . All assets get a version and are in draft publication; the formal publication process is not yet defined, needs tools, and depends on the layer. Three rules follow.

6550.title: 1. Every asset carries a version — and the id is HELD
6550.content: version is universal. Not only the publishable ones. It is enforced by check:publishable, not by the schema: requiring it in the type would break every test fixture that builds a declaration without it, and a sweep that size hides real regressions in the noise. A new layer without a version fails the gate by name, rather than as a parse error in a test fixture. A version is not a publication claim. It distinguishes snapshots of a thing; whether anyone outside may depend on those snapshots is the separate question below. id is not written into declarations. Bootstrapping a different harness must change ONE place — one reference in bootstrap/README.md — and a namespace written into every declaration is many places. So an id must be derived from that single reference, which does not exist yet (bootstrap/README.md carries no outward references, and its tests enforce that). Do not mint ids before then: an id is stable forever, never reused. The namespace rule below stands; only its application waits.

6551.title: 2. Publication is a STATE, and the state is draft
6551.content: publication is not a boolean. draft is the state everything is already in — not an undecided-ness, not an absence. check:publishable does not report a draft layer as undecided. Absence still means draft. Declaring publication: "draft" is legal and says nothing extra; the field exists to reserve the axis and to make rule 3 testable rather than merely intended.

6552.title: 3. published is REFUSED by the schema, not merely reported
6552.content: Because the process does not exist, a flag nothing can verify is refused rather than reported — a gate that only grumbles is a gate somebody switches off: a declaration setting publication: "published" fails to parse, with the error naming what is missing. Falsifier for this whole skill: if published becomes settable by hand before any tool backs it, this is wrong and should be read again. depends on instance is the part not yet designed. When the process arrives it will be per-instance — what publishing means for cat-harness is not what it means for a WHO IG mirror — so expect publication to gain a companion naming that process, rather than to become a second boolean.

6553.title: The id namespace — one rule, no per-instance invention
6553.content: Every layer’s id is io.github.litlfred.folio-assistant.<name>. The rule underneath it is mechanical: reverse the host, append the path. | host + path | id | . | litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant | io.github.litlfred.folio-assistant | . | smart.who.int/base | smart.who.int.base | . The second row is FHIR’s actual published package id for that IG, produced by the same rule: a convention that already yields the right answer for a case we can check is worth more than a scheme chosen for elegance. An id is stable forever and never reused.

6554.title: A MIRROR NEVER TAKES ITS SUBJECT’S IDENTITY
6554.content: The trust-IG mirror here is not the WHO SMART Trust IG. It is this repository’s reconstructed index about that IG. The two are different objects, and the real upstream ids are already held — as data, in the right place: . // <dak-layer>/fhir-artifact-index/chrome.json, ingested at commit 26635f7b { "id": "smart.who.int.trust", "canonical": "http://smart.who.int/trust" } . Giving our layer smart.who.int.trust would claim our mirror is the thing it mirrors. Anything resolving that id would then find two different artefacts answering to it. The same reading governs canonicalUrl. In a mirror’s declaration the URL is READ from upstream, so it is a fact about the upstream IG and not a decision about where that staging directory publishes. For a true mirror, canonicalUrl records the subject. It must not drive our identity. A mirror’s declaration that carries an upstream canonical is describing what it mirrors, not asserting where it lives. Three questions that must not be merged — publication, staging, mirroring . Three different questions answer to “what is this layer’s address”, and each has its own field: . | question | answered by | example | . | Publication identity — where the artefact lives once formally published | the @id its document mints; for a layer staged here for publication elsewhere, its declared canonicalUrl | smart-base → http://smart.who.int/base/smart-base.jsonld | . | Staging location — where this repository’s site serves a draft copy now | the root index’s url, never the @id | a DAK layer → <site>/<name>/<name>.jsonld | . | True mirror — this repository’s index about someone else’s artefact | its own identity on this site; the subject’s ids are held as data | the trust-IG mirror is not the WHO SMART Trust IG | . A layer staged here for publication at its canonicalUrl is not a mirror. It IS the thing that will be published there, so its @id is the publication identity and this site is only where it is staged. The mirror rule above applies to the third row and to nothing else. Never read this site’s address as a layer’s identity: it would mint ids that change the day the artefact is published.

6555.title: Release IRIs — one address, the major, derived from the version
6555.content: Every address a layer mints carries its major version only — <iriBase>v<major>/… — whoever reads it. A namespace, a schema $id, a BPMN xmlns and bpmn:import, a JSON-LD @id, a code-list value, and a page a person reads all take the one form: . | reader | form | example (bootstrap 0.1.1) | . | a program or agent — a namespace, a schema $id, a BPMN xmlns, a JSON-LD @id | <iriBase>v<major>/… | https://litlfred.github.io/bootstrap/v0/ns/ | . | a person — a page to read | <iriBase>v<major>/… | https://litlfred.github.io/bootstrap/v0/ | . The exact release comes from the pin, not the address. A reader is handed a commit by index.lock.json and the needs pins, which already name it exactly; an address that also named the patch would make every patch release rewrite every literal copy of the layer’s addresses. Within one major a minor or patch adds and never breaks — the promise a $schema tag already makes, where a reader accepts any tag of the same major (tagCompatible, below) — so only a breaking change, a new major, changes an address. iriBase and version are written ONCE, in the declaration — the one place a fork edits. iriBase is not canonicalUrl: canonicalUrl says where documents are published and kg-export mints a document @id from it; iriBase says what the identifiers are, and those carry the release’s major. Never type an address or a version. Ask for it: . | in TypeScript, releaseIris(decl) / releaseIri(r, path, "agent" | "human") in bootstrap-tools/schemas/release-iri.ts — gen-bootstrap-schemas mints every $id this way; | in a README template, the release variable (liquid-templates); | on the site, site.data.harness.releases.<instance> (version, major, agent, human), written by sync-docs-harness. | . The copies that cannot ask are synced, and the sync is a gate. An xmlns attribute, a code-list value and a fixture string are literal by nature. bun run iri:sync rewrites every legacy full-version <iriBase><semver>/, whatever the semver, and every <iriBase>v<N>/ of another major, to <iriBase>v<major>/; iri:sync:check fails CI and the pre-commit hook on any that is not. A minor or patch release therefore leaves every copy as it is, and the sync has work to do only on a new major or a move. Moving the base itself (a fork, or a move to a new host) is bun run iri:sync -- --from <old base>, once. beans/ is never rewritten: a work item records what was true when it was written. Transition tolerance — remove when every layer has migrated. Until every layer carries <iriBase>v<major>/, the CHECKS — check:node-iris, iri:sync:check, vocabulary:check — accept a legacy <iriBase><semver>/ copy whose MAJOR is the declared major as deprecated: a warning naming the file, not a failure, so a layer’s CI, which composes the others at main, can go green before they move. The WRITER, iri:sync, still moves every such copy to v<major>/; a full version of another major, or an id at the wrong path, still fails. The tolerance lives in legacyExactSemver / withLegacyMoved in bootstrap-tools/schemas/release-iri.ts. A $schema tag carries its SCHEMA’s semver, not the layer’s: model-registry/1.0.0. A reader accepts any tag of the same major (tagCompatible); a tag change that breaks a reader is a new major. An old tag is accepted until that schema’s next major, and a published schema never names it. Not yet moved, on purpose: the exported document’s own @id (bootstrap.jsonld). kg-export mints it from where the document is actually served, and today that is this site; pointing it at a base that serves nothing would make it dangle. It moves when the bootstrap repository publishes.

6556.title: The release site — what is served where
6556.content: The IRI rule above says what an identifier IS; this says what the layer’s own site must serve so that every identifier dereferences. | path | holds | changes | . | <iriBase>v<major>/ | every file of the latest release of that major exactly where it sits in the repository — schemas, JSON-LD, BPMN, the declaration — plus an extension-less alias for a vocabulary document (processes/ns beside processes/ns.jsonld), and the person-facing pages beside them: READMEs rendered as HTML, the drawn schema page, the diagrams | moves forward with each minor or patch release of that major; a release of a NEW major is a new directory beside it, and the old major’s stays | . | <iriBase> | an index naming the current release of each major, and the versions available | with every release | . One directory serves both audiences, as one address does. A reader that needs the exact bytes of an older patch reads them from the commit its pin names, never from the site. Full-version directories (<iriBase>0.1.0/) are not published; any copy still served there is a leftover, not a release. Three rules follow from the table: . | Publish files where they sit. A published node’s own identifier must be its file’s path under the release address, so copying the release’s tree is enough to serve every identifier. check:node-iris enforces it. | No two artefacts may publish to one path. A generated alias that lands on an authored file’s path hides the authored file — the exported graph’s .json copy at bootstrap/bootstrap.json does exactly that to bootstrap’s own declaration on this site today (the workflow keeps the graph at that address and says so). On bootstrap’s own site the collision cannot occur, because the exported graph is not published there (next rule). | A layer’s own site serves only what its tools generate. For bootstrap that is bootstrap’s files as they sit, the schemas and diagram vocabulary among them, the bs: term vocabulary, and the person-facing pages — all produced by bootstrap-tools. Output a harness computes ABOUT the layer stays on the harness’s site, under the harness’s addresses, naming the layer as its subject: the exported graph bootstrap.jsonld, the swimlane glossary, the QA verdicts, the translation templates. So a new toolset over the same content never has to reproduce a harness’s output to publish the content, and a harness’s output never takes the layer’s identity (kg-separation §”The pair”). | . The JSON-LD context: <iriBase>ns/context/v1.jsonld, published by the layer . One path sits outside the versioned tree: the layer’s @context, generated from the prefixes its own documents use (gen-instance-contexts.ts). It is @protected, so a change that rebinds a term is a new v2 beside it, never an edit under a cached URL. Each repository publishes its own context, through ONE reusable workflow, and the initiation process sets that up. Where its ns is a document, the context goes beside it. A layer holding its vocabulary as ns.jsonld at its root (bootstrap) has ns staged as a FILE (the extensionless ns, and v<major>/ns), so ns/ cannot also be the directory ns/context/v1.jsonld needs, and a static host cannot serve both. Its context is <iriBase>ns.context.v1.jsonld, same v1 rule. The generator decides by what the layer holds (contextPathFor in gen-instance-contexts.ts), the layer’s builtAtPublish and .gitignore name that path, and the workflow publishes at the path the build reports. | The workflow is the tools layer’s .github/workflows/layer-publish-context.yml. A repository calls it from a publish-context.yml of one uses: line, on push to main, with contents: write (path-in-repo: when the layer is a sub-directory, as the DAK layer’s is). It builds only the caller’s context, judges only the caller’s findings, and writes that one path to the caller’s gh-pages. It skips with a notice when the layer declares no iriBase or has no .jsonld documents, and it creates gh-pages when it is absent. | A site that rebuilds gh-pages must keep ns/. An IG deploy or a folio site that cleans the branch lists ns in its clean-exclude, or the next deploy deletes the context. | Initiation. init-folio --instance writes the caller and declares iriBase as https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/ from a github.com origin (--iri-base to choose another). With no such remote it invents none: the workflow skips until one is declared. | The one step that stays the owner’s. GITHUB_TOKEN cannot switch Pages on. After the first run: Settings → Pages → Deploy from a branch: gh-pages, / (root). Then curl -sI <iriBase>ns/context/v1.jsonld answers 200 with content-type: application/ld+json. | . publish-instance-files.ts is the step that copies a layer’s files into a site today — each file as it sits, .md also as .html, README.md as index.html. It serves bootstrap under this site until bootstrap’s own repository publishes itself, at which point the job is bootstrap-tools’. Tags . A standalone repository — one layer, declared at its root — tags a release plainly, v<major>.<minor>.<patch>; a repository of several layers tags <name>-v<major>.<minor>.<patch>, because a plain tag could not say which layer it released. check:version-bump reads both accordingly. The tag is what a site deploy writes /v<major>/ from, so an untagged commit is never an agent-facing release; the tag, like the pin, names the exact version that the address no longer does.

6557.title: What each layer publishes — graph, address, schema, and what is stripped
6557.content: This section is where the publication policy is stated. The files that carry the mechanics point here for the policy. One document per declared layer, of its own directories . Every directory carrying a declaration publishes ONE JSON-LD document, and it holds only the directories that declaration names. A dependency is referenced by IRI, never inlined. The set is read from the declarations (instanceRootsIn), never listed in a workflow, where it would go stale. | layer | document on this site | built by | . | the host, cat-harness | <site>/<stub>/<stub>.jsonld | kg-export.ts --scope instance, its own line in docs-site.yml | . | the checkout root, folio-assistant | <site>/<stub>/<stub>.jsonld | kg-export.ts --instance . | . | bootstrap | <site>/bootstrap/bootstrap.jsonld | bootstrap-tools/scripts/export-graph.ts | . | every other declared layer | <site>/<stub>/<stub>.jsonld | cat-harness-tools/scripts/instance-exports.ts | . | Each document has a .json copy beside it, the same bytes. Pages serves .jsonld as octet-stream, and .json is the only way to get a correct Content-Type out of it. The .jsonld stays canonical, since it is what every @id names. | The host is in the same place as every other layer. Its document, its Tools, its subjects and its glossary are under <site>/<name>/: one rule for every layer, with subjects beside their document. A separate line in the deploy is the only thing different about it. | The first three rows are the only exemptions, and they are PUBLISHED_ELSEWHERE in instance-exports.ts, each with its reason. No other list exists. | The host is built in layer scope, so its document carries only its own nodes. --scope checkout remains for a corpus-wide consumer that says so (the kg search slice). It is never published under the host’s name: PUBLISHED_ELSEWHERE’s pattern for the host refuses it. | . The exporter’s contract (the two scopes, what each collector reads) is kg-export §”Whose nodes — a layer publishes its own”. An @id that moved is not forwarded . An @id that moved — to its owner’s document, from a ….jsonld#<kind>/<id> fragment to a <doc dir>/<kind>/<id> path, or with its document under <site>/<name>/ — keeps NO forwarding node and NO document at the old address. A consumer holding an old @id must re-resolve it. What stays is placedOut, so a deploy step still naming an old --out path writes the document where its @id says it is. Which base an @id is minted against . exportIdentity in kg-export.ts decides. The base is --base-url if given; else the layer’s own canonicalUrl; else, for a layer this repository publishes, the host’s. With no base at all the @id is document-relative and a problem is reported, never a guessed absolute one. Every layer this site publishes, the host included, sits at <base>/<name>/<stub>.jsonld, so <doc dir> for the host’s subjects and Tools is <base>/cat-harness/, never the site root. The one exception is an layer declaring its own canonicalUrl: it is the host of its own base, so its @id is <canonicalUrl>/<stub>.jsonld, and the deploy passes it no --base-url (declaresOwnCanonical in instance-exports.ts) — the tools layer, cat-openapi, the FHIR IG layer and the DAK layer, for example. This site serves their bytes at <site>/<stub>/<stub>.jsonld, and that is their branches/ location, not their identity (§”Three questions that must not be merged” above). The root index records both: @id is the publication identity, url is where this site stages it. Anything that names a node in another layer’s document mints with publishedIdentity, or it names a document nobody writes. iriBase is a different field, for identifiers that carry the release (§”Release IRIs” above). What goes after the base is a path, not a #fragment: a subject is <doc dir>/<kind>/<id>, served as its own file. The rule, its reasons and the ns#Term exception are in kg-export §”Subject IRIs — a path, not a #fragment”. The schema . harness-schema-export.ts writes <site>/<name>/<stub>.schema.json for the host. That is the JSON Schema of the declaration itself, which every <instance>.json is validated against. It also writes tool.schema.json, tool-types.schema.json, tool-types/<Name>.schema.json and each skill’s I/O contract (skills/<skill>/<io>.schema.json) in the same directory, each at the URL its $id names. They sit under the host’s own directory, beside its document, like everything else it publishes. bootstrap’s schemas are published as they sit, by publish-instance-files.ts. Every layer instance-exports.ts publishes also publishes <site>/<stub>/schema/. It holds: . | the layer’s own skill I/O contracts, at schema/skills/<skill>/<io>.schema.json. They are read from <instance>/schemas/skills/, the directory its skills’ input: and output: refs name. The declared schemas graph is not the answer: the science layer declares sources/ as its schemas graph and keeps its contracts under schemas/skills/. | its public Zod schemas, at schema/zod/<module>/<Export>.schema.json (§”Which Zod schemas are public” below). | an index, schema/<stub>.schema.json. It $refs the shared declaration schema (the host’s <stub>.schema.json, by the $id the same build gives it) and lists every contract and every Zod rendering in $defs by $id. | . Every $id is the layer’s publication identity, not this site’s address. The schema base is schema/ beside the document publishedIdentity mints: <site>/<stub>/schema/ for a layer with no canonicalUrl, and <canonicalUrl>/schema/ for one that declares its own. So the DAK layer’s contracts are http://smart.who.int/base/schema/skills/…, and this site stages the bytes at <site>/<dak-layer>/schema/ (§”Three questions that must not be merged”). publishedInstanceSchemas in kg-export.ts is the one place identity and builder meet, and the deploy and the gate both call it. A stored $id in a source contract is never published: with a base the computed one replaces it, and with no base the contract has none. The document links its index with conformsTo (dcterms:conformsTo). It does so exactly when instance-exports.ts writes one, which is when publishesInstanceSchema finds the layer in the plan. The other two exemptions carry no such link. The host links its own <stub>.schema.json, the shared declaration schema, by the $id buildDeclarationSchema mints with the same base. With no base there is no $id, so there is no link: never a relative one. A skill links the contract its own layer publishes. A skill held by a planned layer gets inputSchema / outputSchema set to its contract’s $id as publishedInstanceSchemas mints it, which is the function the deploy writes the file with. That holds in the layer’s own document and in a checkout-scope build that stacks it. A skill whose layer is not in the plan, or whose contract gets no absolute $id, has no link: a guessed address is worse than none. The host’s own skills are unchanged. Which Zod schemas are public . A layer’s public schemas are every exported const whose name ends in Schema and whose value is a Zod schema, in the .ts modules (not *.test.ts) directly inside its schemas directory. That directory is the layer’s declared schemas graph if it declares one, else <root>/schemas/ by convention. The science layer and the IRIS replica declare sources/, which holds JSON descriptors, so they publish none. The rule is the suffix, literally. A Zod value named otherwise is not public, and an export named notASchema matches if its value is Zod. A *Schema export whose value is not Zod is not public either; the scan lists it as notZod and it is not a failure. Publishing a schema says it is reachable, not that it is stable; internal schemas may be exposed. Each one is rendered with namedJsonSchema (to-json-schema.ts), as the host’s own schema documents are, and gets an $id under the same schema base as the contracts. scanInstanceZodSchemas and renderZodSchemas in harness-schema-export.ts do the work, and scannedInstanceSchemas in kg-export.ts is what the deploy and the gate both call. Once the scan has run, the index drops "omitted": ["schemas"], so an index with no zod/ entries means the scan ran and found none. If the directory could not be resolved, omitted stays. A failure fails the publish. A module that will not import, an export the converter cannot represent (z.date(), z.custom()), a value with safeParse that is not a zod-4 schema, and two modules that collide on one path are each reported. They go into the index as unrendered, so “not rendered” never reads as “not there”. instance-exports.ts still writes what did render, then exits 1, which is how it treats a failed kg-export. Logging the failure and exiting 0 would publish a partial zod/ that reads as complete. The host is left out. Its schema documents sit directly in its own directory, <site>/<name>/, not in a per-instance <name>/schema/, so it gets no zod/. The JSON-LD document drops schemas from its own omitted once it links the index. Its module-level Schema collector is still instance-bound and does not run for a foreign layer. But “not looked for” is false when the schemas are published and the document says where. Two cases keep schemas listed. One is a document with no conformsTo: an exemption, or no base. The other is a layer whose schemas directory cannot be resolved (zodSchemaScanDetermined, the scan’s own first step), because its index then says omitted: ["schemas"] too, and the two must not disagree. The gate fails the day a layer’s export lists a Schema node, because nothing yet maps a module node to its per-export renderings. Re-exports are public too. The publisher imports each module and reads every key, so export { FooSchema } from "./x" and export { X as YSchema } are rendered. The gate’s text half reads them as well (declaredExportNames): export const, export { … } lists with or without from, the name after as, and export * as N. A type-only export is not a value and is skipped. A bare export * from is a finding. Its names live in another module’s text, so whether they are published cannot be determined from this one, and could-not-determine is never green. List the names in an export { … } instead. Named subgraphs, and the root index above them . | Named subgraphs: <site>/subgraph/<HARNESS>/<PATH>/, with index.jsonld (direct members as pointers) and index.hydrated.jsonld (every member inline, deep). The harness root has index.jsonld only, because a deep hydrated file there would be a monolith. gen-subgraph-jsonld.ts frames each layer from its OWN export, so no subgraph names a cat-harness.jsonld#<foreign> fragment. The tree is committed under cat-harness/docs/subgraph/, its @context is <site>/ns/subgraph/v1.jsonld, and heavy bodies are content-addressed payloads under cat-harness/docs/payload/sha256/, copied verbatim to <site>/payload/. bootstrap and bootstrap-tools publish their own subgraphs, and the repository index links them with rdfs:seeAlso. The contract: kg-export §”Named subgraphs” and §”Payloads”. | The root index: <site>/index.jsonld and index.json, built at publish time by root-index.ts and never committed: a committed copy conflicts whenever two PRs change the set of harnesses. It names every declared layer at depth 1, with no node of any graph inlined. It exits 1, having written nothing, when a layer’s export is not where its identity says, rather than publish a shorter map. | . What is never in a published graph . | fsh-guts, and every reference to it, is stripped from the KG before publication. The one list is UNPUBLISHED_GRAPH_TYPOLOGIES in schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts. Every emitter filters on it where the document is built, not at upload: isPublishedGraphTypology, isPublishedDirectory (a directory holding ANY unpublished kind), isPublishedSkill and isPublishedSchemaModule, plus a diagram’s documentation prose (publishableDocumentation). The trashcan has its own document, <site>/fsh-guts.jsonld, from fsh-guts-export.ts. That is deliberate: a consumer may fetch it by name and must never arrive by following an edge. Mechanics: kg-export §”fsh-guts NEVER reaches a published graph”; what belongs in it: fsh-guts. | A skill that declares published: false in its front matter (unpublishedSkills in known-skills.ts). The name match and the declaration are two inputs on purpose: one asks whether a skill is NAMED after the trashcan, the other whether it SAID not to publish it. | The nodes of a state graph. The export carries the declared Directory node and its holdsGraph. No collector in kg-export.ts reads a state graph’s files. Where such contents are published, it is as their declared Subgraph node’s own document (todos.jsonld, directory-conventions §”Publishing a subgraph’s contents”), as a SQLite slice built at deploy, or on a branch rather than the site (QA verdicts, on qa-reports). | . The gates . | gate | fails when | . | check:published-instance-exports | the deploy does not run instance-exports.ts, a workflow running it drops an exempt layer’s own publisher, an exemption names no declared layer, or a published export fails or mints a relative @id; or, for a planned layer, a contract its skills name is not written to <stub>/schema/, the index is missing, the document’s conformsTo is not the index’s $id, or the document lists a Schema node the publisher does not render; or an exported Zod *Schema (read from the module text, re-exports included, confirmed Zod by import) is not written to <stub>/schema/zod/ and listed in the index, a module has a bare export * from (undetermined), the publisher did not scan, or it reports an import or render failure | . | root-index.ts at deploy | a layer’s export is missing; the deploy fails rather than publish a shorter map | . | subgraph:jsonld:check | the committed subgraph tree or its payloads are stale | . | check:process-index | a declared BPMN has no Process node in the published subgraphs | . | kg-export.test.ts | the published graph holds a forwarding node, or a published @id dangles | . | fsh-guts-unpublished.test.ts | the string fsh-guts appears anywhere in the built export | . | check:node-iris | a node’s identifier is not its file’s path under the release address (§”The release site”) | .

6558.title: What a consumer may assume of a draft
6558.content: . | That the id is stable. It is the one thing that does not move. | That the version distinguishes snapshots — and nothing more. It carries no promise that a snapshot remains fetchable, or that anyone announced it. | Nothing about availability. No registry, no tarball, no announcement. Draft is not “published somewhere quiet”; it is “the process that would make this depend-on-able has not been built”. | . A layer that wants to be depended upon from outside does not declare its way there. It waits for the process, which is somebody’s work and not a field.

6559.title: Do not
6559.content: . | Do not infer a publication state from evidence. A canonicalUrl, a GitHub Release, a Pages deployment or a dependsOn naming this layer are all things that exist for drafts too. Inferring from them erases the difference between “decided” and “nobody looked”. | Do not mint an id for something that already has one upstream. Record theirs as data, mint ours under the namespace above, and keep them apart. | Do not restate this skill in a work item, a proposal or AGENTS.md. A restatement drifts from its source. Point here instead. | .

6560.title: instance-publication (skill)
6560.content: The skill instance-publication as its source file cat-harness/skills/kg/kg-core/instance-publication.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

6561.title: /interaction-modality — ask in a form the person can answer
6561.content: Skill interaction-modality: Establish how to talk to the person in front of you before deciding what to say — audio, ordinary chat, selectable options for limited hand function, large-type for low vision, plain language — and hold that choice durably so every later session and sibling agent honours it. Covers the accessibility rules a conversational agent can actually keep, the settings surface in the published site, and how to drive a question set from DMN so the SAME logic serves every modality. Use at first contact with a new user, when a user reports difficulty answering, whenever a question is about to be asked, and before any long free-text prompt. Named by: Content acquisition, Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Multi-locale translation, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Ask the person, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Agent activity log, Staging a feature branch preview, and taking it down, Merge manager watch: wake, read the queue live, route, A refused merge-train member, Merge to main, A merge train, Saturation meta-merge: land the ready PRs when the runners are full, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route, Getting started, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . Process: the content core’s processes/conduct/getting-started.bpmn, Task_DetectModality and Task_AskIntent. Preferences: cat-harness/memory/interaction.json (committed, read at session start).

6562.title: Asking the person — the canonical rule (STRICT, read this first)
6562.content: This box is the ONE rule for putting any question or decision to the person. Every other copy (AGENTS.md, the .claude/skills/interaction-modality stub, the ask-well.sh hook, project instructions) points here. If a copy disagrees, this box wins. Every question goes out TWICE, in this order: . | A chat message that states the whole question on its own. What is being decided and why, every PR / work item / link it touches (each id glossed), what happens next, and every option with its letter, a one-line explanation, its trade-off, and which one you recommend. Say what you will do if no answer comes. | Then the tappable card with the same option letters and labels, so the answer is one tap. | . Every question tool counts, whatever the host calls it: AskUserQuestion (Claude Code), request_decision / the “Decision” card (Claude projects), a button card from post_widget, or any selection box a later host adds. Why both, and why the chat copy comes first. Once answered, a card shows only the option that was chosen, and a dismissed card shows nothing. The chat text is the only record of what was asked. This overrides host guidance that says the opposite. The Claude projects request_decision tool tells the agent “Ask once, and do not repeat the question in a message.” Write the full question in the chat anyway, then post the card. Never: . | a card with no full question and options written before it; | a request for a typed reply (“answer 1y 2n”, “reply A or B”): the owner has very limited hand function, and typing is the cost this rule removes; | a pointer instead of the question (“see the card”, “see the issue”). | . If no card tool exists in this host, post the numbered options in chat, say the card tool is unavailable, and keep each answer to a single short choice. In the processes, this box is the skill ask-the-person (input and output schemas) and the subprocess Process_AskThePerson: compose, write in the chat, offer the card, then record the answer or proceed on the default. A diagram step that puts a question to the person is a callActivity with calledElement="Process_AskThePerson", so the association is visible in the diagram rather than remembered. The rest of this skill is the reasoning and the detail: §4.1 for what the context must contain, §4.2 for the form.

6563.title: 0. The failure this prevents
6563.content: An agent that asks a good question in an unusable form has asked nothing. The usual shape of it: a long open prompt — “Tell me about the folio you have in mind, what content types you expect, and how you’d like it organised” — sent to somebody for whom typing is slow and painful. The reply comes back short, the agent reads shortness as low engagement, and asks another open question. @litlfred, this repository’s owner, has very limited hand function. Every question put to that user is to be answerable by selecting, not by typing: numbered or lettered options, a recommended default stated first, and the work proceeding on that default when no answer comes. Free text is always available and never required. Generalise the rule rather than special-casing the person: . A question’s cost is paid by the person answering it. Design the question so the cheapest possible answer is still a complete one.

6564.title: 1. The modality profiles
6564.content: Four axes, independent — a user can be on more than one. | profile | what changes | detection signal | . | low-dexterity | Every question is a selection. Options numbered. One recommended default, first, marked. Never more than ~4 options. Batch decisions so one answer covers several. Long-running work is announced, not confirmed. | user says so; very short replies to open questions; typos of a kind that cost effort to fix; voice input artefacts | . | low-vision | Large type in anything rendered. No information carried by colour alone. Short lines. Tables kept narrow or replaced by lists. ASCII diagrams avoided — they do not survive a screen reader or a 200 % zoom. | user says so; requests to enlarge; screen-reader artefacts | . | audio | Answers read aloud cleanly: no code fences in prose, no tables, no “see the diagram”, spell out identifiers on first use, one idea per sentence. Questions asked one at a time. | the channel is voice; the user is dictating | . | plain-language | Shorter sentences, domain jargon expanded on first use, no nested clauses. Independent of disability — it is also the right default for a second-language reader. | user asks for simpler wording; the folio’s audience | . The default profile — nobody has said anything — is ordinary chat with selectable options wherever there is a genuine choice.

6565.title: 2. Detecting it without an interrogation
6565.content: The detection must not itself be an unusable question. So: . | Read cat-harness/memory/interaction.json first. If it says, you are done. Never re-ask what is recorded. | Read the channel. A voice session is audio without asking. A terminal session is not. | Offer once, as options. At first contact and not again: . How would you like me to ask you things? . | Options I can pick from (recommended — fewest keystrokes) | Ordinary chat | Read aloud / voice | Large type | . (No answer is fine — I’ll use 1.) . | Watch for the signal you were not given. Consistently one-word answers to open questions, or an explicit “hard to type”, moves the user to low-dexterity and is recorded, so no future session re-learns it. | . Never ask a user to name a disability. Ask what form they want the conversation to take. The profile is about the interface, not about them.

6566.title: 3. Where the preference lives
6566.content: cat-harness/memory/interaction.json, committed, so every sibling session reads it rather than asking again. { "$schema": "https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/schemas/interaction.json", "users": { "litlfred@ibiblio.org": { "profiles": ["low-dexterity"], "note": "Very limited hand function. Every question selectable; never require typing.", "source": "stated by the user" } }, "default": { "profiles": [] } } . source is required and is one of stated by the user, inferred from behaviour, or set in the site settings. An inferred profile is honoured and is labelled as inferred, so it can be corrected. 3.1 Who is typing, outside GitHub too . An entry is keyed by a handle, and the session has to work out whose handle it is before the entry can apply. Identity is (provider, handle), GitHub first. One resolver answers for every host: bun run cat auth:login --all (cat-harness-tools/src/core/identity.ts). It prints every identity the session can see, each bare and as provider:handle: . | provider | read from | vouched for by | . | github | the auth Tool’s own resolver: a token, or GITHUB_ACTOR in Actions | GitHub | . | gitlab | GITLAB_USER_LOGIN, only inside GitLab CI | GitLab | . | claude | the agent host’s signed-in account | the agent host | . | any | CAT_HARNESS_PERSON, provider:handle[,…], for this session only | nobody: the person says so | . | any | the user-level store’s identities, and the chosen entry of its profiles | nobody: the person says so | . | git | git config user.email, then user.name | nobody: self-asserted | . So an entry may list gitlab:<handle> or claude:<email> among its aliases, and a person with no GitHub token is still recognised. A self-asserted identity is enough to choose how to TALK to someone, never enough to AUTHORIZE them. Permissions take only what GitHub vouched for (task-authorization §”Asking who you are”). When nothing matches, that is a third state. It is neither “no preference” nor a guess. The session-start sweep says it could not determine who is typing, and applies the strictest profile on record until told otherwise, so an account switch never drops an accommodation. Which agent host runs the session is reported too (cat-harness-tools/src/core/agent-host.ts), because most hosts tell a command nothing about the person. Of Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Codex, Cursor, Antigravity and the Copilot CLI and coding agent, only Claude Code passes the account (CLAUDE_CODE_USER_EMAIL, in its cloud sessions). On the others the resolver adds a note saying the host passes no account, and the person is found from a forge token, CAT_HARNESS_PERSON, the user-level store or the git author. The markers are the ones two independent detectors agree on; a new host is one row in that file’s table. Several people. On a shared machine each person has their own home directory, so their own user-level store. In a shared session or under a shared login, CAT_HARNESS_PERSON names who is typing now. A person with several accounts on one provider lists each one in the store, as entries or as identities: { "github": ["litlfred", "litlfred-bot"] }; every one is a match key, and an entry marked active: true comes first. When the keys match more than one person on record, the sweep says so and the session applies the strictest of their profiles, never the first one listed. Several people in one store. identity.json may hold named profiles, profiles: { "<name>": { identities, interaction } }. The one in use is the profile CAT_HARNESS_PROFILE names, else the store’s activeProfile, else the one whose identities match CAT_HARNESS_PERSON, else the only one. With several profiles and nothing to choose between them, the resolver reports a third state, ambiguous-multi-user, and applies the strictest interaction profile on record until someone says who is typing. The same state is reported when the session matches several people in interaction.json whose profiles differ. A preference that must not be committed lives in the user-level store, ~/.config/cat-harness/identity.json (or $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/…, or the path in CAT_HARNESS_USER_CONFIG), under interaction. It is per machine and never in the repository. The sweep prints it, marked as not committed.

6567.title: 4. Asking a question well
6567.content: §4.1 is what the question has to contain; §4.2 is what shape it has to take. A question can pass every item in §4.2 and still be unanswerable, because none of those say what the options mean. 4.1 Context before the question (STRICT) . Order matters, and it is: context → options → recommendation → question. Never the question first with the explanation available on request. The test is one sentence, and it is checkable in a single pass: . Can the reader answer without opening anything? . If answering needs them to open an issue, a file, a diff or a scrollback, the question is not ready. A link is where somebody goes for more; it is never where the terms are defined. And when a link IS the right thing — a rendered page the reader has to see for themselves — it points at the page, not at the site it is on. The rule and where the page list comes from: feedback-deep-links; the failure it also hides: continual-progress §”Link the PAGE, never the site root”. Six parts, in order: . | What is being decided, in plain words — stated as what will differ depending on the answer, not as the name of the decision. | Every identifier expanded on first use. A work item id, an option name you coined, a field, a Lean declaration, a file path: all opaque without their gloss, above all an option name you coined yourself, because it feels defined to you. | The options, compared — what each does, its pro, its con, what it changes downstream, and how reversible it is. Laid out here, in the prose, where the rows can be read against each other; a selection tool shows one option at a time, so trade-offs written into its labels are not a comparison. decision-comparison carries the columns, why cost and downstream impact are different things, and when a decision is too small to deserve a table. | Your recommendation, and why, stated first and marked. See §4.2. | What happens if they say nothing. Then do that. | The question itself, last. | . This binds every place a decision is handed to the person, not only an explicit question tool: the end-of-turn “next” line, a work item’s ## Done when, a PR body asking the author to choose, a comment on an issue. Those are where it is most often broken, because they feel like reporting rather than asking. A PR body as a whole, not only its question, is governed by pr-description. The prose does not travel — the question object must stand alone (STRICT) . The six parts above assume the reader is in the conversation, reading the prose that precedes the question. Often they are not. A question asked by a background session, a cloud session, a subagent or a scheduled run reaches the person through a channel that carries only the structured fields — the question text, the option labels, the option descriptions. Everything written around the call stays in a transcript the person would have to go and open. The asker’s analysis stays in its own transcript, and a relay has to reconstruct it. So the test grows one clause: . Can the reader answer without opening anything — including the session that asked? . Put in the structured fields everything needed to choose: . | field | carries | . | the question | what will differ depending on the answer, with every identifier expanded. Never a bare noun phrase — “kupb scope” is a topic, not a question. | . | each option’s description | that option’s own consequence and how reversible it is. A reader comparing two options must be able to do it from the two descriptions alone. | . | one option’s description | what happens if they say nothing, marked as the default and phrased as what you will then do. | . The comparison table still belongs in the prose, where rows can be read against each other, but nothing may be load-bearing only in the prose. Two things this rules out: . | A question whose context sits in the paragraph above the call. Correct in a live conversation, invisible through a relay. | An option label carrying the trade-off and a description carrying nothing — or the reverse. A label is a handle; the description is the argument. | . The question goes in the chat too — both, every time (STRICT) . The rule above makes the structured fields stand alone. This is its mirror: the chat must stand alone as well. Every question handed to the person is written in the chat, as text — the question, the numbered options, the recommendation and what happens with no answer — and asked through the selection tool. Neither copy may depend on the other. A question asked only in the selection tool vanishes with one stray tap; for a person with limited hand function a stray tap is the ordinary case. A dismissal is not an answer. The tool reports a dismissed box as “do not proceed”, and the right move is exactly that: proceed on nothing. The question stays open in the chat text, and the next turn re-asks it through the selection tool when the person indicates it was accidental — never treat the dismissal as a choice of any option, including the default. (The stated default governs silence over time, not a dismissal.) . Two things this rules out: . | A question that exists only inside the selection tool. One dismissal, one connection drop or one client that does not render the box, and the decision is gone with no trace in the conversation. | A chat that says “see the question below”. A pointer to the box is not the question; if the box goes, the pointer points at nothing. | . And when you are the one relaying somebody else’s blocked question: say that you are relaying, and say where the answer has to be given. An answer typed at the relay does not reach the asker. The reverse direction, a sibling getting its question to the agent that is talking with the person, and the answer back, is hand-back-to-discussion. Worked example . Unanswerable — every content word is undefined, no option has a cost, and there is no recommendation: . next — cross-agent skill install + prefix. I’d want your call on prefix-at-rest vs prefix-at-install before writing anything. The same decision, askable: . Next up is installing this platform’s skills into whichever agent is running (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor), so each one can load them. Skills would get an fa- prefix so their names cannot collide with the host agent’s own commands: /fa-beans-tui rather than /beans-tui. One decision shapes everything else — where the prefix gets applied: . | When a skill is installed into an agent (recommended) — files in this repo keep their plain names, and the prefix is added as they are emitted. Nothing here has to change. | In this repository itself — rename every skill file. That touches the package manifests, every skill ref in the BPMN diagrams, two doc generators and every cross-reference between skill bodies, and is painful to reverse. | . Say nothing and I will take (1) when I start. A pending question is not a STATUS — ask it (STRICT) . “Stream 3 is blocked on four questions” is not a report. It is a question you declined to ask. Naming a block, linking to where it lives and summarising it still leaves the person unable to answer with a click. Whoever can put the question to the person owns asking it. A question does not “belong to” the session that blocked on it: if you can act on the answer — and an agent with repository access usually can — ask it. If you truly cannot act, ask anyway and carry the answer back. Pointing somewhere is the failure mode, not the fix. “Answer it in that session” moves the whole cost of the decision onto the person. Reserve it for what genuinely cannot be done from here, and say plainly that it cannot. When several are pending, ask the most consequential in full and give a count for the rest — never “which question would you like me to ask?”. §”More than one decision pending” below carries that rule. More than one decision pending — ask ONE, count the rest . The six parts above are per decision. When several are open, stating all in full is a wall, and naming them compactly is a teaser. Ask the one that is actually next, in full. For the others, give a COUNT and no option names. Two other decisions are waiting; I will put each properly when it is next. A count says work is queued without inviting an answer to a question whose terms the reader cannot see. There is no “just listing what’s open” exemption. A wrap-up that names a decision has handed it over, whatever the framing sentence says. Either the options and their costs are there, or the name comes out and a count goes in. Enforced, not remembered — the layers . A rule that depends on being remembered is not enforced. So: . | layer | what it does | what it cannot do | . | .claude/skills/interaction-modality/ | makes this skill offerable by name | triggering is probabilistic; it helps an agent already thinking about asking well | . | PreToolUse on AskUserQuestion → scripts/ask-well.sh | prints the six parts at the one moment the rule certainly applies, on every agent and every session | it sees the tool call, not the prose written before it, so it REMINDS and never blocks — a gate that cannot tell must not refuse | . | schemas/process/decision-request.ts | makes the comparison unomittable: no optionals, so a decision with two options and one comparison does not parse, and renderDecision emits the prose table and the selection from ONE object so they cannot drift | it cannot tell a good con from a lazy one, and does not try — it checks that the question was asked, never that the answer is honest | . | Stop → scripts/decisions-named-not-asked.ts | reads the turn that just ENDED and names the paragraph that handed decisions over bare (e.g. a closing list of open item ids) — the one path the layers keyed on a question tool cannot see | it reads prose, so it is a heuristic; it reminds and never blocks, and a paragraph that happens to carry a comparison suppresses it | . None of these is sufficient on its own. bun test cat-harness-tools/scripts/tests/decision-request.test.ts asserts each refusal, and the Stop hook’s fixtures are real turns rather than invented strings. The posture, and the condition that revisits it . The hook reminds; it does not gate. A gate that refused a well-formed question because the schema turned out too narrow would cost the person the one channel they use to correct an agent. So: . | The hook reminds. It never blocks, and a question always reaches the person, well-formed or not. | renderDecision is the house style for any decision with more than two options, or any decision whose options differ in cost rather than only in kind. Write the object, render the prose, then offer the selection. | Gating is revisited on EVIDENCE, not on a date. | . The condition: twelve RENDERED decision records. bun run cat health reports bean-rendered-decision-records — work items whose decision actually went through {@link renderDecision}, detected from the five-row table it emits. At twelve, a person can read them and judge whether the schema fits the decisions this repository actually has. An ## Options heading is NOT a rendered decision, because work items carry considered-options sections as ordinary practice, so their count grows without anyone using the schema. The counter is a health metric over beans/, not a second store, because a parallel store of decision objects would be a count free to disagree with the work item store’s. The record goes in the work item it belongs to, under ## Options, where madr.md’s two-option floor and bean-thin-decision-records govern it; renderDecision composes the chat message. The unit is WORK ITEMS, not decisions: hasRenderedDecision is a per-bean boolean, so twelve means twelve different work items. The unit is not changed, because moving it without moving the number is a silent re-calibration. A deferral with no trigger is not a deferral: it is indistinguishable a month later from a decision nobody made. 4.2 Form — the checklist . Before any question, all five: . | Could this be a selection? If the answer set is finite, make it one. | Is there a recommended option, and is it first and marked? A user who does not want to decide should be able to pick the first thing and be right. | Is it four options or fewer? Beyond that, split the question. | Does no answer have a safe meaning? Say what you will do if they say nothing, then do that. Silence must never block the work. | Is it blocking at all? Do everything that does not depend on the answer first, and ask at the point where the answer is actually needed. | . And the negative rule: do not ask a question whose answer you could look up. Every fact getting-started reads from the filesystem is a question not asked. This is the largest accessibility win available, and it is invisible. 4.3 After the answer — a ruling is a skill edit, not just an applied answer . The asking is half the loop. The answer comes back, and if it settles how a kind of thing is decided rather than only this one, it is a rule and it is written into the skill that governs it in the same turn: the rule and its reason in the narrative, the quote and date in the skill’s provenance log. Otherwise the next session asks again. The rule, the three questions that identify a rule-level answer, and why it needs no permission: symbiotic-interaction §2. It applies to any author correction, not only to answers to questions asked here.

6568.title: 5. Driving the questions from DMN — one logic, four surfaces
6568.content: Guided questions driven by DMN logic, across modalities, are two separable things: . What to ask next is a decision. It belongs in a DMN table alongside folio-intent.dmn: inputs are the facts known so far, output is the next question’s id (or none, when enough is known). It is authored by whoever owns the process, is reviewable as a table, and is the same for every user. How to render the question is the modality. Options as a numbered list in chat, as spoken alternatives one at a time over audio, as large-type radio buttons on the site. The DMN table never learns about any of this. facts ──▶ [ next-question.dmn ] ──▶ question id ──▶ renderer(profile) ──▶ user ▲ │ └──────────────────── answer recorded as a new fact ─────────────────────┘ . Four properties over an agent improvising the interview: . | The question set is finite and reviewable. You can read the table and know every question the agent can ask. | It terminates. A table whose output can be none has a stopping condition; an improvising agent does not. | Asking becomes obligatory rather than optional. This is the trick folio-intent.dmn already uses: ask is an outcome of the table, so the agent cannot route past it; an agent that decides for itself whether to ask will, under pressure to be helpful, decide not to. | A question skipped is auditable. The facts are recorded; you can replay the table and see which rule fired. | . The limits, stated so nobody is surprised: the FEEL subset this repo implements covers equality, comparison and one-of — no ranges, no not(), no function calls (src/workflow/decision-table.ts). A genuinely open question — “what is this paper about?” — is not a decision and does not belong in a table. And conversation is not a wizard: a user must always be able to say something the table did not anticipate, which is what option 5 of the intent question is for.

6569.title: 6. Grounding — what this follows
6569.content: The rules above are the subset of published accessibility guidance that a conversational agent can actually keep. Named so they can be checked rather than taken on trust: . | WCAG 2.2 AA is the baseline for anything rendered — the docs site, the viewer, a generated PDF. The success criteria that bite hardest here: 1.4.4 Resize text (200 % without loss), 1.4.3 Contrast, 1.4.1 Use of Colour (never colour alone), 2.4.7 Focus Visible, 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions. | WCAG 2.2’s newer criteria are the dexterity ones: 2.5.7 Dragging Movements, 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) — 24 × 24 CSS px — and 3.3.7 Redundant Entry, which says do not make someone enter the same information twice. §3’s committed preferences file is 3.3.7 applied to a conversation. | Cognitive accessibility (WCAG 3.1, and W3C’s COGA guidance) is what §4’s “four options or fewer” and plain-language profile come from. | EN 301 549 is the procurement standard that makes WCAG AA a legal requirement in EU public-sector contexts; Section 508 does the same in the US. Folios published for public-sector use land in those contexts. | Authoring Tool Accessibility Guidelines (ATAG 2.0) is the one most often missed: it covers tools that produce content, which is what this platform is. Part A is the tool being usable; Part B is the tool helping the author produce accessible output. The alt-text and heading-order checks a folio’s QA sweep should carry are Part B. | .

6570.title: 7. The settings surface
6570.content: The published site carries a settings control (gear, top right) writing the same four profiles to localStorage, so a reader who is not the author still gets large type or reduced motion. It is per-viewer and per-browser by construction — it never reaches an agent. cat-harness/memory/interaction.json is the agent-facing record and the site control is the reader-facing one; keep them separate.

6571.title: 8. Anti-patterns
6571.content: . | The question first, the context on request (§4.1), typically in the private vocabulary the agent built while working. “Happy to explain if useful” does not repair it. | Asking someone to describe their disability. Ask about the interface. | Re-asking what cat-harness/memory/interaction.json records (WCAG 3.3.7). | A “quick open question” because the option list felt like overkill. The list is cheaper for the person answering. | Blocking on an answer with no default. State the default, act on it. | Treating an inferred profile as a diagnosis. It is a rendering choice, labelled inferred from behaviour, and the user overrules it. | Accessibility as a rendering concern only. The largest win is §4’s last rule — not asking at all — and no stylesheet delivers it. | .

6573.title: Working an issue — announce, then re-check
6573.content: Skill issue-working: Working a tracked issue — announce the branch when you create it rather than when you finish, and re-check the issue for new AND edited comments while you work. Both rules are about the gap between your view of an issue and everyone else’s. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Agent activity log, Close the bean, Drain the beans, Agent bean lifecycle, Open the bean, Code change and review, Merge the base branch in, A refused merge-train member, Requirements filing: promote, organise, trace, supersede, or retire, SME Review of Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route, Test Data Curation — Fixed Sets and Generated Recipes, Watching a pinned upstream dependency, Adopting an upstream version bump, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Editing and HCI validation, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . Two rules. Both exist because your view of an issue and everyone else’s diverge the moment you start, and neither side can see that it has happened.

6574.title: Announce the branch when you create it, not when you finish
6574.content: Comment on the issue with the branch name, the process and phase, and the work items claimed — at creation. Before it, run the collision review in coordinate §”Starting new work”. A summary posted after the work lands is not a substitute. Until the first comment appears, a sibling session and a human both see an issue with nobody visibly on it, which is precisely the state the work plan exists to prevent and the one no sibling can detect. Announce once, on the single edge into implementation. A process that loops back into implement re-enters on the same branch, and re-announcing each time is noise that trains the reader to skip the announcements that matter.

6575.title: Re-check the issue while you work
6575.content: Checking once at session start is not checking. Requirements change while you are heads-down, and the comment that changes direction is the one you are least likely to see. Track what you have already read as two marks, not one: . | a comment-id high-water mark, and | the newest edit timestamp — because an edited comment keeps its id, and an edited requirement is a changed requirement. A high-water mark alone cannot see an edit at all. | . With no stored mark, everything counts as unseen. A fresh container has read nothing, and defaulting the other way is exactly how the comments that change direction get skipped — silently, because nothing distinguishes read from never looked.

6576.title: When the new material is a large chunk of work, stop
6576.content: Do not fold it into the current run. Say that this is a good stopping point for review, link the artefact, and confirm priorities before continuing. Absorbing it buries a scope change inside a diff nobody asked for, and spends the author’s next review on work they have not agreed to. A large new ask is a decision to hand back, under the usual discipline — context, options with their costs, a marked recommendation, then the question.

6577.title: What an issue is for, against its neighbours
6577.content: They are not synonymous, and conflating them is how an agent closes something it had no standing to close: . |   | what it carries | . | issue | stakeholder sign-off | . | change proposal | code review | . | work item | work-plan tracking | . Never close an issue without explicit authorisation from the analyst or stakeholder. Whether work is done is a judgement, and an agent must never assume completion on its own say-so — the same rule that stops you closing a work item a sibling is mid-flight on. That authorisation may be given in advance: an issue-close waiver, which names the issues it covers and expires. It is the stakeholder answering the same question earlier, which is the whole of what this rule asks for — never the agent supplying the judgement itself. confirmation-waiver.md. After each round of implementation, post a summary on the issue, not only on the change proposal: what was accomplished, what remains, and links to the updated content for review.

6578.title: Milestones and decision points go on the issue, as they happen
6578.content: A round can be long, and the owner follows the issue, not the session or the PR. So between round summaries, post on the issue at two kinds of moment: . | A milestone — a result the owner would want to know before the round ends: a method lands, a benchmark number moves, a tool turns out not to run here, an approach is replaced because measurement reversed it. | A decision point — whenever you put a choice to the owner in the chat, put it on the issue too, in the same shape: context, options with their cost, the marked recommendation, and what happens if nobody answers (interaction-modality). A choice made only in the chat leaves no record where the next reader looks. | . Not every push: a push is reported on the PR. An issue update is for what a stakeholder would act on. Each update must be readable on its own, because it is read days later without the session: status, approach in a line, findings with their numbers and provenance, what landed, and next steps — and a link to the previous update rather than a restatement of it.

6579.title: A sign-off on the issue becomes a record
6579.content: When a requirements document is signed off on its issue — approved, amended, rejected, deferred or cancelled — the comment is the evidence, not the record. The record is a requirement-signoff attestation in the attestations graph (test/attestations/requirement-signoff/<set>.attestations.json): who (kind, id, actor), at, scope, outcome, the stage it moves the requirement set to, the reason, and evidence — the comment’s permalink, …/issues/<n>#issuecomment-<id>. A sign-off given in chat is quoted on the issue first, dated, so the evidence link exists. The agent writes the record of a person’s decision; it never writes one for a decision nobody made, and check:requirements refuses approved or accepted without a human one.

6580.title: Before you publish that something does not exist (STRICT)
6580.content: An issue comment is published, and a false claim in one costs more than a missing true one: it sends the next reader off to verify an accusation, and the correction never reaches everybody the original did. So before an issue comment, PR body or commit message asserts that a file, a function or somebody’s cited precedent does not exist, re-read it from the remote — git show origin/main:<path> — in a command of its own, and check the open branches when the claim is nobody has built this. Grepping your checkout answers “is this in my base”, not “does this exist”, and a git fetch earlier in the same compound command is not a barrier when siblings merge every few minutes. bean-coordination (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan) §”Re-derive from the REMOTE” has the two guards. For the third case, a path that exists only on an open PR’s head, ask the open-work-lookup Tool (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan, work-plan/tools/open-work-lookup/).

6581.title: When the work has a BEAN and no issue (STRICT)
6581.content: A round summary is owed either way. With no issue, it goes on the change proposal AND into the work item — the work item is the durable artefact a sibling reads, and a summary that exists only in a PR thread is invisible to the work plan on main. And a work item that has an issue carries the link BOTH ways: a reader arriving at either object has to be able to reach the other, and a check reports the ones that cannot. When to open an issue at all is crdm-detect §”Issue association” — scan before creating one, and never create one without permission. This section is about what is owed once the work exists, not about manufacturing an issue for every work item.

6583.title: User journey coverage (DRAFT journeys J1 to J4)
6583.content: What the HCERT library must do for each step of the workshop storyline, and whether it does. OHS Player, OHS Stack and the CHW and wallet apps are consumers of the Kotlin library; rendering, scanning, storage, HTTP and FHIR record keeping are theirs. Source: stakeholder directive dir-journeys, 2026-10-20. | Journey step | Library capability | Status | . | J1 Country A clinic issues a DVC for each newborn vaccine (Hep B, polio) | DVCMin payload, one event per certificate (STT-PAY-003); no identity document for a newborn (STT-PAY-005); guardian name gn; any national vaccine code in vp (extensible binding) | Done: HcertIssuer.prepare / finish | . | J1 signs with the clinic’s DSC key held in Android Keystore or an HSM | Two-phase signing, no private key in process (STT-ISS-004, STT-COS-006) | Done | . | J1 printed paper QR, or SMS/MMS | HC1 string is QR Alphanumeric only (STT-QR-001); the app renders it at error correction Q | Done (rendering is the app’s) | . | J1 DEV keys and DEV trust list | Trust store loads GDHCN DID trustlist v2 documents (DEV, UAT, PROD alike) and PEM | Done: addDidDocument, addPem; the app fetches from the trust list distribution endpoints | . | J2 CHW, offline, reads the foreign QR to register the child and refer | Explicitly named unverified read, its result typed as unverified (STT-VER-011) | Done: HcertVerifier.readUnverified | . | J2 alternative: verify offline on the CHW device | Verification is synchronous and offline against a store the app filled earlier (STT-GEN-012, STT-VER-009) | Done; which one J2 uses is the journey’s open question | . | J3 Clinic verifies the foreign DVC | GDHCN verification in the STT-VER-001 order, typed failures (STT-VER-008), EKU check (STT-VER-004) | Done: HcertVerifier.verify, PR 129 vector verifies on JVM and Node | . | J3 imports the immunization into the domestic record | The verified DVCMin fields; mapping to FHIR R4 Immunization/Patient | Not in this library (the app maps). Worked examples in smart-trust-demo: TrustDemoJ3HepB and TrustDemoJ3Bcg, with their verification provenance | . | J3 adds the national schedule code beside the foreign vaccine code | The library passes the issuer’s vp code through unchanged and rejects nothing for an unknown code. The translation is a FHIR ConceptMap ($translate) the clinic EHR applies, adding the national coding and never replacing the issuer’s | Not in this library. Worked example in smart-trust-demo: ConceptMap TrustDemoProductToOnesaEpi (product → national schedule dose of Onesa, the demo’s fictional home country); a product with no entry goes to the nurse, whose decision is recorded (TrustDemoJ3Adjudication) and added to the map | . | J4.0 National portal issues one passcode-protected VHL QR per family member | VHL payload (SHL payload format, flag P) as a CBOR map at HCERT claim -260 key 5 (STT-VHL-001, STT-VHL-002); key generation (STT-VHL-004); JWE dir / A256GCM encryption of each document (STT-VHL-007) | Done: HcertIssuer with Payload.Vhl, HcertVhl.newKey, HcertVhl.encrypt; hosting the manifest and enforcing the passcode are the VHL host’s | . | J4.1 Clinic abroad scans a VHL, fetches with passcode, reads IPS | Verify the VHL HCERT, map or vhlink:/ string at key 5, and the link’s exp (STT-VHL-002, STT-VHL-009); ITI-YY5 request (STT-VHL-005); HTTP Message Signatures (STT-VHL-008); manifest Bundle (STT-VHL-006); decrypt each document (STT-VHL-007) | Done: HcertVerifier.verify, HcertVhl.buildManifestRequest, buildSignatureBase/signatureHeader, parseManifest, decrypt; the HTTP, mutual TLS and AuditEvents are the app’s | .

6584.title: VHL: what the specifications say, and where they disagree
6584.content: Changes raised upstream: WorldHealthOrganization/smart-trust#130 (subclaim 5 is a VHL, a CBOR map), WorldHealthOrganization/smart-trust-phw#17 (payload types match SMART Health Links), and a patch for IHE ITI.VHL in upstream/ihe-iti-vhl/ (ITI-YY3 key 5 as a CBOR map, example fixes). Open issues OI-21 to OI-29. The IHE ITI VHL profile and the WHO VerifiableHealthLinkPayload model share the SMART Health Links payload fields, but: . | IHE’s manifest is a FHIR List search returning a searchset Bundle of DocumentReferences (ITI-YY5), not the SMART Health Links files[] manifest; the Bundle is not signed, and the journey’s “signed VHL manifests” exist in neither specification. | The value at hcert key 5 is a vhlink:/ text string in ITI-YY3 but a decoded JSON object in the ITI-YY4 example; HCERT 3.2.7.1.5 calls it a SMART Health Link (OI-06). | WHO requires type (vhl) and types exp and v as strings; IHE has no type and uses numbers. | JWE alg/enc are not normative (the example is dir / A256GCM); no zip. | Requester authentication (RFC 9421 HTTP signatures, UDAP, or a VC) and the DID trust list’s mapping to a COSE kid are under-specified. | .
