6854.title: Merge-conflict patterns — what a merge may resolve on its own
6854.content: Skill merge-conflict-patterns: Merge the base branch in and resolve, without a person, only the conflicts a DECLARED pattern covers — generated files, generated README regions, QA sidecars — then prove the result with the gate set. Refuses the whole merge when any conflict is authored or undeclared. Use for “merge main”, “resolve the conflicts”, “the PR is conflicted again”, “auto-resolve”, and when adding a pattern for a new kind of churn. Also governs what a merge steward does with a merge-train member it had to refuse: one deduplicated work item under the PR’s own epic, a hand-back to the owning session with a fail condition, one dispatched agent when nobody owns it, one PR comment, and the close. Named by: Merge the base branch in, Merge manager watch: wake, read the queue live, route, A refused merge-train member, Merge to main, A merge train, Saturation meta-merge: land the ready PRs when the runners are full, Guideline Updates . bun run cat merge:main is the command; sdlc/processes/merge-base.bpmn is the process it executes, called from Task_PrepareMerge in code-change-review.bpmn. The patterns themselves are data in cat-harness-tools/scripts/merge-conflict-patterns.ts. This page says what each one is FOR, so a reader can tell a deliberate refusal from a gap. Most main-into-branch merges that conflict do so only on generated files, and every one of those resolves the same way — take the base’s copy, regenerate — so resolving them by hand costs an agent a round and the PR another CI run for nothing.

6855.title: The three rules that make it safe
6855.content: . | All or nothing. Every conflicted path is classified before anything is touched. One refusal ABORTS the merge and restores the tree. Resolving nine generated files and leaving one authored conflict half-done reads as progress, and is not. | Proved, not assumed. After resolving, bun run cat regen asks the checks the CI workflow runs (under merge:main, those whose inputs either side changed since the fork point; --full-regen asks every one) and runs each stale one’s writer until the tree settles. Anything unrepaired aborts the merge. No pattern names its own check: the gate set is derived from the workflow and cannot drift, a hand-kept list of check names can. | Classify with the BASE’s patterns, not your tree’s. pathClass reads PATTERNS from the checkout it is running in. A branch that forked before a pattern was declared therefore classifies by the OLD declaration, and every path in a newly-declared family reads authored — the one verdict that routes work to a person. | . A path that no pattern names is refused. Adding automation is adding a pattern, deliberately, with its reason — never widening a glob on a hunch. Applying rule 3 . A stale tree can be wrong in either direction. A pattern the base has added makes it over-report authored conflicts, which sends a person work the base already declares mechanical. A pattern the base has narrowed, reordered or retired makes it under-report: it takes a side on a path the base now refuses. So git fetch, and classify with the BASE’s own merge-base.ts (from a worktree of the tools at the base, git worktree add --detach <dir> origin/<base>), run against your checkout with --root <your checkout> --base origin/<base> (add --dry-run to classify and change nothing). merge-main.yml does the same: it checks out main’s tools and runs main’s merge-base.ts --root on the PR’s branch. The number that decides whether a human is needed must come from the declaration the merge will actually be resolved under.

6856.title: A merge round — run each check ONCE
6856.content: Most of a round of folding main into a PR is the same question asked twice. What each step costs and adds: . | step | cost | what it adds | . | merge:main, including its own regen | 5–10 min — regen 238–309 s with nothing stale, 601–639 s when a writer runs | THE regen; rule 2 above | . | skill:register | 1–2 min | the derived artefacts the merge left owed | . | a standalone regen after merge:main | 4–5 min | nothing for the merge — same tree; it can only add a pair already stale on both parents, which CI reports anyway | . | full local bun run cat gates | ~24 min (1429 s), nearly all bun test (~21.8k tests) on 3–4 local cores | what CI’s sharded run says in ~5 min, 4 ways | . | regen again in a fresh checkout, to prove a no-op | 4–5 min | what CI’s own clean checkout already proves | . The timings in this section were recorded by 2026-10-08, when cat-harness was seeded. Re-measure with bun run cat measure:merge-round before you quote them. Three of five rows repeat a measurement somebody else, or the same command, has already made. So: . When every conflict is generated — the trimmed round . “Generated” means every conflicted path was resolved by a declared take-base, region or sidecar pattern below, and the merge brought in no authored change of yours to reconcile. | bun run cat state:mount, then bun run cat merge:main. merge:main’s regen IS the regen. Do not run another one after it. | bun run cat skill:register until bun run cat skill:register:check passes. The chain can need two passes: one writer’s output is another’s input. | Targeted checks, and only these: . | skill:register:check and kg:detangle:check — the two reds a generated-only merge actually hit in CI; | subgraph:jsonld:check — a merge or edit that changes a skill also changes its payload hash; skill:register does not run subgraph:jsonld, so run the writer (bun run cat subgraph:jsonld) when the check is red; | check:declared-paths (never with --update here) and check:process-index; | bun run typecheck, and bun run cat lint at 0 errors; | the deletion audit — git diff --name-status --diff-filter=D HEAD^1 HEAD -- '*/test/results/*' must list only files main itself deleted. A gitignored-but-tracked file is dropped by a merge silently, local checks stay green because the writer recreated it on disk, and CI’s fresh checkout fails. merge:main refuses such a drop itself (§”When one side deleted the file”); after a hand merge, restore each one main still tracks with git checkout HEAD^2 -- <path>; | submodule pins equal to main’s — git ls-tree HEAD bootstrap bootstrap-tools against git ls-tree origin/main bootstrap bootstrap-tools. Not git submodule status: merge-queue §”git add -A after a merge silently reverts the submodule gitlinks” says why it cannot see this; | the fsh-guts mount is not committed — git diff --stat origin/main HEAD -- fsh-guts is empty; | git merge-tree --write-tree origin/main HEAD reports 0 conflicts, with the exit status captured on the next line (prepare-merge step 4). | . | Push, never with force. CI’s sharded run is the full gate set. Skip the local full bun run cat gates and the fresh-checkout regen for this kind of merge: each repeats something CI does better. | . When it is NOT generated-only — keep the full local run . An AUTHORED file conflicted, or the merge touched code (a script, test, schema or workflow that conflicted or that you reconciled by hand, on either side): run the full local bun run cat gates before pushing, and read prepare-merge §”What a green LOCAL run entitles you to claim” before quoting it. The targeted list above is chosen for a merge that changed only artefacts with one right answer; it cannot see a semantic conflict such as an import of a module the other side moved (merge-queue §”A train admits only members that STACK cleanly”). Four things a round needs to know . | merge:main has no “continue after a manual fix” mode. When one path blocks it, it aborts and restores the tree (rule 1). Do its steps by hand: git merge origin/main, fix the blocking path, then resolve each declared path by its own pattern’s strategy, never with one command for all of them, and stage each with git add -f <path>: . | take-base: git checkout --theirs <path> when main kept the file; git rm <path> when main deleted it, since a modify/delete has no stage to check out (§”When one side deleted the file”). | owned-tree: take each parent’s committed blob, as takeOwnedTree does (§”subgraph-index and subgraph-payload”). Never --theirs: in a rename/rename it writes conflict-marked bytes under a hash name. | readme-generated-regions: edit the conflict markers in place, hunk by hunk, as resolveGeneratedRegions does. A hunk inside a generated region may take either side, because regen rewrites the region. A hunk outside one, or one that moves a region boundary, is an authored conflict. Never --theirs: it replaces the whole README and drops the branch’s own edits to it, including the ones git merged cleanly. | . Then run the regen it would have run, and both droppedInMerge checks it would have run: once after resolving, and once after regen and git add -A, before committing. Each path git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=D HEAD lists must be one main deleted since the merge base, and each path git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=D MERGE_HEAD lists must be one the branch deleted since the merge base. After regen, a writer’s own deletion also passes, but only when the file is gone from disk too. | Give the regen a long leash. Cold, it needed ≥1200 s of wall time (recorded by 2026-10-08; bun run cat measure:merge-round re-measures). Run it in the background rather than under a default 2-minute tool timeout, which kills it part-way and leaves a half-written tree. | merge:main commits with git’s default message. Amend that commit to add the session’s trailers (git commit --amend) before pushing — it is your unpushed commit, so this is not a rewrite of shared history. | Do not fold main in while another big PR is minutes from landing. Wait for it. Merging now buys a second round the moment it lands (merge-queue). | .

6857.title: A pattern is not always the answer — ask what the file’s record is
6857.content: Read this before declaring a pattern for a path that already has one. The registry answers how a conflict is resolved. It never answers whether one arises, and reaching for it a second time on the same path is the move to stop and check. A declared pattern settles a file whose content is a function of the TREE, and settles nothing about one whose content is a function of the machine that built it — there, take-base is a loop. This section is about a third case: the content is tree-determined, the pattern does resolve it, and the path still conflicts on every merge. The LSI indexes are the example: a one-sentence edit to one skill rewrites most of skills.lsi.json (an SVD rotation is globally sensitive), so the file conflicts on nearly every merge, and the pattern only makes each conflict cheap — and no check on main judges those bytes. So the question to ask is not which strategy, it is: . What is this file’s record, and is main it? . | main is the record — an authored file, or a generated one a reader navigates to by name. Declare the pattern; that is what the registry is for. | main is not the record — the file’s record is the qa-reports entry for its commit, or a build output, and the copy on main is a duplicate kept in step by a gate. Then take it off main, and keep the declaration for the branches still carrying it, where the base has deleted the file and take-base resolves that too (see the next section). | Part of it is, and part is not — the common case, and the one to look for before concluding either of the above. Cut by what each value is a function of: a value the TREE determines stays committed and is reviewable; a value determined by some other artefact’s CONTENT is produced where that artefact lives. docs/lsi/index.md is the worked example — front matter, prose and the verdict table stay, each index’s size, poles and findings go — and the front matter is why it could not be taken off whole: it declares the harness tile, so an uncommitted page is a page with no way in. | . The trap on the way out. Taking a page off its store and leaving it committed can make it worse: a page computed from qa-reports at main reads the latest published entry, so the committed copy goes stale whenever anyone else pushes. Whatever stays committed must be computed from the tree.gitattributes reached the same conclusion from the -merge side and states it plainly: “Removing these conflicts, rather than tidying them, needs the files off main altogether.” Two things make that safe rather than merely tidy, and both are checks, not care: every reader must already cope with the file’s absence, and something must still PRODUCE it where its record lives — qa:refresh decides that per writer, so a family can be removed on its own.

6858.title: When one side deleted the file
6858.content: A modify/delete conflict has no stage for the side that deleted it, so checkout --theirs (or --ours) has nothing to take. Every resolving strategy takes the base’s side of the deletion instead: its copy when the base kept the file, git rm when the base removed it — takeBase in merge-base.ts. Regeneration recreates the file if it is still produced. Classification is by path, so an authored path in a modify/delete conflict is refused exactly like any other conflict on it. The owned-tree patterns are the exception. They read which parent commits hold the path rather than which stages exist, because in a rename/rename “no stage 3” does not mean the base deleted anything (see subgraph-payload below). Taking a deletion is the ONLY way a merge may drop a path, and merge-base.ts checks this before every merge commit. droppedInMerge compares the index with the merge base and both parents. A path either parent tracks that the result lacks is a drop, unless one side deleted it since the merge base. A path both parents hold, or one a side added, must survive. The check runs twice. Right after resolution, before anything else is staged, every drop is refused. After regen and add -A, only a drop the disk still holds is refused, because a writer may delete what it owns: subgraph:jsonld replaces a content-addressed payload when the merge changes its node, and its :check proves that. The check exists because of the gitignored-but-tracked files under */test/results/. Once one of them leaves the index, regen rewrites it on disk and git add -A does not stage it again, since it is now untracked and ignored. The failure signature is green locally, red in CI, with the check reporting the file missing (“has none”). git add -A is not what removes such a file: it only fails to restore one that something else (such as a git rm) already removed from the index. The refusal line says when the dropped file is still on disk, which is the case that local checks cannot see.

6859.title: The patterns
6859.content: kg-qa-manifest — take the base, regenerate . **/test/results/**/kg-qa.manifest.json. One per layer (hosted ones one level deeper), holding only the auditor’s script hash, so any change to kg-audit.ts restamps every one at once. It holds no attestation. qa-results — take the base, regenerate . **/*.qa-results.json. Whole-artefact QA results, rewritten whole by their producer. They change whenever any finding does. derived-results — take the base, regenerate . kg-qa sidecars, LSI indexes, detangle sidecars, tool-run records and translation-qa sidecars under test/results/. Recomputed from the whole corpus, so any concurrent skill or schema change touches them. Attestations live in test/attestations/, which no pattern names and a merge therefore refuses; test/results/ is not committed on main, and a branch still carrying a sidecar takes the base’s side. The LSI half is untracked on main; the globs are kept for branches still carrying it (§”A pattern is not always the answer”). auto-docs — take the base, regenerate . The generated docs index pages, already -merge in .gitattributes. One page per directory, so a new file anywhere changes one. uml — take the base, regenerate . Generated overview diagrams and their SVGs. prov-qaqc — take the base, regenerate . The PROV-O QA/QC report (docs/prov-qaqc/) and its per-instance logs (docs/assets/prov/). Generated WHOLE from the workflow instances under beans/workflows/, so any branch that records an instance — which every branch doing process work does — rewrites the index page and adds a .prov.jsonld. The globs are instance-agnostic (**/docs/prov-qaqc/**), like derived-results and unlike glossary: a dependent folio runs prov:qaqc over its own instances and writes the same two shapes under its own root. It names no check of its own, per rule 2: regen runs prov:qaqc because check:prov-qaqc is a workflow gate, and a pattern that named its own check would be a hand-kept list able to drift from the workflow. glossary — take the base, regenerate . The generated glossary and LSI pages: whole-corpus aggregates where concurrent term additions always collide. The LSI page’s per-index detail is added by the docs-site build rather than committed, and what is left is a function of the tree. The glossary page has no equivalent split: every number on it is a term count over the whole corpus, so there is no half that only the tree moves. That is the second branch of §”A pattern is not always the answer” — main is still the glossary page’s record, and declaring the strategy is all there is to do. translated-glossary — take the base, regenerate . cat-harness/docs/{ar,es,fr,ru,zh}/glossary/index.md. The per-locale glossary pages glossary-page.ts writes whole beside the English one (check:glossary), so they collide exactly when it does. Only the glossary page is named: the rest of each locale directory is authored translation, and a locale no generator writes (de/) is refused. viewer-pages — take the base, regenerate . docs/external-schemas/index.md, docs/methodologies/index.md, docs/processes/*.md, docs/qa/index.html and docs/translation-status/index.html: whole-file viewer pages, each with its writer’s --check in the CI workflow (external-schemas:viz, methodologies:viz, processes:viz, state:visualizer, translation:status). A new schema, diagram or translation anywhere rewrites them. It also holds state:visualizer’s other pages, docs/{beans,todos,health, issue-marks,swimlane-glossary,uploads}/index.html, each headed “Generated by scripts/state-visualizer.ts”. docs/uploads/index.html is the viewer OF uploads/, not an upload, and the uploads refusal’s **/uploads/** would catch it; first match wins, so the viewer entries sit above the refusal. docs/fsh-guts/index.md is not committed: it is derived from fsh-guts/, which is kept on a branch, so it is built at publish by derive:publish and a merge cannot meet it. That is the general answer for any derived page whose input lives on a branch — see directory-conventions §”The storage clock” — and is better than a take-base pattern, which only makes the collision cheap. The archive itself (fsh-guts/**) is kept content and stays refused. viewer-namespace — take the base, regenerate . docs/cat-harness/{catalogue,folio,library,schemas,uploads,voices}/**: the pages gen-library-viz, gen-folio-viz and gen-schema-viz place through viewerPlacement, each rewritten whole from the corpus and checked by its :viz --check. As above, its uploads/ pages render uploads rather than being them. auto-docs/ under the same prefix keeps its own auto-docs entry. navbar-include — take the base, regenerate . docs/_includes/generated/**: the navbar/footer include written whole by gen-navbar-include.ts (navbar:include --check). Any new page, graph or tile rewrites it. Its authored neighbours in docs/_includes/ stay refused. viewer-nav-qa — take the base, regenerate . test/results/viewer-nav/viewer-nav.qa.json: check-viewer-nav’s mechanical layout verdict over every viewer page. Recomputed from the pages, and it carries no reviewer’s attestation. handler-index — take the base, regenerate . docs/cat-harness/published-graphs.md, the handler’s index of every published graph and declared viewer, written whole by gen-handler-index.ts (handler:index:check). Any new graph or viewer rewrites it. skos-glossary-export — take the base, regenerate . **/docs/assets/glossary/*.skos.jsonld: the published SKOS export, written whole by glossary:export (glossary-export.ts, gated by glossary:check). Every layer’s export restamps whenever any declared role, skill or term moves, so two PRs that touch unrelated skills still collide here. It is not the ledger, and that distinction is the whole safety argument. glossary-ledger.json carries forward: glossary-export.ts reads the prior ledger and preserves a concept’s earlier names as skos:hiddenLabel, so taking one side would drop a term’s history. The ledger sits one level up from generated/ and matches no glob here — verified, and pinned by a test. This is .gitattributes’s rule applied to a resolver: the test is not is it generated but does its producer carry anything forward.skos.jsonld does not match site-data’s cat-harness/docs/assets/**/*.json — .jsonld is not .json — which is why it needed its own entry rather than falling through. glossary-generated — take the base, regenerate . **/glossary/generated/**: the per-instance generated glossary JSON, same writer and same check as skos-glossary-export. The glob stops at generated/, so the sibling ledger is untouched. skill-instructions — take the base, regenerate . **/docs/reference/skill-instructions/**: skill instruction bodies, written whole by skills:docs (gen-skill-docs.ts’s OUT_DIR, gated by skills:docs:check). Never hand-edit it. Safe because emit() is compare-or-write with no merge — under --check it compares and records drift, otherwise it writes the content whole — so nothing is carried forward from the file on disk. The authored neighbour is the skill itself. skills/**/*.md is the SOURCE these pages are generated from and stays refuse; a test pins that pair, because resolving the generated copy while taking a side on the source is the mistake this entry would otherwise invite. docs-pages — take the base, regenerate . The cat-harness/docs/**.md pages gen-docs-pages.ts writes whole from the authored blocks under cat-harness/docs/source/<slug>/ (docs:pages, gated by docs:pages:check). Each one says so in its own front matter: . generated: scripts/gen-docs-pages.ts — do not hand-edit; run `bun run cat docs:pages` . Safe because nothing is carried forward. emit() is compare-or-write: the only read of a prior page is inside its --check branch, for the comparison, and every other read in the script is of an INPUT (readBlock over docs/source/, BPMN XML, manifests). Its one walk of the output directory skips files carrying the generated marker. Confirm the writer by reading the script, not by how whole-file it looks. Gated on EXACT content, which is why take-base is verifiable rather than merely convenient. The generator’s own docblock says a difference in a page is “somebody who added a node, renamed a block, ran a first sweep, or moved a sidecar, and did not regenerate”. So after take-base, docs:pages:check proves the regenerated page is right — the resolution is not trusted, it is checked. The slugs are ENUMERATED, not globbed, and that is deliberate. cat-harness/docs/*.md and guides/ mix generated pages with authored ones (architecture.md, index.md, agent-onboarding.md, …). A directory glob would take a side on authored prose — the one thing a resolver must never do. The cost is that a page added to docs/source/ is refused until its slug is declared here, which is the safe direction to be wrong in, and a test reads the pages’ own front matter from the TREE so the enumeration cannot go quietly stale. That test must read the front matter, not the file: the generated body of this skill, docs/reference/skill-instructions/merge-conflict-patterns.md, quotes the marker in the code fence above, and a detector that reads a quotation as a declaration finds its own documentation (audit-coverage). That page’s front matter names gen-skill-docs.ts, and skill-instructions is declared before docs-pages, so the first match gives it the right owner. The authored neighbour is the source, and it stays refused. cat-harness/docs/source/process-publication-workflow/every-workflow-in-the-repo.md is the hand-written INPUT for docs/process/publication-workflow.md. Even when both sides only added rows, a union of additions is a property of that layer and not of the path. A test pins the pair, and pins that nothing under content/ is claimed at any depth. health-report — take the base’s measurement . test/health/results/*.health-report.json. Not a derivation of the tree but a measurement of external state (publish branch, clone size, the work plan), written by bun run cat health and refreshed daily on the base by the health-check workflow, so the base’s copy is simply the newer measurement and a branch’s older one carries nothing worth keeping. check:harness-state judges its producer hash; if the merge changed the producer, bun run cat health rewrites it. qa-witnesses — take the base, regenerate . test/results/witnesses/**: witness projections (qa-witness/v1) and page verdict indexes, written by gen-docs-pages.ts from the kg-qa sidecars and the live subject. A projection, never an attestation, and the docs-site build regenerates them at publish. pot-templates — take the base, regenerate . translations/**/*.pot: gettext templates extracted from the English pages by pot-for-pages.ts (translation:pot:check), so every edit to a source page rewrites its template in every locale. The .po files beside them are authored translations and stay refused. site-data — take the base, regenerate . Generated site data indexes under docs/assets/**/*.json and docs/_data/. subgraph-index and subgraph-payload — owned tree, regenerate . **/docs/subgraph/** holds the subgraph JSON-LD indexes. **/docs/payload/sha256/** holds the content-addressed payloads (<hex> is the sha256 of its bytes, with a <hex>.json sidecar beside it). bun run cat subgraph:jsonld writes both directories whole, and it deletes every file in them that it did not write. Any skill edit rewrites an index and moves a payload. Why not take-base. When both sides change one node’s payload, git reads it as a rename/rename. The base’s hex goes to the branch’s hex on one side and to main’s hex on the other. Git leaves the old name at stage 1 only, the branch’s new name at stage 2 only, and main’s at stage 3 only. Both new stages hold git’s three-way merge of the two bodies, with conflict markers. So take-base fails in two ways: . | It reads “stage 2 only” as “the base deleted it” and git rms the branch’s new payload. That is a path the branch added, so droppedInMerge refuses it at the resolved checkpoint. | checkout --theirs writes marked bytes under a name that is the hash of other bytes. | . The owned-tree strategy (takeOwnedTree in merge-base.ts) reads the parents’ commits, never the stages. For each path: . | it takes the base’s committed blob when the base has the path; | it takes the branch’s committed blob when only the branch has it; | it removes the path only when neither parent has it, which is a deletion both sides made. | . The resolution therefore drops nothing a parent holds, and every kept payload holds the bytes its name hashes. The orphan it keeps is the writer’s to remove. The writer is named in the pattern as prunedBy: "subgraph:jsonld", a writer and not a check: regen still derives the check from the CI workflow. When regen runs that writer, the writer deletes the orphan. Both droppedInMerge checkpoints still hold, and they are why this works. The resolved checkpoint sees no drop. The staged checkpoint sees the writer’s deletion of the superseded payload, a path the branch added, and allows it because the disk no longer holds it either. That is the legitimate replacement of a content-addressed payload, which a single post-regen check would have refused. The test fixture in merge-base.test.ts covers this, and so does its refusal sibling, which shows that take-base on the same merge is refused. Adding another owned-tree pattern needs a writer that deletes what it did not write. Without one, the kept orphan survives regen, and only the writer’s :check can catch it. The test requires every owned-tree pattern to name a prunedBy script that has a :check twin. Under --no-regen (a merge train), the orphan stays in the member’s merge commit until the train’s final regen. navbar-rail-data — owned tree, regenerate . **/docs/assets/navbar/rail-*.js is the navbar’s shared rail data. Each file is named rail-<hash>.js after the content hash of the rail JSON it carries (lib/harness-rail.ts), so a changed rail is a new file and the old one is orphaned. bun run cat navbar:assets deletes every rail file no committed page names, and navbar:assets:check fails on one. Both sides of a merge add their own hash, which is why this is owned-tree and not take-base, for the same reason as subgraph-payload above. The neighbours navbar.js and navbar.css are not covered: they have fixed names and a byte-for-byte check, and stay refused. seed:ready reads the same declaration: deleting or renaming an owned-tree path is not a move of the layer, because a regen renames it anyway. readme-generated-regions — hunk by hunk . Directory READMEs mix authored prose with generated regions (<!-- kg:subgraph:begin --> … :end -->) whose file counts and listings change on every concurrent addition. A hunk inside a region takes the base’s side and the generator rewrites the region; a hunk in authored prose, or one that moves a region boundary, refuses. File-count churn is resolved here; the README keeps its exact counts. standalone-baseline — take the base, regenerate NOTHING . cat-harness-tools/scripts/standalone-baseline.json, check:standalone’s list of accepted standalone failures. It is the one take-base pattern with no regeneration, because it is a ratchet. Re-measuring after a merge would write any new standalone failure into the list unreviewed, which is exactly what the gate exists to stop. Git conflicts on it only when BOTH sides changed the list, so taking the base is fail-closed: if this side’s change was a new failure, its CI goes red until its author runs bun run standalone:baseline on purpose; if it was a fix, all that is lost is a shorter list, and the check reports it. beans — refused, by declaration . Before you go looking for the other session, check whether there is one. A beans/defs/** conflict has two causes and they need different handling: . | cause | how to tell | what to do | . | two sessions edited one work item | the default branch’s claim note names a branch that is not yours | a coordination question — talk to them | . | one session: the claim landed on the default branch, the completion stayed on the branch | the note names your own branch | no coordination needed; keep the completing value and the note | . The second is beans:claim’s normal path, not an edge case: it pushes the claim to the default branch so a sibling sees it before your PR exists, and your branch then edits the same work item to finish it. claim-bean.ts brings the claim COMMIT into the claiming branch after the push: a fast-forward when the branch has nothing of its own yet, otherwise a merge commit. The claim is then in the branch’s merge base, so finishing the work item merges cleanly (copying only the claim’s text still conflicts on updated_at, and a conflicted PR gets no CI at all). The conflict therefore means the claim could NOT be brought in: a detached checkout, local edits in the way, or a merge that would conflict. beans:claim says so (NOT in this branch's history) and falls back to the text mirror (mirrorClaimNote). Resolve the remainder by merging the default branch in, or by keeping the completing branch’s value and the note — and never by unioning the front matter, since a duplicated updated_at is check-bean-front-matter’s recorded defect. Work item definitions are authored work-plan state; two sessions editing one work item is a coordination question (bean-coordination). artefact-verification — refused, by declaration . scripts/artefact-verification.json, the per-check consumer-verification declaration. This is the entry that exists to stop a sweep, not to resolve one — and the one most likely to be globed by mistake, because it reads like a generated sidecar (under scripts/, a .json, its key set derived from package.json). Two facts, either one sufficient: . | task-io.ts classifies check:artefact-verification as TREE_READER, which has no outputs. No script writes the file, so regen has no writer to run and take-base is a silent discard rather than a resolution. | Its own _comment requires every none entry to carry a reason, in prose, and says the file “may only SHRINK”. A branch that adds a gated check adds an authored sentence — precisely what taking base would drop. | . So a conflict here is a genuine editorial merge: both reasons are wanted, and which survives is a judgement. Human merge is the cost of the file’s shape, not a hole in this catalogue. The falsifier: if a --write is ever added that composes the derived key set and carries existing reasons forward, the file becomes regenerable and this entry becomes take-base. Nothing today wants such a writer, and adding one to make merges cheaper would be building a mechanism to serve the merge tool rather than the gate. uploads — refused, by declaration . Uploaded source material: provenance-bearing input, never regenerated.

6860.title: Adding a pattern
6860.content: . | Measure first: replay recent merges with git merge-tree --write-tree and look at what the conflicting lines are, not just which files. | Add an entry with its why and the narrowest glob that covers it. Order matters: the first match decides. | Add a test that the unsafe neighbour is refused, not only that the case resolves. | Add a section here. | .

6861.title: In CI — opt in with the merge-main label
6861.content: .github/workflows/merge-main.yml, which lives in the folio-assistant index and not in this repository, is a second CALLER of the same command, never a second resolver. It runs main’s merge-base.ts --root on the PR’s branch (rule 3). It runs on a push to main, when the label is added, when a labelled PR is marked ready for review, and by hand: . | A sweep (a push to main, or a dispatch naming no PR) merges only a labelled PR that CONFLICTS with main. A PR that merges cleanly is skipped, because its pull_request CI already tests the merge ref (owner ruling 2026-11-05, branch-freshness). Adding the label, or a dispatch naming the PR, still merges a clean one. | Same-repository PRs only, and never a draft. A labelled draft is picked up when it is marked ready. | Runs queue; they are not cancelled in progress. For one PR, runs started by a push to main queue behind each other. A run of any other event (the label, ready-for-review, a dispatch) cancels an earlier run of the same event. Runs of different events can run at once, and the one that pushes second is rejected without overwriting anything. | It pushes only a proved merge, as a fast-forward of the branch it checked out; if the author pushed meanwhile the push is rejected and nothing is overwritten. | A refusal pushes nothing and lists the ✗ paths in its comment. Adding a pattern stays a person’s change, made here. It does NOT label the PR: a label asserting “a person is needed” outlives the condition that set it (merge-queue §”A hold has an EXPIRY and a trigger, or it outlives its reason”). The reason lives in the comment, which is dated and names the run. | A declared resolution that FAILS is a refusal too, not an unexplained red job. If taking the base or resolving a region throws, merge-base prints ` ✗ [: could not resolve] — <git's first error line>` and aborts, so the bot's comment names the path and the error. Staging a conflicted path uses `git add -f` in both resolvers (git exits 1 when staging an unmerged ignored path), safe because the path is one git listed as unmerged. `regen` reporting an unrepaired check is still a red job: that is a defect for a person to read, not a conflict. | One comment per PR, edited in place on every run — except a run that was cancelled (a newer label or ready-for-review run superseded it) or whose merge step reported no status, which leaves the comment untouched. The text is composed by cat-harness-tools/scripts/merge-main-comment.ts, which is unit-tested. | The merge commit is still judged by CI: pushed with the PUSH_BRANCH_TRIGGERING_CI credential (the harness GitHub App, or a repository secret of that name) when one is available, otherwise followed by a dispatch of code-quality-gates.yml on the branch, because a GITHUB_TOKEN push triggers no workflow. | . GitHub runs no pull_request CI on a conflicted PR, and main can move faster than an agent round. Use the label on a PR that is waiting on review rather than on its author; leave it off a branch somebody is pushing to.

6862.title: When a merge-train member is refused: bean, hand back, or dispatch
6862.content: A train is built in one of two ways, and they treat conflicts differently. The automated train (bun run cat merge:train, which merge-train.yml runs; the workflow is proposed in folio-assistant#2960) runs merge-base.ts --no-regen for each member, then one bun run cat regen, then one CI run. A conflict that a declared generated-path pattern covers is resolved at train time, and a conflict in a hand-written file refuses the member (owner ruling 2026-11-05, “Resolve generated only”; merge-queue §”The automated merge train”, proposed in cat-harness#1053). A steward’s hand train admits only members that stack with no conflict at all (merge-queue §”A train admits only members that STACK cleanly”), so it refuses a conflicted member before merging it. In either train, a member is also refused when the train’s combined result fails a gate that the member alone did not fail. The steward drops it and the train goes on without it. sdlc/processes/merge-refusal.bpmn executes what happens to the dropped member. The author’s side, the queue and the bounce-back are merge-queue; the hand-back format is the agent-handoff skill. A refusal has one of three causes: a conflict on a path refused by declaration (two PRs editing one work item, say), an authored or undeclared path, or a gate the combination fails that each member passed alone. Each refusal becomes a work item, because a PR comment or a chat message leaves nothing in the work plan to say it happened. 1. Open one bean per refused PR, and check before you create . beans create dedupes on nothing (see todo-manager §”Check before you create”). The title carries the PR number, so the check is exact: . beans list --json --search 'title:"Merge refused: #1822"' \ | jq -r '.[] | select(.title | startswith("Merge refused: #1822 ")) | select(.status != "completed" and .status != "scrapped") | .id' . | An open work item already exists for this PR: do not create a second one. Add the new refusal to it under ## Attempts with --body-append (never --body-file, which replaces the body). | Otherwise create one: type: bug, titled Merge refused: #<n> <first refused path or gate>. --parent and the create are one action (todo-manager §”After you create”). | . The parent is the epic or story the PR’s own work belongs to, not the steward’s epic. Find it in this order: the work item the PR’s branch adds or claims (git diff --name-only origin/main...<head> -- beans/defs/), then a work item id in the PR body or commit messages. Parent the refusal under that work item’s parent when the PR’s work item is a task, or under the PR’s work item itself when it is an epic or story. Then mark it --blocking <the PR's bean>. Only when the PR names no work item at all does it go under the steward’s own merge-gate epic, and the work item body says so. The body records what the owning session needs in order to act without asking: . PR #1822, head <sha> (the sha the train used), dropped from train `<train name>` (its other members, and the base sha it merged onto). ## Refused - `cat-harness/scripts/gen-library-jsonld.ts`: authored conflict, no declared pattern. Overlaps #1881, which is already in main. ## Done when - [ ] the PR's head merges main with `bun run cat merge:main` and no refusal, and CI is green on that head - [ ] the PR re-enters a train with a new `ready: <sha>`, and lands . For a combined-gate refusal, list the gate, its first failing line, and which other members the train held, because the fix may belong to either side. 2. Hand it back to the owning session, with a fail condition . The owning session is the one in the PR’s Claude-Session: trailer, or in its body. Hand the work item back to it in agent-handoff form: the steward is the coordinator and verifier, the owning session is the executor, and the owner rules on anything authored. The work item carries: . | ## Roles: steward (coordinator, verifier, closes), owning session (executor), owner (authored conflicts, any exception). | ## Report to: the PR. One line per event: <id>: started, <id>: done <sha>, <id>: blocked <why>. | ## Done when: as above. The verifier is the next train, not the executor’s own log. | ## Fails if, the fail condition, which is when the steward takes the work item back: . | no started line on the PR within 4 hours (these hours are as of 2026-10-08, when cat-harness was seeded; merge-manager-watcher acts at 2+ hours and merge-queue calls a PR stale after 24, and the owner decides which governs); | or no push to the PR branch within 24 hours; | or the owning session is gone: archived, failed, or unknown to get_session; | or the executor reports blocked on something it cannot settle. | . | . Send the hand-back to the session itself (send_message), as one line that names the work item and the branch, never the instructions. The instructions are in the work item, on the branch. After that, the steward does not edit the work item, except to add a further refusal (§1), record a dispatch (§3) or close it (§5). Anything else it learns goes to the PR (agent-handoff §1). The fail condition is a takeover, not a reminder, and that differs from agent-handoff §7 on purpose. There, the executor is in another environment and the coordinator cannot do the step, so an expiry only means asking again. Here, the work is in this repository and an agent can do it, so a missed deadline moves to §3. The one thing that is never done is putting a second writer on a branch whose first writer may still be live: before taking over, read the work item’s holder note and the PR’s last push (bean-coordination §”A quiet claim”). 3. When no live owner can be reached, dispatch one agent . If the owning session is gone, or the fail condition has fired, dispatch one agent on the PR’s branch (dispatch-agent). One agent is not a swarm; a second one is, and needs the owner’s per-swarm permission (swarm-management). Its budget is modest: one fix, one push, one report. | It may do what the patterns would have done had they been declared: bring main in with merge:main, regenerate, and fix a gate failure that has one mechanical answer. It pushes merge commits only, and never force-pushes. | It may not decide an authored conflict. Two sibling PRs editing one work item, one script changed differently on both sides, or a page over its budget only in combination: each of these is a choice between authors. The agent writes the question to the owner on the PR, with both sides quoted, the options and a default, and stops (interaction-modality §4.1). | It signs ready: only once it is the owning session. merge:guard takes the PR’s own session from the last session id in the PR body (signingSession in merge-guard.ts), and accepts a ready: <sha> marker only from that session. When the owning session is gone, the agent becomes the owner the way merge-queue §”Stalled for days” step 3 describes, with the owner’s go-ahead as there. It edits the body’s session line to its own session, records “taken over from . (gone)", and then marks the PR ready and signs. The steward never edits that line to itself, and never signs: while a Merge Manager is active, check 2 refuses a merging session that marked the PR ready itself. | The dispatch is recorded on the work item by the steward, before the agent starts: ## Attempts, with the date, the reason the fail condition fired, the agent’s session or task id, and the budget. | . Two failed attempts with the same cause go to the owner instead of a third dispatch (agent-handoff §7). 4. Comment on the PR once, and edit that comment . One comment per refused PR, edited in place as the work item moves on, as merge-main.yml does with its own comment. It names the work item, the head sha, the train, the refused paths, and who holds the fix (the owning session, a dispatched agent, or the owner). A second refusal of the same PR updates the same comment. Remove ready-to-merge (merge-queue). 5. Close the bean when the PR’s fate is settled . The steward is the verifier, so the steward closes: . | the PR lands: completed, with the merge commit as evidence; | the PR is closed unmerged: scrapped, with the reason and a link. The work item is never deleted (bean-coordination). | . A fix that is pushed but has not landed does not close the work item. The member must survive a train first. A refusal work item left open after its PR has gone is a stale hold.

6867.content: Every one of the 11 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Approve the batch cardOwner_Approve | Owner | interaction-modality | In the merge manager’s session only: one card per batch, naming each PR, after its six lines were posted in that chat. A repin+merge: request is re-pinned by the merge manager itself, as its own re-pin PR in a re-pin train, before the requested PR lands; only the merge manager merges or re-pins, and a scheduled routine never merges (owner rulings, 2026-11-13). | . | Announce the hand-overTask_Lapse | Merge steward | merge-manager-watcher | Tell every sibling and the owner, and update the durable note with the session that holds the lane now. Then one card per batch, naming each PR, in priority order: P0 main-red fixes and the re-pin chain, P1 work they unblock, P2 CI speed, P3 the rest. | . | Merge trainCall_Train | Merge steward | calls A merge train | Add the merge-train label instead of merging; the train lands the batch with one CI run. | . | Merge it through merge:guardTask_Direct | Merge steward | merge-manager-watcher | A workflow PR, or a PR in a repository with no train, merges directly. A workflow PR needs no approval beyond the batch card (owner ruling, 2026-11-07, card Workflow PRs, A). | . | Stalled-agent triageCall_Stalled | Merge steward | calls Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route | A PR owner who stalled: tell the owner, then take the stalled PR over. | . | Re-run the failed job onceTask_Rerun | Merge steward | merge-manager-watcher | Infrastructure is re-run, not fixed: re-run the failed job once. A second failure is real and goes back through the sort; a Pages timeout goes to the site-size work. A train that fails only on infrastructure gets its failed job re-run once. Never cancel a main push run that has started. | . | Dispatch a fixerTask_DispatchFixer | Merge steward | merge-manager-watcher | One fixer agent per cause, never one per repository. Give it the failing run, the cause and the repository: pins out of step go to the next re-pin train on the index; the layer’s own bug to a fix PR in that layer; a lower layer’s bug to a fix PR in the lower layer, then a re-pin. It opens a draft fix PR, linked from the main-red issue. The fix is a non-content P0 PR and follows the normal merge rules: the six-line request, the owner’s batch card, full-tier CI green as judged. Close the loop when the next main run is green and the main-red issue closes. Never silence the failure, and never skip, disable or quarantine a gate or a test. | .

6870.title: Merge manager watcher — the loop that runs the merge-steward role
6870.content: Skill merge-manager-watcher: The merge manager agent’s watch loop: what wakes it, how often it looks, how it tells whether it is the active merge manager, what it reads each time, which process each reading sends it to (merge train, saturation meta-merge, stalled-agent takeover), and how it keeps the swarm in step with hold and done broadcasts. Use for “be the merge manager”, “watch the queue”, “who merges”, “the queue is stuck”, and when starting or handing over the merge-steward lane. Named by: Merge manager watch: wake, read the queue live, route, Merge request: find or elect the merge manager, Merge to main, A merge train, Saturation meta-merge: land the ready PRs when the runners are full, Guideline Updates . The merge manager is the agent that holds the merge-steward role on one or more repositories (actor merge-manager). The role says what the steward may decide. The skills say how: what lands next (merge-queue), how it lands (merge-to-main), conflicts (merge-conflict-patterns), shared branches (ref-stewardship), and full runners (saturation-meta-merge). This page covers the loop that runs them: when to look, what to read, and where each reading leads. The process is sdlc/processes/merge-manager-watch.bpmn. It is one of two processes (owner ruling, 2026-11-07), split by phase so each fits a page: . | merge-request.bpmn, the sibling session’s side: find or elect the merge manager, send it the request, and handle a merge manager that stalls; | merge-manager-watch.bpmn, the merge steward’s loop on this page, with the owner lane below it for the batch card. The owner lane sits next to the only lane it talks to. | .

6871.title: Only the merge manager merges and re-pins (STRICT)
6871.content: Owner rulings, 2026-11-13: “they should not merge and only send to you to merge. I have not been initiating any merges”; “send to merge manager to handle merge and repin”; “send to you as merge manager to handle merge AND repin so you can handle trains and CI”. | Only the merge manager merges. No other session merges, enables auto-merge, pushes to main, or posts a ready: <sha> comment on another session’s PR. This holds in every repository. For a PR in a repository the merge manager cannot reach, the merge manager asks the owner by card; the PR’s session still does not merge it. | Sessions do not re-pin just in time. A PR that is green except for a re-pin, or for being behind its pins, goes to the merge manager as repin+merge: <owner/repo>#<n> <sha>, followed by the six lines (§”The merge request: six lines”). The merge manager makes the re-pin (its own PR, remote-mount §”Re-pinning”), sequences re-pin trains and CI, then merges. | A scheduled routine never merges. A routine or check-in that finds a green PR reports a ready: line to the merge manager, and does nothing else. | Standing re-pins and site repositories are the merge manager’s (owner cards, 2026-11-13: “C. No auto-merge”, replacing “A. MM dispatches, auto-merge OK”, and “A. Give MM access”). A standing re-pin run opens or updates its PR, labels it needs-repin, and never merges itself: the merge manager judges it once CI is green and merges it. The merge manager attaches each site repository and runs its re-pin: it dispatches the run, approves the held bot runs, and merges when green (remote-mount §”Standing consent”). | Held runs are approved by the merge manager. A re-pin commit pushed by a bot gets runs held at action_required, and the merge manager approves them before judging the PR. A held run executed nothing, so it is neither red nor green. | merge-guard becomes a required check (owner card, 2026-11-13, “A. merge-guard required status”). Once the tools layer’s workflow posts the merge-guard commit status (full tier, plus ready), the merge manager makes it a required status check on main in the layer repositories, through branch protection. Until then, merge-queue §”A PR lands only through merge:guard” holds as written. | A red index main pauses the re-pin train (owner card, 2026-11-13, “A. #3119, fix main, pause”). While the index repository’s main is red, the merge manager disables the re-pin train workflow, so no re-pin lands on a red base. It re-enables the workflow once main is green, and says so to the siblings and the owner both times. | A one-time consent is quoted where it acts. The owner’s card, with its date, goes in the re-pin PR’s body and in trust.consent’s evidence in index.config.json (remote-mount §”Trust”). | .

6872.title: The sibling’s side: find the merge manager first
6872.content: A coding agent whose PR is ready to merge does not know whether a merge manager exists. It checks, in this order: . | Is a merge manager active? Read the latest merge manager: <session id> announcement in the coordination group, then check that session is live: active, and it answered within the stall window (§”Liveness and stalls”). If so, send it the six-line merge request (below) and wait for its acknowledgement. | If none is active, elect one with the siblings by the fixed rule (§”Am I the active merge manager?”). A lone session is elected alone. The winner announces itself and takes the merge steward lane. Every other sibling notes the holder and sends it the request. Nobody merges while no merge manager holds the lane. | . An agent with no chat to the merge manager (a local agent such as agy, a GitHub Actions job, a scheduled routine, or any tool that only reaches GitHub) signals on its own PR with a label, because the PR is the message (merge-queue §”The PR is the message”; owner, 2026-11-13: “need a way to mark this for agents not able to communicate… label PR?”). It marks the PR ready for review and adds one of two labels: . | ready-to-merge: green; the merge manager merges it. | needs-repin: green except for a re-pin, or for being behind its pins; the merge manager re-pins, then merges. This is the label form of repin+merge:. | . A label is a request, never a merge: only the merge manager acts on either label (§”Only the merge manager merges and re-pins”). The agent puts the six lines in the PR body or a comment, and still asks the owner first (§”Ask the user before submitting” in merge-queue). Every sweep reads the open PRs carrying either label in the repositories the merge manager watches, and treats each as a request. One with no preview, or no six lines, goes back with a comment saying what is missing. Until the tools layer’s merge:guard accepts the label in place of a signed ready: <full head sha> comment (§”What this does not do yet”), the agent also posts that comment on its own PR. Where the announcement lives, so all can use it. The holder sends merge manager: <session id> to every sibling and the owner, and notes it durably on the coordination work item. A sibling started later reads the note, not anybody’s memory. A hand-over updates the note.

6873.title: When is a merge manager needed?
6873.content: This measure was first the condition for holding the lane at all (owner ruling, 2026-11-07: “merge manager needed if lots of conflicting CI runners causing merge slowdown”). Since 2026-11-13 it measures contention only (see below). The queue is contended while both of these hold: . | Two or more active sessions have ready PRs in the same repositories. | The merges are slowing each other down, which shows as either of: . | the runners are contended: more than about 10 queued runs on a repository (the pacing threshold in continual-progress §”Pace the ready marking”), or the oldest queued run is more than about 30 minutes old; | PRs keep conflicting with or superseding each other: duplicate re-pins, or rebases that invalidate each other’s CI. | . | . The lane does not lapse (owner ruling, 2026-11-13, which supersedes the lapse of 2026-11-07). A quiet queue does not hand merging back to each session: a merge manager always holds the lane, and only it merges. The measured condition above now says when the queue is contended. The merge manager then batches through trains and enforces runner relief, rather than landing each PR as it comes.

6874.title: Am I the active merge manager?
6874.content: Exactly one live session holds the lane on each repository. It holds the lane when the owner gave it the lane, when it was elected (below), or when it took the lane over from a stalled holder (stalled-agent-triage) and told the owner. On taking the lane, it announces merge manager: <session id> to every sibling and to the owner, so that every sibling knows where to send PRs. On handing it over, it says to whom. A memory that one existed yesterday does not count, either way. A lone session is its own merge manager (owner ruling, 2026-11-07: “if single, can merge manage self”). When a session is the only active one in its coordination group, it queues its own PRs and asks the owner directly, with the same six-line merge request and the same card per batch. It needs no election and no hand-off. As soon as a second sibling becomes active, the election rule applies. With no merge manager, the siblings elect one (owner ruling, 2026-11-07: “if no merge manager, siblings self-determine which will play that role”). No merge manager is active when none has announced itself, or when the last one has gone inactive. The owner does not have to appoint one. The rule is deterministic, so two sessions cannot both claim the lane: . | The active session that owns the P0 PR (the fix for a red main, or the re-pin chain) takes the lane. | With no P0 PR, the earliest-created active session in the coordination group takes it (the created_at of list_sessions). | With two P0 owners, the earlier-created of the two takes it. | . The elected session announces itself as above, and hands over explicitly when it stops. On 2026-11-07 the previous merge manager, merge-planning, went inactive without a hand-off, and the owner had to appoint one. Liveness and stalls . The merge manager, like any agent, may stall (owner ruling, 2026-11-07). So it has a liveness duty: it acknowledges each merge request within about 10 minutes of receiving it (the role’s holding.heartbeatMinutes; a request wakes it), and posts a heartbeat to the coordination group with each sweep. A sibling treats the lane as vacant when its request has no acknowledgement within about 30 minutes (holding.stalledAfterMinutes), or when the merge manager’s session is inactive. It then runs stalled-agent-triage: it tells the owner, and re-elects without the stalled session. The new holder announces itself, takes over the queue, and tells the owner. A stalled coding agent’s PR is handled the same way, from the other side: the merge manager runs stalled-agent-triage on it (§”Where each reading leads”). Siblings send merge requests here, and the owner approves here (owner ruling, 2026-11-07, card “Approvals”, B: “all siblings should communicate merge requests to you. i will approve here. you queue/prioritize”, and “all my approval is here, not in siblings”): . | There is one merge manager session. | A sibling never merges its own PR. When the PR is ready, the sibling sends the merge manager a merge request in the six-line format below. | The owner approves in the merge manager’s session, with one card per batch that names each PR. An approval the owner gives in a sibling’s session does not authorise a merge. | A pre-approved PR, one the owner said to “merge when green”, needs no second card. | The merge manager queues the PRs in priority order: . | P0: fixes for a red main, and the links of the re-pin chain; | P1: work those unblock; | P2: CI speed; | P3: everything else. | . | . The merge request: six lines . Owner ruling, 2026-11-07: “anything that indicated to merge should have link to PR, claude session, explanation of changes, preview URL”, and “put that in chat then ask to merge by card”. A sibling’s ready: message carries: . | the PR URL and the full 40-hex head SHA; | the claude.ai session URL; | an explanation of the changes, in 1-3 sentences; | the rendered preview URL for that head (feature-staging’s branches/ preview, or the layer’s equivalent), confirmed rendered, or no preview: <reason>; | what to look for in the preview; | the CI verdict on that head (owner ruling, 2026-11-13): full tier green as judged (rule 1 below). For a pin-only PR in a layer repository, line 6 reads pin-only: layer CI judges nothing (it mounts the root's lock), because its “No new failures” job runs no tests or gates and passes without judging anything. The evidence for those pins is the root’s own re-pin PR, not the layer’s green check. | . A PR that is green except for a re-pin is requested as repin+merge: <owner/repo>#<n> <sha> with the same six lines; line 6 then names what the re-pin must move. The merge manager re-pins it (§”Only the merge manager merges and re-pins”). The merge manager posts all six lines in its chat, then asks the owner by card. A request with no rendered preview and no reason goes back to the sibling.

6875.title: What wakes it
6875.content: . | A timer, at the sweep’s cadence (§”The sweep”): every 10-15 minutes while a P0 is in flight, every 30 minutes otherwise. This is a backstop, not the main signal. | A PR event on a subscribed PR: ready for review, CI finished, review submitted, merged or closed. Subscribe to every open non-draft PR in the repositories it holds. | A main run finishing, green or red. | A sibling’s message, for example “ready”, “hold”, or “done”. | . Never poll in a loop inside a turn. End the turn and let the next event wake it.

6876.title: What it reads each time (live, never stored)
6876.content: . | The open PRs: draft or ready, head SHA, mergeable state, owed checks, and whether any open decision is waiting on the owner. | The runner queue on each repository: queued and in-progress runs, and the age of the oldest queued run. | The latest main push run on each repository, and its verdict. | The owners of the PRs: the last push or comment by each owning session. | Every harness repository’s open main-red issue and its newest failed runs on main and gh-pages (§”Red mains and failing runs”). | .

6877.title: Red mains and failing runs: dispatch a fixer
6877.content: Owner, 2026-11-10: “That should be a part of merge manager (dispatch an agent to fix them)”, “Add to process”. A red main mails the owner on every push to it, so watching every harness repository’s main is part of the lane, not something a sibling notices by chance. What it watches. Every repository that runs the layer checks (the harness layers and the layers above them, and the index), whether or not the lane holds a PR there: . | the open main-red issue (kept by layer-main-qa.yml): its failing gates, tests and jobs; | the newest failed run on main, and on gh-pages for Pages deploys. | . Sort each failure into one cause before dispatching, because the fix lands in a different place for each: . | Cause | How to tell | Where the fix goes | . | Pins out of step | The failure names a file or test of ANOTHER layer, and that layer’s own main already differs (a test reads a page the newer layer removed; a heading or type the newer tools already have) | The next re-pin train on the index. A train that fails only on infrastructure gets its failed job re-run once | . | The layer’s own bug | The failure names this layer’s own file, and it fails at this layer’s own main | A fix PR in that layer, opened as a draft by the dispatched agent | . | A lower layer’s bug | The failure names a lower layer’s file, and it fails at that layer’s main too | A fix PR in the lower layer, then a re-pin | . | Infrastructure | “The runner has received a shutdown signal”, a Pages deploy stuck at syncing_files until it times out | Re-run once. A second failure is real: a Pages timeout goes to the site-size work | . Re-run policy (owner, card Q-RERUN-1 B, 2026-11-12). Every run of a PR emails the owner when it fails, and on 11-11 more than half of the failure emails came from re-runs. So a “re-run once” in the table above is bounded by these rules: . | Re-run a PR’s CI only when that PR is about to merge, which means it is approved (or non-content inside a merge window) and nothing else blocks it. | Never re-run held content or committee PRs (smart-ra CS- items, dth-* content, anything without an owner approval). | After a GitHub outage, wait until GitHub status reports healthy before re-running anything. Never re-run PRs in a batch. | Before re-running a re-pin PR, first refresh its pins to the current mains, so the lock-coherence gate does not fail again. | An update-branch also starts a run, so it follows the same rules. | . Dispatch. One fixer agent per cause, never one per repository: a single lower-layer bug can redden every layer above it. Give it the failing run, the cause row above and the repository, and have it open a draft fix PR, linked from the main-red issue. The fix is a P0 (§”Liveness and stalls”). Track it like any other PR in the lane, and close the loop when the next main run is green and the main-red issue closes. What it never does. It does not silence the failure: the report job stays red while main is red (owner, 2026-11-10, card “Merge #1812?”, B “Don’t merge”). It does not skip, disable or quarantine a gate or a test.

6878.title: The sweep
6878.content: Owner ruling, 2026-11-07 (card, about 07:55Z): the merge manager’s sweep is documented and tooled. Cadence. Every 10-15 minutes while a P0 PR (a fix for a red main, or a link of the re-pin chain) is in flight; every 30 minutes otherwise. A PR event, a merge request or a main run finishing may start a sweep early. One sweep, in this order: . | Run merge:watch over every repository the lane holds. It makes the four readings above, and judges each PR by every judge (rule 1 below): . bun run cat merge:watch -- --config merge-watch.json --json . Name the repositories with --repo <owner/name> (repeatable), --repos a,b,c, or --config <file.json> ({"repos": [...], "staleHours": 2}). --stale-hours <n> sets when a silent PR owner is flagged (default 2). The layers whose re-pins need the owner’s consent default to smart-* (the WHO SMART upstream layers; an entry ending in * matches a prefix). --exclude-layer <name> (repeatable) or a config’s excludedLayers replaces the default. Per repository it prints: . | each PR’s verdict, with a route flag: workflow changes go to a direct merge, a folio-assistant PR to the merge train, a pin on an excluded layer needs the owner’s consent, and superseded-by #N marks a duplicate; | the runner queue: queued and in-progress runs, the oldest queued run’s age, by event; | main’s latest push verdict; | each PR owner’s last push or comment, with stale owners flagged; | runner-relief candidates (§”Runner relief”). It only reports them, and never lists a main push run that has started. | . Its verdict is rule 1: every “No new failures” judge passes, each shard’s Q-PIPE-1 table lists 0 new failures, and any run queued or in progress on the head blocks. | Check each green request with bun run cat merge:request:check -- <file|-> (--json for machine output; exit 0 accepted, 1 refused, 2 could not determine). It parses the six lines, and checks that the SHA is the PR’s current head and that the preview was built for that head. Send a refused request back with the reason. Post each accepted request’s six lines in this chat. | Ask the owner with one batch card for all of them, in priority order. Leave off any PR in the pre-approval ledger (below). | Land what is approved. A workflow PR, or a PR in a repository with no train, merges through merge:guard. A folio-assistant PR that does not change .github/workflows/ gets the merge-train label (rule 8 below). | Send landed: <repo>#<n> <sha> to each session that was waiting, or back: <repo>#<n> <reason> for a PR that cannot land. | Post the heartbeat, and re-arm the timer at the cadence above. | . A helper may tabulate, never write. A helper agent may run step 1 and tabulate the result (rule 6 below). It never posts, labels, merges, comments, closes or pushes. Steps 2-6 are the merge manager’s. The pre-approval ledger. When the owner says “merge when green” for a named PR, the merge manager records it: the PR, the owner’s words, and when. It keeps the record on the coordination work item, beside the merge manager: note, so a successor inherits it. A PR in the ledger needs no second card. It lands at the first sweep that finds it green, and then leaves the ledger. The ledger covers only the PRs it names. A standing instruction to “merge everything green” is rule 2’s standing OK, not a ledger entry.

6879.title: Where each reading leads
6879.content: | Reading | Process | . | A merge request for a PR that is all green (rule 1 below) but not yet approved | Post its six lines in chat, then put it on the owner’s next batch card (§”The merge request: six lines”). A request with no rendered preview and no reason goes back | . | A repin+merge: request | Make the re-pin as its own PR, in a re-pin train with any others due, then land the requested PR on top of it (§”Only the merge manager merges and re-pins”) | . | An approved, all-green folio-assistant PR with no .github/workflows/ change | merge-train (Process_MergeTrain): add the merge-train label instead of merging it (rule 8 below) | . | An approved, all-green PR that changes .github/workflows/, or is in a repository with no train | Merge it directly through merge:guard. A workflow PR needs no approval beyond the batch card (owner ruling, 2026-11-07, card “Workflow PRs”, A) | . | Queued runs 60+ minutes old with nothing landed, or the owner says runners are full | First relieve the runners (§”Runner relief”). Then saturation-meta-merge: offer the card, never run without the owner’s tap | . | A PR whose owner has not pushed or answered for 2+ hours | stalled-agent-triage: tell the owner and take it over | . | main red, in any harness repository | §”Red mains and failing runs”: sort the cause, dispatch a fixer. The fix goes to main as its own PR first; when a dispatched post-merge-regen verify run says main is stale, a regen dispatched for the next PR commits the fix and that PR lands with priority (merge-queue §”Merge steward procedure: post-merge verification”). Trains wait for main to be green If it is the index repository’s main, disable the re-pin train until it is green (rule 7 of §”Only the merge manager merges and re-pins”) | . | Nothing to do | End the turn with no message | .

6880.title: Merging across dependent repositories (STRICT)
6880.content: Owner rulings, 2026-11-15 (“prioritize in order of layer dependency”; “update merge manager skills with these (say more generally in terms of dependencies in software PRs)”; “and with all the improvements we made in this thread to process”). The rules are written for any project; names in them are examples only. They hold for any set of repositories where one consumes another, by package, by pin or by submodule. “Lower” means depended on; “dependent” means it consumes a lower repository. | Dependency order. Merge PRs and fix red mains in the lowest repository first. Move up to a dependent only when every repository below it has a green main and none of its ready PRs is left unmerged. Within one repository, finish its ready PRs and fix its red main before leaving it. One exception: a pin update (re-pin) that carries a lower repository’s fix may land as soon as that fix is on the lower repository’s main. | CI queue in dependency order. When runners are scarce, cancel runs that are queued (never running) for dependent repositories, and re-queue them lowest dependency first, feeding each level as runners free up. Never cancel an integration run on main or a re-pin run that has started. | Batching. Combine a repository’s ready non-content PRs into one CI run (a batch or train), merge the batch on the fast checks, and run the full checks on main after it lands. Fix any red on main at once, as a P0. When a batch goes red, split it to find the member at fault, and land the rest. CI backlog playbook (owner, 2026-11-15: “if we get a backlog of CI, then stack PRs and merge together/fix fallout”). Rule 3 is the normal mode; this is what it becomes when CI cannot keep up. | Switch in when, in one repository, the oldest queued run is 60+ minutes old and nothing has landed in that time (the “Saturated” route), or three or more ready PRs are each waiting on their own CI run. | Do: stop running CI per PR. Stack the waiting ready non-content PRs of that repository onto one branch, one merge each, run CI once on the stack, and merge them together when it passes the fast checks. Then watch main’s full run and fix any red on main at once (rule 3), splitting out the member at fault if it cannot be fixed quickly. Cancel the now redundant queued per-PR runs (queued only, rule 2). Re-pins and integration PRs are not stacked with ordinary PRs: they still need full green (rule 9), and content PRs are never stacked (rule 5). | Switch back when that repository’s oldest queued run is under 15 minutes old and its main is green: return to one batch per sweep. | Say in the status report (rule 10) which repositories are in backlog mode, and since when. | . | Stable point. The work is stable when all of these hold, each one checkable: every repository’s main is green on its latest run of each push workflow; every integration and re-pin has landed, so each dependent pins the current main of everything below it and is green on that pin; no ready non-content PR is left unmerged; and every published site is at or after its main’s last publish-relevant commit. Report progress per repository in dependency order, with counts of open, CI running, ready, red and conflicting PRs, and main’s state. Leave content PRs out of the report (they are listed, not counted). | Content PRs (prepare-merge §”Content PRs”): labelled content, never in the queue or the report. They stay drafts until the owner asks to review them. A functional change inside one (code, configuration, pins, schema, CI, tooling) is split out into its own non-content PR and goes through the normal batch. A content PR is brought up to its base’s current main only once every repository it depends on is stable (rule 4), so it is merged once, not chased. | Reviving stale drafts. A draft picked up again is brought in line with current decisions and infrastructure: current main merged in, current pins, current rules, current shared tools in place of older local copies, and anything superseded since it was written dropped. Where it clashes with a later decision, flag it to the owner (a card) instead of pushing the old approach. | Never commit to a shared state branch from a sparse or partial checkout. A commit records the whole tree, so files missing from a sparse checkout are recorded as deleted. On 2026-11-15 one such commit wiped the work-item branch. Use a full checkout (a worktree of the branch, or a full clone at depth 1) for any write to a state branch. A state branch is checked out the same way every time, so a write never depends on how the last session happened to clone it. | One merge manager. Exactly one session merges and re-pins. Every other session hands its PR to it (§”Only the merge manager merges and re-pins”) and never merges, even its own PR. | Re-pins and integration PRs merge only on full green: the full tier on the head, never a fast-tier pass. Small, verified fixes in one repository may stack (land one after another without waiting for main’s full run between them); the merge manager then fixes any fallout on main at once (rule 3). | Status reports at a fixed interval. One report per interval, per repository in dependency order, with total, left and in-progress counts, what is running, blockers, and progress towards the stable point (rule 4). Link the thread or session that owns each item. While the owner is away, hold the reports and send one catch-up when they return. | A draft register. Keep one file (for example drafts.md) listing every open draft PR with its owner and either “being worked on” or “not worked on: ". Act on every stale draft: revive it (rule 6), close it as superseded, or ask the owner. | No idle agents. An agent with nothing in flight either resumes its own to-dos or stands down and says so. Nobody sits idle holding open questions; a question goes to the owner (rule 13) and the agent carries on with what does not depend on it. | Owner questions on tappable cards. Write the question out in full first, with every option, its trade-off and a recommendation, then post one card with the same options. One card per question, and one session asks it: before posting, check that no other session has the same question open. | Approvals are recorded durably. An owner approval is written where the next agent will find it: the PR’s own record (for content, its ## Content review section) or the standing-rules record, citing the card or message. An approval given before a later hold rule still stands for the PRs it named. | Ignored repositories. A repository the owner says to ignore is left out of the work and out of every report until the owner says otherwise. | A lower repository never waits on a higher one (merge-queue §”A lower repository never waits on a higher one” has the CI side) (owner, 2026-11-15: “why are the 2 not merged? they are lowest”). A PR in a lower repository is never blocked on a dependent’s lock or pins. When its only red is a gate that also fails on its own main because CI mounted a dependent’s older pins of it (for example, a generated-file check run with the tools version pinned in a downstream index), that red is not the PR’s, and the PR merges. The lasting fix is for each repository’s CI to test against its own dependencies, never a dependent’s pins. | Ready and green merges at once, lowest first (“ready to merge” is defined in merge-queue §”What ‘ready to merge’ means”). A ready PR that is green on the fast checks, or red only on reds that also fail on main and that it does not cause, merges in the same sweep, in dependency order. It does not wait for the next batch. | Every red PR has an active fixer. A red PR is never left waiting on something else. In the same sweep the merge manager names the thread or session that owns the fix, or dispatches a fix agent, and the draft register (rule 11) and the status report (rule 10) show who is fixing it. | Stall watchdog (owner, 2026-11-15: “things were just sitting there”). If the stable-point report (rule 4) has not moved for 10 minutes (no merge, no main turning green, no red count falling), the merge manager acts on the lowest stuck repository, or posts one line saying what blocks it and who is fixing it. | .

6881.title: Merge-sweep rules (STRICT)
6881.content: . | “All green” is exact. It has three parts. | Finished. Every check run on the head SHA has completed. Anything queued or in progress blocks. Wait for every tier, e2e included. A merge made before the last tier finished broke main (folio-assistant#2955). | Full tier. The “No new failures” judge, or every full test shard, ran. A draft or fast-tier-only pass never counts. | Green as judged, by every judge (owner ruling, 2026-11-07). Where a “No new failures” judge exists, its success is part of the verdict, but an aggregate job covers only the parts it names. folio-assistant’s “Repository gates (hard)” is one such job. Each bun test shard carries its own Q-PIPE-1 “no new failures” table, and each table must list 0 new failures. On 2026-11-06, folio-assistant#2985’s aggregate was green while 4 shards each reported a new failure. A red shard whose failures are all main’s known failures is fine when its table lists 0 new ones. With no judge, each check must have concluded success, skipped or neutral. | .
