7011.title: Opening brief — brief the topic before you touch anything
7011.content: Skill opening-brief: Brief a work item or a topic BEFORE touching anything: what you are doing and why it is worth doing, what you already know and with what provenance, how you plan to do it and what would falsify the approach. Scales with irreversibility, not line count. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Options analysis, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, SWOT situation analysis, Wireframe design review, Agent activity log, Close the bean, Drain the beans, Agent bean lifecycle, Open the bean, Code change and review, Merge the base branch in, A refused merge-train member, Requirements filing: promote, organise, trace, supersede, or retire, SME Review of Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route, Test Data Curation — Fixed Sets and Generated Recipes, Watching a pinned upstream dependency, Adopting an upstream version bump, Questionnaire wireframe review, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Editing and HCI validation, Guideline Updates, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . This skill governs what you say before the work; turn-reporting.md (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) governs what you say during and after it; todo-manager.md (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan) keeps the work item mechanics.

7012.title: Opening brief
7012.content: Claiming a work item records the work. Briefing it is what makes the work resumable. Both are required, and the brief comes first — before the first tool call, in the chat, not in the commit. AGENTS.md §”Opening a bean or a topic” states the rule and when it applies. This is the shape. When it applies — proportionality, so this does not become ceremony . The trigger is irreversibility and surprise, not line count. | A one-line fix with an obvious route needs no brief. Say what you are doing and do it. | Anything touching a shipped gate, a shared artefact, a formal declaration with consumers, or a number a reader sees — brief it. | Anything where you expect to be wrong some of the time — brief it, and say where you expect to be wrong. Research is the case this is most valuable for and most often skipped, on the grounds that the outcome is unknown. The unknown outcome is the reason to write down the route, not a reason to skip it. | . Why it is a rule and not a style preference . Sessions end mid-thread. Containers are reclaimed, context windows fill, a branch is picked up days later by an agent with none of the reasoning that produced it. The work item body and the commit are durable; the chain of inference that made them sensible is not, unless it is written down at the point where it was still obvious. An agent resuming cold should be able to read the brief and continue — not reconstruct its predecessor’s rabbit hole first. It catches wrong work before it is done rather than after. A route stated in advance can be corrected by the author in one line. The same route discovered in a finished diff costs a review cycle and, often, a revert. It is the same discipline as the question frame in interaction-modality §4.1, applied to work instead of decisions: a terse start, like a terse question, makes the author go and find context the agent already had. The four parts . 1. The problem, stated for someone who was not here. Expand every identifier on first use. Not “fixing qou-93hu” but “bean qou-93hu — the CriticalExponent conjecture carrier, whose only field is (3 * 4 : ℕ) = 12, a closed numeral identity with no exponent variable in it, so the class constrains nothing.” . 2. What you know, and how you know it. Every number with its provenance: . | provenance | how to say it | . | measured this session, on this tree | “measured just now: 22 of 22 seeded, 0 missed” | . | measured this session, on a DIFFERENT tree | “grepped 0 on claude/x before branching — not re-run here” | . | carried from a prior session | “recorded 2026-08-24 as 43 drifted; not re-measured” | . | asserted by a work item or a doc | “bean qou-q7lf says X — unverified” | . The last row is the one that bites hardest. A sibling’s work item is not a primary source, and neither is a source file’s ## Status note; both go stale, and a specific, recent, confidently-worded work item is exactly the kind that gets believed. “Measured this session” is not the safe case. A measurement is scoped to the TREE it was taken on, and git switch invalidates every earlier one without saying so. The number is real, recent, and yours; only the tree underneath it moved. So say which tree, and re-run anything load-bearing after a branch change — the re-run costs one command and it is the same command. Part 2 includes the result of the collision review in coordinate (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) §”Starting new work”: the siblings that overlap, or “no overlap found” and what you checked. 3. The route and the gate. How you plan to do it, what you will verify against, and what would falsify the approach. A plan with no failure mode is not a plan; it is an intention. If the gate is a script, name it and its expected output. 4. What you are NOT doing. The adjacent defect you are leaving, the scope you decline to widen into, the thing you will flag rather than fix. Stating it up front is what stops it becoming either silent scope creep or a silent omission — and it puts the scope call where it can still be argued with, which is before the diff. Briefing a sibling or a subagent — pass interaction-modality on (STRICT) . When a coordinating session writes a brief to launch a child session (create_session, send_message) or a background subagent (Agent, invoke_subagent), the brief is the child’s only prompt until it reads the graph. A child whose brief omits how to ask the owner will default to asking in plain prose when it hits a permission wall or a design call. Every sibling brief and subagent prompt written by a coordinating session MUST carry the interaction-modality contract explicitly: . | If the child can reach the person directly (a sibling session with its own chat surface): every question to the owner goes out twice, in order — first the full question in chat (context, what differs, every identifier expanded, at most four numbered or lettered options with pros, cons, downstream impact and reversibility, recommended option first and marked (Recommended), and the stated default on silence), and second the tappable card (AskUserQuestion, request_decision, ask_question, or post_widget) carrying the same option labels. Never ask in prose alone, and never ask the person to type. | If the child is a background subagent or a sibling running beside a live discussion: it does not ask the person in prose either; it returns any owner-facing decision to the coordinating session in the hand-back-to-discussion schema format so the coordinator presents both the full chat block and the tappable card. | Pass it on: if the child itself spawns a helper or a subagent, its brief to that child must carry the same interaction-modality block. | . Before you offer options, check whether it is already ruled (STRICT) . Part two of the brief is what do I already know, with each measurement’s provenance. This is the half that gets skipped, because an unsettled question is more interesting than a settled one and nothing in a checkout announces that a decision exists. Presenting options for a settled question is worse than presenting none. It reopens a decision, spends the owner’s attention on it a second time, and the options offered will not be the ones already weighed. Four places to look, in this order: . | The proposals — the design corpus. They live in the docs/ of the layer whose stub needs them; today that is cat-harness/docs/proposals/ (opt-in cat-harness.proposals), and its index.md is where to start. Resolve the directory rather than remembering this sentence — a stub’s docs/ is where its proposals are, and this path is an example of the rule, not the rule. | The owner’s rulings, in work items and in the declarations that quote them verbatim. A _comment field in a *.json is frequently where a decision was recorded, because that is where it had to be obeyed. | The skill that owns the area — and read it, rather than recalling it. | The commit history — git log -S "<symbol>" over the file you are about to change, and a beans list | grep <topic> that does not filter to open items. A decision that shipped is invisible to every instrument that looks for pending ones — and a recent one is exactly when you are most confident your own reading is current. One git log -S answers it. | . Cite what you read, never what you remember. A half-remembered line used as an authority is the fake-reference failure activity-names-skill exists to prevent, one level up: it is unfalsifiable by the reader, because it sounds like something this repository would say. Worked example . Starting qou-93hu — the CriticalExponent §3b-cond hypothesis class in lean/QOU/AlgebraicSubstrate/ConditionalClasses.lean. The problem. Its single field is alpha_three_eq_four : (3 * 4 : ℕ) = 12 — a closed numeral identity with the values already substituted in, so no exponent variable occurs in it and rfl proves it whatever the physics. Four sibling carriers in the same file are vacuous too, but they are at least the right shape (parameter-quantified inequalities); this one has no quantifier and no free variable at all. What I know. Measured this session: bound as [C] in 5 files; the probe baseline records it proved-vacuous; the class’s own docstring already claims “α = 4/3”, so the target value is not something I need to invent. Not measured: whether any downstream proof depends on the field’s current type. Route. Make α a class parameter — class CriticalExponent (α : ℝ) : Prop where alpha_eq : α = 4/3. A Prop class cannot carry data, so α must be a parameter, not a field. Gate: lean-direct exit 0 on all three affected modules, plus a content probe proving ¬ CriticalExponent 2 — because inhabitability at 4/3 alone would not show the class constrains anything. Falsifier: if ¬ CriticalExponent 2 will not go through, the encoding is not doing what I claim and I stop. Not doing. The other four carriers need analytic setup their docstrings only gesture at — the author’s mathematics, not a cleanup. Also leaving the separate CriticalExponent in core-levi-form.lean, a different carrier in a different namespace. ~200 words, and it would have let a reader stop the work, redirect it, or pick it up cold. What a thin brief looks like, and why it fails . Starting qou-93hu — fixing CriticalExponent. Names the work item and nothing else. It does not say the field is a closed numeral identity with no exponent variable in it, so a reader cannot tell whether this is cosmetic or load-bearing; it does not say the class signature changes, so nobody can warn that every binder in two consumer modules moves with it; and it does not say what “fixed” will be checked against, so the agent is free to declare victory on a compile. Each of those omissions is a place the author could have intervened for the cost of reading one sentence. The failure this prevents . An agent that has spent an hour inside a problem writes in the private vocabulary it built along the way, and a reader — the author, or the next agent — has to reconstruct that vocabulary before evaluating anything. The brief is written at the one moment when the agent still knows which parts are non-obvious, because it has just finished finding them out. Cheapest correct move when you do not want to spend the words: do not start the topic. A task you cannot brief is one you have not understood well enough to begin. The brief’s durable form is the PR description. Once the work exists, pr-description (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) answers the same questions for a reader who arrives after it.

7014.title: Options analysis
7014.content: Process_OptionsAnalysis · strict · 5 step(s) . A decision reached by a NAMED methodology, with its rejected options recorded. Called as a subprocess, never run on its own. WHEN IT APPLIES: the trigger is opening-brief’s — IRREVERSIBILITY AND SURPRISE, not size. A reversible choice needs no subprocess; an irreversible one cannot skip it. A subprocess fired on every decision becomes ceremony, and ceremony is how a gate stops being read. WHY IT IS ONE SUBPROCESS AND NOT A BRANCH PER METHODOLOGY: the methodologies are parallel tracks selected by context, and the selection is a judgement made inside A_Select rather than a gateway. A gateway per methodology would assert the choice is computable from data, which is the claim dmn says to make only when the criteria recur. WHAT IT DOES NOT DO: it does not decide. It produces the options, their trade-offs and a recommendation; the decision and its authorisation belong to whoever owns the calling step. i i i i i

7015.title: How it connects
7015.content: . | Called by: CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, Wireframe design review, Adopting an upstream version bump, Make the content change, Editing and HCI validation | Calls: none | Presented on: no docs page section shows this diagram | Running instances: none recorded | .

7016.title: Lanes — who acts
7016.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | Business analyst | business-analyst | This lane’s deliverable is the recommendation together with the rejected options — a rejected option with no record is a dead end the next agent walks back into — but it never authorises anything; A_Record hands both to whoever called the subprocess, and the decision stays theirs. Answering GW_Trigger no is not a skipped step either: End_TriggerNotMet is recorded as a distinct outcome from a completed comparison, because a caller unable to tell “not needed” from “we chose X” cannot audit either one. | .

7017.title: Steps
7017.content: Every one of the 5 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Frame the decision and check the triggerA_Frame | Business analyst | opening-brief | One sentence naming the KIND of thing being chosen, not the options — “which cache strategy”, never “A or B”. Then the trigger: is this irreversible, or would the answer surprise someone? If neither, say so and stop; the calling step decides without this subprocess. Stopping here is a correct outcome, not a skipped step. | . | Select the methodology by contextA_Select | Business analyst | methodology-adoption | Ask the selection question in order, first yes decides: do the criteria RECUR with the same inputs having to produce the same answer; is this the CERTAINTY of a body of evidence behind a recommendation; is the context a BEAN recording a decision; otherwise a one-off choice among candidates. If none fits, that is a finding — say which question the decision is and that no adopted methodology covers it. Do not improvise one and do not stretch the nearest fit.The declared set is the contents of the methodology graph. Ask for it; do not remember it. | . | Check the selected methodology’s evidence baseA_CheckEvidence | Business analyst | literature-search | Before applying a methodology, establish that the thing being applied is what it claims to be. A methodology is adopted because it is somebody else’s named, external work; this step checks that the origin it cites resolves to a source in a declared library, and reads the methodology-evidence QA sidecar for it.WHY THE CHECK IS HERE AND NOT AT ADOPTION. Adoption happens once; selection happens every time a decision is made. A source that was reachable when the methodology was adopted can stop being so, and a methodology adopted before this axis existed was never checked at all. Measured 2026-09-22: six methodologies cited an origin and NONE had that source in any library, so every selection made until then rested on an unverifiable citation.WHAT A GAP DOES AND DOES NOT DO. A missing source does NOT block the decision, and this step has no branch that stops the process — that would make a documentation gap into an outage, and the owner decides whether an unbacked methodology may still be used. It does two things: it runs literature-search to try to close the gap, and it puts the evidence state into the record A_Record writes, so a reader can tell a decision made on a verified method from one made on a citation nobody could follow.The third state is the one that matters. “Source ingested”, “source located but unreachable from here” and “no source found” are three different facts, and literature-search exists largely to stop the middle one being reported as the last. | . | Apply it, and state each option’s trade-offsA_Apply | Business analyst | methodology-adoption | Follow the selected methodology as written — adopted whole, not blended with another. At least two real options: one option is not a choice, and a straw option is worse than a short list because it makes the analysis look thorough while narrowing it.Never quantify the comparison to make it look measured. Where a method scores and sums, this platform takes the structure and refuses the arithmetic: the weights are invented and a total reads as a measurement. | . | Record the chosen option AND the rejected onesA_Record | Business analyst | decision-audit | The rejected options and why they lost are part of the output, not an appendix. A rejected option with no record is a dead end nobody marked, and the next agent walks into it — the same argument bean-coordination makes for scrapped over deleted.In a bean context the form is MADR’s. Which methodology was followed is named here, so a reader can check the method rather than take the conclusion. | .

7018.title: Decisions
7018.content: Every one of the 1 decision(s) is documented. | decision | what decides it | branches | . | Irreversible or surprising?GW_Trigger | A_Frame has always ENDED with this question — “is this irreversible, or would the answer surprise someone? If neither, say so and stop; the calling step decides without this subprocess. Stopping here is a correct outcome, not a skipped step.” Until this gateway existed, the diagram gave it NO WAY TO STOP: A_Frame’s only outgoing edge went to A_Select, so the prose promised a branch the model did not have.Found by adding the second caller, not by reading. With one caller the straight line looked fine; wiring editing-hci-validation made every write in that process run all four activities, and its corpus-gate tests failed with “Task_RecordDecision is not enabled. Enabled now: A_Frame.” That is the ceremony this process’s own documentation refuses — “a subprocess fired on every decision becomes ceremony, and ceremony is how a gate stops being read” — and it was unreachable as a criticism while the subprocess had a single caller.DELIBERATELY NOT DMN-BACKED, unlike the gateways that are. Irreversibility and surprise are judged, not computed: dmn says to claim computability only when the criteria recur with the same inputs having to produce the same answer, and “would this surprise someone” does not. So the outcome is supplied by whoever is at the step, exactly as Gateway_EditorDecision takes one. | yes → Select the methodology by contextno → Trigger not met — the caller decides without an analysis | .

7020.title: Cutting a package release
7020.content: Skill package-release: Cut a release of a repository’s packages: decide the next version, write the release notes, tag, and create the release — for any repository, the platform or a folio. Publishing the built artefact to a registry is a separate, later step that a person starts. Named by: Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, KG to public portal, The cache process: restore and save every cache a run can use, Alert the publication manager, QA report signing, Adopting an upstream version bump, Incremental IG build, L3 FHIR IG pipeline, An IG site, built from the AST on its cache branch, An IG release: the owner tags, a draft is built, the owner publishes, Content lifecycle, Draft, review and publish, Guideline Updates . A release is a version number that one commit keeps from then on: a tag, notes that say what changed, and a record on the host (a GitHub release). Anything that depends on the package names that version and gets exactly that commit. This skill is general: it is for any repository that publishes packages, including a folio that ships its own. It is not the skill for publishing a folio’s content — that belongs to the content layer above this one, where a person supplies the version when the release is authorised. The two share the word “publish” and nothing else: a package release versions code; a content publication versions a document.

7021.title: The four steps, and who owns each
7021.content: | step | what happens | who | . | 1. Decide the version | the next semver triple, from what changed since the last tag | a mechanism proposes it, a person may raise it | . | 2. Write the notes | what changed, grouped the way a consumer reads it — breaking first | a mechanism drafts them, a person edits | . | 3. Tag and create the release | one tag per package, <package>-v<version>, and the host’s release record | a mechanism, after a person approves | . | 4. Publish the artefact | push the built package to its registry (npm, PyPI, …) | a person starts it, separately | . Step 4 is kept apart on purpose. A tag can be deleted; a version pushed to a public registry cannot be taken back or reused. So the one step nobody can undo is the one step no mechanism takes on its own.

7022.title: Step 1 — where the version comes from
7022.content: Two ways to compute a bump. They can disagree, and the rule for that is below. | From commit messages (conventional commits): feat: is minor, fix: is patch, feat!: or BREAKING CHANGE: is major. Cheap, and what release-please does. Its weakness: a commit message is a claim about a change, not the change. A feat: commit that removed something a consumer uses gives a minor bump and a broken consumer. | From the declared surface: diff what the package exports (for an layer, the graph kg-export walks: graph typologies, skill ids, tool ids, block kinds) between the last tag and HEAD. A removal is major; an addition is minor; neither is patch. | . When both are available, the larger bump wins. You may always release a bigger bump than computed; never a smaller one. A version is an exact triple: no ranges, anywhere. A version that has been tagged is never reused, even if its release was deleted.

7023.title: Step 3 — before you tag
7023.content: . | The package must build from the commit being tagged. Check its manifest’s file list: every entry must exist. A release of a package that cannot be built is worse than no release, because it looks like one. | Only a package declared publishable is released. For a layer, that means publishable: true in its <name>.json (check:publishable). An layer that has not declared it is undecided, not no, and is not released. | The configuration names only what exists. A release tool pointed at a config file that is missing either fails or falls back to guesses. Neither is a release. | .

7024.title: Mechanisms
7024.content: Each Tool that can do this names package-release in its satisfies; ask for them with tool_list rather than relying on this list. | release-please — the GitHub Action or CLI. Does steps 1–3 from commit messages: it opens a release PR, and merging that PR creates the tag and the release. In this repository it is declared but not configured: there is no config. Before one is written, the package must build and the layers to release must declare publishable: true. | By hand — git tag, a CHANGELOG entry and the host’s release form. The same four steps and the same rules; slower, and nothing to misconfigure. | pack-tarball (bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pack-tarball.ts) — packages an layer into an npm .tgz tarball using bun pm pack, computing size and SHA-256 digest into a folio-binary-release/v1 release record. See the npm-kg-distribution skill. | package-release-workflow (gh workflow run release-npm.yml) — dispatches the release workflow across any repository (--repo <owner/repo>) via GitHub Actions. Automates tarball building, tagging, GitHub Release asset upload, and publishing to GitHub Packages / npm registries. Satisfies package-release, npm-kg-distribution, and document-publishing. | .

7025.title: What this skill does not do
7025.content: . | It does not publish a folio’s content (the content layer does). | It does not take in an upstream’s release (upstream-version-adoption). That is the other side of the same event: someone else’s step 3 is the start of your adoption. | It does not push to a registry on its own (step 4, above). | .

Skill id: pcf-consent · Package: fhir-ig-authoring · Layer: fhir-harness · Modules: schemas/pcf-consent.ts (consentToOdrl, decide, evaluatePcfPolicy, PCF_IMPLICIT_POLICY_SETS), schemas/iti-108-consent-client.ts (findAccessConsents, Iti108ConsentClient), schemas/odrl-to-fhir-r5-permission.ts. Standards and scope: . | Specifications: IHE IT Infrastructure Technical Framework Supplement — Privacy Consent on FHIR (PCF) 1.1.0 (Trial Implementation, 2023-08-04) and HL7 FHIR R4 Consent (Trial Use, FMG maturity level 2). | Profiles: IHE PCF Basic (IHE.PCF.consentBasic) and Additional PurposeOfUse (IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate: extended HL7 PurposeOfUse codes and nested provision exceptions). 7032.title: 1. Model — Authoring IHE PCF 1.1.0 Consent in a FHIR IG
7032.content: 1.1 Package dependencies in sushi-config.yaml . An IG that profiles, instantiates, or references IHE PCF consent directives or Verifiable Health Links pins the upstream IHE packages in sushi-config.yaml and references their artefacts by canonical URL only: . dependencies: ihe.iti.pcf: id: ihe_iti_pcf uri: https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/ImplementationGuide/ihe.iti.pcf version: 1.1.0 ihe.iti.vhl: id: ihe_iti_vhl uri: https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/ImplementationGuide/ihe.iti.vhl version: 1.0.0-comment . FHIR R4 Consent in an R5 IG (could-not-determine): ihe.iti.pcf@1.1.0 is an R4 (4.0.1) package. When an R5 (fhirVersion: 5.0.0) IG compiles against it and SUSHI or the IG Publisher rejects cross-version R4-in-R5 profile resolution, report that cross-version outcome explicitly as could-not-determine with the exact tool diagnostic rather than silently dropping the dependency or hand-copying the profile. 1.2 Canonical URLs (never re-declared locally) . Reference the IHE PCF profiles, value sets, and HL7 code systems by their canonical URLs exported in fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts: . | Artefact | Canonical URL | Constant in schemas/pcf-consent.ts | . | PCF Implementation Guide | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF | PCF_IG_CANONICAL | . | PCF Basic Consent profile | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/StructureDefinition/IHE.PCF.consentBasic | PCF_CONSENT_BASIC_PROFILE | . | PCF Intermediate Consent profile | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/StructureDefinition/IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate | PCF_CONSENT_INTERMEDIATE_PROFILE | . | PCF Advanced Consent profile | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/StructureDefinition/IHE.PCF.consentAdvanced | PCF_CONSENT_ADVANCED_PROFILE | . | PCF Basic Purpose ValueSet | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/ValueSet/BasicPurposeVS | PCF_BASIC_PURPOSE_VS | . | PCF Advanced Security Tag ValueSet | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/ValueSet/AdvancedSecurityTagVS | PCF_ADVANCED_SECURITY_TAG_VS | . | HL7 v3 ActReason (PurposeOfUse) | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ActReason | HL7_ACT_REASON_SYSTEM | . | HL7 v3 Confidentiality | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-Confidentiality | HL7_CONFIDENTIALITY_SYSTEM | . | HL7 v3 ActCode | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ActCode | HL7_ACT_CODE_SYSTEM | . | HL7 v3 ParticipationType | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ParticipationType | HL7_PARTICIPATION_TYPE_SYSTEM | . | HL7 ConsentScope | http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/consentscope | HL7_CONSENT_SCOPE_SYSTEM | . | LOINC Privacy policy / Consent | http://loinc.org (59284-0) | LOINC_SYSTEM / LOINC_CONSENT_CODE | . 1.3 Required structure of a PCF Consent instance . Every conformant IHE PCF 1.1.0 Consent resource carries: . | meta.profile: one of IHE.PCF.consentBasic, IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate, or IHE.PCF.consentAdvanced (detectPcfProfile(consent) inspects meta.profile and falls back to structural inspection). | status: "active" for an enforceable consent directive ("draft", "proposed", "rejected", "inactive", and "entered-in-error" carry no active permissions or prohibitions). | scope: http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/consentscope#patient-privacy. | category: includes http://loinc.org#59284-0 (Consent). | patient: reference to the Patient subject (Patient/<id>). | dateTime and performer (the consenting patient or authorized representative, which becomes the ODRL assigner) and organization (the custodian organization). | sourceReference or sourceAttachment: the signed paper/electronic consent artifact or questionnaire response. | policy: policy[].uri naming the overarching privacy policy (such as one of the four IHE PCF Volume 1 §1:53.2.1 implicit policy URIs). | provision: root provision (type: "permit" or "deny"), purpose codings from http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ActReason (TREAT, HPAYMT, HOPERAT in BasicPurposeVS, or extended PurposeOfUse codes such as HRESCH, CLINTRCH, BIORCH, PUBHLTH, ETREAT, BTG, PATRQT), optional period, actor, action, dataPeriod, data, securityLabel, and optional nested provision.provision exceptions. | . No draft purpose vocabularies: W3C DPV is a Community Group report and is refused (dpv:* or /dpv returns false in isKnownHl7PurposeOfUse). Always use HL7 v3 ActReason PurposeOfUse codes.

7033.title: 2. Translate — consentToOdrl() and the Four Implicit Policies
7033.content: consentToOdrl(consent, options) in fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts translates a FHIR R4 Consent into a W3C ODRL 2.2 Set policy (PcfOdrlSet). 2.1 Field-by-field mapping (Consent → ODRL Set) . | FHIR R4 Consent element | ODRL 2.2 Set element | Translation rule | . | id + meta.versionId | uid | consentPolicyUid(consent) → urn:ihe:pcf:consent:<id>:v<versionId> (or urn:ihe:pcf:consent:<id> when unversioned). | . | performer[0] (fallback patient) | assigner | The party granting or withholding consent. | . | status !== "active" | permission: [], prohibition: [] | Non-active consents emit an empty Set, which evaluates to "unknown" (or defers to implicitPolicy). | . | provision.type ("permit" / "deny") | permission / prohibition | Root provision defaults to "permit" when provision.type is omitted, per FHIR R4 Consent.provision.type. | . | provision.purpose[] (v3-ActReason) | constraint (odrl:purpose) | Each HL7 PurposeOfUse code becomes { leftOperand: "odrl:purpose", operator: "odrl:isA", rightOperand: code }, so ontological parent codes (TREAT, HRESCH, ETREAT, …) permit their sub-concepts (CLINTRL, BTG, CLINTRCH, BIORCH, …) via broaderOrSelf over HL7_PURPOSE_OF_USE (IHE PCF Vol 3 §3:5.8.2). Non-HL7 local project codes become odrl:eq. Multiple purpose codings expand into one rule per purpose (logical OR). | . | provision.period (start, end) | constraint (odrl:dateTime) | period.start → { leftOperand: "odrl:dateTime", operator: "odrl:gteq", rightOperand: start }; period.end → { leftOperand: "odrl:dateTime", operator: "odrl:lteq", rightOperand: end }. Date-only bounds (YYYY-MM-DD) expand to 00:00:00.000Z (start) and 23:59:59.999Z (end). | . | provision.actor[].reference | assignee | One rule per actor reference; defaults to ANYONE ("*") when actor is omitted. | . | provision.action[] | action | "read" → "odrl:display", "correct" → "odrl:modify", "access" / "collect" / "use" / "disclose" (and default) → "odrl:use". | . | provision.data[] (meaning: "instance") | target | Direct resource references (DocumentReference/ex-doc, Observation/ex-obs) become rule targets. | . | provision.data[] ("authoredby" / "related") | constraint (pcf:author / pcf:encounter) | meaning: "authoredby" → leftOperand: "pcf:author"; meaning: "related" → leftOperand: "pcf:encounter". | . | provision.dataPeriod | constraint (pcf:dataPeriod) | Clinical data creation/effective period (odrl:gteq / odrl:lteq on pcf:dataPeriod). | . | provision.securityLabel[] | constraint (pcf:securityLabel) | Confidentiality / sensitivity tags (R, V, ETH, PSY, SDV, HIV, …) become odrl:eq or odrl:isAnyOf on pcf:securityLabel. | . | Nested provision.provision[] | permission / prohibition + conflict | Child provisions inherit parent period (intersected via mergePeriods). A root permit with nested deny exceptions sets conflict: "odrl:prohibit". A root deny with nested permit exceptions (e.g. dissent except for Break-Glass BTG) sets conflict: "odrl:perm". | . 2.2 The four IHE PCF Volume 1 §1:53.2.1 implicit-policy Sets . When a patient has no explicit active Consent on file (or when their explicit Consent has expired), IHE PCF Volume 1 §1:53.2.1 and §1:53.4.2.4 define four overarching jurisdictional baseline policies, exported in PCF_IMPLICIT_POLICY_SETS and resolved by getImplicitPolicySet(uriOrAlias): . | Canonical URI (PCF_POLICY_*_URI) | Alias(es) | Constant | Semantics | . | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/Policy-basic-normal | "basic-normal" | PCF_IMPLICIT_BASIC_NORMAL_SET | Permit Clinical Treatment: permits odrl:use when odrl:purpose isA TREAT (including ETREAT, BTG, CLINTRL, POPHLTH); non-treatment purposes return deny. | . | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/Policy-all-normal | "all-normal", "opt-out" | PCF_IMPLICIT_ALL_NORMAL_SET | Permit All Authorized (opt-out baseline): permits odrl:use when odrl:purpose isA PurposeOfUse. | . | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/Policy-break-glass-only | "break-glass-only" | PCF_IMPLICIT_BREAK_GLASS_ONLY_SET | Break-Glass Only: prohibits all uses except when odrl:purpose isA BTG (medical patient-safety override). | . | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/Policy-deny | "deny", "opt-in" | PCF_IMPLICIT_DENY_SET | Deny All (opt-in baseline): prohibits all odrl:use until an explicit active Consent permits access. | .

7034.title: 3. Decide — Three-Valued Evaluation, ITI-108 Reads, obtainConsent, and PROV Citations
7034.content: 3.1 decide() and evaluatePcfPolicy() (permit | deny | unknown) . decide(consentOrPolicy, req, options) in fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts evaluates a PcfDecisionRequest (actor, actorRoles, actorGroups, action, and scope / top-level purpose, dateTime, target, securityLabel, dataPeriod, author, encounter): . | Active explicit Consent governs: if one or more active, non-expired Consent resources (or translated PcfOdrlSets) are supplied, any deny across them returns "deny" (odrl:prohibit), any "permit" (with no "deny") returns "permit", and unresolved scope operands return "unknown". | Missing Scope Operand is "unknown", never "permit": if a rule constrains odrl:purpose, odrl:dateTime, pcf:securityLabel, target, or assignee and the request omits that dimension, evaluation yields "unknown". Under conflict: "odrl:perm" (such as a root deny with a Break-Glass permit exception), if the exception’s constraint is unresolved, evaluatePcfPolicy() returns "unknown" rather than prematurely denying before purpose is supplied. | Expired or absent Consent: . | If options.implicitPolicy is provided, decide() falls back to the configured implicit-policy Set (IHE PCF Vol 1 §1:53.2.2 & §1:53.4.2.5). | If no implicitPolicy is configured: an expired active Consent returns "deny", and an absent or non-active Consent returns "unknown" — never a silent "permit". | . | . 3.2 Reading consents via IHE ITI-108 (findAccessConsents) . findAccessConsents(query) and Iti108ConsentClient in fhir-harness/schemas/iti-108-consent-client.ts implement the IHE ITI-108 (Find Access Consent, [ITI-108]) RESTful search transaction (GET <baseUrl>/Consent) as a Consent Consumer: . | Search parameters (buildIti108SearchUrl): patient / patient.identifier, status (defaults to "active"), actor, purpose, security-label, period, date, data, _profile, and _count. | Client-side validity filtering (evaluateConsentValidity / filterIti108Bundle): every Bundle.entry.resource of type Consent is verified against FhirConsentSchema. Entries whose status !== "active", whose patient does not match the queried patient, or whose provision.period is expired (end < now) or future-dated (start > now) are excluded from consents and recorded in ignored[] with a structured Iti108IgnoredReason ("not-active", "expired", "not-yet-valid", "patient-mismatch", "invalid-period", "invalid-consent"). | Third-state failure handling (status: "unknown"): network failures, DNS errors, request timeouts, non-2xx HTTP responses, malformed JSON, non-searchset payloads, or OperationOutcome errors return { status: "unknown", reason, detail } — never an empty consents: [] that a caller could mistake for “no consent on file”. When passing an ITI-108 result into decide(), check result.status === "unknown" first and propagate "unknown". | . 3.3 Fulfilling odrl:obtainConsent duties on DSAs via injected createPcfConsentEvaluator . cat-harness/schemas/content/odrl.ts holds no FHIR resource types or pcf:* keys. A Data Sharing Agreement (@type: "Agreement") carrying an { action: "odrl:obtainConsent" } duty evaluates consent through an injected consentEvaluator: createPcfConsentEvaluator(consents, options) callback from fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts, which returns { verdict, consent: { id, versionId, uid } } to permits() / permitsWithConsent() / decideWithConsent(): . | DSA + no Consent (or unreachable ITI-108 registry) → "unknown": when odrl:obtainConsent is due and no active matching PCF Consent (or consent-verification record) is provided, permits() returns "unknown". | DSA + matching deny Consent (or expired Consent) → "deny": when the patient’s PCF Consent denies the requested actor, action, purpose, or target, the decision is "deny". | DSA + matching active permit Consent → "permit": when an active, in-period PCF Consent permits the request’s actor, action, purpose, and target (and any other DSA constraints and duties hold), permits() returns "permit". | . 3.3a Consent rules for agreements . Four rules govern consent-based agreements. Rules 2 and 4 are enforced here; rules 1 and 3 are authored in the agreement itself (the dsa document kind and its lifecycle process in folio-assistant-core). | Legal basis. An agreement carries odrl:obtainConsent only when consent is its legal basis. Agreements resting on treatment, public-health law or a research waiver carry no such duty, and this evaluator is never asked. | Version pinning. A Consent names the agreement’s fixed-version URL in R4 Consent.policy.uri. createPcfConsentEvaluator counts a Consent only when that URI equals the agreement’s version (the agreement policy’s uid, or agreementPolicyUri); consentsCitingAgreement() is the filter. An amendment that widens use is a new version URL, so the old Consent no longer counts. An amendment that narrows use needs no new consent: pass the agreement’s DCAT 3 version chain as agreementVersions (each version’s ODRL policy and its dcat:previousVersion), and an older Consent still counts while every step back to its version is a narrowing amendment. isNarrowingAmendment() decides that from the ODRL rules alone: every newer permission sits inside an older one (same or narrower action, same target and assignee, each older constraint matched by one at least as tight, each older duty kept), and every older prohibition and obligation remains. A widening step, a missing version or anything it cannot compare (such as inheritFrom) stops the walk, and new consent is needed. | Plain language. Every agreement that needs consent publishes a plain-language summary, hashed with the agreement. That summary is what the person consents to. | Scale. The jurisdiction picks one of PCF’s implicit default policies (opt-in or opt-out) and passes it as implicitPolicy. Registry reads may be cached: new Iti108ConsentClient(base, defaults, { ttlMs }). An entry ends at its TTL, at the earliest provision.period.end of its Consents, or when consentWithdrawn(id) is called for one of its Consents. | . 3.4 Citing Consent.id + Consent.meta.versionId in PROV-O decision records . Every consent-based access decision recorded in the hash-chained W3C PROV-O decision log (cat-harness/schemas/content/prov.ts, cat-harness-tools/src/workflow/prov-record.ts) must cite the exact Consent resource version used: . | Use extractConsentCitation(consent) / consentPolicyUid(consent) from fhir-harness/schemas/pcf-consent.ts to obtain { id, versionId, uid, status, patient, performer, policyUris }. | Include the translated consent policy uid (urn:ihe:pcf:consent:<id>:v<versionId>) in "cat-harness:underPolicy" on the prov:Activity decision record alongside the governing DSA Agreement uid, and record the Consent’s id and meta.versionId citation so any auditor can verify which version of the patient’s consent directive was in force when the decision hash (cat-harness:recordHash chained via cat-harness:previousHash) was computed. | . 3.5 One-way renderer: ODRL 2.2 Agreement to FHIR R5 Permission (output only) . HL7 FHIR R5 Permission (Trial Use) is output only: W3C ODRL 2.2 is the source of truth and nothing reads Permission back. schemas/odrl-to-fhir-r5-permission.ts provides odrlAgreementToFhirR5Permission(agreement, options) and fhirR5PermissionToFsh(permission, options): . | FhirR5PermissionSchema and its required value-set code lists are built from hl7.fhir.r5.core#5.0.0’s StructureDefinition-Permission.json and CodeSystem-*.json (permission-status, permission-rule-combining, consent-provision-type, consent-data-meaning), so no field outside FHIR R5 Permission is ever invented. | Maps conflict (prohibit / perm) to combining (deny-overrides / permit-overrides); assigner to asserter; shared dateTime constraints to validity; the agreement’s fixed-version uid and dcterms:source to justification.evidence / justification.basis; permission / prohibition to rule.type (permit / deny); target to rule.data.resource; assignee, action (consentaction), and purpose (HL7 v3-ActReason PurposeOfUse) to rule.activity; and delete duty roughly to rule.limit (v3-ActCode#DELAU). | Every ODRL 2.2, DCAT 3, or SPDX term with no exact home in FHIR R5 Permission (including @type, profile, inheritFrom, spdx:checksum, isA, exclusive lt/gt bounds, elapsedTime, refinement, and duties or duty constraints) is returned explicitly in dropped: DroppedOdrlTerm[] rather than dropped silently. | .

7036.title: Inline PDF viewer — a pinned pdf.js, installed at build time
7036.content: Skill pdf-inline-viewer: Show a published PDF inside a generated page — search, scroll, jump to page, print and download — with the pinned pdf.js viewer the site build installs. Which two Tools do it, the publication-gate rule that decides whether a page may embed a document at all, why the viewer opens only allowlisted hosts, and the three pdf.js behaviours that were measured rather than assumed. Read before putting a PDF on a page, before bumping the pdf.js pin, and when an embedded viewer shows an empty frame. Named by: A harness’s default rendering, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . Skill id: pdf-inline-viewer · Package: ui-core · Tools pdf-viewer-install, pdf-viewer-embed · Code cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-viewer.ts . A lightweight inline viewer for PDFs on a CDN: search, scroll, jump to page, print and download. pdf.js is copied onto the built site (not loaded from a CDN) and loaded lazily.

7037.title: The two acts, and which Tool does each
7037.content: | act | who does it | Tool | . | put the viewer into a built site | the site workflow, once per build | pdf-viewer-install | . | show one PDF on one page | a page generator, once per page | pdf-viewer-embed (TypeScript: embed() from pdf-viewer.ts) | . docs-site.yml and feature-staging.yml both run the install right after mount-instance-docs.ts, passing --allow for the repository owner’s cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/<owner>/ and raw.githubusercontent.com/<owner>/. Nothing of pdf.js is committed. The viewer lives at <site root>/assets/vendor/pdfjs/ in the built site only.

7038.title: May this page embed this document? The publication gate decides, not you
7038.content: An embed is a link that also renders. So it follows the same rule as the download link: if the bitstream’s publication gates (copyright, restrictions) are not permitted, the page gets no viewer: the embed returns nothing whenever the download link would be withheld, and the page says only “held here, not published”. Never embed a document to “just preview” it. A preview is publication.

7039.title: Why the viewer opens only allowlisted hosts
7039.content: The pdf.js generic viewer refuses a cross-origin ?file=. That is validateFileURL, whose error is “file origin does not match viewer’s”. It refuses so that a hosted viewer cannot be pointed at any document and lend it the host’s address. Our PDFs are on a CDN, not on Pages, so the build adds a shim (folio-open.js) that opens ?src= instead. It opens a URL only when the URL starts with an --allow prefix, or is on the viewer’s own origin. Anything else is refused on screen and never fetched. | A prefix is a prefix, not a substring. https://evil.example/cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/<owner>/x.pdf is refused, and a unit test pins that. | An empty allowlist is a usage error, not a default. Forgetting --allow would otherwise ship a viewer that refuses every CDN document while the build reports success. Write --allow same-origin-only when that really is what you want. | .

7040.title: Three things measured rather than assumed (pdf.js 6.4.299)
7040.content: All three are listed under binds in the pdfjs entry of upstream-pins.json, so a version bump re-checks them. | The modern build needs a very new browser. It calls Map.prototype.getOrInsertComputed. Chromium 140 lacks it, threw during startup and never opened the document. The install uses the legacy build, which carries its own polyfills. | webviewerloaded fires on parent.document when the viewer is framed by a same-origin page, and on its own document only otherwise. An embed on this site is the same-origin case, so a listener on document alone never fires and the frame stays empty. The shim listens on both, and checks detail.source. | defaultUrl is the tracemonkey sample paper. The shim sets it to empty, so a missing or refused ?src= shows an empty viewer rather than somebody else’s document. | .

7041.title: The embed, and what it does when it cannot work
7041.content: . | Site root from the browser. One generated page is served at several depths (/<folio>/, /folio-assistant/<folio>/, /branches/<branch>/<folio>/). The caller passes the route pattern, using the folio-mount.ts convention (group 1 is the root), and the inlined client applies it. A page off the route gets a frame saying so, never a 404 inside the frame. | Lazy. The frame is pointed at the viewer only when it comes within 200px of the viewport. This uses an IntersectionObserver, because how engines treat loading="lazy" on a script-set src varies. A reader who never scrolls there downloads nothing. | Plain links always. “Open the PDF on its own” and “Download” sit under the frame whether or not the viewer works. They are not a fallback that appears on failure. | .

7042.title: Caching: why the frame’s address carries a version tag
7042.content: GitHub Pages serves every file with max-age=600 through a CDN, so a hard reload can still be answered from a copy up to ten minutes old. | The frame’s address ends &v=<rev>.<deploy>. <rev> is VIEWER_REV, a hash of the pinned release, the shim and the patch. <deploy> comes from the host page’s document.lastModified, which Pages sets at deploy time. So the frame is exactly as fresh as the page around it. A reader who sees the new page gets the new viewer. | The shim is fetched as folio-open.js?v=<rev>, so a change to it cannot be masked by a cached copy. | Where a server sends no Last-Modified (a local preview), the browser reports the current time, so the frame is simply never cached there. That is correct, just slower. | . The outer page itself is outside this. If the green staging banner shows an older commit than the deploy, the whole page is a cached copy. Wait out the ten minutes, or use a private window.

7043.title: The site’s own post-build passes leave the viewer alone
7043.content: viewer.html is Mozilla’s markup with one <script> added. minify-site.ts skips it (rewriting it would ship bytes no pdf.js release contains), and check:duplicate-ids and publish-verify’s html-unique-ids count it out of scope, not passed. It declares id="buttons" twice upstream. That finding is real, and nobody here can fix it without forking pdf.js. They ask isVendoredViewer(), so there is one answer to “is this ours”. The two passes that INJECT into every page skip it too. These are the staging banner and the standalone navigation rail; otherwise both draw inside the PDF frame. Any new pass that writes into every *.html in _site owes the same exclusion. standalone-rail.test.ts and pdf-viewer.test.ts each assert it for the existing two.

7044.title: Cost
7044.content: About a 7 MB download per build, adding about 12 MB (404 files) to the built site. The size matters most for staging previews, each of which carries its own copy on gh-pages. bun run cat health reports the size of gh-pages. Nothing is added to a clone.

7045.title: Verifying a change here
7045.content: Unit tests (cat-harness-tools/scripts/tests/pdf-viewer.test.ts) run the shipped shim and client against stubs: the allowlist, the parent-document listener, the root derivation at three depths, and lazy loading. They cannot check that pdf.js opens, searches and prints. For that, install into a scratch site with --zip, serve it, and drive it in a browser (see rendered-verification). Check, and screenshot for the author: the page count shows, a search finds matches, the page box jumps, print and download are present, and a narrow viewport does not load the viewer until it is scrolled to.

Named by: Hand back to the discussion, Drain the beans, A refused merge-train member, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route . Quick status display. Read-only. Run any time to answer “where am I?” or “what did I say I was going to do?”.

7048.title: What it shows

From STATUS.md: which goal(s) the current PR touches. | Master ledger intent. The “INTENT” cell of the current session-log row in docs/coordination/<goal>.md. | .

7049.title: Output format (compact)
7049.content: ## Session pending — 2026-01-01 14:32 UTC Branch: claude/<feature-slug> PR: #1580 — <PR title> Beans (via `beans list`): [epic-123] Session tracker (In Progress) [task-124] Subtask 1 (Completed) [task-125] Subtask 2 (In Progress) Goal: <goal-slug> (also touches: <other-goal>) Ledger intent (docs/coordination/<goal>.md): (1) create ledger + STATUS.md, (2) coord with #1577, .

Sources (read order): . | git branch --show-current | mcp__github__list_pull_requests({head: "<branch>"}) for PR number | Run the CLI tool beans list to find tasks matching the current scope. | STATUS.md — find row where “Active PRs” contains current PR | docs/coordination/<goal>.md — find session-log row for current branch | .

7051.title: When to invoke
7051.content: . | User asks “what are you working on?” / “what’s left?” / “status?”. | Mid-session checkpoint — ensure ledger is consistent with Work items state. | Before a context handoff (compaction event, end of session). | .

7053.title: Pickup Skill
7053.content: Skill pickup: Pick up / continue work on one or more existing open PRs efficiently. Resolves each PR’s REAL branch + title + checklist + reviews + CI in one batched pass, classifies CI as billing-vs-real, then dispatches one worktree sub-agent per PR with a filled-in brief, and applies the safe class of review-nit fixes (eval→ast.literal_eval, dead-code/unused-var removal, etc.). Use when the user says “pick up PR N”, “continue 1543/1576/1571”, “work these PRs”, “address the review on PR N”, or “take over PR N”. Named by: Hand back to the discussion, Drain the beans, A refused merge-train member, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route . Continue work on existing open change proposals — pull requests (PRs) — with minimal wasted tokens. This skill exists because the expensive failure mode is acting on a remembered or assumed branch name / scope and then re-discovering reality mid-task. The cure is: resolve ground truth first, in one batch, then dispatch. Read repo-root AGENTS.md first. This skill operates under the branch/PR workflow, the project’s production-vs-exploratory and content validation discipline, and CI-billing-failure rules. It does not override them.

7054.title: Hard rules
7054.content: . | NEVER trust a remembered branch name or PR title. A PR number is the only stable handle. git ls-remote / a branch you “recall” is not — branch names drift and a PR number you were given may map to a different PR than its scope suggests. Always resolve head.ref, title, and body checklist by reading the PR (the read change proposal forge-operation Tool) for the literal number before doing anything. | A review targets a commit SHA — re-verify the nit is still live. Gemini/Copilot review the commit at review time. Later commits on the branch may have already fixed the flagged issue. Before “fixing” anything from a review, grep the current file: if eval( / the unused symbol / the dead dict is already gone, reply noting it’s resolved — do not re-apply or hallucinate a fix. | Verify the file before trusting any description of it — including the review’s, the PR body’s, and your own earlier read if the output looked corrupted. Read the real bytes (capture to a temp file and Read it if terminal display garbles output). | Commit-early in every sub-agent. Long sub-agents hit idle/stream timeouts. A sub-agent that explores for 80 tool-calls then dies without committing loses everything. Brief sub-agents to commit after the first substantive edit and push after each commit. | Classify CI before diagnosing it. Multiple jobs failing in ≤5 s with identical started_at is the GitHub Actions billing signature, not a code failure (integration-watcher §5f). Do not push retrigger commits; note it and move on. Real failures take ≥30 s. | Never merge. Merge needs explicit user permission via /prepare-merge. This skill prepares and reports; it does not merge. | .

7055.title: Arguments
7055.content: /pickup <PR#> [<PR#> ...] # full pickup: discover + dispatch each /pickup <PR#> --reviews-only # just apply the safe review-nit fixes /pickup <PR#> --discover-only # print the resolved brief, do not dispatch . With no arg, ask the user which open PR(s) to pick up (offer the recently-updated claude/* PRs, listed with the list change proposals forge-operation Tool).

7056.title: Procedure
7056.content: Step 0 — Load tools . Resolve the forge-operation Tools from the tools graph, picking the node for the forge the checkout’s remote is on (skills-and-tools). This skill uses read change proposal (details, check runs, reviews, review comments), list change proposals, comment on change proposal and request review. Where the session offers the Tool’s MCP arm, those tools are deferred — load them before Step 1; otherwise its shell arm serves. If neither is reachable, say so and stop: a PR not resolved is not ground truth. Step 1 — Resolve ground truth (ONE batched pass per PR) . For each PR number, in a single message issue parallel calls: . | read change proposal → head.ref (the REAL branch), title, body (checklist), base.ref, mergeable_state, state. Act on mergeable_state only when it reads dirty. This endpoint can serve a merged PR’s PRE-MERGE view for a long time, so clean and unknown can both be describing a PR that is already gone; unknown additionally means not computed yet rather than cannot be determined. For “has this landed?”, ask git: git merge-base --is-ancestor origin/<head> origin/<base>. | its check runs → CI state. | its reviews and review comments → review bodies + inline threads (these are often rate-limited; tolerate failure and proceed with what you have). | . Parse the body for unchecked - [ ] items — that is the work queue. Classify CI per Hard Rule 5. If --discover-only: print, per PR, the resolved branch, title, unchecked checklist items, CI verdict (billing/real/green), and open review nits. Stop. Step 2 — Triage review nits into safe vs unsafe . Safe class (auto-apply after re-verifying live per Hard Rule 2): . | eval( / exec( → ast.literal_eval (or a real parser). | Unused function / import / variable / dict removal (dead code). | Obvious typos in comments/docstrings. | f-string / format trivialities, missing r on regex literals. | . Unsafe class (never auto-apply — AskUserQuestion or defer): . | Anything touching math/numerics, a witness value, or a canonical formula (production-vs-exploratory discipline applies). | Anything changing a formal statement, a proof, or a content validation invariant. | Architectural / multi-file refactors, API changes. | A reviewer suggestion that conflicts with the PR’s stated intent. | . Step 3 — Dispatch one worktree sub-agent per PR . For each PR with non-trivial remaining work, spawn a background Agent(isolation: "worktree", run_in_background: true). The brief MUST contain (filled from Step 1, not assumed): . | the resolved branch name (git fetch origin <ref> + git checkout -B <ref> origin/<ref>; “do NOT create a new branch”); | the literal PR title + the unchecked checklist items; | the relevant AGENTS.md discipline pointers for that PR’s domain (content validation / production-vs-exploratory / formal-proof / precision-goals — whichever apply); | commit-early-and-push instruction (Hard Rule 4) with the session URL line for commit bodies and 4× exp-backoff push retry; | “validate before pushing content (bun run validate <paper>); never add a status field; do NOT open a new PR (it exists); do NOT merge”; | “if blocked on a bad premise / a gate / a missing toolchain, STOP and report — do NOT fabricate work or numbers.” | . Keep each brief single-focus where possible; a sub-agent with one clear deliverable is far less likely to time out than one with a broad survey. For purely mechanical review-nit fixes, do them inline (Step 4) rather than spawning an agent. Step 4 — Apply safe review-nit fixes inline . For --reviews-only or small nit batches, do it in the foreground via a temp worktree (keeps the working branch clean): . git worktree add -f /tmp/pick-wt <resolved-branch> # edit in /tmp/pick-wt, re-verify the nit is live first python3 -c "import ast,sys; ast.parse(open(P).read())" # syntax gate for .py # run the script/test if cheap, to confirm no behavior change git -C /tmp/pick-wt commit -am "<msg>"; push with retry git worktree remove --force /tmp/pick-wt . Commit message: style(<area>): <fix> — address <reviewer> review. Commit body ends with the session’s attribution lines. Step 5 — Reply frugally + report . | Reply to a review only if it resolves the thread or raises a question — be frugal. For “already fixed in a later commit” nits, one short note is enough; don’t reply per-nit. | If Copilot’s review errored (“unable to review”), request its review again (the request review forge-operation Tool). | Report per PR: resolved branch, what was done / dispatched, commit SHAs, CI verdict, blob URLs (.md primary), and any blocked items with reasons. Never claim a formal artifact compiles/verifies unless a checker actually confirmed it; say “verification pending” otherwise. | .

7057.title: Worktree hygiene
7057.content: Sub-agent worktrees are auto-locked while running. After completion, git worktree prune then git worktree remove --force .claude/worktrees/agent-<id> for finished ones. Remove any /tmp/*-wt you created. Never rm -rf a tracked path to “clean up” — check git ls-tree first (a path tracked on base is not leftover junk).

7060.title: Placement — decide where it goes before you write it
7060.content: Skill placement: Establish where a new node belongs BEFORE you create it — which layer, which declared graph, which kind of node, and which of the two “stub” conventions applies. Read before adding a skill, role, actor, workflow, decision table, schema, tool or content object, and before writing any literal that names one folio. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Code node review, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Agent activity log, Close the bean, Drain the beans, Agent bean lifecycle, Open the bean, Code change and review, Merge the base branch in, A refused merge-train member, Requirements filing: promote, organise, trace, supersede, or retire, SME Review of Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route, Test Data Curation — Fixed Sets and Generated Recipes, Watching a pinned upstream dependency, Adopting an upstream version bump, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Editing and HCI validation, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . One question, answered before the first file exists: . Which layer owns this, which of its declared graphs does it go in, and what kind of node is it? . An agent that starts writing and works the answer out afterwards produces a node in the wrong repository, under a hardcoded path, named by a composed string. All three are silent: the tests pass, and the damage lands on the next consumer. This is a decision procedure. Four steps and a stop. Run it in order; the later steps are meaningless if an earlier one is a guess.

7061.title: Step 1 — which layer?
7061.content: folio-assistant is the platform, not the content. It holds skills, schemas, the pipeline and the MCP server an agent uses to author a folio — a paper, a WHO SMART Guideline, an IG — and the folio lives in a separate repository. Ask of the thing you are about to write: . Does this name, assume, or default to one folio? . A paper directory, a document title, a badge URL, an owner/repo, a Lake library prefix, a workflow filename, a simulator path, a licence block, a vocabulary, a constant with a subject-matter value. If the answer is yes, it does not belong in platform code. There are three destinations, not two, and collapsing the third is the common mistake: . | destination | what goes there | test | . | the platform | the mechanism, parameterised | the same code is correct for every folio | . | the folio’s tree | the subject matter itself | a reader of that folio would look for it | . | the folio’s config | the value the mechanism reads | it varies per folio but platform code needs it | . A value that varies per folio and is consumed by platform code is a config field — <name>.config.json, <name>.json, lakefile.toml — never a literal in a script and never a file the platform has to go and find. A Lake prefix, for example, is read from lakefile.toml, and left unprefixed when no lakefile names one, because a wrong namespace is worse than none. Do not infer the layer from the directory you are standing in. Read the declaration at the repository root, carrying name, stub and directories. basename($PWD) is not an identity — a repo cloned into a differently-named directory resolves to nothing, and reports no config rather than an error.

7062.title: Step 2 — which declared graph, and where does that layer put it?
7062.content: A node’s location is not a path you memorise. Every layer declares the directories it scans in <name>.json, and each entry names the kind of graph it holds — cat-harness (skills, roles, workflows, decisions, requirements, permissions), schemas, tools, qa, beans, folio and the rest. The vocabulary is open. | Ask for a skill, do not open a file. skill_list for what exists here, skill_fetch to load one, work_plan_prime for the work plan. With no MCP, resolve the graph from the declaration (readDeclaration in schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts) and read the directory it names. | In this repository the skills graph’s path is skills/. That is a fact about this layer, not a convention you may carry to another one. Ids are stable across a relocation; paths are not. | Overrides match on the entry’s id, never on its path. A layer that sites its knowledge graph elsewhere redeclares the same id with a different path. Matching on path makes two knowledge graphs out of one relocation, and every consumer then scans a directory that is not there. | Declare only what exists. A declared-but-absent directory is worse than an undeclared one: every consumer scans nothing and reports a clean run over it. | . Full rules, inheritance order and the three read states: directory-conventions.md. The docs graph, and the filing question it answers . docs is an authorable destination like the others, and the one an agent most often forgets to consider when it derives a destination list: deriving the list is not enough if the derivation drops a declared graph. What goes there: a design-memory asset — something produced while BUILDING, rather than the thing built. kg-contribution-offer carries the one question that identifies the class and why fsh-guts is the tempting wrong answer (its content may be thrown away; a design record’s value is that it survives). WHOSE docs/ comes first, and it is Step 1’s question again. Detailed information, design and planning for a harness, feature or tool go into that harness’s docs/: docs is a declared graph, and the layer that owns the feature owns the record of why it is shaped that way. A feature’s reasoning filed in the wrong layer’s docs/ reads fine and is unreachable from the place that needs it. Then where inside it, which is this skill’s question and not kg-contribution-offer’s: . | the asset is | it files under | . | why a subsystem is shaped as it is — requirements, options, rulings | <instance>/docs/architecture/, with parent: Architecture in the front matter | . | options for a decision not yet taken, with what each costs | <instance>/docs/proposals/, kind: proposal, and a row in its index.md | . | what was FOUND — prior art, a survey, a measurement, a comparison — that informs a decision without proposing one | <instance>/docs/research-and-analysis/, kind: research, and a row in its index.md | . | how a person does a task with it | <instance>/docs/guides/ | . | how to REACH a data source the content describes — endpoints, shapes, quirks | <instance>/docs/, beside the subject it serves | . | what a declared thing IS, generated from source | <instance>/docs/reference/ — never hand-edited | . Three rules that catch the usual mistakes: . | A design record is dated and says what it was true OF. It is history, so it carries the commit, PR or issue it describes. A record written in the present tense becomes a claim about today, and goes stale invisibly. | It states what it could NOT establish. A requirement referenced but never defined, a measurement not taken: named as such. A design record that reads complete when it is not is worse than a short one. | It is prose for a person, not instructions for an agent. If you find yourself writing “the agent SHALL”, it is a skill and it is in the wrong graph. | . The line between the two, stated as a test: . A skill carries what a competent practitioner needs IN ORDER TO DO the task. Anything beyond that is documentation. Background, derivations, options not taken, an API’s full surface when the task touches three calls: real, worth keeping, and none of it needed to act. Both directions fail silently — a skill that swallows them makes every agent read a chapter to find a rule, and a rule filed in docs/ because it arrived with context is a rule skill_fetch will never serve. Inheritance . A layer inherits its dependencies’ directories and skills, deepest dependency first and root last so the root wins: declarationChain + resolveDirectories for directories, and resolveSkillDirs in schemas/kg/harness-config.ts for the cross-layer skill overlay. So a skill placed in the platform reaches a downstream folio through its declaration; never copy a skill into the folio, which mints a second copy free to drift.

7063.title: Step 3 — which KIND of node?
7063.content: The axes below are distinct. Ask the separating question; do not pattern-match on what the thing resembles. | you are about to write | ask | the two answers | . | a new content type | does it need different code, or only different rules? | different code → an adapter; only rules → a profile plus a subclass | . | something a participant is or does | must the performer know it, or may the participant do it? | know → a skill, on the lane’s role; do → a permission, on the actor | . | a participant | does it persist across processes, or is it a position inside one? | persists → an actor; a position → a role, which is the BPMN swimlane | . | a sequence of steps | does it have actors, activities and a control flow? | yes → BPMN under the workflows directory, not a Mermaid fence and not prose | . | a branch at a gateway | is the answer computed from facts, or chosen by a person? | computed → a DMN table plus a <cat-harness.processes:decision/> ref; chosen → an ordinary gateway | . | a durable fact for one agent | does it govern, or summarise what governs? | governs → a skill; summarises → a memory entry under the memory nodes | . | subject matter | would a reader of one folio look for it? | yes → the folio, as data — never the platform | . Adapter vs profile is the expensive one. Adapters (paper, dak) partition block kinds into disjoint namespaces, and adapterForKind — what QA-criterion scoping reads — must stay total and unambiguous. Profiles (document, paper) nest: every document kind is also a paper kind. Making document a third adapter would make adapterForKind ambiguous on every shared kind. Actor / role / skill / permission. One sentence carries the model — an actor performs a task in a process as a role, using that role’s skills. Permissions stay on the actor: moving them onto Role, which looks right, conflicts wherever a permission is held by some but not all actors sharing a role. Resolution rules, how to bind a lane, and how to add a role: role-model.md. Do not re-derive them here. A .md under the cat-harness path that declares its own $schema is not a skill. The audit walks that directory recursively; declaration beats location, the same contract part-of: carries. Adding a graph typology is a registry change, not a new top-level directory. If nothing in the open vocabulary fits, that is a decision to hand over (Step 5), not one to settle by creating a folder.

7064.title: Step 4 — which stub? There are two, and they are unrelated
7064.content: This is the step most often skipped, because “stub” reads as one word. The agent-file stub — a pointer, never a home . AGENTS.md is the agent-generic source of truth. CLAUDE.md and GEMINI.md are thin stubs whose entire content is a pointer to it; scripts/init-folio.ts writes all three for a new folio. | Never put guidance in a stub. It reaches one tool’s agents and nobody else, and the other two stubs are then quietly wrong. | And prefer not to put it in AGENTS.md either. That file’s own banner says it: it is a bootstrap pointer, and the discipline lives in the skills graph. A rule that exists only in AGENTS.md is not in the generated reference, not in the published skill docs, and not found by an agent that went looking for the skill first. | . So: new guidance is a skill. Add a pointer from AGENTS.md if it needs one, and register the skill in its package manifest. The artefact stub — resolve it, never compose it . The declaration carries stub, the filename stem of every artefact this layer publishes. artefactStub() is the one function that answers it (stub when declared, otherwise name), and renderingPath() / siteDir() derive the published paths from it: . <base>/<name>/<stub>.jsonld <base>/<name>/<stub>.json <base>/<name>/<stub>.schema.json <base>/<stub>/ docs/<stub>/ . The graph document is under the layer’s own directory, the host’s included: one rule for every layer, with subjects beside their document (instance-publication §”Which base an @id is minted against”). Compose nothing; resolve everything. A hand-written path such as /kg/ 404s, because the real path comes out of renderingPath. A naive guess is not merely fragile, it is wrong on real layers. WHO’s SMART Base IG publishes under a stub shorter than its repository name, so “the stub is the repo name” fails on the reference implementation the convention was modelled on. The declaration file itself is NOT stub-named: it is <name>.json, found by findDeclarationFile() matching a file’s stem to its own name. Everything it describes is named after the stub, because by the time you fetch those you have read the declaration that names them.

7065.title: Step 5 — when you cannot tell, stop and ask
7065.content: Placement has three states, like everything else here: determined, determined-empty (this layer genuinely has no such directory — a real answer), and could-not-determine. The third is never to be rendered as the first. Do not guess and do not pick the repository you happen to be standing in. A misplaced node is not a typo: it is a second copy of something, free to drift, that a later agent will find and believe. Hand the decision over the way interaction-modality.md §4.1 requires — context → options with what each costs → your recommendation, marked → what happens if they say nothing → the question. The test is one pass: . Can the reader answer without opening anything? . Every identifier expanded on first use. A link is where somebody goes for more; it is never where the terms are defined. I need to place <thing>, which <one sentence on what it does>. Two candidates: A. <instance/graph> — costs <what this makes harder, concretely> B. <instance/graph> — costs <…> Recommend B, because <the property that decides it>. If you say nothing I will do B and note it in the PR body. A or B? .

7066.title: The worked failure this skill exists to prevent
7066.content: A platform script that writes a whole README holding one folio’s title, badges and licence destroys the README of every other folio it runs in, because prose about a folio belongs to that folio. Every step above catches it: Step 1, the content names one folio; Step 2, a helper path is composed rather than resolved; Step 4, published paths are built by convention and checked against nothing. The pattern that replaces it: the folio owns the file; the platform owns the markers, and writes a section only where the README carries its marker pair (readme-sections).

7067.title: Checklist
7067.content: Before you create a skill, role, actor, workflow, decision, schema, tool or content object: . | Layer — platform, folio, or the folio’s config? Does anything in it name one folio? | Graph — which declared entry, resolved from <name>.json by id? Not a path you remember. | Kind — which side of the separating question in Step 3, and can you say why in one sentence? | Stub — if it is guidance, is it a skill rather than a stub or AGENTS.md? If it publishes, does every path come from artefactStub() / renderingPath()? | Registered — bun run cat skill:register (skill-registration), and bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/gen-skill-docs.ts run, so the published mirror is not stale. | Could not determine? Stop. Ask in the Step 5 frame. Do not default to the repo you are in. | .

One command: . bun run cat gates # the fast set bun run cat gates --all # plus the jobs that need a browser bun run cat gates:list # see them without running them .
