7340.title: Render a Knowledge Graph to GitHub Pages
7340.content: Skill render-kg-to-github-pages: Render a Knowledge Graph, or a list of its Subgraphs, to GitHub Pages at a publication root URL, and report the push: a status (pushed, not pushed, could not determine) and one message carrying the deployed commit and the QA result. The same steps for a staging preview and for a release; only the root URL differs. Named by: Render a Knowledge Graph to GitHub Pages . Inputs, each named by whoever starts the process: . | input | what | default | . | the Knowledge Graph | a layer root, the directory holding its <name>.json | none; required | . | Subgraphs | a list of directory ids from that declaration | the whole graph | . | publication root URL | where the rendering is served | the declaration’s iriBase, else https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/ | . Output: a status and a message, and nothing else a caller must read. | status | when | . | pushed | the staged tree had no problem, the root URL answers, its README page (README.html) answers, and every document address answers | . | not-pushed | a check ran and failed: a staging problem, or a 404 at the root or at a document address | . | could-not-determine | nothing failed, but an answer was about the way here (403, 407, 5xx, no network) | . The message is one line a caller posts as it stands: pushed 1a2b3c4 to <root> — QA: staged ok (N files, M documents); root 200; README.html 200; documents M/M answer. The commit is which bytes are live: the commit on the gh-pages branch the site is served from. Staging and release are not two processes. A preview is this process with a root under the release root (…/branches/<slug>/, say) and a release is it with the release root. Anything that differs between them (who may start it, what must be reviewed first) belongs to the process that calls this one, never in here.

7341.title: The steps
7341.content: Drawn in processes/render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn. Every command below is run from bootstrap-tools, with the layer as --root. | Resolve the inputs. Read the declaration; check every Subgraph id is one it declares; settle the root URL. An unknown id is refused, never rendered as a smaller site. | Make sure gh-pages exists and Pages serves it. Pages cannot be switched on to serve a branch that does not exist, so in order: . | git ls-remote --heads origin gh-pages; if absent, push an orphan placeholder (index.html + .nojekyll); | Pages on, Source = branch gh-pages, folder /: gh api -X POST repos/<o>/<r>/pages -f 'source[branch]=gh-pages' -f 'source[path]=/' when gh is signed in, otherwise the manual step (Settings → Pages → Deploy from a branch → gh-pages, / (root)). bun run scripts/init.ts --root <instance> runs both as site:branch and site:enabled. This provisioning belongs to this process, not to the publication step that calls it. | . | Stage the rendering. bun run scripts/site.ts --root <instance> --out <dir> [--subgraph <id>]…: every JSON Schema and JSON-LD document at the IRI it names, the files as they sit, the README page as README.md — served at <root>/README.html — and index.html, a redirect to it. The redirect is only the default: a layer that carries its own index.html or index.md at its root gets that as its landing page instead. Every generated page opens with a notice naming bootstrap-tools and the script that wrote it, and its footer links the generator and its source rather than GitHub’s editor, which would edit the gh-pages copy the next publish overwrites. | Check what was staged. site.ts --check and bun run scripts/readme-book.ts --root <instance> --check. Any problem stops here: the report says not-pushed and names the problem, and nothing is deployed. A push of a tree known to be broken is not a push to report. | Deploy. Commit the staged tree onto gh-pages as a full replace with bun run scripts/publish-site.ts --site <dir> --remote <git url>: the layer’s Pages workflow runs it on a push to main, and an agent runs it with its own git credentials for a layer that carries no workflow (bootstrap). GitHub Pages builds the branch (Jekyll, unless .nojekyll). A rejected push is rebuilt and retried, never rebased. The gh-pages commit is the one the message names. | Check what is served, and report. bun run scripts/pages-status.ts --root <instance> [--url <root>] [--sha <commit>] [--subgraph <id>]… asks the root URL and every document address, and prints the message; --json gives the whole record. Exit 0 pushed, 1 not-pushed, 3 could-not-determine. | .

7342.title: What this is not
7342.content: It is one target. A harness above these tools may have several ways of putting a rendering in front of readers, and treat GitHub Pages as one of them; nothing here needs to know that, and nothing here names it. It does not decide who may publish, whether review has happened, or what happens to other previews on the same host: those are the calling process’s.

7350.title: Render logging — the publish branch keeps its own history
7350.content: Skill render-logging: Log every render to the publish branch — what was published, removed, restored or deliberately retained — to an append-only log that lives beside what it describes. Use when adding or removing anything on gh-pages, when asking “what happened to this preview”, or before writing a workflow step that deletes a published artefact. Named by: Render log — the publish branch keeps its own history, Staging a feature branch preview, and taking it down .

7351.title: The question it exists to answer
7351.content: What happened to branches/<slug>, and why? . A preview can be cleaned up because its pull request closed, removed by a dispatch somebody confirmed, or deleted by an unrelated merge to main. Without a record on the publish branch itself, which one happened is not recoverable.

7352.title: Append-only, and never anything else
7352.content: A removal is a new entry, not the erasure of an old one. The pair — the rendered and the removed that follows it — IS the history. scripts/render-log.ts offers no verb that could lose an entry: no --remove, no --edit, no id to overwrite. The never-delete property is a shape of the tool, so a caller cannot be written wrongly. Emptying a log is a person’s decision, taken deliberately, with the confirmation every durable artefact here requires (deletion-requires-confirmation). No tool and no workflow does it.

7353.title: The four events, and why retained earns its place
7353.content: | event | what it records | . | rendered | published, or re-published over itself — so “when was this last built” needs no commit archaeology | . | removed | taken down. Requires a reason, refused without one | . | restored | carried across a full-replace deploy by restore-staging. Its own event, because “somebody pushed this branch” and “an unrelated merge nearly deleted it” are different facts | . | retained | a removal was considered and refused. Also requires a reason | . retained answers “why is this still up”: a preview still standing because a liveness signal fired leaves no trace otherwise.

7354.title: Where it lives, and why that is structural
7354.content: _render-log/<YYYY-MM-DD>.jsonl, at the root of the publish branch. Outside branches/, deliberately. The cleanup runs rm -rf "branches/$SLUG", and a branch named to collide with a directory under branches/ slugifies to exactly that name. A store outside branches/ is unreachable by that command whatever the slug says; a guard you have to remember is weaker than a location that cannot be reached. One file per UTC day, not one growing file and not one per entry. Six workflows publish to this branch; a read-modify-write of a single file loses whatever landed in between, and the tool appends a line rather than rewriting. One file per entry would make “what happened this week” a directory walk.

7355.title: It does NOT survive a deploy on its own — this is the part to get right
7355.content: docs-site.yml is a full replace: git rm -r --ignore-unmatch '*' over the whole branch, then copies _site in. It is the only one of this repository’s six gh-pages publishers without keep_files: true, and it is the one that fires on every push to main. So the log is carried across that deploy by restore-staging.ts, unconditionally — not gated on open pull requests the way previews are. A preview belongs to an open PR; a log entry about a closed one is exactly what nothing would carry, and exactly what a reader needs most. A log a deploy truncates is worse than no log, because a reader will believe its entries persisted. docs-site.yml runs restore-staging.ts from main, so a change to what the restore carries is not in force until it merges. --verify checks the carried prefixes as well as branches/, because a verifier blind to half of what the restore carried reports a clean run over the loss it exists to catch. A lost prefix is reported as not recoverable by re-running anything: a preview can be rebuilt from its workflow, and a record of what was already removed cannot. Only the prefixes the restore reported as carried are verified. A determined absent was never there to lose, and asserting on it would fail every deploy before the first entry is ever written. CARRIED_PREFIXES is where that is declared; it is a list, so another carried store is a new row, not a new code path. The carry runs before the preview check, so the log is carried even when there are no previews. A carry that could not be determined is not a warning. It collapses into the restore’s own unknown, exit 2, which fails the deploy step: continuing would run the full replace and delete the record. A determined absence — the branch is readable and has no log yet — is reported rather than omitted, because “there is no log yet” and “the carry never ran” look identical in a silent report and only the second is a defect.

7356.title: Who writes an entry
7356.content: Every path that can change branches/ writes one, and scripts/tests/workflow-yaml.test.ts asserts that by job rather than leaving it to be remembered: . | path | event | how it lands | . | feature-staging.yml → stage | rendered | the same commit as the deploy. The entry goes to the root _render-log/, never into _site, which would land it at branches/<slug>/_render-log/ — inside the directory a cleanup removes | . | feature-staging.yml → stage, preview cap | removed, one per rotated preview | the same commit as the deploy, written by staging-rotate.ts; the reason names the size budget, and the summary gives slug, age and size | . | feature-staging.yml → cleanup, confirmed | removed | the same commit as the removal | . | feature-staging.yml → cleanup, refused | retained | its own commit | . | feature-staging.yml → cleanup-dispatch | removed | the same commit as the removal | . | docs-site.yml → restore | carried, not written | restore-staging.ts | . The reason is the gate’s own, never a restatement of one branch of it. cleanup emits merged | labelled | closed-unmerged-and-unlabelled and the entry carries that value. A hardcoded reason would name the wrong rule for some of them, and a wrong reason reads as evidence. A removal and its record are one commit. A separate log push can fail on its own and leave a preview that vanished with nothing saying why. The rendered and retained entries are continue-on-error. A preview that deployed and whose entry did not is a gap in the record, not a failed deploy, and failing the job there would turn a logging problem into a lost review surface. The step goes red in the run, so the gap is visible. A removed entry has no such fallback and needs none: it cannot fail separately from the removal it describes.

7357.title: Writing an entry
7357.content: bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/render-log.ts --dir <gh-pages-checkout> \ --event rendered --kind staging-preview --path branches/<slug> --slug <slug> \ --summary "preview published" --branch "$BRANCH" --commit "$SHA" --run "$RUN_URL" . The tool writes into a directory and never pushes. The workflows that call it already hold a gh-pages checkout with their own retry and concurrency handling; a second pusher racing those is a new way to lose a deploy. One job knows how to push, this one knows what to write. Reading back: --read [--day YYYY-MM-DD]. It exits 1 when any line could not be read, and prints which — a short count must be visible as short, never passed off as complete. Same rule as ci-health: could-not-determine is never rendered as clean.

7358.title: A path is checked by VALUE, never trusted by provenance
7358.content: --path is refused unless it is / or a sequence of plain segments — no .., no leading /, no backslash. The staging slug sanitiser can emit .. (input .. gives output ..), and is safe only because git rejects every ref name containing it. That invariant holds for a slug taken from a ref and does not hold for one taken from a dispatch input — and cleanup-dispatch takes exactly that. So the check is on the value, not on where it came from.

7359.title: It is a specialisation of folio-log/v1, not a rival
7359.content: schemas/sdlc/log-entry.ts already answers “what does an entry look like”, and a render entry reuses those spellings: id, at, summary, detail, references, capture. Three things differ, each deliberately: . |   | activity log | render log | . | subject | what an agent did | what was published | . | store | fsh-guts/logs/, in the repo | the publish branch | . | published | no | yes | . An agent’s audit trail is not published; a record of what is on the publish branch belongs where its subject’s absence can be seen.

7362.title: Rendered impact — which rendered files a Change Set changes
7362.content: Skill rendered-impact: The list of rendered files a Change Set alters, and how a reviewer approves against it. Each renderer maps the input files a change touched to the rendered files of its site through its dependency cone, before any build; a build diff then confirms the prediction. Use when opening or reviewing a Change Set PR, when asked “which pages does this change”, when a prediction and a build disagree, or when adding a renderer. Named by: Human Translation Workflow, Translation review and adjudication, Translation round trip (untainted), Translation Workflow, Review task, Adjudication, Criterion adjudication, A harness’s default rendering, Theme and UI review — at ingestion, Wireframe design review, Prose and the code it describes, SME Review of Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Adopting an upstream version bump, Is the incremental IG AST what a full build would have produced?, Incremental IG build, L3 FHIR IG pipeline, Questionnaire wireframe review, Committee review of a content change, Merge and publish a content change, Stage the content change, Content Change and Review, Content lifecycle, Draft, review and publish, Editing and HCI validation, Guideline Updates, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Public comment on a review draft, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Review and publish a folio, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate . Skill id: rendered-impact · Package: sdlc-core . A Change Set’s PR is approved against what it does to the rendered site, not only against its source diff. A one-line FSH edit can re-render one page of 722 or all of them, and a reviewer cannot tell which from the diff. So every renderer answers one question, and the PR shows the answer.

7363.title: Scope
7363.content: . | Every renderer maps a list of changed input files to the list of changed rendered files, from its dependency cone. | The public-comment Change Set (changeset/1.0.0) is the Change Set for ANY folio change, and the rendered list is one of its fields. | The original stays in library/; a Change Set applies to the folio materialised in folio/, never to the library source. | .

7364.title: The contract: rendered-impact/v1
7364.content: Declared in cat-harness/schemas/ui/rendered-impact.ts. A renderer takes the changed input files and returns: . | field | says | . | files[] | each rendered file the change alters: path in the built site, change (changed, added, removed), role (content, data, index) and via, the chain that reached it | . | files[].anchors | for a page that assembles many units (a document page), the fragment ids the change alters; the review list links path#anchor | . | undetermined[] | each input the renderer could NOT place, with its reason, and scope: all when it can change any page | . | method | cone (predicted before a build) or build-diff (measured after one) | . Three rules, each one a refusal: . | Could-not-determine is never “no change”. An empty files with a non-empty undetermined is “not known”, and the PR says so in those words. A renderer that drops an input it cannot map is broken. | Index files are listed and marked, not dropped. The reviewer’s list (reviewList) leaves out role: index (search data, sitemaps, an artefact index) because review is of content, not indexes. The renderer marks the role; the reader filters. | A page whose bytes do not change can still change. An AST artefact page loads its resource in the browser, so the cone names the page AND its data file, and a build diff sees only the data file. That is unconfirmed, not a defect. | .

7365.title: Checking a prediction: the one comparison that matters
7365.content: comparePrediction(predicted, measured) sorts every file into three groups: . | missed: the build changed it, the cone did not predict it. A cone defect, never a pass. Report it on the PR and fix the renderer: the next Change Set relies on the same cone to tell the reviewer what to open. | confirmed: predicted and measured. | unconfirmed: predicted, not measured. Expected for content pages that load their data (rule 3). For anything else it means the cone is too wide: it is safe, but say so. | .

7366.title: The renderers today
7366.content: | renderer | maps | how | status | . | fhir-ig-pages | .fsh, .cql, input/pagecontent/*.md | fsh-cone forward cone → SUSHI’s fsh-index.json → AST artefact page + served JSON; a page → itself and every page that includes it | in the FHIR layer, documented with its AST tooling (skill_fetch ig-ast-delta) | . | document-site, public-comment-site, library-site | a block, a document/chapter/section manifest, media/*, the public-comment store, a file in a declared library entry or a folio review-anchors.json naming one (the entry’s Document view and doc.json; its structure.json also the library index) | loaded from the published changeset.json (each changed block’s label and file) and outline.json (the documents), never from source: a block lands on its document’s page, anchored at its label (anchors) — on a LAZY page (outline.json lazy) on its blocks/NNN.json chunk and index.hydrated.html instead, and a block added, removed, renamed or moved reshapes the shell and every chunk from its position on; a file no builder of the site reads is an input with no page: each builder in the folio’s build command exports siteReads (the folio; the comment store; every directory of a typology holding a kind it renders), and a file outside all of them, the submodules, .github/ and the root’s non-Markdown files reaches nothing — so beans/ reaches no page, while todos/, whose pages are rendered, still may. A step that exports no siteReads excludes nothing; never decide it from the layer’s declaration, which also declares what no builder reads | in the document layer, with the ChangeSet Tool | . | docs-site | any file | a file in the COMPOSED Jekyll tree (docsLayers, composedInstances) → its page (permalink, or .md → .html) or asset; an include → the pages that include it, transitively; _data → the pages and includes that read it; a layout, a THEME include (read from the installed theme; unreadable means every include) or an include nothing calls → any page; any page change → the search index; a file outside the tree → undetermined when the staging cone carries any directory, nothing when it reaches none | cat-harness-tools/scripts/docs-rendered-impact.ts | . | published-provenance | a mounted layer’s skill, process or schema (anything a generator renders) | the published root’s own record of what each page was generated from — the “Generated from <path>” note and data-src on the edit link — read back as source → pages; a new source has no page yet and an index names no source, so both stay for the QA diff | cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-changes.ts (predictByProvenance) | . Two builds of one commit differ in every page by a ?v=<build time> cache-buster, so diffBuiltSites blanks BUILD_STAMPS before hashing; without that, every page reads as missed. A renderer’s command line belongs to the layer that owns it; this layer names none above it.

7367.title: In the review process
7367.content: content-change-review.bpmn: . | Produce: the staging build writes rendered-impact.json beside the preview and puts the review list in the PR comment. Each entry links to the preview and to main’s copy of the page. | Read: at Compare main vs staging, the reviewer opens every file on the review list, not only the pages the author mentions. Use before-after-preview for the pairs, and visual-diff for figures. | Measure: the staging job diffs its build against main’s published site (measure-rendered-impact.ts, before the banner goes on) and writes rendered-measured.json: what changed, and what the prediction MISSED. Only when that site was built from the PR’s base does it count (status: known); otherwise main’s own changes would read as misses (not-base). No published main site, no file: “not measured”, never “nothing missed”. The review page shows it under the list, as the PR comment does: a run started by dispatch finds its PR from the branch, so the comment is not lost when no pull_request event started the run. | Show: every docs-site preview also carries branches/<slug>/changes/ (cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-changes.ts): the changed sources, with a re-pinned mount in index.lock.json expanded into the files its repository changed between the two pins (a re-pin handed to a renderer as one JSON line predicts nothing); the cone’s files and its undetermined inputs; and the build diffed against the site at the gh-pages root, its missed files listed as changed, not in the cone. That diff folds the preview’s base URL to the root’s, blanks BUILD_STAMPS and compares a page’s <main>, because a preview’s chrome differs on every page; a removed file is listed apart, by directory, since most are parts of the site the preview does not carry. The root records its build commit in build.json; a root not built from the PR’s base is said on the page, never read as this branch’s change. | Gate: review-coverage-gate.dmn reads three page counts beside the block counts, each with a status fact so an uncomputed count is never 0: . | unreviewedPages: review-list files nobody has reviewed at their current pin. A page is reviewed by a page: verdict, or block by block when every block anchored on it has a verdict; a data file goes with a reviewed page that shares its pin. | undeterminedInputs: inputs no renderer placed, until an input: verdict or waiver (with a reason) says somebody looked. | missedPages: measured but not predicted, until a page: verdict. | . A pin is the hash of the git blobs of the changed inputs on a file’s via (pinImpact), never the built bytes, which carry a per-build banner. An edit after review reopens exactly the pages it touched. The tag is in review-comments. | .

7368.title: Adding a renderer
7368.content: . | Map each input kind the renderer reads to the rendered files it writes, through the dependency information the renderer ALREADY has. Never re-derive a mapping the renderer’s own tool records (SUSHI’s fsh-index is the authority for FSH → resource). | Put every other input in undetermined, unless the renderer cannot read it at all: then it is an input with no file. Decide that from what the layer declares, never from a list of names here. | Test it against a real build with comparePrediction: 0 missed is the bar. | .

7370.title: /rendered-verification — look at it, then send the picture
7370.content: Skill rendered-verification: Confirm a UI change by LOOKING at it in a browser and sending the screenshots to the author, rather than describing it. Use whenever a change touches CSS, a Liquid/HTML template, a generated page, the navbar, a board, a sticky or any rendered surface — before claiming it works, and before asking the author to review it. Covers building the site locally, taking the REAL CI build off gh-pages when the question is theme chrome or layout, driving it with Playwright in this environment, measuring computed style rather than reading the stylesheet, hit-testing a control’s centre because visible is not usable, asserting the conditions so a check cannot pass over an unstyled page, and the defect classes that are invisible to a green gate set. Named by: Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file . continual-progress holds that a human cannot assess a rendered artefact from a description of it. Neither can the agent that wrote it. A stylesheet is not a rendering, a generator’s output is not a page, and a green gate set is not a screenshot.

7371.title: The rule
7371.content: A change to a rendered surface is not done until you have looked at it in a browser and sent the author the picture. Not “ran the tests”. Not “checked the CSS”. Opened it, measured the computed result, and attached the image to the turn. Sending the screenshot is part of the rule, not a courtesy: an image lets the author disagree with you in one glance.

7372.title: Check the page the owner opened, and that it is LIVE
7372.content: Owner, 2026-11-14: “why I am having to ask for the same requests multiple times?” An audit of five repeated requests found the same four failures: . | Merged and pinned is not live. The layer’s publish run failed at a guard, nothing recorded it, and the site kept serving pages from an older pin, so three merged fixes never reached the owner. Before saying a fix is done, find the layer’s latest publish run for the pinned commit and say whether it succeeded; if it failed, say so and hand it on. | The fix went to a different surface. “Cap + hover” for long titles was applied to the library table and not to the rail the owner was looking at. Screenshot the URL the owner named, not a page you chose. | The fix covered a batch, not the owner’s entry. A figures fix scoped to one family of entries left the owner’s entry with none. Check the entry the owner named, and say which entries the fix does not reach. | An older ruling outlived a newer one. A November 10 card chose wrapping for short menu names; three days later the owner asked for one line with hover for long titles, and the code still cited the old ruling. When a new request contradicts a recorded ruling, ask on a card which one wins, then change the code comment and the test that cite the old ruling. | .

7373.title: Why a green gate set does not cover this
7373.content: Defect classes no test catches, because the source was right and the rendering was not: . | what happens | why the suite is green | . | a generator emits raw <h3>, kramdown assigns no ids, and every heading on a page shares one anchor | the generator’s own output looks right | . | two files hold their own copy of a shared size (a rail at 40px, a sidebar at 56px) | each file has a test asserting its own copy | . | a component renders with no colour | an invalid custom-property substitution fails silently — no parse error, no console warning, just the initial value | . | a region lays out below the viewport, rendered and unreachable | the markup is correct; a !important in the theme makes the flex column inert | .

7374.title: Measure the COMPUTED result, never the stylesheet
7374.content: getComputedStyle and getBoundingClientRect are the instruments. Reading the CSS tells you what was authored; only the browser tells you what won. Measure every time: . | display, flex, min-height on a region you believe is a flex child. A !important from a theme utility class silently makes every flex value below it inert. | scrollHeight against clientHeight. A region that “does not scroll” and a region whose content is ten times its height look identical in a screenshot of the top of it. | the resolved colour, not the declaration. A custom property holding a hue substituted into color-mix() yields rgba(0,0,0,0) and no error. | . Use a control. When you suspect a value is invalid, build the minimal element in the page and read it back, rather than reasoning from the spec: the probe is a measurement, and reasoning from the spec is a claim. const probe = document.createElement("div"); probe.style.cssText = "--h:268;background:color-mix(in oklab, var(--h) 28%, transparent)"; document.body.appendChild(probe); getComputedStyle(probe).backgroundColor; // rgba(0, 0, 0, 0) -> invalid .

7375.title: A before/after pair beats an after
7375.content: Build the base branch too and shoot the same element. Without it “the dividers have colour now” is unfalsifiable. git worktree add <dir> origin/main --detach is the cheap way; symlink node_modules and the docs vendor/.bundle into it rather than re-installing. When the pair goes to a reviewer rather than confirming the change to yourself, before-after-preview (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) governs it: one build with one variable where possible, stable capture, a k of n count with its method, the status line, and where the preview sits in the review processes. It also covers papers, FHIR IGs and slide decks.

7376.title: Running it here
7376.content: Building the site is preview:site, whose header carries the two things that make a naive bundle exec jekyll fail in this repo. It is not what CI builds — CI uses the pinned remote_theme, this uses the gem — so read a theme-chrome question off the staging preview (next section), not off this. Liquid and kramdown are identical, and so is our own stylesheet. Two environment facts: . | Serve it under its baseurl. _config.yml pins baseurl: "/folio-assistant", so every stylesheet is requested at /folio-assistant/assets/…. Serving the build directory at / returns 200 for the HTML and 404 for every stylesheet — and an unstyled page renders, so the failure looks like a CSS bug rather than a 404. Symlink <serve>/folio-assistant -> <build> and serve the parent. | Pin the browser. Chromium is pre-installed but its build number will not match whatever playwright-core resolves to, and playwright install is not available. Launch with executablePath: "/opt/pw-browsers/chromium". | . Drive the control a reader would drive. page.click(".side-bar .site-title") (the avatar, which opens and closes the sidebar from 50rem up), not element.classList.add(…). A state you set by hand is a state you have not tested the way in to. And check that the state actually changed. Setting data-fa-scheme directly does not switch the scheme — the real toggle is jtd.setTheme(name). A test that silently does nothing reports the old state as the new one. Assert the switch landed (for example, the sidebar background changed) before reading anything off it. Know what that toggle does: setTheme swaps the theme’s first stylesheet, so while the new file is in flight the page has no ground but the browser’s white canvas, and it flashes white. A scheme check that only reads the SETTLED page cannot see it — hold the new sheet in flight with page.route and read the ground then, as first-paint-scheme.e2e.ts does. The rule itself lives in theme-artefacts (opt-in cat-harness.platform-ui) §”The page ground: the first paint is DARK”.

7377.title: The REAL build is reachable — take it off gh-pages
7377.content: This environment’s proxy refuses litlfred.github.io, but feature-staging.yml deploys each preview into branches/<slug>/ on the gh-pages branch, and git reaches what HTTP cannot: . git fetch origin gh-pages S=claude-my-branch-slug # the deploy comment names it mkdir -p "/tmp/rv/folio-assistant/branches/$S" git archive "FETCH_HEAD:branches/$S" | tar -x -C "/tmp/rv/folio-assistant/branches/$S" cd /tmp/rv && nohup python3 -m http.server 8091 >/dev/null 2>&1 & # → http://127.0.0.1:8091/folio-assistant/branches/$S/<page>.html . That is the pinned remote_theme, the composed tree, the mounted layers and the post-Jekyll steps — the thing CI publishes. A whole preview is ~90 MB; git archive FETCH_HEAD:branches/$S page.html assets takes just what a page needs. Mount it at the branches/ path, not at the site root. A staged page requests /folio-assistant/branches/<slug>/assets/…, so serving the extract at /folio-assistant/ 404s every stylesheet.

7378.title: Assert the CONDITIONS, or the check passes over nothing
7378.content: An unstyled page still renders. It still answers elementFromPoint. It still returns PASS. A run mounted at the wrong path reports a pass over a page with zero stylesheets; what gives it away is the numbers beside the verdict, not the verdict. So every rendered check reports, beside its verdict: . | document.styleSheets.length — zero or one means the page is bare; | a count of responses with status >= 400, collected from page.on("response"); | the precondition the defect needs — the class, the state, the element count. If the bug only appears when fa-has-fullwidth is set, a run where it is unset has not tested anything. | . A check that cannot tell a styled page from a bare one is not a check: could-not-determine rendered as a pass. A COUNT over the built site needs its instrument validated first . Before trusting any “N of M pages have X”, run the instrument on a known positive AND a known negative, and on one positive of each way X can appear. Naive instruments give confident wrong numbers: an exact class match misses the theme’s own variant, a substring match counts the class name quoted in prose, a link count takes a stylesheet href as a way out. For navigated pages, the instrument that holds is <nav class="fa-nav" OR id="site-nav". For a count of NODES with a page, an IRI and a folder-page row, do not write an instrument: bun run cat node-views:report -- --site <dir> is that count, validated by its tests, and it says unknown rather than 0 where it could not ask. It reads a folder’s data files, so rows a script draws are counted. For a site-wide count, the gh-pages route above scales. Use a --filter=blob:none --sparse clone of gh-pages, with sparse patterns for the files counted, and exclude branches/. All HTML is about 1.7 GB and takes minutes; one directory takes seconds.

7379.title: Visible is not usable — hit-test the control’s CENTRE
7379.content: A control can have the right size, the right colour and the right label, and still be un-clickable because something is painted over it — for example a wrapper that computes to height 0 because its only child is position: absolute, letting a flow sibling paint across the field. const b = el.getBoundingClientRect(); const hit = document.elementFromPoint( Math.round(b.x + b.width / 2), Math.round(b.y + b.height / 2)); const usable = hit && (hit === el || el.contains(hit) || hit.contains(el)); . Two ways this test lies: . | It resolves INSIDE the control. elementFromPoint returns the deepest element, often an <svg> or <span> within a button. hit === el alone reports a working control as covered — which is what the contains pair above is for. | It reports a preview-only overlay. The staging banner (a <div> with no class, z-index: 9999, a child of <body>) exists only on previews. Identify the coverer (document.elementsFromPoint(x, y).slice(0, 3)) before calling it a defect: what is on top decides whether it ships. | . Where the covered control is the ONLY route back to a state — the magnifier that reopens a collapsed search — being un-clickable means an action whose inverse is not reachable.

7380.title: Two environment facts that cost cycles rather than correctness
7380.content: . | Never pkill -f "http.server" from the shell running one. The pattern matches your own process group and kills the command issuing it — exit 144, no output, looks like the tool failed. Start each server on a fresh port in its own invocation instead. | Probe scripts must not be left in the repository root. check:undeclared-files fails the gate set on a stray probe.mjs. Playwright needs the script where playwright resolves, so write it to the repo root, run it, and delete it in the same command. | .

7381.title: What to send
7381.content: The frames that answer a question the author would otherwise have to ask: . | before and after of the same element, same viewport; | the surface in both colour schemes, if the change touches colour; | the state that is hard to describe — a region scrolled to its end, a menu open, an empty case. | . Caption them with what to look at, not with what they are. “The nav crushed to a 64px sliver, no home link” is a caption; “navbar screenshot” is a filename. SendUserFile is the mechanism; write into the working directory or the scratchpad, since a file the author cannot open is not a deliverable.

7382.title: Accessibility is measured here too
7382.content: Unique heading anchors and the 3:1 bar for meaningful non-text content are rendered facts: compute the contrast from the two resolved colours rather than from the tokens, because the token you authored and the colour that won are different questions.

7383.title: Listen for pageerror, or a crash reads as a missing feature
7383.content: A throw early in a page’s init() takes the rest of init() with it. The symptom is a feature that is simply not there — which looks exactly like a feature that did not mount — and a swallowed init is silent in a screenshot. So: attach the listener, and assert zero. page.on("pageerror", (e) => errors.push(e.stack || e.message)); . And check the base branch before you claim a crash is yours — or before you claim it is not. One run against a build of origin/main tells “something I just broke” from “a live defect nobody had reported”.

7384.title: A STATIC read of a client-rendered page is not verification — in either direction
7384.content: This skill stops a false red as well as a false green. Grepping a page’s committed HTML for content the page fetches at runtime proves nothing. The content is absent whether the page works or not. A library viewer, for example, carries DATA_HREF = "../../../assets/library/index.json", fetches it, and filters by layer. Its committed index.html never holds the entry names, so grepping it for them returns the same answer for a working page and a broken one. Loading it in Chromium settles it in one command. A false red files a bug against working code and sends the next agent to rewrite a correct generator, and because the report carries measurements it reads as thoroughly evidenced. If a page assembles any of its content after load, open it. The tell is cheap to check: a fetch, an XMLHttpRequest, a DATA_HREF, a <script> that writes into the DOM. Finding one means a static read cannot answer the question, and §"Running it here" above is how to answer it instead.

7385.title: Print it too, when the page defers anything
7385.content: A page that lazy-loads (images, a tree built on toggle, a listing drawn on first open, text kept for a popout) must print complete (owner, 2026-11-14). Check it the way a reader prints: emulate print media, run the page’s print preparation (its Print button with window.print stubbed, or a dispatched beforeprint), assert every image is loaded (complete && naturalWidth) and the deferred text is present, then page.pdf() and look at a page of it.

7386.title: What this does NOT replace
7386.content: The gate set. This is the layer above it: gates catch what is checkable from the source, and this catches what is only true once a browser has laid it out. A change that skips either is unverified.

7388.title: /repo-conversion — folio-assistant over a repo that already has a life
7388.content: Skill repo-conversion: Lay folio-assistant over a repository that already exists, without losing or silently moving what is in it. Scans the tree read-only, classifies candidate files into library (external source) and content (authored here) with an explicit third bucket for what it cannot classify, scans outside the content tree for mathematical evidence and refutations, lists the content markers (an IG, a DAK, processes, work items, library, Lean, folio manifests) the harness could declare and declares only the ones the person picks, puts the three questions the scan cannot answer to the author as selections, and hands ingestion to one agent or a small swarm. Use when a user wants an existing repo converted to a folio, asks to import what is already there, asks whether their PDFs/notes/drafts can come along, or asks what else in a repository an existing harness could declare. Named by: Content acquisition, Copy out materialized content — to work on somebody else’s bytes, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Adopt a methodology from a source document, Multi-locale translation, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Agent activity log, Staging a feature branch preview, and taking it down, Merge manager watch: wake, read the queue live, route, Merge to main, A merge train, Saturation meta-merge: land the ready PRs when the runners are full, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route, Getting started, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . Process: the content core’s processes/conduct/getting-started.bpmn, Task_ScanRepo, Task_ChooseHarnessed and Task_ConfirmImport (both non-relaxable). Scanner: bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts.

7389.title: 0. The one rule
7389.content: Scan, show, ask, then move — and never in any other order. The author’s repository is the thing of value; the scaffolding is replaceable. A wrong import is not fixed by a git checkout, because the author has to work out what the agent did. Task_ConfirmImport is marked relaxable="false" in the BPMN, and a content package may not declare it away.

7390.title: 1. Scan — read-only, and honest about its limits
7390.content: bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts # human-readable report bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts --json # same, as facts . It walks the working tree (respecting .gitignore) and sorts what it finds into three buckets: . | bucket | means | typical | . | library | external source material — something somebody else wrote, that the folio will cite or ingest | PDFs, papers, scans, datasets, references/, papers/, sources/ | . | content | material authored here, that could become folio blocks | Markdown prose, docs/, notes/, drafts/, .tex | . | unclassified | it could not tell | everything else, and it is reported, not hidden | . unclassified is reported, never forced. A two-bucket scanner’s mistakes arrive as moved files; this one reports what it could not place, and the author disposes of it. The classification is by path convention and extension only. It does not read file contents or call a model, so the author can disagree with any row of it in one word. Outside-content candidate scanning — preserving evidence and refutations . In repositories with formal, analytical, or domain-specific content, crucial verification scripts, macros, and counterexamples often live outside the primary content tree (content/ or folio/); a conversion that carries only that tree drops the evidence that some claims are false. scan-repo-content.ts scans outside the content tree and classifies these artifacts into read-only candidate classifications (defined by the content-type layer’s conversion refinement skill), reporting source location, rationale, and linkStatus (linked when referenced by at least one content block, or unlinked when orphaned). Like the general scan, candidate scanning never writes, moves, or modifies files; it presents the candidates to the author and agent so decisions can be made before importing.

7391.title: 2. Show, then ask — three questions, all as selections
7391.content: Present the scan as counts and a handful of examples per bucket, never as a 1,400-line file list. Then three questions, each answerable by picking. Load interaction-modality first. Q1 — import at all? . | Import everything the scan found (recommended) | Import only the library bucket — sources now, prose later | Import nothing; just set up folio-assistant | Let me pick bucket by bucket | . Q2 — where does each group go? Only for groups the scan was not confident about, and only when Q1 was not “nothing”. Offer library/ vs content/ per directory, not per file (a per-file interrogation is the accessibility failure in interaction-modality §0). Q3 — leave in place, or reorganise? . | Leave everything where it is (recommended) — the folio references the files at their current paths. Nothing moves, every existing link still works, and the decision stays open. | Reorganise into library/ and content/ — tidier, and it rewrites paths. Offer this only on a clean working tree, do it in its own commit, and use git mv so history follows. | . Recommend leave in place by default: a broken relative link in somebody’s README is a defect.

7392.title: 2a. Markers — choose what the harness reads (declare, don’t slurp)
7392.content: A harness declares what it reads in a repository; it does not take all of its content. The principle is directory-conventions §”A marker declares what is read, and nothing else is”. The scan’s fourth section, markers, lists the content a harness COULD be told to read: a sushi-config.yaml (an IG: contentTypes.ig), a legacy dak.json (contentTypes.dak), .bpmn processes, a work items store, library/, uploads/, Lean (contentType: paper) and folio manifests (contentType: document). For each it gives the paths, whether it is already declared — declared, not-declared, or unknown when there is no readable index.config.json to ask — and the snippet that would declare it, with where it goes (index.config.json#contentTypes, or a local layer’s <name>.json#directories). Content types come from the registry (defaultContentTypes; an { indexSection } type is checked against contentTypes.<id>), directory facets are checked against the registered graph typologies, and only the evidence the registries cannot state is a short table in cat-harness-tools/scripts/lib/content-markers.ts. Where each kind of content lives is directory-conventions. bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts [dir] --markers # the list bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts [dir] --markers --json # same, as facts . A plain command: any agent host (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Antigravity, Cursor, Copilot) or a person at a shell runs it, with no MCP server. It writes nothing. Q0 — which of these should the harness read? (Task_ChooseHarnessed, non-relaxable). Ask it the interaction-modality way — the full question in the chat, then a tap card where the host has one, otherwise a numbered pick-list with its default stated. Never a typed reply. Offer only the markers that are not-declared (or unknown), one option each: . | None of these for now (the default) — nothing is declared; the scan can be run again any time | contentTypes.ig — sushi-config.yaml, input/fsh/, … (the FHIR IG) | directories: processes — processes/ (7 BPMN files) | Let me pick several — the same options as a multi-select | . The default declares nothing, and the agent never declares a marker the person did not pick. Declare exactly the picks — the scan’s suggestion snippet, at its suggestion.at — in the scaffolding commit, or in its own commit on a layer that already exists. After setup, too. The same question fits any layer at any time: “what else could this harness declare?” is --markers on the layer’s repository, then Q0. Rows already declared are shown for context and are not offered. A content type registered by a higher harness layer appears as a hint when that layer is not loaded, with a note saying where the type lives. Declaring a scoped content type is not a boolean flag: its include list states everything that layer’s readers will read, so confirm the list with the person and consult that layer’s build-pipeline skill for how additional paths are added later.

7393.title: 3. Dispatch the ingestion
7393.content: Ingestion proper is library/processes/document-ingestion.bpmn (and the content layer’s document-intake refinement skill when converting into a content folio). What this skill decides is how much parallelism, and it is a question for the author because it spends their tokens: . | scale | when | how | . | inline | under ~10 documents | do it here, no subagents | . | one agent | tens of documents, one kind | a single background agent, reporting per document | . | small swarm | hundreds, or several distinct kinds | dispatch-agent (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) — 2–4 agents partitioned by directory, never by file count | . Partition by directory because a per-file partition puts two agents in the same manifest, and the conflicts cost more than the parallelism saves. Open one work item per ingestion front before dispatching — running the existence check in todo-manager.md (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan) §”Check before you create” first — so a session that dies mid-import leaves a plan behind rather than a half-full library/.

7394.title: 4. The conversion itself
7394.content: Once Q1–Q3 are answered, folio_init against the existing directory. It refuses rather than overwrites where a file is already present, which on this branch is the common case (README.md, .gitignore, a docs/). Read its report rather than assuming; the files it declined to write are the ones you now merge by hand: . | AGENTS.md — if one exists, merge; do not replace. It is the most valuable file in the repository for the next agent. | README.md — never replaced. readme-sections.ts only writes inside marker pairs the author has opted into, so offer to add markers rather than content. | .gitignore — append the folio entries; keep theirs. | . If the remote is empty, push main first. A repository with work locally can still have an empty remote, and GitHub makes the first branch pushed to an empty repository its default. Run init-folio or push main before any feature branch. If main has no harness yet, land a setup-only PR first. A fork or an existing repository whose main has no index.config.json and index.lock.json gives the full PR checks nothing to compare against: the base side fails before any test runs, and the PR’s own gates are skipped. So open one small PR with only what folio_init writes and the pins, merge it, and only then branch for content. Draft-tier checks never build the base, so this does not show until the content PR leaves draft. The setup-only PR has a Tool: instantiate-harness. It pins the harness and every layer it needs, mounts them, commits the setup on harness/<harness>, opens that PR, and renders the branch’s preview at gh-pages:branches/<branch>/. On a repository with nothing mounted yet, run it from a fresh clone of the tools layer: . git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/litlfred/cat-harness-tools /tmp/cht echo "<where the author consented>" | bun run /tmp/cht/scripts/instantiate-harness.ts \ --repo . --harness <owner/repo> --consent-by <who> [--plan | --local] . The setup also writes .github/cat.ts and .github/mount-from-lock.sh and sets the root’s cat script to bun .github/cat.ts, so after the merge a fresh clone needs no mount step: the first bun run cat … mounts the layers. --plan prints the closure and every step and writes nothing; --local commits on the branch and pushes nothing. The harness’s own adoption steps are its checkout scripts instantiate:<harness> (files it declares, committed with the setup) and prepare:<harness> (what the site is built from, never committed). For an IG on a FHIR harness these declare contentTypes.ig and build the IG’s first AST. A harness built on this platform may add adoption steps of its own for its kind of repository, for example about CI that already publishes a site on every push. Ask skill_list for the skill governing that kind before calling the conversion done.

7395.title: 5. Publishing — provision gh-pages first; an overlay needs it too
7395.content: An overlay never reaches getting-started §5 by itself, so this section repeats the one step a publishing route cannot skip: provision gh-pages before GitHub Pages is switched on. The step is Task_ProvisionGhPages (“Provision gh-pages”) in getting-started.bpmn, on the shared path after scaffolding and before the Pages build, and it carries the semantics of A_Provision in bootstrap-tools’ render-kg-to-github-pages.bpmn. The tool is pages-bootstrap: . bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pages-bootstrap.ts # reports `unprovisioned` (exit 3) and the exact command when gh-pages is absent bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pages-bootstrap.ts --provision # pushes an orphan gh-pages: placeholder index.html + .nojekyll . --provision is idempotent and never forces a push, and nothing creates a remote branch without it. Then switch Pages on with Source: “Deploy from a branch: gh-pages, / (root)” — the script prints the source it expects. When the repository’s publish workflow pushes gh-pages, “GitHub Actions” is the wrong source: the workflow would push a branch Pages was never told to serve. The same holds for an overlay that remote-mounts its dependencies. A mount brings layers in; it does not provision anything on the downstream’s remote.

7396.title: 6. Anti-patterns
7396.content: . | Moving a file before Q3 is answered. | Reporting a two-bucket classification. If unclassified is empty on a real repository, suspect the scanner rather than celebrate it. | A per-file confirmation loop. See §2. | Swarming a 12-document import. The dispatch overhead exceeds the work. | Replacing an existing AGENTS.md or README.md. Merge, or leave. | Treating the scan as ingestion. It reads; it never writes. Ingestion is a separate process with its own diagram and its own gate. | Switching Pages on before gh-pages exists, or choosing “GitHub Actions” for a workflow that pushes gh-pages. See §5. | Dropping outside-content math artifacts or unlinked audit refutations. Carrying only the primary content tree (content/ or folio/) drops outside proofs, computations, and refutations showing that some paper claims are false. See §1. | .

7398.title: Is the repository itself healthy?
7398.content: Process_RepoHealth · strict · 2 step(s) . Is the repository itself healthy — what the review previews cost the publish branch, what a clone costs, whether the work plan holds duplicates or unhonoured claims — reported in one tracking issue and never acted on. THE SAME SHAPE AS ci-health, ONE LEVEL OUT. That one asks whether the WORKFLOWS pass; this asks about the REPOSITORY — how much of gh-pages the review previews occupy, how big a clone costs, whether the work plan has duplicates or unhonoured claims. IT REPORTS AND NEVER ACTS. Four of the five checks are about artefacts accumulating, and every finding’s action names something a PERSON does. That is deletion-requires-confirmation applied to the tool that most wants to break it: the skill’s own worked example is bean plj1, a workflow whose shape deleted every open PR’s preview without anybody deciding it. There is no removal task on this diagram, and its absence is the rule being followed rather than an omission. THE REPORT IS KEPT WHETHER OR NOT THE CHECKS SUCCEED (if: always()), which is why Run the health checks says “keeping the report either way”. A sweep whose output survives only on success cannot be used to investigate the run that failed. The daily cron is at 06:41, OFF THE HOUR deliberately: GitHub’s scheduler queues heavily at :00, and a delayed run is a run whose report is stamped later than the state it describes. THE THIRD STATE IS THE WHOLE POINT, AND IT IS THE ONLY ONE THAT FAILS THE JOB. Verified 2026-09-20 by reading the if: guards: unknown runs exit 1; a finding does NOT. A repository in trouble leaves this workflow GREEN and speaks through the tracking issue, while a sweep that could not look turns the job red. That inversion is deliberate and is invisible from the run list, which is the argument for drawing it. ONE TRACKING ISSUE, EDITED IN PLACE, never a comment and never a second issue — a feed nobody reads is the failure mode a watchdog invites. On unknown the issue is left UNTOUCHED: not closed, not opened, not edited. Closing it would assert the thing the sweep just failed to establish. Ensure the tracking label exists sits AFTER Could we tell? and before the split, because both issue paths need the label — the clean path filters on it too, and on a repository where nothing has ever gone wrong it would not otherwise exist. It is skipped on unknown, where neither path runs and a label hiccup must not be what fails the job. The verdict is reported through the shared tracked-watch process (Process_TrackedWatch), with the label repo-health. Its three ends say what happened: unknown (job red, issue untouched), clean (issue closed), or found (issue opened or edited, job green). i i

7415.title: Review comments — from a PR comment to a structured todo
7415.content: Skill review-comments: Reviewer comments on a folio’s edit-set, from a tagged pull-request comment to a structured todo on the review page. Covers the tag a reviewer types, how the comments are ingested into review-comment/1.0.0 todos, where the published review-comments.json comes from and when it refreshes, how a comment follows a renamed block and survives a removed one, who may change a comment’s status, and how to change this process. Use when a reviewer asks how to comment on a block, when the review page shows no comments or a wrong one, when editing the ingestion, or when a folio’s staging workflow is set up. Named by: Committee review of a content change . Skill id: review-comments · Package: content-lifecycle-ext Tools: folio-review-comments (ingest), folio-review-comment-move (record a decision) . A reviewer comments on one block of a folio by writing an ordinary comment on the edit-set’s pull request, starting with a tag that names the block. The review process turns each tagged comment into a todo of a special kind, review-comment/1.0.0. The review page lists those todos beside the blocks they are about.

7416.title: Design
7416.content: | rule | why | . | The channel is a PR conversation comment tagged with the block label | Needs nothing installed, sits beside the approve, and is anchored by LABEL, so it survives a block moving. A line review comment is anchored to a file line and is lost when the block moves. | . | The record is a todo subtype declared by core, in the dynamic KG | A board, heat map or reader that understands todos reads a review comment without knowing about review. | . | The preview gets comments from a file the workflow writes | Works for private and public repositories, and no token ever reaches a browser. | . | A status change is committed to the folio’s todos/ on the edit-set’s feature branch | Reviewed with the edit it is about, lands on main only when that branch merges, and is part of the KG. | . The PR comment is the write channel; the todo is the canonical record.

7417.title: Writing a comment: the tag
7417.content: Start a conversation comment on the pull request with header lines, then a blank line, then what you want to say: . block: prose:overview kind: defect role: clinical-sme The dose in the second sentence contradicts table 3. | header | required | values | default | . | block: | yes | the block’s label, exactly as the review page shows it | — | . | kind: | no | question, defect, suggestion, editorial | question, which asserts least | . | role: | no | the lane you are reviewing in, a role id from roles.json | reviewer | . | The headers must be the very first lines. The first line that is not key: value ends the header. | block: takes the rest of the line, because labels contain colons (prose:overview). It must be ONE label. | A comment without block: is conversation, not a review comment, and is left alone. A PR thread is also where people talk. | A malformed tag is reported, never dropped. An unknown kind, or two words after block:, appears in malformed with the comment’s link, so the reviewer can fix it. | . The review page shows the exact block: <label> line for every changed block, ready to copy, and links to the pull request. GitHub cannot pre-fill a comment box, so copying the line is the one manual step.

7418.title: What a review comment IS
7418.content: review-comment/1.0.0, in folio-assistant-core/schemas/review-comment.ts. It is declared with nodeKind and its one parent is the harness todo, which itself is carried-note + themed. So it IS a todo: . | targetLabel is required. A general todo may float free; a review comment is always about one block. | status is closed: open, addressed, resolved, adjudicated, withdrawn. | Everything review-specific sits under one field, review: the repository, PR, comment id and URL, reviewer, role, kind, the block’s content hash and the commit when ingested, orphaned, anchoredFrom, and the decision that closed it. | . Keeping the review fields under one key means no field here can collide with one a parent adds later, which is the collision nodeKind refuses at load.

7419.title: Who may change a status: only the process
7419.content: A status moves only through transition(comment, to, {process, task}), and only along a row of REVIEW_TRANSITIONS. Anything else throws. | move | from | to | by (BPMN task) | needs a Decision | . | ingest | — | open | Process_ContentChangeReviewCommittee#Task_IngestComments |   | . | address | open | addressed | Process_Review#Task_EditorDecides |   | . | send back | addressed | open | Process_Review#Task_EditorDecides |   | . | resolve | addressed | resolved | Process_Review#Task_EditorDecides | yes | . | adjudicate | open, addressed | adjudicated | Process_Adjudication#A_RecordEntry | yes | . | withdraw | open, addressed | withdrawn | Process_ContentChangeReviewCommittee#Task_WithdrawComment |   | . A comment’s status is what the coverage gate counts, so a comment closed outside the process would count as reviewed when nobody decided anything. A test holds every row to a task that exists in its .bpmn. Ingestion is the review coordinator’s first step in content-change-review.bpmn’s committee phase, content-change-review-committee.bpmn; withdrawal is the reviewer’s step there after the slices come back.

7420.title: Ingestion: the Tool
7420.content: bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/review-comments.ts \ --repo owner/name --pr 7 --out _site/review-comments.json \ --folio folio --blocks-out _site/blocks.json \ --existing <previous review-comments.json> . Declared as the Tool folio-review-comments in folio-assistant-core/tools/folio-review-comments/, whose satisfies names this skill. | Read the comments. All pages of the PR’s conversation comments, with GITHUB_TOKEN when set. --comments <file> reads them from a file instead, for offline runs and tests. | Know the blocks. Either --folio <dir>, which reads the manifests as text and executes nothing, or --blocks <blocks.json> from an earlier run. | Keep everything already ingested. Every comment in --existing is kept, status included. A comment’s id is review-pr<N>-c<commentId>, so a re-run finds it rather than adding a second one. | Add the new ones. Each tagged comment not yet ingested becomes an open todo. A defect gets priority high; the others get medium. | Re-anchor every comment against the head’s blocks (reanchorToBlocks): . | the label is present: anchored; | a block lists the label in its renamedFrom: the comment moves to that block, and the old label goes into review.anchoredFrom; | neither: orphaned: true. Kept and shown, never dropped. | . | Write review-comments.json, folio-review-comments/v1. Its comments ARE the todo kind, each validated as one. The envelope adds only what one node cannot: provenance (repo, pr, commit, generatedAt), the malformed list, and the untagged count. So “no comments” and “comments nobody could parse” can be told apart. | . Why re-anchor against renamedFrom and not the ChangeSet. A ChangeSet compares against main. A block ADDED in the pull request and then renamed inside it is “added” both times, so the comment made on its first label would be orphaned. The block’s own renamedFrom (guarded by id-stable) says where it came from whatever the base. reanchor() over a ChangeSet also exists, for a caller that has only that.

7421.title: Recording a decision: commit to the feature branch
7421.content: When an editor or adjudicator decides what happens to a comment, the decision is committed to the feature branch that carries the edit-set, the same branch the edits are on: . bun run folio-assistant-core/scripts/review-comment-move.ts \ --id review-pr7-c1 --to addressed \ --process Process_Review --task Task_EditorDecides \ --published _site/review-comments.json --commit . | The move goes through transition(), so --process and --task must be a task allowed to make it, and resolved / adjudicated need --decision. The command is not a back door around the table above. | A new folio already has the directory. init-folio writes todos/todos.json declaring items and feedback (todo-feedback), and creates both. An older folio that lacks it gets an error naming the remedy. | The file goes where the graph says. That is the todos graph’s directory of kind todo-feedback (“todos raised against a specific block, carrying the submitter’s identity”), read from todos/todos.json. A graph that declares none gets an error naming the remedy. | The file IS the node: <feedback dir>/<id>.json, one review-comment/1.0.0, the same object the published file carries. It is JSON, not Markdown, because the todo reader’s front matter is flat and a review comment has a nested review field. | --commit refuses the base branch (default main, change it with --base) and a detached HEAD. The check runs before anything is written, so a refused commit leaves nothing behind. A status committed straight to main would record a review outcome that no merge ever accepted. | The first move reads the published file, where a comment first exists after ingestion. Every later move reads the committed file, which is the reviewed record. | . How it reaches the page. The commit is a push to the feature branch, which rebuilds the preview. That build’s ingestion reads the committed comments (--todos) and a committed comment wins over the previously published copy. The comment-triggered refresh checks out no branch code, so it cannot read them and keeps what the last build published. Nothing is lost between the two. What it costs. One extra commit on the edit-set’s branch per decision, and a PR from a fork cannot be written to by anyone but its author.

7422.title: Verdicts: “I read this version”
7422.content: A comment asks for something. A verdict records that a reviewer read a block, and what they judged. The coverage gate needs verdicts, because comments cannot say whether a block with none was read. The channel is the same tagged PR comment, with a verdict: or waive: line instead of kind:. block: prose:dose prose:schedule verdict: ok role: clinical-sme . | line | means | . | verdict: ok | read, no objection | . | verdict: changes | read, and it needs changing. The reasons go in review COMMENTS; the verdict only records the reading | . | waive: <reason> | the block needs no review (a pure rename, say). The reason is required and kept | . | block: may name several labels, so one comment can close a slice. One verdict is recorded per label. | A comment is a verdict or a review comment, never both. A tag with kind: as well is refused and shown as malformed, so nothing is counted twice under two meanings. The comment parser passes every verdict tag over. | A verdict is pinned to the block’s hash. It counts only while the block is at that version. An edit after review reopens exactly the blocks it touched. The old verdict is kept and shown as “on an earlier version”. | A verdict on a label the head does not carry is malformed, not recorded. | . Pages and inputs no block reaches. A page changed by a manifest or media file, the comment pages and every FHIR IG page have no block to give a verdict on, and an input no renderer could place may have changed any page. The same tag takes them, beside or instead of block:: . page: en/dpi-h-ra/index.html verdict: ok . input: sushi-config.yaml waive: only the version string changed . page: names a path in the preview’s rendered-impact.json, or a page the build measured and the prediction missed; input: names one of its undetermined inputs. Each is pinned to that file’s hash there, so it reopens when an input that reaches it is edited. A page or input the build does not list, or a build that published no rendered impact, is reported malformed with the reason. See rendered-impact (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc). The folio-review-comments Tool ingests verdicts into the same review-comments.json, as its verdicts array (folio-review-verdict/v1, folio-assistant-core/schemas/review-verdict.ts). Coverage. The folio-review-coverage Tool computes every fact GW_Covered reads (uncoveredBlocks, openDefects, and, with --rendered and --measured, the page counts with their rendered and measured statuses) and prints them as JSON on stdout, ready for workflow_complete. Every fact is always printed, because the engine refuses a missing one. With --todos <root> --commit it writes the verdicts into the todos graph’s declared review-verdicts directory and commits them to the feature branch, as comment statuses are, and it refuses the base branch and a detached HEAD. init-folio declares that directory (todos/verdicts/) for every new folio.

7423.title: Publication: where the file comes from, and when
7423.content: folio-staging.yml (the reusable workflow a folio calls) has two jobs: . | job | runs on | blocks from | what it writes | . | stage | the folio’s pull request (including a push that records a decision) | --folio, the checked-out feature branch; statuses from --todos | the site, changeset.json, blocks.json, review-comments.json | . | comments | a new or edited PR comment containing block: | the published blocks.json | review-comments.json only | . The comments job never checks out or runs the pull request’s code. It is started by anyone who can comment, and it holds a token that can write to the publish branch. Checking out a PR’s code in such a job is the well-known way to hand that token to a stranger. So it checks out only: . | the platform, at platform_ref (never a copy the PR carries); | the publish branch, which holds only what earlier trusted builds wrote. | . A comment body is parsed as data and never reaches a shell. The job also skips bot comments, so the preview comment the workflow itself posts cannot start it. Freshness. A new comment appears on the page about a minute later, after the comments job runs. A push rebuilds everything and keeps every comment. Nothing refreshes on a comment when there is no preview yet (no blocks.json), and the job says so rather than failing. The caller must opt in. A folio’s own workflow has to list issue_comment among its triggers for the comments job ever to run. init-folio writes that for a document folio.

7424.title: The review page
7424.content: en/review/index.html in the preview reads review-comments.json beside changeset.json, at the preview’s root, when it is opened: . | each changed block lists its comments: kind, status, reviewer and role, the first line, a link to the PR comment, the resolve: <id> tag for an open or addressed comment, and the recorded decision for a closed one; | a comment filter (Show comments) filters the listed comments by status (open, addressed, resolved, adjudicated, withdrawn, or open and addressed) or kind (defect, question, suggestion, editorial); | a comment on a block this PR did not change is listed separately, since a review of a whole document comments on unchanged text too; | orphaned comments are listed under their own heading, with the label they were made on; | malformed tags are listed with their links, so the reviewer can fix them; | every changed block shows its block: <label> line and a link to the PR, for writing a new comment; | no review-comments.json means the page SAYS it has no comment data. An empty list would read as “nobody commented”. | .

7425.title: Changing this process
7425.content: The process is a Skill and a Tool rather than YAML steps, so it can be changed here: . | to change | edit | and | . | the tag grammar | parseReviewTag in schemas/review-comment.ts | this skill’s tag table; the tests | . | a status or who may move it | REVIEW_COMMENT_STATUSES / REVIEW_TRANSITIONS | the BPMN task it names; this skill’s table | . | where a decision is recorded | folio-assistant-core/scripts/review-comment-move.ts | the folio-review-comment-move Tool node | . | a field on the record | ReviewFieldsSchema | the page, if it shows it | . | what the ingestion does | folio-assistant-core/scripts/review-comments.ts | the Tool node’s io if a flag changes | . | when it runs | folio-staging.yml and init-folio’s caller template | the trust notes above | .

7426.title: Deciding from the review page: a resolve: comment
7426.content: The page decides through the same channel it comments through. Under each open or addressed comment it shows the tag to post as a pull-request conversation comment, with the words that comment’s status allows: . resolve: review-pr7-c123 decision: resolved The dose now matches table 3. | The words are transitions of the table above: addressed (address), reopened (send-back), resolved (resolve), adjudicated (adjudicate), withdrawn (withdraw). Anything the table refuses is refused here too. | Who. A repository owner, member or collaborator (GitHub’s author_association) decides; the comment’s own author may withdraw it. Anyone else’s tag is refused, because a PR conversation is open to every GitHub user and a status is what the coverage gate counts. | The Decision that closes a comment is the decision comment’s URL. | Once. Each applied decision’s comment id is kept in review.decisions, so a rebuild, or a committed copy that already carries it, applies nothing twice. | Never dropped. A tag that cannot be read or applied is listed under “Tags that could not be read or applied”, with its reason. | . The build (folio-review-comments, and stage-local for a site.build folio) applies the tags after ingestion, so the published file and the page show the decided status. With --write-decided the Tool also writes each newly decided comment into the todos graph’s feedback directory, as folio-review-comment-move writes it; stage-local passes it and then runs state:push for a todos graph kept on its own state branch (dth-hrh’s cat/dth-hrh/todos), so the decision is recorded without anyone running a command. A todos graph in the feature branch’s tree is left for the editor to commit.

7427.title: Not yet decided
7427.content: . | Committing a page decision to an in-tree todos graph automatically. | A reviewer who edits a comment after ingest. The edit is not re-read, so a record an editor has already acted on is not silently rewritten. Whether an edit should reopen the comment is open. | Line review comments are not read. A reviewer who uses one gets no todo. | .
