An extra column is reported and ignored. A dropdown value outside the master’s values, or a page or line that is not in the frozen review version, rejects the row. | Sort. Every row with feedback is put in a group. Imported CS# and PC# numbers are hints, never keys. | Group | When | . | Add to existing | same number and same title: the changed human cells | . | Conflict | same number, another title (the number is wrong or reused); or a cell changed both offline and in the master since the copy was taken | . | Possible duplicate | no such number, but the same words as another row | . | New | none of these: the master gives it a number | . | Rejected | it failed validation | . --base is the archived workbook the copy was taken from (git show <commit>:<file>). With it, a cell changed only in the master is kept. Without it, a filled master cell may only be extended offline, and any other change to it is a conflict. | A person selects. Post the review list the check printed and ask which rows to import. Give the lettered or numbered choices, with a recommendation: usually every Add and New, no Conflict. | Plan. review-log-import.ts plan report.json --log <node> --select <numbers> [--accept-conflicts] --out plan.json gives the cell writes: A1 range and value, human columns only. A new row goes below the last row, and the sheet’s script numbers it. A new comment from the PDF feedback template has only the script’s columns (page, line, comment). It is not typed into the sheet. It goes to --intake-out <csv> for public-comment.ts import --channel comment-matrix, which numbers and places it. That CSV may hold names, so it stays out of the repository. | Write the planned cells to the master log, and nothing else. Editor (orange), agent (green) and script (grey) cells are never written. The watcher then picks the new feedback up as usual. | .

7478.title: Published with the document’s site
7478.content: scripts/review-sheet-site.ts --out <site> (package script site:review-sheet in a folio, a sourceSteps entry of its site build) writes <site>/review-sheet/: the generic Code.gs, each review/<mode>/sheet-sync.json as <mode>.config-rows.json, review-sheet.jsonld (the script as schema:SoftwareSourceCode with its SHA-256 and commit; each document’s settings as a schema:Dataset linked to its sheet and to the Tool), and an index.html with the setup steps and the SHA-256 to check a pasted copy against. Point people there rather than sending the file.

7479.title: Trusting the script
7479.content: A copy of a sheet carries its Apps Script, so anyone starting from a template should know what they are running. | Nothing runs until the sheet’s owner allows it. The owner runs installTriggers; Google then shows the scopes, and the triggers run as the owner, whoever’s edit fires them. So an editor’s edit makes owner code read what they typed: the script therefore never writes typed text as a formula (asText, q), and touches only this sheet. | Security review. tools/review-sheet-sync/security-review.md records the threat model and findings F1 to F10, each fixed with a test or accepted with its reason. Re-review on any new write sink, service, or editor-writable tab. | The agent caps new issues (finding F6): it opens a change set’s issue only for a row with a Title or feedback text, and asks a person before opening more than 20 in one sync. | This sheet only. The template starts with @OnlyCurrentDoc, so the consent screen asks for “this spreadsheet”, not all of the owner’s spreadsheets. The script uses only SpreadsheetApp, PropertiesService, LockService and ScriptApp: no UrlFetchApp, mail or Drive, so it sends nothing out. review-sheet-security.test.ts fails if one of those, or eval/new Function, appears. | Three permissions, one file. Google works out a script’s permissions from its code, and @OnlyCurrentDoc narrows the spreadsheet one to this sheet. So the consent screen asks for exactly three: this spreadsheet, the script’s own triggers, and its menu. tools/review-sheet-sync/appsscript.json records those three for the security test, which fails if the code would need more. It is a record, not a file to paste. | Plain ASCII. The built script escapes every non-ASCII character, so a paste cannot mangle it. The build prints its SHA-256; compare it with the pasted copy. | Wrong sheet. Pasted into a sheet it was not built for, it stops with a message naming the config and tab it expected, before installing triggers. | Check a copy against its source. The script is the same for every document, so one review covers all copies. Its header names the folio-assistant-core commit it was built from. Build again at that commit with the folio’s config and compare; or ignore the copied script and paste one you built yourself. | “Google hasn’t verified this app.” Bound scripts are unverified, so the owner clicks Advanced to continue. Publishing as a verified Workspace add-on would remove the warning. | .

7480.title: Drafting mode: editors’ and contributors’ feedback
7480.content: Before a document goes to public comment, editors and contributors give feedback on the working draft. That needs a simpler sheet: no Public Comment Source, no Review Public Comments, no TWGs. Each row of feedback is a change set (CS: a list of related comments on one topic), and each change set gets a GitHub issue. Tabs. | tab | who writes | columns | . | Contributor Feedback | people, plus the Apps Script | one row per change set. Grey, mechanical: Change-set (the script gives a used row the next CS-nnn once; it stays with the row). Blue, people: Title; Selected Sections (a multi-select dropdown of the document’s table of contents, each section indented under its chapter by three U+2800 blanks per level, since a dropdown cannot nest; not real spaces, because Sheets trims a multi-select cell and the first chip would lose them and read as Invalid; plain, because a dropdown chip cannot carry a link); any number of Contributor Feedback (…) columns, one per contributor, with their initials or name in the brackets (e.g. Contributor Feedback (CL); the script reads every column whose header is Contributor Feedback or starts Contributor Feedback (); Disposition (a dropdown: Pending, Accepted, Partially accepted, Not accepted, Noted, Duplicate, Out of scope), the committee’s verdict on the row. Orange, editors: Ready for agent (Yes, No, Completed), Ready for merge (Yes/No). Grey, by the script: Section links (each selected section on its own line, linked to its place on the document page, like the Sections column of the public-comment log). Green, by the agent: Feedback (agent), right of Ready for merge, the agent’s proposed direction (not a person’s feedback: the script leaves it out of the Contributor Feedback columns, and it decides nothing). Green, by the script from Agent: Issue (<repo>#n, linked), Agentic status (as in public-comment mode: one line per PR, <repo>#n (status, completed) · what it changed), Staging review (a “review” link to the change set’s review page on its staging preview, branches/<branch>/en/review/, while its PR is open), Agentic status (filter) (the change set’s status as one plain value, for the “By agentic status” filter view) | . | Agent | the agent only | one row per change set: Change-set, Issue (URL), Agentic status, Pull request (change set), What the PRs changed (change set), Agent completed (UTC, change set), Staging review page (change set), Feedback basis (change set). The agent writes it as each step completes, by the steps of the review-sheet-agent-columns skill; a drafting sheet has no per-comment rows, so only its change-set columns apply | . | TOC (hidden) | the script | the Sections dropdown’s list and each entry’s link. Rewritten on every refresh, so it follows the document | . Colours as in public-comment mode: grey mechanical, blue human, orange editor gates, green agent-derived. Built from the folio’s review-anchors.json: each chapter (Ch 3 Digital Transformation Approach), each numbered section (3.1 DIIG alignment) and each unnumbered section, prefixed by its chapter (Ch 3 · Objectives and key messages). A multi-select cell joins its choices with , , so commas in titles become ;. Each links to sectionUrl + the anchor (sec:3-1, chap:<dir>), which the document page carries as element ids. Config, review/drafting/sheet-sync.json: . { "mode": "drafting", "anchors": "folio/<doc>/review-anchors.json", "sectionUrl": "en/<doc>/#" } . Write the URLs relative to the folio’s site: the build resolves them against iriBase in the folio’s <instance>.json (e.g. https://litlfred.github.io/dth-hrh/), so no organisation name is written in sheet-sync.json and a folio that moves changes one iriBase and rewrites its Config. An absolute https:// URL is taken as written. tabs and columns (draft, draftAgent) override the headers as in public-comment mode. Write its Config with --config review/drafting/sheet-sync.json and install as above. The Sections dropdown is a data validation “dropdown from a range” on TOC!A2:A with Allow multiple selections ticked (step 6 below). Without the tick, a cell with two or more sections shows “Invalid: Input must fall within specified range”. The agent’s part: every change set has an issue. On each sync, for every Contributor Feedback row with a Change-set: . | If the Agent tab has no row for it, add one (Change-set, Agentic status Not started). | If that row has no Issue, open a GitHub issue in the folio’s repository: title CS-nnn: <Title> (or the first feedback line while Title is empty), body the linked sections, every Contributor Feedback (…) cell verbatim, and a link back to the sheet row. Write its URL into Issue. | When feedback is added to a row later, comment the new text on its issue. | Propose a direction in Feedback (agent) for every new row (from an issue, a person or a TWG workbook) and whenever the row changes, whoever changed it. The watcher does this on its next wake (skill review-log-watch, step 5). A question for people goes there too, as a Decision needed: block (§”Inputs and outputs”). On each sync compute feedbackBasis(header, row) (tools/review-sheet-sync/feedback-issue.ts: a short hash of Title, Selected Sections and the people’s Contributor Feedback columns). Where it differs from the Agent tab’s Feedback basis (change set), or the proposal cell is empty (a person clears it to ask for a fresh one), write a new proposal and the new basis. The script’s own writes (ids, links, tree marks) do not change the basis. | Work a change set only when Ready for agent is Yes; its PRs say Closes #n for the change set’s issue, and go to Agent’s PR columns. | When you pick a row up, say so first: set its Agent status to Working and put the URL of your conversation (the session, thread or PR discussion) in Agent conversation (change set). Agentic status then opens with An agent is working on it: conversation, linked. The script finds that column by header; on a sheet that lacks it, the agent adds it at the right of the Agent (change sets) tab. | . Title is the people’s on both kinds of sheet: the agent never writes it. In public-comment mode a Title-only row on Review Change Sets is a new change set, and the agent’s title is only the first value of a row it adds (skill review-log-watch, “Change sets people make”). Feedback from the site. A folio with .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/block-feedback.yml (copy the shared templates/issue-forms/block-feedback.yml) gets 📣 feedback links that open that form with Content, Section, Block, page and Source prefilled; the contributor picks a Type and writes Comment and Proposed change. On each sync the agent lists open issues labelled feedback that no Agent row names, and for each appends a Contributor Feedback row from tools/review-sheet-sync/feedback-issue.ts (feedbackRow): Sections the block’s TOC entry, Title a draft (<section>: <first sentence>, which people may rewrite), Contributor Feedback @login (Type): comment plus Proposed: …. The script then gives it a CS id, and the agent writes the issue’s URL into that change set’s Agent row: the feedback issue is the change set’s issue, so step 2 above opens none. A comment added to the issue later is added to the row’s next empty Contributor Feedback cell. Linked templates. Each mode keeps one template sheet in the informatics.avengers Drive, laid out as above, script installed, no rows. A new document starts from its “make a copy” link (table at the end); then the agent writes the new document’s Config tab, and the owner runs installTriggers. The script in the template needs no change. Locks in a template and its copies: every cell is locked to the owner except the blue, human-controlled columns, and the heads of the Contributor Feedback (or Committee Feedback) columns, where each contributor writes their initials. The lock covers the other headers, the grey mechanical and green agent-derived columns, the Config tab, the Agent tab and the hidden TOC. The orange Ready-for-agent and Ready-for-merge columns have a lock of their own, “Ready columns: editors”, which starts with only the owner; the owner adds each document editor to it in each copy (step 4 below). Setting up a sheet for a new document . The owner (informatics.avengers) does steps 1 to 6; the agent does step 3. | Copy the template. Open the “make a copy” link for the mode (table at the end), name the copy “ Contributor Log" or " Public Comment Log", and keep it in the informatics.avengers Drive. A file copy keeps tabs, colours, dropdowns, locks and the script. **Always copy the file** (File, then Make a copy); never build a log by copying tabs into a blank spreadsheet, which leaves the script behind. The owner keeps the latest `dist/Code.gs` pasted into both templates, so a copy starts current. | Share it. Share > add contributors or reviewers as Editor. The locks still keep them to the blue columns. | Link it to the repository (agent). Give the agent the copy’s URL and the document’s repository. The agent follows “Linking a sheet to a repository” below. Until it does, Config holds only its Instructions, Key and EDITORS rows and the Selected Sections dropdown is empty. The sheet says what to do next: the first line of each tab’s Instructions starts with ⚠ and names the next step, “Not set up yet. Step 1 of 2: ask the agent to link this sheet …” (the templates carry it, so a copy starts with it), then, once linked, “Almost set up. Step 2 of 2: choose Folio Assistant, then Install”. A short toast says the same when the sheet opens, and every run of an unlinked sheet stops with “Ask the agent to link this sheet to its document: give it this sheet’s link (ID …)”. Once installed (the timerMinutes document property installTriggers sets), the ⚠ line goes and each tab’s Instructions ends with a Document: <site> Repository: <repo> line; Config has an Instructions - Links row with the site, the repository and the sheet’s settings file. | Name the editors (owner). Type their emails in Config’s orange EDITORS row, or leave it empty so only the owner can set the Ready columns (below). | Install the script: §”Installing the script, step by step” below. A copy of the template already holds the script, so the paste is needed only when the script changes; installTriggers is needed in every copy, because triggers and the owner’s permission do not copy. A copy keeps the version it was made with: when Code.gs changes, paste it again into each sheet in use, and into the template. | Drafting only: finish the Selected Sections dropdown. installTriggers adds the rule (a dropdown from TOC!A2:A) when the column has none, and leaves an existing one alone (a rewrite would clear its tick). One setting is a person’s, once per sheet: . | click the column letter above “Selected Sections” to select the column; | choose Data, then Data validation; | open the rule for that column (the sidebar lists it by its range, such as 'Contributor Feedback'!E2:E1000, as “Dropdown (from a range)”); | under Advanced options, check that Display style is Chip; | tick Allow multiple selections; | press Done. | . The tick is greyed out unless the style is Chip. A rule that Apps Script writes (requireValueInRange) gets the Arrow style, which Apps Script cannot change. The agent therefore sets the style through the Sheets API at setup, and whenever a log’s rule reads customUiMode: ARROW: setDataValidation with the same ONE_OF_RANGE condition and "showCustomUi": true, "customUiMode": "CHIP", "strict": false. The API reads the tick (condition.allowMultipleSelections) but sets it only for ONE_OF_LIST rules, so ticking it on the range rule stays the person’s step. installTriggers cannot check either directly. It shows the steps in a 30-second toast unless it has evidence they are done: a cell already holding two sections from the list (or dropdownDone). It is a toast, never a dialog: a dialog waits for an answer in the sheet, and an Install run from the Apps Script editor then hangs until Apps Script stops it at 6 minutes (“Exceeded maximum execution time”). Only the menu’s “Which version is this?” opens a dialog. Copies made after the template has them keep them. The same steps are in the Config tab’s Instructions - Dropdown row; the script ignores that row. | . Installing the script, step by step . For the sheet’s owner, once per sheet. The Config tab’s Instructions - Install script row carries the same steps and links here. | Get the latest Code.gs. Open dist/Code.gs on GitHub and press Copy raw file (the two-squares button at the top right of the code), or open the raw file, select all and copy. It is the build of review-sheet.gs on core’s main, rewritten by build-review-sheet-script.ts --dist; a test fails when it is stale. | Open the editor. In the sheet: Extensions, then Apps Script. It opens in a new tab. “Sorry, unable to open the file at this time” (in German, “Datei kann derzeit nicht geöffnet werden”) means the browser is signed in to several Google accounts and Apps Script opened under the default one (/u/0/), which cannot see the sheet: use a private window with only the owner’s account, or change /u/0/ in the failing address to /u/1/, /u/2/, and so on. | Name the project after the sheet. Click Untitled project at the top left, type the spreadsheet’s own name (e.g. “DTH-PC Contributor Log”), and press Rename, so it is found by name in script.google.com, where bound projects are listed apart from their sheets. | Paste. Click Code.gs in the Files list on the left. Select all (Ctrl+A, or Cmd+A on a Mac), delete, paste, and save (Ctrl+S or Cmd+S, or the disk icon). Code.gs is the only file to paste: leave the project’s manifest as it is. | Run installTriggers. Reload the sheet and choose Folio Assistant, then Install. Or, in the editor, the function list next to Run and Debug shows installTriggers (it is the first function, so the default; not onOpen, which only adds the menu); press Run. | Allow it. Review permissions, pick the owner’s account. Google shows “Google hasn’t verified this app. The app is requesting access to sensitive info in your Google Account.” That is expected for a sheet’s own script, which Google never verifies: press Advanced, then **Go to (unsafe)**, then **Allow** ([why](https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/7454865)). | Check it. The log shows “Execution completed”. Back in the sheet tab, reload: a Folio Assistant menu appears; Folio Assistant, then Refresh now, checks it. | Drafting sheets only: tick Allow multiple selections on the Selected Sections dropdown (step 6 of “Setting up a sheet for a new document”). | . Updating later: steps 1, 2 and 4, then Folio Assistant, then Refresh now; the automatic refresh stays installed. Sheets may run older builds: Folio Assistant, then Which version is this? shows the build the sheet runs (SCRIPT_VERSION, the stamp on the script’s header line), the Code.gs copy page, and “✓ Up to date” or “New build available” by comparing with the Config tab’s CFG.LATEST_BUILD. The agent writes LATEST_BUILD (the content stamp of the build it publishes, latestBuild()) with the Config rows, so rewrite each sheet’s Config when a new build goes out. The script never fetches. The menu is named Folio Assistant and ends with About Folio Assistant, which points to https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/; the same link is the last line of each tab’s Instructions. The library builds the menu (addMenu) and the stub asks it, so every sheet shows the same menu and a rename needs no new stub. A stub that builds its own “Review links” menu is out of date: paste dist/Stub.gs over it once. A copy of the template needs none of this: the script came with the file. Reload the copy, choose Folio Assistant, then Install, and allow it as in step 6. The menu runs installTriggers, so the editor is never opened. Renaming the bound project (step 3) is optional: a copied project is named “Copy of …” by Google. One library, a stub in each sheet . The code lives once, in a standalone Apps Script project, Folio Review Library, owned by the sheets’ owner, and every sheet runs its latest code (HEAD). Each sheet keeps only dist/Stub.gs, which never changes. Setting the library up, once: . | At script.google.com, New project; name it Folio Review Library. | Replace its code with dist/Code.gs; save. | Project settings (the gear): copy the Script ID. The library is 1us7_ApIq_XvDG-V1XtqdcyHucF0hSlST0qracv1Tw9KTb4-lAFvK1bMQ; the Config tab’s install steps and the stub name it. | . Each sheet, once (templates first, so copies inherit it): . | Extensions, then Apps Script. Replace Code.gs with dist/Stub.gs; save. | Libraries +: paste the Script ID, Look up, Version HEAD (Development mode), Identifier Review, Add. | In the sheet, Folio Assistant > Install. | . An update needs no paste. The library also holds dist/Updater.gs; updateFromGitHub, run from the library’s editor, fetches dist/Code.gs from main and writes it over the library’s Code.gs through the Apps Script API, leaving the library’s other files alone. It refuses anything that is not the review-sheet script (an error page, the stub) and logs “Updated to <version>” or “Already current”. There is no timer: an update runs when the owner runs it. Every sheet runs the new code from its next open, edit or timer. Adding the updater, once: . | Turn on the Apps Script API at https://script.google.com/home/usersettings. | In the library, Files +, Script, name it Updater; paste dist/Updater.gs; save. | Project settings: tick “Show appsscript.json manifest file in editor”, then replace appsscript.json with dist/library-appsscript.json (it adds the script.projects and script.external_request scopes); save. | Pick updateFromGitHub in the function list, Run, and allow it. | . After that an update is step 4 alone. Without the updater, an update is one paste of the new dist/Code.gs into the library. “Which version is this?” reports the library’s stamp. The stub hands its services over (Review.init) because a library has no spreadsheet of its own, so its document properties, document lock and triggers would not be the sheet’s. The stub passes its own PropertiesService, LockService and ScriptApp, and the triggers it installs name the stub’s functions. Pasted straight into a sheet, Code.gs still works alone: without init it uses the sheet’s services. HEAD runs only for people with edit access to the library. The triggers run as the owner who installed them, so that is the owner alone; an editor who uses Refresh now by hand needs the library shared with them as an editor. Linking a sheet to a repository . A copied sheet knows nothing about its document until the agent links it. Linking is repository work first and sheet work second, in this order: . | The folio has a section list. A drafting sheet’s dropdown is the document’s chapters and sections, read from folio/<doc>/review-anchors.json. The folio’s package.json declares review:anchors and check:review-anchors, both running folio-assistant-core/scripts/review-anchors-from-folio.ts --document <doc>. A document seeded from a library file adds `–library --source --source-label `; one authored from scratch (dth-pc, dth-sc) leaves all three out. Run `review:anchors` and commit the file. A new document folio declares both scripts from its first commit. | The folio names the sheet, and the rows are built: one command. From the folio’s root, with the link the person pasted: bun run folio-assistant-core/tools/review-sheet-sync/build-review-sheet-script.ts --link <sheet link or id> --document <doc> --out config-rows.json --toc-out toc-rows.json. It writes review/drafting/sheet-sync.json ({"mode":"drafting","anchors":"folio/<doc>/review-anchors.json","sectionUrl":"en/<doc>/#","sheet":"<spreadsheet id>"}; an existing file keeps its settings and only gets the new sheet), then the rows. The site and repository links come from the folio’s iriBase (https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/ is https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>); a folio on another host sets "repository" in sheet-sync.json. Public comment, or to rebuild after a structural change: --config review/<mode>/sheet-sync.json instead of --link. | The agent writes the sheet. With the Sheets connector, it writes the rows from step 2: the whole Config tab from A1, keeping the sheet’s EDITORS value (the Instructions - Links row sits above Key, so the CFG, COLS and DATA rows land below EDITORS), and for drafting the TOC rows into the TOC tab from A1. The connector writes values, not colours, so the agent also colours Config: the Key row a Grey header (#b7b7b7, bold), EDITORS Orange (#f4b26b), and CFG, COLS, DATA and their continuation rows Grey (#efefef), and fits the Instructions rows’ heights to their text (a Sheets API autoResizeDimensions; an inserted row otherwise inherits its neighbour’s height). Every refresh re-applies these (styleConfig), so a sheet the script runs in heals on its own. The TOC rows are exactly what the script’s refresh writes, so the dropdown works before anyone pastes the script. | The agent says what is left for a person: paste Code.gs and run installTriggers (step 5 above), and tick Allow multiple selections (step 6). | . When the branch carrying the folio is not merged yet, the agent may run steps 1 and 3 from that branch without pushing to it, and write the sheet; the branch’s owner commits the anchors and sheet-sync.json. Re-run step 3 after any structural change to the document (a section added, moved or renamed). Who may set the Ready columns: the EDITORS row. Everyone who works in a log is shared as Editor; protected ranges decide what each can change. Blue columns are open to all of them. The orange Ready for agent and Ready for merge columns are for editors only, and the owner names them in the Config tab’s EDITORS row, column B: plain emails, no names, one per line (Ctrl+Enter or Cmd+Enter starts a line inside a cell), or separated by commas or semicolons. The format is spelled out, with an example, in the Instructions - Editors row and in a note on the cell itself. Anything that is not an email is left out, and the refresh names it in a toast. installTriggers and Folio Assistant > Refresh now lock each Ready for ... column to the owner plus those emails, under a protection the script owns and rebuilds each time (other protections are left alone). An empty row locks them to the owner alone, which is how every new sheet starts; a Config with no EDITORS row leaves them as they are. Both templates carry the Orange EDITORS row, empty. EDITORS is the one Config row a person keeps: the agent writes it empty and keeps the sheet’s value whenever it rewrites the tab, and the emails never go into sheet-sync.json, which is committed. To delegate who decides, the owner can add a delegate to the Config tab’s protection, or send the agent the list. The Instructions rows. Every visible tab opens with an Instructions row that says what that tab is for and how it works, in that tab’s own terms; tabInstructions() in the builder writes the text for each tab. On a people’s tab (RPC, RCS, Contributor Feedback) the row is frozen with the header and grey like it, a lighter grey than the header. Its first line is the colour key: Column colours: then one phrase per colour, in the order Blue, Green, Orange, Grey, worded for the mode by colourKey() and naming no colour (§”Sheet conventions”): . | Blue: input by people, named by their process role: the Feedback Review Committee in public-comment mode, the Authoring Committee in drafting mode; | Green: the agent; | Orange: an Editor (the Ready for ... columns); | Grey: the script. | . Then come the steps for that tab, one per line, naming columns, never colours. On a change-set tab they are the human-to-agent workflow, worded by process role: people write their feedback, the agent proposes, an Editor sets Ready for agent, the agent opens one pull request for the row whose Staging review opens the changes, new feedback marks the proposal stale, a second reviewer checks the dispositions and the QA report, and an Editor sets Ready for merge and the agent merges. On Review Public Comments the steps say that decisions are made per change set. Last come the filter views, and a link to the harness’s page for the process the sheet runs: public-comment.html for public comment and contributor-feedback.html for drafting, under en/cat-harness/processes/ on the folio-assistant site (processPage(); CFG.PROCESS overrides it). The first cell reads Instructions, and the text is one merged cell across the rest of the row. The script reads any leading rows whose first cell starts Instructions (or Colour key) as for people: the header is the row after them, and every write, lock and edit range starts below the header. Insert the row only after the sheet runs a Code.gs that knows it; an older script reads the legend as the header and finds no columns. Filter views and protections start at the header row, so shift them down by one row when the row is inserted. A filter view’s custom formula does not move when a column is inserted, so rewrite it. The Config tab keeps its Instructions short, one subject per row, so no row is taller than the window: Instructions (the tab’s purpose: nothing here needs you unless you install the script), Instructions - Install script (setupSteps(): copy Code.gs, Extensions > Apps Script, name the project after the spreadsheet, paste and save, run installTriggers, allow it, reload), on a drafting sheet Instructions - Dropdown (dropdownSteps()), and Instructions - Editors (editorSteps()), then the Key | Value header. Its rows are not frozen. The EDITORS row is Orange, like the Ready columns it controls, because a person keeps it; the rows the agent writes stay grey. The script reads Config keys by name, so it ignores these rows. A stale proposal hands control back to an Editor. When a row’s proposal turns stale (a blue cell changed since the agent wrote it), the script sets that row’s Ready for agent from Yes to No, once, on the turn. The agent does not act on the row until an Editor sets Yes again, which is the signal to update the row’s pull request. A Yes set while the row is still stale stays. One row, one branch, one active pull request. A change-set row keeps one branch for its whole life, and at most one pull request is open on it. Every later agent run pushes to that branch and updates that PR, so the row’s Staging review link stays the same. If the PR is closed and the committee or contributors want the work back, the agent reopens it, or opens a new PR on the same branch when it cannot be reopened. It never starts a second branch for the row. Each earlier PR stays listed in the row’s Agentic status, one line per PR. Filter views. Each template carries saved filter views, which copy with it. Use Data > Filter views, never a plain filter: a plain filter changes the view for everyone, a filter view only for whoever opens it. Each view is named for who uses it and what it shows. | sheet | view | who | shows | . | drafting: Contributor Feedback | Open | everyone | rows with a Title, Ready for merge not Yes | . |   | Needs contributor feedback | contributors | rows with a Title and every Contributor Feedback column empty | . |   | Waiting for editor (Ready for agent not Yes) | editors | rows with a Title, Ready for agent not Yes | . |   | Merge decision due (PR open, not merged) | editors | Agentic status (filter) is PR open, Ready for merge not Yes | . |   | Needs you (answer the agent’s question) | editors, owner | Agentic status (filter) starts with “Needs you” | . |   | Stale (agent proposal or staging out of date) | owner | the agent proposal starts with ⚠, or the staging link says stale | . |   | Decided (Ready for merge Yes) | everyone | Ready for merge is Yes | . |   | By agentic status (pick values) | everyone | every row; pick values in the Agentic status (filter) column’s filter (a plain copy of the change set’s Agent status) | . | public comment: Review Change Sets | Change sets: the same eight | as above | on its own columns; “Needs architect feedback” checks the three Committee Feedback (initials) columns | . | public comment: Review Public Comments | Comments: Open (no Disposition) | everyone | a No., Disposition empty | . |   | Comments: No change set yet | review coordinator | a No., Change Set empty | . |   | Comments: Needs architect feedback | the Feedback Review Committee | a No., every Committee Feedback (initials) column empty | . |   | Comments: Decided (Disposition set) | everyone | Disposition filled | . The “needs feedback” and “stale” views use a custom formula that names columns by letter, so a column move breaks them: after moving columns, the agent checks each view’s formula against the headers. A filter view covers the rows the tab had when the view was made; when rows are added past that, widen its range (Data > Filter views > the view > Options > Update range). Keeping the section list current (agent). The dropdown’s list is the hidden TOC tab, and the script writes it from DATA.TOC in the Config tab on every refresh. So when the document’s chapters or sections change (any PR that changes review-anchors.json, the same moment review:anchors runs), the agent rebuilds the Config rows (--config review/drafting/sheet-sync.json --out config-rows.json) and writes them into each drafting sheet the folio names, in the same change. Nobody edits the TOC tab by hand. How picks stay valid. On each refresh the script repairs Selected Sections before anything else: . | the pick | what the script does | . | a current section, with or without its indent (or a “└ “ mark) | rewrites it to the dropdown’s name, indent included | . | a section renamed or renumbered since it was picked | finds it by its anchor (the TOC tab’s column C keeps the anchors of the names it offered before) and rewrites it to the new name | . | a section no longer in the document | keeps it, so nothing a person chose is lost, and adds a line in Section links: ⚠ “" is not in the document now: pick its section again | . So “Invalid” after a document change clears by itself at the next refresh, except for a section that was removed, which a person repicks. Change-set ids. Any row a person has filled in gets the next CS-nnn at the next refresh, whichever column they started in. A cell holding only “No” (a Yes/No dropdown’s default) and the script’s own columns do not count. Selected Sections shows “Invalid”. Three causes: a pick of a section removed from the document (Section links flags it; pick again); a cell with several sections where the rule does not allow multiple selections (tick it, step 6); or a cell that carries links. Sections must be plain text, the links belong in Section links: clear the cell’s formatting (Format > Clear formatting) and the script keeps it plain. Check it. Folio Assistant > Refresh now. In drafting mode a filled-in row gets a CS id and its picked sections appear, linked, in Section links; in public-comment mode each No. becomes a link. An error names what is missing: no Config tab, a Config row, or a tab the Config names. | mode | template (owned by informatics.avengers) | make a copy | . | public-comment | Folio Assistant - Public Comment Review Template, 14PtLd2U_tBQV5OHoEEVRJK1EKfsbZEBPP_MIqo2E3o4 | https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/14PtLd2U_tBQV5OHoEEVRJK1EKfsbZEBPP_MIqo2E3o4/copy | . | drafting | Folio Assistant - Contributor Template, 1PtcNJgLQIA1BjapU51pAQzqQjGylBHYNKlCPzZkwVag | https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1PtcNJgLQIA1BjapU51pAQzqQjGylBHYNKlCPzZkwVag/copy | . A copy keeps tabs, colours, dropdowns and formulas. It does not keep protected ranges (re-add them: Agent whole tab; the grey and green columns), and its TOC tab is empty until the script’s first refresh. A document’s own sheet is named in its sheet-sync.json as sheet (the spreadsheet id), so the agent’s sync knows where to read and write.

7482.title: Review task
7482.content: Process_Review · advisory · 6 step(s) . The generic review position: classify what changed, descend into the review that fits it, consolidate what comes back, and accept or send back. You are in this process for any change under review. It is a DISPATCHER — the actor takes on the inner lane’s role for the call path only — which is why prose and code can both be reviewed without either reviewer having to know the other’s criteria. A change that is both — prose and the code it describes — takes a branch of its own, which reviews the two against each other; the gateway is exclusive and takes exactly one branch. The accept-or-send-back decision lives here and nowhere beneath it. The subprocesses produce findings; this is the only lane entitled to turn findings into an outcome, so “who decided” stays answerable. i i i i i i

7494.title: Roles are swimlanes
7494.content: Skill role-model: Actors, roles and skills — who performs a BPMN task, under which swimlane, with which skills. How a role’s skill set is resolved through inherits and through a subprocess call chain, how a lane binds to a declared role, and how kg:audit finds a dangling skill, lane, role or decision. Named by: A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Cut over to the separated graph, Move the graph into its repositories, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Actor and role administration . One sentence carries the whole model: . An actor performs a task in a process as a role, using that role’s skills. Six objects, each with a home: . | object | what it is | declared in | . | Actor | a concrete participant. Human, agentic or mechanical. Persists across every process. | scenarios/actors/*.json (the declared scenarios graph, beside the roles) | . | Role | the swimlane — a persona an actor takes on because of the lane it is acting in. Carries a collection of Skills. | scenarios/roles.json | . | Skill | an instruction body: what the actor needs to know to perform the task it was handed. | skills/<pkg>/*.md (naming its input:/output: contracts, usually under schemas/skills/<name>/); JSON SkillDefinitions in each owning layer’s skills/skill-definitions/ | . | Process / Decision | BPMN and DMN. Lanes bind roles; activities name skills; gateways may compute their branch from a table. | processes/**/*.bpmn, processes/**/decisions/*.dmn | . | Requirement | a conformance obligation, pointed at by what discharges it: a skill or capability names the statement in satisfies: req:<id>#<key>. The requirement points at actors (who is bound) and derivedFrom (the broader requirement it specialises). | skills/requirements/*.json | . | Permission | what an actor is allowed to do. Cross-cuts roles. A W3C ODRL 2.2 rule, scoped by Process, Task or Role when it needs to be. | actions: skills/permissions/permissions.json; who holds them: policies/*.jsonld | . WHO’s “actor” is this model’s Role. An actor in the WHO DPI-H Reference Architecture’s conformance model (§3.7.2, an abstract information-processing role) and a DAK generic persona each map to a folio-assistant Role, never to an Actor. The RA’s system realising an actor maps to a mechanical Actor taking on that role. The comparison is on the DAK layer’s findings/dth-terms.md. Schema: schemas/process/role-graph.ts. Audit: scripts/kg-audit.ts, sidecar schema schemas/sdlc/kg-qa.ts. Not every skill is PERFORMED — consulted: true . Reference material belongs in no lane, by its nature. build-pdf and proof-triage are tasks somebody carries out; directory-conventions, untrusted-input and turn-reporting are what the performer READS. Both kinds are skills; only the first can sit in a swimlane. A skill that is reference material declares consulted: true in its front matter. Absent means performed: the exception is annotated, not the rule, because an axis whose default costs an edit in every skill file does not get adopted. No mechanical signal (a sibling SkillDefinition, an allowed-tools: line) tells the two kinds apart, so it must be declared. It is checked in BOTH directions, which is what stops it being an opt-out. skill-in-role-or-process skips a consulted skill; the separate consulted-skill-not-performed reports one that a role carries or an activity names, because a skill cannot be reference material and a step somebody performs. Which of the two declarations is wrong takes a person, so the criterion reports both rather than choosing. A skill does not carry roles: front matter . Do not write roles: in a skill’s front matter. bun run cat check:retired-front-matter fails if it appears, because copying an adjacent skill’s front matter brings the field back. To learn who performs a skill, read scenarios/roles.json; the registry is the only answer that resolves. A role→skill edge for a skill above the harness is an extensions entry in that layer’s role graph (§”A higher layer EXTENDS a role by id”). roles: in a folio-memory/v1 entry is a DIFFERENT field and stays. memoryForRoles filters on tags.roles, and an untagged entry would be seen by every lane. Sharing a key name across graph typologies is not sharing a field, and check:retired-front-matter keys its exemption on $schema, never on the directory. Whether a skill should declare its performer is undecided; if it ever does, the field is declared in the schema before it is written.

7495.title: Why a lane names a role, and the role is not the person
7495.content: A lane is not itself a role: a lane names the Role its tasks are performed in, not an Actor. The same actor is a different thing in two diagrams, and two different actors are the same thing in one. In crdm-requirements.bpmn the session agent acts in Lane_Agent. In bean-lifecycle.bpmn that very same session agent is, from the other diagram’s point of view, the sibling session — the lane that exists precisely to mark what is not yours to close. The skills differ because the lane differs, not because the actor did. So nothing is “a reviewer”. Somebody acts as reviewer, inside a process, for the duration of a lane. An actor carries roles[], never inherits. “Can review” and “can push” are properties of a position, not of a person, so the inherits lattice lives in the role graph. An actor lists the roles it may take on. roles: [] and an absent roles mean different things. [] says the actor takes on no role, which is the honest value for a read-only identity that never appears in a swimlane; absent says nothing has been asserted. The actor-is-not-a-role criterion reports an actor that carries inherits, because a registry written by hand reaches for inherits again. Roles played by mechanical actors are real roles, because the diagrams hand them tasks. Work plan (beans), Corpus, Publish target, a build pipeline and the external registries are roles a machine or an outside party plays. Their skills are their contract: the responsibilities they must perform, which a test can hold them to — a contract skill names its tests in front matter as tested-by:. The QA report lists a mechanical role whose skills name no test as mechanical-role-untested, and role-has-actor asks what actor plays each such role. A store is a mechanical role with a store block, and is drawn as a data store, not a lane. work-plan, corpus, log and session-record keep things rather than do them. Each stays a Role, so its skills are still its contract, and adds store: what it holds (typology ids), its api (one entry per transport, in that transport’s own format: openapi, fhir-capability, graphql, cli tools, json-schema-files, git), what it is realisedBy, and whether it is published. Only a role played by system or external actors may declare one. The role id is the store id: each layer declares <bpmn:dataStore id="<role id>"> once in processes/global-tasks.bpmn, and a process draws a dataStoreReference pointing at it, with dataInputAssociation for a read and dataOutputAssociation for a write. A system that does its own step (validates, decides, returns a result) keeps a lane; one that only keeps what others write is a data store. The same store is an ArchiMate application component (its interfaces, data objects and services hang off it) and, in a FHIR layer, an ActorDefinition of type system whose capabilities or reference points at its API. Some roles perform, but by judgement. stakeholder carries judgementOnly: true: somebody really does sign off, deliberates and is accountable — they simply cannot be handed a procedure that produces the answer. That is a different thing from a mechanical role, which has no judgement to exercise and whose skills are a contract it can be tested against. Do not give such a role a skill. The flag exists because a decision recorded only in a role’s summary is one the next agent re-litigates. activity-names-skill records n/a for activities in its lane, which lets that criterion gate on the undeclared ones.

7496.title: An actor is one of three kinds — human, agentic, mechanical
7496.content: { "id": "ci-pipeline", "title": "CI pipeline", "kind": "system", … } . kind takes one of four values, and three of them are the classification that matters. external is the fourth: a participant outside this layer, which is not ours to task at all. | kind | the kind it names | what it can be handed | . | person | human | a skill to read, and a judgement to make | . | agent | agentic | a skill to read, and a judgement to make | . | system | mechanical | a program to run, and nothing to decide | . | external | outside this layer | nothing | . The line is judgement. An agent and a person can both be handed an instruction body and asked to decide something; a mechanical system executes a procedure and decides nothing. That says whether a given step may be given to a given participant, so one value covering an LLM agent and a CI runner alike would leave “which tasks can this actor perform” unanswerable. The vocabulary is declared once, in schemas/kg/skill-package.ts (the zod-only base both the registry schema and the role graph import), and re-exported from schemas/process/role-graph.ts, where it is ACTOR_KINDS. A legacy type still loads, and is never read as agent. An unmigrated downstream registry has not said whether its non-person actors exercise judgement, so they read as system — the reading that refuses a judgement task rather than granting one on a guess. Guessing from an id ending in -agent would put an unreviewed claim into the graph wearing the appearance of data. An unrecognised kind throws: coercing a typo to system would silently disqualify an actor from every task it exists to perform.

7497.title: A task declares which actor kinds may fulfil it — mostly without saying so
7497.content: Tasks can be fulfilled by only certain actor types. activity-fulfilment-kind checks that against the lane’s role, and almost no diagram has to declare anything, because BPMN already answers it and nothing was reading the answer: . | task type | who may perform it | from | . | bpmn:userTask | person | the spec: “performed by a human being with the assistance of a software application” | . | bpmn:serviceTask | agent, system | the spec: “uses some sort of service … a Web service or an automated application” — no human in the loop | . | bpmn:task | nothing asserted | the abstract task says nothing, so neither does the check | . | bpmn:callActivity | nothing asserted | the constraint belongs to the called process’s own steps | . fulfilmentKindsForBpmnType returns undefined for the last two, never []. An empty list would read as “no kind may perform this” and fail every activity drawn as a plain task — the third state, in the place it is easiest to lose. Scoped like activity-names-skill. An activity whose lane is unbound or absent is already reported by lane-binds-role and activity-in-lane, so it is not reported twice here. Override it only when the derived answer is genuinely wrong: . <bpmn:extensionElements> <cat-harness.processes:fulfilment kinds="person agent" reason="a person or an agent drafts this; a pipeline cannot." /> </bpmn:extensionElements> . The reason is required at load time and a reasonless declaration does not parse — the same rule <cat-harness.processes:no-skill reason> follows, and for the same reason. Widening kinds is the cheapest way to make this criterion pass, so silencing it has to cost a sentence somebody reads in the diff. Read a failure as a question with three answers, not one. The task type may be wrong, the lane may be wrong, or the step may really admit that kind — and only the third is a <cat-harness.processes:fulfilment/>. Reaching for the exemption first turns it into a rubber stamp.

7498.title: Three questions about an actor, and only two are answered on the actor
7498.content: // cat-harness/scenarios/actors/admin.json { "id": "admin", "roles": ["programme-manager", "publication-manager", "editor", "author", "reviewer"], "capabilities": ["git-push"] } // policies/folio-defaults.jsonld: a W3C ODRL 2.2 Set { "permission": [ { "assignee": "admin", "action": "role-management" }, … ] } . | question | answered by | scope | . | what may it act AS? | roles on the actor | per lane | . | what may it DO? | ODRL rules in policies/ naming it as assignee | everywhere, or as narrow as a rule’s cat-harness:process, cat-harness:task and cat-harness:role constraints | . | what does its machine have? | capabilities on the actor | the environment | . What an actor may DO is not on the actor. It is a W3C ODRL 2.2 rule per action in policies/: . | Inheritance. Each action in permissions.json says which broader actions it is includedIn, ending at ODRL’s own (odrl:display, odrl:modify, odrl:execute, …). A grant of a broader action permits everything included in it. The graph need not be a tree and may have cycles. | Scope. A rule may be limited to a Process, a Task or a Role. No constraint means everywhere. | One question, three answers. permits() in schemas/content/odrl.ts returns permit, deny or unknown, and unknown is never permit. Performing a task in a lane needs the permission and the lane’s role, so eligibility (roles) and permission stay separate, as below. | Anyone. cat-harness:anyone is an unauthenticated reader: a person with no login, whoever they are. It may visualize and render, and nothing else. | . Identity is not here. Which login is which actor is the data store’s to know. No actor file and no policy carries a login, and workflow history names the actor, never the login: the repository owner’s steps are recorded as owner, and the data store maps the login to owner. Who reads all three before a task runs: the BPMN executor. Before any task or decision is recorded, authorizeTask asks whether the actor is authenticated, eligible for the lane’s role (roles), and permitted by policy to perform-task here and on this content. A role mismatch or a deny refuses, and so does unknown, because the engine runs strict. The HTTP routes ask the same policies through src/core/rbac.ts. See task-authorization. Adding a permission: declare the action in permissions.json with its includedIn, then add a rule to a policy in policies/. Never add a permissions list to an actor file: the audit reads it (an unmigrated downstream registry still works), but a list there is invisible to every scoped decision. Permissions do not belong on Role either. A permission cross-cuts: one action is held by actors taking on several different roles, and not by every actor sharing a role. The line that does hold: a skill answers what the performer of this task needs to KNOW, and belongs to the lane. A permission answers what this participant may DO, and travels with the participant through every lane it enters. Both are audited and both are critical — actor-permissions-resolve (which also checks that every policy rule names a declared action and a declared actor or cat-harness:anyone) and actor-capabilities-resolve.

7499.title: Requirements are the fifth node kind, and they only point
7499.content: A requirement is not a skill and not a role. It is an obligation about them, kept in the kg graph so that every agent reads it and its joins are audited: . { "id": "req:commit-hygiene", "derivedFrom": ["req:agent-workflow"], "actors": ["author", "admin"], "statements": [ { "key": "no-secrets", "conformance": "SHALL", "requirement": "Commits SHALL NOT include secrets, API keys, tokens…" } ] } . and a skill that discharges a statement says so in its own front matter: . satisfies: - "req:commit-hygiene#no-secrets" . The statement names no satisfier: a requirement is written once, and what discharges it arrives later, so the pointer lives on the arrival. The references are audited. satisfies-resolves, requirement-actors-resolve and requirement-derived-from-resolves are critical, because a reader following a broken one gets nothing — the same test as a dangling <bootstrap.processes:skill ref>. requirement-statement-satisfied is minor coverage: a statement nothing claims is visible only from the requirement’s side. requirement-statements-graded is major: an ungraded statement is readable, it just cannot be conformance-tested, and SHALL-vs-SHOULD is the whole reason to write a requirement rather than a note. Do not fold a requirement into the skill that satisfies it. The grading, the derivedFrom lattice, the actor binding and the many-to-many satisfies are the only machine-checkable things about it, and prose in a skill doc carries none of them. satisfies is many-to-many in both directions — one skill discharges statements in several requirements — so inlining duplicates rather than relocates.

7500.title: Two compositions, and they are not the same
7500.content: inherits — a role IS-A role. qc-reviewer inherits reviewer and gets its skills everywhere, in every process, forever. Static. resolveRoleSkills closes over it breadth-first, so a skill’s reported via is the nearest ancestor that supplies it. The subprocess stack — a role acting INSIDE another role’s task. A process calls a subprocess and the actor keeps acting: it does not stop being the outer role, it additionally takes on the inner lane’s role. The skills available at that task are the union along the whole call path. resolveRoleStack takes the path outermost-first and keeps each skill’s provenance, because a reader needs to know not only that a skill was available but which level supplied it. resolveRoleSkills(graph, "qc-reviewer") // static: + everything reviewer has resolveRoleStack(graph, ["editor", "viewer"]) // scoped: the union for this call only . Do not merge them. A flat union would make reviewer permanently hold every skill any caller ever had, and a closure that broad cannot fail an audit, which is the same as not having one.

7501.title: A higher layer EXTENDS a role by id — it never edits it
7501.content: A third relation, across layers rather than within one graph. When a skill belongs above the harness (a core cataloguing skill, a sci Lean skill), the role→skill edge naming it must not stay in cat-harness/scenarios/roles.json — that is an upward reference. So the dependent holds the pointer, the way a voice points at the role it addresses and a story at the role it is told as: . // <content-core>/scenarios/roles.json { "name": "<content-core>", "roles": [], "extensions": [{ "role": "librarian", "skills": ["filing-dublin-core"] }] } . | a dependent’s scenarios/ may | it may NOT | . | add skills to a lower role (extensions) | change its title, description, inherits, actorKinds or persona | . | add a NEW role, which may inherits a lower one | redeclare a lower id — refused, “extend it instead” (one exception, below) | . | extend a lower actor: actors/<f>.json with "extends": "<id>", adding roles / capabilities | carry any other field on an extension | . | extend a capability: "extends" adding requires; or add a new probe | point an extension UP or sideways — only at an id declared below it | . The one exception — a move in flight. Moving a role, actor, capability or policy up a layer is two pull requests: the higher layer adds it, then the lower layer removes it, and in between both declare the id. A redeclaration that only adds — every field the lower declaration carries is there unchanged (the same scalar, every member of an array, a nested object by the same rule), and it may carry more, such as the skills it used to add by extension — is accepted with a warning that names the id and both layers, and the higher declaration is used. The warning is the move’s to-do: remove the lower copy. A redeclaration that changes or drops anything the lower one said is still refused. schemas/process/scenario-overlay.ts applies it (checkoutRoleGraph, checkoutActors, checkoutCapabilities, checkoutPolicies; the exception is onlyAdds); the layers are the checkout’s layers that depend on the role’s owner, deepest first. Resolved alone, the harness sees only its own roles. kg:audit, check:raci, check:fallback-roles, check:actor-reach, kg-export and the stakeholder map read the checkout’s view on the platform’s own run. The edge stays on a role graph — the graph of the layer that owns the skill — never in skill front matter.

7502.title: A lane binds its role with partitionElementRef
7502.content: Lane names are free text, and several spellings name one position, so a name alone joins a lane to nothing and an undefined lane is a silence rather than a finding. So a lane binds its role itself, with BPMN’s own partitionElementRef: the role is declared once per diagram as a top-level <bpmn:resource> whose id is the role id verbatim and whose name is its title, before the collaboration and the process. The role lists no lanes: a role is the general node and a lane the dependent one, and a general node never names its users (data-modelling step 8). <bpmn:resource id="reviewer" name="Reviewer"/> ... <bpmn:lane id="Lane_Reviewer" name="Reviewer" partitionElementRef="reviewer"> ... </bpmn:lane> . A <bootstrap.processes:role ref="reviewer"/> in the lane’s extensionElements is read, with a warning, only when partitionElementRef is absent (laneRoleRef in schemas/process/role-graph.ts); the QA report lists it as lane-role-legacy-binding. <bootstrap.processes:role variable="true"/> stays: it declares a performer who is whoever invoked the process. An explicit binding wins over name matching: a diagram that has said which role it means must not be second-guessed by a string table. A ref naming no declared role is a critical finding — it is not quietly name-matched instead.

7503.title: The audit — bun run cat kg:audit
7503.content: One criterion per join in the sentence at the top. The list below is the actor→role→skill→task core; KG_CRITERIA in schemas/sdlc/kg-qa.ts is the registry, and it is longer — it also covers requirements, skill bodies and the graph as a whole. activity ──names────▶ skill skill-ref-resolves critical gateway ──computes─▶ decision decision-ref-resolves critical lane ──is───────▶ role role-ref-resolves critical activity ──sits in──▶ lane activity-in-lane major task type─can be done by▶ kind activity-fulfilment-kind major lane ──is───────▶ role lane-binds-role major role ──carries──▶ skill role-carries-activity-skill major decision ──is used──▶ gateway decision-outcomes-used major role ──carries──▶ skill role-skills-resolve critical role ──is-a─────▶ role role-inherits-resolves critical activity ──names────▶ skill activity-names-skill minor role ──is used──▶ lane role-binds-a-lane minor actor ──takes on─▶ role role-has-actor minor skill ──any way in▶ anything skill-has-entry-point minor skill ──modelled?▶ role/task skill-in-role-or-process minor actor ──is not a─▶ role actor-is-not-a-role minor . | command | does | . | bun run cat kg:audit | write the sidecars, print the summary | . | bun run cat kg:audit:check | fail on a critical finding, or on a stale sidecar | . | bun run cat kg:audit:strict | …and on major too | . | bun run scripts/kg-audit.ts --json | the full report set, for a tool | . Why sidecars rather than a console report . check-workflow-refs.ts prints and exits, so its previous answer is gone. That makes “this lane has been unbound since the day it was drawn” and “this lane broke in the commit under review” indistinguishable, and a reviewer cannot separate a new defect from inherited debt. The sidecars are committed, under kg-qa/ beside whatever they audit, so the diff says exactly which findings a change introduced. Same argument and same file shape as the block sweep’s *.qa.json and the script sweep’s *.script-qa.json. Where the sidecars for another layer go — hosted, not written into it . A layer that declares no qa directory does not receive sidecars inside its own tree: kgQaHomeFor (schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts) puts them in the auditing harness’s qa directory under the layer’s stub — cat-harness/test/results/bootstrap/ for bootstrap (a working copy, stored on the qa-reports branch with the rest of that qa directory; a JUDGEMENT about it is hosted the same way, under test/attestations/). A verdict ABOUT an layer is the auditor’s output, and bootstrap is the layer that must read cleanly with no harness present. The same holds once bootstrap is its own repository: the verdicts stay with the harness that computed them, against the pinned bootstrap (kg-separation §”The pair”). Three states, and what unknown costs . A criterion returns pass, fail, n/a (does not apply to this subject) or unknown (could not be evaluated — the file would not parse, a dependency was absent). unknown is never written as a pass. It counts as a failure at its criterion’s own severity. It is not promoted to major either: a diagram that will not load records unknown against its critical criteria too, so it still fails the gate, while an unevaluable minor criterion does not gate the build: a gate that fires on something nobody agreed was blocking gets switched off. Severity, and why coverage is only minor . critical is a broken reference — something names a thing that does not exist, and a consumer following it gets nothing. major is a missing join — the graph is intact but a question has no answer, e.g. a lane bound to no role. minor is coverage: a real gap with legitimate instances. A human signing something off is not implemented by a markdown file, so failing on activity-names-skill would force a fake ref onto a real step, which is worse than the gap. Never quote a count from prose — run the audit . A number written in a document is a claim; only a run is evidence. Two criteria ask different reachability questions, and only one of them is about the role model: . | skill-has-entry-point — is there ANY way in: servable, in the harness, carried by a role, or named by an activity? The servable clause alone covers nearly the whole corpus, so this passes near-trivially; its green is not an answer to the coverage question. | skill-in-role-or-process — what does the actor → role → task model actually reach? This is the real coverage question, and it must never gate. A skill invoked directly by name is doing its job without appearing in any diagram, and driving the number to zero would mean inventing roles and activities to absorb tools that do not want them. Watch it move; do not read it as a defect list. | .

7504.title: What counts as a skill
7504.content: scripts/known-skills.ts is the single answer, shared by kg-audit and check-workflow-refs so the two cannot disagree. Not every group under a skills directory holds skills: actors/ holds participants, capabilities/ holds environment probes (docker, pandoc, python3), roles/ holds an assignment table and hooks/ holds a shell script. NON_SKILL_GROUPS excludes them, so <bootstrap.processes:skill ref="viewer"/> does not resolve. It is a deny-list of groups known not to hold skills, not an allow-list of local/, so a new group of real skills is picked up automatically and a new group of something else is a one-line addition.

7505.title: Administration IS a swimlane
7505.content: The role graph is the substrate every diagram’s lanes bind to. Changing it — adding an actor, opening a role, granting a permission, retiring a participant — is therefore a process like any other, and it is drawn: actor-role-administration.bpmn, in the administrator lane. Do not invent a role to make a diagram drawable. A role minted for a picture is a role no audit can fail, because nothing was ever true of it — the closure-widening failure of §”Two compositions”, from the other end. What follows from administration being a lane: . |   |   | . | administration is a lane | so role-management is exercised somewhere a reader can find | . | the lane is person-only | a permission grant is a standing decision, not a task; the agentic/mechanical line is judgement, and this one is authority | . | the mechanics are NOT re-drawn | the diagram calls code-change-review; a second description of branch-gates-review is a second thing free to disagree with the first | . | the audit runs after | every criterion is a join, so what an administrative edit breaks is never in the file it edited | .

7506.title: Adding a role
7506.content: . | Add it to scenarios/roles.json with a description that says what the position is, not what it is called. actorKinds is a SET drawn from person, agent, system and external — human, agentic, mechanical, or outside this layer. It is what activity-fulfilment-kind checks the lane’s steps against, so it is a claim about who can actually stand there, not a label. Use title/description (the two labels every knowledge-graph node carries), never summary, and actorKinds, never actorKind: Zod strips an unknown key, so a misnamed field type-checks, parses, and is silently lost. | Bind its lanes: each diagram declares <bpmn:resource id="<role id>" name="<title>"/> once, and each lane that names this role carries partitionElementRef="<role id>". The role lists no lanes, since a role is the general node and a lane the dependent one (data-modelling step 8). A lane with no ref is unbound, whatever its name. | Give it the skills its lane’s activities name. role-carries-activity-skill fails if an activity demands something its performer was never given. | bun run cat kg:audit. The kg-qa sidecars it writes are derived results whose record the CI job qa-publish stores on the qa-reports branch. | . A role that binds no lane in any diagram is reported by role-binds-a-lane: either a lane name has drifted, or the role is dead.

7507.title: Renaming a role, and a role’s other names
7507.content: Never let a name go silently. A role carries every name it goes by: . | otherNames — names in use today: synonyms, a local title, an example. The same field, and meaning, as otherNames on WHO SMART Base’s Generic Persona. Published as skos:altLabel, beside the names the role’s lanes are drawn with. | formerNames — { "name", "retiredOn" } for each name it no longer goes by. Published as skos:hiddenLabel on the role, and the old name’s concept is owl:deprecated and dcterms:isReplacedBy the role, so a reader holding the old name from older text is sent to the current one. | . To rename: change title, and add the old one to formerNames with today’s date, in the same commit. readRoleGraph refuses a name — title, other or former — that two roles share, so a retired name cannot be quietly given to a new role. The glossary ledger still records, from the harness’s side, every name a swimlane has derived; the role’s own lists are the authored record a README can show (kg:roles, written by bootstrap-tools).

7508.title: role-model (skill)
7508.content: The skill role-model as its source file cat-harness/skills/process/process-core/role-model.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

7509.title: The root README, and the one fact it must carry
7509.content: Skill root-readme: Write the repository’s root README when there is none, carrying a link to the harness that was installed and the overall install status. Never replaces one that exists. It runs only once the install has succeeded. Named by: Complete initialization, Determine the harness and repositories, Initialize a harness . You are the Bootstrapping Agent, and the install has just succeeded. The repository now is a layer instantiating a harness, and — unless somebody wrote one before you got here — nothing at its root says so. People and agents read README.md first, so the README says it.

7510.title: Writing it is not the write the layer rule forbids
7510.content: An instance-readme is read at session start and never written by a running process. That rule governs a process operating on a layer that exists; initialization brings the layer into being, so it may create the README.

7511.title: When it is absent — write it
7511.content: Two things, and no more: . | A link to the harness that was installed. Whatever reference the Requestor gave when the harness was confirmed, resolved to something clickable. | The overall install status. Not one line per location dug out of a log — the question a reader has is “is this repository set up, and as what”, and that is what you answer. Say how many locations the install touched and whether every one of them succeeded. | . Write nothing else: the harness’s own README tool fills the rest, in marker pairs, once it is installed. Say which locations, when there is more than one. “Installed” over three locations where one failed is a false statement about the repository, and the reader who acts on it is the person who set it up.

7512.title: When one is already there — do NOT replace it
7512.content: Add the link and the status inside a marker pair instead, so the harness’s README tool owns that region from then on and the rest of the file stays the author’s. If you cannot tell whether an existing file is authored or a leftover, it is authored: that is the assumption whose failure mode is a duplicated sentence rather than a lost page.

7513.title: What you do not decide here
7513.content: Whether the install succeeded — the install step decided that, and you are on the path where it did. Which harness it was — the Requestor decided that. What the README should eventually say — its author decides that, and you are not its author. If the write fails (no permission, a read-only checkout), say so and end installed anyway: the harness is installed.

7514.title: root-readme (skill)
7514.content: The skill root-readme as its source file bootstrap/skills/root-readme.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

7515.title: Sample import
7515.content: Skill sample-import: Testing an import of a SAMPLE of a remote source into a knowledge graph or other structured store: scope it, let materialize-remote gate it, land it in the library (permanent) or the kept, unpublished trashcan (trial), import it, and test the import. The gates are called, never copied. Named by: Sample import into a structured data store . The SDLC for trying out a remote source before committing to it: take a sample, land it, import it into the store you care about, and find out what breaks. The process is cat-harness/library/processes/sample-import.bpmn. IRIS is the worked instance (the IRIS replica); nothing here is WHO-specific.

7516.title: The gates are not here
7516.content: Size, restrictions, copyright, retention and source loss are asked once, by materialize-remote, and this process only reads the outcome. A second copy would be a second answer free to disagree with the first. What each gate refuses on is in that skill. What this skill adds is what happens around it.

7517.title: 1. Scope — three answers before anything is fetched
7517.content: | question | why it is asked first | . | Which items? By the source’s identifiers, or a subset strategy its descriptor (in the owning instance’s declared sources/, e.g. the IRIS replica’s sources/) supports. | the size gate needs a request to measure | . | Which store? The graph or database the import is tested against. | the test in step 4 is against this store’s schema | . | Permanent or trial? | it decides where the copy lands, and moving a landed copy later means moving it under the wrong obligations | . There is no default for the third. An unscoped sample goes back to the person who proposed it.

7518.title: 2. Materialize — call, and branch on the outcome
7518.content: Call Process_MaterializeRemote. referenced (any gate refused or unknown) ends the sample: nothing is imported, and the refusing gate’s reason is recorded so the next attempt does not re-litigate it.

7519.title: 3. Land it where its permanence says
7519.content: A sample that is not intended to be permanent is materialized to fsh-guts/. |   | permanent | trial | . | destination | library/ | fsh-guts/ | . | published | yes, with the library | no — kept, addressable, exported, never rendered | . | refreshed | yes, by refresh-materialized | no — it records what the source looked like when tried | . | provenance | the materialization record | $schema: folio-fsh-guts/v1, plus the work item or issue it was written under. Never a movedFrom: it was not moved from anywhere, and inventing one is false provenance. | . Promoting a trial means running the process again with permanent. The gates are asked afresh; a trial’s answers were given for a trial.

7520.title: 4. Import and test
7520.content: Load the landed sample into the store and check: . | completeness — every requested item arrived (count against the request); | identifiers — the descriptor’s authoritative identifiers survived; | structure — each node validates against the store’s schema; | provenance — source, revision and fixity are attached to each node. | . A check that could not run is a failure, not a pass. That is the whole reason the gateway is labelled “no, or could not run”.

7521.title: 5. Record the outcome — every path
7521.content: . | passed → where it landed and what was checked; | failed → which check, on which items, with the evidence. The landed copy stays: a failed import is information about the source or the store, and removing the copy destroys it (deletion-requires-confirmation). | .

7522.title: Why bootstrap does not call this
7522.content: bootstrap is the floor (needs: []) and these processes live in cat-harness, which needs bootstrap. A call from bootstrap up to cat-harness is an edge layer-direction.ts reports as wrong-direction.

7523.title: sample-import (skill)
7523.content: The skill sample-import as its source file cat-harness/library/skills/large-datasets/sample-import.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

7524.doc: Sample import into a structured data store
7524.title: Sample import into a structured data store
7524.content: Process_SampleImport · strict · 7 step(s) . The SDLC for testing an import of a SAMPLE of a remote source into a knowledge graph or other structured store. It covers data size, retention, source loss and copyright. General, not WHO-specific: IRIS is the worked instance, and who-iris/ is what this is exercised on. THE GATES ARE CALLED, NOT COPIED.
