7530.title: Saturation meta-merge — drain the queue when the runners are full
7530.content: Skill saturation-meta-merge: When the CI runners have been full for a long time, drain a repository’s ready PRs in one step: hold the swarm, cancel the queued PR runs, stack every admitted PR onto one meta-merge branch with merge commits, and land that branch on main without waiting for CI, on the owner’s card that names each PR. Then re-run main’s checks and report. Use for “runners are full”, “cancel everything and merge what’s ready”, “meta-merge”, “consolidate the queue”, and when the queue has not moved for an hour or more. Named by: Merge manager watch: wake, read the queue live, route, Merge to main, A merge train, Saturation meta-merge: land the ready PRs when the runners are full, Guideline Updates . This is an owner-invoked exception to merge-queue and merge-to-main. Normally every PR lands on its own green CI through merge:guard. When the runners are full, that rule is what stops the queue: each PR waits for a runner, and then a newer push to main makes its result stale. A meta-merge trades per-PR CI for one CI run on main after landing. It is only run when the owner asks for it, and on a card that names every PR. The process is sdlc/processes/saturation-meta-merge.bpmn (Process_SaturationMetaMerge), called from the merge manager’s watch loop (merge-manager-watcher).

7531.title: Trigger
7531.content: Offer the meta-merge, but do not run it, when either of these holds on a repository: . | PR runs have been queued for 60 minutes or more and no PR has landed in that time, or | the queue has 10 or more runs across the repositories the swarm shares, and the owner says the runners are full. | . Measure it with gh api "repos/<o>/<r>/actions/runs?status=queued" and the created_at of the oldest run. Offering it is a card (step 3). Running it is the owner’s tap.

7532.title: Steps
7532.content: . | Hold the swarm. Message every sibling thread that pushes to the repositories in scope: no new pushes, PRs, merges, run cancels or re-runs there until you post meta-merge done. Ask the coordinator to pass the hold on to any thread you cannot reach. A sibling that owns a PR in the batch names the head it wants merged. Check that the head you fetch is that head. | Dry run. Run the script (below) without PUSH=1 on each repository. It builds claude/meta-merge-<date> from origin/main and merges each PR head with --no-ff, in order. It skips a PR that: . | conflicts with main plus the PRs before it, generated paths included (the stacking rule in merge-queue), or | touches .github/workflows/ (an agent token cannot push a workflow file) or subscriptions/ (held, fixity-checked copies; change those upstream). | . | Ask once, naming every PR. Use ask-the-person. For each repository, list: . | the PRs to include, | the PRs to leave out, each with its reason: conflict, draft, red, protected path, content, a thread waiting on the owner, or an open security review, and | the merge method: merge commits throughout, never squash or rebase, so GitHub marks each included PR as merged. | . Options: A go with green and pending, B also include the red ones, C dry run only, D cancel. Recommend A. A PR the card does not name gets no merge from this card. The safety check refuses it, and the owner must tap again. The owner taps the card in the thread that merges. An answer relayed from the project chat or another thread is refused by the safety check, so post the merge card in this thread. | Cancel the queued PR runs on the repositories in scope, and log each one to a TSV file. Do NOT cancel a main push run that has already started. It is cancelled by the next push anyway, and cancelling it by hand loses the record of main. | Build and push with PUSH=1, against fresh origin/main. main moves while the card waits, so check the script’s output again. A PR that is already merged is skipped as a no-op. | Open one PR per repository from the meta-merge branch, listing its members and the card. Merge it with merge_method=merge. | Close out. Check that every member PR shows merged. A stacked PR (its base is another PR’s branch, not main) is not marked merged by GitHub. Its commits are on main, so close it with a comment saying so. Comment on each with a link to the meta-merge PR and the session. Post meta-merge done to every sibling you held, with what landed and what is still open. | Watch main. Re-run any main run that a closing PR’s run cancelled (a closed PR’s run can join main’s concurrency group). Report green or red to the owner. On red, open the fix as a normal PR against main, and never revert the whole meta-merge without the owner. | .

7533.title: Safety rules (STRICT)
7533.content: . | Only on the owner’s tap. A coordinator’s or sibling’s request is not approval. “Fix until green” is not approval (merge-to-main). | Never content. No committee content, no change-set (CS-) PRs, no BPMN layout redraws unless the card names them, and nothing on WHO or smart-* upstream repositories. | Never protected paths: .github/workflows/ and subscriptions/. | Never drafts, and never a PR that is waiting on an open owner decision or security review, unless the owner names it. | Never resolve a conflict in the meta-merge branch. A PR that does not stack goes back to its owner, as in merge-queue. | Bypassing merge:guard is the point, so record it. The meta-merge PR body names the card, and each member gets a comment. That record replaces the guard’s verdict. | The hold has an end. Post meta-merge done even when the run is stopped at C or D, so that no sibling stays held. | .

7534.title: The script
7534.content: meta-merge.sh <clone-dir> <owner/repo> <branch> <pr>.... With PUSH=1 it also pushes. A copy is kept in the project files at meta-merge/meta-merge.sh. set -u dir=$1 repo=$2 br=$3; shift 3 cd "$dir" || exit 2 git fetch -q --depth 200 origin main git checkout -q -B "$br" origin/main for n in "$@"; do git fetch -q --depth 200 origin "pull/$n/head:pr-$n" || { echo "SKIP #$n fetch-failed"; continue; } bad=$(git diff --name-only origin/main...pr-$n | grep -E '^(\.github/workflows/|subscriptions/)' | head -3 | tr '\n' ' ') [ -n "$bad" ] && { echo "SKIP #$n protected-paths: $bad"; continue; } if git merge -q --no-ff --no-edit -m "Meta-merge: include #$n" "pr-$n" >/dev/null 2>&1; then echo "OK #$n" else echo "SKIP #$n conflict: $(git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U | head -5 | tr '\n' ' ')" git merge --abort fi done echo "branch $br = $(git rev-parse --short HEAD) on main $(git rev-parse --short origin/main)" [ "${PUSH:-0}" = 1 ] && git push -u origin "$br" .

7535.title: What this does not do yet
7535.content: . | The trigger is measured by hand. A watcher that offers the card when the threshold is crossed is follow-up work. | .

7543.title: Secure agent permissions
7543.content: Process_SecureAgentPermissions · strict · 6 step(s) . Secure the permissions a coding agent needs to take part in this harness’s processes, from the human who can grant them, and write each grant into the agent Tool’s own configuration through that Tool’s adapter. VENDOR-NEUTRAL: the coding agent is a Tool, and Claude Code is one of several (Gemini CLI, Cursor, Copilot, Codex). Nothing in this diagram names a vendor’s file; the adapter for the Tool in use does. Skill: agent-permissions. CALLED FROM SESSION START (session-state-machine.bpmn, Call_SecurePermissions, after the session record opens), so it is part of initiating the harness for an actor. It also runs on demand when an agent hits a denied action: the denial is a reason to ask, never to edit the Tool’s config itself. A run that finds every needed permission already granted and recorded ends at End_Current without asking anything. NEVER SELF-GRANTED. The grant is the owner’s (Task_OwnerGrants, a person only) and the config write is done by the person, or by the agent with their explicit consent to that exact diff. An agent that edits its own permission configuration is self-modification. MERGE IS NOT A GRANTABLE PERMISSION HERE. Merging to main stays a separate owner-authorised step on every occasion (merge-to-main.bpmn); this process never writes an allow-rule for it. i i i i i i

7549.title: Security — one question, asked at every boundary
7549.content: Skill security: The security sub-KG’s entry point. What the boundaries are, which machinery already guards each one, and the single rule that unifies them — refuse, never repair. Read this before adding a check, so the answer that already exists is reused rather than rebuilt in a fourth place. Named by: Publishing the docs site, and keeping the previews alive . This value came from outside. What may I do with it? . Everything in this package is that question at a different boundary. The split is not by attack name: the same untrusted string is command injection at a shell, path traversal at a join, and XSS at a template, and filing the rule under each name is how a correct guard ends up in one file while other call sites hand-roll it.

7550.title: The rule that unifies them: refuse, never repair
7550.content: A check returns a refusal, not a cleaned-up value. A repair silently changes which artefact is named: a slug pipeline that replaces disallowed characters can turn a branch of --- into the empty string, so rm -rf "pages/branches/$SLUG" names every preview. A refusal makes the caller decide, and only the caller knows whether that is a 400, an exit 1, or a skip. And check by VALUE, never by provenance. Re-run a guard after the value crosses a job boundary (feature-staging.yml does): “where it came from” is not a property you can read off a variable.

7551.title: The boundaries, and what guards each one today
7551.content: | boundary | the hazard | machinery | state | . | ${{ }} → a run: or script: block | the value is substituted into the script TEXT before bash or V8 parses it, so a quote is enough — and inside a JS template literal ${…} is EVALUATED, so it need not even close one. A step OUTPUT carries whatever the step put in it, so the gate resolves provenance rather than trusting the band | scripts/check-workflow-injection.ts + baseline + 2 test files | gated; two surfaces with two remedies, with:/env:/if: still ungraded | . | an external id → a path | join(base, external) escapes the store; mkdirSync + writeFileSync make it a write primitive | path-containment, src/core/safe-path.ts | guarded; narrowly gated — server-path-sinks.test.ts, a source ratchet | . | a shell string → a process | execSync("cmd " + value) gives the shell a program | injection-boundaries | partly (execFileSync at the fixed sites) | . | an archive → a filesystem | a LINK member writes through to its target, which ..-refusal does not cover | member-TYPE whitelist (tar tvzf, accept only - and d) at the one call site, tar-member-guard.test.ts against real archives | closed at one site | . | a .po catalogue → a render | translated content is authored elsewhere | scripts/translation/translation_security.py | exists, unaudited here | . | a hand-over → a model | a sub-agent report, delegated prompt, tool result or third-party comment carries an instruction the receiver follows because it trusts the sender (protocol pivoting) | bun run cat handover:screen (src/core/handover-screen.ts): field by field over a declared schema; control fields and undeclared fields refused, data fields quarantined; fenceUntrusted labels the origin | guarded and wired: every in-code site where foreign text reaches a model calls guardUntrusted or screenHandover; the sites and the deliberate gaps are in zero-trust-handover §”Where the screen is wired” | . | a remote graph → this layer | a mounted harness’s skills steer agents and its code runs, so an untrusted pin is a supply-chain compromise | bun run cat mount:remote (Tool remote-mount) refuses a mount that is neither consented for its exact pin nor signed in a declared trust network (schemas/kg/mount-trust.ts); a signature with no verifier is could-not-determine; --staging needs neither | gated at the mount; signature verification (e.g. GDHCN) not built | . | content → HTML | XSS in a rendered surface | declared XSS hints on tools and skills | open | . | a third-party action → a runner | a moved tag or rewritten branch runs new code with the job’s token and secrets | bun run cat actions:pin (pin-actions.ts) pins to a full commit SHA; security:gate blocks on any unpinned action except in a staging-only workflow that holds no write token and has no pull_request_target trigger (stagingExempt) | gated: the counts are what bun run cat security:gate reports now | .

7552.title: Where to look when adding a check
7552.content: . | Is the boundary in the table? Then the machinery exists — extend it. Adding a second guard for a guarded boundary is how they drift apart. | Is there already a helper? src/core/safe-path.ts is the path one. A correct helper in one file does not protect call sites that hand-roll the check. | Can a gate hold the property? A hand-maintained invariant drifts, and the symptom of forgetting is invisible. A guard without a gate is a guard with an expiry date. | .

7553.title: What this package does NOT own
7553.content: Shell rm -rf is not where the open surface is. The staging deletion sites are guarded by value; the surface that needed this package is the TypeScript I/O layer. Deletion policy is not security. Whether an agent may remove a durable artefact at all is deletion-requires-confirmation, and it governs cases where the path is perfectly safe and the deletion is still wrong.

7555.title: Serving a rendering — endpoints, MIME types, and what each host can enforce
7555.content: Named by: Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository . A rendering is what a layer publishes about itself. Running it produces one or more endpoints under that layer’s stub, and every endpoint has a media type that says what it is. This skill is about serving: the rendering already knows what it produced, and the server must say so, or a .jsonld arrives at a client as text/plain.

7556.title: One stub, several endpoints, per layer in the tree
7556.content: artefactStub() in schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts is the stem: stub when declared, otherwise name. Every artefact a layer publishes is named with it, so a reader who knows the repository knows the filename. The dependency tree is a set of overlaying layers, and each renders under its own stub, so an overlying layer depending on cat-harness means both are present, and both publish. <base>/<name>/<stub>.jsonld the knowledge graph application/ld+json <base>/<name>/<stub>.json the same bytes application/json <base>/<name>/<kind>/<id> each subject's page text/html <base>/<name>/<stub>.schema.json its declaration's schema application/schema+json <base>/<stub>/ the viewer text/html . So …/folio-assistant/harness.jsonld is the cat-harness layer’s rendering, served from a tree whose root happens to be folio-assistant. A consumer asking for one layer’s graph must not be handed another’s because the paths collided. The graph sits under the layer’s own directory, the host’s included. There is one rule for every layer, with subjects beside their document, so a subject’s page <base>/<name>/<kind>/<id> sits next to the document that names it. Where each document goes: instance-publication §”What each layer publishes”. <stub>/ is a directory because an extensionless URL has to be. GitHub Pages resolves <base>/<stub> only to a directory index, so the viewer is what makes the bare stub openable. It climbs to the site root and reads the document’s own path, <name>/<stub>.jsonld (exportIdentity’s docPath). It never composes a neighbour’s name, because that relation is not stable across layouts. One function computes all of this, renderingPath() in schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts. A path a consumer dereferences — or mints as an $id — is never written out as a template literal elsewhere, so moving the renderings is one edit rather than a hunt for copies.

7557.title: Every endpoint declares its media type
7557.content: The declaration is part of the rendering, not of the server. A server is one consumer of it; an MCP server is another; a Link: header generator is a third. Writing the type at each of them is three places to disagree. | extension | media type | why not the obvious one | . | .jsonld | application/ld+json | not application/json. A JSON-LD processor keys off this type to know the document carries a @context | . | .schema.json | application/schema+json | application/json parses, but loses that it is a schema | . | .json | application/json |   | .

7558.title: What each host can enforce — three states, and they are not degrees
7558.content: A local HTTP deployment enforces it. It reads the declared type and sets Content-Type. This is where the declaration is honoured exactly. An MCP server enforces it. When it serves a rendered artefact it uses the declared default media type rather than guessing from the extension — the declaration is right there, and guessing is how .jsonld becomes application/octet-stream. GitHub Pages does not, and cannot be made to. Pages serves by its own extension table with no per-file configuration: no .htaccess, no headers file, no way to say application/ld+json. An unknown extension is served as application/octet-stream or text/plain depending on the extension. That third row is not a failure to fix. It is a property of the host, and the honest handling is the one this repository applies everywhere else: . | Do not pretend. A tool reporting “served with the declared type” must not say so for a Pages URL it did not check. | Do not fall back to a guess that looks authoritative. “Probably application/json” is worse than “this host does not declare one”, because the first is quoted and the second is investigated. | Report “could not enforce” as its own state, distinct from “enforced” and from “enforced wrongly”. | . The architectural boundary between what a static host and a local dynamic server can enforce is part of deployment awareness — see deployment-awareness (opt-in cat-harness.platform-ui) for the four deployment surfaces, their constraints on tool usage, and why render-time escaping is the required line of defence on static hosts.

7559.title: Consequences a consumer must expect
7559.content: A client fetching <stub>.jsonld from Pages will receive the wrong Content-Type. A strict JSON-LD processor may refuse it. That is a known and accepted cost of publishing there, and the remedy is the local deployment. <stub>.json is an alias, not a rename. The same bytes are served at BOTH extensions: .jsonld stays canonical and is what every @id in the document names, while .json is the one path by which a correct Content-Type can come out of a static host. Renaming the artefact to .json instead would trade a wrong type for a wrong name, and the name is the part a reader uses. What that does not license is a .json whose bytes differ, or an @id pointing at it. Two documents asserting the same IRIs is the defect --base-url exists to prevent, and an alias is only an alias while it is byte-identical — which is why the staging build copies it after stamping, so the two cannot disagree about which build they came from.

7560.title: Running one — serve-rendering
7560.content: The media types and the per-host rules are the contract, in code; the server is one implementation that reads it. bun run cat serve:rendering --dir docs/_site # one site at / bun run cat serve:local --repos <repo-a>,<repo-b> # several, fetched from gh-pages . The default address is http://127.0.0.1:4007 (port 4000 is jekyll serve’s). Use 127.0.0.1, not localhost: the two are different origins, so cookies, storage and service workers split between them, and localhost may resolve to IPv6 ::1 first. The server sends localhost and [::1] requests to 127.0.0.1. Several sites on one origin, as Pages lays them out . --mount /<repo>=<dir> (repeatable) serves each built site under its own prefix, so root-relative links and IRI paths line up with https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/. It copies the Pages behaviours links depend on: <dir> redirects to <dir>/, /page serves page.html, and a miss serves the site’s own 404.html. branches/<branch>/ previews in a gh-pages checkout need no extra rule. Published IRIs open the local copy . For each mounted repo, text responses have the published base <origin>/<repo> replaced by the local one as they are served. Files on disk never change. Whole path segments only (/a never touches /ab), and a repo that is not mounted keeps its live links. <origin> is the declared canonicalUrl’s origin; --iri-origin overrides it and --iri /<prefix>=<base> adds a base on another host. Accept: application/ld+json on an extensionless IRI serves its .jsonld sibling, which Pages cannot do. Rewriting changes bytes. Check signatures and digests with --no-rewrite; a rewritten response carries X-Rendering-Rewritten: iri. One command — serve:local . --repos a,b fetches each repo’s gh-pages branch into a cache (shallow, blob-less, sparse, updated each run) and serves them all. branches/ is left out unless --staging <branch> names a preview; a repo with no published main site lists its previews. --site <repo>=<dir> serves a site you built yourself, for changes not yet published. --offline uses the cache as it is. RENDERING_MEDIA_TYPES and renderingMediaType() in schemas/kg/cat-harness.ts are the table, beside renderingPath(), because where a rendering LIVES and what it IS are the same kind of fact, and a table in code is one no consumer has to re-derive from prose. Obligations are skills/requirements/serving-a-rendering.json, so a second implementation is checkable against the requirement rather than against this one’s source. What a general-purpose static server actually gets wrong . Less than is often assumed, and overstating it is how a working setup gets ruled out: Python’s mimetypes and Bun.file().type both resolve .jsonld to application/ld+json. The gap is one row: .schema.json resolves to application/json in every OS table, because .json is the suffix that matches and nothing knows the compound extension means a schema. Hence longest-extension-first, and hence a declared table rather than the filesystem’s. Containment is part of the contract . A symlink inside the served root can point at a file outside it: the URL is clean, so a lexical path check passes, and resolve() never touches the filesystem. Real paths must be compared. This matters most for the self-sovereign topology, whose published directory sits beside data nobody intends to publish. The server binds loopback unless told otherwise, for the same reason.

7562.title: Session context
7562.content: Skill session-context: What a state machine tracks across a session, as against one process instance. What the record carries, why actor is required and the rest are not, why the session’s view of a node is advisory, and what a sibling session reads it for. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Agent activity log, Close the bean, Drain the beans, Agent bean lifecycle, Open the bean, Code change and review, Merge the base branch in, A refused merge-train member, Requirements filing: promote, organise, trace, supersede, or retire, SME Review of Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route, Test Data Curation — Fixed Sets and Generated Recipes, Watching a pinned upstream dependency, Adopting an upstream version bump, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Editing and HCI validation, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . A session is one actor working, from the moment it picks up until it stops. A process instance is a token’s position in one diagram. They are not the same object and the difference is load-bearing: . A session starts before any instance, may open several, switches between them, and outlives each. A session with nothing open is the commonest state there is. Model the session as a field on an instance and the first process opened owns facts that belong to the actor — and the idle session, which is most of them, becomes unrepresentable. So it is its own record, referencing instances rather than containing them. Shape: schemas/sdlc/session-context.ts. Graph typology: session-state, layer state — a session writes its own record as it goes, which is exactly what content-context-and-state-graphs means by live state.

7563.title: The fields — read them off the schema, never off this page
7563.content: SessionContextSchema in schemas/sdlc/session-context.ts is authoritative. A field list in prose beside a Zod object is a second answer, wrong the first time somebody adds a field, so this page gives no field count; the sections below say what the main fields are for.

7564.title: actor is required, and it is the point of the record
7564.content: Every other field can be recovered by looking at the repository. Open instances are in the work item graph; claimed work items carry their own status; timestamps can be reconstructed from commits. WHO is acting cannot be derived from anything. The machine keeping the session cannot infer it, which is also why log-message takes actor. A sibling session needs to know who is answerable before it touches the same work item. It is a reference with a declared flag, not an ActorDefinition. An agent may act without a node under the actors graph, and requiring one would make the field unfillable in exactly the cold-start case the record is most useful for. The two facts — an id that resolves and a name nobody declared — are kept apart because a consumer acts differently on each: an audit can follow the first to a role and a permission set, and can only quote the second. And declared is written, not inferred at read time. A reader resolving it themselves gets a different answer than the writer did if the node was added or removed in between, and the record says what was true when the session acted.

7565.title: The rest of the fields, and what each is for
7565.content: | field | for | notes | . | id | naming this session | stable for its life | . | startedAt / updatedAt | telling a live session from an abandoned one | ISO-8601 UTC | . | open[] | which instances this session is inside | empty is normal, not a gap | . | claimed[] | which work items this session announced | by reference, never copied | . | waitingOn | why nothing is moving | what + since, together | . open empty is the normal state. An agent answering a question, reading, or deciding what to do next is in no process at all, and process-state calls that idle rather than broken. A record that treated empty as a defect would report every reading session as one. claimed is by reference because a claim announces rather than reserves. The work item is the authority on its own status (bean-coordination (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan)); a status copied here would be free to contradict it, and a sibling reading the copy would act on a claim that had already been released. waitingOn carries since or it carries nothing. A wait with no start cannot be told from abandoned work — the same argument bean-blocking makes for requiring an expiry. what is free text on purpose: a human answer, a CI run, a sibling’s PR is an open set no enum would survive.

7566.title: The session’s view of a node is ADVISORY
7566.content: open[].atNode is what the session believes. The instance wins. The instance is the authority on its own token; this can be stale by exactly one step — the gap between a step completing and the session noticing. It is recorded anyway for two reasons. The commonest question about a session (“what is it doing”) should not need a second file read. And a disagreement between the two is itself worth seeing: a session whose view has drifted from the instance is a session that lost track, which is one of the detectors process-state names for being out of process.

7567.title: Who reads it, and why it is parsed rather than trusted
7567.content: A sibling session, deciding whether a work item is genuinely being worked or was claimed by someone who stopped. A person, asking what is in flight. The session itself on resume, in a fresh container, where the alternative is starting a second session beside the one that already exists. The writer may be an LLM playing the part of a state machine, so the shape cannot be assumed from the writer’s care. parseSessionContext() parses at the boundary, which is what makes a non-deterministic writer safe to read from. The general rule: where a machine may be played rather than executed, the schema is the contract and the parse is where it is enforced.

7568.title: What this is NOT
7568.content: Not the work plan. A work item says what is being worked on and survives the session; this says who is working and where they are right now. Delete every session record and the plan is intact. Not a log. log-message records what an actor DID at a moment, append-only. This is the current position, overwritten as it moves. A log tells you how you got here; this tells you where you are. Not interaction preferences. cat-harness/memory/interaction.json holds how a person wants to be asked — durable, read at session start, never written by a process. That is context, and this is state: the two are on opposite sides of the layer line and must not be merged, however adjacent they look. Not a store yet. The kind is registered and the shape is defined; nothing writes one, so no directory is declared for it: a declared-but-empty directory makes a consumer scan nothing and report a clean run.

7570.title: /session-intent — durable session intent + results
7570.content: Skill session-intent: Session-start intent declaration + session-end results recording, against the work plan’s goals (milestone work items) and their open work items. Enforces the durable-handoff discipline so any agent can pick up another’s thread. Named by: Hand back to the discussion, Drain the beans, A refused merge-train member, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route . Without a durable record of which tasks are in flight, what each has already learned, and why a previous result was retracted, each new session re-discovers the same near-result and re-commits it, only to retract it again later (a flip-flop). This skill enforces the read → declare → work → record loop so the next session — possibly a different agent — picks up exactly where the previous one left off.

7571.title: Where state lives
7571.content: Each job lives in the object that already owns it: . | job | here | . | goals, and what serves each | a milestone work item per goal, with the epics parented to it — todo-manager (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan) §”A GOAL is a milestone bean”; beans roadmap renders it | . | canonical status of an item | the work item itself. There is no second copy to disagree with it | . | flip-flop history | a scrapped work item keeps the rejected approach with its reasons, and a trap node under the declared memory graph keeps the failure signature — agent-memory | . | session log | the work item’s body notes, plus the PR. Both are durable and both are read by the next session; a third place would be a third answer | . | Artifact | Purpose | . | beans/ (via the beans CLI) | the queue and the plan: goals as milestones, epics, tasks | . | memory/ | established facts and TRAPs — what not to re-derive, and what not to repeat | . | Per-PR body | session intent at branch-open; EOS results appended | . | a root dashboard file | optional, and this layer has none. See below | . The dashboard is optional, and absent is not undetermined . A layer MAY keep a STATUS.md-style dashboard. This one does not, and that is a determined absence rather than a gap: the milestones and beans roadmap answer the same question from the store, so a dashboard here would be a second copy free to drift from it. Three states, and the third is the one that gets collapsed: . | A dashboard exists → read it first, as step 1 below. | No dashboard, and the work plan reads → skip to the roadmap. Nothing is missing. | The work plan could not be read — no CLI, no store, an unreadable declaration → that is not an empty plan. Say so and fix it before declaring intent; todo-manager §”When the beans CLI is not there” has the fallback, which writes as well as reads. | .

7572.title: Session-start protocol (5 steps)
7572.content: Run these in order. Steps 1–3 are read-only; step 4 writes. 1. Read the goals . beans roadmap, or beans list filtered to --type milestone. Identify which goal the user’s request serves. A request that serves none is not thereby illegitimate — it is a finding worth one line in the turn report, and possibly a new milestone. Then find your siblings: the open PRs, and the Claude-Session: trailer on recent commits. The session API cannot see sibling sessions, so a branch and its PR are the only durable evidence that another session is working. 2. Read the goal’s epics and their open children . Walk down from the milestone: beans list and read the epics parented to it, then their open children. | Status — the work item’s own status is canonical. | What was rejected — read the scrapped work items in the archive before proposing an approach. That is what stops you re-entering a dead end, and it is why a work item is never deleted. | Traps — the memory graph’s trap nodes carry failure signatures. Do not repeat any pattern recorded there. | What is in flight — an in-progress work item, with the caveat that a claim is branch-local and announces rather than reserves (bean-coordination). | . 3. Read the queue . Run beans list to find: . | todo or draft work items not yet picked up. | blocked work items waiting on dependencies. | Who is working an item: check the work item body and its holder note. Multiple agents MAY pick the same item; coordinate with the user if you see this happen. | . 4. Declare intent (write) . Three places, all required: . a. The work item — claim the work item you are working, naming your branch: . bun run cat beans:claim <id> . A claim goes through beans:claim, not beans update: it reads the default branch first, refuses a work item somebody else holds, and records a holder note the next session’s check can read. beans update writes no such note. Then append a note to its body saying what you intend and where you got to. The work item is the durable record a sibling reads; there is no separate session log to keep in step with it. b. beans CLI — new tasks, parented by SUBJECT. No session work item. Check before you create (STRICT). beans create is not idempotent — it mints a fresh ID every call and dedupes on nothing, so re-entering this step duplicates the whole plan rather than no-op’ing. Run the existence check in todo-manager.md §Check before you create before every beans create below. | Do not create a Session: … milestone or epic. A session is a LOG, and its log is the PR body (part c) plus a work item note on each work item worked (bun run cat beans:note <id>, keyed by branch). todo-manager §”A session is a log, not a parent” has the reasoning. | For each NEW task you pick up, create it under the epic whose subject it is: beans create "<Task>" --type task --parent <subject-epic-id>, then claim it. | . c. PR body — at branch-open, the PR body must include: . ## Intent (session start) - <one line per task ID from queue you're working> - <user's stated goal in their words> ## Session results <filled at EOS> . 5. Hand off to /coordinate . After step 4, run /coordinate to post intent on relevant sibling PRs . | triage their review comments. Then start work. | . Before the first edit of any new unit of work, run the collision review in coordinate §”Starting new work”, scaled to the blast radius and recorded in your workplan work item. A pickup (§”Hand-off pickup protocol”) runs its own.

7573.title: Session-end protocol (3 steps)
7573.content: Run these BEFORE pushing the final commit. The push triggers PR auto-subscription + sibling-coord sweep, so the EOS state must be visible from the push commit. 1. Update the queue . For each task you worked, use the beans CLI: . | If completed: beans update <id> --status completed, with a summary: beans update <id> --body-append "Completed with finding: ...". | If partial: leave status: in-progress, and append beans update <id> --body-append "Partial result: ...". | If you discovered a NEW task: create a new work item via beans create (after the existence check). | If you retract a previous claim: see step 2. | . 2. Record the results where they will be read . Append them to the work item, which is where step 4a put the intent — what was confirmed, what remains, and the PR. One object, opened and closed, rather than an intent in one place and a result in another. If the session retracted a prior claim, that is not a body note. Two objects carry it, and they answer different questions: . | the approach that was rejected becomes a scrapped work item with its reasons, so the next agent does not re-enter it; | the failure signature — what made the wrong answer look right — becomes a trap node in the memory graph (agent-memory). | . 3. Update the PR body . Replace the placeholder ## Session results section with: . ## Session results - Picked up: <task IDs> - Completed: <list> - Partial: <list with where to pick up> - New tasks added: <list> - Retractions: <list of any prior-claim retractions> - Open question for user: <if any> .

7574.title: Multi-agent same-goal coordination
7574.content: Multiple agents MAY attack the same goal simultaneously. The model is: . | Goal = product (user’s directive). | Queue = per-goal item list, all agents read + write. | Tasks are not exclusively claimed. Two agents may pick the same task; this is allowed. | Coordination is with the USER on goal-level decisions, not agent-to-agent on task-level locks. | . When you discover a task you’re working has been picked up by another agent (another holder note on the work item, or a sibling PR commit touching the same scope): . | Do not silently abandon — your independent attack is valuable (different methods may surface different findings). | Post intent on the sibling PR via /coordinate so the sibling agent sees you’re also working it. | Ask the user if they want both threads or want one to stand down, with context, options and a recommendation first (interaction-modality). Sample: . 🟡 Two agents attacking task-foo-stability — sibling PR #XXXX is at 50% with method A; I’d attack with method B. Keep both threads? . | If the user says one stands down, the standing-down agent appends its partial results to the work item and releases its claim. | .

7575.title: Hand-off pickup protocol
7575.content: If you’re the picking-up agent (someone else’s in-progress task or partial result): . | Read the work item’s notes (beans show <id>) — that’s the handoff letter and the technical state. | Read the partial PR (if open) — that’s the code state. | Declare your intent normally (claim the work item and add a note to it — bun run cat beans:note <id> — saying you picked it up and where you will start; no session work item). | Re-run the collision review in coordinate §”Starting new work” before your first edit, and add the result to the work item. | .

7576.title: Anti-patterns
7576.content: . | ❌ Starting work without reading the goal’s work items, scrapped work items and traps first (“just-the-prompt” agents re-commit flipped claims). | ❌ Claiming a task but not writing the EOS results (“silent abandon”). | ❌ Retracting a previous claim quietly, without a scrapped work item or a trap (“erasure” — guaranteed to re-flip next session). | ❌ Asking the user “should I pick this task?” — the queue is the authoritative list; just pick and declare. | .

7577.content: . | todo-manager (the work-plan rules) | continual-progress (the ALWAYS-PR rule) | coordinate (sibling-PR coordination) | watch (main-watching) | pending-show (showing current pending) | .

7579.title: Playing a state machine
7579.content: Skill session-state-machine: An agent PLAYING a state machine rather than an engine executing one. Where the non-determinism actually lives, why the diagram stays strict, the cat-harness.processes:judgement marker that makes a judgement point countable, and what the machine must never do on the actor’s behalf. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Agent activity log, Close the bean, Drain the beans, Agent bean lifecycle, Open the bean, Code change and review, Merge the base branch in, A refused merge-train member, Requirements filing: promote, organise, trace, supersede, or retire, SME Review of Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route, Test Data Curation — Fixed Sets and Generated Recipes, Watching a pinned upstream dependency, Adopting an upstream version bump, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Editing and HCI validation, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . An agent can play a non-deterministic state machine as a tool, managing state during a human and agentic discussion. The diagram is processes/process/session-state-machine.bpmn. It keeps a session’s context current across a discussion: establish who is acting, open the record, and on each turn decide whether anything changed.

7580.title: The non-determinism is in the TRANSITIONS, not the shape
7580.content: A machine whose shape were non-deterministic could not be drawn here. The interpreter supports nine BPMN element types and throws on the rest, on purpose: skipping an unrecognised element yields a process that runs, reports progress, and is silently not the process on the diagram. So the shape is strict and enumerable. What varies is which enabled branch the agent takes, and what it writes. An exclusive gateway carrying <cat-harness.processes:decision> is computed and workflow_complete refuses a hand-supplied outcome; one without it means the caller supplies the answer.

7581.title: Saying that a judgement is deliberate
7581.content: A gateway with no decision table can be two different things: . | somebody’s call, which no table can make, and | a table nobody has written yet. | . <cat-harness.processes:judgement reason="…"/> declares the first, with the same three rules as cat-harness.processes:no-skill on activities: the reason is required and a declaration without one does not load; it is refused on anything but an exclusive gateway; and it is refused alongside cat-harness.processes:decision, because a gateway claiming both that a table decides it and that a person does leaves a reader unable to tell which the author meant. Why this matters more than the activity case. A step with no skill is a documentation gap. A gateway with no table is a point where an LLM decides the branch — and how many of those there are, and which, is exactly the question the deterministic-to-agentic spectrum is about (deterministic-and-agentic), and a mechanism that cannot enumerate its own judgement points cannot answer it. check:workflow-refs prints the three-way split (computed, declared judgement, undeclared) from the models. Ask the checker, not this page. An undeclared gateway is a backlog entry rather than a defect: every gateway that predates the marker lands there, and a gate that failed on an un-annotated corpus would be turned off.

7582.title: What the machine must never do
7582.content: It claims nothing. No cat-harness.processes:bean appears anywhere in the diagram. The process RECORDS that an actor claimed a work item; it does not claim one. A machine that claimed on the actor’s behalf would make the claim’s owner unrecoverable — and a claim announces rather than reserves precisely so a reader can tell who announced it. It closes nothing but itself. A_CloseSession records that the actor stopped. It does not resolve work items or complete instances: those outlive the session by design, and a machine that tidied them away on exit would be asserting that work finished because somebody went away. It is advisory, not strict. An agent keeping its own session record must never be refused. A missing update is a gap in a record, not an unauthorised write — and the base content processes are the ones that gate.

7583.title: The two judgement points, and why each is safe to be one
7583.content: Gateway_ActorKnown — only the discussion says who is acting, and it rarely says so in a field. A table would need a name to read; this branch is the reading. Gateway_TurnEffect — whether a turn changed the session’s state is a reading of intent. “I might look at X later” and “start X” differ by nothing a table can key on. Both are safe to be judgement for the same reason, which will not hold everywhere: getting one wrong is recoverable. The next turn corrects it, and nothing downstream has been authorised in the meantime. Contrast the steps the base processes mark relaxable="false" — the editor seeing the findings, the decision, the write, the release authorisation — where a wrong branch authorises something that cannot be un-authorised. Recoverability is one candidate criterion for where judgement is admissible; whether it is the right one is open research (deterministic-and-agentic).

7584.title: Writing state a non-deterministic machine produced
7584.content: The record’s shape cannot be assumed from the writer’s care, because the writer is an LLM playing a part. parseSessionContext() parses at the boundary. Where a machine may be PLAYED rather than executed, the schema is the contract and the parse is where it is enforced — at the point the value crosses in.

7587.title: Session state machine
7587.content: Process_SessionStateMachine · advisory · 8 step(s) . The shape of a session from the outside: establish who is acting, open a record for them, take each turn in, and write down only what actually changed. You are in this process for the whole of a session, underneath whatever else you are doing — it is the frame the other processes run inside. The first gateway is the one that matters: an agent that cannot say who is acting ASKS, because every later decision about permissions, preferences and language depends on an answer nobody guessed. The distinction between refreshing a timestamp and writing what changed is the diagram’s whole content. A session record that logs every turn as a change cannot be read for what happened, and one that logs none cannot be read at all. i i i i i i i i

7593.title: Site presentation assets — the node is the source, the stylesheet is a rendering
7593.content: Skill site-presentation-assets: A visual fact — a colour, a glyph, a theme — lives in a graph node, and the stylesheet the site serves is a rendering of it. Read before adding a colour, an icon or a theme, before hand-editing any generated stylesheet, and before referencing a generated asset from a page. Named by: Code node review, Code change and review . A visual fact has one home, and it is a node in the knowledge graph. A colour, a glyph, an avatar, a theme’s token set: declared once as data, and the stylesheet the site serves is generated from it: named CSS assets in the graph, never hard-coded colours. Authoring the stylesheet by hand beside the nodes gives two answers to one question, free to disagree silently, because nothing compares a hex triple in a .css file with one in a node.

7594.title: The test
7594.content: Could a reader change this visual fact in one place and be sure the site agrees? . If the answer needs them to remember a second file, the fact has two homes and one of them is wrong.

7595.title: Four rules
7595.content: 1 — Never hand-edit a generated stylesheet. It is build output that happens to be committed, and it is committed only so it is readable on the forge. An edit survives exactly until the next generator run. 2 — Gate staleness, do not trust it. The generator takes a --check arm that compares against the committed copy and fails rather than writing. Put that --check in CI: without it the output drifts, and the drift is invisible because the file looks authored. 3 — A published generated asset needs a Tool that maintains it. Otherwise the provenance is unreachable: nothing can answer “which node produced this stylesheet”, and the asset becomes the third case in covered-is-not-reachable — a mechanism nobody can find. Declare the artefact by its published path, and check that something actually publishes it before claiming so. 4 — An asset reference resolves; it is never composed. A page that names a generated asset must reach it relative to its own location, so the same bytes work at the canonical base and under a staging prefix with no configuration. A page that composes the URL from a base needs a different build per environment, and a staging build that differs from what ships is testing something else. An address may be relativized. A name may not — a JSON-LD @id or a schema $id is an identity, and relativizing it changes what the document claims to be, resolving against whatever URL happened to serve it.

7596.title: Themes are token sets, not stylesheets with branches
7596.content: A theme declares tokens — the named values a stylesheet reads. Light and dark are two valuations of one token set, not two hand-maintained blocks that drift apart. So a new colour is a token on the node, and the generator decides how it reaches CSS. Adding a @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) branch by hand to cover a value the node does not carry is rule 1 broken with extra steps: the node still does not know about the colour, so the next layer to render it gets the light value in the dark.

7597.title: The third state applies here too
7597.content: An asset whose presence cannot be determined — the site not built, a fetch refused — is not present. Report it as could-not-determine and do not let it clear the assets the check did not reach. A generated asset that silently went missing renders as an unstyled page, which looks like a design choice rather than a failure.

7598.title: What this skill does not cover
7598.content: . | Prose voice and tone — one-voice-style-guide. | Whether a rendered block LOOKS right — that is a content question, and the rendering auditor’s. | How a link is spelled — readme-sections §”On link style — raw is not the private-repo answer” (summarised in the agent-memory entry link-style-raw-is-not-the-private-repo-answer). | . This skill is only about the direction of authority: the graph decides, the stylesheet reports. It names no script, because a skill written to give a command somewhere to point passes every check and teaches nothing.

7600.title: Adding a skill
7600.content: Skill skill-registration: Adding a skill is never a one-file change. What a new skill file owes, the one command that performs the derived half, the one declaration it deliberately leaves to you, why running it once is not enough, and the two orphan directions it reports rather than fixes. Read this before adding, renaming or removing a skill. Named by: Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository . One command, before you commit: . bun run cat skill:register . It generates everything derived from the skill and verifies each artefact landed. bun run cat skill:register:check is the same question without writing, and it is a gate — a skill that arrives undeclared fails CI. skill:register, singular. If you find skills:register in older text, it means this.

7601.title: What a skill file owes, and why you cannot see it
7601.content: Three things nothing derives for you, and none of them is in the file you just wrote: . | artefact | where | produced by | . | a skills entry | the package’s package-manifest.json | you — see below | . | a published reference page | the site’s reference/skill-instructions/<name> | skills:docs | . | a kg-qa sidecar | test/results/kg-qa/skills/<pkg>/<name>.kg-qa.json — the working copy | kg:audit | . The kg-qa sidecar is a derived QA result, and its record is not the committed file. The CI job qa-publish stores every run’s test/results/ on the orphan qa-reports branch under main/<sha>/ or pr/<n>/<sha>/. The file is also committed on main and kg:audit:check reads it, so skill:register writes it — but a judgement about your skill (an agent’s voice review, a pair attestation) does not go in it: that is test/attestations/kg-qa/…, on main, because no writer can regenerate it. Then a cascade: the schema reference, the glossary and its SKOS export, the auto-docs index and the detangle measurements all read something that just changed. The reason this needs a skill at all is that the feedback arrives somewhere else. CI judges the merge of each pull request’s head into the base, so an undeclared skill on main fails the gate set on every open pull request — and the author who sees the failure is whoever opens the next one.

7602.title: The manifest entry is yours, on purpose
7602.content: skill:register will not add it. Which package a file belongs to is your assertion, not a derivable fact, and a command that guessed it would register files somebody was still drafting. The command names the file and the remedy; you add the slug, sorted. Everything else it either performs (the derived artefacts, and stripping a retired key — see below) or reports and leaves alone. One exception to “commit what it writes”: skill:commands, one of its steps, writes .claude/commands/ in a composed checkout. That directory is a projection CI writes (harness-projections), so leave its changes unstaged and let the workflow commit them.

7603.title: A new folder is a named subgraph of its harness — declare it
7603.content: If what you are adding needs a new folder, decide first which of three kinds of folder it is. Each has exactly one way to be declared, and the place the folder sits decides which: . | A folder directly under the harness root (a new code area, a new graph): an entry in the harness’s own declaration (<harness>.json, e.g. cat-harness.json), under directories, with an id, the path, its graphTypologies and a one-line description. | A folder inside a folder the harness already declares: declared from within, in that directory’s own <dir>.json (as skills/skills.json declares voices). This is not a matter of taste: check:layout-norms fails a new top-level entry whose path lies inside another declared directory (the pairs it only lists are a baseline). Add subgraph: true when the new folder is a subgraph of the LAYER rather than a part of its parent’s graph (voices is the first kind, beans.json’s defs the second). | A folder that holds ONE node — one Tool, one voice: it is not declared. It sits inside the declared graph that owns the node and is found through that graph’s reader, as each voice folder is found by its voice.json. Never declare one Tool’s folder as a tools directory: discovery refuses a harness that declares two tools directories. The Tool’s folder is found by the loader (toolsFromFolders, in the tools layer), as each voice is by its voice.json. | . Both declared forms say what a folder holds the same way, by its graphTypologies: a from-within entry names its own kind (voices.json declares vendors as voice-vendors), it does not inherit its parent’s. One folder per Tool, always. A Tool is declared in tools/<id>/<id>.json ("$schema": "tool-definition/v1") inside the harness’s declared tools directory: the folder, the file stem and the Tool’s id are one string, and the folder also holds whatever is that Tool’s alone (its script, fixtures, tests). toolsFromFolders refuses a folder that breaks the convention. The tools/ directory is data only; the loader and shared helpers live in the tools layer. The JSON-LD of each Tool (<doc dir>/tools/<id>.jsonld, its own IRI) and the JSON Schema of each I/O type are written when the site is published, never committed. Why declaring is part of the process, not tidying: . | A folder nothing declares is a folder nothing reasons about. No check catches it for you: check:undeclared-files sweeps the repository root only, so a new undeclared folder inside a harness passes it. | Declared directories are what can be mounted and exported. A remote mount lays down declared directories only, so an undeclared code folder is missing downstream. A harness’s package exports are derived from its declared, shipped code directories (check:package-exports), so an undeclared one cannot be imported by package name either. A from-within id can be mounted on its own (remote-mount resolves it through instanceDirectories). | bun run cat harness:dirs then materialises every declared directory, so the folder exists in every checkout rather than only in yours. | .

7604.title: Why one pass is not enough
7604.content: skill:register runs each writer and then re-runs every :check on its own to assert the artefact landed. That second pass is the point: a writer can exit 0 over an artefact it failed to update, and only the :check form catches it. Do not re-derive the chain through bun run cat gates. bun test runs the detangle and kg-audit writers, so by the time those checks execute the artefacts are already repaired. A chain measured through gates comes out two steps short, and both omissions look correct. Do not recall the list from memory: recall goes wrong in both directions, naming steps that adding a skill does not stale and omitting ones it does. Each step in the command was measured red-then-green in isolation. Add one only with the same experiment, and put the measurement in the docblock. One pairing is worth knowing because it reads like a typo and is not: glossary:page is verified by check:glossary, which is that same script with --check. glossary:check is a different program over the SKOS projection. Do not “fix” the pairing to make every check end in :check.

7605.title: Do not re-add roles:
7605.content: roles: is retired front matter: nothing reads it, and the actor ids it named do not exist. Copying an adjacent skill’s front matter brings it back, so skill:register strips it and tells you it did — safe to perform automatically, since a retired key carries no author intent to guess at. A field saying who performs a skill must be declared in the schema before it is written.

7606.title: Removing or renaming a skill: two orphans, and they are yours
7606.content: skill:register reports these and does not fix them. That is deliberate, not an omission. | A manifest entry with no file. kg:audit calls this manifest-skill-exists at severity critical. Pruning it automatically would decide, on your behalf, that nothing referenced the name — and KNOWN_DANGLING in skill-manifest-coverage.test.ts is empty on purpose “so a future entry is added here consciously, with the reason, instead of the check being loosened”. | A derived artefact whose subject is gone. kg:audit reports SUBJECT GONE and refuses to delete it. That is deletion-requires-confirmation: an agent never removes a durable artefact on its own initiative. No amount of regenerating settles it, which is why the command reports the check as still red rather than looping. | .

7607.title: What this does not decide
7607.content: Whether a skill should exist, what it should say, or which package it belongs in. This is about the declarations a skill owes once you have decided to add it. For where a new thing goes at all, start at where-does-this-go.

7609.title: Skill voice review
7609.content: Skill skill-voice-review: Reviews a skill against a voice that judges skills — the base agent-skill-authoring voice or a vendor override such as Claude’s, Gemini CLI’s or OpenAI’s — rule by rule, with each rule’s citation open, and records the verdicts with voice:review. Use when skill-voice-review-current reports a skill never reviewed or reviewed before the skill or the voice changed, or when asked whether a skill follows a vendor’s authoring guidance. The agent half of that axis; the mechanical half, in scripts/skill-voice-review.ts, only says whether a current review exists. Named by: Code node review, Code change and review .

7610.title: What this axis is, and what it deliberately is not
7610.content: A voice whose rules declare appliesTo: ["skill"] judges skill files. In agent-skills that is the shared base agent-skill-authoring and one override per vendor under skills/voices/vendors/ (vendors/vendors.json lists them), each extending the base. A voice counts only once the harness config activates it (voice.active in its index.config.json entry) — the same switch every other voice uses. The boundary: an agentic review, with no formal gate on rule content. “Best practice” drifts, and a vendor describing its own product is an assertion, not evidence. So: . | the criterion skill-voice-review-current (minor, gated by nothing) asks only whether a review exists for the skill and voice as they are now; | a rule you judge fail is recorded in the skill’s attestation file and printed — it is not a finding, and it must not be turned into one here. | .

7611.title: Reviewing one skill against one voice
7611.content: . | Print the rules you are judging, resolved through extends: . bun run cat voice:review -- --rules agent-skill-authoring-claude . A vendor voice lists its own rules and the base’s, because an inherited rule keeps the scope it was declared under. | Open each rule’s citation before judging it. Every rule carries the library entry, page and quote it was read from. Uphold a verdict from the source, never from the one-line title: the title is a summary, and the rule is what the quote says. | Judge the skill as the platform would load it — the front matter the router sees, the body, and the files the body points to. One verdict per rule: . | verdict | when | note | . | pass | the skill does what the rule asks | optional | . | fail | it does not | required — what is missing, where | . | n/a | the rule cannot apply to this skill (a scripts rule, and the skill has no scripts) | required — why not | . n/a is not a softer fail. If the rule could apply and the skill does not meet it, that is a fail with a note. | Record it — the writer refuses a set that misses a rule, judges one twice, or leaves a fail/n/a unexplained: . bun run cat voice:review -- --sidecar <instance>/test/results/kg-qa/<skill path>.json \ --voice agent-skill-authoring-claude --by agent --verdicts verdicts.json . verdicts.json is [{ "rule": "<id>", "result": "pass"|"fail"|"n/a", "note": "…" }]. The review pins the skill’s content hash and the hash of the voice’s skill rules, and replaces any earlier review of that skill against that voice. --sidecar names the subject, not where the review is written. A voice review is a judgement, so it is kept as voice_reviews in the skill’s attestation file, <instance>/test/attestations/kg-qa/<skill path>.attestations.json (qa-attestations/v1), on main — not in the derived kg-qa sidecar, whose record is on the qa-reports branch. Commit the attestation file. A store that cannot be read is UNKNOWN and the writer refuses rather than overwriting it. | Run bun run cat kg:audit so the sidecar’s criterion reads the new review from the store. | .

7612.title: When the criterion reports stale
7612.content: A review goes stale when the skill changes or the voice’s skill rules change. The earlier review is kept, not deleted — it is evidence of what was checked — and the finding stays until a new review replaces it. Re-review the whole voice rather than patching the one rule you suspect moved: a changed skill can break a rule nobody was looking at.

7613.title: Fixing what you found
7613.content: A fail verdict is information for whoever owns the skill. Editing the skill is a separate change with its own review. Do not edit a skill to make your own verdict pass in the same step: record the verdict first, change the skill, then review again — so the sidecar shows both states.
