The dependency graph comes from: . | uses[] field in content .ts manifests (narrative dependency) | any formalization import statements (formal-layer dependency) | dependency-graph.svg generated by CI | .

7763.title: When to write a test
7763.content: . | A bug was found — write a regression test before fixing. | A new script or config file is added — test its contract. | A rendering macro is changed — test extraction still works. | A new formal-layer project is added — auto-discovered, but verify. | A review skill detects a potential error — it will ask the user whether to write a test. If yes, this skill writes it. | .

7764.title: How to write a test
7764.content: // In scripts/tests/<suite>.test.ts import { describe, test, expect } from "bun:test"; import { REPO_ROOT, ... } from "./helpers"; describe("Feature under test", () => { test("specific behavior", () => { // Arrange // Act // Assert expect(result).toBe(expected); }); }); . Conventions . | One test file per concern: create new files for new concerns. | Use helpers.ts: Don’t hardcode paths or re-implement discovery. | Informational vs. blocking: Tests that report data quality (coverage gaps, label mismatches) should log and pass. Tests that verify contracts (JSON validity, required fields, file existence) should fail. | Comment the failure point: Each test should document what bug or failure it prevents. | Types from schemas/formalization-types.ts: Use TestResult, TestReport, CoverageEntry etc. when generating structured output. | . A test never reads test/results/ as a fixture . Derived QA results live on the orphan qa-reports branch: the checkout’s <instance>/test/results/** is an ignored working copy, and the record is the commit-keyed entry qa-publish stores. A test that reads that tree reads a file that may not be there: it fails when the corpus is absent, or worse, passes by iterating over zero files. | Build the fixture, or run the producer in-process over one, and assert on what it computed. A verdict is not a fixture: the corpus is supposed to change (see qa-witness). | If a test must read a stored result, read it through qa-store (readQa) and treat miss, corrupt and unknown as states to assert, never as an empty pass. | A loop over a corpus needs a “there are some” guard beside it, or it is green over nothing. | Never write into test/attestations/ from a test. It is the judgement store on main; a test that needs one builds it in a temporary root. | . Every test has a Gherkin (STRICT) . A test is not finished until a Gherkin Scenario says what it tests. The Scenario is the specification a reader can review without reading code; the test function is one way of executing it. A test with no Scenario is a defect, not missing documentation. | Every executable test maps to exactly one Scenario. An executable test is whatever the language’s runner discovers, ignored or skipped ones included: a Rust #[test], a Kotlin/JUnit @Test, a bun or vitest test() / it(), a pytest test_*. A parameterised test (test.each, @pytest.mark.parametrize, @ParameterizedTest) is ONE test and maps to one Scenario or Scenario Outline. A test’s title is a fixed string: a test titled by a loop variable or a ${…} template has no name a tag can carry, so the check reports it (test-name-not-static). Give it a literal title, or write the loop as test.each(…)("… %s"). | The link is a tag on the Scenario, never on the Feature: line (a Feature tag would be inherited by every Scenario under it): . @test:tools/verify/tests/signature.rs::rejects_expired_key Scenario: an expired signing key is refused . | The tag grammar is one grammar for every language — @test:<file>::<scope>::…::<name>: . | <file> is the test’s source file, relative to the repository root, with / separators; | then the enclosing scopes in source order (a Rust mod, a Kotlin or Python class, a describe() title), then the test’s own name, each segment separated by ::; | whitespace inside a segment is written as _, because a Gherkin tag ends at whitespace. The checker normalises both sides the same way and reports two tests that normalise to one tag as ambiguous. | . | runner | test | tag | . | Rust | fn parses_cbor() in mod tests of src/cose.rs | @test:src/cose.rs::tests::parses_cbor | . | Rust | fn round_trip() in tests/hcert.rs | @test:tests/hcert.rs::round_trip | . | Kotlin | @Test fun decodes() in class QrTest | @test:app/src/test/kotlin/x/QrTest.kt::QrTest::decodes | . | bun / vitest | test("reads a plan") in describe("loader") | @test:scripts/loader.test.ts::loader::reads_a_plan | . | pytest | def test_load() in class TestPlan | @test:tests/test_plan.py::TestPlan::test_load | . The pytest form is pytest’s own node id, so it can be pasted from the runner’s output. | A Scenario may name more than one test when several tests execute one behaviour, by carrying one tag per test. A Scenario with no @test: tag is specification nobody executes, and is a finding too; mark it @manual when a person executes it, and the checker counts it as linked. | Binding is by tag, and a Scenario may bind an external test case. Besides @test:, a Scenario may carry @itb:<testSuite id>/<testCase id> for a WHO-ITB (GITB TDL) test case, named by the id attribute of the <testsuite> and of the <testcase> it references: ids, not paths, since ITB reports results by id. The tag resolves against a checkout of the suites at a pinned commit; without one it is reported unresolved, never passed. External cases are checked one way only (the tag must name a case that exists), because an external suite is not this repository’s to cover. The schemes are an extensible list, so a new kind of external test is a new prefix and a resolver. | A .feature may be written in any Gherkin dialect, declared by its first-line # language: <code> comment. A translated file stays valid; the @test: and @itb: tags are not translated. | A specification for implementers is not a test of this tree (owner, 2026-11-13). Some .feature files specify tests for whoever implements the content (a DAK’s L2 scenarios, for one); they do not test the repository’s code. A repository says so in its harness configuration, never by a path or a type the checker names: testSpecifications, a list of repository-relative paths (a directory ends in /), on the section of contentTypes in its index.config.json whose specifications they are, for example "dak": { …, "testSpecifications": ["input/testing/"] }. The key reads the same on every type. Only the .feature files under those paths are specifications. A malformed list is refused, not read as empty. In a declared specification a Scenario with no binding is counted as a specification, not reported. Once it carries a binding (@itb: to an external suite, or @test:) it is checked like any other. Nothing else is relaxed: every test still needs its Scenario. | Each test-plan case names its .feature (testCases[].feature in test-plan/v1.1); the tests that execute the case are found through the @test: tags of that file, not listed again in the plan. | . bun run cat check:test-gherkin reports orphans both ways: a test no Scenario names, a tag that names no test, a test named by two Scenarios, a Scenario that names no test, a tag on a Feature: line, an @itb: tag naming no case or whose source is not held, and an unknown dialect. It reads any tree (--root, --under, --itb, --json); it is not a gate until a repository has backfilled. Once a layer reports 0 findings, it gates on it: a check:test-gherkin:<layer> entry beside the layer’s other check:* gates (a script name may be declared by only one layer). The kg-audit criterion test-has-gherkin records the same gap for a layer, and adds every test-plan case whose .feature is missing or does not resolve. Adding a new formal-layer project . When a new formal-layer library is added to the build manifest: . | discoverProjects() in helpers.ts auto-discovers it | the project test suite automatically tests it (directory, files, audits) | No manual test registration needed | . Test categories (from TestCategory type) . | Category | What it tests | . | formal-compile | formal-layer files exist, have imports, are non-empty | . | formal-library | toolchain, build manifest, dependencies declared | . | formal-gap | unproved-gap count per project/file | . | render-coverage | render tags resolve, statement coverage, consistency | . | doc-structure | labels, cross-refs, environments | . | schema-validity | JSON manifests match their schemas | . | infrastructure | server config, scripts, deploy, .gitignore | . | content-validation | content objects pass Zod + constraint + AST checks | . Content-object tests . Test content objects using the validation pipeline: . import { validateObjects } from "../../pipeline/validate"; describe("Content objects", () => { test("all objects pass schema validation", async () => { const result = await validateObjects("content/<paper>/<section>/"); const errors = result.issues.filter(i => i.level === "error"); expect(errors).toHaveLength(0); }); test("rendered output passes AST validation", async () => { // The validation pipeline includes AST checks automatically const result = await validateObjects("content/<paper>/<section>/"); expect(result.valid).toBe(true); }); }); .

7768.title: Running a test plan — from a request to a signed certification
7768.content: Skill test-plan-execution: Run a test-plan/v1 against a system under test and take it to a certification decision — the five lanes of test-plan-execution.bpmn (requester, tester, untainted checker, certifier, attestation service), how the test data is bound, what the run and the report must record, the facts the certification table reads, and the kg-audit criteria that judge a run afterwards. Read before executing a plan, re-executing a sample, or certifying a result. Named by: KG to public portal, QA report signing, SME Review of Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Test Data Curation — Fixed Sets and Generated Recipes, Test-plan execution . Skill id: test-plan-execution · Package: sdlc-core · Process: test-plan-execution.bpmn · Decision: test-certification.dmn . A system is tested against a plan, by somebody who is not the system, and certified by somebody who did not run the test. Everything below is that sentence made operational. This skill is the PROCESS. How to write a test is test-engineer; how a folio’s content is tested is content-test; why the checker sees only a controlled context is untainted-verification; how a signature is routed by reach is qa-report-signing. Read those for their halves — this one does not restate them.

7769.title: The nodes, and who points at whom
7769.content: | node | schema | where it lives | . | the plan | test-plan/v1 — schemas/sdlc/test-plan.ts | authored content (test-plan kind) | . | the system under test | the systemUnderTest facet on an actor — schemas/kg/skill-package.ts | scenarios/actors/*.json | . | the run | folio-test-run/v1 with plan + sut — schemas/sdlc/test-run.ts | the declared qa directory | . | the report | test-report/v1 — schemas/sdlc/test-report.ts | the qa-reports branch, tests/<plan>/<sut>/<run>/ | . | the certification | a judgement, qa-attestations/v1 | the declared attestations graph, on main | . The run points at the plan; the plan names no run. A plan is reused across runs and systems, so a back-pointer would turn authored content into live state. Same direction for the report → run and the certification → report. The platform model is FHIR-free. FHIR R5 TestPlan informed test-plan/v1 and is a DOWNSTREAM export target, in the FHIR IG layer. Never read a FHIR TestPlan as the source of a plan here.

7770.title: The system under test is a facet, not a role
7770.content: Being tested is not a lane anybody takes on. An actor that can be executed — agent or system, never a person or an external — declares: . // an illustration, not a declared actor { "id": "example-mcp-tool", "kind": "system", "reach": "internet", "systemUnderTest": { "kind": "tool", "version": "0.1.0" } } . kind is the closed list SUT_KINDS (skill, agent, tool, machine, ig, process) — the same vocabulary as a plan’s scope.kind, so the two are compared, not translated. Reach is the actor’s own reach, read by sutRefFor; absent is unknown, never internet.

7771.title: The five lanes
7771.content: | lane | role | does | . | Requester / SUT | test-requester | asks for certification of system S against plan P, naming P’s id and version | . | Tester | tester | resolves P, binds its data, executes every case, writes the run and the report | . | Untainted checker | untainted-checker | re-executes a SAMPLE of cases, blind to the tester’s verdicts | . | Certifier | certifier | applies the plan’s exitCriteria table, then records the decision | . | Attestation service | attestation-service | signs, via qa-report-signing.bpmn, and files the certification | . The tester is untainted from the system under test. The SUT may request; it may never be the tester, the checker or the certifier, and it never writes a verdict about itself — test-report/v1 refuses a reviewer whose id or actor is the SUT’s actor, and test-sut-not-self-judged audits it. Tester . | Resolve the plan. P parses as test-plan/v1.1 (a test-plan/v1 plan still parses, deprecated), names at least one req: requirement, its exitCriteria.decision resolves to a decision in a .dmn that exists, and its scope.kind matches the SUT actor’s facet kind. A plan that does not resolve is not run. Every case names the .feature it is written in, and every test that executes it carries that file’s @test: tag (test-engineer). | Bind the test data (test-data-sets). A fixed set is a committed path and is evidence only once reviewed (isEvidence). A generated set is a template + params + seed and is never materialised into the repository. Both feed the run’s data hash; runner, configuration and scenario bank feed its process hash, and the two bases must be disjoint (buildTestRun refuses otherwise). | Execute. Every case is executed, or recorded skipped with a reason. A case with no verdict at the end of a terminal run is a finding, not an omission (checkAgainstPlan). | Write the run and the report. The run records plan {id, version} and sut {actor, version, reach}; the report rolls up per plan, never across plans, and testReportPath says where it goes. | . Untainted checker . Re-executes a sample of the cases from the plan and the data alone — never the tester’s verdicts — and reports agree, disagree or unknown. It RULES ON NOTHING (untainted-verification rule 3): the comparison is a fact the certification table reads, not a verdict the checker writes. Certifier . The gateway is computed. Pass the facts; never assert the branch — the engine refuses a hand-supplied outcome on a DMN gateway. | fact | from | . | reportStatus | the report’s status | . | dataHashKnown | the run’s data.hash is not unknown | . | unexecutedCases | checkAgainstPlan(...).filter(kind === "unexecuted-case").length | . | checker | the untainted checker’s agree / disagree / unknown | . | failedCases | rollup.fail | . | passedCases | rollup.pass | . The table returns certified, refused or undetermined. undetermined is the third state — a running or aborted report, an unknown data hash, an unexecuted case, a checker that disagreed or could not run, or a report in which nothing passed. It is never rendered as certified, and it is not a refusal either: it says the evidence does not decide, so nothing is signed. The certification decision is a judgement. The table says whether the exit criteria are met; the certifier — a person, a specialisation of stakeholder — records the decision, and it lives with the other judgements under the declared attestations graph, never on the qa-reports branch with derived results. Attestation service . Call_Sign runs qa-report-signing.bpmn unchanged; its route (API or a human release authority) is chosen there by the signer’s reach. Then the signed certification is filed under attestations.

7772.title: The kg-audit criteria
7772.content: Registered in KG_CRITERIA (schemas/sdlc/kg-qa.ts), implemented in scripts/test-plan-audit.ts, recorded on the graph roll-up: . | criterion | fails when | severity | . | test-plan-resolves | a plan does not parse, its exit DMN does not resolve, or a run/report names a plan, version or SUT that does not resolve (or a SUT whose facet kind is not the plan’s scope) | critical | . | test-case-executed-or-skipped | a terminal report leaves a plan case with no verdict, or names a case the plan lacks | major | . | test-data-hash-present | a plan-run’s data hash is unknown, or a report’s run carries none | major | . | test-sut-not-self-judged | any verdict’s reviewer is the system under test | critical | . | test-has-gherkin | a test no Gherkin Scenario names, a @test: tag naming no test, or a plan case whose .feature is missing or does not resolve (test-engineer) | major | . Each records n/a when there is nothing of its kind to judge — no plan, no plan-run, no report — and never a pass over nothing.

7774.title: Test-plan execution
7774.content: Process_TestPlanExecution · strict · 13 step(s) . Executing a test-plan/v1 against a system under test and taking the result to a certification decision: requested by (or for) the system, run by a tester, re-executed in sample by an untainted checker, decided by a certifier through the plan’s exit-criteria table, and signed through qa-report-signing.bpmn. You are in this process when somebody wants a system — a skill, an agent, a tool, a machine, an IG or a process — certified against a named plan. Executing a plan with no certification in view is still this process; it ends at undetermined or refused without anything being signed. The run, the report and the certification are three records, and they point backwards: the run at the plan, the report at the run, the certification at the report. The certification is a judgement and lives under the declared attestations graph, on main; the report is derived and lives on the qa-reports branch. i i i i i i i i i i i i i

7775.title: How it connects
7775.content: . | Called by: no call activity names this process | Calls: Close the bean, Open the bean, QA report signing | Presented on: no docs page section shows this diagram | Skill: test-plan-execution | Running instances: none running; 1 finished: crdm-detect-evaluation-r-3554a15543fc-54762ece6646 | .

7776.title: Lanes — who acts
7776.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | Requester / system under test | test-requester | The system under test, or whoever speaks for it, asking for certification against plan P at a named version. Its only task is the request, and that is the design rather than an omission: the system under test never writes a verdict about itself, so after this lane it is the SUBJECT of the process and never a performer in it. | . | Tester | tester | Runs the plan against the system: resolves it, binds its fixed or generated test data, executes every case or skips it with a reason, and writes the folio-test-run/v1 and the test-report/v1. Untainted from the system under test — never the same actor — and it does not certify: what it writes is what the certifier decides on. | . | Untainted checker | untainted-checker | A second party re-executing a sample of the cases from the plan and the data alone, never from the tester’s verdicts. It rules on nothing: whether it agrees is a fact the certification table reads. One party doing both halves is not this check — it would compare a run with its own paraphrase of itself. | . | Certifier | certifier | The accountable party for the decision, a specialisation of the stakeholder. The gateway is computed from the plan’s exit-criteria table; what the certifier adds, and what makes it a judgement, is recording the decision under their name. Never the tester and never the system under test. | . | Attestation service | attestation-service | Signs the certification and files it. Reached only from certified: a refusal and an undetermined result are recorded by the certifier and signed by nobody. The signature itself is qa-report-signing.bpmn, called unchanged, whose own gateway chooses the API or a human release authority by the signer’s reach. | .

7777.title: Steps
7777.content: Every one of the 13 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Request certification of the system against plan PA_Request | Requester / system under test | test-plan-execution | Name the plan by id AND version, and the system under test by actor id. The actor must carry the systemUnderTest facet: an actor that has not said it can be tested is not run against a plan by default. The bean this instance tracks is claimed here. | . | Resolve the planA_ResolvePlan | Tester | test-plan-execution | The plan parses, names at least one req: requirement, its exitCriteria resolves to a decision in a .dmn that exists, and its scope.kind is the system’s facet kind. A plan that does not resolve is not run — test-plan-resolves audits the same join afterwards. Reads a test-plan/v1. | . | Bind the test dataA_BindData | Tester | test-plan-execution | Per bean vm6m: a fixed set is a committed path and counts as evidence only once reviewed; a generated set is template + params + seed and is never materialised. 7780.title: Theme art intake
7780.content: Skill theme-art-intake: Accept or refuse a set of three theme/avatar layouts arriving through document ingestion, with a named reason for every refusal. Named by: Content acquisition, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — ingest a theme, Theme and UI review — at ingestion, Public comment on a review draft, L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, Publish extracted statements with source links . Art arrives — three crops for a theme or an avatar — and the answer is either accepted, with the declaration written, or refused, with what to fix.

7781.title: This is a step in document ingestion, not a process beside it
7781.content: Document ingestion already answers the question art arrival poses — something unstructured has arrived; is it acceptable, and if not, why not — with a pipeline and a completeness gate. Theme art is the same event with a different payload, so what exists is a check keyed on the payload, not a second pipeline: a parallel “avatar ingestion” would be a second answer to one question, free to disagree with the first. |   | where | . | the check | schemas/library/theme-art-intake.ts — pure, no I/O, no clock | . | the CLI face | scripts/check-theme-art.ts, bun run cat check:theme-art | . | the arrival | uploads/, per content-acquisition and document-intake | .

7782.title: The constraints
7782.content: Each constraint answers a failure that has happened. Do not add one that has not: a rule with no failure behind it is one whose next maintainer cannot tell whether it still matters. | constraint | verdict | why | . | all three layouts | refuse | resolveThemeBackdrop refuses an incomplete backdrop wholesale, so a theme missing one crop renders with no art — not two thirds of it. | . | distinct content | refuse | two byte-identical files for two named layouts or avatars means one is missing. | . | orientation per layout | refuse | a portrait crop is not a landscape crop scaled down. The quiet area the sticky’s text sits in moves. | . | a declared destination | refuse | art outside a declared directory (at the repository root, say) is seen by no gate: check-declared-assets walks declared→disk. | . | dimensions measured | structural | intake takes bytes and emits the declaration, so there is nowhere for a retyped (or copied) number to enter. | . | weight and format | report | heavy PNGs still render, so refusing them would block work over a bandwidth judgement. | .

7783.title: Refuse, report, or neither
7783.content: . | Refuse when the art cannot do its job, or when intake cannot tell which of two readings is intended. A missing crop and two identical files are both “somebody has to decide something”. | Report when the art works but costs. Weight and format are the cases: a 1.6 MB PNG renders correctly. | Neither — say nothing — for anything intake did not actually measure. | . remedy is a required field on every failure: a refusal that says invalid teaches nobody what to fix. All failures are collected rather than thrown one at a time, because art arrives as a batch, and reporting the first problem of three means three round trips to learn three things.

7784.title: Do not repair somebody’s art
7784.content: deletion-requires-confirmation applies, and so does its spirit. When intake refuses, the outputs are the report and a work-plan item — not a re-crop, not a converted file, and not a quietly removed declaration. What looks like a missing crop may be a duplicate that was uploaded by mistake, and that is a question for the person who has the original. check:theme-art:check runs in CI, so a refusal of declared art is a regression.

7785.title: Reading the report
7785.content: ✓ landing-engineer: 3 layouts accepted · laptop 1672×941 docs/assets/img/harness/landing-engineer-laptop.png ! [heavy] laptop: … is 1560 KB, over the 391 KB budget → convert to webp — the measured gap on this art was about 16× ✗ landing-architecture: refused, 1 problem(s) · [missing-layout] mobile: no file offered for the mobile layout → supply all three layouts … . Three rules for reading it, the same three ci-health states: . | declared-but-absent is not a refusal and not a pass. The declaration names a file that is not on disk. It is reported on its own line because “the file is not there” and “the file is the wrong shape” are different facts, and a reader who cannot tell them apart fixes the wrong one. | A check that fires on every subject is wrong. docs/ is not a declared directory, and should not be — a declared entry names a graph, and the site is the render target — so art under it is not undeclared-destination. When a new check’s first run lights up broadly, ask which of these are correct? before how do I fix the repository?, and test any exclusion in both directions: a test of the excluded case alone passes equally for a check that never fires. A check that fires on legitimate subjects gets switched off, and a switched-off check still reads as coverage. | Warnings do not accumulate into a refusal. Twelve heavy files are twelve reports, not a failure. | .

7786.title: Adding a constraint
7786.content: . | Name the failure it answers. No failure, no constraint. | Decide refuse vs report by the line above — can the art do its job? | Write the remedy before the detection. If you cannot say what to do about it, the check is not ready. | Prove it fires, with a test that fails when the check is removed. | Check it against art already shipped. The aspect bands are deliberately wide because the shipped laptop crops run 1.50–1.78; a tighter band would refuse work that is fine. | . The stages of theming, and which owns which question, are in theming.

7789.title: At ingestion, and only at ingestion
7789.content: Skill theme-ui-review: Review graphical assets AS THEY ARE INGESTED, in the context of the website or app design they are for — accessibility, branding, languages — to determine what the assets and the UI will be. At ingestion only; called from ingest-theme. Measures rather than asserts, and raises findings rather than fixing them. Named by: Content acquisition, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — ingest a theme, Theme and UI review — at ingestion, Public comment on a review draft, L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, Publish extracted statements with source links . This skill runs in exactly one place: theme-ui-review.bpmn, called from ingest-theme.bpmn Task_Review, whose agent lane is ingestion-agent. It is not part of a post-MVP SDLC step and is not called from crdm-deliver.bpmn.

7790.title: What it reviews
7790.content: It looks at the arriving graphical assets laid out in the design they are for, so a finding is a decision about what the assets will be, taken while it is still cheap. The questions: accessibility measured rather than asserted, branding against the layer’s own declaration, and every declared locale. Theme choice is an authoring judgement. There is no role-to-theme mapping (theme.ts records why), so nothing here checks a binding. What gets reviewed is the ingested art in its design context.

7791.title: What this gives up — accepted
7791.content: An ingestion review answers “what will this turn into?” only as far as the assets can be laid out in their design before the site exists — not how a crop reads in the finished page. That gap is accepted; do not add a post-MVP review call on your own initiative.

7792.title: A person is in the loop, inside ingestion
7792.content: R_Judge is a human step: a person looks at the assets laid out at a web and a mobile width, so ingesting a theme source is attended at that step. Ingesting anything else stays unattended — Gateway_ThemeSource in document-ingestion.bpmn routes non-theme documents past ingest-theme.bpmn entirely.

7793.title: Measure; do not assert
7793.content: Contrast is computed, against the real ground. A theme with a backdrop has no single ratio — ink over a photograph varies pixel to pixel — so the number that matters is the worst case the art can present. Every shipped scrim in this repository is measured over pure black for that reason, and the check is written so it can fail: without a case that fails at a thin scrim, passing assertions prove nothing about the value. Colour is never the sole carrier (SC 1.4.1). Where it carries meaning, look for the second channel — the priority stripe is a width as well as a hue precisely so a monochrome reader still sees it. An automated pass is necessary and not sufficient: . | axe accepts a non-empty placeholder as an accessible name, so a label removed from the accessibility tree can pass the automated check. | A CSS selector that matches nothing raises no error in any tool, and can leave a backdrop at its intrinsic size across the viewport with every gate green. | . So a person looks at the assets laid out in their design (R_Judge). That is a step in the diagram, not an optional extra, because no automated check catches either case above.

7794.title: Branding is a question about the LAYER, not about taste
7794.content: Marks, palettes and art are checked against the layer’s own declaration rather than a remembered style. The sharpest form of the question comes from downstream: would a folio depending on this platform inherit something it did not choose? landing.html states it as a rule — “a downstream folio should not inherit a grumpy cat it did not choose” — and it is why a theme names an image role rather than a path.

7795.title: Languages: new UI is where untranslated strings enter
7795.content: Check that every user-facing string reaches the .pot, that each declared locale renders without clipping, and that right-to-left is laid out rather than mirrored by accident. The distinction worth keeping: a name is translatable and a value is not. A theme’s display name goes through the pipeline; its palette does not, because a colour is not language-dependent and translating one invites a locale to diverge on a value the CSS must agree on.

7796.title: Raise findings; do not fix them
7796.content: A finding goes back to whoever authored the choice, because the choice was theirs. There is no mapping to correct instead, and a reviewer who quietly re-themes a note has substituted their judgement for the author’s without saying so — which is the same objection decision-audit makes to editing a finding rather than overruling it with a note. The one exception is the one this repository already allows everywhere: a defect that is not a judgement call at all — a selector matching nothing, a string missing from the .pot, a contrast ratio below the floor — is a bug, and bugs get fixed.

7797.title: What this does NOT cover
7797.content: Not the choice itself. Whether a sticky should be engineer or library is an authoring decision, and this review does not second-guess it; it asks whether what was ingested will render legibly, consistently and in every declared language in the design it is for.

7798.title: Both viewports, always
7798.content: . | Every surface is inventoried and judged at a web width and at a mobile width. | A review done at one width is incomplete, not passed. | The surface’s wireframe, in wireframe-design-review, states what each layout was meant to be, so the review compares the build against an intent rather than against memory. | .

7807.title: Installing beans (fresh sandbox / cloud container)
7807.content: beans is the hmans/beans Go binary — a flat-file issue tracker storing issues as markdown under beans/. Cloud sandboxes do not ship it, so reinstall on demand (Go ships in the sandbox): . cat-harness-tools/scripts/install-beans.sh # idempotent; installs into a PATH dir # equivalently, the one-liner it runs: GOBIN="$HOME/.local/bin" go install github.com/hmans/beans@latest . Note: the npm package named beans is an unrelated abandoned tool — do not npm install beans. Verify with beans list && beans check.

7808.title: What the session-start sweep emits, and why in that order
7808.content: A session-start hook runs the sweep where a hook runs at all. It installs the CLI when it is genuinely missing — bounded and quiet, falling through to the degraded reader rather than failing the hook — and prepends the install directory when the binary is already there, so a second session does not reinstall. If the sweep still reports the CLI missing, it could not be installed there. The sweep installs rather than recommends, because an instruction somebody has to act on is weaker than the act itself. The order is not arbitrary: . | Interaction preferences — first, because they change the form of every question that follows. A question asked before them may have to be asked again. | Work-plan priming and the open list. | The roadmap. A flat list of a hundred ids in creation order is data, not a plan; the milestone/epic structure is what lets an end-of-turn report say what is next and why. | The commands the person can run themselves, the interactive browser first. An agent cannot drive a TUI on somebody’s behalf, so the only useful thing to do with one is print it where they will see it — with a copy-pasteable line whose path and branch are computed, never written in. | Default-branch delta, sibling branch activity, CI health. | . Heavy triage of new commits belongs in a background subagent, not the foreground. The sweep’s job is to tell you what changed, not to spend your first minutes reading it.

7809.title: Core Directives for Sessions
7809.content: . | A session is a LOG, never an epic or a milestone. Do not create a Session: … work item. What one sitting did is recorded in two places that already exist and are already read: the PR body (## Intent / ## Session results, session-intent) and a work item note on each work item you worked — bun run cat beans:note <id> --title "…", written to the declared notes directory of beans/beans.json and keyed by branch, so it is one file per session per work item by construction (bean-coordination §”Adding to a bean”). See §”A session is a log, not a parent” below for why. | Every todo is a work item, parented by SUBJECT. Each task, probe or action item is a work item (--type task) under the epic whose subject it is — §”WHICH parent” — not under anything representing the session. beans create "<Task Title>" --type task --parent <subject-epic-id> | No manual .md checklists: Never use session-beans.md or raw Markdown - [ ] checklists to track global tasks. Always use the beans CLI to prevent namespace pollution and maintain the official project tracking. | Check before you create: beans create is not idempotent. Run the existence check below before every beans create — no exceptions. | Brief before you work: claiming a work item records which item is taken; the opening brief records what it is taken for. Write it before the first tool call, in the chat. See §”Opening brief” below. | Write work items to the work-plan store, never into a code PR: create, claim, note and status changes go to the store through its Tool. The store’s operations are in work-plan-store; how the Tool in use performs them (today the git state branch, work-plan-store-git-branch) is on that Tool’s page. Do not commit work item files to code PR branches on main. | .

7810.title: Where beans live
7810.content: The work plan is a data store with a contract, work-plan-store, and this skill uses it only through that contract’s operations (get, list, create, update, note, history, positions). Which Tool backs it is the deployment’s choice Today every checkout uses the git state branch; how to mount it, which commands perform each operation and how changes are pushed are on its page, work-plan-store-git-branch. | Never bundle work items in code PR commits. Code PRs touch code and documentation; work item changes go to the store, which keeps the work plan current for every session without merge conflicts or spurious CI runs. | .

7811.title: Check before you create — beans create is not idempotent (STRICT)
7811.content: beans create mints a fresh random ID on every call and dedupes on nothing. Re-running a work-plan step is therefore not a no-op — it creates a second work item. Before every beans create, check whether the work item exists: . T="Prove Foo.bar" beans list --json --search "title:\"$T\"" | python3 -c ' import json, sys t = sys.argv[1] m = [b for b in json.load(sys.stdin) if b["title"] == t] print(f"{len(m)} exact match(es)") [print(" ", b["id"], b["status"]) for b in m]' "$T" . | ≥ 1 match → do not create. Claim the existing work item instead, with bun run cat beans:claim <id> — which reads the shared store first, refuses a work item a sibling holds or one already closed, and records a holder note so the next session’s check can see you. Not beans update <id> --status in-progress. It writes no holder note, so the claim is invisible to beans:claim’s own already-claimed check. Read the outcome — three of them are refusals, and held-unknown means it could not tell a live sibling from an abandoned claim: bean-coordination.md §”bun run cat beans:claim <id> — how it behaves”. | 0 matches → run the semantic check before creating: . bun run cat lsi:near "$T" # add --body "<first paragraph>" when you have one . The exact-title check above catches the same WORDS; this catches the same work in other words. It folds the title into an LSI index of every work item (all statuses — a completed one is often the answer) and prints the nearest five plus the closest epic. Read every hit marked ← (cosine ≥ 0.7) before creating. If one is the same work, claim or reopen it rather than create; if it is related, create and say so in the body. The score proposes; whether a hit IS the same work is your call (method lsi, refusal 3). | A work item ABOUT ONE OBJECT is keyed on the object, not the title. When the work targets a single named thing (a Lean declaration, a block label, a file), titles drift: “Prove Foo.bar”, “PROVE(lean): Foo.bar”, “close sorry in Foo.bar”. Neither check above is guaranteed to pair them, and generator re-runs are the usual source of such duplicates. So write the key into the work item as a line of its own, Target: lean:Foo.bar (or block:<label>, file:<path>), and before creating search the WHOLE store for that line, archive included, because a completed work item is often the answer: . grep -rlF "Target: lean:Foo.bar" beans/defs/ # the archive is beans/defs/archive/ . A hit is the same work: claim it, reopen it with a note, or link to it. A generator that files work items MUST write the key and run this check, since a re-run is exactly the case the title checks miss. | Still new → beans create "$T" --type task, under the epic lsi:near printed if it fits (§”WHICH parent — the criterion nobody wrote down” below). | . --search is a fuzzy Bleve query, so the exact-title comparison inside the pipe is load-bearing — do not drop it and trust --search alone. Why this is STRICT. Because create is unconditional, an agent that re-runs a work-plan step in a loop mints thousands of duplicates: the sweep and the backlog then read mostly noise, duplicates can collide with real work item ids, and corpus searches over beans/ are inflated. An unguarded create is what the rule prevents. It is platform-level so every folio inherits it.

7812.title: Check before you UPDATE — --body-file REPLACES the body (STRICT)
7812.content: beans create is not idempotent; beans update is not additive. They are different failures and both cost a durable artefact, so they sit together. A work item’s body is an append-only record of who found what, when. Every note in it is dated and signed, and later notes cite earlier ones. Replace the body and you have deleted findings that other work items, commits and issues point at. beans update offers four ways to write one, and only one of them appends: . | flag | what it does | . | --body-append <text> | --body-append - | appends. - reads stdin | . | --body-file <path> | REPLACES the whole body with the file | . | --body <text> | --body - | REPLACES | . | --body-replace-old/-new | replaces one substring; leaves the rest | . --body-file replaces with exit 0, no warning, no diff, no prompt: nothing in the output distinguishes it from an append. For a long, multi-paragraph note, use --body-append -: . beans update <id> --status completed --body-append - <<'NOTE' _2026-09-22T06:51:22Z_ — what you found, and how you know it. NOTE . Do not reach for --body-file because the note is long. (beans create rejects --body-file - with a heredoc, so the two subcommands also disagree about that flag.) . The timestamp prefix is an authored convention, not a CLI feature — no flag adds it. Write it yourself or the note joins the previous paragraph undated. Recovery, if it has already happened. The store is committed, which is the whole reason this is survivable: git show HEAD:<bean-file> returns the body as of the last commit, and the lost notes can be reassembled with the new front matter. Recover from git, not from your own scrollback — a transcript is a copy you made, and the repository is the artefact. Then say plainly what was lost and restored; a silent repair leaves the next reader unable to tell a reconstruction from an original.

7813.title: WHICH parent — the criterion nobody wrote down
7813.content: A work item’s parent is the epic whose SUBJECT it is, not the epic you happen to be working in. Nothing catches a wrong parent. check-bean-parents tests exactly two things: that an open work item HAS a parent, and that the parent NAMES A WORK ITEM THAT EXISTS. A work item filed under the wrong epic satisfies both, so it is textually clean, the guard is green, and it is only findable by a person reading the roadmap. The check cannot distinguish a right parent from a wrong one, so the criterion has to live here or nowhere. How to choose . | beans list and read the EPICS first — there are many, each with a thematic scope in its title. Do this BEFORE beans create, at the same time as §”Check before you create”; both are questions about where a work item belongs, and both are cheaper before the file exists. | Ask what the work item is ABOUT, not what you were doing when you wrote it. A visualiser whose blocker is an unrecorded ingest relation is an ingest work item. A sticky’s art is a rendering work item. The topic that makes the work hard is usually the right epic. | When two epics both fit, pick the one whose OTHER children you would want read alongside it, and say in the body why the other was not chosen — a parent is a claim about where somebody should go looking. | . A session is a log, not a parent . Do not create a Session: … epic or milestone. It turns the roadmap’s top level into a diary, and: . | An epic is a claim about where to look for a SUBJECT. A session epic points at one sitting, which ended; nobody looks there for the work, so its children are lost to the next agent filing by subject. | It defeats the guards. check-bean-parents passes a task parented to a session epic, because the parent exists and is an epic. The wrong parent is textually clean. | Its status lies. A session epic stays in-progress after its session ends, so it is a stale claim from birth, and the quiet-claim findings fill with logs. | . Where the log goes instead — each already declared, already read: . | what the session wants to keep | where | . | what it intended and what it got done | the PR body, ## Intent / ## Session results (session-intent) | . | what it found about a work item | a note: bun run cat beans:note <id> → beans/notes/<bean>--<date>--<branch>.md | . | a survey of a commit window it read | beans/surveys/ (session-survey) — only if it surveyed one | . | a handover to whoever comes next | a note on the work item being handed over, plus handover-report | . A handover is the same case. A Handoff: … or Handover: … work item typed epic or milestone is a session log with a different title. bun run cat health reports it — the bean-store check’s bean-session-log-roots finding names every OPEN work item whose title starts Session, Handoff or Handover and whose type is epic or milestone. Report-only: the remedy is a person’s (or a reviewed work-plan-restructure plan’s) — re-parent the children by subject, move the narrative into a note, then set the log to completed or scrapped with a pointer. Never beans delete it: other work items, commits and PRs cite its id.

7814.title: A GOAL is a milestone bean, and an epic joins one by parenting to it
7814.content: A “goal-scoped” queue needs the goal to exist as an object, or every review re-derives the classification from scratch. A goal is a milestone work item, in the owner’s own words, and the epics serving it are parented to it. beans create "<the goal, verbatim>" --type milestone # after the existence check above beans update <epic-id> --parent <milestone-id> . Three properties make this the cheap answer rather than a new mechanism: . | The type exists and check-bean-parents permits an epic under a milestone. | beans roadmap groups by parent:, so the goals become the roadmap’s top level the moment the epics are parented — which is what a roadmap was always for. | “Prioritise against the goals” becomes a query: walk down from the milestone. An item under no goal is then visible as such, which is itself the finding a review wants. | . Verbatim, and this is not a style note. A goal is the owner’s sentence, and a tidied paraphrase is a different claim that nobody agreed to — the same rule confirmation-waiver applies to a waiver’s quote, and for the same reason: the reader auditing the classification has only that string to check it against. If you do not have the owner’s words, you do not have the goal — record the paraphrase as a paraphrase, say so, and ask. This does not conflict with filing by subject (§”WHICH parent”). A milestone sits ABOVE the epics; a work item is still parented to the epic whose subject it is, and the epic is parented to the goal it serves. Two levels, one criterion at each.

7815.title: A WORK PLAN is an epic or milestone that names the process it runs
7815.content: Owner, 2026-11-05: “At the beginning of a large process (like creating a new collaborative document, or adding software features,) there should / may be a work plan. Not every process needs a work plan. Docs/proposals/ once approved become workplans”, and on the card, “Epic is the plan”. So a work plan is not a new kind of file. It is the epic (or milestone) that already groups the work, with two tags saying what it runs and where it came from: . beans update <epic-id> --tag process:<bpmn:process id> # what it instantiates; repeat for several beans update <epic-id> --tag proposal:<repo-relative path> # the approved proposal it was made from beans list --tag process:<bpmn:process id> # every plan that runs that process . | Tags, not front-matter fields. The beans CLI drops every front-matter key it does not know on its next write (measured 2026-11-05), and keeps tags. | A process: tag is what makes it a plan. A proposal: tag alone does not: a proposal with no process to run is not a plan yet. A plan filed as a feature or a story is reported, not refused (the work-plan schema in the tools layer reports it). | Start the process under the plan: workflow_start with plan: <epic-id> (bun run cat workflow:start <process> <subject> --plan <epic-id>). The instance names its plan, as it names its work item; the plan does not list its instances, because where the work is lives in the instances. | Not every process needs one. A small process tracked by one work item runs with no plan, exactly as before. | The work items under the plan are its work: parented to the epic, as always. A work item is a memory record with more structure; a work plan is a work item that says which process it runs. | . The work-plan page marks each plan in its tree with its process, its proposal and how many instances are running under it. Approving a proposal seeds its plan . When the owner approves a proposal (owner, 2026-11-05, card “Proposal seeds plan”), one command writes both ends, so neither is kept by hand: . bun run cat proposal:approve <path/to/proposal.md> --process <bpmn:process id> [--process …] \ [--plan <epic or milestone id>] [--parent <goal id>] [--dry-run] . | With no --plan it creates an epic titled as the proposal. With --plan it tags that epic or milestone instead; a feature or a story is refused. | The plan gets the process: and proposal: tags. The proposal’s front matter gets status: approved, approvedOn: <date> and plan: <id>. | At least one --process is required, unless --plan already names one: a plan is defined by what it runs. | Approve only on the owner’s word. The command records an approval; it does not decide one. Run it with --dry-run first and show the owner what it will write. | bun run cat proposal:approve --check <proposals dir> checks the two ends against each other and reports rather than fails: an approved proposal with no plan, a plan id that is no work item, a plan that names no process, or a plan whose proposal: tag names another file. | .

7816.title: After you create — parent it, and re-run the guard before you push
7816.content: check-bean-parents fails on an open work item with no parent, because such a work item lands in the roadmap’s Miscellaneous section where nobody looks for it. Two ways past it: . | A multi-flag beans update can apply only some of its flags and still report success (-s in-progress --parent <epic> can set the status and leave the parent unset). After setting several properties at once, read the front matter back — grep -n "^status:\|^parent:\|^priority:" beans/defs/<file>.md — rather than trusting the “Updated …” line. | A work item created after your last test run is an unguarded work item. | . So: beans create and the --parent that follows it are one action, and touching the work item store invalidates your last test run. Re-run at least bun test cat-harness-tools/scripts/tests/check-bean-parents.test.ts before pushing. A green suite is green for the tree you ran it against. A new bean also owes readme:subgraphs — and this is the most-missed step . beans/README.md is GENERATED and carries per-subdirectory counts, so creating or archiving a work item makes it stale. Nothing in the beans CLI regenerates it, and the gate that catches it is named for the generic case rather than for work items: . Repository gates (hard) · step 65: "Every declared directory's README is current" . That is readme:subgraphs:check. Run its writer before you push: . bun run cat readme:subgraphs # updates beans/README.md; push state via the store Tool bun run cat readme:subgraphs:check # must exit 0 bun run cat state:push # when the store Tool is git-branch (work-plan-store-git-branch.md) . The check’s name gives no hint that adding a work item dirtied it, so a session that reads only the name looks at directories and never at the work item it just created. Read the failing STEP, and remember that beans/ is a declared directory like any other. The same shape applies one door along: editing a skill owes bun run cat skill:register, which skill-registration carries in full. Both are instances of one rule — a declared artefact has generated neighbours, and the CLI that writes the artefact does not write them.

7817.title: When the beans CLI is not there — you are still not read-only
7817.content: scripts/beans-fallback.ts writes the same store in the same layout: same files, same front matter, same id shape, read from .beans.yml. The CLI reads everything it writes once installed. There is no import step and no second store. bun run cat beans:fallback list --status todo bun run cat beans:fallback show <id> bun run cat beans:fallback claim <id> bun run cat beans:fallback create "<title>" --status in-progress bun run cat beans:fallback note <id> "<what you found>" . A read-only fallback would let a session see its plan but not claim it, so it would do its work unclaimed. Its create refuses an exact duplicate title and names the work item to claim instead; the CLI’s create does not. --force exists for a genuinely intended duplicate and has to be typed.

7818.title: Check before you WORK — a checkbox is a claim, not a measurement (STRICT)
7818.content: beans create is not idempotent, and §”Check before you create” above is the guard. This is its twin at the other end: a work item’s stated state is a claim somebody wrote down once, and the code has moved since. Re-measure a work item’s open items against the code before you act on them. The cost of skipping this is not wasted effort; it is acting on a stale claim. The two failures this prevents, and they are different . 1. Doing work that exists. Siblings finish items without ticking the box. 2. Undoing a decision that was recorded elsewhere. An open item can read like a gap when the absence is deliberate and explained in a comment in the file the work item is about. Doing the obvious thing then re-introduces the defect the decision avoids. The decision is in the file, not the work item. What “re-measure” means, concretely . | Run the thing — the audit or check that measures the item. | Read the body, not just the boxes. | Date it. git log -S on the symbol or the file against the work item’s created_at separates fixed since from wrong when written. | Read the file the work item is about, for a comment saying why it is the way it is. That is where a deliberate absence lives. | . And a bean you re-measure, you record . Leave what you found in the work item, with the commits and the times — a stale checkbox you silently worked around is one the next agent meets unchanged. Tick what is done and name who did it; withdraw a done-when you no longer believe, with reasons, rather than leaving it unmet. Where the work item and the code disagree, the code is what is true and the work item is what is wrong — the same rule AGENTS.md states for a skill against that file. This is the work-plan half. The cross-session half is bean-coordination §”Claims are global via the branch store”.

7819.title: Working with Beans
7819.content: 1. Finding Tasks & Graph Analytics (beans:query / bean_query) Use beans list for simple listing, or bun run beans:query (and the bean_query MCP tool) for fast in-memory SPARQL 1.1 analytics over the work item store (loads ~1,000 work items into an Oxigraph store in ~70 ms): . | bun run beans:query --named safe_drain_candidates: leaves with >= 2 open siblings under their parent container (safe against check:bean-rollup) | bun run beans:query --named actionable_leaves: open/todo leaf work items with zero open blockers, ready for an agent to claim immediately | bun run beans:query --named critical_path_blockers: blockers ranked by how many open work items they directly hold up | bun run beans:query --named epic_burndown: per-epic child status breakdown (total, open, completed, scrapped, and completion percentage) | bun run beans:query --named rollup_invariant_violations: completed containers with open children, or in-progress containers with 0 open children | bun run beans:query --named stale_claims: in-progress work items whose updated_at timestamp is older than 7 days | bun run beans:query --named unparented_open_tasks: open non-epic work items that have no epic or milestone parent | bun run beans:query --named circular_blockers: circular blocking deadlocks | bun run beans:query --named high_fanout_epics: epics with high fanout (>= 15 direct children) that may need decomposition | Arbitrary SPARQL: bun run beans:query --sparql "SELECT ?id ?title WHERE { ?b bean:id ?id ; bean:title ?title }" | Export RDF graph: bun run beans:query --export-nq beans.nq | . 2. Setting Dependencies You can map out sequence blockers using: beans update <id> --blocked-by <blocker-id> beans update <id> --blocking <blocked-id> . 3. Updating Status & Adding Comments . | When starting work: bun run cat beans:claim <id> — a claim goes through the claim tool, never through beans update, so it is visible to the next session’s check | When completed: beans update <id> --status completed | To add notes or discussion: beans update <id> --body-append "Your note", or --body-append - with a heredoc when it runs to paragraphs. Never --body-file — it replaces the whole body, silently, exit 0: §”Check before you UPDATE”. | . 4. A work item that delivers a requirement copies its success criteria When a work item is part of a work plan — it delivers one or more req: statements (or a plan’s REQ-### / FR-###) — it names them in its body and its ## Done when is copied from their success criteria, one checkbox per criterion, with the criterion’s key. Closing the work item is then judging those criteria. The work item ids are also listed in the requirement set’s workPlan — a set at planned with none is refused by check:requirements. The rule and an example are in the content layer’s requirement-definition skill (skill_fetch requirement-definition) §”The work plan is beans”.

7820.title: Archiving — two dispositions, and they answer different questions
7820.content: beans archive moves every completed or scrapped work item out of the working set. It moves, never deletes: an archived work item is still resolvable by id, which is what makes it a disposal an agent may perform at all (deletion-requires-confirmation). There are two ways it can be driven, they are not alternatives, and a process author needs to know which one they are reaching for. |   | a per-activity op | a periodic sweep | . | what it is | a step inside one process — a fourth <cat-harness.processes:bean op> beside claim, note, resolve | a scheduled run over the whole store | . | the question it answers | is this item’s work over? | is the store still readable? | . | what decides | the process reaching a step that means completion | a uniform, process-independent criterion — completed or scrapped | . | what the archive then records | why — “archived because the release shipped” | when — “archived in the sweep of that date” | . | what it cannot do | reach a work item no process resolved | know that this release is what terminated this item | . Why neither replaces the other . The op cannot cover the store. A work item resolved by a process with no archive step, by hand, or by a sibling session, is never reached; coverage would depend on every path having been drawn, and paths are added faster than they are wired. The sweep cannot carry authority. It knows only status. It cannot say that a requirement was archived because the stakeholder signed off, which is the fact an audit of the CRDM close would want — and crdm-close.bpmn is precisely where that authority exists. So the honest shape is: the sweep is the floor, the op is the exception. The sweep guarantees the store stays readable whatever anyone forgot; an op is worth adding only where a process’s completion is itself the reason, and recording that reason is worth the extra edge on the diagram. Where this sits against resolve — two layers, not two spellings . resolve is the process saying “I am done with this item.” Archiving is the store saying “this is no longer in the working set.” They are different layers and they are allowed to be far apart in time — which is why resolve must never imply an archive, and why the sweep is still needed. The per-activity op: a step carrying <cat-harness.processes:bean op="archive"/> moves the instance’s work item into beans/defs/archive/, with a line saying which process closed it. It does so only once the process has finished and the work item is completed or scrapped; otherwise it leaves the work item in place with a note saying why, because check:bean-archive allows only terminal work items in the archive. Where the bean ops live — OPEN and CLOSE, called by every process . The claim, resolve and archive ops live in two called processes, and nowhere else, so no process can open a work item it never closes: . |   | process | what it does | ops it carries | . | OPEN | Process_BeanOpen (sdlc/processes/bean-open.bpmn) | check before you create, create, whose work item, claim — or leave it alone | claim | . | CLOSE | Process_BeanClose (sdlc/processes/bean-close.bpmn) | outcome: complete, or scrap with reasons, then one shared archive step; or record the blocker and hand back | resolve, archive (and a note for the blocker) | . Process_BeanLifecycle is OPEN → work → CLOSE, calling both. Process_BeanDrain (sdlc/processes/bean-drain.bpmn) is the same over a queue: build the queue grouped by owner, then for each work item OPEN → work → CLOSE, and refill when a drainer’s list runs dry. A work item OPEN finds is someone else’s is marked skip on the queue, not worked. How a process uses them. Call Process_BeanOpen where the work item becomes the process’s own — usually its first step — and follow it with a gateway (claimed / not yours): the engine hands a called process the caller’s work item but not its end event, so the caller reads which end OPEN reached, and not yours stops at an end of its own without touching the work item. Call Process_BeanClose straight before each end the process reaches after OPEN. Straight before matters: resolve counts the process as finished when nothing but archive steps is left (onlyArchiveLeft), and a CLOSE followed by more work turns its resolve into a note. note ops stay where the work happens. A called phase does not open or close again. A process only ever called by another (the CRDM phases under crdm-requirements.bpmn) runs on its caller’s work item, so the caller opens and closes it. A process that is both run on its own and called (code-change-review, upstream-version-adoption, editing-hci-validation) keeps its own pair: nested, OPEN’s claim is idempotent and CLOSE notes instead of closing while the outer process still has work. The check. check:bean-calls (also run inside check:workflow-refs, which CI gates) fails on a claim, resolve or archive op outside OPEN and CLOSE, on a process that calls one of them without the other, and on an entry process that names a work item by ref without calling both. A process whose only marks are note (or a bare <cat-harness.processes:bean/>) and that nothing calls is reported, not failed: it writes on whatever work item its instance was started with and never decides that work item’s fate. The sweep is still beans archive, run deliberately — the floor under every process that never reached CLOSE. Note the CLI prints .beans/archive/ but honours path: from .beans.yml; here that means beans/defs/archive/.

7821.title: Status Display Format
7821.content: When the user asks “status” or “show beans”, run beans list and display the work items this session touched under their subject epics — the epic is the heading because it is where the work lives; the session is a filter, not a node: . ## Beans this session touched (branch <branch-name>) - [abcd] PROCESS: how an agent decides what it is doing (epic) - [task-124] Task A (completed) - [task-125] Task B (in-progress) - [efgh] QA: verdicts, sidecars and the audited review record (epic) - [task-126] Task C (todo) .

7822.title: Coordination discipline
7822.content: . | Claim before you work, with bun run cat beans:claim <id>, so sibling sessions working the same goal do not duplicate the effort. Also check the open PR list for the work item id and its subject before you start: a claim announces the item is taken, but a sibling may already have a PR. Full rule: bean-coordination.md §”Claims are global via the branch store”. Brief it in the same turn you claim it — opening-brief.md. The claim tells a sibling the item is taken; the brief tells them, and the author, what it is being taken for. | One source of truth per concern. Do not fork a work item into a parallel todos/*.json queue; link to the queue from the work item instead. | Move wiring and script together. When relocating a hook-backed script, move its hook reference in the same change — a script without its wiring, or a hook reference without its script, leaves a dangling reference. | Close on landing. When the work lands, close the tracking work item and update any cross-repo ownership note. | .

7823.title: Relationship to other surfaces
7823.content: . | bean-coordination.md — the cross-session claim and handoff lifecycle, and why a claim is not a lock. | bean-blocking.md — a real block carries what it waits on, since when, an expiry and a handoff. | scripts/session-start-coord-sweep.sh — the CLI-independent session-start surface: fetches origin/main and summarises sibling branch activity. Works even when the beans CLI is absent. | cat-harness-tools/scripts/install-beans.sh — provisions the CLI. | .

7824.title: todo-manager (skill)
7824.content: The skill todo-manager as its source file cat-harness/work-plan/skills/work-plan/todo-manager.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

7825.title: Todo Review Skill
7825.content: Skill todo-review: Monitor and triage open feedback across all content blocks. At session start, ask the author if they’d like to work on feedback. Provide overview, let them pick a chapter/section, then review and iterate until done. Named by: Adjudication, Wireframe design review, Public comment on a review draft . Disambiguation: . | todo-review (this file) = triage of content feedback stored under feedback/<paper>/ (paper-scope; persistent across sessions; surfaced via /todos dashboard). | todo-manager = the agent’s session work-plan via work items (durable, committed under beans/). | . Both can be active in one session: the agent’s work-plan (todo-manager) may include “process N feedback items via todo-review” as a single task.

7826.title: Where the feedback came FROM — this skill starts mid-air without it
7826.content: Materialized content (held by reference or materialized from elsewhere) is read-only; a reviewer cannot annotate it in place. The first step of review is copy-out-materialized (diagram: library/processes/copy-out-materialized.bpmn): the reviewer copies the materialized sub-graph into their own folio/, carrying provenance.local back to the original, annotates the copy, and those annotations arrive here. While triaging: . | Feedback is on the COPY, not on the original. Resolving an item edits the copy. The original still hashes to its recorded digest, and check:materialized-fixity fails if somebody annotated held content in place. | provenance.local makes a resolved item traceable to the thing it was about; without it the copy is indistinguishable from original work one rename later. | .

7827.title: Role
7827.content: Monitor open feedback across the manuscript. At session start, offer a structured todo workflow. Provide triage, context-aware selection, and a feedback cycle until the author is satisfied.

7828.title: When to Use This Skill
7828.content: . | Session start (automatic): ask if author wants to work on feedback | User asks: “show todos”, “what feedback is pending”, “review todos” | User asks: “what needs attention”, “any open items”, “work on todos” | After completing a block of work, to check if related items can be closed | .

7829.title: Feedback Storage
7829.content: Feedback lives in feedback/<paper-dir>/ (tracked in git, committed to main via worktree). Each content block with feedback has a TypeScript file: . feedback/ <paper-dir>/ <block-a>.ts <block-b>.ts ... Each file exports an array of FeedbackItem (extends TodoItem with author/authorEmail): . import type { FeedbackItem } from "../../schemas/types"; export default [ { "id": "todo-mn159z53", "summary": "short description of the issue", "comment": "longer description of the issue", "status": "open", "priority": "medium", "origin": "human", "assignee": "editor-agent", "createdAt": "2026-03-22T02:35:33.543Z" } ] satisfies FeedbackItem[]; .

7830.title: Session Start: Todo Workflow
7830.content: When the editor skill enters the session start protocol and open feedback exists, follow this flow: . Step 0 — Offer the todo workflow . Present a brief overview and ask: . You have N open feedback items (X critical, Y high, Z medium). Would you like to work on feedback today? . Options: . | Yes, let’s review feedback → proceed to Step 1 | No, I have something else in mind → exit to normal triage | . Step 1 — Overview and scope selection . Show a quick summary grouped by chapter: . ## Feedback Overview | Chapter | Open | Critical/High | Sample |---------|------|---------------|--------| Ch 1: Introduction | 12 | 3 | "this does not need to hold in general" | Ch 4: Methods | 4 | 1 | "missing cross-ref to prior section" | Ch 11: Results | 6 | 0 | "clarify the derivation" | . Then ask: . Where would you like to start? . Options (dynamically generated): . | High priority first — all critical + high items across paper | **Ch N: ** — one option per chapter that has feedback | Show all — flat list sorted by priority | . Step 2 — Present the selected feedback . Show the filtered items as a table: . ## Open Feedback — Ch 1 (12 items) | # | Priority | Block | Summary |---|----------|-------|---------| 1 | high | initial-conditions | this does not need to hold in general | 2 | high | main-point | need a supporting statement for the claim | 3 | medium | core-definition | clarify notation convention | ... | . Ask: Which item(s) would you like to address? (pick by number or “all”) . Step 3 — Review and address each item . For each selected feedback item: . | Show the feedback — full comment, author, date, priority | Read the block — load content/<paper>/<chapter>/<rootName>.md and .ts manifest for context | Propose a fix — suggest specific edits to the .md content | Ask for approval — show the proposed changes and ask: Does this address the feedback? (yes / revise / skip) . | Apply if approved — edit the file, mark todo as in_progress | Iterate if “revise” — ask what to change, re-propose | . Step 4 — After each item, offer next steps . After completing (or skipping) an item: . Done with “this does not need to hold in general”. What next? . Options (context-aware): . | Next item on this block (if more exist) | Next item in this section/chapter | Back to overview — re-show the chapter summary | Done for now — exit todo workflow | . Step 5 — Wrap up . When the author says “done” or all items in scope are addressed: . Session feedback summary: . | Reviewed: 5 items | Addressed: 3 (edits applied) | Skipped: 2 | Remaining open: 9 | . The addressed items are marked in_progress. You can resolve them from the viewer feedback panel when you’re satisfied with the changes.

7831.title: Resolving Feedback
7831.content: Only the human author may resolve or remove a FeedbackItem. Agents must never set status to resolved or wontfix, and must never delete items. Agents may set status to in_progress after making edits. Resolution happens in the viewer’s feedback panel (click the status badge on any feedback item).

7835.doc: Report a verdict on one tracking issue
7835.title: Report a verdict on one tracking issue
7835.content: Process_TrackedWatch · strict · 3 step(s) . Report a check’s verdict on one tracking issue: close the issue when the check found nothing, open or edit it when the check found something, and leave it untouched when the check could not tell. Every watch that keeps one tracking issue runs this, with its own label: ci-health-watch (ci-health), repository-health-watch (repo-health) and pr-checks-present (pr-no-checks). Before 2026-11-01 each of them drew these seven steps itself (shared block G2 of the BPMN guidance review, owner Q-BR-2 C). THE THIRD STATE IS THE WHOLE POINT, AND IT IS THE ONLY ONE THAT FAILS THE JOB. unknown runs exit 1; a finding does NOT. A repository in trouble leaves the watch GREEN and speaks through the tracking issue, while a sweep that could not look turns the job red. That inversion is deliberate and is invisible from the run list, which is the argument for drawing it. ONE TRACKING ISSUE, EDITED IN PLACE, never a comment and never a second issue: a feed nobody reads is the failure mode a watchdog invites. On unknown the issue is left UNTOUCHED: not closed, not opened, not edited. Closing it would assert the thing the sweep just failed to establish. Ensure the tracking label exists sits AFTER Could we tell? and before the split, because both issue paths need the label: the clean path filters on it too, and on a repository where nothing has ever gone wrong it would not otherwise exist. It is skipped on unknown, where neither path runs and a label hiccup must not be what fails the job. The verdict is the calling watch’s: its check writes a report file before any exit path, exit 0 is clean, 1 is a finding, 2 is could-not-check, and an exit 1 with no report file is a crash, read as could-not-check. Each watch’s own gateway documentation in its workflow says which step writes it. i i i
