7906.title: Untainted verification — the producer never writes the verdict
7906.content: Skill untainted-verification: The party that produced an artefact does not write the verdict on it. How a checker and an adjudicator are dispatched with controlled context, the three rules that make it a measurement rather than a ritual, and the third state that lets it gate at all. Named by: Translation review and adjudication, Translation round trip (untainted), Translation Workflow, Adjudication, Criterion adjudication, Wireframe design review, Test-plan execution, Is the incremental IG AST what a full build would have produced?, Incremental IG build, L3 FHIR IG pipeline, Make a decided public comment change, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate . Skill id: untainted-verification · Package: sdlc-core . A secret scan, a schema validation, a back-translation and a systematic literature search differ in what they read and in what counts as a finding. They do not differ in this: . The party that produced the artefact does not get to write the verdict on it, and the checking party is given a controlled context rather than the run of the repository. Everything below is that sentence made operational, for any domain, because taking the translation vocabulary out of it changes nothing structural; translation-manager.md §”The agentic round trip” is the translation instance.

7907.title: The parties
7907.content: | party | is given | produces | . | producer | the task | the artefact | . | checker | the artefact’s declared checker_sees, and nothing that would let it shortcut | an independent rendering or finding | . | adjudicator | adjudicator_sees and the checker’s output — never the artefact itself | pass / warn / fail, each drift named | .

7908.title: Three rules, and the failure each one stops
7908.content: 1. Neither party sees what would let it shortcut. A back-translator shown the English writes the English back and the check passes vacuously. An adjudicator shown the French can talk itself into any reading of the back-translation. Neither failure raises an error; both produce a green verdict that measured nothing, which is worse than a red one. 2. The checker uses no tools, and says so. The artefact is in the repository. A checker with filesystem access can find what it was not given, and the verdict then measures its search rather than the artefact. Ask for a TOOLS_USED line and record the answer — UntaintedParty.tools_used. Absent means nobody asked, which is not the same as “no”. 3. One party doing both halves is not this check. It compares a thing with its own paraphrase of itself.

7909.title: The context is declared, not composed
7909.content: UntaintedDispatch on the criterion (schemas/sdlc/block-qa.ts) declares checker_sees, checker_withheld, adjudicator_sees and drift. A caller names a subject and a criterion; it does not hand-assemble a brief. That is not ceremony — the party composing a brief by hand is the producer, and rule 1 then breaks silently, one call site at a time. A declaration is also checkable, and untaintedPartitionDefects checks it: . | defect | what it means | . | undeclared | no untainted block. Reported, never skipped: nobody said is not nothing to check | . | overlap | a role visible to both parties — one of them is grading its own input | . | unpartitioned | a companion in depends_on that is in neither visible set; usually a role added later. Nobody decided | . | phantom | a role named in the declaration that the criterion does not depend on — the declaration describes something else | . Totality is the point of checker_withheld. Without it a newly-added companion role defaults into the checker’s view, or out of it, and either way the separation moves without anybody choosing. With it, the partition simply stops being total, which has a name. drift must say both halves. Told only what to look for, an adjudicator returns a style review and everything fails. The translation round trip states it well: synonyms, articles and re-ordering are not drift; a claim added, dropped, weakened, strengthened or reversed is. The check verifies the string is non-empty and nothing more — “states what is not drift as well as what is” is a reading, and a gate pretending to measure it would be the exact defect this skill exists to stop.

7910.title: Three states, and the third is what lets it gate
7910.content: . | verified — the adjudicator ruled. Two entries, adjudicator first. | could not dispatch — no dispatch capability was available. One entry, result: "n/a", metrics.dispatch: "unavailable", and a required reason. The producer may write this one, and only this one. | not attempted — no entry at all. | . Without state 2 the discipline cannot gate anywhere: a producer forbidden from writing a verdict has nothing to write in an environment with no subagents, so the gate reads an absence it cannot tell from negligence. Recording it keeps “could not dispatch” distinguishable from “nobody tried”. It is never a pass. isVerified() is the predicate a gate asks, and it is false for state 2 and for state 3 alike. A consumer that reads n/a as “nothing to see” turns the honest gap straight back into the silent one.

7911.title: Recording
7911.content: Both parties are written as witnesses. The adjudicator leads — the first entry per criterion is the operative one everywhere in this repo. The checker sits behind it with result: "n/a" and its output in notes, because a reader asking on what basis? needs the intermediate and a reader asking who did this? needs both names. Record model with model_source, or not at all. A subagent’s serving model is not observable from the session that dispatched it: it inherits the parent unless the harness overrides, and the hand-back does not say which model served the turn. A bare model string is an inference printed as a fact. Absent both, a reader gets “not recorded”, which is true and acceptable. A sweep replaces only entries whose reviewer is itself. mergeUntainted carries everything else through, so an unrelated re-run never silently deletes another party’s verdict. A human ruling is never superseded here. A verdict is hashed to what it was about. Edit the subject and the verdict goes stale. This matters more for an agent ruling than a script one, because nobody can cheaply re-run it. Where the verdict is kept: the attestation store, not the derived file . Both entries are judgements — reviewer.kind is agent (or human) — so their durable home is the attestations graph, test/attestations/<family>/<mirrored subject path>.attestations.json (qa-attestations/v1), on main. The derived test/results/ file beside them is a working copy whose record lives on the qa-reports branch, and a regeneration cannot reproduce an agent ruling. recordUntainted writes the store first, through the same resolvePrior / finalizeCriteria API as every other attesting writer, and refreshes the derived report only if one already exists — it never invents one. So the verdict lands whether or not the derived file is on the branch, and the store file it returns is the one to commit. What puts a subject in scope is the subject existing (<subject>.md or .ts), not its derived report, which does not live beside it. A corrupt or unreadable store reads UNKNOWN and is refused, with nothing written, rather than overwritten.

7912.title: Why the instrument is the thing to watch
7912.content: A measurement whose author has to explain it away is about the instrument, not the subject — for example a failure count that is really a count of entries missing from the checker’s reference map. Remove such a measurement rather than publish it. translation-manager §”The instrument, not the translation” has the worked case.

7913.title: This is one rule with two homes
7913.content: It is not a platform invention. Guideline methodology separates the systematic review team from the guideline development group for the same reason, and the identical rule applies to evidence-based literature review for living guidelines. When adding a domain’s rules here, run them through domain-fencing (opt-in cat-harness.kg-ops)’s three questions first: a rule that fails all three is a folio’s rule, correctly located, and fencing it and saying so is the honest move.

It deliberately does not call a model: the payload is written by whatever ran the parties, so recording works the same for two subagents, two API calls, or two people. | .

7916.title: Upload naming — the name is normalised, not the link escaped
7916.content: Skill upload-naming: What an ingested file may be CALLED. Read before adding anything to an uploads or library graph, before writing a generator that links to one, and before “fixing” a broken link in a generated README. Covers which characters break what, why the name is normalised as well as the link escaped, how a sidecar stays paired with its source, and the one case the fixer refuses. Named by: Content acquisition, Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/, Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess, Refresh materialized remote content, Sample import into a structured data store, Subscribe to an external knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — ingest a theme, Theme and UI review — at ingestion, Public comment on a review draft, L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graph, Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assets, Ingestion subprocess — extract structure, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate, Publish extracted statements with source links . A file in an uploads or library graph is named by whoever uploaded it, and that name reaches a generated Markdown link. So the name is an interface, not a label. It is a library-core skill, beside uploads-watch and library-ingestion, because what an ingested file may be called is a question about acquiring and ingesting sources. bun run cat check:upload-names reports; check:upload-names:check gates; check:upload-names:fix renames with git mv.

7917.title: The rule
7917.content: A name may not contain any of . space , ( ) [ ] { } # ? & % ' " ` < > | . Everything else is left exactly as uploaded. The fixer replaces a run of those with a single -, trims, and preserves the extension and any sidecar suffix. A name with no unsafe character is returned untouched. Collapsing and trimming happen only to names that were going to change anyway; a double dash, a leading dash or a trailing dash is not this check’s business. Case is not a defect either: README.md stays README.md, because renaming it breaks every link to it and every generator that writes one. Rewriting a name that was already safe breaks whatever looks it up by that name, such as a generator that lists a section file. Both are pinned by tests.

7918.title: What each character breaks
7918.content: | character | what it breaks | . | space, (, ) | a Markdown link target ends at the first ) | . | [ ] | the label half of the link | . | < > \| | the angle-bracket link form, and tables | . | # ? | a fragment and a query to every URL parser | . | & % quotes backtick | escaping in a shell, an href, or both | . | , | nothing — included for the stub convention | .

7919.title: Why the NAME as well as the link
7919.content: uploads/X (2).pdf produces the link target X (2).pdf, which resolves to X (2. Two layers answer this, and neither subsumes the other: . | layer | reaches | fails when | . | linkTarget (in subgraph-readmes.ts) / decodeLinkTarget (in check-subgraphs.ts) | every generated README link, in every graph typology, including directory names | never — it percent-encodes every segment of what the generator writes (parentheses included, because an unbalanced one ends a CommonMark destination as surely as a space), and the check decodes before asking the filesystem | . | this check | uploads and library names, before anything links them | a name reaches something that is not that generator | . The encoder keeps generated READMEs valid. This check keeps a filename usable in a shell, an href, a CI log line, a curl, and any later generator. Escaping is per-generator; a name is per-file, so a name that is safe everywhere is safe once. A rename churns downstream references, and that is accepted: they are repaired, not abandoned. After a rename, repoint the hand-maintained path fields (files[].path in intake.json; container and assets[].path in *.extraction.json; provenance.source in catalogue records; file and source_file in structure.json and manifest.jsonld; hardcoded paths in tests and scripts). Leave a hand-authored wireframe alone: what it depicts is a design decision, not a consequence of the rename. Then regenerate in dependency order: library:graph → library:viz → library:readmes → readme:subgraphs, then skill:register. Out of order, a later writer stales an earlier one’s output, which reads exactly like a real failure. Build the old-name list for a reference sweep from git diff --name-status -M split on tabs (awk -F'\t'), not on whitespace: the filenames being renamed contain spaces. A sweep that finds nothing must be shown to have had something to look for.

7920.title: A sidecar suffix is not an extension
7920.content: X.pdf pairs with X.pdf.extraction.json. Two ways to break that: . | rename the source and not the sidecar → the extraction is orphaned | normalise the sidecar by a different rule than its source → same | . So the fixer strips the sidecar suffix first, normalises the remaining name by the one rule, and restores the suffix. The pair moves together by construction. The stem is normalised and the extension left alone, because a whole-filename slug destroys the extension (…(2).pdf → …-2-pdf).

7921.title: Findings are not the size of a rename
7921.content: The check reports only what is still unnormalised, so once part of the corpus has been renamed its count is the tail of the work, not its size. Measure a rename from git diff --name-status -M.

7922.title: The one case it refuses
7922.content: Two files that normalise to one name. The fixer reports the collision and renames neither: picking a winner silently destroys an upload, and an upload is somebody’s source material. Rename one by hand. That is deletion-requires-confirmation applied to a rename — a git mv that overwrites is a deletion with a friendlier name.

7923.title: What this does NOT cover
7923.content: . | Directory names. The check reads files; a directory with a space in it is not graded. | Content. It reads names and never opens a file, which is why it is harness-layer rather than folio-layer in the repo partition. | Whether a file should be there at all. That is ingestion’s question, not naming’s. | .

7925.title: Two mechanisms and a persona
7925.content: Skill upload-routes: How a file actually REACHES uploads/ — the two mechanisms that write bytes into a declared queue, the persona that performs one of them on somebody’s behalf, and what each writer owes that the route does not do for them. The step before intake and after acquisition. Named by: Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/ . content-acquisition decides what channel a resource comes in on — a file, a link, or a description somebody gives in their own words. This skill starts one step later, where the answer was a file: what writes the bytes into the declared queue, and what does the writer owe? . It ends the moment the file is in the queue. uploads-watch notices it arrived; library-ingestion and document-intake take it from there.

7926.title: The answer is two, not three, and the third is a persona
7926.content: Two mechanisms write bytes: a git commit, and the forge’s web UI. A file handed to an agent in a conversation is route 1 performed by a different actor. A persona inherits every obligation of the mechanism it performs, so the question about an agent is “did the agent discharge the git route’s obligations, and what does it owe on top?” Treating it as a third route would invite a third, shorter list of obligations. What it owes on top is provenance. A commit records its own author and message; a web upload records the account that made it. Neither records “this arrived in a conversation, from this person, for this reason” — that fact exists only in the session, which is ephemeral. If the agent does not write it down when it places the file, it is gone: for the other two routes a commit exists to go back to, and for a conversation nothing does.

7927.title: Route 1 — a git commit from a working tree
7927.content: git add the file under the queue, commit, push, open a PR. A working tree is where the pre-commit hook and bun run cat gates run — if you run them. What you owe. |   |   | . | put it in the declared queue of the layer that will own it | see §”Which queue” | . | run the generators the file stales | uploads/README.md is generated and lists every file, so any addition stales it. bun run cat readme:subgraphs, then bun run cat gates for the rest | . | open a PR | so CI judges it, and so a sibling session can see the queue grew | . | record where it came from | the commit message is the only place this route has for it | . You do not owe ingestion. Placing and ingesting are different acts by different skills, and uploads-watch is explicit that a drop is somebody handing over a file, not an instruction to publish it.

7928.title: Route 2 — the forge’s web UI
7928.content: GitHub’s “Add files via upload”. Never write the URL by hand — run bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/upload-url.ts [branch], which composes it from the declaration. The declared path uploads/ is relative to the layer, and a forge URL needs it relative to the repository. There is no working tree, so there is no pre-commit hook and no generator run. The commit is minted server-side from the bytes you selected and nothing else. Two hazards: . | It commits to the path you are LOOKING at. A file outside the declared queue reads as absent to every consumer, because each resolves the queue from the declaration. | It lets you commit to any branch, including the default one. A commit straight to main skips the PR, which is the only place CI would have run: no hook locally and no CI remotely. The generated uploads/README.md is then stale on the default branch, and readme:subgraphs:check — a blocking gate — fails for whoever opens the next pull request. | . What you owe. Everything route 1 owes, discharged afterwards from a checkout, because the web UI cannot discharge any of it: . | choose the branch, not main, unless you are also going to run the generators immediately; | navigate to the declared queue directory before uploading, not to the repository root; | pull, run bun run cat readme:subgraphs and bun run cat gates, and push the result — or ask an agent to, which is the persona below. | .

7929.title: The persona — a file handed to an agent in a conversation
7929.content: This is route 1, performed by an agent. It inherits every obligation above. Three things are the agent’s own: . Materialise the bytes before anything else. A file that exists only in the conversation exists nowhere the repository can see. Write it into the declared queue under a name that will still mean something — not ChatGPT Image Sep 20, 2026, 08_26_47 AM.png or a bare UUID. Write down what the conversation knows and the commit does not — who provided it, when, what they said it was, and why it was wanted. Put it in the commit message at minimum. This is the obligation the other two routes do not have, and the reason the persona is named although it is not a mechanism. Do not ingest on your own say-so, and do not delete. Both are other skills’ decisions — library-ingestion and deletion-requires-confirmation. A processed upload still looks spent and still is not.

7930.title: What the routes are NOT responsible for
7930.content: The same three for every route, stated once so no route’s section can shorten the list: . | deciding the file belongs in the corpus. That is acquisition’s question, answered before this step. | ingestion. A file in the queue is a file in the queue; library/ is a judgement call somebody else owns. | cleaning the queue. uploads/ is the raw record of what was handed over and a derived library/ entry does not replace it. | .

7931.title: Which queue — there can be more than one, and they belong to different layers
7931.content: A checkout that includes several layers can carry several uploads queues — for example uploads/ declared by the layer at the repository root and cat-harness/uploads/ declared by the cat-harness layer. They are not one directory declared twice: they are two layers’ queues that share an id. So “put it in uploads/” is not an instruction — it does not say whose. Resolve the queue from the declaration of the layer that will own the material, which is what queueRepoRelative in scripts/upload-url.ts does and what the upload-url Tool exposes. Pass that layer’s root; do not paste a path.

7932.title: Unsettled
7932.content: . | Which layer owns a given file. Nothing states the rule for choosing between two declared queues. Ask, or follow whatever the surrounding work already uses. | Whether an arrival without an intake record should be refused. A gate would fail main on arrival, which is the opposite of accepting what somebody offers (content-acquisition). Whether the record is owed by the placer or minted by intake is undecided. | .

7934.title: Watching the queue
7934.content: Skill uploads-watch: Notice what has landed in the acquisition queue, and tell an arrival from a backlog. Reports; it never deletes, and never ingests on its own say-so. Named by: Content acquisition . uploads/ is the acquisition queue — content-acquisition puts things in it, library-ingestion takes them out. This is the step between: seeing that something arrived. The queue path is read from the declaration, never written down. It is uploads/ relative to the layer, which is not where a repository-relative consumer would look. queueRepoRelative in scripts/upload-url.ts is the one place that arithmetic lives.

7935.title: An arrival is not a backlog
7935.content: A file sitting in the queue says nothing on its own: it may have landed a minute ago or been waiting since before this session. Do not report a queue’s contents as news: a watcher that does becomes noise that gets ignored, and an ignored watcher reads as coverage. So report against a mark: what was there when this session began, or when the watch last ran. What is new since the mark is an arrival. Everything else is the backlog, and the backlog is mentioned once, as a count. A backlog is still a finding. A queue that has held the same file for weeks means acquisition happened and ingestion did not, and nobody noticed. That is worth one line — not silence, and not a repeated alarm.

7936.title: It reports; it does not act
7936.content: Never ingest on a watcher’s say-so. A drop is somebody handing over a file, not an instruction to publish it: ingestion decides a bib slug, writes into library/, and is a judgement call that library-ingestion owns. Never delete anything from the queue — that is deletion-requires-confirmation applied where it is most tempting, because a processed file looks spent. It is not: uploads/ is the raw record of what was handed over, and the derived entry in library/ is not a substitute for it. Report what could go, with sizes and ages, and wait to be told.

7937.title: What to say when something arrived
7937.content: Name the file, say when it landed, say what it appears to be — and then say the next step is ingestion and whether you are taking it. An arrival reported without a next step hands the reader a fact and a chore.

7938.title: What to say when nothing did
7938.content: Nothing, unless you were asked. A watch that reports every quiet interval trains its reader to skip it, including the round that matters.

7940.title: Watching a pinned upstream dependency
7940.content: Process_UpstreamPinWatch · strict · 8 step(s) . Has a pinned upstream dependency fallen behind a release: check each pin, keep one tracking issue, and enter the adoption subprocess for each dependency that is behind. THE WATCHER’S DISPATCH POINT, drawn rather than described. Bean 29ij records the rule this follows: a watcher fires on specific events, and those events are process events — they belong in a diagram, not in prose that no tool reads. Everything up to the tracking issue is MECHANICAL and sits in a system lane: read the registry, list upstream’s releases, compare, and maintain ONE issue. No step here exercises judgement, which is what makes build-pipeline the correct lane rather than a convenient one. Three outcomes and the middle one is the point. Current closes the issue; behind opens or edits it; COULD NOT TELL leaves the issue exactly as it is and fails the job, because a watchdog that has gone blind must not read as good news — check-ci-health.ts’s rule, and the reason this repository has a watchdog at all. The adoption itself is a call activity, so the judgement half lives in its own reusable process and this one stays free of it. i i i i i i i i

It hands off at the first sign of judgement: the moment a bump needs adopting, that is Lane_Agent’s, never this one’s. | . | Agent | authoring-agent | Entered only once Lane_Ci has confirmed a pin is behind and filed the issue, never to make that determination itself: A_PickUp’s claim is what stops two sessions adopting the same bump. The judgement of adoption is not drawn here either — Call_Adopt hands it to its own reusable process, so this lane is only the hand-off from mechanical detection to judgement, not the judgement itself. | .

An unpinned dependency is an unreviewed commit from a stranger, merged on every build. A pinned one is a commitment that somebody has to revisit. This skill is the second half: what happens between upstream cut a release and we are running it. It implements two diagrams, and the diagram is the source of truth for ordering: . | Diagram | What it is | . | upstream-pin-watch.bpmn (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) | The watcher. Scheduled, mechanical, ends at either “every pin is current” or “one tracking issue says which is not”. | . | upstream-version-adoption.bpmn (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) | The reusable subprocess, entered once per stale pin. Scope → impact → MVP → review → decide. | . The second is called, not copied: calledElement="Process_UpstreamAdoption". Any pinned upstream dependency enters it the same way, and a new tenant is a registry row plus a call activity — never a second diagram that says the same thing in different words.

7947.title: The registry is the tenant list, and it does not hold the version
7947.content: upstream/upstream-pins.json — in this harness’s declared upstream/ directory — declares each pinned dependency, with each pinnedIn resolved against the harness root: the upstream repo, the file the pin literal actually lives in, the pattern that reads it, what of ours binds to it, and the commands that constitute its MVP. It deliberately does not store the pinned version. The version lives in exactly one place — site-chrome/_config.yml for the theme — and the registry says how to read it from there. A registry that carried its own copy would be a second answer to “what are we running”, free to disagree with the build. bun run cat check:upstream-pins reads the literal out of the declared file; a pattern that matches nothing is reported as an error, not as “no pin”. binds and mvp are the reason the registry exists at all rather than the check simply grepping for version strings. They are what turn impact analysis and MVP from words in a box into a list somebody can work through.

7948.title: 1 — Watch
7948.content: bun run cat check:upstream-pins, weekly from .github/workflows/upstream-pins.yml and on demand. For each row: read the pinned ref out of its declared file, list the upstream tags that match tagPattern, and compare. Exit codes, and the middle one is the point: . | Exit | Meaning | What the workflow does | . | 0 | every pin is at the newest matching release | closes the tracking issue if one is open | . | 1 | at least one pin is behind | opens one issue labelled upstream-pin, or edits the existing one | . | 2 | could not determine — upstream unreachable, pattern did not match | leaves the issue untouched and fails the job | . Three rules it inherits from check-ci-health.ts, and they are not optional: . | “Could not check” is never rendered as current. An unreachable upstream is exit 2, not exit 0. A watchdog that goes blind must not read as good news. | One issue, edited in place. An edit does not notify, so a pin that stays stale for months stays one unread item rather than many. | The job fails on exit 2, which makes this workflow itself red on the default branch, which check:ci-health reports. The watchdog is watched. | .

7949.title: 2 — Impact analysis
7949.content: Scope the delta first, and scope it to what reaches our output. The upstream changelog is the claim; the diff is the evidence. For a Jekyll theme that means _sass, _includes, _layouts and assets — a change to upstream’s own docs, CI or tests cannot reach us: . git -C <upstream-clone> diff --stat <pinned>..<candidate> -- _sass _includes _layouts assets . Then ask what of ours binds to it, from the row’s binds list. This is the half that a changelog cannot tell you, because upstream does not know what you reached into. For the theme it is concrete and small: site-chrome/assets/js/docs-ui.js moves the theme’s own search markup into the action launcher, binding .search, #search-input and .search-label; site-chrome/assets/css/docs-ui.css overrides .side-bar, .site-header and .main-header; and three e2e specs assert the structure the theme emits. An upstream rename of any of those is not a build failure — it is a shipped feature that quietly stops working, which is the failure mode a pin exists to convert into a decision. Write the analysis down as the work item’s note before building anything. A candidate that touches nothing we bind to is a different conversation from one that renames a selector we depend on, and the reviewer needs to know which they are looking at before they look.

7950.title: 3 — MVP
7950.content: An MVP is a deployed build, not a description of one. Move the pin on a branch, let feature-staging.yml publish it under branches/<branch-slug>/, and run the row’s mvp commands. For the theme: . rm -rf _kg _site bun test # unit tests CI=1 bun run cat test:e2e # a11y, action tiles, sidebar panels, qa panel bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/site-links.ts --site ./_site # every navbar tile resolves in the BUILT site . site-links.ts checks the tiles against the real _site rather than against the attribute, which is what catches a tile that 404s. A red gate is evidence, not an exit. It does not end the process and it does not loop on its own — it goes to the reviewer with everything else, because “this version breaks us” is a finding the decider needs, not a reason to stop before they see it.

7951.title: 4 — Review
7951.content: Post the staging URL, the gate results and the impact analysis on the PR, then hand it over. The reviewer’s question is narrower than “is the new version good”: it is does anything in binds still hold, checked against the deployed page rather than against a screenshot. Findings the agent can fix — our overlay adapting to a renamed class, a test fixture updated to the markup the theme now emits — loop back into impact analysis on the same branch. Findings that are upstream’s behaviour rather than ours go to the decision as they are.

7952.title: 5 — Decide
7952.content: A person decides, and the diagram says so. PM_Decide is a bpmn:userTask in the publication manager’s lane, and that role admits person only, so activity-fulfilment-kind fails the moment somebody tries to make an agent the accepting party. It also carries <cat-harness.processes:policy relaxable="false"/>: no package may relax it. The lane is the publication manager’s rather than the editor’s because the pin is not a change to the corpus — it is a change to what the published artefact is built from, and that role is the one “accountable for what is live”. The gateway is not DMN-backed, and that is deliberate. Every other computed gateway in this repository reduces to arithmetic over tool output; this one weighs a rendering nobody can score against the cost of staying behind. A table here would look authoritative and would not be. Three outcomes: . | Adopt — move the pin, open the PR, and say in the body what the version range changed in rendered output. Record the evidence you used, not just the verdict. | Hold — record it as a block with an expiry and a revisit trigger (bean-blocking.md (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan)). A hold with no expiry cannot be told from abandoned work, and the next watcher run will re-raise the same pin with no memory of why it was left. | Decline — record the reasons on the work item and scrap it. A scrapped work item is what stops the next agent re-entering the same dead end; a deleted one leaves them unable to tell a decision from an accident. | . In every case the decision is written down before the process ends. The work item is resolved from the terminal step, so a run that stops at “we looked and said no” is as finished as one that moved the pin.

7953.title: Adding a tenant
7953.content: . | Pin the literal wherever the tool reads it, with a comment saying which process governs moving it. | Add a row to upstream-pins.json: repo, pinnedIn, pattern, tagPattern, binds, mvp. | Run bun run cat check:upstream-pins and confirm it reads your pin back. A pattern that does not match is exit 2 — “could not determine” — and the row is not watched until it does. | . No diagram changes. That is what reusable means here.

7954.title: How to pick the pinned version when you first pin something
7954.content: Pin what is running, not what is newest. Those are different changes, and doing both at once means neither is reviewable — a regression cannot be attributed to the pin or to the bump. Establish what is running by fingerprint, not by assumption. For the theme that meant finding a declaration in the deployed CSS on gh-pages (text-wrap: balance, in _sass/navigation.scss) that entered upstream after the newest release, which proved the live site was tracking the default branch rather than any tag. The newest release at or below that point is the pin, and the PR states the residual delta — one CSS declaration — rather than claiming there is none. If no fingerprint discriminates, say so and pin the newest release anyway; an unverified pin is still strictly better than an unpinned dependency, and “could not determine” written down is worth more than a confident guess.

7962.title: uses[] Editorial Review
7962.content: Skill uses-editorial-review: Adjudicate uses-editorial-completeness — read a block as a reader would and judge whether its uses[] is complete and genuinely expository. The human/agent half of the uses QA axis; the mechanical half runs in qa-checkers-uses.ts. Named by: Narrative review, Voice overlay review, Committee review of a content change .

7963.title: The relation you are auditing
7963.content: uses[] is the editorial dependency relation: what must a reader have read to follow this block? It is authored content — a deliberate judgement about narrative order — and it is maintained by agents and humans, not generated. The same relation exists at term scale: a glossary term’s requires, and a schema term’s uses in bootstrap’s graph.schema.json, say what a reader must know before the definition. Same discipline — AUTHORED, never inferred, with a text matcher kept only as a guard that list and prose agree (see the glossary ordering discipline, §”Ordered glossaries”). It is not any machine-derived dependency graph. A content type with a formal layer also derives a formal relation, from what its proofs actually invoke, and the two relations answer different questions and diverge in both directions, correctly. The layer that ships such a content type holds that comparison and names this skill from its side (for a paper folio, the science layer).

7964.title: interprets is the same relation under a second field name
7964.content: uses[] is the curated list. interprets states the same reader-facing fact for a remark or example about one specific block, and the content graph counts both. Each editorial edge carries editorialField so a tool proposing an edit can still tell which field an author wrote: they are interchangeable to a reader and not to a writer, and collapsing them would make an automated edit rewrite the wrong field. Two caveats, both of which change what a number means: . | detangler-no-forward-ref builds its own uses-only adjacency and does not consume the shared graph, so forward-pointing interprets edges are outside what it counts. | The editorial graph is not acyclic. Counting both fields reveals genuine editorial cycles. Do not “fix” one without reading whether it is real. | . Do not quote a count from prose — run the check against the corpus in front of you. A number in a document is a claim; only a run is evidence. For impact questions — what breaks if this changes? — use the union, via the content graph’s accessors, which default to it.

7965.title: The prime directive
7965.content: Never populate uses[] from a machine-derived dependency graph. Copying derived dependencies in destroys the editorial signal and inflates every ordering metric computed from it (graph energy, forward refs, cone size, PageRank). Never “sync” the two. When reviewing, do not open a block’s formal or generated sibling to decide what belongs in uses[]. The question is about the reader.

7966.title: Workflow
7966.content: . | Read the .md as a reader. Cold. Do not read the .ts first — you want your own sense of what the block presumes before you see what the author declared. | List what the narrative actually leans on. Note every point where the prose: . | uses notation it does not introduce, | names an object (“the canonical $X$”) defined elsewhere, | argues against or refines a prior result, | presumes a construction the reader would otherwise have to reconstruct. | . | Now read uses[] in the .ts manifest and compare both ways. | Judge completeness. Anything from step 2 missing from uses[] that a reader would genuinely stumble over ⇒ fail (major). A reader who could carry on unbothered ⇒ at most warn. | Judge editorial fitness. For each listed entry, ask: would a reader be worse off having not read this first? . | Yes ⇒ fine. | No, and it looks like a derived artefact (an entry the prose never mentions, copied from a generated dependency list) ⇒ fail (major). This is the pollution case. | No, but it is defensible context ⇒ warn. | . | Write the sidecar entry under uses-editorial-completeness with reviewer.kind: "agent" (or "human"), citing file:line and a verbatim quote for every finding — the block-QA evidence contract. | .

7967.title: Verdict rubric
7967.content: | Verdict | When | . | pass | List reads as a deliberate editorial judgement; nothing a reader needs is missing; nothing present is dead weight. | . | warn | A marginal entry, or a missing dependency a reader could shrug off. | . | fail | A missing dependency a reader would stumble over, or an entry that is plainly a copied-in derived dependency. | .

7968.title: Forward references and foreshadows[]
7968.content: A uses[] entry pointing at a block that appears later in the chapter is a detangler-no-forward-ref finding. Sometimes that is right — the exposition really does defer — and foreshadows[] records it. foreshadows[] is independent of uses[], so a chapter overview can name results it previews without asserting a dependency that is not real. It covers two cases you must keep apart: . | case | in uses[]? | who records it | cost | . | Pure forward pointer — the prose names something coming later and does not depend on it | no | derived from the .md, not authored | zero by construction: it never enters the dependency graph | . | Deferred prerequisite — a real dependency the paper states later on purpose | yes | declared by the author, and only the author | exempt from ordering cost; still counted for cycles, cones and depth | . Do not hand-author the first case. deriveForeshadows reads the block’s own markdown links and backticked labels, keeps those that resolve to a real block sitting later in reading order and are not already in uses[], and loadChapterGraph re-derives on every load. Writing them into the manifest duplicates the prose into metadata, where it goes stale. The derivation never reads deferral language; it matches links and labels only (phrasing detection misreads e.g. “Below $n^*$”, a numeric comparison).

7969.title: Declaring the second case
7969.content: Only a deferred prerequisite needs your judgement: it exempts a real uses[] edge from the ordering metrics, hiding a genuine defect behind an authored claim that the disorder was intended, and nothing downstream re-opens it. The contract in BlockBase.foreshadows is strict — the prose must frame the reference as deferred (“we will need X, proved in chapter 9”). The bar is a first-person authorial hand-off that says the treatment happens elsewhere: “we establish this in X”, “we work this out separately”, “the derivation is recorded in X”. | Looks like a deferral | Actually | . | Bare cross-reference — “See [X] in Chapter 7” | ordering. Says nothing about direction. | . | Organizational pointer — “these tables are projections of this master table” | ordering. About structure, not sequence. | . | Block asserts the target’s conclusion as background, then reasons onward from it | ordering. Consuming a result is the opposite of deferring it. | . | Target listed under “## Rigorous results” / “## Consumers / downstream” | ordering — and check the direction; these often run target→source. | . | A forward-looking word (“below”, “later”, “we must show”) | ordering unless the sentence is about this target’s placement. “Below $n^*$” is a numeric comparison; “we must show” is usually about research, not chapter order. | . Two failure modes survive a verbatim quote, so check both before declaring: . | False locator. “the functor of the next subsection” where the target is 21 sections and ~300 blocks away. The prose defers; it does not defer this far, and the edge is a real defect. | Mis-aimed deferral. The quoted sentence hands off to a different block than the edge under review. A deferral pointed elsewhere cannot exempt this one. | . Both are about the declared case only. A derived pointer is aimed by the link itself, so it cannot be mis-aimed, and it carries no exemption to abuse. Two rules police the field: foreshadows-resolve (every target must exist) and foreshadows-not-self. The foreshadows-point-forward criterion catches a target the reader has already passed, which is either a prerequisite filed in the wrong field or an inert back-reference.

7970.title: A block’s uses[] may be carrying the whole family
7970.content: Never judge an entry from the block’s own .md alone. A block is the head of a family — X-proof, X-interpretation, X-tableN-data — and the dependency you are looking for is often in a child while the declaration sits on the parent. | Table children. Pointer-style blocks (“See Table 3”) keep their substance in tbl:…-data. A name-and-notation search of the parent’s .md reports an absence that is not real. | Proof children. A proof cites what the statement assumes. The parent’s prose may never name a target its proof child cites by label; if the proof declares no uses[] of its own, the parent’s entry is the sole record of the dependency, and deleting it as “unsupported by the prose” erases the edge entirely. | . So before removing an entry, check whether any child leans on the target, and whether that child declares anything itself. An entry that looks like dead weight on the parent may be the family’s only declaration. Searching for the target’s words also misses a lean on the target’s object — a source writing “the canonical $\tilde w_\lambda$” depends on whatever defines the undeformed $w_\lambda$, whether or not it ever says so.

7971.title: Sibling parity is evidence only until a bulk edit touched the family
7971.content: “All the siblings declare nothing, so declaring it here would be the anomaly” is evidence only if no bulk operation has run over the family: a bulk edit (for example a transitive-prune pass) produces parity by construction, so parity cannot distinguish a shared convention from shared damage. Before resting on it, check the family’s history, not just the block’s: . git log --oneline -- <chapter>/<sibling>.ts # for two or three siblings . A convention shows up as blocks that were authored empty. Damage shows up as one commit emptying all of them on the same day. If the emptiness has a single commit behind it, parity tells you nothing about intent. The same caution applies to any evidence drawn from what “the corpus does”: a corpus that has been swept is a record of the sweep as much as of the authors.

7972.title: One reading is not the standard
7972.content: A single careful pass is not enough: on re-review, destructive uses[] verdicts and foreshadow declarations are overturned often, and keyword search over the .md alone misses real dependencies. Use two readers who cannot see each other’s verdicts for anything that edits the graph, and treat agreement as the signal. Where they disagree, or where either is unsure, leave the edge alone: a wrongly deleted editorial edge silently corrupts every ordering metric computed from the graph. A retarget carries both burdens. It asserts this edge is wrong and that one is right, so it needs evidence for each half separately. When only the second half holds, it is an addition, not a swap.

7973.title: Reading the mechanical findings first

7991.title: Visual diff — see a figure change
7991.content: Skill visual-diff: Pictures of a changed figure, diagram or table, before and after, and how much of it changed. Says when to use it, what the percentage means and must NOT be read as, what a missing picture means, and how the staging job and the review process call it. Use when a reviewer asks “what does this figure look like now”, when a table’s markup diff is unreadable, or when a staging preview’s pictures are missing. Named by: Human Translation Workflow, Translation review and adjudication, Translation round trip (untainted), Translation Workflow, Review task, Adjudication, Criterion adjudication, A harness’s default rendering, Theme and UI review — at ingestion, Wireframe design review, Prose and the code it describes, SME Review of Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Adopting an upstream version bump, Is the incremental IG AST what a full build would have produced?, Incremental IG build, L3 FHIR IG pipeline, Questionnaire wireframe review, Committee review of a content change, Merge and publish a content change, Content Change and Review, Content lifecycle, Draft, review and publish, Editing and HCI validation, Make a decided public comment change, Release a draft for public comment, Public comment on a review draft, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Review and publish a folio, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate . Skill id: visual-diff · Package: sdlc-core . For a figure, a diagram, a table, an equation or a simulator, the change a reviewer must judge is how the block LOOKS. The Markdown or SVG diff of a recoloured bar chart is noise. So the staging job pictures each such block on both sides, and the review page shows the pictures. For a before/after of anything the staging job does not picture (page chrome, scroll behaviour, a PDF page, an IG page, a slide), and for the rules every reviewer-facing pair follows, see before-after-preview.

7992.title: Design rules
7992.content: . | A Skill and a Tool, built into the processes. The steps live in the folio-block-screenshots Tool and in this skill. The staging workflow and the review process CALL them; nobody copies them. | No new dependency. The pictures are taken with Playwright, which the platform already uses, and the comparison runs in Chromium’s own canvas, so nothing new needs a licence. | One key or one click; never a drag. The page offers four views as radio buttons, not a slider. | .

7993.title: What the reviewer sees
7993.content: On the review page, a visual block opens on “Pictures, before and after”. It shows: . | a sentence stating how much changed: “12.3% of the block’s pixels changed”, or “No pixel changed beyond anti-aliasing”, or “Only one side could be pictured”; | four views, each one click (or an arrow key): | . | view | shows | . | Changed pixels | the after picture faded to grey, with every changed pixel marked in magenta | . | Before | the block on the published site | . | After | the block on this preview | . | Both | before and after side by side | . When a build published no pictures, the block opens side by side (the live pages in frames) instead, because the page takes the first view that can run and lists the block’s kind.

7994.title: What the percentage means, and must NOT be read as
7994.content: | it is | it is not | . | the share of the block’s pixels, in the larger of the two pictures, that differ by more than a small tolerance (24 of 255 per channel, to absorb anti-aliasing) | whether the change is right. A one-pixel line through a chart can be the whole point | . | counted over the larger picture, so a block that grew counts the new area as changed | a measure of text change: a reworded caption moves many pixels | . | of the light theme only | a check of dark mode | . Zero means nothing changed that the eye would see. A block the ChangeSet lists as changed with 0% is still worth a look at its markup: the change may be in alt text, a label or a link.

7995.title: When a picture is missing
7995.content: A missing picture is said, never drawn blank: . | message | means | what to do | . | “Not on main: this block is new.” | an added block has no before | nothing: there is nothing to compare | . | “Its page is not in the published site” | the before side has no page for the block’s document | the document is new, or main was never published. A folio publishes main when its staging caller lists push to main; the build log warns when _main-site.json is absent | . | “Its anchor is not on the … page” | the page exists, but has no <a id="<label>"> for the block | the block was renamed without renamedFrom, or the build dropped it. Check the id-stable QA criterion | .

7996.title: How a picture is taken
7996.content: The site build writes an empty <a id="<label>"> before each labelled block. There is no element that wraps the block. So a block’s picture is the region from its anchor down to the next anchor, as wide as the anchor’s container. A page with anchors out of order pictures the wrong region, so if a picture looks wrong, check the anchors first.

7997.title: The Tool
7997.content: # how many blocks would be pictured (no browser needed) bun run <platform>/cat-harness-tools/scripts/block-screenshots.ts --changeset _site/changeset.json --count # picture and compare bun run <platform>/cat-harness-tools/scripts/block-screenshots.ts \ --changeset _site/changeset.json --base pages --head _site --out _site . It writes visual-diff.json (folio-visual-diff/v1) and visual/*.png next to the site. The review page reads ../visual-diff.json.

It runs after the step “Choose the before side”, which picks: . | main’s site, at the publish branch’s root, published by the same workflow’s publish-main job on every push to main; | for a stacked PR, its base branch’s preview, branches/<base-slug>/, so the pictures and the ChangeSet compare with the same branch. It installs Chromium only when --count is above zero. | publish-main (same workflow) deletes only files its own manifest, _main-site.json, lists. branches/, _render-log/ and anything a person put at the root are never touched, and the first publish removes nothing. | content-change-review.bpmn, task Compare main vs staging. The reviewer’s comparison names this skill beside staging-review, so a reviewer handed that task is told the pictures exist. | .

8001.title: Visualizer loading — the page is layout, the graph is fetched
8001.content: Skill visualizer-loading: The general strategy for a complex visualizer: the generated page carries identity, layout and a pointer, and its bulky or repeated content is fetched from the Knowledge Graph in the browser rather than baked into every page. What must stay server-side, how to fetch, how to stay equivalent to the render being replaced, and how to verify a page whose content is not in its HTML. Read before generating any page that shows a KG node’s data at length: an IG artefact view, a graph viewer, a schema or sidecar view. Named by: A harness’s default rendering, Board: open and close content, Board: relocate content to the trashcan . Skill id: visualizer-loading · Package: ui-core .

8002.title: The rule
8002.content: A generated page for a complex visualizer holds three things: . | Identity: the title, description and front matter that navigation, search and a link preview read. | Layout: headings, tabs and links, arranged by a template (liquid-templates). | A pointer: the KG file the content comes from, resolved by the generator. | . The content (a sidecar file, a node’s properties at length, a table derived from the graph) is fetched by the browser from the committed KG artefact. It is never copied into the page. Each copy is a second answer, free to drift from the first, and copied into a thousand pages it is most of the site’s bytes. kg-viewer is an instance of the pattern: one page that fetches its sibling graph document and computes back-links at load.

8003.title: What stays server-side
8003.content: Moving content client-side has costs: a reader without JavaScript loses it, a search index loses it, and so does the first paint. So these stay in the page: . | What navigation and search need: title, description, headings, and the link labels a reader scans for. | The way to reach the data without JavaScript: a link to the raw file, under <noscript> if nowhere else. A view that renders nothing without scripts must still say where its content is. | Anything short and unique to the page. A one-line value is not bloat, and fetching it costs a request to save a few bytes. | . Move a block when it is large or repeated and already a KG file. A block that would need a new file published just to be fetched is a design question for the owner, not a default.

8004.title: Where the data is served from — served: true
8004.content: The fetched file is the KG’s own, published verbatim. A directory declares served: true in its layer’s <instance>.json, and mount-instance-docs copies its bytes to /<instance>/<path> after Jekyll: no Liquid, no layout, no index page. Pages under the layer’s composed docs then reach it with a relative path. Never copy the file into docs/ beside the page instead — a gate flags it as an unknown file family in a docs directory. A generator whose data is not served writes no page that would fetch it, and says why.

8005.title: How to fetch
8005.content: . | Relative to the page’s own location, never via a configured base URL, so the same bytes work in production and in a staging preview (kg-viewer §”The page is generated, not committed”). | One shared loader per visualizer kind, published once and referenced by every page, never inlined in each page. | No dependencies: no CDN or framework. Same reason as kg-viewer: the data is this repository’s, and a third party in its trust boundary is at odds with that. | Three states on the page: loading, loaded, and could not load, which names the file and the error. A failed fetch that leaves a blank or a permanent “Loading…” is the silent-gap defect in another form. | .

8006.title: Stay equivalent to the render you replace
8006.content: When the page replaces another renderer’s page (for example the IG Publisher’s, which every phase must render equivalent to), compute the display the same way that renderer does, and then check it. For example, a page that shows a file as JSON.stringify(parsed, null, 2) differs from the file’s own bytes whenever the file has integer-like keys, which JavaScript orders first; showing the raw bytes would look right and be wrong.

8007.title: Printing and PDFs
8007.content: A browser prints the page as it is at that moment, so fetched content prints once it has loaded and not before: a PDF taken at domcontentloaded holds “Loading…”. | Every loader signals completion. Each counts itself in and out of window.__kgLoads, and the last one to finish sets <html data-kg-loaded>, on success or failure. A failed fetch still ends the wait, and its message is what prints. | Anything that prints or renders a PDF waits for that attribute, never for a fixed delay. That includes a Playwright page.pdf(), a PDF build step and a screenshot test. A page with no loader never sets it, so a tool that waits must first check whether the page loads one of the loader scripts. | A reader pressing Ctrl+P gets the page as loaded. The loaders are fast, but a print from a cold cache can still catch “Loading…”. That is a visible, honest state, not a blank. | .

8008.title: Verify in a browser, not in the HTML
8008.content: A static check cannot see fetched content: the built HTML holds only “Loading…”. Verification therefore means loading each page in a browser (Playwright, with the pre-installed Chromium) and comparing what it displays against the reference, as rendered-verification requires of any rendered artefact.

8009.title: Finding what to move
8009.content: A QA review over a built site: . | The mechanical half measures per-page bytes, blocks repeated across pages, and blocks matching a committed KG file, and writes a QA sidecar. | The agentic half judges each candidate against §”What stays server-side”. | . Repetition is a measurement, but whether a block may leave the page is a judgement.

8010.title: Do not
8010.content: . | Bake a KG file’s text into a page “for now”. That copy is what the next person will have to find and remove. | Move navigation or search terms client-side to save bytes. The saving is small and the loss is the page being findable. | Add a framework to fetch a JSON file. fetch and textContent are the whole loader. | .

8012.title: Voice editorial review
8012.content: Skill voice-editorial-review: Adjudicate a voice-* finding — read the flagged passage as a reader of THAT genre would and decide whether the register is wrong, the criterion is out of scope, or the block is a stated exception. The human/agent half of the voice QA axis; the mechanical half runs in qa-checkers-voice.ts. Named by: Narrative review, Voice overlay review .

8013.title: The axis you are adjudicating
8013.content: Six criteria in pipeline/qa-criteria-registry.ts describe one house voice: . | criterion | what it matches | severity | . | voice-status-leak | status markers and derivation-status speech in body prose | critical | . | voice-scholarly-default | second-person address, lecturer-cadence openers, paper-past-tense narration | major | . | voice-author-notes-pollution | status banners, PR/commit refs, agent names, ISO dates | major | . | voice-emoji-content | emoji as content outside tables | major | . | voice-first-person-work | first-person work tone — “we’ll add”, “let me”, “needs more work” | major | . | voice-editorializing | “surprisingly”, “it is worth noting that”, “rather than merely …” | minor | . They are heuristics over phrase lists. A match is a question, not a verdict; a reviewer entry on the same sidecar confirms or overrules it.

8014.title: The scoping question comes first, and it is usually the answer
8014.content: Every criterion above was written for a paper: a scholarly artefact in third person, where a status marker really is a leak of the work tracker into the published text. A criterion without profiles scoping also runs over documentation, whose register addresses the reader: “you need bun, latexmk and Lean” is a correct sentence in a prerequisites page and a voice-scholarly-default match. Ask which is true before touching the prose: . | The register is wrong for this genre. Fix the passage. | The criterion does not belong in this genre. Add profiles: ["paper"] to it in the registry. One edit clears the finding for every document folio and records why. | The criterion belongs and this block is an exception. Record a reviewer entry on the sidecar saying why. It leads the criterion, so the block reads pass with the reasoning attached, and nothing is silently rewritten. | . Many instances of one criterion across many guide pages is evidence about the criterion’s scope, not about the authors.

8015.title: What the criterion cannot know
8015.content: The checkers match text. They do not know what the page is about. Typical false positives: . | voice-status-leak on a page that is a deliberate inventory of gaps (**Not yet implemented:** is its subject, not a leak). | voice-status-leak on prose about a work-plan lane: prose about a to-do store contains the words of a to-do store. | voice-emoji-content inside a transcript of an agent session, quoted as data. | . Each is a criterion reading a quotation as an assertion, and the reviewer entry says so in those words.

8016.title: Adjudicating one finding
8016.content: . | Open the block, not just the evidence line. The sidecar quotes one line; the register is a property of the passage around it. | Name the genre. Paper, guide, reference, transcript. That decides which of the three outcomes applies before you read another word. | Record the outcome where the next reader will find it — a prose edit, a registry edit with profiles, or a reviewer entry. A finding left open comes back on the next sweep. | Re-run the sweep — bun run pipeline/qa-sweep.ts --root docs/source — so the sidecar, the icon and the panel agree with what you decided. | .

8017.title: Where the open findings are
8017.content: Tracked in the work plan, one item per criterion, each carrying its blocks with file, line and the matched text: . beans list | grep "Voice axis" . The evidence itself lives in <block>.qa.json beside each block, and is published per block on the docs site: the QA icon opens the criterion, and the criterion opens the witness that ruled on it — which checker, at which script_hash, and whether the verdict still matches the file on disk.

8018.title: Do not
8018.content: . | Do not edit prose to silence a criterion you believe is out of scope. That hides the scoping defect and costs the next folio the same argument. | Do not mass-apply one finding’s resolution across its siblings without reading them; one criterion can fire for different causes. | Do not treat critical as “fix first”. Severity ranks the criterion’s authors’ concern, not the confidence of this match. | Do not delete a finding from a sidecar. The sweep rewrites its own entries; a hand-removed one comes back with no record that anyone looked. | .

8020.title: Voice overlay review
8020.content: Skill voice-overlay-review: Review a block against the active voices’ rules and record the verdict on its QA sidecar. The human/agent half of the voice overlay; the mechanical half is whatever patterns and terminology a rule carries. Named by: Human Translation Workflow, Translation review and adjudication, Translation round trip (untainted), Translation Workflow, Narrative review, Review task, Voice overlay review, Adjudication, Criterion adjudication, A harness’s default rendering, Theme and UI review — at ingestion, Wireframe design review, Prose and the code it describes, SME Review of Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Adopting an upstream version bump, Is the incremental IG AST what a full build would have produced?, Incremental IG build, L3 FHIR IG pipeline, Questionnaire wireframe review, Committee review of a content change, Merge and publish a content change, Content Change and Review, Content lifecycle, Draft, review and publish, Editing and HCI validation, Make a decided public comment change, Public comment on a review draft, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Review and publish a folio, Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gate .

8021.title: What you are reviewing, and against what
8021.content: One block, against the rules of the voices the folio has activated — not every voice it ships. The layer’s config (its index.config.json entry) holds the list; an empty list means there is nothing for this skill to do and that is a pass, not a gap. bun run cat check:voices # the voices, their rule counts, and that every citation resolves .

8022.title: The rule’s citation is the argument, so open it
8022.content: Every voice rule carries a source that resolves to a real file — a library/<doc>/sections/<section>.md for a rule read from an ingested document, or a path for a house standard. It also carries the quote the rule was read from. Open the citation before upholding a finding. | A reviewer who has read the source can say why the rule applies to this block. | The rule may be wrong. A rule derived from a document can misread it. If the quote does not support the rule, the rule is the defect and the work item goes against the voice, not against the block. | .

8023.title: Three outcomes, as with the house voice axis
8023.content: Identical to voice-editorial-review: . | The finding stands — the register is wrong for this block. Fix the prose. | The rule does not apply to this content — record it, and consider whether the rule needs appliesTo scoping on the voice. One scoping edit beats many per-block overrules. | The rule applies and this block is an exception — a reviewer entry on the sidecar saying why. It leads the criterion, so the block reads pass with the reasoning attached and nothing is silently rewritten. | .

8024.title: A mechanical match is a question
8024.content: A pattern is a regex over text; it does not know what the block is about. Examples of non-defects it matches: . | voice-scholarly-default on documentation pages whose register is correctly second-person. | voice-editorializing on merely inside a comparative, where the contrast is the block’s claim. | voice-editorializing on clearly used as proof economy. | . Verify before upholding, and when a rule fires repeatedly across a corpus on the same non-defect, that is evidence about the RULE.

8025.title: Recording the verdict
8025.content: Voice findings go on the block’s QA sidecar like any other, through the same writer, so the icon and the published witness agree with what you decided: . bun run pipeline/qa-merge-findings.ts --file findings.json . insertAdjudication places your entry ahead of the script entry, because list[0] is a criterion’s effective verdict. The script’s entry is kept beneath yours, because the disagreement between a checker and a reviewer is information.

8026.title: Do not
8026.content: . | Do not uphold a finding you have not traced to its quote. A rule that misreads its source is the failure this design exists to prevent. | Do not review against a voice the folio has not activated. | Do not delete a script finding from a sidecar. The sweep rewrites its own entries; a hand-removed one returns with no record that anyone looked. | Do not resolve a conflict between two active voices in the prose. Both rules stand: name them and let the editor decide. | .

8028.title: Voice overlay review
8028.content: Process_VoiceReview · advisory · 6 step(s) . The voice axis: load whichever editorial voices are active, run each rule’s mechanical half, and decide — for each finding — whether the prose is wrong, the rule does not apply to this content, or this block is a stated exception. You are in this process after the base voice has been adjudicated, and only if a voice is active at all: the first gateway ends the process honestly when none is, rather than reporting a clean review of nothing. Three outcomes, all legitimate, and the third is the one that needs recording: an exception without a reviewer entry is indistinguishable from a rule nobody ran. There is also a fourth path the diagram draws deliberately — if the rule’s own citation does not support it, the RULE is the defect, and that becomes a bean rather than a finding against the prose. i i i i i i

At each citation, this lane also has to route the defect to the right place: a rule its own citation does not support goes to Task_RuleIsWrong as a finding against the VOICE, never into Task_Adjudicate, which only ever judges the block. | .
