A unified watcher that handles branches (poll git ls-remote) and change proposals — pull requests, PRs — (subscribe to their activity through the session platform; subscribing is not a forge operation). On every event, walk the §3 integration checklist and either act, defer, or flag the user.

8035.title: Invocation
8035.content: The user’s request maps to one of three modes; pick the right one without asking: . | user phrase | mode | how | . | “watch main” / “watch upstream” / no target | branch:main | poll origin/main every 5 min | . | “watch PR 516” / “watch the PR” / “watch this PR” | pr:N | subscribe to its activity — the session platform’s subscription (event-driven) | . | “watch branch foo/bar” / “watch claude/x-y” | branch:foo/bar | poll origin/foo/bar every 5 min | . | “watch foo/bar PR 42” | pr:42 + maybe branch | subscribe + poll | . If ambiguous, default to branch:main.

8036.title: 1.  Stash the baseline
8036.content: Before arming anything, record the current state so the §3 review compares cleanly: . # Explicit refspec, ALWAYS. `git fetch origin <BRANCH>` writes FETCH_HEAD and # refreshes refs/remotes/origin/<BRANCH> only when the clone's configured # refspec covers it — and exits 0 either way. A baseline read from a tracking # ref that was never updated is not a baseline. git fetch origin "+refs/heads/<BRANCH>:refs/remotes/origin/<BRANCH>" 2>/dev/null # Sanitize branch name for use in a file path: replace `/` with `_` # (e.g. `feature/foo` → `feature_foo`). Without this, branches with # slashes silently land in non-existent directory trees. SAFE_BRANCH=$(printf '%s' "<BRANCH>" | tr '/' '_') git rev-parse "origin/<BRANCH>" > "/tmp/_watch_baseline_${SAFE_BRANCH}.sha" . For PR mode, instead capture the latest PR head SHA: read PR N with the read change proposal forge-operation Tool and stash its head commit SHA.

8037.title: 2.  Arm the watcher
8037.content: Branch mode — Monitor with poll loop . Use the Monitor tool, persistent: true, 5-minute poll: . Monitor: description: "origin/<BRANCH> new commits" persistent: true command: | BRANCH="<BRANCH>" last=$(git ls-remote origin "$BRANCH" | cut -f1) while true; do cur=$(git ls-remote origin "$BRANCH" 2>/dev/null | cut -f1) if [ -n "$cur" ] && [ "$cur" != "$last" ]; then git fetch origin "$BRANCH" 2>/dev/null # one line per new commit, oldest first git log --reverse --oneline "$last..$cur" | head -20 last=$cur fi sleep 300 done . Each new commit becomes one notification line. PR mode — activity subscription . Subscribe to the PR’s activity through the session platform (in a Claude Code remote session, its PR-activity subscription). This is not a forge operation, so no forge Tool node offers it. Already event-driven — no polling needed. The harness delivers <github-webhook-activity> events for comments, CI status, reviews, and merges. See the existing PR-subscription guidance in the system prompt for handling.

8038.title: 3.  Per-event integration checklist
8038.content: For every notification (branch commit or PR event), run through these four questions in order — stop at the first “no” or “no action”: . Q1 — Should we integrate? . | Is the change on a file we touch in this branch? Quick check: git diff --name-only HEAD <NEW_SHA> -- $(git diff --name-only $(git merge-base HEAD origin/main)..HEAD). | If yes and the change is small, rebase / pull now. | If yes but large, defer until the immediate task ships and add a TODO. | If no overlap, skip Q2/Q3/Q4 and acknowledge with a one-liner. | . Q2 — Does it conflict? . | Try a dry rebase in a fresh worktree. Use mktemp -d so the path is unique (avoids collisions with previous failed runs and with parallel /watch invocations) and clean up unconditionally via trap: . PROBE=$(mktemp -d /tmp/rebase-probe.XXXXXX) trap 'git worktree remove --force "$PROBE" 2>/dev/null; rm -rf "$PROBE"' EXIT git worktree add "$PROBE" HEAD >/dev/null ( cd "$PROBE" && git rebase "origin/<BRANCH>" ) status=$? # trap fires on EXIT . | Conflicts (status != 0) → first attempt auto-resolve for the recurring drift-conflict pattern (see §2a below); only flag the user if auto-resolve fails or the conflict is non-trivial (overlapping logic edits, schema rewrites, etc.). | . §2a — Auto-resolve drift-conflict pattern (CI-regenerated artifacts) . Some artifacts (*.witness.json sidecars, generated caches, derived reference files) are routinely regenerated by the CI validate job and frequently conflict on rebase against fast-moving main. These conflicts are always the same shape: our branch’s committed artifact was regenerated against an older main; main now has a fresher version. Resolution is mechanical: regenerate against current main and recommit. The recipe (run on the real branch, not the probe worktree): . # When `git rebase origin/<BRANCH>` halts with a regenerated artifact # in the conflict list, do NOT hand-merge the JSON. Instead: # 1. If the conflicting commit was a pure regen of these generated # artifacts (no other changes), skip it — main already has the regen: git diff --name-only --cached | grep -qE '\.witness\.json$' && \ ! git diff --name-only --cached | grep -vE '\.witness\.json$' && \ git rebase --skip # 2. Otherwise, abort the rebase, regenerate the artifacts # on the rebased branch, then re-rebase. This produces a clean # apply because the regenerated artifact now matches main. git rebase --abort git rebase origin/<BRANCH> # re-rebase, skipping bad commits as above # regenerate the affected artifacts via the project's generator(s), e.g. bun run cat regen git add <regenerated-artifact-paths> git commit -m "Regen generated artifacts post-rebase against latest main" git push --force-with-lease . Only flag the user if: . | The conflict is in a source file (.py, .lean, .ts, .md) — those are real semantic conflicts that need human judgment. | The conflict is in a generated artifact whose regenerated content differs substantively from a simple drift (e.g. a numerical value changed, not just a timestamp/hash) — that means a CI-run generator on main produced different output, which deserves a closer look before blindly accepting. | The auto-resolve recipe itself fails (regen script errors out, push rejected for non-fast-forward reasons, etc.). | . For generated artifacts specifically: if upstream regenerated files our branch also touched, prefer rebase-and-regenerate over hand-merging. Drift is structural; merging is fragile. Q3 — Can we reuse? . Apply four reuse questions: . | Definitions / lemmas / helpers / witnesses — does the new commit add something our branch is duplicating, paraphrasing, or reinventing? Replace with uses[] / a citation and delete the local stand-in. | Proofs — does a new lemma or tactic discharge a hypothesis, collapse a chain, or close a gap? Apply via the project’s proof-simplification / build-fix skills. | Exposition — does our .md re-derive what main now defines upstream? Replace with a forward-reference; route through the project’s accuracy / readability skills. | Computation — does a new script or witness supersede a hand-rolled loop or stale witness in our branch? Swap in and regenerate the artifact. (See §2a for the routine drift-conflict pattern.) . | When the upstream commit adds or modifies a prop: / thm: / lem: / cor: block (or its sibling formalization), delegate to the project’s compute-integration watcher to check whether the new claim is wired into the production compute chain. Capture the verdict here and feed it into Q4. | . | . Q3a — Did upstream land a new skill file? . For each main-refresh, check whether a skill directory the layer declares in its kg graph (skill_list names them) gained a new file between this branch’s prior baseline and the new origin/main: . git diff --name-only --diff-filter=A "$LAST_BASE..origin/main" -- <skill-dirs> . For each new skill file: . | Read its frontmatter — extract name, roles, description, and any inherits field. | Match against branch scope — does the skill’s description overlap with what this branch is doing? Heuristics: . | skill description mentions a file kind / domain / pattern that appears in this branch’s git diff origin/main..HEAD --name-only, OR | skill is a new integration-watcher child (inherits: local/integration-watcher) and your branch is itself an integration-watcher PR, OR | skill is a content-block QA skill (e.g. one-voice-*, proof-*, compute-*) and your branch touches .md / .ts / .lean content blocks. | . | Surface to the user via AskUserQuestion with the standard 3-chip pattern: . New skill <name> landed on main: . <one-line description from frontmatter> . This branch’s scope overlaps because <one-line match rationale + file paths>. 1) Adopt now — invoke the skill on the relevant subset of this branch’s diff before continuing. 2) Defer to follow-up branch — record the decision and note for the next branch; don’t change this branch. 3) Not relevant — record so the watcher doesn’t re-prompt on future main-refreshes. | Record the decision as a note on the watcher’s work item (or in chat for the bare /watch flow) so subsequent main-refreshes don’t re-prompt for the same skill. | . This rule applies to skill files only. Skills landing on sibling PRs that haven’t merged yet do NOT trigger this check — only main commits count, mirroring the §2 “watch origin/main” scope. Q4 — Report or act? . | Acted (made the change): one-line summary + the new commit SHA. | Will act after current task: add a TODO with what + why. | Skipped: one-line reason (“no overlap”, “blocked on $TASK”). | .

8039.title: 4.  Stop the watcher
8039.content: Stop when the branch ships (PR merged, or you switch branches): . | Branch mode: call TaskStop on the Monitor task ID. | PR mode: the harness auto-unsubscribes when the PR merges/closes; otherwise unsubscribe through the session platform. | .

8040.title: 5.  Common upstream patterns (heuristics)
8040.content: . | Artifact drift: upstream regenerated generated artifacts (*.witness.json, caches) while we also modified them → rebase-and-regenerate, never hand-merge. | Toolchain version bumps: a dependency/toolchain hash changed → check our branch’s toolchain pin aligns before continuing a build. | Schema or generator changes: run bun run cat regen before continuing. | Routine review-cycle commits (Gemini/Copilot fixes on unrelated PRs): almost always Q1 = no overlap = skip with one-liner. | .

8041.title: 5b.  Monitor-timeout recovery (MANDATORY when re-arming)
8041.content: Background Monitors time out ([Monitor timed out — re-arm if needed]). Do not just re-arm and continue — between the last event and the timeout, main may have moved substantially. Mandatory steps on timeout-recovery: . # Compare the stashed baseline against the WATCHED BRANCH's actual head. # # This fetched `main` and then measured `origin/<BRANCH>` — a different ref # from the one it refreshed. The recovery step that exists to catch what was # missed while the watcher was down therefore compared the baseline against a # tracking ref nothing had updated, found them equal, and reported 0 missed # every time. Fetch the ref you are about to read, with an explicit refspec so # the tracking ref is actually written. git fetch origin "+refs/heads/<BRANCH>:refs/remotes/origin/<BRANCH>" 2>/dev/null SAFE=$(echo "<BRANCH>" | tr '/' '_') LAST=$(cat /tmp/_watch_baseline_${SAFE}.sha 2>/dev/null || echo "") CUR=$(git rev-parse origin/<BRANCH>) if [ "$LAST" != "$CUR" ]; then MISSED=$(git log --oneline "$LAST..$CUR" 2>/dev/null | wc -l) echo "MISSED $MISSED commits while watcher was down" git log --oneline "$LAST..$CUR" | head -10 # Update baseline AFTER reporting git rev-parse origin/<BRANCH> > /tmp/_watch_baseline_${SAFE}.sha fi . If MISSED >= 5 OR any missed commit touches a file in your branch’s diff, run the §3 integration checklist on the missed range BEFORE arming a fresh monitor. This catches main moving many commits ahead during a long focused session while the watcher is timed out.

8042.title: 6.  Output style
8042.content: Follow interaction-modality: . | One sentence per commit / event by default | Numbered choices when integration is non-obvious | Run small fixes proactively; flag big ones | .

8050.title: Web apps — an app is content, the harness publishes it
8050.content: Skill web-apps: Interactive web apps as knowledge-graph content: a layer holds an app’s source in a directory of kind web-app (one web-app.json), its UI strings go through the harness’s translation process like any template, and the harness’s apps visualiser (Tool web-app-build) builds it at publish and writes it to its own route with no site chrome, loaded only when a reader opens it. Read before adding an app to any layer, before writing a publish script for one (do not), and when an app’s build or translations fail. Named by: Publish a web app — declared, translated, built at its own route . Skill id: web-apps · Package: ui-core · Kind: web-app · Tool: web-app-build (bun run cat web-apps:build) · Process: web-app-publish .

8051.title: The rule
8051.content: A layer that carries an app declares it; it does not publish it. Owner, 2026-11-11 (cards Q-GAME-5 A and Q-GAME-7 A): a content layer with an app (a WHO onboarding game was the first) must not become a harness to ship it, and the one-off route VaxLink used (web/ + its own publish.sh + site.build.keep) is retired. The kind and its visualiser are the harness’s, so every layer that mounts cat-harness gets them. Before writing an app at all, ask whether it is a journey: a walkthrough of people and steps is a user-scenario and a workshop drawn by the journeys-viewer, not an app. An app is for what a page cannot be: a game, a simulation, a 3D world.

8052.title: Declaring one
8052.content: . | Put the app’s source in a directory of the layer, with its package.json and a lockfile (package-lock.json for npm, bun.lock for bun): the build installs exact versions only. | Declare the directory in the layer’s <name>.json with "graphTypologies": ["web-app"]. | Put a web-app.json (web-app/0.1.0, the schema the Tool web-app-build reads) at its root: | . { "$schema": "web-app/0.1.0", "id": "onboarding-game", "title": "Join the Network", "description": "A country onboards to the GDHCN, one choice at a time.", "build": { "installer": "npm", "script": "build", "outDir": "dist" }, "locales": ["en", "ar", "es", "fr", "ru", "zh"], "i18n": { "catalog": "src/i18n/en.json", "out": "public/i18n" }, "contentFrom": ["business-processes", "glossary"], "sizeBudgetMB": 45, "license": "Apache-2.0", "source": { "repository": "https://github.com/carlsbox/gdhcn-onboarding-game", "commit": "bd4c34c" } } . | field | rule | . | id | lower-case kebab; the route segment. Two layers claiming one id is a declaration error naming both. | . | build | defaults npm / build / dist. The app must build with relative asset paths (Vite base: './'), since its route is computed, not chosen. | . | chrome | always none (the default): the app draws its own frame. | . | locales | the first is the source language. A WHO layer ships the six UN languages: ar, en, es, fr, ru, zh. Arabic is right to left: the app sets dir="rtl" for it. | . | contentFrom | the layer’s own directory ids the app reads at build time. An app reads the layer’s content (its BPMN, glossary, actors, instances) at build time rather than copying it into code, so it cannot drift. | . | sizeBudgetMB | the index flags an app over it; the site size review reads it. | . | license, source | for a copied app: keep its LICENSE and a NOTICE naming the source commit. | .

8053.title: Where it is published, and why it loads only when opened
8053.content: | route | what | . | <locale>/<harness>/apps/ | the index, in the site’s chrome: one entry per app, its languages and size | . | <locale>/<harness>/apps/<id>/ | the app’s build, every page marked <meta name="folio-navbar" content="none"> and rendered-by: web-app-build | . The route is computed by visualiserRoute, as for every visualiser (harness-tiles). No other page embeds an app or loads its scripts: a tile, an IG page or a journey links to it. So a reader downloads an app only by opening its route. Inside the app, put heavy parts (a 3D engine, films) behind a dynamic import() or preload="none" so the first screen paints first. Lazy on screen, complete in print . Defer what a reader may never reach (owner, 2026-11-14: “do lazy load content and libs”): images with loading="lazy" and decoding="async", libraries behind a dynamic import() on first use, a hidden panel or a closed <details> drawn on its first open, a popout built when it is opened. Every deferral has a print path (owner, 2026-11-14: “make sure printing loads all of the content before it renders the PDF on the browser”). On beforeprint, and in a Print button that waits before it calls window.print(): switch lazy images to eager and wait for them, build and open what is built on toggle, and write out text that only a popout shows. afterprint closes again what the preparation opened. The library entry page (cat-harness-tools/scripts/lib/library-document.ts, docPrintPrep) is the worked example.

8060.title: Two uses
8060.content: | use | candidates | review | . | Design: a new or changed UI | at least two, compared blind | per-criterion, then adjudication, then options analysis | . | As-is: an existing visualiser, drawn as it renders on main | exactly one, marked as-is | the same criteria. A finding becomes a work item against the visualiser, not a redesign | .

8061.title: 1. Intent
8061.content: A few sentences: who the screen is for, what they need to do, and what it must show. For an as-is wireframe, the intent is read off the visualiser’s own declaration and generator, not invented.

8062.title: 2. Candidates
8062.content: . | Mid-fidelity HTML: monochrome, real content from the graph it shows, semantic icons, and no placeholder text. | Web and mobile in every candidate, through responsive CSS or two layouts. A candidate with one layout does not enter review. | .

8063.title: 3. Mechanical checks (wireframe-viewport-check)
8063.content: bun run cat wireframe:check --use as-is --topic <topic> --surface <visualiser ref> bun run cat wireframe:check --use design --topic <slug> --surface <surface> . The three flags are this skill’s input. --topic picks the directory in the table above and every candidate in it (name candidates to check fewer; one outside it is refused), and the report goes to its checks/. --use design needs at least two candidates; --use as-is needs each marked as-is in its file name, and a --surface that is the topic or a ref index.json says it covers. The use, topic and surface are recorded in report.json. This renders each candidate at web (1280×800) and mobile (390×844) sizes. It records script entries for renders, no-overflow and no-placeholder, each pass or fail with a note, and writes a screenshot per viewport. Any fail sends the candidate back to step 2.

8064.title: 4. Blind review, per criterion
8064.content: Reviewers include at least one agent that did not author the candidate and one human. For Design use called from CRDM, the human is the requester or the BA who owns the request: the person who will accept the delivered feature chooses its design. They see the intent, the screenshots and the HTML, without the authors. For each criterion they record pass, warn or fail, with a reason: . | criterion | question | . | intent-fit | Does it do what the intent says, for the person it names? | . | web usability | Can the task be done at desktop width? | . | mobile usability | Can the task be done at phone width, by touch? | . | accessibility | Contrast, a non-colour channel, accessible names, keyboard, reading order | . | alternatives | Do the candidates differ in the ways that matter? (Design use only) | . There are no scores and no averages (methodology-adoption, Refusals).

8065.title: 5. Adjudication and choice
8065.content: . | When entries for one criterion disagree, call Process_Adjudication. The adjudication leads, the checker’s entry is kept, and a dispensation needs its reason. | The choice between surviving candidates is Process_OptionsAnalysis. Rejected candidates stay, each with the reason it lost. | .

8066.title: Staging links
8066.content: When a staging preview exists, every request this skill makes for feedback, review or sign-off carries it: one deep link per changed page, to the anchor where the change sits, with the same page on main as before. Where the skill declares an output contract, they go in its stagingLinks field. The rule, and where the page list comes from: feedback-deep-links.

8067.title: Showing it to the requester
8067.content: Design use from CRDM ends in a person’s choice, so the candidates must be in front of that person before implementation starts: . | Commit the candidates, intent.md, checks/ (screenshots) and reviews/ under docs/proposals/<slug>/wireframes/ on the feature branch, so feature-staging publishes them with the rest of the branch. | Show them where the requester will look, chosen from context: the conversation, the issue the request came from, the pull request, or more than one of these. Where it goes is a judgement (feedback-deep-links, point 5); every place chosen carries the same content: a short narrative of what each candidate does differently; branches/ deep links to each candidate’s HTML (not the site root); and its web and mobile screenshots shown as images, not only linked. Say which could not be linked or rendered, and why. | Ask the requester or BA to choose, with the comparison (one row per candidate, from A_CompareOptions) and a recommendation, per interaction-modality where it applies. | Record their choice in the proposal and in the output’s chosen. An agent never chooses on their behalf. Implementation (CRDM Phase 6) builds against the chosen candidate, and the delivery summary links it beside the after-screenshot. | .

8077.title: Restructuring a work plan — a reviewed plan, not a bulk edit
8077.content: Skill work-plan-restructure: Reorganise a work plan that has outgrown one-bean-at-a-time repair — session logs typed as epics, duplicate families, generated template work items, stale claims, unparented work — through a reviewed PLAN rather than in bulk. The taxonomy is stated as data, a dry-run plan lists one row per work item (action, new parent, new status, evidence, note) with its before-state so the plan is its own inverse, the owner approves it by class or by row, and the apply is batched and reversible. Scrap, never delete. Read before changing the parent, type or status of more than a handful of work items at once. Named by: Hand back to the discussion, Drain the beans, A refused merge-train member, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route . lsi-indexing §”Epic filing” ends with “never apply the proposal in bulk”. A store that needs thousands of moves — session logs typed as epics, stale claims, duplicate groups, generated template families — cannot be repaired one work item at a time either. This skill is the middle path: a plan file a person reads, approves, and can undo. Applying a rule across thousands of work items unread is what deletion-requires-confirmation and the lsi method’s refusal 3 forbid; the plan is how the rule gets read without each work item being read alone.

8078.title: 1. State the taxonomy as data, first
8078.content: A restructure is a claim about what each level MEANS. If that claim stays implicit, the plan cannot be reviewed: the owner would be approving moves whose criterion they never saw. So the plan file opens with the taxonomy it applies: . { "taxonomy": { "milestone": "a GOAL, in the owner's verbatim words (todo-manager §A GOAL is a milestone bean)", "epic": "a SUBJECT that outlives any session; >= 2 children, or it is a task", "feature": "a deliverable a person can accept or reject on its own", "task|bug": "one pull request's worth of work", "never a level": ["a session", "a handover", "a generator run", "a PR"] }, "rules": { "max-depth-below-milestone": 3, "epic-min-children": 2 } } . Defaults are the ones this repository already states: todo-manager for goals, subjects and a session is a log, and release-epic-planning (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) for epic → feature → task. The types must be the ones .beans.yml lets the CLI write. A level the store cannot hold, such as a story type it does not configure, is a proposal to the owner. It is not a row.

8079.title: 2. Generate the dry-run plan — one row per bean, with its before-state
8079.content: | column | what it carries | . | bean | the id, or new:<slug> for an epic the plan creates | . | action | keep · reparent · retype · scrap-duplicate · scrap-generated · close-landed · reset-claim · create-epic | . | from-parent → to-parent | before and after | . | from-type → to-type | before and after | . | from-status → to-status | before and after | . | evidence | explicit · rule:<name> · latent:<cosine>/<margin> — never blank | . | note | what a reviewer needs: the survivor of a duplicate, the commit that landed it, the rule that fired | . The from- columns make the plan its own inverse. Swap every from-* and to-* and you have the plan that undoes it. Nothing has to be remembered to reverse it, and that matters most when the session that applied it is gone. The evidence comes from tools that already exist. Do not re-derive any of it: . | row source | tool | evidence class | . | reparent an open work item | lsi:epics: a parent: chain or a work item id in commits first, cosine second | explicit, else latent | . | session log typed as epic or milestone | sessionLogRootBeans in test/health/checks.ts (the bean-session-log-roots finding) | rule:session-log | . | duplicate | the bean-store duplicate groups; the target-object key in todo-manager §”Check before you create” | rule:same-title, rule:same-target | . | landed work still open | branch-archaeology: patch-id equivalence on main | explicit | . | stale claim | bean-stale-in-progress / bean-quiet-claims in bun run cat health, network-checked by check:quiet-claims | rule:stale-claim | . | unparented | check:bean-parents | rule:orphan | . lsi:epics prints a calibration line, and the plan carries it. Its agreement rate is well short of certain, so a latent row is a proposal, never presented as a finding. Write the plan as a work item note on the work item that owns the restructure (bun run cat beans:note <id>), with the summary first and the rows as a table. The notes directory is declared and keyed by branch, so the plan is committed and reviewed in the PR diff without inventing a new directory. A plan too large for one note is split by action class, one note per class, because that is how the owner approves it.

8080.title: 3. The owner gate — approve by class, never by silence
8080.content: Present the summary before any row, following interaction-modality §4.1 (context → options → recommendation → question): . | counts per action; | open children per epic, before and after; | orphans after (it must be 0); | every row whose to-status is scrapped or completed. | . Then ask: . | A class approval covers explicit and rule: rows only. Latent rows are approved row by row, or by the owner’s explicit words extending the approval to them. A latent row that was not approved stays keep. It is never applied on the strength of its cosine. | Scrap and close are the deletion-shaped actions. They take the owner’s word under deletion-requires-confirmation, or a recorded confirmation-waiver for the deletion gate that names this plan. | No answer is not approval. Say what happens if they say nothing: the plan stays a note, and the store is untouched. | .

8081.title: 4. Apply in batches, re-reading each bean first
8081.content: . | One action class per commit, at most ~100 rows. The commit message names the plan note and the class. A bad batch is then one git revert. | Re-read each work item before you write it (todo-manager §”Check before you WORK”). If its current parent, type or status differs from the row’s from-*, a sibling moved it after the plan was made. Skip the row and report it; do not overwrite. | Respect live claims. Leave alone any work item that is mid-flight under bean-coordination: touched within 72 h, or named by an open PR. The exception is the owner naming that work item. | One flag per beans update, then read the front matter back. A multi-flag update can apply only some of its flags and still report success (todo-manager §”After you create”). | Notes go in by note or --body-append, never --body-file. --body-file replaces the body silently. | Scrap, never delete. scrap-duplicate names the survivor in the scrapped work item. scrap-generated names the generator and the sidecar or queue that should have held the item instead (work items are not sidecars). A session log is closed or scrapped with a pointer to where its children went. Archiving is a view, not an exit (bean-coordination §”Archiving is a VIEW”). | After each batch: bun run cat check:bean-parents, bun run cat readme:subgraphs and bun run cat health. The batch is not done until the guards agree with the plan’s “after” column. | .

8082.title: 5. Reversing it
8082.content: If nothing has landed on the store since, revert the batch commits; the store is committed, which is what makes that possible. If siblings have edited it since, apply the swapped plan: the from-* columns become the targets. Its rows go through the same re-read rule in step 4.2, so a row that a sibling has since moved is skipped rather than clobbered.

8083.title: What this skill does not do
8083.content: . | Decide the taxonomy. It states one for the owner to accept or amend. A disputed filing (symptom against subject, as lsi-indexing puts it) is the owner’s call, not the score’s. | Run unattended. No step from 3 onward happens without the owner’s approval for that plan. | Fix the cause. If a generator or a skill is minting the work items being scrapped, fix that first. Otherwise the plan is repaired again next week. | .

8085.title: The work plan’s contract
8085.content: Skill work-plan-store: The contract the work plan (work items) keeps as a data store, as operations any Tool must provide: get, list, create, update with ifMatch, note, history, and where a work item is in its processes. Give back a work item exactly as written, keep ids unique and links whole, keep status and type to their closed lists, lose nothing to concurrent writers, and answer a work item’s history. A mechanical Actor plays this Role through whichever Tool the deployment names. Named by: Authoring a document . The work plan is a data store, and this is its contract. work-plan in scenarios/roles.json is a mechanical Role with a store block: what it holds, and how it is reached. This skill is the other half, what it must do. How an agent USES the plan is todo-manager; this file says what the plan promises back. This contract names no Tool. A process or skill that touches the work plan says which operation below it performs (“note the bean”, “claim it”), never which command does it. How one Tool performs an operation belongs on that Tool’s page, listed in §”Tools”. The Tool in use is chosen by the deployment description, per checkout. A diagram draws the store as a data store, never a lane: a dataStoreReference with dataStoreRef="work-plan", declared once in processes/global-tasks.bpmn. A task that opens or closes a work item writes to it with a dataOutputAssociation; a task that reads the plan has a dataInputAssociation from it. The task sits in the lane of whoever does it.

8086.title: What it holds
8086.content: | Kind | What | . | bean-defs | work items ($schema: bean/1.0.0), shaped by schemas/kinds/bean-defs.schema.json | . | bean-notes | addenda to a work item, one per writer, never rewritten | . | workflow-state | running and finished BPMN instances (folio-workflow-instance/v1) | .

8087.title: Operations
8087.content: Every Tool provides these. Each line says what a caller can rely on. | Operation | Guarantee | . | get(id) | the work item as last written, or “none”. A short id resolves to exactly one work item or to none | . | list(filter) | work items by status, type, tag or parent; archived work items only when the filter asks for them | . | create(bean) | the id is unique; the work item is readable by get once create returns | . | update(id, change, ifMatch) | refused when ifMatch names a version that is no longer current; a retry on the current version lands. archived: true archives the work item | . | note(id, text, by) | appended to the work item’s notes, never rewriting earlier ones | . | history(id) | every change to the work item, oldest first: when, by whom, what changed, and which process step made it when one did | . | positions(id) | every workflow instance that names the work item: process, step(s), instance status, last move | . | beansAt(process, step?) | the work items with a token at that process (and step) | . Archiving is a field, not an operation. update(id, { archived: true }, ifMatch) is refused unless the work item is completed or scrapped, and the work item keeps its status. get still finds an archived work item; list leaves it out unless asked. Where an archived work item lives is the Tool’s choice, stated on its page. A work item’s position lives only in the workflow instances. The work item records no process or step of its own; positions and beansAt read the instances the store holds. A tag such as process:code-change-review may label a work item for people, and is never read as its position.

8088.title: Responsibilities
8088.content: Each line is something a test can check against any Tool. | Give back what was written. get after create or update returns, byte for byte, the work item written. | Keep ids unique. No two work items share an id. | Keep links whole. parent, blocking and blocked_by name work items that exist. | Keep the lists closed. status and type take only the values the schema declares. | Lose nothing to a race. Two writers at once both land: the second update with a stale ifMatch is refused, retried on the current version, and lands. Nothing is overwritten unread. | Keep the history. history(id) answers who changed what and when, and which process step did it. | Archive only what is finished. archived: true on a work item that is not completed or scrapped is refused. | Know where a work item is. positions and beansAt agree with the instances the store holds. | .

8089.title: Tools
8089.content: | Tool | Backed by | Page | . | git state branch | a branch per graph (cat/<harness>/beans), mounted at beans/, written with the beans CLI (beans-cli) or by hand (beans-manual), read with bean-query | work-plan-store-git-branch | . | work items server | beans-serve GraphQL (schema); its mutations already take ifMatch | proposed | . | MCP service | an MCP server over the same operations | proposed | . | run-scoped store | in memory or a scratch branch, one per benchmark run, never the real plan (req:model-benchmark) | proposed | .

8090.title: Tests
8090.content: The conformance suite lives in the tools layer (scripts/tests/sdlc/work-plan-store-conformance.ts, one describe per responsibility above) and runs against both of the git Tool’s access modes. Until this file carries a tested-by: line, kg-audit reports this role as mechanical-role-untested.

8091.title: Not its responsibility
8091.content: Deciding what to work on, who claims a work item, or whether work is done. Those are judgements made in the lanes of the people and agents who read and write the plan.

8093.title: State in a running process
8093.content: Skill workflow-state: Where a running process keeps what it knows, and which store answers which question. The three records a step may touch, the one it may not, what <cat-harness.processes:bean op> actually performs, and why an instance and a work item must be one answer rather than two. Named by: Adopt a methodology from a source document, Translation Workflow, Copy a knowledge-graph asset into a folio, A sub-graph wants to leave, Authorise the extraction, Move the graph into its repositories, Prepare a graph to stand alone, A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories, Build and publish a per-slice SQLite file, A sub-KG is staged in place, then leaves for its own repository, Ask the person, CRDM close-out, CRDM data model, CRDM Phase 6 — implement, MVP, acceptance, CRDM — link the work to an issue, CRDM Phase 1 — needs, CRDM Phases 2–4 — BPA and requirements, CRDM requirements, CRDM Phase 5 — beans and sign-off, Hand back to the discussion, Related work: find, sort, summarize, ask to coordinate, Secure agent permissions, Session state machine, Wireframe design review, Agent activity log, Close the bean, Drain the beans, Agent bean lifecycle, Open the bean, Code change and review, Merge the base branch in, A refused merge-train member, Requirements filing: promote, organise, trace, supersede, or retire, SME Review of Decision Support and Indicator Test Data, Stalled-agent triage: collect handovers, consolidate themes, recommend, re-route, Test Data Curation — Fixed Sets and Generated Recipes, Watching a pinned upstream dependency, Adopting an upstream version bump, Getting started, Authoring a document, Make the content change, Content Change and Review, Editing and HCI validation, Contributor feedback on a working draft, Record agent step, Review-log watch . A process instance is not self-contained. It walks a diagram that lives somewhere else, records its position somewhere else again, and reads facts it must not change. Five stores; confusing any two of them is how a work plan comes to disagree with itself.

8094.title: Which store answers which question
8094.content: | question | store | graph typology | layer | . | what does this process DO? | processes/**/*.bpmn | cat-harness | content | . | where did this instance GET TO? | the workflow-state node of the work item graph | workflow-state | state | . | what is being worked on? | the bean-defs node of the work item graph | bean-defs | state | . | what does a PERSON still owe? | todos/ | todo-items | state | . | what do I already know? | agent memory | memory | context | . The layer column says what a step may do. A step may write to a state graph; that is what state is for. A step that writes to context is a defect, not an update: memory changes when a human directs an authoring act, outside any instance. content-context-and-state-graphs carries the axis; processMayWrite() is the predicate.

8095.title: The diagram is content and the instance is state, and that is the whole model
8095.content: A .bpmn is authored, reviewed, versioned and read by anyone — it stands on its own. An instance is a token position in that diagram plus a history: it means nothing detached from the file it walks. That is why the two live in different graphs and why an instance names its process rather than embedding it. Two consequences: . An instance is never edited by hand. It carries "$schema": "folio-workflow-instance/v1" and the interpreter owns it. Hand- editing a token is asserting a step happened, which is precisely what the gate exists to refuse. A diagram change does not rewrite history. An instance records where it got to under the diagram as it stood. If a step is renamed, the honest answer is that the old instance names a node that no longer exists — not that it retroactively took a different path.

8096.title: Beans and instances are ONE answer, not two
8096.content: bean-defs says what is being worked on; workflow-state says where it got to. Those must be one answer or they diverge, and a work plan that disagrees with itself is worse than one that is merely coarse. The loop is closed by <cat-harness.processes:bean op="…"> on an activity. A bean-marked step is not a step about the work plan — it IS the work-plan operation, so completing the step performs it: . | op | on completing the step | . | claim | status → in-progress, idempotent | . | note | append the caller’s note to the body | . | resolve | status → completed, only if the instance itself finished (or only archive steps are left) | . | archive | move a completed or scrapped work item into the archive, only once the instance finished | . claim is drawn only in Process_BeanOpen, and resolve and archive only in Process_BeanClose; every process that works on a work item calls both (check:bean-calls). note is drawn where the work happens. resolve is the careful one. A work item is never closed on somebody else’s judgement, so it does not fire on the caller’s say-so: the work item completes only when the instance tracking it has completed, which is a fact derived from the process rather than asserted by the agent calling it. A still-running instance gets a note. An op the build does not implement fails at process load. A step that says it resolves a work item and quietly does nothing is exactly the divergence the extension exists to close.

8097.title: What state does NOT buy you
8097.content: Ordering is not quality. A completed instance means the gates ran in order and a person saw the findings. Whether the content is correct is what the QA axes, the build and the validators are for. A green process must never be read as a reviewed artefact, and any dashboard built on this has to say so. A position is not a claim. An instance at Task_Commit says the token arrived, not that the commit is good.

8098.title: Where running instances live — the state graph on the branch store
8098.content: Running instances are part of the work-plan store (workflow-state graph typology; positions in work-plan-store (opt-in cat-harness.work-plan)). Where the deployment uses the git state-branch Tool, the store is mounted and pushed as described in work-plan-store-git-branch. The container is ephemeral and a work plan only one agent can see is not a work plan. Instance state lives in the shared work-plan store for the same reason work item definitions do: a sibling session, or the same session resumed in a fresh container, reads the store to find the position that exists rather than starting a second one beside it. When an instance advances, its state is written through the store’s Tool (bun run cat state:push when backed by the git state branch). This keeps instance state globally visible without cluttering code PR diffs on main. Instance ids are derived from the subject rather than random, so re-entering a step finds the instance that is already there: beans create is not idempotent and dedupes on nothing, so an id you can recompute is what prevents duplicates.

8099.title: Reading the state you did not write
8099.content: Before acting on an instance you did not start, ask what it is waiting on. A work item’s status defaults to non-blocking; a real block carries what it waits on, since when, an expiry and a handoff — because a block with no expiry cannot be told from abandoned work. bean-blocking carries that, and bean-coordination carries the rule that a claim announces rather than reserves until your PR exists.
